Amazing grid-style dungeon crawler/western style RPG. I love pretty much everything about this game and the mysterious, dangerous, puzzled filled and monster infested island that my 4 shipwrecked escaped prisoners find themselves stranded on.
Modern visuals/sound/execution, with a retro style, classic heart.
Some people don't seem to care for the more "live action" combat style, and I was a little iffy on it, at first, myself. I warmed up to it though, and I don't think a more turn based fighting system would suit the game. It might make for a difficult time at first, if you have never played a game like this before, but its well made and very well balanced, once you get the hang of it.
I absolutely recommend this game, with one suggestion: look up some character builds before setting out, even if you ultimately decide to branch out and do something completely different. Understanding the strengths of each class, what perks and traits benefit the playstyle you have in mind, and knowing what to do with your points as you level is paramount to having a good time on this island. I won't say its impossible to build a hybrid character but you typically won't have any points to spare or waste, and you also probably won't have nearly as many of them (or levels) as you envision - and spreading yourself too thin is a huge mistake in this place.

I hesitate calling this a game. Simulation is a better name for it. So as far as recommending this 'game', I cant, but I can recommend this farm town sim. Banished consists of building homes for townsfolk and building places for them to work. You are going to need food to feed your people, tools to help them work, clothes to keep them warm and resources to build all of the above. Banished starts off slow and will continue to be slow, even if you crank up the game speed to 10x it will still take about a half hour to get through one harvest. Keep it at that speed though and your town will quickly starve.
For the first 10 or so hours of your town your going to need to keep a close eye on it. Once you get enough people and resources you can kinda let your town run on its own. This was my biggest issue with the sim. At a certain point Banished no longer need you, just check in with it every once in awhile and build some houses or farm plots and let your citizens do the work. You can of course watch them, or tell them what to do but keep in mind that they all have a hiararchy of need to to fulfil before they do what their overlord tells them. Its alot like an ant farm. Its cool to see what comes of your town after fifty hours, but do you really what to invest that time?

Ampu-Tea is a very lackluster and unpolished game. The first thing you are greeted with after launching the game is a poorly textured language selection screen, after which you are thrown into a room as a prosthetic hand, and tasked with making tea according to the instructions. This clearly looks like YouTube bait and/or an engine test.
Comparisons may be drawn to Surgeon Simulator. It involves the same idea where you control each digit of the hand with a separate key and are tasked with fulfilling a task requiring very precise control. The difference however, is that Surgeon Simulator looks and feels more competent, more streamlined graphics, physics, sound and control-wise while also offering a ton of more content than Ampu-Tea.

In case you've been living under a rock for the past 5 years, I will quickly try to explain why this is one of the best video games of the last generation. Enter Fallout: A post-apocolyptic RPG, set in a strange "commie-hatin" 1950's setting. As you adventure through the 'Capitol Wasteland' (the ruins of Washington DC), your specially created character levels up various skills, gains new abilities, and finds various weapons and armors. All of course, to fight enemies, finish quests, and find the best loot available.
Released in 2008, Fallout certainly looks and handles 'last-gen'. Textures are poor, no iron-sights to speak of, and NPCs look like strange play-doh monsters. Yet, current PCs can handle it at a butter smooth 90+ FPS, with incredible draw distances. Mods can easily fix any texture problems, and make NPCs actually look human. Just hop onto
, install the NexusModManager, and this 6 year old game will look and handle like it came out yesterday.
As you run along to various hits from the 50s, the 'Vault-Tech Assting Targeting System' deviates from the standard first-person shooter fare, and allows you to spend 'action points' to target specific areas of enemies bodies, crippling limbs, or shooting the gun staright from their hands. Be warned, the game is a wee bit violent, courtesy of fully destructible body parts. Expect to see limbs being blown off by grenades, and flying red streaks through the air. Combat can be fought with energy weapons, projectiles, grenades, melee weapons, rockets, or even your fists. Those with less imagination can opt for small or heavy firearms. Points can be spent upon leveling up, making your character more proficient in these skills. Various perks give you more bonuses from "Lead-Belly' (Reduced radiation taken from food) to 'Bloody-Mess'. (enemies yave a chance to explode into a bloody paste, FUN!) Ultimately, comabt is varied, and can be quite challenging. Various enemy types require different weapons to tackle, and various ways to defend against them. Super Mutants deem worthy for a couple precise rockets, while mole rats are more deserving of a couple whacks with a sledgehammer.
Various quests will keep you entertained for hours upon hours, with everything from entering a simulation of typical 1950's America, helping write a book about wastleand survival, or settling the differences between 2 would be superheroes; the Antagonizer and the Mechanist. Dialouge trees allow you to open secret 'options' for missions, as well as craft your charcters personailty. A karma system offers various buffs as well. This is all topped off by some witty humor, and occasional darker, more metaphoric writing.
The wasteland is massive, filled with places to explore, enemies to fight, and incredible vistas to view. Building and camps dot the countryside, and contain everything from raider settlements, abandon military blockades, to border clashes between power armored supertroops and giant ants. A truly wonderfully crafted and realised world.
Ultimately; an incredible game. Hours of entertainment, character buidling, addictive combat, and exploring, for $10. Install mods, for an even better experience.

The biggest problem by far is the resource management: there are games when I'm either stuck on 2-3 mana and keep pulling cards I can't afford or I _only_ get mana cards for 5-6 rounds so by the time I finally get a unit it's already too late.
I don't really see how this random mana system improves the game but if it absolutely has to be there then at least let me affect it in some manner. For example let me pick how often I get a guaranteed mana drop: every 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th turn or something.
I played mostly against the AI because that is reasonably fun: there are some easy wins, there are some quick defeats (due to mana starve/flood) but often the match is tight and feels fair regardless the outcome.
To finish some quests I did play against people in ranked and draft but it was not fun at all: I got beaten so fast that I usually never even landed a single hit. (I won once tho, for some weird reason. :)
EDIT: There are two key things which helps with power issues:
- Manually manage your power cards (can be turned on in the options). After a few games you'll have a feel if you have too many/too few power cards so you can adjust the deck accordingly.
- If you mulligan your opening draw you are guaranteed to have 2-4 power cards in there. If I don't see a clear way to get through the first 3-4 rounds then I mulligan and hope for the best.
Keeping these things in mind I haven't got mana flood for a while now and starving is also much less of an issue. Now, playing exclusively against AI, I recommend the game. :)

First off, I am a LONG time flight simmer, and a pilot, so I do have some qualifications to speak intelligently about this sim.
I have a modest rig, i7 Sandy Bridge OC'ed to 3.9Ghz (Slight OC), 32Gb Ripjaw Mem, GTX760 2Gb, and several Terabytes of
drives. I noticed several things, some of the recip engined aircraft have Turbine Inlet Temperature guages, those are usually only seen on turbine engined aircraft.
The sim was smooth for me, (I don't quote framerates beyond 30, since eyes can't tell the difference too well beyond that.)
No maps to pull up yet during flight to see ILS freqs and airport comms freqs. ATC window did not popup AND close with the Tilde key.
Pause key was not working either, had to go to options tab at top of the screen to pause. (very tough to do if you're not trimmed out and all your hardware is on the right, and kybd is on the left, LoLz!
Shaders are too bright, washed out the runways and taxiway guidance striping. Some of the GPS and radio settings could only be done in the popup windows,
not a big deal, just had to be aware of it.
It took a bit of getting accustomed to the European voicing for ATC, and their special way of pronouncing certain words. the sim interface itself was done well, just not enough options yet, I know that will happen over time.
Changing the parameters of a flight during it is a needed feature, such as time of day, weather, ETC.
It would be great to have real-time weather as well, need to be able to use FSRealWeather Lite, or FSGRW, something like that with this sim. And of course all the 3rd-party Add-Ons that we all enjoy so much in FSX and others.
If they do not allow a 3rd-party community to develop around this sim, then I fear it will be relegated to Arcade game status, and hard-core simmers will not latch on to it.
Personally, I would not have gone to Steam to release this, I would have Self-Published, and let the chips fall where they may.
MSFS in all it's iterations was released into the wild pretty much on it's own merits, and it has lasted the 30 years I have been Flying and Simming.
So if Dovetail does this right, it, too, will stand the test of time, I have high hopes for this, they are on the right track, just need to add some things in and polish the brass and chrome a bit, optimize the code some more, it will be well on it's way!
I would be happy to Beta-Test for them, since I do have experience with this.

This has to be one of the weirdest titles I’ve read in a long time. Along with that: it is also one of the more imaginative games I’ve played in a long time. Mixing up platforming with player-created-on-the-spot levels is genius.
While this game can be played with two people, or yourself and three other controllers, The Ultimate Chicken Horse is a dish best served with three other people (always better with friends)! As the level changes after every round as dictated by each player, the levels only get crazier and crazier. Unless someone uses the bomb and cleans it up a little. However, sometimes some spring cleaning is in order unless you don’t really want to progress.
Allowing on-line play was one of the smartest moves for Clever Endeavour Games. It’s not something that I can remember many small party games like this having missed lately, but it is something I could see someone taking a stance on. “Get your friends over like we did back in the day.” That’s weird to some people, but that was the norm back when I was a kid. It’s buggy currently, but they are diligently working on it. All this to say: it will still be more fun with your buds right there to punch.
I can understand the way multplayer is done currently, but it’s not my favorite. Given the flavor of the game, a more open multiplayer would have been more appreciated. However, since trying to make my own game and getting caught up with tiny details not working, if it was this “port-forwarding-friend-menu”method or nothing, then this trumps any complaint. I simply got used to this method of connecting with Magicite, but didn’t really appreciate it because of the lack of friends playing the same game. I like these type of games while not many of my buds would be willing to drop as little change down as Ultimate Chicken Horse costs. A more fluid, server-based multiplayer would have opened the floodgates to a more populated online experience in an ideal world. It could very well have been a lot of time spent coding and then been underused and that time could have been better spent. There are to many variables and let’s just say that I’m happy to at least have the option.
Score: Tasty!
Ultimate Chicken Horse is pretty darn unique. It still surprises me that some devs can come up with something like this out of nowhere when it feels like it should have been a part of our gaming library for a long time now. There are a lot of tools to hinder you and your friends with and enough levels to add some variety to the gameplay. Ultimate Chicken Horse is definitely worth picking up if you’ve got some buds that enjoy good platforming fun-time.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I really want to recommend this game, but it's hard to bring myself to do that when I am looking for other games to play before I have even finished this one.
I played the first game and I LOVED it. I couldn't wait for the second one to come out. Now that I have finally managed to get around to playing it (I have tons of games and sometimes I don't get around to it) the second doesn't live up to the first.
The first game was fairly linear. You go through a level of the dungeon, find everything and move on. Sometimes you come across a puzzle, usually very satisfying with a little bit of chin stroking, and feel a sense of accomplisment when you were done.
In the second game however, when you come across a puzzle or an area that you can't seem to pass, you have to ask yourself, "Am I missing something? Something that I am just not seeing? Or do I have another objective on the other side of the damned game map that I have to finish first?" Annoying as♥♥♥♥♥♥
Don't get me wrong, the puzzles are smartly made, but if I have to travel to the ends of the Earth and back just to get an item to pass this puzzle, I would like a clue that tells me as much. That's a major problem with this game, it doesn't tell you if you are stuck because the puzzle is either that hard, or you are missing an item, switch, or button.
I have found myself skipping large areas because I thought I had to come back later, then I got stuck in another area, ran around the map for HOURS trying to figure out what to do next, then I finally came back to the original area only to find out I missed a God forsaken button....♥♥♥♥! I have a wife and 4 kids, I don't have hours to stick my thumb up my butt looking for buttons.

A superb sequel that brings everything the original had back to the table, and adds so much more to enjoy!
While maintaining the atmospheric emersion of the first game, Legend of Grimrock 2 presents us with a plethora of new settings.  A bright sunny beach is the first, which will welcome you and ease you into the game.  Soon enough you'll be making your way carefully through the dense murk of the swamps, or plumbing the lake depths to see what secrets they hold.  Each location has its own personality, and while dungeon crawling through actual dungeons is still a significant portion of the game, the diversity really helps to mix things up.
Speaking of diversity, there are more enemies which have a much broader array of attack patterns.  Some can leap or charge at you from one square away.  Some can hop over you to attack your side.  Some will burrow through the ground to pop out and ambush you.  Added to this are a number of bosses!  Each has it own powerful attacks, and most also have an array of minions to trap you.
The puzzles and secrets are back in force, and clever gamers will find no end to the rewards that can be found with a little patience and a good eye.  Character creation now has quite a number of new and interesting options, including the Alchemist and the Battle Mage.  If you're looking for a challenge you can also take the handicap class, the Farmer.  Generally speaking the Farmer is intentionally worse than the other classes, but dedicated gamers can make them into forces to be reckoned with!
Legend of Grimrock 2 is truly an excellent game, and I would recommend it to all fans of the genre.

My full review and thoughts on Just Cause 2.
The Positive:
- A very Lenghty game. Takes a very long time to complete 100%.
- Infinite parachutes are very cool to have.
- The grapple wire is fun to use and adds a lot to the game.
- The story is interesting.
- The character of Rico is indept and interesting.
- The grapple wire is a very important part in the game and is more like your primary weapon than a gun.
- The story gets straight to the point and not slow or repetitive.
- Its nice to have a open world with the most biggest map ingame that I have ever seen when it came out.
- The black market is very usefull and a lot of items are available.
- Great Gameplay.
- Playing the whole game could last you over 85 - 100 hours!
The Negative
- The grapple wire could have gone a bit further.
- The story missions itself was very short (but having literally over a hundred side missions kind off payed off)
- There are a few bugs here and there.
- The gunplay is terrible. I can not physically aim!
- Driving handling is a bit slippery.
- There are very few weapons and you can only hold few at a time with less ammo than usual third person open world games.
- Voice could glitch out and be out of sync a couple of times.
Most negative points are about the bugs in the game. This does not mean that the game is not fun. The game is absolutely brilliant and I had a lot of fun playing it on my old account. Definately worth 15 dollars!

First of all, this game isn't optimized for 32bit systems and requires some unorthodox system tuning to make it work properly (or at all!). Why is it this way, when it uses now really dated Unreal engine, is a question for the devs.
The game is not as nearly as scary as the hype made it out to be. A lot of horror is derived from gore, which is, in my opinion, always a cheap trick. There are some jump scares too, but they are not overused. The main terror factor is that you are completely helpless when confronted with anybody/anything that wants to hurt you and have to rely or running fast to a hiding place. This, combined with the camera's night vision mode provides the same effect as one we already seen in Amnesia: A Dark Descent. - player is left feeling vulnerable and helpless, the feeling that is only strenghtened by main characters unwilling sobs and heavy breathing. On the other hand, the fact that it takes several hits for enemies to end your life (at least on normal difficulty) diminishes the overall feeling and could have been made harder on the player.
Music, environmental sounds and animation have all been done beautifully and with much detail and serve to enrich the environment and the atmosphere. Graphics are solid, even rough at places (some textures look like from a 10 year old game), so it only adds weight to the question of unusual system requirements.
The story is told via documents you find while roaming through the asylum, notes that the protagonist makes and, on a rare occasion, by NPC characters you interact with in some way. This is a formula used by many games, but it has not been done well. It's both hard to follow and uninteresting (several cliches jumbled one atop another), so you'll probably stop caring somewhere along the way, which kinda defeats the purpose of you playing as a journalist who wants to expose what has been happening behind the walls of the asylum.
There are some interesting moments to the story though, but they revolve around things that concern the player and not the 'big picture'.
Overall, even though not a masterpiece of horror, Outlast is still quite enjoyable and is bound to send more than a couple of chills down your spine.

Come on, this game as 92% positive review and you are still wonder if you'll like the game? Well, let's see what I can say about this game then.
The Good:
1) Extras. Game theme music and game manual provided is a nice touch as an add-on.
2) Good Music
3) Good Graphics
4) Good RPG elements. Leveling up and character builds are interesting, diverse and well implemented.
5) Good Controls. Real time combats where inventory and maps doesn't pause anything. Controls are hard and you can tell its intentionally made that way. This makes the game feels more real.
6) Good Enemy AI: Dodge/Chase-down intelligently based on player's action. This makes sometimes even a weak enemy alittle problemetic to deal with. Moves intelligently. Will standstill or take detour just to corner player making enemies quite deadly at 3 or more in numbers. Strategy seems well written since players need to take damage in order to get out of being surrounded, sometimes its even impossible to get out and player will have to brace themsevles.
7) Story is more rich as they have added abit more lore in.
8) Good riddles and puzzles and traps as usual.
9) Good value for $$$.
The Bad:
1) Low replay value. The game is great and epic but replay value is even lower now that there's not even a Toorum mode a.k.a. one imba character for player to replay the whole game with new strategy or in a new light. I feel tired just by the thought of having to play the whole epic adventure once more just to try out a new team build.
1b) A solution might be for newgame+ or allowing changing class and skillpoint distribution once game has been completed. Just to make trying out different stuff much less daunting.
2) Uneven use of enemies.. I find the diversity of enemies great and I have mentioned how wonderful their AI is. However, I find myself fighting undeads most of the time.... I mean.. Come on, there's 2 entire regions here undead is the primary enemy. I feel like I want to fight other types of enemies more often and less undead.. At least double the encounter for all other types of enemies and at least half encounters for undead.
There you go. That's what I'll like to say about the game. All in all great game. I'm a stingy motherfker and I personally wouldn't buy the game at full price but I can't honestly say its not worth it. The game is definitely worth every dollar spent even if bought at full price.

Legend of Grimrock 2 is similar to the first game in a lot of ways but this game is set outdoors on the Island of Nex which allowed for bigger areas. The skill system has been overhauled and way less linear as you can increase any type of skill regardless of your class, classes only provide some bonuses and such but you can progress whatever you want. They also retained the unique rune based magic grid casting system but instead of clicking on each rune you have to connect a line between runes to cast spells. Another thing this sequel retains is the amazing atmosphere and story through notes you find throughout the game. Their are 5 races which are humans, insectoids, minotaurs, lizardmen, and ratlings. you can create 4 characters for your party like the first game and they also added firearms to the game as a new weapon type and skill as well as overhauling the alchemy system by adding an alchemy skill and a plethora of ingredients and potions which are very useful as well as elemental bombs. I hope my review has convinced you to buy this amazing game but I recommend you play the first one as it is easier to learn and get players into the genre of party based dungeon crawlers of the olden days. Hopefully the Legend of Grimrock series gets more players into this type of RPG because their are a handful of these kinds of games from the 90s that are amazing such as the Might and Magic franchise or Eye of the Beholder series and much more. Thank you if you read this review and please buy Legend of Grimrock 2 as it is a sequel done right in every single way but Legend of Grimrock 1 is an amazing game as well and much better at getting players into these games.

I haven't had this much fun playing a card game since Yu-Gi-Oh. While Hearthstone is fun to play it suffers from a really bad free to play model because the only way for you to grind gold is through the daily quests and those usually require you to play against other players. As a new player this isn't something you want to do because almost everyone you duel will have a better deck than you.
In Eternal you actually have a way to grind gold by playing against the A.I. in the Gauntlet game mode which is completely free to play. From there you can buy your way into the Forge. And if you are good enough to make it all the way through the Forge you will win back about 2,000 gold to help you enter the Forge again. OR if you get really lucky (like I did) you will win every match except the last one, but your gold reward will turn into a diamond reward which pays out a lot of gold (I do believe it was 2,000). So far I have played two forges back to back for free (not counting the very first Forge which is given to you for free) and I'm about to play through it for a third time back to back. For new players, I highly suggest doing this because all the cards that you draft in the Forge you get to keep. You can get way more rares and even the possibility of a legendary this way, plus you also win booster packs on top of that. I don't suggest buying booster packs like I did the first two or three times as you can get way more bang for your buck by playing through the Forge.
If you want to support the game, I do suggest buying Jekk's bounty as it is very fun to play through with the exception of Jekk the final boss. He is frustratingly hard to win against but it's definitely not impossible. You will find yourself making a bunch of crazy decks (that would never work in pvp) in order to win against some of the crazy rules that are added in this campaign.
Another great thing this game has going for it is a bunch of new mechanics that I haven't seen in card games before and they are really fun. (edit) I'm adding this link for anyone who is interested in some of the mechanics this game has to offer:
My only complaint is that after buying 1050 gems and spending 1000 of it on Jekk's bounty, I'm left with 50 gems that I can't buy anything with. I really hope they make it so you can either turn your leftover gems into gold or shiftstone (which is equivalent to Hearthstone's dust). It's only about 50 cents that you're wasting but still, money is money. (Edit: the store prices were changed in patch 1.19 so this no longer applies; thanks to the Devs for listening to the community.)
Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys Hearthstone or Shadowverse but wishes that these games were more free to play friendly. As long as Eternal keeps its current free to play model and continues to expand and listen to the community, I can easily see it becoming more popular than Shadowverse and maybe even Hearthstone.

At first what I want to say I’m not a flight simmer, I’m a gamer and everything I say is from my perspective. I’m not one those flight simmers who spend thousands on poor quality DLC.
First flight sim I tried was FSX. It looked like crap but it was forgivable because the game is old and I tried it only couple of years ago. With mods you can make it look pretty good.
Now FSW releases. As a 2017 product it should look as good or better as fully modded FSX. Sadly FSW looks bad. When you’re flying low the ground looks terrible and here you will fly low often because game has only small general aviation planes. From the high up textures look better and at times they look pretty good. But poor draw distance ruins it, you can clearly see a line where draw distance ends and blurry textures with no trees starts. The most important thing to me is a good and as accurate as possible world scenery. X-plane 11 does this much better out of the box, i can easily find where i live, there are even the smallest details, i can point my home in about 20 meters accuracy.
FSW feels like a reworked FSX. It is based on FSX engine. Compared to vanilla FSX it looks slightly better, but overexposed lighting system and bloom makes it look bad. Shadows are ridiculous. It's like a separate object under your plane, like a second plane only black.
Well in 2017 game I would expect it would have the same or at least similar amount of content as more than 10 years old FSX. There are no jets and commercial airliners. This is a big letdown. I hope they will come for free with future updates. It would be nice to have them in pilot training missions and learn to fly. Competition – X-plane 11 and Aerofly FS2 has them.
FSW lacks graphics options. You can't even choose what AA to use, there’s only on/off for AA. And there are only few other graphics options. FSW runs bad, really bad. With maxed settings @1080p sometimes I get as low as 25fps which is absolutely unacceptable seeing how the game looks.
Planes on the other hand looks awesome. They are really detailed and I have nothing bad to say about them. Rain effects on the windshield looks very cool too.
Finally a sim with a flight school, missions and achievements. And it has cards too, that was a surprise. From this you can see Dovetail aims for much wider audience than all other sims which don’t want to let new people in and community don’t like new people and tries to reject them. Training missions are fun, maybe a bit buggy at times, but it tries to teach you how to fly, I really like it. Various scenario missions exist too and I hope Dovetail will add more missions with each update. It would be nice to have a career mode. Also i hope for more achievements in the future.
I’m not a real pilot so I can’t tell much about flight model and physics. For me X-plane 11 feels better, but FSW is nowhere near bad, it’s very decent, you will need a good skill to control the planes and make a good landing. FSW is waaay more accessible, that’s a big thumbs up for FSW.
Another thing is airports. Don’t think I want all the airports to be close to their real counterparts, that would be crazy. All I want is auto-generated airports. Now airports are just a runway in a field, no buildings or anything. It’s not hard to make the game to generate simple airports, at least make 10 airports of different sizes and apply them automatically depending on real world airport size.
What I want to see is steam workshop integration and let people create new planes, airports and scenery. If Dovetail will add workshop support and encourage people to create free content providing them easy to access tools, it would be +5 respect points from me.
I know it’s an early access release so it may change same as my review later. If Dovetail fixes the performance problems, graphics, world scenery and add airliners and jets I may change this review. But for now it is not worth purchasing. Dovetail took the easy path and decided to just rework FSX a bit, only with 50% features and content taken out. Just save your time and money and buy XP11 or Aerofly FS2 or stay with FSX. All these three are much better than outdated FSW.
EDIT: so it seems this game is done. Like i thought DLC is releasing one after another while the game is still in early access and that DLC is ridiculous. Like they charge money for a moving map and camera. Yes they charge money for camera. How is this even a thing? They will ask money for colors next? Or will they make shadows as a payware option? Pathetic. This game is already done and forgotten even before it's out.

Released in 2005, Bone: Escape from Boneville is both an adaption of the first issue of Jeff Smith’s classic comic book series but also Telltale’s first point-and-click adventure game.
Unfortunately Telltale’s first leap into the adventure game genre proves to be quite mediocre as the game suffers from a few flaws that really hold it back and make it hard to recommend to anyone who isn’t a fan of the comics.
Pros:
-	The characters are likeable and the game does present an interesting lore that makes me want to check out the comics
-	The game has a good sense of humour
-	Knows how to create a mysterious atmosphere when needed for the occasion
Cons:
-	The game is too short clocking in at about an hour, this is understandable with most Telltale titles as they’re generally episodic, however this one wasn’t and instead was released as a standalone title, not part of a seasonal pack such as their later releases
-	The audio mixing is awful, sometimes the music will overshadow the characters’ dialogues
-	Help mode is overbearing to a point where it will just outright state the answer to a puzzle
Bone: Out From Boneville
[Point-and-Click Adventure]  [Comedy] [Fantasy] [Easy]
The game is all about the Bone cousins as they’re chased out of their hometown, along their way discover the mystical thorn valley which holds many secrets and monsters for our heroes to handle.
While the characters are likeable, the game does fall flat with how simple the puzzles can be, with one in particular being especially frustrating – not helped by the fact that this puzzle, which requires you to play hide-and-seek with the Possum kids twice, both times ruining the game’s general pacing and artificially extending the playthrough time.
As noted before, yes the game is very short and can be beaten within 2 hours, especially since there’s absolutely no challenge at all. The puzzles are easy with a hint box that will spell everything out to you if selected enough times – this ruins any challenge the game had going for it and ruins one of the key fundamentals established from within this particular genre as point and click games need to have some reasonably tricky puzzles to test the player regardless of age.
From a visual standpoint, yes the game has aged and the lower budget is quite noticeable (e.g. Backgrounds are hand painted instead of 3D models and don’t mix with the foreground that well) but the simple style does a good job capturing the simple look of the comics that’s pleasing to the eyes.
In short, while a fun little distraction, I can’t really bring myself to recommend this game to others due to its short comings such as being too short and nothing really feeling properly fleshed out. With that said, you’re probably better off checking out the comics instead
5.5/10

Please Note: This reveiw is coming from someone who has never played this type of game before.
So this game came in one of the Humble Bundle packages that I purchased, and it was not the game i was purchasing it for.
It took me a while to install it even though it is a small game only about 1 gig, and this was due to me not being sure if this type of game would appeal to me or not.
Now.. like I said I have never played a game like this before. It is a real time Dungeon crawling game where you build a party of four. There are different classes for customization of weapons and skills that you will use throughout. I wasnt quite sure what i was getting into because i have played games where you have a party and go adventuring in the world towards your goal whatever it may be and gain levels acuire new abilitys and such but this was much different and far from the Final fantasy and secret of mana type games that I enjoy.
This game has some pretty decent visuals. You play in a first person perspective so you get to see the environment upclose. It has some great looking areas and some dull but that is almost every game now because lets be honest we have almost seen it all before. The dangerous creatures that you face as you travel through have a decent design to them and feel like they belong in the game which i like. There are also several different types that you will encounter which keeps the combat fresh as they all can do something different.
Your movement is grid based so you move forward, back and left to right as you would in most games except you only take one step which moves you 1 square so to speak. At first it seemed strange to me but after a bit of playing i got used to it and it worked well with how the map is designed.
Combat is pretty easy to grasp except for the mage which can take some memorization of different rune combinations so that you can cast your assortment of spells. It has some decent boss battles with some unique mechanics and overall felt nice. There are a few puzzles in here that i enjoyed and added to the overall experience of the game.
It offers different modes that you can play that change the dynamics of the game like the pen and paper mode which takes away the digital map and only lets you plot with pen and paper which i thought was neat. There is also an ironman mode which can appeal to some people but I didnt try it as I am new to this type of genre.
Overall I had a good experience with this game and it felt really fresh to me and i would recommend this game if its on sale to all that enjoy this genre or to those seeking something fresh that they have never really tried before. Do not be put off by this game because you have never played something like it. If you havent I recommend that you do. It might be the next hidden gem in your library

While there is a lot of good about this game, the bad things make it a range of unfun to unplayable.
Positives:
Touting more of a genuine WWI feeling than Battlefield (not explicitly, but we all know what they're talking about), Verdun's weapons seem less like gimmiky "experimental" weapons that we all really know are just re-skins of WWII weapons, and seem actually legitimately from their time. Rifles are toploaders, and bolt-action, and those facts are not just aesthetic. The genuine feeling also extends to the gameplay, a tough, stubborn style of gameplay with often slow line movements, mimicking how a WWI battle might actually feel (although it does move significantly faster, obviously, to still make it a fun game you don't have to play for weeks). The gas mask/mustard gas mechanic is also a lot of fun, and does make you feel claustrophobic as you don a mask.
Negatives:
The negatives from this game come less from the actual gameplay, and more from the class system. Each game is divided into 2 teams and each team is divided into 4(ish) "Squads" of 4 players each. To add some depth to the game, squads can have different nationalities, which goes beyond just the uniform, and actually dictates which kinds of weapons and classes the squad has available. In a squad, there are 4 different positions, and no 2 people can be the same position, forcing an actual squad feeling, which would be cool except that about 25% of the classes are pure♥♥♥♥♥♥
You may be thinking "Well, maybe some of those classes fit someone else's play style better than yours" but this leads us to the main issue which is that certain play styles seem to be heavily favored. When joining a game you can either "quick join" into any random open spot (which is usually a terrible class), or you can browse through the open positions on teams that are currently playing. What you see is that a certain subset of classes that are unpopular remain open on squads with the other 3 classes full. Joining as these bad classes will put you at a disadvantage against all the better-armed classes on the map, making the game incredibly unfun.
This gets worse if you, like me, are really better at one style of combat. I excel at sniping, and do it in most every game I play, but apparently so do many, many other people because finding an open sniping slot is like winning the lottery (except on the French squads whose snipers apparently use paintball guns for how weak they are).
Your other option is to create your own squad, which sounds great. You can choose your nationality, and your role before anyone else gets a pick, but then you have to wait unspecified lengths in the lobby waiting to be matched with at least 8 other patient players, a process of which I have yet to see the end.
So I'm disappointed I can't recommend this game because when I had 2 straight hours in a sniper position it was a ton of fun, but the reason I can't recommend that is that I've spent almost as much time looking to just play the class I want to play as I have spent playing the game.

The FFX/X-2 Remasters are simply fantastic remakes and well worth the price.
For starters they revamped the UI to be slick, COMPLETELY remastered the Final Fantasy X soundtrack for a new experience (old one still available), and improved and cleaned up the graphics overall. Despite being from 2001 and 2003 both games still have quite exceptional visuals. On top of those improvements they added some new content and post-campaign bosses for the hardcore fans and players that are quite challenging. The gameplay itself of party based combat and item hunting still holds up as enjoyable aswell. That aside...........
The main reason these are such great games are the story and lore. There aren't many tales in video games like this one that make you completely dissolve into the world emotionally. The unique characters, futuristic yet somehow post-medival art style, and well weaved out social and cultural dynamics of Spira really capture the intrigue of the player and make you further invested in the already beaufitul story telling of a party of outcasts that are trying to save a world that seems against them at every plot twist.
If the campaigns alone aren't enough to keep you satisfied for the 100 hours it takes to beat them there is enough detail, side missions, lore and difficult quests to keep you busy for another 100 hours. After you've done everything it'll be long enough that you'll want to start over again. The value for cost is unmatched for most single player games out there.
Games like THIS are what gaming is about. This is a must play for anybody interested in RPG games having played them or not. Perfect 10/10.

Just finished the entire game with achievements, and despite some problems, I still recommend it.
[PROS]
- Original concept that you don't see much. Nice for working out your typing skills, multitasking skills, reading speed, and memory.
- Nice graphics for a 2D game.
- Lean and intuitive UI.
- Achievements are actually doable in a lifetime.
- Addictive.
[CONS]
- Makes you hungry.
- Your girlfriend will think you're taking cooking lessons and have more expectations.
- Balancing problems between various foods. Some complicated foods provide little reward. So why make them? Fish, for example, are quick and easy to make (even fully upgraded, they only have 2 recipe cards), attract customers and have a very rapid return-on-investment. So why make anything else?
- The game quickly becomes repetitive. You come to expect more content out of improving your restaurant other than just a skin change and customers with more patience.
- The game describes itself as hardcore but is actually very easy. Can be done completely without ever using the optional VIPs, bets and dating mechanisms.
- It feels like the New Game Plus mode was added as a last-minute afterthought. It induces even more balancing problems and the game actually becomes even easier than before. Feels very untested.
[SPECIAL NOTES ABOUT NG+]
- Because of the constant 50% positive buzz, you'll never be in trouble of lacking customers.
- You'll actually be trying to artificially decrease the number of customers by keeping the same fatty foods on your menu for a long time and putting alcohol on the menu (going against everything you learnt in the previous game mode).
- By the time you get to a 2-star restaurant and because of all the customers, you should have enough money to get through the whole game.
- After this point, you can even go through days without touching your keyboard, failing all your food orders. The only consequence will be less customers the following day, which is actually a good thing!
Finally, the game has a major design oversight: by leaving cooked foods burning on the stove / grill (for example steak, chicken or fish), you can block several / all your prep stations from receiving new customers. This allows you to make the game simpler by effectively removing a number of prep stations for the day at 0 negative buzz (I'm not an expert at cooking, but steak burnt for 13 hours should not be viewed by customers as "average"...).
In NG+, you can use this to take a 5-minute break away from your computer or laugh at 8 idiots watching their food burn for a whole day while effectively avoiding super rush hours ("extreme difficulty" achievement :-)), robberies, chores and it gives you a free pass to safety inspections! Once you've satisfied the other items on your level-up checklist, it's a quick and easy way to go through the remaining days unaffected.

My full review and thoughts on Just Cause 2.
The Positive:
- A very Lenghty game. Takes a very long time to complete 100%.
- Infinite parachutes are very cool to have.
- The grapple wire is fun to use and adds a lot to the game.
- The story is interesting.
- The character of Rico is indept and interesting.
- The grapple wire is a very important part in the game and is more like your primary weapon than a gun.
- The story gets straight to the point and not slow or repetitive.
- Its nice to have a open world with the most biggest map ingame that I have ever seen when it came out.
- The black market is very usefull and a lot of items are available.
- Great Gameplay.
- Playing the whole game could last you over 85 - 100 hours!
The Negative
- The grapple wire could have gone a bit further.
- The story missions itself was very short (but having literally over a hundred side missions kind off payed off)
- There are a few bugs here and there.
- The gunplay is terrible. I can not physically aim!
- Driving handling is a bit slippery.
- There are very few weapons and you can only hold few at a time with less ammo than usual third person open world games.
- Voice could glitch out and be out of sync a couple of times.
Most negative points are about the bugs in the game. This does not mean that the game is not fun. The game is absolutely brilliant and I had a lot of fun playing it on my old account. Definately worth 15 dollars!

Thumbs down to Doodles Navigating a Sidewalk: the Videogame!
Okay, okay.  That was uncalled for.  Actually, Drew and the Floating Labyrinth does a few things well, but not enough to recommend it to most people and certainly not for anything approaching the eight dollar asking price.
Floating Labyrinth is a puzzle game in which you attempt to navigate a path of floating cubes obscured by various visual tricks.  The puzzles are largely well designed with each unique trick having 10 short levels dedicated to it, which - with the exception of a few outliars - increase in difficulty from a tutorial level to a fairly complex challenge that will take your average adult player a few goes to get right.  It all comes together in the last approximately 20 levels where all the various visual conundrums are combined to good effect.  For the most part, Floating Labyrinth never feels too easy or controller-snappingly difficult, though there were a fair amount that I ended up solving by tricky jumps rather than actually using logic and a few that are less puzzles than they are exercises in patience.
One could argue the biggest drawback of the puzzling in Drew is its small offering of gameplay.  Now, 80 levels sounds like a good deal on paper, but when you ignore levels that are purely vehicles for the story and effortless tutorial levels, it feels short.  I finished the game completely in less than two hours of casual play.  If the quality of the game is dragged down by its length, perhaps it could bring a strong story and visual style to the table.  If it did, 60 or so competently designed levels might even be a perfect length; ending before the game overstays its welcome.  Unfortunately, while the minimalist sketch-like visuals and use of color are pleasing to the eye, the narrative framework is weak.
You play as a young girl seeking a way home, guided only by a soothing voice revealed to belong to a bird that offers periodic (and just a bit too repetitive) advice.  Already we have the indie formula of "small child navigates a bleak, frightening world," so it's fair to say there will be a loss of innocence and possibly some kind of twist or pseudo-philosophical pretensions.  Yes, Floating Labyrinth did indeed hit evey branch on its fall out of the indie tree, and basic awareness of "artsy" games will leave you feeling a bit blasé at the end; exactly the opposite of the emotional impact the game is fishing for.  Ultimately, though, I believe the narrative fails because it lacks the dialogue-free story open to interpretation of something like Limbo, nor does it offer enough to characterize Drew, her guide, and their relationship as done right by, say, Portal.  The dialogue between them consists of only a handful of vague sentences for the entire first half of the game and I just never felt invested.
Technically, Drew is okay.  It does noticably lack polish that quickly identifies it as being largely the work of one man; I assume a student showing off the culmination of all their hard work.  You can tell by minor things like the inability to rebind keys after launching the game and an entirely royalty-free soundtrack (which is very samey between levels).  That said, it played fine, I encountered no bugs, and it looks genuinely good.
So by now you might be thinking, "if the game has some good puzzles and a unique visual style, surely it's still worth my time?"  Well, no.  I can't really recommend it on that alone.  Sure, some puzzle aficionados or lovers of good art design might enjoy Drew, but at the end of the day it's a middling experience.  And it's a middling experience being offered for more money than better indie puzzlers, as well as some free ones.  I'd place Floating Labyrinth above something you get for free to play on your phone, but sadly, only just.  I'd get this game for maybe one or two dollars tops to enjoy the bite of artsy puzzling goodness it offers, but I'd suggest you leave off otherwise.
I do hope we see more from Dust Scratch Games in the future, though.  With more amibitous writing, a little more polish, and a willingness to keep trying new ideas, the result could be a great game.

Well....
It's a fairly interesting puzzle platform game (yes, platform, not platformer).  If you think you would enjoy a puzzle game in which you are trying to use clues to traverse a path of blocks, I do recommend it.  I enjoyed it, with the exception of one of the levels which had absolutely no way to "solve" it without simply doing trial-and-error and falling again and again.
That brings me to the first complaint I had.  The companion Drew has helping her through this puzzle space is very willing to tell you the advice for the current sequence of stages.  The first time he says "shadows can tell you something about your surroundings" [slightly paraphrased], it's helpful... the eighth time he says the same thing, I started having flashbacks to Zelda OOT's Navi "Hey Listen!".  This could be solved by putting an option to turn off the random "help" in the options, but the option screen is somewhat bare, with no option to turn off the repetitive comments.
My second issue: Its length.  This game is very short.  I completed the whole game blind [no previous information] in 90 minutes, which is actually much shorter than how long it took to download the game (how is this game so big and so short?).  Anyway, that's really just a minor issue in my book, but I figure I should mention it just in case it's important to you.
My third issue: Every time you finish a level, which in some cases can be <15 seconds, it sends you back to the level selection screen.  This seems fairly redundant, as unless you want to skip levels (and make the game even shorter!), you'll just be going to the next level.  It makes the game feel less like a contiguous story and more like a free flash game you would play online.
Again, I do recommend it, as long as you're in the target audience.  The first and third issues above could theoretically be fixed by a small patch.  The second could make-or-break-it for you, but I find length less important than other issues.

Played through one cycle, but haven't tried NG+ yet. Compared to the previous games in the series, the monster placement/quantity in some areas is punitive rather than challenging. There are certain points at which you'll be so overwhelmed that it feels "gimmicky" instead of challenging. On occasion, DS2:SOTFS crosses over the line from "tough but fair" like the predecessors, into unnecessarily cheap.
You'll also find bosses that play more like the DLC bosses from DS1 than the original DS1 bosses. Fast and hard-hitting attacks that almost always stagger you or break your guard when you block, as well as many many more unblockable attacks. There are also some environmental gimmicks (Flexile Sentry room flooding is one example) that make things more difficult. You have to shift your mentality from good timing with blocking to good timing with dodging.
It's fun overall, but certainly not as memorable as DS1. There are some memorable boss fights and areas (very impressive visuals in the Dragon Aerie/Dragon Shrine), but overall it doesn't leave as deep of an impression as DS1. Who can forget Quelaag, Sif, Smough/Ornstein, Crossbreed Priscilla, Moonlight Butterfly, and many others from DS1? I'm having a hard time remembering many from DS2:SOTFS, except a few that killed me repeatedly in questionable ways that caused more frustration than normal.
I ended up not bothering with the DLC areas and bosses. The ultimate weapons (boss weapons) are also nondescript compared to DS1, and I ended up using an upgraded Craftsman's Hammer for the vast majority of the game. There are some really impressive new spells though, compared to DS1. DS2:SOTFS gives you the impression that it was made for spellcasters and PvPers, which is good for those audiences. But I played for the complete package, which even by "Souls" standards is threadbare at best. The bosses mostly seem like an assortment of DS1 "cutting room floor" ideas that don't convey the same depth and continuity as the ones from DS1.
If you like the "Souls" games and get this for a discount during a special or sale, you'll have fun. It's not bad, it's just not as memorable as its predecessors. It gets off to a very slow start, and you'll find more interesting areas and bosses as you get deeper (more than halfway) through the game.
(For frame of reference: I've played Demons' Souls and Dark Souls 1 through multiple NG+ rounds each. I did not play vanilla (non-SOTFS) DS2.)

Ozapell Basic is a retro-styled programming language. It is advertised as both an educational tool to learn the basics of programming and a game development tool for simple retro games.
I was really, really torn on the final verdict of this review. I've actually enjoyed playing with Ozapell Basic quite a bit. It's fairly simple to pick up and play with. It took me back to my youth for a few hours and that was worth the money to me. But it's also flawed. So would I recommend it? Not to the audience it seems to be aimed at...
Using this as an educational tool seems a bit like teaching someone to drive in Ford Model T. The principles may still apply, but it lacks so many modern conveniences that I'm not sure if it's a worthwhile task. There's no IDE here and therefore no syntax highlighting, GUI, contextual help etc. This isn't a complaint as such - it is what appealed to me in the first place. I just take issue with inflicting these archaic limitations on a beginner. Something like Mu (
) would seem to be a much better choice. It still has much of the simplicity and immediacy of Ozapell Basic, but lacks the artificial outmoded limitations. As an additional bonus, since it is python-based, much more help is available.
The syntax is "inspired by JavaScript, with BASIC keywords." And it's certainly unusual. For example, an if-then construct:
I would have thought the need for the RESULT keyword was a odd limitation of the interpretor. Others might call it horrific. But it's apparently an intentional design choice:
I'm not an educator. This may well be a good way to learn. But I remain unconvinced it should be enforced by the language. If I'm honest, I have to wonder if this is in fact less of a design choice and more a limitation of the way Ozapell Basic is implemented.
So what about as a game development tool? Ozapell says "It could be fun for someone who wants to program or make retro style games but doesn't want to learn a complicated modern language." You certainly could develop complete games with Ozapell Basic and it could be fun, but I think only in a 'what can I do with limitations' kind of way. If you want to develop something without learning a complicated language. I'd recommend Game Maker Studio instead. Anything you wanted to make with Ozapell Basic, you could make with Game Maker in a fraction of the time. It would be much easier to pick up and learn too. Plus you can delve deeper in to code if you wish. Game Maker is also great for children.
Finally a minor complaint, Ozapell Basic doesn't seem to respect your keyboard's layout. Particularly annoying for UK layouts where the double quote key is in a different position. Also the numpad doesn't seem to work at all. I'm pretty disappointed this bug made it out of the beta, to be honest.

Here we have another dialect of BASIC. “Ozapell Basic is a programming language simple enough to teach the basics of programming - Blah, blah, blah… etc.” It’s is true that you can program using Ozapell Basic but let’s just be honest with ourselves it is not a good idea in 2017. And for beginners who never programmed in their lives it’s just bad. Don’t get me wrong I’m not one of those people who think BASIC is a horrible language and should never be learned; it’s just my opinion. For beginners I would strongly recommend to start with something like python or JavaScript. This languages are easy to learn and you don’t need an IDE to write your programs. Moreover, there are thousands of tutorials how to program games using these languages and a lot of them are free. If you are getting started with a dialect of BASIC, it is extremely hard to even find a good tutorial which is going to help you understand how to program.
In my opinion these kind of dialects aimed towards people who already know how to program and they are just interested in learning something new. I myself program C++ and some front-end work with JS & jQuery. For me, it is interesting to have a look at software like Ozapell Basic on my weekends. However, the lack of good community, steam workshop, informative tutorials and having the idea that it is still BASIC and it is 2017 now kind of kill my motivation to invest my time in building a decent program using Ozapell Basic.
As for the compiler itself, I wish we could have a 2 window mode where we can use Ozapell Basic like emacs. One window for compilation/debugging only and the other one is for writing code. It’s really uncomfortable to save my file and close it each time I try to compile my program. I mean productivity just decreases. It would be also nice if the developer could implement steam cloud and workshop because sharing something that you’ve built is kind of awesome and could motivate others to give this software a try. “It was created using Ozapell Basic” – “ Wow, really?! No joke?! That’s awesome!”
I like the way this software looks. It gives me some kind of retro feel. I never had a computer like Atari 800, Apple2 or Commodore 64 where BASIC was the main language. I started with Borland compliers on Windows XP :P. Nowadays, I use IDEs, vim and emacs. Frankly, after using Brackets, VS: Community and other IDEs, Ozapell Basic just feels refreshing. I can really feel the struggle of people who were programming 40-30 years ago looking at monochrome monitors, not having good debugging tools and there was no IntelliSense!!!! This was a nightmare!
In a nutshell, I have no problem paying for this software. Developer described everything it could do and everything is true. However, don’t think you can do serious game dev using Ozapell Basic and it is certainly not the easiest thing to get started with. Just because it is not beginner-friendly. In my opinion this software is focused towards programming enthusiasts.
Keep up all the good work bud! It is really nice to see that steam’s adding more software. Good luck!

Gone Home is about a story of two sisters. Samantha is stuck at home while her sister, Katie, is off traveling the world. So she writes down her every thought to share with her sister when she gets back. However when Kate arrives home the house is empty. There’s a note on the front door stating that Sam left for some unknown reason.
This is a touching story. It purely represents how people can’t ever really go home again and expect life to be the exact same as when they left. It slowly, but bluntly, tells you how time changes everything and pushes people forward, or even away from each other. The game is every blatant about this with the many clues it leaves around. However it is the very definition of first world problems and is slightly riddled with stereotypical teen angst groaning you’d find in any American’s 1980s teen movies, but without any actual reason for conflict.
At first I was intrigued because it gives a somewhat approving approach to letting me be a completely voyeur into someone’s family. As I wondered around I would get to read into each persons life and their problems. This ability only poked at my curiosity to go further. Even the storm outside the house made the dark hallways seem somber rather then creepy. With a few steps here and there it opens up other parts of the house and even shows you secret entrances and old remnants of the previous owner of the house. This was intriguing to only a limited extent.
Then there are other parts of the story that are just completely bland. There’s multiple clues lying around that would have suggested a troubled marriage or the parents having trouble dealing with their more rebellious daughter. However I found myself not caring, because I would only be able to find 1 or 2 notes on what one parent thought about the situation. The other parent (most of the time this was the father) would be completely left out by the fact that there wouldn’t be anything of his to read or analyze.
Other times the clues were handwritten notes that were completely illegible. Want to find out about the house and why it’s nicknamed? Well guess what? You probably won’t be able to read what happened since it looks like a small gerbil had a seizure while holding a pen on one of the only notes from the owner. This only left me frustrated and I ended up not caring at all about what happened. So this made it feel like half of the story was incomplete.
This was followed by the continued girl-to-woman story of Sam. While this was cute and heart warming to reading about a girl finding herself, it left me wondering if I should have just read a book instead. Whatever item you pick up plays a diary page of Sam’s and it belts out over the soft music in the background and the occasional thunder. None of it was too interesting, and as said before: it is riddled with clichés. The 90’s punk and girl grunge references even come off as cliché due to the same standard writing all over the posters of ‘fighting the man’ and what not. It’s like they rebel against a establishment without any clear reason to do so.
It lacks basic game play mechanics and good exploring rewards. Like with most games it might have clues as to what to do next that are clear and help continue the story. Yes, this was partly my fault, but after having such limited interaction with items I started looking less and less for items to fiddle with. It doesn’t interest me to pick up a 3d plate, or 3d tooth brush, and spin it around. The 3d books serve little to no purpose, except for one. Then the story items are so blatantly obvious they aren’t misable or they look so generic that I didn’t bother picking it up considering it was only the 900 th random piece of paper strung about in the house.
In the end Gone Home is another video game experiment that doesn’t feel complete. Many gamers, including myself, will be greatly disappointed with this. This is due to the lack of just about everything that makes video games playable. Yes it’s filled with every artistic metaphors and emotional impact that would be in most video games. Although for me the story was lost due to the stereotypical storyline of the subject matter, plot holes, and illegible clues. If it went on for a few more hours and explained everyone else’s view point I would have probably enjoyed it a lot more.
Either skip this or get it on the cheap (i.e. below $10). It’s only 2 hours worth of gameplay and has ZERO replay value.

Wild Run Update: WR is out and after a few hours with it I can safely say that literally none of the concerns I have stated below has been fixed, in fact the game has gotten noticeable worse including, but not limited to:
The new vehicles included in this expansion are even more expensive in the in-game money/real life bought money conversion. While a high-end car would set you back roughly 15-20 euros/dollars(!) in the original game, the new high-end cars will be over double that. You're looking at almost 40(!!) euros/dollars for a single car and that is without any upgrade which will easily be another 20 euros/dollars if you don't have 3-4 hours to grind the in-game money for it! Also they included something called "Smart loot" which instead of having you travel around to certain areas of the map for challenges, you can now instead just do the same challenge over and over and over again for 5 hours and eventually you'll have your fully upgraded cars. The new extreme modes, monster trucks, bikes and drifting are essentially gimmicks that will be fun for roughly an hour.
The idea around The Summit is on paper a good idea but the execution of it is probably one of the worst ideas in a while. I could go into why at lenght but just know that unless you are ready to spend several hundreds (Yes, no joke) of hours in the game, it will leave you feeling unfulfilled and that you've wasted your time because The Summit requires you to compete against other players and only the best gets rewarded properly. I could go on and on and on, with how the side walks in the game are now actual edges that will make you car fly randomly or how drifting is 90% like driving in the snow in the vanilla game or how the game is so poorly optimized that the wet roads will make your computer stutter (Even on a 980 Ti!) and how the graphical update overall is a complete disappointment and the thousand other things I haven't mentioned.
I'm going to have to stop writing here as I realize the more I think about it, the more I am actually going from thinking that the game was an okay game to directly hating it and regretting this purchase full stop.
The Crew and The Wild Run could've been so much more but instead we got this...
Original game review:
I tried being positive about this game, but in the end I can't justify it from a gameplay perspective. I like exotic cars a lot which is what has kept me at this game for so long, but I doubt a lot of people have my level of "addiction" to exotic cars to justify it and end up disappointed in the game. Be aware that this is an arcady game, so if you're looking for a realistic simulation game, this is not it.
The traffic is poorly implemented so if a player in your session has a bad connection, the traffic will swerve left and right and it will be hard to overtake.
The max number of players in a FreeDrive session is capped at 8 which in 2015 is hilariously low for a game so heavily focused on multiplayer. In addition to that, you have no control over what session you end up in. And that is without going into the required always-on DRM that will eventually happen to kick you out of the game (That is a promise) that will set your progress back 5 to 45 minutes.
The graphics are mediocre and everything in the world except player cars looks like something that was made in 2010. The sound is bordering on the ridiculous (Sorry UbiSoft, but a Koeniggsegg does not sound like a BMW with a custom exhaust) and the forced disconnect if you are AFK for 10 minutes (You are returned to the start Splash screen, not even disconnected where you parked your car before going AFK) gives this game a overall poor immersion.
The price decrease came too late and the game population has sort of fizzled out - That being said, it was briefly revived by the announcement of the upcoming expansion pack and the 2 hour trial. A trial that was poorly implemented. When you play the trial you meet people which makes this game a lot better, but by the end of the trial people are straight up disconnected with no chance of saying anything to the other drivers the person was driving with - The only way around this is to add them to your UbiSoft friendlist - But good luck remembering the names of the players!
The game gets grindy real fast. The laughable short story does not reward you in any way towards a full upgraded car, nor does it provide you enough cash to have an acceptable level of cars with upgrades. The game essentially forces you into buying in-game cash for real money to a gross extent. 20 euros will roughly be the equivalent of 5 hours of gaming.
Speaking of Euros, having encountered a bunch of Americans in the game they have proudly told me that they pay in dollars instead. In UbiSoft's world 20 euros = 20 dollars.
If you ignore all of the above and you spend the 30 euros/$30 just to cruise around and complete the main story the game is fine.
However, if you know cars you will cringe. If you're a completionist you will burn out fast as the game has Tetris levels of variety in gameplay.
With all that being said, will I continue to play it just for cruising around in the single car I spend 15 hours to upgrade fully? Yes, I probably will.

Solid gameplay, although you should be ready for a vertical learning curve at the beginning. In faithfully recreating the Western Front experience of World War One, Verdun presents the player with an environment that is hazardous in ways you may not expect.
The most common weapon you'll get is a bolt-action rifle with iron sights, which you will spend your first 20 or so deaths learning how to aim. Practice timing your shots with the amount of time it takes to cycle the bolt. Press 4 to equip a gas mask that will blind you slightly less than the gas itself. Some classes get grenades, which you can deploy by pressing G and then drop at your feet when you're shot in the head by one of the sniper classes that actually get an optical scope.
There are no ammo pickups, which you will not live long enough to need anyway.
The game is hard initially but rewarding once you get the hang of it.

Let me begin by saying I was skeptical about how fun exactly this game would be. A friend got it for me for my birthday, and I tried it. Welp.
I've played RTS games since the original AOE (I was seven when it came out, got my mom to buy it for me saying it was a history learning game lol), and I never learned the hotkey frenzy that seems to be popular with some players. I'm definitely not "good," at RTS's, as I got my♥♥♥♥♥whooped in many a multiplayer match back in the day before I gave up playing against real people.
This isn't AOE. This isn't Warcraft, or anything of the like. There are no weapons, no barracks, no special unit types. There's just you and good old mother nature. It's a RTS about...real life.
It's faster paced than some have made it out to be (however I always keep the time multiplier on 2x), and takes some getting used to. Sometimes the villagers are frustratingly dumb and don't do what you want them to, but then you figure out why, and go "Ohhh," sometimes out loud, making your SO or roommate or pet look at you funny. The first time I played it, I wondered how the heck it got to be three in the morning when I distinctly remember it being 9pm just a few minutes prior.
Every new game is different. Sometimes, it snows in early summer and everyone freezes to death. Other times you think you're doing great because you've got 6000 food stockpiled and then suddenly it's winter, and half your adults starve to death because they couldn't walk all the way to the barn where all the food was. Sometimes a tornado comes through and destroys literally everything, and that's just how Banished works.
Final note: The help files are grammatically hilarious. But it's one dude, what do you expect.
A game everyone should own.

After you manage to find your way out and escape Mount Grimrock, you become shipwrecked on an island and your only objective is to find a way out and survive, will you manage?
Legend of Grimrock 2 is a game developed and published by Almost Human Games and is the sequel to the first dungeon crawler game; Legend of Grimrock. Legend of Grimrock 2 puts you in control of a group of four prisoners aiming to find their way out off an island. Search for secrets, find clothes, weapons and armours and continuously upgrade the abilities of your party members
It is a wonderful game if you are willing to immerse into it. But it requires a lot of patience and endurance because it's a very difficult game. The game allows you to set up your personal party, choosing the race and abilities of your members or you can simply start by using a pre-defined group. As an old-fashioned dungeon crawler you can only move one step at a time in one direction
Legend of Grimrock 2 has great atmosphere with nice and improved graphics from the first game and addictive game with extremely good and varied puzzle design with many different and gradually stronger enemies and mysterious hints that gradually reveal the story and are very rewarding
The mazes can be maddening at times but at the same time this adds to the claustrophobic mood the game is trying to portray, however, Legend of Grimrock 2 isn't easy so be prepared to die a lot
Overall, Legend of Grimrock 2 is a fun dungeon crawler to play in bursts and is a great return to the Legend of Grimrock series!

I got it because many said it was similar to Life is Strange, and I can see how. I loved Life is Strange. I teared up and can't listen to Obstacles by Syd Matters without "feelings" lol. I did not expect it to be the same, but I did expect a nice story based game.

I get it. The extraordinary within the ordinary, simplicity, beauty, life, sentiment, etc. I "understand" that.
It's just that I could have watched all of the movies I ever seen in my teen years on IFC, LOGO, and Sundance etc, things that i've seen many times (that i LOVE)..... and even with that, the story left me feeling like..."so?? yea..? and??". My personal experience with it felt more generic than captivating or  touching.
You know the feeling you get when there's a book/movie that's a big  hit and everyone is recommending it and you finally read/watch it and you're like "wait.....that's all? am i missing something? what's the fuss about?". That feeling.
Perhaps because I have been accustomed to seeking out many things like it in the past in the form of film. The story was nice and "real" and all...and intentionally "simple"..which is fine...but it was just too basic. That is, if you've already been accustomed to stories/ideas just like it.
