If you are thinking about buying this game, read the negative reviews (many reviews bring up the same issues)(sort by "most recent" too). I would recommend this game when it is on sale, but not at full price.
Barely WWI. Gas and barbed wire and graphics are the only thing that is WWI. But barbed wire does not kill in 5 seconds irl. No WWI feel.
Summary-  CLUNKY CONTROLS (this deserves caps), too few players per map (16 per side). bad map design, lack of sound effects or battle atmosphere, game cant handle lag, and weak pistols. It is also a pain to pick a full sever. "Squad" is weird and not useful.
As others have said - clunky controls. Your character goes to crouch or prone like he is an old man doing some gardening, not like an 18 year old getting shot at. Often times you press the run button and your guy doesnt seem to do much. One of the problems seems to be the "crouch" position, I dont think the game can transition to a run from a crouch. There is no jogging crouch like in RO. Coming from from a game like Red Orchestra, this game's controls are horible for a game in 2017.
**Edit** I have been experimenting with the clunky controls to figure out why they are so bad and I have dicovered a few things. First off, your stamina bar only lasts for 9 seconds of running. After that 9 seconds you stop, then start walking. In a game like, oh I dont know, RO, if you are sprinting and run out of stamina is keep going at a slow jog. In Verdun you are either sprinting OR walking. Secondly, when you hit the prone button your character does not drop to the ground. He transitions (for a split second) into a crouch then he goes prone. Sometimes the game seems to stop (or slow way down) at the crouch position. This leads you to press the prone button multiple times. But Verdun plays a trick on you. The prone button is used to stand up too. You will press the prone button frantically to avoid fire, but you will find yourself standing up into fire. Lastly, the game allows you to hold an aim when it shouldnt. If you are aiming and crouch you still hold your ami. You stand up, you hold your aim. When you go prone I think you still hold your aim (I will have to check this in game). This leads to a lot (I mean a lot) of jack-in-the-box shooting. Other games like RO your gun collides with the terrian, so in a lot of instances you cant pop down then up (without losing your aim). These clunky controls, makes me feel like your character is in boot camp and the drill instructor is yelling "DONT GET YOUR GUN DIRTY PRIVATE!!!" When you hit crouch, your character takes his time and holds his gun up. When you go prone, the game transitions in to a crouch (carefully) then goes prone. It feels like your character is trying to keep his gun from getting scratches. It reminds me of the pictures of Vietnam, with the soldiers holding their guns over their head while crossing a stream.
Here are some other cons:
-Too few players per map. There are only 16 player per side and in another post one of the developers said that the maps are narrower so the player count isnt noticed. No, this is not true. At any given time you are attacking or defending a trench 100-200 yards wide with 8 guys, because half of your team is always dead or just spawned and running up. With 8 guys per 100 yards, this does not seem like a WW1 game, and this leads to a lot of running and gunning.
**Edit** Besides the low player count per map, the "squad" system makes it hard to pick a map to join. The "squad" is not useful and I think the only reason it was added was to shut people up, and to stop them from asking, "Why didnt you add americans?" and "Why didnt you add Canadians?" Each squad member having a job plays no part in this game. Each side is sooooo small (only 16 people MAX) you are really just watching out for your side as a whole. If you have a sniper on your squad, he is not going to be watching out for you squad, he is going to be watching out for your whole team (heck it is only a few more people). The squad system over complicates the screen to join a server and it over complicates choosing your weapon. Your squad does not stick together. You stick with the people you spawn with. Period.
-Bad map design (or you could call it "spawn" design). You spawn either right where the other team is trying to attack or you spawn right in front of where the other team already is. About 25% you will get killed within 5 seconds of spawning. Spawning within 10 feet of an enemy is common. He will just sit there and kill your whole wave, or you will have to joy of spawning in front of an MG. It is possible to spawn in the middle of a gas attack.
-Another spawn issue - Each time you spawn (or maybe it is random) you alternate sides of the map. You spawn on the left flank then the right flank. This makes it VERY hard for new people to learn the battle field. Every time you spawn, you think to yourself, "Where the hell am I ?" You whole team spawning back and forth does not make sense. It makes even less sense when you are defending. Once you find a nice spot, but dont see any enemies, dont worry! A whole group of them will spawn on your side of the battlefield in about 12 seconds. This makes defending VERY predicable (and this makes attacking hard, not because of any other factors).
-Other map issues - wierd bunkers. In many maps there are sandbag walls with holes for shooting, but the designers of the games made the firing "slits" 3 feet wide and 12 inches high. These firing "slits" act less like firing ports and more like frames so the enemy can shoot you. To make matters worse, on a slightly curved bunker there will be 3 or 4 slits across the front and sides so the enemy can shoot you from any direction. The developers of this game need to get some shovels and sandbags and make a little bunker in their office's flowerbeds. A firing slit doesnt have to be big to cover a large arc. I think 8 inches high and 12 inches wide would be plenty.
-No atmoshere. The lack of good sound effects and battlefield conditions make the game very unconvicing. There is no fog or dust either. Once again, the game Red Orchestra is better. In RO, artillery booms, mg fire buzzes overhead, people are yelling. Verdun has got to (please, I beg) add a blackout system when artillery and genades hit near by. And mg fire needs to scare your character. Even though RO is many years old, it has a system for these things. A rifle fired from 100 yards away in real life is still LOUD, but in Verdun you only way you know people are shooting at you is when you are dead. Gas masks to not block hearing or vision. In fact the enemy will attack through their own gas just because new players dont put on their masks. Gas is no problem with a mask (or I should say masks are no problem).
**Edit** My new "favorite" sound effect is when you are trying to crawl it sounds like you are digging in your pocket for your keys but your pocket is full of other stuff: keys, bottle caps, old receits, lose change. You cant crawl an inch without those sound effects. VERY easy to hear people crawling on the other side of a wall.
-Lag, or how the game handles lag is bad. I have a 50-80 ping and it is common to see other players warping around the map. I was going to say that the balistics are bad, but I think it is how the game handles lag.
-Pistols are worthless (**Edit - Revolvers are worthless. Semi-auto 45 is like a 7 shot machinegun). I heard pistols were nerfed. Pistols are under powered and do not slow down someone you hit. I think pistols should cause a one second stun (or at least a stun that is as long the hit enemy could say, "Owww"). Torso shots should be 1 hit kill or bleed, wait there is no bleeding death, that is Red Orchestra (good job 2011).
-Weapon cycle times. Pistols and bolt action rifle cycle (fire) at a similar rate. I started with a pistol hoping to kick butt in trenches but a rifle's one hit kill, at the same rate of fire, is better.

Fallout 3 has got to be one of the best RPG's ever made.
Your character is a lone wanderer, born into an underground vault shelter in Washington D.C., in the aftermath of a great nuclear war that happened more than 200 years ago. One day, your father leaves the vault for unknown reasons. You are now forced to leave the safety of your vault and venture into an unforgiving, ravaged wasteland in search of him to find out why he left. But of course, you are now free to do whatever you desire until then, in this massive, open world.
There are many side quests, locations, charcters, and enemies along the way to encounter. Along with an array of weapons available ranging from a simple baseball bat...to a mini-nuke launcher! Not to mention armor from your standard vault outfit to the cool looking armor you see on the cover of this game. Will you be a saviour? Or will you make a name as the most evil wanderer the wastes has ever known? The choice is all yours.
Even after 5 years since this game has came out, I still find myself discovering things that I haven't before and am still captivated each time. I highly recommend Fallout 3 for anyone looking for a great RPG or just a truly, well made game that's fun to play and something you can immerse yourself in for many hours, days, months...years! Also, I recommend you checkout the DLC's for this game. Broken Steel is almost essential.
Thank you for reading my review and have a good day!

First impression:  North Korea?  That's just silly and really ruins the immersion immediately.  China would be more plausible.  Good graphics, though, and at a discounted price, there's fun to be had.
Later in the day:  Quite enjoyable moving through a ruined city with your squad and taking out enemy-held locations.  Various missions to see to.  The designers put a lot of work into this, and it's appreciated.
A couple of days later: Still enjoying. I'm playing the campaign, not the multiplayer, running around the city stopping the enemy police from abusing the people, doing acts of subterfuge, gathering fighters and taking objectives in the war zones, storyline missions...It's all been quite entertaining, and the voice acting is very good. I don't know what it was like when it was first released or in multiplayer, but right now bugs are few and nothing critical. Even at a higher price, this would be a good buy, and the developers should be proud of their achievement.
Final take after 50 hours (including DLC):
I wish there were a "save whenever you want to" feature; I find it upsetting when games leave this out.  If you want to torture yourself, make checkpoints with no saves an option rather than an unchangeable function. Having to do over a difficult scenario several times can become tedious, and this is not the way you want your game to be perceived.  Overall, though, this is an engaging, entertaining game, and I recommend it for anyone who is into first person war shooters.

Let me contain my gushing and try to do this succinctly. CSD is a restaurant "sim" in the same sense that a bag of potato chips is food. It's quick, accessible, and makes you hungry for more. The core of the gameplay is serving a steady stream of customers via barrages of QTE's as apparently the sole existing employee, in something like Cooking Mama meets Wario Ware on crack -- especially during rush hours. Then, in your downtime between days you get to buy new foods, upgrades to existing ones, bits of equipment, and cycle your active menu to keep your "buzz" level (customer traffic) high. That's as far as the sim portion goes. The old Giant Bomb quicklook with the late great Ryan Davis sums it up well:
Since release, it's also gotten a slew of free new content including about a dozen new foods, controller support, local co-op and competitive modes, Iron Chef challenges, and more. The dev is pretty active and friendly with the community, and now there's even a sequel on the way.
The art is, while largely static, easy on the eyes, while the sound design complements it perfectly and really gives the game its captivating energy. The music is fitting for both the everyday activity and rush hours, and each part of an order you assemble is punctuated by various chops, whacks, slaps, and splashes. I wouldn't change a thing about it.
For as much as I love the game, though, it does get off to a frustratingly slow start. The main metric of your progress is accumulating star ratings for your restaurant, which typically require getting a handful of perfect combos, passing a few safety inspections, doing the currently available catering side events... and playing for 20 (in-game) days since your last star upgrade. You will LONG be finished the other requirements by the time this elapses, and getting to 1 and 2 stars is a bit of a drag. On the flipside, though, by the time you get to 3 stars you'll likely be wishing that span was longer, as the game starts to ramp up in challenge FAST. I would strongly recommend you be a competent touch typist if you want to play this!
All in all, highly addictive, pretty cheap, the dev's nice, and it's easily earned a spot on my favourites list.

So, first off, to get it out of the way - for the price point this is a pretty short one all in all. If it were a little closer to $5 I think it'd be more fitting what most people expect..
Despite that I'm gonna give it a thumbs up, with a few caveats, but an overall positive expression.
The aesthetic is pretty solid - they have a solid and consistent pixel style, it's a pretty extra-old grungy early PC-era days look, but it works, and they run with it. Ultimate Chicken Horse is a competitive multiplayer platformer, with a twist. You need to place objects in the world to make it possible for you to reach the end, but harder for others to follow you.
The strength of this game lies in the ever-evolving levels. What once was as simple as jumping across five platforms, soon turns into a death race with black holes and death traps everywhere. The game is arguably going to be at its best when played locally because of how easy it is to communicate, plot and yell at your friends. It might still be fun using skype or similar, but it remains to be seen how well this game holds up when playing with complete strangers whom you can’t talk to.
This game features a fair amount of unlockable stages and costume pieces, so the game will remain fun as you keep playing it. The process of unlocking could easily have been a grind, but they managed to avoid that by adding something new after every game. The process of gaining the levels or costume is very interesting and unique: you have to, while competing, build something to get to the box that contains the unlockable. This leads to a team effort to mess everybody’s chances of winning up, and more often than not makes the rest of that match a lot more interesting.
There are a lot of parts, all of which can be used together in amazing ways. For example, you can use the rather ordinary platform with a saw, put some honey on it, and have an instant death trap for anyone who lands on it. And it only gets crazier as the game goes on, as more and more parts get placed. And if the level gets too hard, you always can still destroy some particularly troublesome parts. No parts will ever be used in the exact same way twice, and no game will be the same. It’s the perfect system to give infinite replayability.
Each game will take about 5 minutes to complete, which is the perfect length for this game. Play sessions will generally be longer than that though, when everyone keeps wanting to play one more time. All of the game rules can be changed – if there’s something that’s not quite right for what you currently want, you can most likely change that.
+ Ever changing levels
+ Lots of parts
+ Interesting possibilities for interactions between parts
+ Short games and simple to set up
(-) Online may not be as good as local play
I can find nothing bad to say about this game. The only thing that could possibly keep me from playing this, is its local play requirement and limited fun otherwise. But if you’re looking for local play game, then look no further than this.

Jeff Smith's Bone series is a brilliant mix of fantasy world-building and timeless comedy... also, it's conspicuously absent from the description of this game. That seems a major oversight as Bone: Out From Boneville functions as a highlight reel of the first few issues, realized in 3D form. For fans of the series, there's nothing new here... which is fine, since the wit and wonder still works, even in Windows 10.
Despite the comments to the contrary, I never experienced any installation errors or gamebreaking bugs. In fact, my only complaints about Boneville are its relatively short runtime (2-3 hours) and the visual depiction of Rose. While Gran'ma Ben's exaggerated features translated well to cartoonish rendering, the more 'human' Rose looks more like the cgi monstrosities of a Dire Straits video (ask your parents), but her voicework saves the performance.
The puzzles are fairly light and simplistic (hide-n-seek as an integral plot point, for example), making the game appropriate for younger audiences. Admittedly, there are multiple references to smoking and gambling, but nothing more hardcore than the films of my childhood, the now-classic Goonies and Gremlins... again, ask your parents...
Beyond the seeming straightforwardness, Out From includes branching conversational paths and puzzles with multiple solutions, prompting different later dialogue, so you would need to replay sections to hear all of the voice acting. Therefore, while the game itself can be finished rather quickly, there is enough content to recommend the title at its non-sale price, currently set as half of a $10 bundle. As for me, I'm off to the Cow Races...

Bone: Out From Boneville was one of the first point and click adventure games released by Telltale Games. It was also one of their first licensed properties to help them get over a hurdle for their start in their gaming business. Based on the highly acclaimed comic series by Jeff Smith, Bone started off as a cult comic but years later it would become a household franchise recognized by various libraries and comic award committees. It was only logical that it should get it's own game. Anyways even if you never read the comic, this game is a direct adaption of the first volume under the same title. It's a cross between the Peanuts comics and the Lord of the Rings series which is the best way to describe it. The main protagnogists are white anthropomorphic creatures that don't resemble anything else seen in the series. Which is part of the appeal of the series is that they are easy to recognize and to isolate them from the other more realisticly drawn characters. Now for the plot: the game starts off with our main hero Fone Bone who is out in the middle of a wasteland with his cousins Smiley & Phoney Bone. They were ran out of Boneville due to Phoeny Bone's election for town mayor went sour. With food and water becoming scarce, they need to find civilazation if they want to survive. When Fone Bone finds a map, they spouted a upcoming swarm of locusts and have to run for their own lives. Upon the encounter of the swarm, Fone Bone got seperated from his cousins and is now alone. Not willing to give up Fone uses his best outdoor skills to track his cousins and soon finds himself in a forest region that is more lively than the barren wasteland. A stranger in this unknown land to Fone, he soon makes new friends with the locals and with enough luck will soon find out what became of his cousins. The mechanics of the point and click system are at times a little off but since this was Telltale Games' first attempt in the genre, I will forgive them on that small error. Otherwise this game is easy to play, and while it's not a lengthy game keep in mind it's only covering one volume of a nine volume comic series so it was intended to pile each installment upon the other. Anyone who loves the comics will enjoy this game for certain.

What do you like? Would you like to plunge your enemies into the chaos of the deep darkness lurking in all hollows, use the power of hexes to your advantage. How about hit someone with a 200 pound sword and fling them around like a ragdoll? Or perhaps nimbly slide around enemies and stunlock them with your quick and agile moves. I'm not even going to get into the subcategory of weaponry. Also fasion souls.
Moving on to more considerable measures, the gameplay aspect is fantastic and all but the movment system is really what puts the strawberry on top of the mouthwatering double chocolate cake. We can spend hours on hours talking about said movment system. To keep things reasonably short, for any fans or people familiar with Dark Souls 1, this is a direct upgrade upon the movment system introducing better I-frames, directional rolling, less sensitivity on sprinting, controller support, all in all better optimisation. Basically your character stopped going to McDoalds and lost 100 pounds.
The leveling system original to the series was also introduced in Dark Souls II, variety really started to shine through, the game is still hard so what makes this such a bad Dark Souls game? Simply the backstory, the lore does not connect, the game doesn't have the depressing "I'm going to painfully die and come back sufforing being stuck in an undying cycle" feeling. It also doesn't share the same disturbing factor as say Dark Souls 3. Demon of Song being the acception. Although similarity the areas are still breathtaking, out of all the disaster and giants you topple there's a pretty sunset at the end or after getting pelted with greatbow arrows and killing demons you see a pretty lava lake. As in life, beauty comes in natural situations conventionally, sometimes you just need a clever eye. I'll stop myself before this needless praising gets out of hand. Not sure what you're waiting for, perhaps a friend to play through the game with? Or how about 5 of them? (They also changed that in SotFS) Anyways, thanks for reading and showing support. Have fun!

Probably the best digital card game currently.
The dev took the best of MTG but adapted some of the mechanics to fit the digital world. For example, cards keep their "counters" and other statuses when they go to the graveyard or are shuffled back to your deck or hand.
They also tried to make as fast paced as possible with a UI similar to Hearthstone, while still giving you a chance to react on the opponents turn. You do not have as many situations where you can react, but you can on the most important (when an opponent casts a spell, plays a creature, when blocking and blockers are declared and after the opponent's turn). That gives you a lot of options but still keeps the game flow smooth.
The land (mana) system is also a bit simplified in comparison to MTG. You have available power and influence over a color. You do not tap a land of a specific color, you spend power to play cards. But you need to have enough influence over a color to play some of the more powerful cards.
The free to play system is probably the best from what I've seen, the game gives you cards and gold constantly (literally every single win awards you with a chest that has at least one card and some gold). Also if you do a draft you get to keep the cards.
There's a lot of optional "vs AI" game modes (campaign, arena style draft and a gauntlet where you play increasingly more difficult AIs with the same deck for better and better rewards) for people who don't like playing vs other players or for testing out new decks.
TL;DR: The best of MTG mechanics brought to a digital world with a very generous F2P systems. Highly recommended.

I'm going to say this straight up.  You need to have a lot of patience if you want to have any hope of beating this game.  This game is *hard.*
Now that that's out of the way, on to the review.  The game, VVVVVV, is a hardcore platformer designed around the manipulation of gravity.  The controls are very simple:  left, right, and change the gravitational pull.  However, do not be fooled by its apparent simplicity.  This game, from beginning to end, is meant to challenge and frustrate, and only the most patient and skilled of players will be able to succeed.  There are various different "levels" connected by a hub world, with each level presenting a different mechanic, such as wires that instantly switch gravity to auto-scrolling levels, for the player to learn.  While the beginnings of these levels are meant to ease the player in, by the end of each section, the player will be required to have mastered the mechanic, if he or she wishes to succeed and move on.  This all culminates in a final level designed to test even the best of players.
While a story is present, it's mainly just filler between levels, like many platformers.  However, in a game like this, I find one unnecessary, as that's not what the game is ultimately about.  I would even argue that too much story is present at times, as it can be a bit irritating to be forced to scroll through conversations to get to the next area.
Finally, I must say that I love its music, a fast-paced ode to the older days of the NES and SNES.  It really fits the tone of the game and gets you pumped and ready for the challenges to come.
Overall, this is a great game, and I fully recommend it to any who want to truly test their platforming skills.  This receives, from me, a 9/10.

On the one hand it's a good game that will provide several hours of enjoyment. On the other hand there's not much challenge once you “figure it out” and so the replay-ability is not there. Overall, I might think $10 justifiable if it were a final game (and give it a different rating then), but as it's not complete yet I think it's overpriced considering what you get. If you are considering this purchase, I would say wait until a 'final' version is released and hopefully some more features will have been added to justify the cost (and hopefully the price won't go up).
The Good
What Banished does well, it does really well. It is quick to learn and much of it is very intuitive. Most of what you need to know is right in the tutorials which don't suck up your time but leave you feeling like you are ready to tackle the world.
The interface is easy to use and you won't find yourself going from window to window trying to figure out what just happened and why. There are information windows, but these can be kept open and put out of the way so that “the game” is what's going on in your city, not how goo you are at micro managing.
The graphics are great and large cities look amazing. I would love to be able to zoom in more and maybe follow a person around from their perspective, but what is there is really good. One bit that I found wasn't great was the lakes and rivers which (on some maps especially) when you zoom out far enough looked kinda like someone used a pain tool to draw them on the map. The solution, of course, is to not zoom out too far.
Once you get going on a city you do tend to loose yourself in the game, at least for the first 200 citizens. The whole “just one more turn” effect applies to this game (even though it's not turn based) until you reach larger sizes. It's easy to play the same way a good wine is easy to taste. (Who am I kidding, I'll drink any wine.)
The Bad
Banished is simple to learn and easy to play because it's an easy, simple game. Yes, you will have a challenge on your hands to figure out the secret to starting a successful city without losing settlers, but once you figure that out there's not much left. (I should note that I've never played anything except the hardest difficulty.) This is NOT Dwarf Fortress (complex and hard to play), but it is also not Sim City (complex but easy to play).
The list of challenges in the game include:
(1) Not dying that first year (or two). Once you figure out the trick this is no longer an issue.
(2) Surviving minor disasters. People (and crops) die, get used to it...and plan for it.
(3) Surviving major disasters. Few and far between in the games I've played, but having a large enough stock of everything seems to make this more of a hassle than a game-changer (with the notable exception of fires).
(4) Build big and accomplish some challenges (things like population levels, # of buildings of certain type, etc). These are not in-game challenges and they don't have in-game rewards (that I've noticed), so there's not much point to them except to say you've done them.
The lack of challenges means that the game suffers in the replay-ability aspect and fails to hold attention beyond managing to create a large city (which is easy, just time consuming).
There is also a distinct lack of variety in the game. This can be seen in both the graphics (well done, just not many different homes, bridges, or wildlife as examples) and the basic resources (logs, stone, and iron metal – no different types of these things, that's it – oh, and coal which is all but useless). You can't plant trees along the paths or build a monument to yourself in the centre of town. The one exception is crops – there are many different types here which can be used to make a city look interesting (they are really not needed to survive, or even thrive, at all).
The lack of variety means that every city will look and feel about the same and there's no way to put your own signature on any given map. You will be able to mod the game eventually, but that seems like it's up to the players to make it a good game, which I have never bought into.
Final Thought
So, on one hand I *do* recommend the game because it's well done and for the first few tries you will have great fun (for me that was about 20 hours). On the other hand I *don't* recommend the game because there's just not enough there to justify the cost. However, if more features are added or if you see this game on sale...

I'm only two to three hours in, but I feel like I don't really want to go on--it's taken this long to even get within sight of any meaningful gameplay change.
The game starts with you managing 4 prep stations (which sometimes get bogged down with chores) to prepare food. Yes over the course of the beginning of the game you acquire money to buy new foods to put on the menu, and upgrade those foods, but a lot of the content is gated behind how many stars your restaurant is--you start with zero stars, and you have to go through 20 days to even get to being a two star restaurant (in addition to a bunch of other things that you'd have to be really bad to not have done by day 20). I believe I satisfied all of the other requirements within 8-10 days (around the first hour and a half-ish), and the past ~7 days have all just been the same thing waiting to unlock the next star.
The game is neat, and I've enjoyed it, but if this is the pace the rest of the game is going to have I'm not going to be playing much longer. As of right now I'm not even sure I'm going to come back to play out the next three days. I half expect a hard requirement of 50 more to reach two stars.
If the trailer, which accurately represents the game, looks like fun to you, the game is most certainly worth a couple bucks to take a look. It seems to have a lot of other modes and whatnot that I'm not terribly interested in but might be good for a go (co-op looks possibly interesting), just be warned of the hard cap on pacing in story mode--it may make you lose interest before you fully get a chance to enjoy the game.

This game was made as a challenge, the 7 Day First Person Shooter challenge in 2012.
It quickly became my favorite game to kill time with. The play sessions don't last long for me, as they don't need to. This game is unforgiving, will end abruptly if not cautious, and will often leave you angry at yourself for not checking the proper corners.
You begin with a sidearm, nothing else, perhaps a magazine and a handful of ammunition. The weapon starts in a random condition, with the saftey off or on, a round in the chamber, the hammer not cocked, or with an empty magazine.
The first step in Receiver, should always be get your weapon to condition one. Condition one being, loaded magazine in the weapon, round in the chamber, hammer cocked, and ready to kill drones. Drones are the enemies in this procedural world, of which there are two types. The flying taser drone, and the stationary turret drone. They beep when they are alerted to your presence, and beep again when they have lost sight of you.
Killing drones is easy and requires only one well placed shot. However, you may find yourself against multiple drones coming at you from multiple directions with nothing but quick reaction time and sheer luck to save your skin. Firing your weapon wildy at the drones homing in on you from above and behind your weapon clicks an empty chamber and you die.
You hadn't even gather or listened to a single tape. Dang. Perhaps better luck next time. There will always be the next time. You are now in a new room, unfamiliar and just as alone as the last time. Find your weapon, load a magazine, and chamber a round. Find the tapes. Kill the drones.
And stay woke.

Despite all the negative reviews here and on youtube, I have to say I disagree with a lot of them. I actually really love this game, I was instantly hooked from the beginning, turning off most of the HUD and just exploring and knowing that you are part of a dwindling resistance up against an army that overpowers you is so cool because you have something they don't, people.
You're progress in this game shows, from the city changing to you gathering more forces. The gunplay is fun, it can be quite crazy and strategic at times due to the fact that the enemy is better than you in almost every way, leaving you the only option of running, which isn't bad, because you will return and with a greater force. I didn't mind the story at all, sure it was average but thats ok, not every story needs to be a epic, not every story needs to be a great one, I can enjoy average. The graphics are pretty damn good, the gameplay is pretty good, I like the exploration too, the missions are fun as I really like the idea of being apart of a resistance and this game handles it pretty well. Despite all the faults, I can see the passion behind it. This game is nowhere near perfect, but I love this game, it just hit a cord with me. Perhaps its because I went in with not a lot of hope after seeing so many reviews.
All I can say was I was instantly immersed, it felt like a mixture of the last of us gameplay meets a bit of fallout 4 with a bit of call of duty.
Some cons?
Well, a few graphical bugs here and there.
The mouths of characters when they speak do not match with the voice acting most of the time.
The player does not speak, which normally isn't a bad thing, but the script of the game was done in such a way that it is more noticable and would gain a bit if the main character was able to speak.
Resistance mode is lacking. Instead of being a choose a stage/mission, I feel as though it should have been a fully open world experience like the singleplayer mode, although a bit more fleshed out and far more activities, as this game is a shooter, but I feel as it should be secondary as this game should and could have had far more important things to it. As I said above, I do believe immersion is something this game does well for what it is.
Overall, for 8 dollars you can't go wrong, give it a try.

We have all heard now plenty of times how this sim is in early access, and plenty of other user reviews have been negative tawords this new sim.
My personal opinion is that this sim is a very good starting base for Dovetails new flight simulator.
It actually has minimal bugs and runs very well on my system on ultra settings.
- Now I run an I7 6700k - GTX 970 and I get 60fps in most areas only dropping to 20fps around New York.
- I play it in windows mode and turn traffic off
Now obviously we are all hearing how this compares so far to the old FSX. Well in my case I have about $600 worth of addons for FSX and in that current state FSX cant be beaten. yet....
This sim in its vanilla state is a great start to the new successor to fsx as it has many more features out of the box than what fsx had. The default aircraft in this are a lot more advanced as is the graphics and default winds and weather. The plane reacts a lot more realistically when flying in severe weather. To have this level of detail in fsx you would need to purchase add ons.
A lot of users have complained about there being no commercial airliners or jets so far in the sim, but i think the way in which dovetail have only implemented GA aircraft is a much better way to test the sim and also forces users back to basics of flying.
The flying dynamicks have also been improved with the addition of accufeel and also the sounds of the sim seem to have been improved. Being able to see raindrops hitting the windscreen looks amazing. Ive never seen weather conditions look so good without a purchased add on.
Anyway I think this is a great starting base for the next gen flight sim. Dont expect it to beat fsx with all of its add ons and content, but in the near future once dovetail further enhance the sim and once third party developers get onboard, I think we may have an amazing flight sim that will last long into the future just as fsx did. Exceeded my expectations.

The game mechanics of this game are absolutely amazing. Hard to master at first, you will spend ages just staring at the help screen, wondering what kind of a madman created those keybindings (especially when using a different keyboard layout than the US).
But after a while, your fingers develop muscle memory. You start to automatically press the right buttons, even the most complicated key stroke sequences become intuition. This brings a profound sense of both accomplishment and control. This is the closest a pacifist like me will ever get to actually handling a gun.
The rest of the gameplay is accordingly simple. Explore a mace of procedurally generated rooms, shoot some turrets and run away screaming when one of the drones homes in on you.
In most games, the complicated gun mechanics would probably draw to much focus away from the game itself. But this game is an excellent example of how to get immersion right. Immersion is not about graphics, soundtracks or realism. Immersion is all about control.
TL;DR: Steep learning curve, totally worth it!

Probably the best digital card game currently.
The dev took the best of MTG but adapted some of the mechanics to fit the digital world. For example, cards keep their "counters" and other statuses when they go to the graveyard or are shuffled back to your deck or hand.
They also tried to make as fast paced as possible with a UI similar to Hearthstone, while still giving you a chance to react on the opponents turn. You do not have as many situations where you can react, but you can on the most important (when an opponent casts a spell, plays a creature, when blocking and blockers are declared and after the opponent's turn). That gives you a lot of options but still keeps the game flow smooth.
The land (mana) system is also a bit simplified in comparison to MTG. You have available power and influence over a color. You do not tap a land of a specific color, you spend power to play cards. But you need to have enough influence over a color to play some of the more powerful cards.
The free to play system is probably the best from what I've seen, the game gives you cards and gold constantly (literally every single win awards you with a chest that has at least one card and some gold). Also if you do a draft you get to keep the cards.
There's a lot of optional "vs AI" game modes (campaign, arena style draft and a gauntlet where you play increasingly more difficult AIs with the same deck for better and better rewards) for people who don't like playing vs other players or for testing out new decks.
TL;DR: The best of MTG mechanics brought to a digital world with a very generous F2P systems. Highly recommended.

Receiver is a perfect metaphor for life itself: harsh, unforgiving and complex to start, but also immensely rewarding to people who take the time to learn its ins and outs. Invariably stumbling to learn the controls for the seemingly simple act of reloading a sidearm, players who persist and perservere in mastering the controls soon find themselves experts at reloading. It feels like a major accomplishment to be able to reload each of the game's weapons from memory without looking at the keystrokes, and this leaves players free to begin tackling the game's task of finding the tapes, which itself is no easy feat. Death comes swiftly for the unaware, and even cautious players can lose everything in an instant. However, when success is reached, and the combination of weapons proficiency overlap with a game where things fall into play, one can collect all eleven tapes. Far more than any other game in my library, Receiver is a title that provides players with a sense of pride and accomplishment for gathering all the tapes in a single perfect run. My first victory came after thirty hours of time spent in this game: what's yours?

I played this game for a couple of hours before I returned it. I understand that it is an early access game, but it is literally FSX with some "polish". It's like they compliled some third party sceneries and effects from FSX, reboxed it, and changed the menus and logos.
The performance is the same as FSX, since it is FSX, and favors multicore hyperthreaded cpu's. I recommend at least a quad core with hyperthreading, so something like an i7. I have an i5 6600k with a GTX 1060 and was getting low 30's and high 20's on the ground, with about an average of 60+ fps in the air in 3440x1440.
The flight model does however feel a bit better than FSX. I noticed in some aircraft in this game you have a lot more rudder authority than their FSX counterparts. That being said; with the sliders on the most "realistic" settings, the p-factor and torque is way more exaggerated than they were in FSX.
A couple of the missions were fun to play, but the rest were just weird. For whatever reason they split them up into multiple parts. It'd have you take off, fly a few miles out, then it would abruptly and say "Mission Complete", prompting you to fly the next part.
Overall I do not recommend this game. Simply because it is literally FSX with less included aircraft,  subjectively better scenery (it looks like they only added more autogen scenery to me), and IMO a regression in the camera mechanism, for all the same price as FSX Steam Edition. Wait for their next sim. This is FSX, so it's still only 32 bit which means the same VAS issues as FSX.
I recommend you buy FSX Steam Edition instead of this if you don't already have it and you're looking at getting a good flight sim.

Played through one cycle, but haven't tried NG+ yet. Compared to the previous games in the series, the monster placement/quantity in some areas is punitive rather than challenging. There are certain points at which you'll be so overwhelmed that it feels "gimmicky" instead of challenging. On occasion, DS2:SOTFS crosses over the line from "tough but fair" like the predecessors, into unnecessarily cheap.
You'll also find bosses that play more like the DLC bosses from DS1 than the original DS1 bosses. Fast and hard-hitting attacks that almost always stagger you or break your guard when you block, as well as many many more unblockable attacks. There are also some environmental gimmicks (Flexile Sentry room flooding is one example) that make things more difficult. You have to shift your mentality from good timing with blocking to good timing with dodging.
It's fun overall, but certainly not as memorable as DS1. There are some memorable boss fights and areas (very impressive visuals in the Dragon Aerie/Dragon Shrine), but overall it doesn't leave as deep of an impression as DS1. Who can forget Quelaag, Sif, Smough/Ornstein, Crossbreed Priscilla, Moonlight Butterfly, and many others from DS1? I'm having a hard time remembering many from DS2:SOTFS, except a few that killed me repeatedly in questionable ways that caused more frustration than normal.
I ended up not bothering with the DLC areas and bosses. The ultimate weapons (boss weapons) are also nondescript compared to DS1, and I ended up using an upgraded Craftsman's Hammer for the vast majority of the game. There are some really impressive new spells though, compared to DS1. DS2:SOTFS gives you the impression that it was made for spellcasters and PvPers, which is good for those audiences. But I played for the complete package, which even by "Souls" standards is threadbare at best. The bosses mostly seem like an assortment of DS1 "cutting room floor" ideas that don't convey the same depth and continuity as the ones from DS1.
If you like the "Souls" games and get this for a discount during a special or sale, you'll have fun. It's not bad, it's just not as memorable as its predecessors. It gets off to a very slow start, and you'll find more interesting areas and bosses as you get deeper (more than halfway) through the game.
(For frame of reference: I've played Demons' Souls and Dark Souls 1 through multiple NG+ rounds each. I did not play vanilla (non-SOTFS) DS2.)

First of all, it's important to rememeber that this software has been released prior to being finished, hence the 'early access', so I consider it a beta version.
The fundamentals and familiarity are all there for those who are used to MS Flight Simulator. The same shortcuts seem to apply across the board, though there are not comprehensive instructions or prompts on all shortcuts and controls as yet so I found myself frantically trying to work them out in the air.
Many people have expressed issues with the frame refresh rate. The graphical details are fantastic, and just like MS Flight Simulator, the more detail you want, the refresh rate is impacted, however I can only assume that this will be a work in progress for Dovetail. After all, there's no joy in a cluncky flight sim, so it's in their best interest to trim it down wherever possible.
As yet, the only controls available are the mouse and the keyboard; I cannot work out how to get it to recognise my MS Sidewinder joystick.
Overall, I give this release a 6/10 remembering that it is unfinished, and there is plenty more to come, and I have no hesitation in expecting a much higher rating when the commercial release is available.

Outlast, like Portal, takes a simple premise and polishes it to the point where the game becomes an engrossing experience. Armed with only a HD nightvision camcorder, easily frayed nerves and the keen instincts of a journalist, you traverse an apparently abandoned asylum where you heard some weird stuff was going down.
Scary moments in Outlast go from spooky to downright frightening. The creepiness is ratcheted up way beyond Amnesia: The Dark Descent and that's only within the first fifteen minutes. Halfway through the game you're finding darkness by far the least scary thing this place has to offer.
The story is remarkably well told in class act horror scenes, along with notes and documents that characterise both you, the journalist, and other major figures in the asylum. Pacing in this game never fatigues you, instead, you might find yourself having to quit the game every half hour with being too terrified to continue. I know I was quitting and removing my headphones from the intensity.
You rely on nightvision in the HD camcorder to navigate the darkness. This could have easily turned into a gimmick, but Outlast makes the camcorder your only companion in this nightmare and your only hope of getting past. Outlast uses the 'found footage' horror genre better than Paranormal Activity, better than Cloverfield and I'd view the game on par with the Blair Witch Project.
Disturbing, chilling, full of dread and mystery, Outlast is a rollercoaster of a game that should be played if you fancy yourself having the courage to face the truly frightening.

Wow, just wow. I have had my eye on this series but since the first installement seemed too much of a dungeon crawler, I didn't end up bying it. Now got this from the humblebundle and had to play it from start to finish in just few days. Although I consider myself a gaming veteran this genre is totally unknown to me. So for me everything was pretty much new. For me the closest thing that is anything similar would be Dark Souls with a touch of Baldur's Gate.
I started the game with premaid party and normal difficulty. Turned out to be the just right option for me as the game was challenging from start to finish although it never had moments where I felt that I couldn't get forward without leveling. LoG2 is basically a grid based action rpg, where you guide 4 man group in a hostile island. Island's master taunts you in every turn to beat his monsters and puzzles. The game is a hybrid of sandbox and tunnel, most areas have a clear starting point and path from there to finish, yet one can visit most of the areas in any order. There is a certain lack of interaction with the world, meaning there are no characters to talk to or dialogue. There are random pieces of information scattered all over the island that helps with puzzles, finding treasures or taking the next step to completing the mystery.
As one can see from the screenshots, the game looks stunning and has atmosphere in almost all levels. Although the island is a very hostile place, it never feels as unwelcoming as in Dark Souls. Clearing enemies guarantees some peace for a time and there's rarely any rush to explore or go forward. Because the game is gridbased it gives a player certain guarantee that quite many dead ends and awkward corners actually contain something valuable. And since there are no excess of stuff in game apart from late game, one feels compelled to search every corner and try to figure out even the vaguest of puzzles.
In a sense the game sucks you into the world just by being interesting. Although some might argue that without any narration and clear direction the game is too open, I say that it is exactly the reason that kept me going forward, just like Dark Souls. The loot is interesting, varied(although hardly exciting) and actually quite rare. Although the game gives the player a decent amount of stuff to handle, it feels like that most of the items could've been useful if my characters were different or I had arrived there earlier. There are no stores or shops and almost no respawning items, so one cannot just spend stuff because the situation needs it. The more sensible way is to play the situation again and try to beat it with better solution. So unlike most of the current generation RPGs where loot is abundant and totally redundant, this game makes you go after it even though it might hamper you by losing some items most likely needed later in game.
Like I said, the items are oddly boring, and so are the characters. Although I used premade, there isn't too many options to make it different enough to play it again any time soon. Items are mostly just "axe, sword, bow" with different stats, and even the special items are somewhat lacking or "too special", meaning one must drag that dispel dagger with you unless you know the secret of dispel spell. I would like to see more imagination put into the weapons and items in game, so that there would have to be a real building of a balanced group. Now I could just take the best items and forget most spells. Most enemies take damage from all sources, apart from some elementals. So basically taking the best sword or axe is enough.
The game is puzzle heavy, if these are not your thing, you're not going to enjoy the game much. Most areas contain multiple puzzles to crack and most of the time tips to solving are scarce or vague. For me this was the biggest flaw. Although most of the puzzles were interesting and challenging there was just too many pressureplates and hidden buttons. I ended up watching too much of the same wall textures just to find a secret button to secret room or throwing rocks in certain order to pressure plates. In the end it felt somewhat tedious. Some puzzles had clues way too far away to make any sense and considering the fact that moving in this game isn't exactly fast and consumes precious food, I felt compelled occasionally to skip solving the mystery. Towards the end I started using walkthrough to 'skip' some of the more vague puzzles(under under over and all over again) and to get few achievements.
Another problem is something that is a problem in most of the rpg and action rpg games. The mechanics are not explained. It would be fine if this was real world, but these games have different rules and finding out what works and what does not, takes too much time even before we can actually solve the puzzle. So basically few puzzles are not about finding the solution but finding the key mechanic that hasn't been introduced before. This is mostly because they want you to play the game and then play it again knowing most of the stuff, but that's not the case these days. Most games are not played again, so I would like to have a full experience without going to some wiki to find out what is actually what and how it works. Although this game is a lot clearer than most, I still had to go check how wizardry was supposed to work, after using 100 times the fire spell and nothing else.
What I found odd was the fact that although being a gridbased game, the game acts in real time. This gives the player a huge advantage over the enemies who rarely knows sidestepping and seem somewhat playing with turn based rules(as if taking turns while the player does not). I found this a weird design choice although it worked in making the situations feel more urgent. I actually most of the time just decided to stand there and take the beating rather than dancing around the enemy and hitting him from the side just because it felt like fairer for the enemy. Although there are moments where multiple(Even dozens) enemies are coming at you one rarely loses control because the grid gives option to tunnel the enemies into something more manageable.
Even with these flaws I felt I'm not going to play anything similar and as good as this one until they come up with LoG3. Definately one of the best games I've played this year, although I feel like I exhausted the mechanic for some time now and might not return to the Island until the third one.

I picked it up without any familiarity to the series.  It's basically a mashup between an old-school square based dungeon crawler and a point-and-click adventure game.
Things to note: there are zero visual indicators that anything is important, or that you can interact with anything.  You have 4 "party" members, that all occupy the same square except that their position in the party dictates whether they can or cannot interact with things.
The game starts with one of the characters highlighted and basically no indication of what to do (pick up the stick).  However, if you're foolish enough to drop the stick in the hands that are highlighted (or were highlighted when I started the game) you can't actually hit the door - because you're too far away from it.  Had to watch a tutorial video to hit a door with a stick, because the mechanics of party positioning and item usage are left to you to figure out.
My wizard died before I escaped the cage, because I had the audacity to click some of my buttons (that have no readout or description as to what they are or do).
If you enjoyed older games where you had to click everything on the screen to find something that moves, this is one of those.  Looking around doesn't serve much purpose, since after you release the look button your return immediately to a centered view.  Trying to move where you can't will cause a motion bump - this and the terrible look system will both induce motion sickness if you suffer from it.
When I was younger, I enjoyed games like this because there seemed to be a lot of "mystery".  As I've grown more familiar with game design, I've come to realize that this is really just a disguise for a poor, unintuitive layout that eats time via having the user search for interaction.
If you want to customize your character, be prepared to play Dungeons and Dragons (TM).  Every character has a sheet with 15-20 skills, a handful of which will get just a couple of points, a few traits and other things that you can pick from.  The classes are thoroughly uninspiring.  Wizard, fighter, fighter wizard.  Don't forget the rogue!
I'm sure there are plenty of interesting things to play with in the spells system and lots of things to discover, if you just click enough.

I want to give a concise, effective, and interesting review of Gone Home, but I'm not sure I can do it.
Do I like it? Yes. Why? Well, that's not so simple.
Technically, this game is fairly unremarkable. The graphics are fine, the controls are so simple that it would have been a feat to screw them up, the music does its job properly but doesn't amaze. To be honest, that's by and large how it goes - every component of the game is perfectly sufficient to do its job but fails to go above and beyond what is expected.
The sole exception to that, from a technical standpoint, is the level design. While it all takes place in one "level," the house that is the setting is masterfully designed to direct the player towards the next step of the journey while never feeling too restrictive. It directs the player in a linear experience while feeling like it is the player themself who is deciding where to go next (with a few notable, but natural exceptions).
Of course, this is a story-driven game, so the technical aspects might be considered secondary for its appeal, but even there I am not as completely and utterly amazed as some reviewers have been. The story itself is good, and the way its told is interesting and novel. It is this narrative delivery (something that is inextricably tied to the aforementioend level design) that deserves the most praise.
Unfortunately, a narrative delivery mechanism alone is not enough to carry a game, and while the narrative it delivers is good, it left me wanting. I got the sense that when I reached the end of the game, what I had really reached was the end of the first act of a bigger story. I appreciate the attempt for an open-ended narrative, but I felt that much of the most interesting content in the story was what happened next. This disappointed me.
Of course, when the biggest quibble is that there isn't enough of something, obviously whatever is happening, it's doing something right. So, overall, yes, I would recommend this game. Specifically, I recommend it to people who enjoy exploration narratives with a heavy character focus, clever design, and impressive atmosphere. If you're looking for engaging gameplay, epic story, massive worlds, or anything besides an interesting, small story, do not look here, because you will be left wanting. If however, you come to this seeking a small piece of beautiful, understandable, relatable humanity, give Gone Home a try.

I was surprised by how much I enjoyed this game. I'm also surprised by how much I LEARNED from this game. For instance: did you know that when cooking in a restaurant, you only have one single shot at ANY order to get it right? I didn't know that! I thought I could throw it away and start over! Not so! Here are a few other free lessons before you open your own restaurant.
1- Customers are impatient jerks. If you can't cook and put together a burger within 30 seconds they are OUTTA THERE.
2- Customers are also not an understanding bunch. "Just get robbed? TS, idiot, give me my burger!"
3- When you become successful and start earning some decent money, you can still never hire employees to take care of trash and dishes or serve food. Like a real restaurant! It's all you, buddy! No employees, no payroll! Screw those guys! People want to eat food prepared by the person who cleans dishes, throws out garbage, and sets rat traps, anyway, just like the pros!
4- A secret clan of ninja cooks exist. I now fear for my life.
Those are a few of the things you'll learn about cooking. I've also greatly expanded my cooking skills in real life, too. When I'm trying to prepare a potato, for instance, I'm pressing "1" over and over again but it doesn't start baking. Eventually someone feels sorry for me and puts the potato in the oven. Success.
I've had less success eating out, however, because of this game, sadly. The waiter kept asking what I want and since I was confused why I wasn't talking to the chef, I just kept looking around the place, wondering if other people were being harassed by this guy, too. Evidently he was annoying EVERYBODY because they were too shy or scared to even look at me and were eating or drinking their single item they could order. I played along and just wrote on a piece of paper that I wanted a burger with "L", "C", and "T" with a couple of "P". He pretended to be all confused and I insisted he take it to the chef. He came back about 10 minutes later with a leek, cabbage, truffles, and pubic hair burger. Success.
All in all, this is a great game worth your time. Play it as fast as you can before the ninjas test your karate baking skill.

Overall this sim is a modest improvement compared to FSX. However, with the sim currently in the early access stage of development, I would expect in the coming years for this sim to easily surpass FSX. At the moment there are quite a few glitches or things that don't appear to be finished yet, but so far so good.
If you were a fan of the default FSX autogen then this sim is sure to please. Airports and autogen buildings look pretty similar compared to stock FSX. What has been significantly improved however, are the ground textures, which I believe are from FTX Global. The road system is much better as well, but cars only seem to drive on major interstates, even with traffic on ultra. The only major problem with the scenery at this time is the night textures. When flying at night, the ground textures are almost completely black, making the buildings and roads seem to float above the ground. I expect this will be fixed in an update soon, but right now flying is basically restricted to daytime.
The stock aircraft are simply amazing. They are payware quality planes, with high quality textures and LOTS of attention to detail. The overall model of the aircrafts are very nice, with beautiful animation, such as a rotating beacon lights. I think there are multiple textures for each of the default planes, but I haven't figured out how to access them from the menu yet. While the outside is nice, the virtual cockpit is clearly where most of the time and resources went. You can press almost every button, and it actually does something, unlike stock FSX aircraft. Shadows that move across the cockpit when turning are also a nice touch, but they aren't even the best feature. For me at least, the best and coolest feature is the vibrations in the cockpit. Everything from the sun visors to the needles on the gauges vibrate. Overall the stock aircraft are fantastic, but only GA, no airliners. Hopefully jets will be included in future updates, as at the time their absence would be my only complaint about
Currently it seems weather has only received minor improvements. The sky textures seem pretty realistic, so no real complaints there. Clouds are a little overly white, and look a little washed out, especially the cumulous clouds. Storms are okay, my only complaint would be the lightning, as it seems to still use the crappy FSX lightning textures. The default weather scenarios are similar to the default FSX ones, with a few new additions. At this time I don’t think live weather is an option, so hopefully that will be included in a future update.
One amazing feature that has been added is the raindrop effect on the windshield of the virtual cockpit. It is very realistic, and the drops move with varying speed depending on the speed of the aircraft. Flying in the rain is very enjoyable because of this. I would be willing to bet this is one of the few 100% finished features of the game.
I haven’t experienced too much lag on my system with settings ranging from high to ultra. I am currently running an AMD FX-8320 (4 Ghz) and a GTX 750 with 8 gb of ram. Obviously FPS will not be as good at LAX during a thunderstorm, but most of the time the sim ran smoothly with an occasional stutter. Overall it seems to be a modest improvement on FSX.
Dovetail is seems to have built a very solid platform to expand upon. While the sim is decent as is, there are a few things I’d like to see added such as: updated rivers/coastlines (Or at least smooth out the existing data, as most water features don’t have 45-90 degree angles), jets, ability to start at specific gates, LIVE WEATHER UPDATES, improved autogen around the world and at airports, more cars both at airports and on the road, and probably most important BETTER NIGHT TEXTURES.
All in all for the price, this sim is an incredible value. It isn’t perfect yet and it shouldn’t be, that’s what early access is for. I would recommend this for anyone who doesn’t have a heavily modded X-Plane or FSX, and anyone new looking to try out a flight simulator. If you have a heavily modded flight sim already right now at least, Flight Sim World will probably be a step down (I expect this to change with future updates). This sim has a lot of potential though, and with continued support, updates, and a bit of patience, this could be the successor to FSX we’ve been waiting for.

My negative rating isn't really a knock against the game, but rather the disaster that is Windows 10. The two Telltale-developed Bone point-and-click adventures don't play nice with Microsoft's latest muck up.
1) Both Bone games crash unless you delete prefs.prop from each directory.
2) The games will continue to crash if fullscreen mode is selected.
3) Resolution settings are limited, meaning -- depending on your screen size and resolution -- the window is nigh unplayable.
3b) To solve this, a third-party application needs to be downloaded
.
Finally, I was able to start and play the game. I love how it captured the look and spirit of the Bone comic series, one of my all-time favourites. The interface and movements are significantly clunkier than in modern Telltale games, so definitely take that under advisement.
After a while, I decided to save and quit. The reason? I found that Steam's screenshot tool wasn't working, possibly due to the custom resolution tool, and I enjoy snapping shots of my games. Anyhow, I reset the resolution and booted the game up again.
It couldn't find my save.
At that point, I decided enough was enough. I really do think that the games, at least an hour in, respect the source material. Unfortunately, I may never know if that continues. Seeing as I doubt this game will ever be patched to play nice with this awful operation system (after all, it's not like Steam is GOG -- they don't care), I simply have to rate it down and move on. Maybe, just maybe, I'll be able to play it again someday but I'm not holding my breath.
I guess I'll just read the comic again when I need to get my fix for Jeff Smith's wonderful characters, story, and world. Sigh...

If you really want to know about this game, you should read my review.
I have played plenty of games but this is the only game I have ever chose to be the first game I would write a review for. That is because I support this game and wish to see it explode more into popularity yet I still will describe some concerns that Eternal needs to address.
If you are an avid card game fanatic, this is the card game that you have been looking for. I have played over 40 different card games besides other genres, of which all the card game titles are the major ones in the market, and this one stands above the rest. It is indeed a baby child of Magic the Gathering and Hearthstone combined, but more MtG than HS. This is what people with a high intellect have been looking for, over the child's game of RNG and non-critical thinking that is of HS. This is also the copyright-safe version of what MtG Online should of been but cheaper and more F2P (free to play) friendly if you can invest a lot of time. This game is designed by Direwood Digital with the help of some famous Magic the Gathering celebrities such as Luis Scott Vargas and others. Overall, it's a very high quality and polished game in terms of card mechanics.
To address the concerns of a larger deck size that some people don't understand is that, when you play a card game, you want replayability and each game to feel different than the one before per person you verse. If you have a smaller minimum deck size, you will be playing with the same cards over and over, have fewer selections for card choice, and each matchup will be too consistent and boring. Also, you will not see deck variety and only 1 or 2 decks will be tier 1 and trump over the rest. In the beginning when I first started, I too thought 75 card minimum was too much until I spent over 750 hours in the game, climbed to top 100 masters in both ranked and draft and understood the mentioned reasons for such a necessity. The 75 deck size is perfect for keeping the game feeling fresh which was a problem that I felt was always a repeated offense in other card games. In addition, more opportunity for card selection and avoidance of overwhelming repeated card consistency prevents infinite combos and hyper-aggro all-in decks for a full on brainless hit face aggression (smorc) that anyone with an IQ over 20 would not want to face against.
To address the concern of being power screwed, I completely agree. Getting screwed when you don't get your power source or being overflooded completely sucks, but I foresee the Direwood Devs to address this issue further along the line because they have an excellent dev to player connection. There is a feedback button in game that lets you input your comments and thoughts for review. Being power screwed happens less in constructed in contrast to draft, which is more frequent where you get flooded with, or completely deprived of power. But when it does happen, it's brutal. Nothing is worse than losing due to power screw. This is one aspect from MtG that Eternal definitely and strongly should NOT have taken with them, but instead, should have been improved upon. Perhaps they will design cards that help with power consistencies in the future. Right now it is really painful and might cause players to be left with a distasteful approach about the game left in the mouth.
In addition, today, March 30th 2017, they upgraded to a better mulligan system for initial hand draws but we will have to see of its fruitfulness, but it does not address progressive power screw problems after the 7 card hand.
My biggest concern of to date is; as any card game, it needs a large card base to increase creativity, interactions, and variety. One of the positives of MtG is that their card base is huge, which makes the game extremely diverse and enjoyable. Hearthstone also has the model of very frequently releasing new sets to keep the game fresh. Eternal is missing this aspect and is still stuck on the first set, but the game is still in BETA. The best model would be a new set every 3-4 months, as I am feeling bored from just two months with the collection, with a lot of players just stop playing in  anticipation for a new set. I foresee that once the card base is as diverse as MtG, this game will be the best card game in existence.
Pros:
Complex and requires IQ to play
Almost no RNG in the card text
Each versus game feels fresh instead of droning the same cards/combos over and over
Free to play friendly if you can invest time
Not pay to win
You get to keep the cards in drafting
Player interaction of cards and card text is the most important thing in any card game which allows decision making and variety
User interface flows smoothly while retaining response windows
Phone/tablet compability
Excellent community, fan-based tournaments, reddit page, and fan websites/database
Cons:
Huge problem with power draws of unfortunate RNG
Still in beta and infrequent release of card sets
Small card base; therefore, nowhere as diverse for complexity, strategy, and variety
You cannot infinitely draft for free as drafting does not allow you to reuse packs as entry fee and gold rewards only pay back for your drafting fee if you 7-x max win
No official tournaments, therefore no sideboards (sideboarding is only necessary if there are matches)
In addition, some of the most important things to a successful card game from my experience is:
1. Replay value - (Each game feeling unique and therefore, not boring, is the best RNG aspect for a card game)
2. Large card base - (Allows diversity, creativity, complexity, and strategy)
3. Card text interaction - (Most important thing in any card game is allowing player decisions within the match that decides wins or losses and game variety, two players can run the same deck, but the better player makes the better decisions)
4. Free to play - (Allows the game to be popular and kept alive)
5. E-Sports Viability - (Tournament value for rewarding good players makes a game explode)

Best online card game I've played. Simple and intuitive ui like games like hearthstone, and depth and strategic diversity like games like Magic the Gathering. This is what I've always wanted in a card game and it's one of the first ones that's genuinely reasonable to play FTP. There are tons of budget options for decks that, while maybe not good enough for Master Tier, will get you plenty of ranked game wins or wins in the gauntlet (a game mode that is against AI). On top of that there are 4 super fun diverse game modes: Ranked, Gauntlet, Forge, and Draft that allow you to play however you want.
Draft mode is very similar to the MTG drafting system for those looking for something in that vein, where you open a pack of 12 cards, take one and pass it, and repeat that. In this mode you get a total of 4 packs opened and passed, and you get to keep ALL CARDS YOU DRAFT! Not only that but you can win rewards up to 3 packs and 6K gold (for 7 wins) which is more than the gold it takes to enter in the first place. This allows good players to grow their collection without putting in any money.
Forge is similar to Hearthstone's Arena. You get 45 "pick 1 of 3" options and then play games with the cards you picked. Again you get to keep all cards you draft, and you get additional rewards at the end based on performance. The one big difference is that this is against AI, so it's a bit easier to get 7 wins than in draft (though the rewards are less).
Gauntlet is a mode played with preconstructed decks. These decks can contain any cards you have in your collection. It is played against prebuilt AI decks that can actually be somewhat challenging (for an AI opponent). You can unlock rewards in this mode as well.
Ranked is the mainstay of any online game, and is where you go to pit your best decks against other players. While the level of competition is much higher here, I've been able to win a considerable number of games without any legendaries in the deck, and with few rares. As my collection grew I obviously began building decks with the cards that were most interesting to me (which often included rares and legendaries of course) but I certainly go back and play my budget common/uncommon decks just for fun.
Overall if you are looking for an online card game to try out, I would definitely give this one a go. The biggest key to trying it out is to make sure to play at least a few games after you finish the tutorial campaign, as the campaign is a very preliminary look at the mechanics, and you won't get a true feel for the depth until you've played some of your own decks.

The controls are WASD (or the arrows) for moving left and right and the space bar for flipping gravity, which is the only gameplay mechanic. What makes the game difficult is the fact that you can only flip gravity when you land on a platform, not in mid-air, so you have to be able to react quickly. Around each level are frequent checkpoints that allow you to respawn when you die, making this game a lot less frustrating.
The level design is pretty well done, and the soundtrack fits the game nicely. The game is not too difficult, and can be completed in just a few hours. Overall a great game providing a few hours' worth of fun.

Gone Home is a wonderful small gem among such game genres. The voice acting is really good and more often that not I just stopped playing to properly listen to the narrator. It's described as a Walking Simulator in the tags, but I would describe it more of Exploration than that. The best thing about this game is that there is no set path per se; you can start at any point of the house you wish and go from there. While the story is linear, or better understood as such, you can have fun with the game and go off the beaten path; the ending will still be the same no matter what.
Speaking of the story, it was a stunning story that even today can be considered modern. I loved how it developed and I loved how it was presented. To make things even better, the narrator fills the criteria needed to make it as realistic as possible.
I was impressed by the sheer details of the game and the work that was put into to make the atmosphere feel like the 90s. Every corner of the house hit me like a nostalgia truck and it never grew old for me. The graphics have aged well and the gameplay was right what this game needed, just a Point and Click without complicating what you really need to do.
However, if you are thinking of spending a lot of hours in this game, you will be greatly mistaken. Even if you take your sweet time with it, you can clear it under 2 hours with ease. In fact, you will discover this after you finish the game, but you can actually clear the game in literally under 1 minute.
The only thing I disliked however wasn't how short the game was, or other bugs I found while I was playing; the game itself was just so good that I could forgive them. However asking 20 euros for this is just way too much. The price ratio for the time you will be playing the game is just not worth it. Wait for a Sale to get this one. However, you should get it when you have the chance, it's too good to just pass it!
TLDR
PROS
+ Fantastic Story
+ True 90s Atmosphere
+ Great Voice Acting/Narration
CONS
- Short Game
- Zero Replaybility
- Too expensive
