Gone Home is one of the best examples of the walking simulator genre. It has a single story it wants to tell, and it tells it well. More importantly, however, it sets up an atmosphere and a world that is worth exploring every nook and cranny to get as many details as possible. While there's one overarching story, there are plenty of side stories that all add depth to these characters and their relationships with each other. These character moments cover the whole emotional spectrum: I often found myself laughing one minute at a silly detail that made the characters very real in my mind, only to feel heartbroken minutes later by one of the background stories and the context it brings to the whole venture. I won't bring up any particular story moments since this game is best explored without any knowledge of what to expect, but I will say that every additional detail you find is rewarding. Completionists will find an extra level of depth that makes the experience feel satisfying.
When I played this game, I was living abroad in Scotland for University. The story of our protagonist coming home from school only to find the house empty and having to put together the details for herself...yeah, that hit me. I carried myself into the game, and I was rewarded for it with a story I still remember years later. If you enjoy this style of game, do yourself a favor and get it already. It's absolutely worth it.

After little flying on FSW (early access) here are my following pro's and con's and what can be worked and improved on:
Pros:
1. The Graphics are Amazing! Including: Scenery and Aircrafts etc. (GREAT JOB!!!)
2. The interface is very simple and way to access things.
3. Being able to create flight plans and set home base airport on the map is pretty cool.
4. The weather themes are very nice.
5. ORBX did a great job and making the scenery look really nice and detailed.
6. The raindrops on the windows of the aircrafts are very realistic and make it more real when flying in real-life.
7. The flying dynamics of the aircrafts are pretty descent not bad at all.
8. Flying on Multiplayer interface is really good.
Cons:
1. The ATC needs improvement, and more realistic interface.
2. The lighting of the sun at the airport grounds (somewhat) is overpowering.
3. Starting at a runway not a gate or parking should be choosen by the player.
4. Some gauges and autopilot needs to be worked and doesn't work at all in some aicrafts when setting ALT, VS and etc.
5. Not be able to go into my settings while flying (display, traffic, etc).
What needs to be worked on or improved:
1. FSW needs "advacement" settings for people to set the scenery the way they want to not just low, med-high, high etc.
2. ATC needs a lot improvements sounds to slow and needs to be more clear.
3. Need to be able to allow to add FSX aircrafts to the simulator (which I looked inside the installer files and looks very much the same as the Steam Edition).
4. The raindrops effects can take a framerate hit if that could be fixed to make it more FPS friendly that would be awesome!
5. Being able to have updated SIDS and STARS, Airport Charts etc. like real pilots use for HIGH ALT AIRWAYS AND LOW ALT AIRWAYS would be great on the maps when creating flight plans on the map (not just direct).
6. Adding more aircrafts in the near future.
7. I heard the DTG is working on a better weather interface so I'm hoping to better and more realistic as for METARS and ATIS.
8. Default airport textures, clouds, sun etc. could be better (maybe partner with REX Simulations in the near future?) to make it more FPS Friendly.
So overall as far FSW goes as early acess not bad at all for the price! A lot people need to understand this just an early access and I believe DTG is working very hard to listen to the community and what we want and to make improvements and adjustments and to fix bugs. I really believe DTG would make sure that they will take the suggestions above very seriously and work hard to make it happen. As for me personally, FSW still needs a lot worked to be done before I switch from Steam Edition but overal I'm very impressed with the worked that has already been done to FSW and I can't wait for what the future holds for FSW!
So do I recommend this game? Yes, very much so, as it being early access!

Receiver is something like an infiltration mission with the Matrix-like backstory (If that's what you want to call it.  It barely has story at all.)  The game is incredibly fun and difficult if you get caught in a bad situation.  There is no difficulty levels, just one solid playthrough with the objective to collect 11 recorded tapes.  (Note : I have yet to beat this game.)  Though the game is fun, it does not exempt it from the problems at hand.
The game is fun and VERY challenging.  You can shoot down sentries and drones with ease and progress to the next tape relatively easy.  The positioning of the sentries and drones can catch you off guard sometimes.  Therefore, I can not stress how important it is for you to CHECK YOUR CORNERS when playing this game.  You can EASILY be taken down in one shot by the sentries or tased by the Taser Drone.  The easiest way to deal with the drones is to clear some distance between you and the drone so that you have time to peek back around and fire more rounds at it.  The necessity of these drones are important because they can scare you into sentry guns which, in turn, will gun you down.
I find the controls entirely too clunky.  I love the ammo management system, however, I find it incredibly annoying having to constantly cycle my hotbar of items to load rounds in, remove magazines, insert magazines, etc.  I feel like that is entirely way too much to be working with.  It would honestly be better if I could just click one button and it would unload the current magazine in my gun so that I can cycle to the next magazine on my hotbar and reload that magazine back into my gun.  Instead of making this complicated system of clicking back and forth on my keyboard, you could make it a couple keystrokes shorter.  There is also no keybind settings so you are stuck with a static set of controls the game gives you.  As for the Sentries, I find it cheesy that you can sit around a corner and take pot shots at the Sentry without it being able to retaliate.  I find drones also have a problems getting through doorways to give me chase as I can easily lose them by transitioning from outside to indoors.
I have to say the most annoying things in the game (for me) is the hotbar.  It's so cumbersome on the screen and it's incredibly annoying.  At least put it lower on the character like in most VR games.  Having a magazine constantly in your view as your trying to find/avoid enemies is SO DAMN ANNOYING.  Also, falling to your death is EASY and ridiculous.  You can fall 5 feet in this game and suddenly both your ankles are broken, your knees are folded inward, and both your femurs are annihilated.  Just.  By.  Falling.  5.  Feet.  Having to mash the W key just to run is such a stupid idea as well.

I think the main problem with this game and the mixed feelings in the reviews is the expectation created by Dovetail. I think if Dovetail had been more honest, people would have reacted differently.
Why did you promote this game as a "next generation" or "major breakthrough" in flight simulation? It's not.
Dovetail website reads "Dovetail Games has signed a global licensing deal with Microsoft, granting exclusive rights to develop and publish all-new flight simulation products based on Microsoft’s genre-defining technology".
And that's what you'll find in this game: an improved version of FSX, with the same guts, same menus, same general feeling. Basically FSX with a new GUI, ORBX terrain, AccuFeel, and a few payware-quality General Aviation model planes.
So if you already have FSX and a few add-ons, I think you will be disappointed. Especially because  you'll still miss things, like jets. That being said, Dovetail did a great job. And the price is terrific. For the price you are basically getting a "General Aviation FSX on steroids", so I would totally recommend it to new simmers.
As general feedback and as a software engineer, it really worries me the path that flight simulators are taking. We are now requiring users to buy a PC with a 4GHz CPU and a $500 dedicated GPU or otherwise "they might not have a good experience". However, I can run FSX completely maxed out at 1440p with add-on weather, add-on terrain, add-on airport, add-on plane, peripherals, an external program for ATC on a... 1.6GHz i5 NUC with Intel integrated graphics!!! It runs smooth and provides a great flight simulation experience.
Honestly, what is going on? I thought all the bragging about using "64-bits", "completely rewritten", "new libraries", etc... would actually at least mean much better performance. But it's just the opposite. Now you need much better hardware to get a worse experience.
I think the efforts are going in the wrong direction. How come are we still pressing keys and listening to robotic voices for ATC, when wecan ask Siri, Alexa or Google anything on a $100 phone?
Bottom line. This is a great game for the price, especially if you are new. Unfortunately, there has been no breakthrough and the flight simulator scene has stayed where it was. But now you need ultra-powerful hardware if you want to be part of it.

After spending about 90 minutes playing with Dovetail Games latest Flight Simulator released for early access, I figured I’d take a moment to set my thoughts down in writing.
Flight Sim World Issues
1.	Default fair weather scenery is blindingly bright.  Need a method to configure lighting.
2.	AI ATC is a step backwards from FSX.  Just leave the AI ATC alone.  What came with FSX is good enough.
3.	The weather engine needs more work.  Currently, It’s fine.  But we need to be able to fly real world weather (i.e. download from Metar service and inject into simulator).  Also, we need to be able to configure weather to a specific set of METAR conditions.
4.	The user Interface is good, but can get confusing
a.	Don’t assume everyone knows sliders to left means low and sliders to right means high.  Need to document this better.
b.	When loading, we need  %complete meter to get an idea of loading status
c.	Don’t make flight planning a requirement in order to do a flight.  Most of us do our flight planning outside the sim anyways.
d.	For aircraft realism, make default max realism.
5.	Need a fly now button at the home page.  All simulators back in the day had a fly now feature for folks to anxious to get started.  Just drop them in the cockpit (select random plane) at the runway of their home airport with engine running.
6.	Need to be able to swap out aircraft while in the simulator (on the ground or in flight).  Currently, you have to end your mission to swap out the planes.
7.	The trim setting is way too un-sensitive.  I have to hold down the button I map to trim up or down for several seconds before the trim responds.
8.	When you start a flight, the simulator places you at the foot of the runway at the airport you selected.  For most of my flights, I prefer to start at the ramp.  Please don’t remove that option.
What I liked
1.	The stock aircraft are very good.  Not great.  But very good.  I was expecting the texture and alpha numeric schemes to be a lot sharper – but I like the default aircrafts.  More than what I was expecting.
2.	The flight dynamics appear spot on.  The planes felt real, and not cartoonish.
3.	The fact that everything was modeled in the GA aircraft shows attention to detail.  Loved that.
4.	The rain effect on the glass is fantastic.
5.	Load times were good.  Didn’t have to wait to get going.
What I would like to see:
1.	I would like to see a basic instructor station implemented.  Checkout Luis Gordo’s implementation of his instructor station software.  Something to consider for the long term?  After all, what good is a simulator if you’re not challenged?
2.	Shared cockpit for the stock GA aircraft.
3.	ATC controller – That came out of the box with FSX, didn’t it?
Potential Show Stopper – Frame Rates
Another youtuber who didn’t have the time to do a complete evaluation simply fired up xplane 11 set all the sliders to max, took a screen shot.  Then he fired up FSW with everything on Max, took a screen shot and compared the two .  Xplane frames was 35 fps.  FSW frames was 12.  And he was running a decent rig with Nvidia 1080 Graphics card.  Why is this a show stopper?  Simple.  There are folks out there still running FS9 for the sole reason that they get great frames.  People spend hundreds of dollars and many hours tinkering  with their sim and Operating System to get the max frames.  That FSW out of the box gives no noticeable increase in frame rate is going to turn off a lot of people.
Final Report.
First thing to remember is FSW is an early release product.  DTG is new to Flight Simulator development business, so as a community we have a duty to provide constructive feedback, exercise patience, and give them a chance to right the ship.  Many will compare FSW to Xplane or P3D.  That is not a fair comparison.  Lockheed Martin and Laminar Research had many years to refine their products, whereas DTG is just getting started.
I recommend DTG developers spend a few hours flying P3D, Xplane, and Aerofly  to determine their best in practice features and capabilities – then implement them in FSW.  Good artists copy, great artists steal.
In the meantime, I’m going to be doing my part to help DTG move the sim along by playing it and providing feedback.  So far, I think they have done a great job, and I’m excited by it potential and future prospects.

Great couch co-op game. I enjoyed the alpha builds a lot, and the addition of online play, more maps and characters, and new mechanics like ice and sticking stuff together has just made it better.

The bad:
- I really wanted to see the singleplayer mode that was teased in an early trailer. Shame.
- (Minor) The alpha build had stronger walljumping which allowed for some skilled maneuvers, so I was a bit miffed to discover that the full release nerfed walljumping a bit.

Telltale's first adventure game is a fairly short, graphically charming game which is clearly aimed at children. The humour would appeal to young kids and the puzzles are pretty easy. The minigames can be skipped if anyone finds them too difficult. It's not a great game, but it's not terrible either. Others have mentioned bugs, but apart from two moments of silence when characters should have been speaking, I didn't encounter any.
The pace of the game is quite slow, characters move ponderously and dialogue can't be skipped. For a point and click adventure there aren't that many things to click on. There are very few objects to find and even fewer puzzles that require using those objects. The game is mainly dialogue driven with lots of talking and is very linear, interspersed with set piece games and puzzles. These are quite simplistic and frankly I found them rather tedious, although kids would probably enjoy them.
I would not recommend this game for adults, but I would recommend it for the audience it was clearly intended for, young children.
EDIT: It's not obvious from the title, but this game is Act 1 of a two part series. The Great Cow Race is Act 2, so they should be played in order. Unfortunately the story is not complete, they should have made more episodes but didn't.

Best online card game I've played. Simple and intuitive ui like games like hearthstone, and depth and strategic diversity like games like Magic the Gathering. This is what I've always wanted in a card game and it's one of the first ones that's genuinely reasonable to play FTP. There are tons of budget options for decks that, while maybe not good enough for Master Tier, will get you plenty of ranked game wins or wins in the gauntlet (a game mode that is against AI). On top of that there are 4 super fun diverse game modes: Ranked, Gauntlet, Forge, and Draft that allow you to play however you want.
Draft mode is very similar to the MTG drafting system for those looking for something in that vein, where you open a pack of 12 cards, take one and pass it, and repeat that. In this mode you get a total of 4 packs opened and passed, and you get to keep ALL CARDS YOU DRAFT! Not only that but you can win rewards up to 3 packs and 6K gold (for 7 wins) which is more than the gold it takes to enter in the first place. This allows good players to grow their collection without putting in any money.
Forge is similar to Hearthstone's Arena. You get 45 "pick 1 of 3" options and then play games with the cards you picked. Again you get to keep all cards you draft, and you get additional rewards at the end based on performance. The one big difference is that this is against AI, so it's a bit easier to get 7 wins than in draft (though the rewards are less).
Gauntlet is a mode played with preconstructed decks. These decks can contain any cards you have in your collection. It is played against prebuilt AI decks that can actually be somewhat challenging (for an AI opponent). You can unlock rewards in this mode as well.
Ranked is the mainstay of any online game, and is where you go to pit your best decks against other players. While the level of competition is much higher here, I've been able to win a considerable number of games without any legendaries in the deck, and with few rares. As my collection grew I obviously began building decks with the cards that were most interesting to me (which often included rares and legendaries of course) but I certainly go back and play my budget common/uncommon decks just for fun.
Overall if you are looking for an online card game to try out, I would definitely give this one a go. The biggest key to trying it out is to make sure to play at least a few games after you finish the tutorial campaign, as the campaign is a very preliminary look at the mechanics, and you won't get a true feel for the depth until you've played some of your own decks.

Why do people hate on this game so much? This is Telltale's first game ever! Cut them some slack! Anyway, this is what you would expect from Telltale, point-and-click greatness. It basically follows the Bone series of graphic novels made by Jeff Smith. The series ran from 1991 to 2004 and DAMN were these good books. But the game however..is lacking. As expected from Telltale's first game, this one isn't as long as say, TWD or BTTF. No, this won't take very long. The graphics fit the feel of the comics to a t, and features voice acting to go with it. Everyone sounds on par to me, just how I would imagine them in the comics. Although, Grandma Ben and Smiley Bone can get on your nerves real quick. But other than that, both the graphics and voice acting are decent. However, the puzzles, as explained in previous reviews, are what break the pacing. Finding the possum kids was a snoozefest in itself, and guiding Ted through the river was a hellish ♥♥♥♥ing nightmare. I swear to God if it wasn't for a guide for a game aimed at 7-11 year olds, I would have been stuck there for HOURS. Yes, there are some crashing issues and bugs, but that did not stop me from enjoying this gem. Recommended for fans of the comics? Yes. Recommended for fans of the Telltale games? Well...that's all up to you.

In overall this game is super cheap and poor in terms of game design and certainly not worth to buy it.
1. Graphics - game represent 10 yer old picture, same as DS1 without a single change, more than that developers copypaste tons of content from first game and DS2 looks almost the same as first one, some areas strongly remind the areas from DS1, same with bosses.
2. Gameplay - i want to dispel the myth that this game is "Hard and challenging" NO NO and NO. 90% of your gameplay time is runing form bonefire to boss location(very few Bosses have bonefire right before them, most bosses have ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ distance from bonefire to their location with tons of mobs or lift and other trash that's make travel is more annoying), 5% is boss fights and only rest 5% is actual world/lore discovering.  90% of bosses is supper easy while the rest is pure RNG based especially if you have low adaptability.
With base adaptability you will have aroud 150ms -> 0.15 second of IFrame during roll it's fkn ridiculous thrash, even if you have outstanding reaction and know absolutely all enemy attack it's pure gamble to dodging most of the attacks, in order to make roll somehow reliable you have to lvl adaptability to 36+ and your iframe will be ~0.4 seconds, which is still low even for player who have reaction above average.
About controlls - this game have no free strafe and you are forced to strafe during "focus target" mode and this "focus targed" tends ot make your character uncontrolable, i had tons of situations when my UGS hit absolutely different direction from my target(even when i dirrect my LS to the target). Parry in DS2 is pure gamble compared to DS1 where i could parry with very low chance to ♥♥♥♥ up. Backstab is another annoying trash, you can be right behind mob/player and will fail on attempt to backstab while in other situation you can face side of an enemy and perform backstab or just start animation of backstab while your target is free and smashing your face while you stuned for 2+ sec in animation, in other words another RNG trash. All projectiles(even arrows) and atacks that mobs perform is "homing" while your atacks/projectile NOT(although projectile is also homing durring "Focus target" mode), in example mob can do jump attack and do almost 360 degree rotation right in middle of animation(being in air) in order to set your♥♥♥♥♥on fire.
About boss fights - they are so fkn poorly designed, instead of make unique mechanics wich require certain actions from player thye just have made tons of RNG which player should bypass with "roll", in result all bosses looks the same especially humanoid ones, bosses with tons of adds is more annoyng than hard, as i said before there is no HARD or CHALLENGING bosses, fight vs RNG isn't challenging/hard. Most from illusions of "hard" bosses is made of long distance from bonefire to boss location, since you have very few timeframe where you can atleast receive an opportuinty to see attacks of the boss in order to learn it, RNG dependence adds more to this illusion.
Melee fight is so gimped compared to ranged, sorcery/hex/miracle/pyro builds is soo overpowerd(reduce RNG dependence by a lot) that this game is become a lot less time consumption.
About RNG in boss/mobs fight, this is mostly because of how they telegraph their actions, there is a lot of attacks that have no any telegraph or they are so short that there is no way you can react and mostly you have to just predict, also thereis some enemies that have two different attacks with absolutely the same telegraph animation, but this attacks is differ with speed and if you roll too early you will be hit by slow attack, but if you roll to late you will be hit by fast attack and this is pure gamble.
PVP in this game another gamble, unless you are high lvl mage vs pure melee character.
3. Items - a lot of items is recycling from 1st game, 90% of items are useless crap, there is also no progression during story in terms of obtaining better equipment, in example Greatsword which can be found early in game is better than majority of unque UGS's, while provide almost the same perfomance compared to best UGS's. Armor in this game is completely useless even if not consider drawbacks of heavy armors there is almost no difference betwen naked and best heavy armor(difference in damage reduction is hardly notable), only advantage of heavy armor is POISE what is neglegible atleast in PVE.
4. World and lore - extremely poor, majority of NPC is just a part of decorations, story is so dumb and straight, lack of motivation of your character and especially of other hollows that are considered as you enemy, why the hell??? they are same hollows like you, what the♥♥♥♥♥ why the hell 99% of living creature in the world want you ded especialy other hollows, how the hell they recognize you and don't atack each others?
Conclusions: DS2 is huge downgrade from DS1, i didn't like a lot of things in DS1 but in DS2 they've become even worse. I can compare DS2 with casino game like roulette in example they have absolutely the same way of attraction - passion/desire to taste a luck. In order to maximize your pleasure from this game you should be very lucky and be a exremely patient, your personal skill is not really mater, in overal this game is very easy. I can note only one good thing in DS series as a part of a potentially good "Game" is the stamina system, but developers ruined it with high RNG dependence.

Excellent card game. GUI and game flow reminds me of HS and the depth and complexity reminds me of MTG, but with enough new features to make it feel unique.
The game is also not Pay to Win at all. You can build some top tier decks without a single legendary (Hooru Control and Stonescar Burn being some good examples at the time this review was written) and even the legendaries are very easy to get compared to other F2P CGs.
Another good point is that in the drafting formats (Forge and Draft) you are allowed to keep the cards you draft, which makes it very interesting, making you balance between the cards you need to do well in the draft and the cards you want to have after the draft.
The only thing I would point as a negative is that the forge and gauntlet (PVE formats) have ranks that don't reset, ever. Which makes them a little unappealing after you achieve master rank. If they would reset each month, it would be fun to play until master every month, getting the rewards along the way (even if the rewards were worse to compensate).
Aside from that, one of the best in the genre, in my humble opinion.

Gone Home is a beautiful and heart warming story. It has great voice acting and a fairly well designed setting. It's also good at creating an ominous tone and atmosphere, until you begin to ease into the story. You play as the sister of the narrator, returning home from a trip to an empty house. There's the main story, and smaller subplots that you discover as you go through the game. The game does very well with the idea "show, don't tell", and makes sure the things you interact with are beneficial to the plot. This chosen form of narration and storytelling is unique, relying on your involvement and discovery of the story for it to unravel.
This being said, I can't quite label this as a full fleged game due to its really short playtime and overall limited experience. Your actions don't affect the end/outcome of the game, and there is no other goal than to get to the end of its one main story. Gone Home excells cinematically and in terms of a narrative; It's a great interactive story, but it fails to deliver a genuine experience as a "game" especially at its base $20 price point.
Endpoint: Don't buy this game at full price; wait for a sale or something. Do still get the game at some point, as the story is gives you is worth experiencing.

Verdun is nothing like your average online fps. Unlike most fps games, this one is slow paced and MUCH MUCH more team-based. You can't defend or capture by yourself - you need the help of your team. Same as you need their help, as what truly adds the feeling that you MUST work as a team is the fact that 99% of the classes are limited to 1 player per match. Moreover, unlike most games, this one has a really nice community. You won't find the school kids spamming the voice chat. You won't find imbecills doing useless♥♥♥♥♥♥ You won't find camping snipers killing you from the directly opposite side of the map. You won't find idiots saying "rekt" after each kill, or throwing "yo mama" jokes left and right. Speaking of kills, expect to die. A LOT. And kill a lot. Artillery, martars, and, of course, gas all adds to the atmosphere.
The game is tuly authentic, and the developers are aiming to make it as historically accurate as it is bloody possible.
Now, why I see this game better than it's direct concurent, Battlefield 1:
1. It was released earlier.
2. It's cheaper. Around $150 cheaper.
3. The reason I used BF1's full ~$170 price is because I included all DLC. Verdun has no DLC. It's full from the beginning. Something very few games have, and I hope it will stay so for Verdun.
4. Atmosphere. Unlike BF1, it does not feel like "yet another shooter game". It is truly unique.
5. Authentic. It's not exactly historically accurate of all the fast running around in BF1. In WW1, the military was still using some of the concepts of the line combat of 18th centry. Take the British at Somme, for example, who charged machine gun positions, over open ground, at a walking man's pace, under the cover of daylight. Also, you can find most players in BF1 charging in with SMG or hipfireing an LMG. While in Verdun it is impossible to hipfire an LMG - it must be deployed on it's bipod. And hipfire is helpfull only at point-blank range. I mean, you can miss the enemy at the distance of just 2 meters if you're hipfiring.
What else can I add? I fully on recommend this marvelous game.

Banished
Banished is a sort of Civilisation, or City Simulator based in the past, where the general theme is to expand your town/city while managing your resources and citizens closely.
Visually I find this game very pleasing. The trees, water and even rocks look very nice, and the animations are also done well. There isn’t a huge amount to say about the audio, but it does the job.
The game itself is hard to talk about. You start with a small number of villagers, and have to have them collect resources such as wood, stone, and food, while building new houses for them to live in. Houses allow your population to grow, giving you more children, which eventually will become adults and workers. That all sounds fairly standard, and even simplistic, but do not be fooled; this game can destroy you. That may sound somewhat strange, when you consider the fact there are no roaming barbarians, vicious animals, or in fact any enemies at all. No, the difficulty is the extent of micro management that is required to keep your town functioning. It’s about finding balance. You might want to build several houses for your villagers, so they can sleep, and take shelter from the weather. That’s all well and good, but that one simple choice now has several consequences such as the need for more wood to be converted to firewood to keep the people warm, it will also increase the population as people start to have children. More children will eventually mean more workers, but in the short term they’re just more mouths to consume precious food. You also have to consider the materials used for the house, and how many people you assign to build it, will no longer be collecting those resources for the time it takes to build. This is just one example, but that is the kind of thing that makes it what it is. Every choice has to be thought through, even the positioning of the houses. A house too far away from the occupants work area means less efficiency and less resources gathered.
Your citizens will need to be closely monitored, as they have general health, which can be maintained with a Herbalist making remedies, happiness which is very hard to manage, but can be helped with buildings like Taverns, and Hunger needs to be monitored so they don’t starve to death. Interestingly your citizens will grow old, and they will die of old age, which is an easy thing to forget, and if you do, you may end up with a very old town, incapable of having children, and so you lose by attrition. Weather affects them too, meaning you need to make some warm clothes for winter, and light for summer, and maintain a steady supply of tools for people to actually do their jobs with.
Overall the mechanics are very solid and are easy to understand, but difficult to master. However, it’s not all sunshine and rainbows for the game, unfortunately. The pacing of the game can be extremely slow, even when you manually adjust the timer to the fastest setting. Some of the controls, like having someone stop their current job and start doing something else (or work somewhere else) seems very much in the hands of the AI. Sometimes people just won’t do what you want. The biggest thing with Banished though, is ‘the point’. As in ‘what’s the point?’. Truth be told, there isn’t one. There are no technologies to advance, no enemies to conquer, no end of the game or unlocks. You simply just go until you fill the map (which looks quite small). Now, I appreciate that not all games have ‘a point’ per se (ex: Minecraft, Space Engineers, Garry’s Mod) but the majority do, and the ones that don’t are usually based on the player creating something unique, and are multiplayer. Banished has none of those features.
Conclusion; to wrap it up I’d say that Banished is a well made and balanced game, with an emphasis on resource and micro-management in a slow paced environment. A recommendation really depends on the person considering buying the game. If you’re the sort of person that likes to pick up a game, play it from start to finish and put it down for a while, this game is likely not for you, so avoid it at all costs. However, if you’re the sort of person that likes a nice, slow paced game, with heavy man-management systems and are not too bothered by campaigns or story driven games, then this is right up your street.
Assuming you’re the latter category, I’d give it 8.5/10

How to fix freezes/crashes on Windows 7 or above.
Go to documents/my games/Fallout3
Click FALLOUT.ini or just FALLOUT if the .ini isn't present.
Edit it with notepad or notepad++. Press control+F and type "bUseThreadedAI"
It will say bUseThreadedAI=0, change the 0 to a 1.
Press enter and type EXACTLY this: iNumHWThreads=2
Save the file.
Boot up Fallout 3, than ALT+TAB out.
Open task manager and look for Fallout3.
Right click it and go to properties.
Up the top, press compatibilty.
Than, select what operating system you have.
I hope this helped!

I have flown many different flight sims in my life.
I started with stuff like "Flight Sim 1.0" and "F-29 Retaliator".
Up untill this day i've been playing FSX.
The biggest upside of the FS games is the community.
I've repainted countless of airplanes, downloaded thousands of freeware aircraft and have bought several 3rd party payware add-ons.
I have logged about 5000 hours in the FS series (yes, i kept track) so I was kinda excited to read that DTG bought the rights and would actively develop a new version.
However, knowing DTG's reputation when it comes to taking over franchises I was a bit worried as well.
The fear is that DTG wants to cash as much as possible on this game by adding expensive DLC's.
My biggest fear however, is that we won't be able to add our own developed aircraft / scenery anymore.
CPU: Intel Core I5 6600K
RAM: 16GB
GPU: GeForce GTX 980Ti
Display: Asus MG279 @ 2560x1440 144hz
Doing a quick inspection of the installation folders tells me this is the exact folder layout as FSX.
When starting up the game for the first time there's a Flight Simulator X  feeling.
It generates indexes at the start like it does in Flight Simulator X.
I'm impressed by the main menu at this point. Very nice lay-out and it looks slick.
Graphical settings are set to medium by default and I turn them all the way up.
I like the fact there's a flying school and the addition of extra missions is also a plus!
All planes handle as you expect of a FS successor, no issues here.
But now, the performance of the game engine:
The game runs at 15-20 frames on ultra, i can get them up to 30 on ultra @ 1080p.
Some textures' saturation is completely wrong and trees are rendered in a horrible way.
Since it's an EA title there's still room for improvement.
Well, the community factor is very low on this one.
However they implemented a server browser to make it easy to play online with other people, they didn't do much for the community.
There is no way to import any freeware / payware aircraft. Neither does it seem there's any planned support for it.
Was I looking forward to this game? Yes!
Did FSW fullfill my hopes and wishes? No!
+ Low entrance level (Flight School)
- Graphical issues
- Lack of freeware / payware support of earlier titles
- DTG seems wanting to make as much cash on an old obsolete product as possbile
So I wouldn't recommend the game at this time. The graphics need work, the engine needs polishing and the lack of freeware / 3rd party payware add-ons are crucial issues DTG needs to fix before getting this game out of Early Access.

Rush hours make you actually feel stressed due to the sheer ammount of customers that walk inside and hearing the bell signaling the end of rush hour is so satisfying.
With that said, the game can get a bit frustating when you cook certain items because they either take too long or require a lot of attention, making you distracted from your other dishes. All and all, pretty good game, fair price and good simulator.

Okay, so I've been playing the game for over two hundred hours at the time of this review, mouse and keyboard.  This is my first actual Dark Souls that I've grown dedicated to, DSI to a degree after buying this.  I'd certainly buy this if you're looking to get into a Souls game and do not own the others, unlike a lot of folks are probably telling you.  It's not like Dark Souls 1, for certain, but if you're getting into DSI on PC, you're in for a rude awakening.  You have to jump through numerous amounts of hoops to even get it to work half decent, and you just might end up with an unbearably low resolution.
Dark Souls 2, on the other hand, is a good port to the PC and has mouse controls and the such, and you really do not have to modify the game at all with any third party fixes.
I haven't played the original DSII, but from other reviews, people aren't really happy about buying that and then SotFS, claiming it to be nothing more than lighting overhauls and such.  To that, I say, if you already have the original Dark Souls II, DO NOT BUY THIS.  Otherwise, if you wish to play Dark Souls II and are confused whether you should get this or the original, definitely buy this.  The DLCs are much more integrated into the world from what I've read, and there are quite a few other overhauls.
The game is still very much alive, duels being held on the bridge around SL150, summons existing, and invaders crushing orbs to this day.  It may not be as active as DSIII, but it sure as hell is more populated than DSI, and unlike DSIII, it has a working poise system.
It's not Dark Souls 1, but it still is a great game, with excellent PvP where estoc/rapier spam is not a good idea and still has that signature Dark Souls difficulty spike to it, although probably not as hard as usual.
Pros
+ Good PvP
+ Nice environments
+ Multiplayer still alive, weekends most active
+ Poise
+ You really do not have to fiddle with third party programs to get it working right.
+ Sun praising
+ Onion armor
Cons
- Lucatiel not as good as Solaire
- Soul memory, seriously, it can go to hell
- Not Dark Souls 1
- Spells easily abused, but you can get by those if you learn to roll properly.
- The Executioner's Chariot

Now, I fail to understand why there is quite a divide among those who appreciate Dark Souls II and those who do not. I see Dark Souls II as a "best of both worlds" in terms of a combination of mechanics from "Demon's Souls" and "Dark Souls".
For a long time I read negative reviews about this game and thus I avoided it. But then I saw the game on sale and figured, "You know what? Screw what others have to say about this game. I'm gonna give it a shot". And it's a good thing I did.
I love the fact that the game serves up a good challenge and at no point felt the AI pulled a cheap move. There is always something to study from the enemies' moves and oh yeah, I felt good knowing their weaknesses.
Graphics held up very well, beautiful environments. Bosses were plenty. There really was no need for me to farm at all for souls, which felt like a real waste of time for me in DS1.
The ability to summon more than one spirit really helps you move forward, but you are still expected to pitch in and help them out to defeat the bosses. Although some spirits felt a bit too overpowered, but it was really no biggie for me.
I've yet to try the DLC but I'm sure I'll enjoy it. It was worth playing this game. Heck, I think I like it more than DS1.

At first blush, Luckslinger may come off as Gunman Clive with some pixel-based clothes. But stylistically, it's a slower-paced low-key turntablist demake b-side remix to the PSX ultra-cult hit Rising Zan: Samurai Gunman. Only here, the bombastic swordplay is traded out for fascinating luck mechanics, cool plaformer-based combat techniques, and one of the better soundracks found in a pixel art game. Worth your time if you want something that feels familiar with a few new welcome gameplay tricks and a lot of style.

If this should be recommended probably depends on the other acts of this series. As it is, Out From Boneville feels pretty unfinished, as if it didn't even make to the polishing phase. Altogether this seems to be more of a proof-of-concept adventure for the TellTale engine. From design (protagonists' models and movements are somewhat similar to Max's) and voice actors (e.g. main protagonist's voice is Sam's) I'd say this adventure was done to show the Sam & Max adventures could be done, which incidentially are what I would recommend everyone to play way before touching this game.
+ It's an adventure
+ TellTale engine: 3D world, camera 'following' the player
+ Good voice acting: David Nowlin (Sam) and other voices from TellTale's Sam & Max
- Way too short and still somewhat boring
- Story almost completely developed in introduction cutscene
- Awful controls in action sequences
- Skipping dialogue parts may skip more than can be read at the time
The story builds little momentum, mainly driven by the introduction cutscene and by some pieces of dialogue that appear disconnected at times. And the first act is over in nearly no time.
Puzzles are very easy. Basically it's combining the few things you find with the environment, the main obstacle here is finding items as they are not highlighted in any way (which I'm fine with). Other times your current objective is helped by dialogue.
There are three scenes with their own puzzle mechanics
which is nice.
Using items inconsistently makes the mouse cursor that object or the standard 'use' cursor.
There are two
in which you have to escape whatever follows you. They are bad because your control options - jump, go left, go right (as opposed to turn left or right) - are executed with the mouse and the left-right movement control is nothing close to tight. There is no indication as to how far you just moved the character before it stops moving in that direction which can feel pretty long after you let go of your mouse and make you run into obstacles - not fit for reaction sequence. Both sequences are short but not short enough to not bore. Then again you can simply fail them after which the game offers to skip them.
Personal preference: I don't like it when the played character, one of two, behaves like a prick, more so if that interferes in no way with completing objectives. Maybe that's why the 'protagonists' are from Boneville.
I may recommend this act after playing the next one as piece of the overall experience but I don't expect the second part to take it away.
For now, I don't recomment Out From Boneville.

This review is from someone who is not a racing or sports fan at all but my all time favourite racing game which actually got me into trying some racing games is Need for Speed Most Wanted 2005:
The Crew is a bit close to NFSMW 2005 since it has a story line + car tuning + cop chases + helicopter supports and different type of racing methods such as circuit or just a straight racing line or just like NFS 2005 time trials in addition it also has "Raid" and "Dirt" racing too which completely makes it different than other racing games. story line is not that good or amazing it is just there to help you progress faster and unlock more stuff before you jump into multiplayer so do not expect an amazing ending or something totally unique.
Pros:
- a complete racing game for those who want to experience every type of racing methods in one game.
- handling the car can be really realistic if you put it on hardcore, unlike NFS it is much harder to handle the car here it is more realistic.
- perks which can help you to finish the game easier.
- good online compared to other UBI games this one is one of the few games which has a good online, COOP is really nice if you are stuck in a mission just find someone to do COOP with it is alot easier to pass the campaign missions in the COOP than solo.
- huge map and a lot of different areas to test your car in.
- different tones of online game modes which can be selected by voting before the match starts.
Cons:
- if you have a wireless gamepad your game detects it as driving wheel and therfore keys dont work properly at all.
- sometimes you need to restart the game completley to avoid some minor bugs such as not showing a friend online or in your crew when they join you.
- for a $60 game there is too much cut out contents being sold as DLC, for example the biggest joke is all Mercedes cars in this game are DLC none of them can be unlocked without paying real money which is a shame for a $60 game.
- some missions are extremly stupidly designed specially the raid ones. they have no racing feeling at all and in some of them yu have to drive in middle of trees at night so you crash a lot and it is really really annoying.
- not all cars can be tuned to what you want, the tuning is just a side option in this game it is not actually tuning like in NFS 2005, you have nearly no options for tuning your car except accepting what game forces you to buy for the missions.
- finding a multiplayer match is so hard, first you need to search automatically for a game and as long as not enough players are found the lobby wont get started, when it does players have to vote for what type of game mode and race they wanna play, you can not select what game mode you want before searching so you exactly get what you want. you select what you want in the lobby and so do other players so if you are lucky you get what you want if not then you have to play what others want.
- you can not test your favourite car in every race you want as most of the cars do not have much tuning options for Raid and Dirt. for example if your car is aston martin you can only play it in "performance missions" if a mission is dirt or street you have to use a street car and aston martin can not be tuned for any other race than "performance".
- for a 2014 game i was expecting a lot better graphics for this game but sadly only cars are really detailed and well designed people and the city enviroment have the graphics of GTA back in 2000s. The Crew. A game that I'd followed for a fair few months before its BETA release, and then jumped off the train to "buyingit-ville" very shortly before release. For another 8 months I fondled with the idea of buying it, but never did. I didn't really know why... until now.
Now, before I start, I should clarify that no, I didn't "thumbs it up" by mistake. I bought this game on sale for £12 and I feel it's worth that. But a penny more? No.
An open world, multi-purpose racing game with vast amounts of custimization that is also an MMO. Sounds great, right? Let me further clarify those for you.
Open World
...and then some. Oh boy, the map's huge! I always thought GTA V's map was big, but this must be at least 4x the size of Los Santos. Not only is it big, based around the entirety of the USA and time-consuming to travel across, but it's also incredibly detailed. The sale price was worth it for the gametime on that map alone. Even without missions, it would still be enjoyable for me. You might want to get a plane if you're going from NY to LA though.
Multi Purpose Racing/Customization
You betcha! Dirt, Raid, Perf(ormance), Street and Circuit specs will make sure that you definitely have the right tool for the job (or the race, in this case)! The car detailing with these specs is very nice. Cars look crisp, although some more than others, for some reason, and there's a lot to do in the customization front (bumpers, fenders etc.).
The A.I. however is a joke. It would seem that Ubisoft believe that you should have to hard brake around track corners in a specially circuit-tuned race car that should turn on a dime, only to fall off track and lose your first place position to the guy in last 1 mile back. But, the guy behind you in a Chevy V8, with tyres the size of a standard London road-lane and the turning circle of a cruise ship? Oh, no trouble there! In fact, they don't have to even brake! Their car has high-performance, rubberised glue... apparently. Oh, and if you can actually manage to pull off a first place medal against the sling-shotting A.I., don't expect it to be gold. You're going to need a harrier jet for that. Available in the new DLC , which you'll be able to grab in your nearest showroom for the low, low price of £25.
M.M.O
Ha! Yeah right. I haven't played W.O.W in a few years, but unless their servers have changed to allowing a whopping 8 players in one match(!), then it is an insult to even put this into the same category.
Conclusion
It's a fun game. Has a lot of bugs but a lot of them are rarely noticable. It's a great time-waster and the cars look good, especially when you put a big ol' body kit on 'em. Buy it, but don't pay full price for it, even if that is only £25. Also, be prepared for a ton of in-game currency being thrown in your face. Seriously, it's like hitting a wasps nest with a baseball bat; overwhelming and really, really stupid.

A strategy city building game which feels like what would happen if Maxis did two things:
1. Broke free from the iron-grip of EA.
2. Made a Sim City set in the 1800s.
Except I noticed that I do a hell of a lot better in this game than I ever did in any Sim City games.
Maybe its because the AI is a lot better and more intelligent, maybe its because the game itself is more user friendly, maybe its because lets face it when I'd play Sim City anything I'd just summon the monster and watch it go batshit on my city and this game doesn't have that option.
You take the role of mayor of a small community during the 1800s and have to guide your village by deciding where roads go, directing villagers to create farms, orchards, and pastures to raise food, hunting lodges and fishing docks to catch or hunt food, gather wood, stone, and ore to create new buildings, tools, and such, and slowly grow your little village from a tiny collection of about ten houses into a massive city of it's own that spans the entire map.
This isn't as easy as it sounds however. You have to match your growth carefully to your resources. Build too many houses too fast and suddenly winter will come but you won't have enough food or firewood to get through it and half your village will starve or freeze to death. Expand too many farms without building houses and you'll wind up without enough workers to go around, half your fields winding up empty until the weeds and forests reclaim them. Not to mention your villagers will still age and die. Don't build houses fast enough? Oops, now there's nobody left in town to do anything because they all got old and croaked while you were watching the trees grow.
A good title for taking a break between shooting aliens from outer space and stabbing dragons for their souls that I get an oddly zen-like relaxation playing... at least until it suddenly starts yelling at me that the reserve of firewood is running low and that one of my quarry workers got smushed into paste when a rock broke loose. Still, if you like sim games this one is a winner.

How to fix freezes/crashes on Windows 7 or above.
Go to documents/my games/Fallout3
Click FALLOUT.ini or just FALLOUT if the .ini isn't present.
Edit it with notepad or notepad++. Press control+F and type "bUseThreadedAI"
It will say bUseThreadedAI=0, change the 0 to a 1.
Press enter and type EXACTLY this: iNumHWThreads=2
Save the file.
Boot up Fallout 3, than ALT+TAB out.
Open task manager and look for Fallout3.
Right click it and go to properties.
Up the top, press compatibilty.
Than, select what operating system you have.
I hope this helped!

A really disappointing title based on an interesting premise (albeit a reimagining of the first Homefont). It's a title with very repetitive, bland and buggy gameplay. Some issues: crouch near a curb and go sliding to the right, spinning boxes, random lights floating in mid air as well as some pickups, NPCs getting stuck in crates, NPCs disappearing in front of you, vehicles spawning inside walls, flashlight not functioning correctly in some areas (why do we pull the flashlight out from over our left shoulder?), a constant head bob that is extrodinarily off-putting, a poor choice of colour palette exacerbates this issue making it very difficult to focus in some areas and a need to mod the game to get a decent FOV, among many others.
The story made little sense, most characters had very poor dialogue, as well as back stories and implied motivation plot holes. It felt like we were supposed to empathise with most of the main characters but for many there was nothing to care about. Most of the cutscenes were unappealing, character motivations were at times all over the place, they would express one reason or motivation for a decision and then contradict it soon after. Some characters were downright annoying. In the end the only character I personally found interesting was the gun shop guy, and I don't remember his name! Also, the ending felt rushed, uninspired and most of the control was taken away from you. At least let us pull the switch!
Sound was generally decent but off-putting with things like ricochet effects occuring on surfaces that shouldn't have them. Also, the sound of far off battle playing on the other side of a wall you're next to is immersion breaking. The background conversations from NPCs bring some liveliness to the environment but at times they seems very confused, e.g. "Yeah, let's do this", followed up quickly with "Save me!", then when you save them it's all "Yeah, we did it!". Gameplay was cookie cutter from one section to another. This game is right up my alley. Unfortunately, the game is a technical disaster that barely runs, fraught with so much microstutter that just walking around is next to impossible. You won't notice this issue until the very first "here's a gun, have at 'em" moment. At least, that's where it crept up for me. Otherwise, the game was a solid, perfect 60 fps at high settings. I guess the high performance came from the fact that the beginning area's a scripted setpiece. Once the game adds actual enemy AIs into the mix, performance goes into the toilet.
Casually looking up the problem shows that it's a widespread issue that never really got addressed or fixed. Bummer.
So is the game worth the buy, even at such a low price? No, I'm afraid not. The performance issues are just too much. Having the entire game hitch up every 20 seconds or so isn't something that you can just ignore or work around.
Disclaimer - played the game for free during its trial period. Honestly bummed that the technical issues prevented me from enjoying the experience. Otherwise, I can tell a lot of work went into the game as a whole.

Sidescroll 'em up western with Commodore 64-esque graphics that allows you to store up luck to use as a resource and manipulate certain behind the scenes dicerolls to your favor (or against). Prevelant throughout is a minamalist hip-hop theme that mixes with the spaghetti western setting to create something extremely surreal - which is saying something for a title that also features a trusty duck companion who only acts
like a mallard.
While the game begins charming and is an easy venture to get into the groove of (shoot, roll, jump and knifetoss to victory with the occasional item/luck medallion usage) certain gameplay flaws quickly become apparent. Reloading is an easily interrupted though setting appropriate juncture and there will be plenty of times where you'll be flanked on both sides stuck dodging while reloading one bullet at a time to peck away at enemies with. Throw in melee enemies that just run straight at you while the shooters are still there and you've got yourself the perfect formula for annoyance. Expect to meet such a gauntlet near the end of almost every level. On top of this is that getting hit and/or losing a life depletes your luck
Bosses are a mixed bag of characters every last bit as crazy as the townfolk, my personal favorite being the saloon girl (incorporates a game of chance to determine how much of a disadvantage you start at) and the cultist priest being by far the most annoying (the battle IS the aforementioned gauntlet full of endless rushing melee enemies while having to dodge a fast giant coin). If you're unlucky enough to lose at a boss you don't get to start straight at the fight; you'll have to mash through the cutscene every single time. Not even the sick in-town skateboarding or freestyle instrumental recording you can do is enough to forgive such a thing in the modern day.
Had Luckslinger kept its initial impression it'd definitely be a thing to reccomend (though perhaps a stretch at that asking price), but it sadly ended up skipping a few too many beats and firing more blanks than lead for me.

One of my favorite card games in a long run of board- and card-game playing; I must've played it at least a hundred times over the last five-six years.  You get the full amount of enjoyment of a good game, but condensed down to about 15 or 20 minutes - making it perfect for an idle waiting period.

I would've liked perhaps some way to customize the ruleset - with the physical card game, for example, the homeworld selection can become non-random or you could change the ending conditions if you want a longer game - or you could set up challenges or partial decks.
There's also a couple ways to do a "solitaire" version with the actual cards - granted, having an AI offers much the same advantage, but you can't do a "score attack" challenge as easily.
There's a couple of expansions that aren't in this version yet - I assume they'll come out later.
On the whole, I definitely recommend this to both fans of the card game and those looking for a fun way to spend a few minutes.  Current price is seven dollars, with expansions four dollars each - the expansions seem a bit on the pricy side, all things considered, but I'd recommend buying the base game, trying it out and then buying the DLC once you know if you'll continue enjoying it.

You would expect the immediate comparison of Eternal to be to Hearthstone. However unlike Hearthsone, Eternal allows actions on your opponents turns, has a much more complex combat system, and doesn't have many powerful cards that rely heavily on randomness,
Magic: The Gathering ends up being a much better comparison. Eternal borrows a good number of mechanics, but with its own twists. It utilizes the digital format effectively, such as allowing buffs on the next creature in your deck, or keeping track of stat changes through different zones. It also streamlines the turns, to the point where it's actually playable on mobile (apparently an IOS client is in the works).  Eternal also has a draft format, where you draft against actual players, while keeping the cards you draft,
Ultimately if you are looking for a more streamlined mobile-friendly version of Magic, I would suggest giving Eternal a try. Or if you are bored of the myriad "do a random thing" effects from Hearthstone, the more deterministic cards here may be welcome.

Real big fan of Eternal.  I played Magic: The Gathering many years ago and recently got the itch to get back into something similar.  Eternal scratches that itch really well.  The game is clearly built on the basics of MTG but really expand into the digital space well.  Modifications to cards can be permanent and persist between deck, hand, play, and the void (graveyard).
The intro tutorial/campaign is currently awful and one of the biggest barriers to success.  If you can slug through it, you will be rewarded with a rich metagame that includes PVP and PVE modes.  Both modes are generous with their rewards.  You don't need to purchase gems/packs to be competitive (although it of course helps improve your collection).  Draft lets you purchase 4 packs for $5 with a chance to win 3 more packs and enough gold to draft again for free for only 7 wins (compared to 12 in hearthstone for the best reward).
The biggest complaint I've heard from new players is the sigil system which is based on MTG's land system.  New players generally don't know how to effectively build a power base and this creates problems as the game doesn't help with deck building at all.  I'll say that even with the occasional powerscrew/flood, the sigil system allows for a broad metagame with many color combinations being represented.  Player aren't boxed in to specific cardsets based on an overriding class (Like hearthstone).
Big fan, will keep playing.

This game is worse than the original Dark Souls in most ways, so if you haven't played a Dark Souls game before, then I recommend you play the first game instead. But if you've already played the first game to death and want more, then you should enjoy this one as well. It also has more players online now.
The gameplay is much the same as the first Dark Souls, but the level design is a bit worse since you start out with the ability to teleport at the beginning of the game rather than acquiring it late, so they put less thought into compact level designs. The level designs are also less interesting, with few or no destinations visible on the horizon in most places. I've seen few areas and no amazing characters so far, although the graphical quality is definitely nice. In the first game, I even felt sad to fight or refused to kill some bosses (like Sif and Priscilla respectively). Even some regular enemies were just creatures defending their homes. In this game, all the enemies have been pure monsters so far. The world building and lore suffers too, as this game has less in the way of ambient world-building. I know the story isn't the main draw of a Dark Souls game, but all those small touches made the first game special. I also miss the ability to kick in combat, since kicking the occasional enemy or invader off a cliff was a lot of fun. It's just a minor thing, though. On the plus side, I haven't seen any of the sadistic level designs (that cause death through falling) from the first game. There's also a lot less grinding needed. You'll probably obtain at least a dozen titanite slabs, enough to fully level up a couple suits of equipment. And grinding sucks, so that's nice.
The game is much easier than the original Dark Souls. While I'm not a fan of brutal difficulties, I thought the first Dark Souls was well-balanced. The enemies and bosses were a challenge, and some were quite hard, and beating them solo was a real accomplishment. (Some, like Ornstein and Smough, I never managed on my own despite over a dozen tries.) In Dark Souls II, I've solo'd every boss, almost all of them on my very first try, and several times on my first try as a hollow with 55% max health and minus a few Estus flasks. They're just really easy compared to Dark Souls bosses, and that's a shame because I've never had the thrill of a hard-fought win in Dark Souls II. Some reviewers say the game throws multiple easy enemies at you rather than throwing challenging enemies at you. That's true, and it sucks to be ganged up on, but overall I haven't found it to be a problem.
Making enemies stop spawning after you've killed them ten times also sucks, because rather than forcing me to actually get good at the game it just lets me grind through the enemies until there aren't any left. (Similarly, rather than forcing them to really balance a level, they can just let you grind through it.) On the other hand, it limits grinding for souls and items, and since I'm weak-willed when it comes to resisting that kind of thing I appreciate it a bit.
As for multiplayer, I'm glad they made it possible to be invaded while hollow, and I don't mind the effect of losing max health after death since it drops slowly and gives players an incentive to become human again. That gets and keeps more players involved in multiplayer, which is a good thing. There are some minor improvements, like your summon sign disappearing less frequently, so you can play more while waiting to be summoned. The covenants, like the rest of the lore, are rather less inspiring and interesting in this game, but I guess they get the job done. I don't like the use of Soul Memory (i.e. the total number of souls ever collected) as opposed to character level for matchmaking. It means you can't stay at your desired sweet spot for PvP. In Dark Souls, there were clear tiers, like the 40-level PvP, the 80-level PvP, and the 120-level PvP, and you could build a character for one tier and stay there. In Dark Souls II, you can't stay with the build you want, since over time you'll be matched with ever-harder opponents even if you never level up. (There is a ring that can prevent you from gaining souls, though, if you don't mind losing a ring slot.) I have seen some cheaters, but it's about the same as the original game.
Speaking of levels, levelling up means less in Dark Souls II. At the end of Dark Souls, I was at level 65. In Dark Souls II, I hit level 100 when I was less than a quarter of the way through the game. So you can get high values in almost every stat if you want, and probably will, which means most characters can probably do everything fairly well rather than being specialized like in the first game. My current character is a level 125 tank / dodger / pyromancer / archer and I'm not even half way through the game yet. And speaking of dodging, they made characters able to dodge quickly while wearing a lot more, so there's little need to be concerned about weight, which means almost every character will be able to both dodge and tank simultaneously, again limiting specialization and making opponents feel too similar and generic.
The graphics are a bit better in this game, mostly in the textures and environmental effects, but the animations are often less impressive. (For example, the backstab and riposte actions are much less satisfying.) The sound design is about as good, but also less impressive in some places.
Overall, the first Dark Souls is a much better game so by comparison this one is a bit of a disappointment, but just judging it on its own I'm still having fun so I guess I have to recommend it.

Great game. Very intense, with a very good gameplay. Despite being an independent game, it truly feels like an AAA production.
The chasing and hide-and-seek sequences inspired by Amnesia are actually way better than Amnesia. Though the level design is a bit too forgiving early game, making the encounters easier than they should. It gets better later, but at that point the player is not surprised anymore. Though I suppose it's to allow everyone to be able to go past the beginning.
I tend to hate cheap jumpscares, but I actually found the jumpscares in Outcast very well thought out. They surprise but do not feel cheap, and they achieve the best possible result: scare the player when he feels safe, then keep the player on edge when there is nothing to fear.
It all seems well, what's the catch?
The game can feel a bit repetitive, though it's always enjoyable thanks to the good gameplay and the 'mirror's edge'-like body awareness and movement.
The real bummer is the story that falls a bit short towards the end. It's all blood and guts, not a fascinating story and atmosphere. Unlike Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs, that outdoes Outlast in the fascinating 'psychological horror' department.

Positives: It's short, like two hours or under.  The characters look about like you'd expect.
Negatives: It's tedious and boring, making it feel much longer than the short runtime.
'Bone' is one of my favorite books (graphic or otherwise) ever.  It's a wonderful fantasy adventure.  I also enjoy TellTale's games (though they aren't perfect).  So I should love this, right?  I wish.
Every task you're asked to complete is clearly busy work.  None of the "puzzles" is truly driven by the story.  They're just hoops to jump through in order to get to the next screen.  The worst offender is when you're asked to guide Ted the bug across the river.  Without a walkthrough, I never would have gotten across as the logic dicated by the pattern of his jumps breaks down when you get close to the other side.  It looks like I should be able to make the jumps necessary as the stones are spaced just like rest, and I tried multiple spots to lead from, but there is only one single way to get across, and if you don't follow it, it won't allow you to make the jumps.
An additional crime, less painful but still aggravating, is the inability to skip voiced dialogue.  I can generally read the text much faster than the voice actor will deliver it, and when I'm in the middle of an extended Q&A, I want to get it over with as soon as possible.  But perhaps that's my impatience with the overall game.  I just wanted to be done and wished I could speed up any little bit of it.  This lack of skipability carries over into the end credits.  They're slowly scrolled and, for some heinous reason, quadruple spaced.  And you... can't... skip them.
To be fair, the early sections of the book are relatively uneventful, but maybe that should have been a sign to TellTale.  'Bone' would make a phenomenal animated movie, but videogames are an interactive medium, and that interaction needs to feel meaningful.  The source material here, as much as I love it, doesn't bear the weight of player interaction.
Unless you're the most die-hard fan of TellTale's games, skip this one.  Fans of the book?  Stay away.

Overall, I was happily impressed with my time with Race for the Galaxy. Had I not had someone there to hold my hand and explain things to me, I probably would have written it off. However, I’ve got friends who play this and we talk via Blizzard chat and we have a fun time. It’s fairly fun by myself as well now, but it’s still a card game and RNG can really suppress a plan that you could be concocting and that can be very frustrating if you’re not willing to switch it up and pick a new tactic. I tend to be stubborn soooo… yeh. There’s a lot of strategy to be had here and you’ll have to keep an eye on your opponents cards so you don’t end up helping them. Race for the Galaxy is fun and I do turn it on frequently to get a game in or two against the medium ai, but the lack of real-life interaction between friends keeps this game from being first-rate. I’m not entirely sure that comes off as fair to judge a videogame like that, but I rate for fun and my card-based fun is more fully enjoyed in real life.
Full Review:
As a reviewer, I tend to shy away from games that I don’t find all that interesting. Ever notice how many card games I’ve reviewed on this site? Kind of slim eh? Yeh, I don’t like digital card games. I love Blizzard, but I haven’t touched Hearthstone. I love The Witcher, but I won’t go near The Witcher Adventure Game (even though it’s mostly a board game). I’ll play them in person, but digital just doesn’t click for me. Why would I touch Race for the Galaxy then? Well a good friend of mine asked me to take a look. Does Race for the Galaxy justify my disdain for the digital card game concept or did it birth a new genre for me to embrace and enjoy? Let me break it down for you.
Let’s start with the basic issue I had with the game. Have you ever played a card game with a lot of rules and strategies before? Are you one of those people who had a fair bit of trouble wrapping your mind around it and had to ask a few questions of your friends? I have. There in part lies one of my biggest issues with Race for the Galaxy (RFTG from here on out): it’s complicated. Now, I’m all for a challenge, but the difference here is that all you’ve got are the provided tutorials. They do an OK job of laying down some of the basics of how the game can be played in three different ways. None of them are purely one way or the other because the games cards are not commonly given out when you need them as is the case in real life. Sometimes luck is with you and other times you just can’t draw the right card to save your life. Given that, and there are a lot of details that aren’t fully explained in the tutorials and you’re left up to pick up the rest yourself since it’s digital and unless you or a bud has played the card game before, this may be tough. It’s not impossible, but it’s tough.
There is also no in-game chat which some people have complained about. However, I don’t think I really want to hear about the many ways someone close to me has been violated over the internet so I’m OK with that. I tend to only really want to play games with my friends anyway. How many other chat programs are out there? Skype? Raidcall? Blizzard and Steam have a chat function. Discord even? Pick one and you’ll be set. Some people do want to talk to the rando’s and that’s fine, but that’s not me. I’ll take the atmospheric music over some drivel any day.
On the same note of not being able to talk to your opponents with some in-game tool in RFTG, finding a match can be kind of difficult as well. Not impossible, but I’ve been told that you need to manually refresh the online search. This isn’t really a problem either. To note, whenever I go on, there is usually someone looking to play a game even if I’m not willing to play with them. I’ll shoot random people in Overwatch, but I don’t want to play card games with random people over the internet. Again, that’s just a thing for me.
There are two expansions to play with alongside the vanilla game. It’s easy enough to select which ones you want to play with, but if you’re having trouble learning the game, don’t play with any of the expansions (except the first) because they compound the difficulty that’s already there. The basic mode has three main ways of winning. You can mass a military and take over worlds to get victory points. You can gather worlds that produce goods and then trade them for victory points. Then there is production and that comes off to me as gathering specific cards that require other cards that gives multiple victory points depending on how many requirements you’ve met on specific cards. There is, of course, the possibility of playing a mix of these three to win as well. The expansion Gathering Storm adds some side conditions to earning extra victory points as well as adding additional cards. Rebel Vs. Imperium adds the ability to actually attack other players cards and take over planets. That’s pretty cool and adds a bit of variety for not too much cost (about $3.99 I believe). In all honesty though, I like the basic card game with the NW (the one I mentioned at the top of this paragraph) expansion and I’ve no idea what that stands for, but there’s more cards for more vanilla action and that’s cool.
With all that, RFTG was a super frustrating experience at first. I got to play with Theresa “The Reza” Duringer one of the devs on a Skype’d game where she screen-hacked her way to victory (sarcasm) all in the attempt to teach me how to play. After that, we took it public and on-line in our latest episode of 2 Newbs and a Game where we did a 1v1v1v1 and she straight rocked us all, every time. However, I had a lot of fun. That’s one of the huge stipulations to RFTG for me. If you’ve got buds that will chat with you somehow while playing, RFTG can be a boat-load of fun. If you don’t have any promising leads on buds that will play with you, then I’d say to either get some, be able to play solo (which is actually pretty cool), or be competitive and have fun going online beating rando’s. I was not having much fun with RFTG until I learned the ropes and when my co-op buddy joined me. Having my wife play as well and adding Theresa in the mix only sweetened the pot.

Hello simmers,
With the huge amount of negative reviews I saw, I want to add my voice. First of all a few considerations...
Flight Sim World: a no go?
We have to keep in mind that it is an early access. Some games won't change a lot from EA to the finished product... others change a lot (Minecraft, Empyrion,...). This product may become the long awaited new FSX... if only we give it the chance.
Is it worth its price?
At the current state no. But this is not a finished product. You are paying for the final game, not the game as it is today. So, if Dovetail Games play it right... it may become a 60 USD game easily.
First impressions:
The menu is a bit slow and need a bit of extra work. Since I haven't a lot of time these days I just started a flight from LSZL (Locarno, Switzerland)... Obviously with a storm and everything on max. I experienced no lag except some short spikes every 10-20 seconds: but those spikes were so short they did not ruin the experience. Sure... it would be better to smooth them out.
Raindrops and atmosphere were really nice.
Towns, road and railroads: those need a bit of work. Rounded streets and rail turns, bridges, ... those could definitely be better. The towns seems correctly placed but, at least in this area, they are too small, and there are too many trees as a replacement. For VFR this should be upgraded.
Keyboard (I haven't tried my saitek setup yet nor a joystick, does those work yet?) keys are similar as FSX and the on screen messages too. A bad thing? A good thing? I think it is a personal choice, but for me it is a good thing.
Airplane models: those looks good... but... too few and all small prop plane. A bigger jet could have cheered everyone up a bit.
Crashes... and not game crashes... it would be nice to have some simulation of those... not just a frozen image as FSX.... I used Passenger X with FSX and it made a huge difference in emergencies.
Let's hope that in the future there will be cheap addons... Paying a lot for addons may ruin this game.

As this is an Early Access title I find it hard to really leave a review of what is in effect a product in it's beta stage of development. Therefore I will limit my review to a few comments.
After using FSW for over 3 hours I ended up feeling that it is like a cleaned up and slightly improved version of FSX SE such to the point that I consider it like a v1.1 of such. I feel it does have potential, if DTG seriously improve it but it needs a lot of work (and time) to match anything like PrePar3D v3.x or X-Plane 11. The price of $25 is pretty fair but be aware it is quite unstable and full of issues at the moment. I am guessing the low price is because DTG expect to make the real money from all the addons that will soon start to appear on Steam.
Coming from X-Plane 11 and PrePar3D and accepting FSW as a 'beta' product I did like it but the big unknown is, can DTG pull it off and make FSW into a polished mature flight sim in time. At the moment I think it could just as well sink as suceed.
