First impressions?
Awesome and this game shows a ton of potential. Sure, it can definitely be considered a reskinned FSX...but honestly, that to me is what was needed. It takes a lot of what FSX presented and applies modern engines and graphical updates. All the people complaining about FPS crap, sure, the game definitely isn't going to be in its most optimized state, as it is EARLY ACCESS, first release at that.
I was able to run this at 4k, ultra everything with a i7 6700, 16gb ram, and gtx1080, at 30-40fps. That is definitely probably a potential outlier as a rig for a lot of sim hobbyists, but as this is a modern game running in 64 bit, with directx11, it is going to require some beefy hardware. A lot of the complaining I have seen where people complain about crap frame rate and then they list their graphics card, well they have the bare minimum (GTX970). Here lies a couple issues; Sure, maybe we can blame this on a♥♥♥♥♥♥optimization, early access, screw dovetail blah blah blah!!!!!, or realize ya sure. The minimum specs are what basically allow the game to run. If you want it to look good and run well, well, it is going to require some beefier hardware as this game is being made to take advantage of what the modern engines have to offer!
The airplanes are gorgeous. Absolutely stunning I gotta say. The team did a really good job on modeling and the details look very good in the planes I have hopped in.
Now! MY MAJOR GRIPE!!!!!!!!! WTF IS GOING ON WITH THE PHYSICS OF THE PA-28? (I am ripping this one as this is the plane I fly 2-3 times a week). Straight and level flight, 50% power. Other than that, felt good and I am VERY optimistic about the future of this game as DoveTail continues the development, bug fixes, and optimization of this.

I've stopped for a while in most locations to take a closer look at the beatiful surroundings and envinronment, but it was harder to feel the world, even summons felt more boring than in Dark Souls I. Besides little flaws, Dark Souls 2 did everything better, combat and movement felt more smooth, returning idea from Demon Souls to have a base, or a little encampment I should say, was also cool, while there still were some important NPC's scattered around locations, really liked that. Controls for keyboard and mouse (I don't have any pad, so yeah, I play the "hard way") were easier to learn and comfortable to manage later on, and, most importantly, connection system was really working this time, so I had multiple chances to finally enjoy jolly cooperation with friends, without struggling to see each other signs. PVP is also more fun, but that's just my opinion.

I remembered this fondly from years ago and frequently I would think about the mini-game blitzball, which was a joy none of the other Final Fantasy incarnations had reached.  When I realised that the game had been remastered, I was apprehensive - what if my memory had been making it seem better?  I shouldn't have worried - it is still fantastic.  I am not even that deep into the game proper this time around, since the mini-game, which you can access from any save point, is worth the full price of the game on its own.  Blitzball is basically like underwater soccer/volleyball where your team develops over leagues and cups and you can recruit players to fit the needs of your team.
If you are going to get any of the FF titles then get this one.  The basic game has all the elements you could want from a RPG and has plenty to offer on its own.

I didn't think much of the first Homefront and I was largely disinterested in any prospect of a sequel, so when The Revolution rolled around and the reviews were lukewarm at best, I can't say I was surprised. Regardless, I like trying free games and gave this one a shot. The result was an experience I wouldn't pay money for. Revolution is the sort of game that is best defined by the games it isn't, and in this case that's not a good thing. Somebody described it as being Tom Clancy's The Division except worse, so I guess its like Destiny except much worse and with no campaign coop. Or double jumping. And motorcycles that handle like crap.
First off, the damage model is heinously bad. I am so bored of games where you can take about as much punishment as a dying mosquito and see the game over screen faster then it takes to blink. Even in the first Homefront you could take more punishment then you can in Revolution. It's a mess, and dooms the entire experience from the first gunfight. To make matters worse, player movment is unsually sluggish, even for a military shooter. You needed a slide manuever or leaning around corners and there is neither. They give you the durability of a call of duty protagonist but then give you a dwindling stack of medkits, leaving you♥♥♥♥♥♥out of luck when they run out. Weapon selection is fairly limited and restricted further by progression.
While It has a richer color palette and better sound design then a lot of contemporary "realistic" shooters, that's about all it has going for it. That and the inclusion of a coop mode, compared to the sloppily-designed Battlefield-knockoff versus mode of the first game or its developer's previous work, the incredibly forgettable Frontlines: Fuel of War.
Although its a bit older then such, the best way for me to describe this game is an inferior version of Wolfenstein 2: The New Colossus. Both games deal with a totalitarian occupation of the US, both have open areas with side objectives and collectibles, and both games provoked some controversy in their public perception. But where Wolfenstein's B.J. Blazkowicz has both dialogue and monologue to humanize him and care for his friends, Revolution's protagonist, whose name already eludes me, is the typical FPS mute with no motivation or characterization. Where Wolfenstein offers dual-wielding, rotary automatic shotguns, grenade pistols, lasers and flamethrowing mechanical dogs, Revolution offers the same boring♥♥♥♥♥military shooter guns with a coat of grime and graffiti to make them look "resistance-y". Where Wolfenstein gives you piles of health and armor pickups to sustain you through pitched gunfights, Revolution expects you to hide behind a box and take potshots with guns that recoil like a kindergardner was holding them. And though Wolfenstein offers no multiplayer, Revolution's coop is of a type that was better executed by Mass Effect 3, Vermintide and even Call of Duty Ghosts' Extinction mode.
For the sale price of $7.49 you could do considerably worse. But ultimately I can't recommend Revolution simply on the basis that there many better games.

Race for the Galaxy is, as far as I'm concerned, the finest card game out there. It plays lightning quick, 15-30 minutes per game, but packs more interesting decisions in that time than most games 10 times as long.
In RftG, you have a hand of cards, each card corresponds to a planet or development. Each card usually has one or two powers on it, perhaps it gains a resource in the production phase, perhaps it gives a discount or a bonus card on future developments, perhaps it sells goods into victory points...
These cards are also your cash though, so for that 3 cost card, you will have to throw away 3 other cards to play it, which means three other options.
In addition, the various "phases" of the game turn have to be called before they happen. Each turn begins with players simultaneously revealing what they would like to do that turn. If nobody calls develop, nobody will develop that turn. The person who called develop will get to develop with a slight bonus, and everyone else may develop at cost unless they called it too. So if call the "get more cards" phase, everyone else will get a card too. This gets complicated fast as once people start building their empires, they start amassing such bonuses in certain phases that you don't want to call that action. Your goods-producing empire gets threatened fast when someone gets a world that lets them draw 2 cards every time produce occurs.
This leads to a lot of different strategies. Do you want to corner the market on shipping goods? Expand with military power? Flood the board with settled planets or developments to try to get those victory points? And how are you feeding these empires? Are you trading goods to refill your hand? Do you have enough goods producing worlds to do that without falling behind? It is a RACE for the galaxy, after all. But, since you have to more or less toss your hand to make any play, you usually are trying to cobble together an engine from one of the 4-6 parts the deck is willing to give you. Do you keep the big scoring combo card in your hand for most of the game as dead weight until you have what it takes to get it out and score big? Or do you pitch it and try to stay mobile?
The port is solid and lovely, with AI and online options, including the incredibly powerful Keldon AI. RftG takes a while to learn but you'll soon see why it is my favorite card game if you give it a shot.

My background: I played Hearthstone ferociously for about six months before growing tired of its stale metas. I moved onto Duelyst and found I enjoyed the more complex, board-based gameplay, but recent expansions have promoted flashy, swingy games with increasing amounts of RNG. I also tried other popular alternative CCGs such as Shadowverse and Elder Scrolls: Legends. Neither hooked me.
Eternal drew me in with its diverse set of game modes. Feel like grinding? Gauntlet lets you play constructed decks versus the AI for decent, continuous rewards. Ladder shows greater diversity than games like Hearthstone, owing in part to the large deck sizes which allow for common archetypes to exist in a variety of forms and combinations. Draft is excellent, featuring its own ladder with end of the month rewards. It's an awesome way to build your collection, as you get to keep the cards you draft. This allows for a wonderfully direct way to customize your collection, especially as you're starting out.
While the diversity of game modes is what drew me in, the rich gameplay is what has really hooked me. Mechanics such as Echo (when an Echo card is drawn it automatically creates a copy of itself that also goes in hand), Relic Weapons (hero weapons whose live totals can be modified through a variety of means providing you with extra attacking and removal options that can last a long time if used strategically), defender-prescribed blocking, and Fast Spells (spells that can be played in response to an opponent's actions including on their turn) make for some deep, strategic, and interactive gameplay that is much more rewarding than the back-and-forth nature of Hearthstone.
The card-based power mechanics (reminiscent of Magic's Lands) makes deck building very flexible and multi-faceted. Three-faction decks are common and strike a nice balance between the power of having more options and the increased challenge necessary to pilot such a deck. At the same time mono-faction decks are quite valiable, with two faction decks perhaps the most common and presently supported. Deck construction can be as streamlined or multifaceted as you desire.
Eternal's meta is regularly in flux owing to consistent tuning by the developers (who show more willingness and tact to nerf or buff than Hearthstone's Team 5), but is generally much more friendly to slower decks than the other aforementioned CCGs I've played.
The game is intensely F2P friendly. In addition to the ability to keep the cards you draft in draft modes, each win in constructed nets you a chest which awards both gold and cards (the rarity of which increases as the chest rarity rises). Packs provide twelve cards: 8 common, 3 uncommon (equivalent to a rare in Hearthstone or Duelyst), and 1 rare ("epic") or legendary. Gold-level chests award packs, and Draft and Forge (draft versus the AI) also award chests at a run's completion. All this is to say, regularly play is very well rewarded and allows for the amassing of an extensive collection.
I've enjoyed Eternal tremendously for its rich gameplay. It's hard to believe the game is still in Beta. Future features like in-client tournament modes and best out of 3 play will only further round out this already stellar game. If you're a fan of card games, especially deeper ones, I can't recommend Eternal strongly enough.

I think this is a great implementation of a really good card game. The AI is plenty strong to hone your skills.  If you have a iOS or android version, you can link your account to keep up with your games on the go.  The developers did a good job of avoiding common digital board game pitfalls (unnecessary 3d graphics, slow gameplay, lack of online play), and I can't wait to see what future patches will hold for it.  I would love to see other boardgames get this treatment.

The best card game there is, especially for two players. A beautiful design that squeezes an enormous amount of tough decisions into a fifteen minute time frame. There's no need to build decks, collect new cards, or grind for booster packs - Everything you need is included. You'll easily get hundreds of plays from just the base deck of 114 cards, and still feel like you haven't explored all the possibilities and can improve further.
In Race, people will not beat you because they've spent more money on the game than you - They'll beat you because they know the game better than you. And then, in single player mode, the truly excellent AI will pummel you some more. This is to be expected, since some people have been playing this game for ten years already. However, the Steam implementation is a great way to start getting ready to face the folks who only agree to play the fabled "GS/RvI/BoW Arc".
Some people will tell you the game is hard to learn. Sure, there's a learning curve. Race is quite different from the card games you might be familiar with. The Steam version helps a lot, though, since you cannot make illegal plays.
Other people will tell you this game is multiplayer solitaire. But the more you play, the more you'll realize that reading your opponent and planning accordingly is absolutely crucial. Staring only at your own cards will not work.
Some people will tell you Magic the Gathering is the better game. Unfortunately, there's no helping those folks.

This game is a perfect example of why Steam reviews need a "Kinda Recommended" button instead of yes or no, because Luckslinger has a lot of good, that is sadly bogged down by some questionable design choices and insipid difficulty.
* Presentation
The game looks fairly average at best. The low-detail pixel art is ugly at times, but the use of colour and the emotions presented in animations give the game life. The different locations are all visually unique and sport some cool design choices, and each one has great atmosphere. The music is also really damn good, with some excellent hip-hop choices that really compliment the atmosphere. Overall the game has a great sense of charm with little details, like how people speak in record-vinyl scratching, or the clickclickclick of reloading your pistol. The story of the game is also really good, with some great dialouge that gives life to the characters- special note given to the main 6 bad guys of the game, who each have some interesting reasons for doing what they do.
* Gameplay
The game has a number of great ideas. It is a run and gun shooter with emphasis placed on Luck above all things- Luck is in fact a collectable, and can be used to turn bullets away from you, drop rewards and so on. This works in reverse too- low luck means bad things happen, and this puts an interesting spin on things. The game has a number of little details that make it fun, like a duck assist character,  a 6 shot ammo limit for your gun, and a throwing knife. The controls, however, make what could be an interesting take on a run and gun extremely frustrating. The Luckslinger frankly controls like ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥ His jump arc is really impercise, his dodge roll is useful for exclusively bullets (meaning everything else must be dodged over) and has a cooldown, meaning it's useless to use in a firefight with a lot of people, which the game throws at you with alarm.  The game style, however, is simply not built for this kind of hectic firefight, so you end up dying a lot. Add the fact that your invincibility frames are non-existent to very small and you get a game trying to be a bullet hell that cannot handle being one. Oh, and he also cancels reloading by jumping or rolling, which makes reloading (which the game will NOT auto do for you) a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ and more of a detriment than a factor of the game you need to work around, like Carry Capacity in Dark Souls. It's extremely frustrating to play this game because underneath the terrible controls is a genuinely intelligent spin on the run and gun genre, and to see such amateur failures bog it down is disheartening.
* Design
And here is where the game really ♥♥♥♥♥ the bed. Luckslinger is too hard for it's own good- in an attempt to be "oh so #Oldschool" Duckbridge made a game that is hard for the wrong reasons, including the aforementioned flaws in the gameplay section, but this extends into design. For starters, the basic difficulty mode is extremely cruel- there are checkpoints, but lose all your lives and you're back to the start. In any game like Castlevania, this is fine- most stages in that game are like 10 minutes long. In here, the stages easily surpass 20 minutes, which can make backtracking through the whooooolllleeee damn stage a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ and not fun at all. Losing luck after every hit is also extremely annoying, as it causes a cycle of hurting every time you get hit, meaning you'll just keep losing. The game's level design leaves a lot to be desired, as instead of coming up with unique scenarios for you to fight through, it just swamps you with foes and says "deal with it". For a game that obviously wants to be played fast and risky, it sure is easy and reliable to cheese. These design and gameplay problems come together to for a game that tries to be hard and forgets to be fair- in a hard game like Super Meat Boy, every death is my fault and I know it, because the controls are so tight and the design is so fair that I never got frustrated at the game. Here, Luckslinger just made me want to put down the game and never play it again because I always felt my deaths were not preventable, which is a shame because the game does have some replay value and some great uses of player choice.
Overall, Luckslinger could have been a must buy with some great ideas and pretty good excecution, but in it's current state, plagued with rookie mistakes, it simply lies as an okay game that should be examined as how to NOT do difficulty.
Luckslinger receives an 5/10. Only get it on sale, if you even want it.

Eternal Card Game, or Eternal as I wish it were called, is an interesting game in today's Hearthstone copypasta world. While the former throws away any standard TCG phases, and allows you to do whatever you please whenever you'd like during your turn, Eternal reminds us of the refreshing appeal of such lost mechanics. To the opposite of many, I don't find this as a Hearthstone the Gathering if you will, but more of a young heir to the empire of MTG. You have your red wins decks, midrange control decks, arguably the most frustrating, Clockroach decks, and really any sort of deck you desire (just build the clockroach deck. I know you don't understand yet, but just do it).
While we are talking about these phases, it really is a refreshing reminder of why Magic has stood the test of time for so long. You basically have your Standby phase, Main phase, Attack Phase, and second Main Phase. There are instant spells you can cast any time duruing a particular phase, ambush units that are creatures who act like instant spells, flying units, and my favorite which are the warcry units. Everytime these units attack the next unit or weapon in your deck gets +1/+1. There are more unit types on top of the ones I listed, but these were the first that came to mind right away. These unit mechanics on top of the phases makes for a true strategic experience that many TCG's are missing as of late. It adds that layer of card quality I've desired ever since Hearthstone♥♥♥♥♥♥on any strategy but "♥♥♥♥ it, give me strength RNG gods."
Although Eternal certainly has it's positive moments, there are also the negatives, such as drawing 13 mana in a row against red wins. There are also the occasional mechanical hiccups, such as units with aegis (they ignore one spell or effect and then lose the shield) being destroyed by kill spells regardless if they still have the shield, or the ever so broken cards such as clockroach (seriously, you Hearthstone boys think Jades are bad, you have not seen the infuriating power of clockroach).
With that said, I have seem to been never the less entranced by a particular part of the game known as the Gauntlet. This completely Player vs AI gamemode allows you to pick one of your currently constructed decks and face off against multiple computer oppents with increasing difficulty. As you win your rewards are increased further, and after multiple fights you will face a sort of boss. Unlike the fights before this one, there is a unique mechanic to these fights. From all multi-faction units gaining +1/+1, to every player drawing two cards at the beginning of each of their respective turns. Win against every opponenet and you earn yourself three silver chests and a new rank in this particular mode. This game mode alone allows you to rack up a good amount of gold, used to buy packs, and a solid card collection as well. If you're honestly looking to see the best of this game I suggest you dive into this as soon as you have a decent competive deck(Aggro Warcry works fantastic).
In the end, there is much of this game I have left out of this review. Let's go over them real quick. First, there are multiple factions to choose from (just think Magic and you will be fine). Second, Ranked so far is nothing to cheer about, and the other game modes like forge and draft will increase in value as more sets are released. Third, the campaign is utterly boring, and even locks specific cards behind it (the game won't even allow you to craft them until you buy the bonus campaign for $10).
Right now, I think the best idea is to atleast install the game and give a run at the Gauntlet. It will give you a clear understanding of how the game plays, and the different deck archetypes that work best. I see a strong future for Eternal Card Game if the developers keep an honest effort into increasing the total card count, and doing whatever it takes to build a solid player base. They are heading in the right direction with giving away plenty of gold for packs, and even guarenteeing legendaries if you actually choose to spend your hard earned cash. With this said, we have seen plenty of games pushed through the gutters of developer greed, something I hope to never see for a game with so much potential.

This is one of those times where Steam really needs a "neutral" option. I've only just started this game and so far I find it enjoyable enough but I can completely understand why people don't like it.
First, let's deal with the elephant in the room: microtransactions in a $60 game, DLC is overpriced for what you get, DRM in the form of vague and unnecessary MMO-elements, and Uplay is a thing. Basically, Ubisoft is Ubisoft and ♥♥♥♥ Ubisoft.
How about some positives? The world is enormous and quite beatiful too. I can't remember where I read this but I saw that someone did a road trip from NYC to LA and it took 39 minutes, averaging 150 MPH, to give you a sense of scale. There's plenty of missions and things to do, tons of hours of gameplay if you're willing to invest the time. Car customisation is fairly extensive. You have to unlock most of the parts but there are plenty as areas that can be customised, including the interior, which is something I haven't come across in other racing/car games.
And now for the negatives. As you probably expect, the story is rubbish: you avenge the death of a character you've barely met as a character you won't care about. Hmm, now where have I seen this before? Oh, that's right, every other Ubisoft game of 2014! You play as Alex, a former streetracer who is working with police to takedown an illegal street racing/gun smuggling/drug sumggling gang. Like his Watch Dogs counterpart Aiden, he has all the personality of a wet napkin and is completely forgettable. And he also looks like Gordon Freeman's idiot cousin. The car list has some nice selections but it is short, only about 50 cars. The cars themselves have terrible physics that are neither realistic nor particularly fun. They feel very heavy but have little grip, and all seem to snap-oversteer at unusual times with bad understeer the rest of the time; adjusting steering sensitivity hasn't changed this. Spins that would easily be saveable with the throttle and countersteer in other games with proper physics are impossible to save here. I've only played with a 360 controller so far but I'll try my racing wheel at some point to see how that goes. Side quests (mostly small challenges scattered throughough the world) unlock new performance parts but are very repetitive and mostly "meh" anyway.
So why do I recommend this game? Personally, I get a lot of enjoyment from just cruising around the world, discovering landmarks and locations along the way. That factor alone has actually the purchase for me, and the fact I got it on sale made the deal much better. Overall, while I haven't played the most recent games in the series, The Crew feels on par with most of the Need For Speed games I've played: not much in the way of a good narrative but a decent car game, if you're into that sort of thing. If you own an Xbox One (I don't but often use my friend's), I'd recommend picking up Forza Horizon 2 instead; it's a substantially better game on the whole. If you don't, you could do worse than this. The reason I enjoy it is very likely in the minority but to each his/her own. There is a free 2 hour demo, so download that and see what you think.

This game has had many changes recently - many for the better, some for the worse. There's a lot of ongoing development, which is great and keeps things from being stagnant, but the core of the game remains fun. If you only want to play cooperatively, you can do that. If you only want to play PvP, you can do that too. With the recent change from first-win bonus being once per gamemode instead of once in coop and once in PvP, it's a lot easier to earn Warface cash and not have to worry about repair costs- something many players complained of previously.
It's true that if you work super hard and buy permanent gear that's for all the best available, the repair costs are very high, but I see that partly as a way to balance the game. That prevents everyone from always haveing a full set of the best armor and all the best weapons. However, it's still easily affordable to use the best weapons and not the best armor, and if you're good enough with a weapon you'll still come out on top. Armor that is only a bit worse than the best is like half as expensive, and same for weapons, both in purchase price and repairs. There are also daily weapon rewards a few time a week if you come back and frequent rank up bonuses so you don't need to rely only on what you buy.
There's another thing worth mentioning: rentals. Currently, you can only buy permanent items or rent for one day, but if you play a few rounds then with the first win bonuses you'll afford enough to buy a weapon or piece of armor every single day over and over for tyhe rental and not pay any repair costs on it. That means you can try out basically every gun with little loss before deciding to blow your cash on one. See if it works for you, see how easy it is to use, if it makes a big difference to your performance, etc. Same for armor.
There's also the matter of unlockables. These are actually very good weapons and armor which are frequently used by really high level players and cannot simply be bought until unlocked. They have far lower purchase repair costs than comparable weapons and armor from the store - especially when it comes to snipers, where the difference between one 1-hit-kill rifle and another barely matters. This steadily rewards players for playing and lets them incrementally upgrade their gear even playing casually and not always going for the cash bonuses and buying items. You choose a weapon, armor, or attachment, and each round some VP go towards unlocking that item. They get incrementally harder to unlock the next. I ignored armor unlocks almost entirely until rank 28 and now I can unlock some in like 3 rounds, while weapons and attachments take dozens.
All in all, there may be some balance issues here and there, but this game is very fun and can easily be enjoyed casually or competatively.

So this game has really been with me my entire childhood leading onwards. Much of my gaming as a child in elementary was actually spent playing this game on PS2, and since then, this game still evokes nostalgia. Though this may seem like a personal value, and though it may strongly be, I justify that this game has been able to grasp me and never really let go. It's narrative is beautiful, remeniscent of some previous Final Fantasy games, but on its own, it is unique, touching upon religion, the fragility of such, and dreams of the individual. For its powerful and emotional story, there is no critique. The characters felt comical at first, but as the game progresses, there is a tie that formed between myself and the characters, and with each moment of desperation, I felt it alongside, though relatively. This is a game that truly outlasts the flood of copies, imitations, and fillers, and from this release of a remastered version, I can only say that I am overjoyed to experience my youth once again, and to me, there is no greater game in value, albiet personal. Without hesitation, as objectively as I may speak, Final Fantasy X is more about the story than the gameplay, as the latter is standard JRPG, and X-2 is similar, but more for the fans, therefore I see it as an addon of the original X game. Regardless, with no particular exaggeration, I claim that Final Fantasy X/X-2 HD Remaster is a must-play masterpiece.

FFX - 44 hours
Another Final Fantasy game and obviously I'll recommend it. This is good, really good. But also different than the previous titles. The first fully 3D game in the series (no pre-rendered static backgrounds) so the game feels a bit more alive. Yet also a bit more dull. The 3D graphics are not the best, I mean the game was released in 2001 and even with the HD remaster you can see the grapichs are a bit plain. But tbh we don't play FF games for the graphics.
The battle system is perfect. I'd actually say this is the best battle system in any FF game. It's turn based but no ATB so you can just chill in the battle and really think out what should be your next step. But the game is a bit "easy" so you shouldn't really have any problem with any battles at all. There are several ways to constantly deal maximum damage in every battle so the game shouldn't be a headache. Ofc that depends on your playstyle too (are you willing too farm some items and do some side quests or not). You can get Hyper Mighty G and Trio of 9999 around mid game and finish basically every boss battle in a few turns. For that I can once again highly recommend the Jegged walkthrough guide
Or just check the mixes and where you can get the items you need
The sphere grid system is also really good. While it's a bit linear you still have some flexibility. You can turn any character into a magic or physical damage dealing one. It's really fun yet not too complicated. Actually it later inspired the Path of Exile developers. If you play that game you can see how the two skill systems are really similar. The only negative thing is Kimahri. He doesn't have his own path so from the start you can go any routes and basically become a (weaker) copycat of another character. So in the end you will not play Kimahri that much (tho there is one boss fight where you have to, so it can be a problem if you didn't level him)
The story is... You know... It's Final Fantasy, it's always good. Kinda a cliché but this really the truth. You will laugh a lot yet cry like a baby in the end. Also you will have a lot of questions (bit like FF8). I still think tho that FF9 has a better story than this. But in the end you can't really compare the games. Yeah I'm contradicting myself here.
The music is also phenomenal. I used the original soundtrack not the arranged one. The voice acting is also good. Sometimes a bit cheesy and the lip sync is usually off but that's because of the japanes VO.
In the end you should play this game. I can only repeat myself: it's Final Fantasy, it's good, it's moving. It's everything you want from a video game.
"You'll cry. You're gonna cry. You always cry, see? You're crying."?
FFX-2 - 38 hours
After finishing FFX you should obviously play FFX-2. It is the first sequel game in the whole FF franchise. It's a good game but has its problems and mostly with the story not the gameplay.
First the gameplay: it is totally different than FFX. ATB is back so no more chilling in the battle, you have to act as soon as possible. Instead of the sphere grids we have dresspheres and garment grids. Dresspheres are basically jobs. If you played the old NES/SNES FF games they will be really familiar. Black mage, white mage, warrior, thief etc. All classic jobs are available and ofc new ones too. Most of the better and more strong dresspheres have to be unlocked in several side quests so not something you get automatically. In my experience the Death Knight + Alchemist + Lady Luck combo is the best. But to some extent it doesn't really matter becasue the game is incredibly easy. Garment grids are similar to the sphere grid in the first game. But instead of unlocking skills and stat points you equip your dresspheres. And each garment grid gives you different bonuses. For example more stats, special abilites etc. And in battles you can change between dresspheres you have equipped on the garment grid so one turn you can be a white mage, than black mage, than gunner etc. The combination is only limited by your imagination (tho it's recommended to stick one character with DPS jobs, one with magical etc.)
So the gameplay is really fun. I mentioned that the game is really easy and yeah... it's really really easy. You can get a Bloodlust item (Berserk + 60 STR) in the Bevelle underground at chapter 2. And that makes the whole game a cakewalk. Put it on Paine with Warrior than later with Death Knight and you have an automatic kill machine. You can't control her but have a healer and a mage in your party and the game is done (as I said above: Death Knight + Alchemist + Lady Luck is the best combo imo). No Jegged guide for this game so I used this:
Now the story. That's the main problem with the whole game: some of the endings are invalidating the first game. And there are multiple endings. There is a sad, a normal, a good, and the perfect one. And there are enough differences that they make the first game less good if I can say that. It's really strange actually because FFX had a really strong message (like FFVII) and a certain tone or mood. Well everything like that is gone in FFX-2. It's more lightweight and more cheesy. That's obviously not should be a problem on its own. It's only a problem because this game is a sequel to a pretty strong main line FF title which considered to be one of the best. So the difference between the two games' story and the quality of the story is day and night.
In the end I think FFX is a better game. And while FFX-2 has a really fun gameplay the story makes the whole game less good as it could have been. Some can even say that even the mere existence of this game puts the story of FFX under question as the ending of that game was pretty much perfect.
But I still recommend to play this game. It's Final Fantasy after all.

Do you want a true battlefield experience? Then look no further than Verdun. Never have I played a FPS that made me sweat at the idea of running across no man's land trying to invade the enemy's trench. This is not the kind of game where you rank up kills while soaking bullets like some kind of super soldier. If one bullet hits you, you are dead. You better get used to the idea because that's all you're going to do at the start of your first assault. You will quickly realize just how serious the situation is when you start seeing your comrades fall to the ground as the sound of mortars pierce your ears, all while trying to dodge machine gun fire and hopefully not get sniped for the 100th time as you slowly make your way through all the chaos. Your accuracy has never been more important than now. Having fast reflexes is essential if you want to stay alive. In order to improve you need to practice, so I suggest playing Squad Defense mode - it's basically where players fight off endless waves of enemy bots, which sounds less realistic, but consider it a target practice mode that will help you a lot in the beginning.
Verdun set out to recreate the horror that was WW 1 by putting players in the shoes of the brave men that fought in it. In my opinion the game succeeds with flying colors and is one of the best war games you can play. Highly recommended!

This game seems on the surface to be a casual cooking/managment game that you often find on free online games websites. This is a cooking game, and a management game, but it is quite debateable whether or not it is 'casual', although I am not saying all casual games are bad, as I have played some good ones, but it does seem to not have as many fatures as a casual game, as cooking and casual aren't always the same thing.
The reason I say this isn't a casual game, is because when you think of casual games, you would normally think of a relaxing and easy-to-play game, something where you don't need to think. This game is far from relaxing, it is a great simulation of having a panic attack. There is no easy mode, only normal and extreme, and even normal mode can seem quite impossible. Juggling all these different foods, while at the same time having to do chores, such as flush the toilet, because we all know that's a chef's job.
The gameplay in this is not only intense, but it is also centred around typing. It would be easy if it was simply typing out words, such as what the food/recipe was, but no, you have to prapere the food, and each ingrediant/action is one letter, meaning you will end up muttering to yourself while you type a ridiculous combo of letters and numbers.
PSCR PSCR PSCR
Once you get use to one combonation of letters for a certain meal, you will then, upgrade it as you go, and struggle to learn even more keys. As well as prapering foods for consumtion, you need to amke sure they don't burn, that you don't accidentally press 4 when you meant to press 5 and serve the food undercooked.
There is so much more to be said about this game: the graphics, the music, the humour and references, the progression, the events, etc. But all that needs to be said for it, is that you should buy it and play it, as it is quite worth it's money, and is a very enjoyable game, with a very high replay value.

What if Quentin Tarantino directed a videogame Western for the Atari 7800? That's Luckslinger in a nut-shell. You're a man with no name, whose deeds will become legend, when you deal with the nastiest, most ruthless, and luckiest outlaws in the West. This action-packed shooter puts up a decent enough challenge, but it's the attention to detail and excellent soundtrack that'll preserve it's long-term appeal.
I really can't say enough about how good the music is in this game. It's somewhere between spaghetti western and hip-hop. There aren't any weak tracks in the game. The sound-design is on point as well. The minimal dialogue is "voiced" by record scratches, which perfectly fits the lo-fi aesthetics. I also appreciate that the other sound-effects aren't bleeps and blurps. Just because it looks like an Atari game, doesn't mean it has to sound like one.
With that aside, visually this game is very impressive. I'd describe it as a "less is more" approach, and a lot of effort was put into those pixels. A number of characters have interesting animations, some more subtle than others. A lot of the great imagery is in the finer details. Grand vistas and extravagant backgrounds would distract from the core of this game. This is a fairly tough adventure, and proper visual-design is a must. Overall, Luckslinger is a fantastic audiovisual experience.
The action-platformer is a genre almost as old as time itself, so a lot of different ideas are necessary. On the surface, these games can look alot alike, so it takes some thoughtful game-design to carve out an identity. In this respect, Luckslinger continues to impress. The protagonist carries a gun, but it can only fire six shots. He has unlimited ammo, but can only reload while on the ground. These design-decisions lead to a different style of play. Your adversaries tend to use guns as well, so you'll have to jump (or dodge-roll) their shots, while finding opportunities just to reload.
It can be argued that this mechanic prolongs gun-battles, but I think it works perfectly for the game. It forces you to pay more attention to enemy patterns. In platformers with a heavy emphasis on shooting, we depend on tried and true strategies like "mash the fire button" and "get close and shoot until its dead". Since this game limits your abilities, you'll spend more time moving around, seeing what your foes are capable of, and so on. It's thoughtful game-design, and doesn't take anything away from the pacing. Furthermore, your arsenal includes a throwing knife. As you play, you'll discover more ways to incorporate this handy weapon into your strategy.
Luck plays a part in the game as well. Whenever you kill an enemy, there's a chance they'll drop a "shiny". No, I don't know what it's called, so bear with me. Shinies raise the chance that good things happen to you. This includes everything from bullets harmlessly curving around you to birds & giant moles(?) saving you from bottomless pits. You lose shinies whenever you take damage (or die), so naturally the better you play, the luckier you'll stay. I'm of the old school when it comes to game difficulty. I believe that games should become easier if the player is having trouble, and harder if they're getting better. Luckslinger reverses this concept, and surprisingly I agree with how it is handled.
Most of the other reviews you'll see on this page point out the game's difficulty. They're certainly not wrong, because some of the later stages and bosses can be really tough. However, this is also a game where the second play-through is much easier than the first. Once you understand the enemy locations, the boss patterns, and your abilities as the Luckslinger, you'll have no problems holding onto shinies. The extra boost of luck will it make it easier for veteran players to grab all of the gold bars for the best ending.
However, if you think that maybe things have gotten a little too easy, then there's the unlockable difficulty. In this mode, everything kills in one hit. I can see the appeal, but I would have preferred something a bit more substantial. A mode with new/tougher enemies, more intricate boss-patterns, and slightly longer stages would have been amazing. On the plus side, the mechanics are more than suitable for a potential no-hit run. I say potential because there's no way I'd have the patience for it. The irony that someone with a Cave avatar just wrote this is not lost on me.
As far as nitpicks go, I would have liked an option to "chill" in Clovercreek. Over the course of the game, this ghost town eventually flourishes, but once you complete the last bounty, you have to part ways. Since this game constantly auto-saves, I had to restart and replay most of the game, just to unlock all of the NPCs and other extras. All told, there's not THAT much to do in the town, but it'd be nice to work on my beer-chugging and skateboarding. There's also the minor annoyance that is losing a game of Russian Roulette, even when my luck is maxed out. That's probably something I shouldn't pay a lot of mind to. I mean, it's called luck for a reason.
In conclusion, Luckslinger is a very good game. It's a testament to the early days of game-development. All it took was three people (one designer, one programmer, and one composer) to put together this high-quality adventure. Nowadays, eh well..perhaps I shouldn't talk about nowadays. It's better to appreciate the fact that even today, unique games like this one can be made.

64 bit. Yeah. About time for this FSX  platform. Enough of the OOMs with FSX/P3D. Enough of having to strip down all the ORBX stuff just to make a woeful 32 bit memory address constraint. If you have flown flight sims, and particularly the FSX/P3D series for decades as I have, it bloody well is the next generation i.e., 64 bit. It's too bad it took so long to get here as XP 10 had already done it a couple of years back. But here we are. And knowing the years of curmudgeons set in their ways about the FS incarnations and the money spent on addons like any new incarnation there will be crying and handwringing. For the reasons noted above everyone should be clapping and moving forward that the pathetic memory constraints of the 32 bit platform can now be a thing of the past. As it is you can port over numerous of your payware airports with some  degree of success - see the thread on discussions for that.
Easy settings for input devices. I have the T.Flight Hotas4, Saitek yoke and quadrant and CH pedals. Recognized all the connected devices and I was easily able to set them re throttle, mixture, flaps, etc. Child's play.

Welcome to the wild west where you are a lone gunslinger whose destiny changes when you receive a luck ring. If you can harness the powers you can become the luckiest gunman there is, but if you neglect your luck you will find that the bullets will always find you and your death will come quick.
In Luckslinger, developed by Duckbridge, you are not going to be blown away with the 2D sidescroller graphics, actually you'll probably be having fits of nostalgia with the 8-bit graphic approach. The thing is that its the game mechanics and the pusic that is going to keep you hooked.
I highly recommend that you play this game with a controller, it definitely feels like the more solid of the control choices. You will notice that depending on your luck you can be saved by what would otherwise be costly mistakes while controlling the game.
Now I mention the music, and I've said this about a million times in my videos to this point, it has that level of professionalism that reminds me of the record scratching you would find in a high end anime like Samurai Champloo. There's just something about it that makes you get into the beat and get lost in the game.
So lets go over the main game mechanic, and that is the luck mechanic. You are going to be gifted a luck ring, and there will be others out there with one too, and of course you will have to, when the time comes, take down those people. So here's the deal you are going to want to shoot, kill, and discover hidden secrets as much as possible because you can then use what you find to fill up your luck ring, and when you get enough luck bullets will change directions away from you, you will be caught from falling, and much more. Now the flip side is that things will try to fall on you, you're going to have to be much more careful around enemies, etc.
I will also admit that this is a game that is not the easiest to pick up, you are going to have to learn the ends and outs of the game, you will have to make damn sure you don't take too much damage because when you do you lose some of that luck, and if you lose enough, you are going to find yourself being gunned down, getting crushed to death, or of course falling into a very deep and very deadly hole.
In the end this is a game I would recommend for those who are looking for a challenge, want a piece of their childhood, but at the same time have the beats to make it feel new. So if you think you are a gunslinger, then take on this challenge, and find those who are abusing the luck rings. This game gets an 8.1 out of 10.

Banished is a wonderful vacation from the typical Real-Time Strategy (RTS) which always seems to see your labors of building a grand city demolished by invading forces.  Banished has no war aspect, no invaders, no pirates, and no lions lurking in the shadows waiting to eat your exploring villager.
You control a township that breaks away from the thick of thin things to build a self-sustaining town:  woodcutters, farmers, fishermen (and women), gatherers, herbalists, miners, stonecutters, etc.  Each villager can be reassigned as needs shift, seasons change, or quarry is stripped.
Bottom line:  This is definitely a welcome change to the standard RTS format.

Quantum Rush Champions is an anti-gravity single-player racing game. Boasting a Career Mode with 9 different challenge (race mode) types, 21 Bosses and 14 racing tracks, a considerable amount of time will be required to see everything this game has to offer.
Career mode starts with choosing one of three racer Manufacturers. Ion Energy Systems specializes in racers with extraordinary shields. Nitroid Racing focuses on improving their racers' boosters while Nanofabric Motorworks aims to produce the most balanced and steady racers. After choosing a Tier (racer), 6+ different Challenge types must be completed in order to progress. Each subsequent Tier (7 Tiers for each manufacturer) is unlocked by achieving a required number of medals and defeating the Tier's Boss. These medals are received upon fulfilling certain challenge requirements. The following 9 challenge types are listed below.
:
Throughout the race, an on-board weapon can be used to shoot enemies down. These weapons are part of random awards received at the end of each successful challenge. Some of the weapons include pulse-fire shooters or lasers. Due to the curvature of the track and the weapons' inability to lock-on, it can be very difficult to effectively utilize them. To supplement this, pickup items at designated locations are also provided for support. Three items can be carried at once and toggled for situational use. Unfortunately, these items can not be fired backwards (excluding mines). Some of the items include: armor, shields, lock-on rockets, AOE fire and straight-fire rockets. Although using these items are crucial to success, the hitbox for the pickup items are rather small. Even though they are presented as holographic squares that are the size of an average racer, a direct collision through the center of the item is required for it to register as received.
Arcade mode provides freely configurable challenges to allow customized races. Every challenge type is available for modification with the exception of boss races. The race parameters that can be altered are listed below.
:
The graphics and aesthetics for QRC is very similar to other high octane/anti-gravity racers. A futuristic feel is generated with the use of the darker spectrum of the color palette and many vertical lines, imitating a sense of traveling through tubes, tunnels or wires. The tight level design helps create a sense of speed. QRC is a far cry from the common indie graphics seen in many shovelware that utilize the most basic native engine assets.
The HUD presents three different meters located at each corner of the screen (Energy, Speed, Heat) and an armor meter with 3 item pickup icons located at the top. Due to the nature of the high speed racing and intense action, it can be very difficult to look away from the center of the screen to observe the various meters. A more centralized location with the 3 meters in a condensed form would allow for more effictive utilization.
Although QRC has full controller support, this game should have went through more QA testing to fix all of the minor grievances observed while playing with a controller. One such grievance is the fact that the controller does not work on the title menu. Continuing with the troubles, the item toggle button is mapped to a very difficult to reach location and re-mapping it causes the "Summary/Detail/Custom" options to be unusable with any other mapped button. Also, the Alt-Tab feature has caused the game to freeze multiple times.
Even with these minor annoyances, the handling of the racers during gameplay is fairly fluid. The racer is responsive enough to the analog control and the two airbrakes sufficiently allow for fine turning around sharp corners.
The current state of the game may be a bit troubling to some players. The developers seemed to have moved on from this game to their other IPs. It's been exactly one year from this review's posting since an official update was published; Steam News announcements involve GameArt's newer titles. A quick look through the Steam Discussions will reveal a lack of developer-authored posts. What the game has to offer in this state is essentially its "complete" form.
With everything taken into consideration, Quantum Rush Champions is only recommended to those that are fans of anti-gravity single-player racers. The minor bugs and problematic UI navigation can be forgiven, but the lack of online multiplayer/local coop and continued updates will be difficult for many veteran gamers to accept.

I found it hard to even start this game? It's sort of like.. "so what?". I didn't like the idea of starting with free houses and supplies because I'd like to make a well structured city; keeping in mind that civilians can apparently die simply due to the sheer size of a town (they go to get food when they're hungry and die on the way back to their house). The BIGGEST issue I had was the map seeds constantly being extremely awkward for building and planning. There are almost no plains or flat areas, just bumpy, hilly, mountainy, river split areas.
Simply put, starting this game is extremely awkward. I cycled through over 10 map seeds, all of which had mountains and rivers every where. With no way to flatten the area or adjust the terrain you literally have to hope you get lucky, which isn't so bad to some but to me (some what OCD and a perfectionist) it made me LITERALLY throw my hands in the air 3 times, quit the game and give up before I could start. I want to start on the hard "difficulty" (not being given a lot of stuff for free) and I want to be able to construct the basics in a way that I can expand on later without moutains or rivers getting in the way. Finding room to have a well constructed city is just IMPOSSIBLE, once again, keeping in mind the bug that causes civilians to die from starvation during the trip to pick up food.
I'd also like to be able to costumize my stockpiles so that I can order my villagers to have a minimal amount of fireword in there or something, so there can be stockpiles near my houses, you know, so the trip to pick the stuff up isn't lethal. Honestly though, this game is great but for someone who thinks of the long term, its just impossible to start. If you're a "living in the moment" sort of person, this might suit you, as you randomly plonk relevant structures around without guidance of any kind, but after your town really kicks off you're just going to have to accept that because you didn't build to suit the game but instead built to suit the situation, you're villagers will be knocking off one by one from extremely novel situations.
EDIT 1: This being said, I'll try the "wing it" system and disregard the terrain and bugs and then post a much smaller review in 'EDIT 2'.
EDIT 2: Okay so I've been playing this game for 3 days and done and seen everything it has to offer. Ultimately, I cycled through (what felt like hundreds) of map seeds until I came across one that had a reasonably big flat area some where in the map.
I winged it, building stuff as it was needed and adjusting workers to suit circumstances but I've noticed a few things... You're either going to play this game speed x10 or paused. There's simply no reason to play it slowly and because of this it's extremely quick to "finish" (just a days worth of playing). I also tried to move my town to another area that was clear of mountains and rivers so I could work on a functional town that would have everything I needed without being seperated by terrain; people died because they couldn't reach food in time and they were still pretty close. After setting up the foundational buildings, I attempted to remove the stufff from the old town and move it all into the other town. I still was working on food constantly but people were dying from starvation like crazy. Some how, I had about 95% of the community working on gathering food and I was still running low. This ended up as "game over" despite my 2 days of effort of hording massive amounts of food and only building structures to the other town closest to the my old town which they only needed to pass through a tunnel to reach..? I started again on hard difficulty thinking I had the knowledge to get it done but seriously, unless you build exactly the right stuff immediately people start dying like crazy.
Basically I think there needs to be more consideration into the end game content. I don't even nessacarily add more, but instead have a "plains" option for map seeds, this way you can support a large town without falling victim to this games mechanics. I personally don't think it's worth the money because after only 3 days I doubt I'll be touching it anymore because the funnest part is starting over and then once the game kicks off you realize there isn't much point because building a nice end game town that functions perfectly for a 300+ people town is almost impossible to fit in due to the amount of mountains and rivers blocking construction.

Just when you think your town is going well, BOOM... starvation, a lack of tools, or another disaster kicks in.  Say goodbye to all of your little people!
I've played this game over 100 hours and just yesterday had my first really successful town of 800 people.  And that was only after a helpful tip from another player.  That lasted for 57 in-game years, then 150 of them died off, one at a time.  Despite how mad this game makes me -- because of my own bad decisions -- I find myself playing it again, and again, and again... DETERMINED to have a really great town.
Applause to the developer!  You have me hooked!
Update: 600 hours and it still has me addicted!

There are really two types of people in this world. Those who hate maddeningly frustrating twitch platformers like this one, and those who hate maddeningly frustrating twitch platformers like this one so much, they can't stop playing them. Spiritual elder sibling to "You Have To Win The Game," VVVVVV is to the Commodore 64 platformer of yore what its CGA cousin is to the DOS platformer of yore, and I cannot possibly recommend both games enough.
To paraphrase the words that prefaced the Dungeons and Dragons rulebook so many years ago, those gamers who lack patience, those who don't care for Monty Mole's adventures through sprawling maps of tricky-to-navigate rooms, who feel no thrill upon waking up with Lester in the suspended cage in that famously Another World, who do not enjoy rubbing their palmheel raw on the molded plastic grip of an old one-button joystick with a nine-pin connector or trying hundreds of times to see what lies beyond that maddening gauntlet of hazards, even if it's just a blank room that hasn't been visited before, will not be likely to find VVVVVV to their tastes. But those whose curiosity knows no bounds and whose frustration tolerance rivals that of a Zen master will find this game the answer to their SID-soundtracked, load-star-comma-eight-comma-one prayers.
The very simple graphics may put you off; don't let them. The six Vs of the title, the cast of the game, take a little getting-used-to, certainly, and I admit, I would have liked a slightly less stylized (if still period-appropriate) character model, but their simple Carcassone-like iconic cuteness grows on you, or at least a tolerance to it accumulates. The characters have two recognizable facial expressions, and their paddle-like, boxy heads are sized, I suspect, to accommodate those easily-recognizable expression changes. Without sharing spoilers, I should note that it becomes clear, later in the game, that their box-headed design was thematically intentional. If you don't like it, relax, and don't let that stop you from enjoying this amazing game.
The backgrounds, with their stylized metal plating, single-color enemies, and two-plane-deep parallax scrolling gamefield, will be immediately recognizable to C64 fans, as will the bombastic, cheerful, strident soundtrack of in-game looped hits by Magnus Pålsson. While You Have To Win The Game offers only monophonic sound cues, in line with its pre-soundcard DOS-and-PC-speaker pedigree, VVVVVV feels much less stark and empty for its consistently cheerful, upbeat and hopeful tone, and the soundtrack plays a huge role in creating that atmosphere of "Let's play space explorers!" Saturday morning excitement.
Again, like its cousin, the massive, sprawling map is liberally dotted with continue points, which make recovering from one of the game's many nigh-inevitable deaths less painful, as little ground must be regained afterward. Like its cousin, exploration is key, and will be rewarded -- the map view offers a tantalizing glimpse of area not yet traveled, and the desire to wipe away all the blank areas on it is strong. Like its cousin, the game's locales can be revisited after winning, explored anew, and there's a reward in store for completionists. Like its cousin, spikes are an ever-present and vexing environmental hazard. Like its cousin, there are a few graphic options that help to recreate a much more obviously retro gaming platform experience. (I love Analogue Mode, though I wish there was a way to reduce the frequency of vertical hold failures, or to turn off vertical hold failures completely.)
So, you might be asking, how does VVVVVV differ from You Have To Win The Game? Quite significantly, despite their many similarities. First, the bombastic, upbeat optimism of the game is a stark contrast to YHTWTG's quiet and emptiness. There are no friends to be found in YHTWTG, while in VVVVVV, reuniting the titular Vs is, in fact, the primary goal of the game's main arc. (This is not a spoiler, for not; it's stated from the get-go.) Furthermore, while YHTWTG uses a fairly conventional run-and-jump platformer mechanic, there is no jump button in VVVVVV. Rather, the protagonist can reverse personal gravity, and elect to "fall up" rather than down, more or less at will.
More or less, indeed. To flip gravity, one must first be standing on (at least momentarily) solid ground. A flip in progress must complete, and land successfully, before the player can flip again. Our brave Captain Viridian can steer mid-fall, but can't stop a fall. It is entirely possible to end up missing a safe landing point this way. Be grateful for those ubiquitous continue-points. You'll need them. At least, mercifully, one can't die from too long a fall.
I've already mentioned the difference in mood, but beyond this, VVVVVV is communicative in a way YHTWTG isn't. The landscape is dotted with computer terminals hosting messages, and of course, there are five crew members to find and rescue. While YHTWTG offers no clues about its landscape, VVVVVV tells a coherent narrative, and while many questions are left unanswered, one leaves VVVVVV with a better sense of the events of the game in a narrative context than the state in which one leaves YHTWTG.
VVVVVV offers some really spectacular accessibility features for gamers who would normally not be able to play this sort of game, too. One can slow down the game incrementally, turn off moving backgrounds and screen effects, or set the protagonist invincible. The granularity of slowdown control allows you to easily notch the game's reflexes-related difficulty back to a point where it's still challenging but playable, for those who can't react quickly enough at full game speed. This option, as opposed to simply implementing the invulnerability switch, shows a real solid understanding of not only what such a player might need, but how to provide it while preserving as much of the challenge of the game as said player wishes to face. It's rare that this much thought goes into accessibility accommodations, let alone in an indie game.
Finally, VVVVVV offers tools to build one's own levels and scenarios, to bundle them up, and to share them with others. There are quite a few fan-made levels out there, and they're often quite impressive. Terry Cavanagh offers a free "Make and Play" edition of VVVVVV that creates and plays fan-made levels, allowing you to easily and legally share what you make with others. That feature alone extends VVVVVV far beyond the scope of YHTWTG, and makes it a real must-have at its $5 price point. (Frankly, it was more than worth its original $15 price point, too, but I'm glad the price dropped, and VVVVVV became a much more comfortable impulse buy for the still-unconvinced gamer.)
VVVVVV will frustrate you. It will vex you. It will make you scream in frustration and insist it's 'impossible' at least once or twice, but then you'll sail past a difficult level and the palpable joy of your triumph will eclipse the frustration. (Veni Vidi Vici, anyone...?) If your frustration tolerance is limited, this is probably not the game for you. If you can't get beyond the lo-fi visual style, if "chiptunes" annoy you, if dying over and over again bothers you, and especially if you're not not a twitch-reflexes run-and-jumper (run-and-flipper?), then this is probably not your game.
You're probably either put off or curious now. I hope you're curious. VVVVVV rewards curiosity, as long as it's tempered with a healthy dose of patience. Jump in, flip gravity, and rock out the soundtrack. This is a fun, sunny, bombastic return to Saturday mornings on the Commodore 64, in all the very best of ways.

Receiver fails to establish that the complexity of gun handling matters. The detailed reloading scheme doesn't speak to the story, the aesthetic, or the other mechanics. Receiver doesn't treat aiming or shooting the weapon with the same carefulness it reserves for reloading, and doesn't fiddle much with the basics of movement, yet running and shooting are the core verbs of the game. By making the world randomly generated, the developers give up the opportunity to design encounters where efficient reloading matters. As a consequence, becoming more skilled with the game's most intricate systems doesn't make a player any more likely to succeed. Receiver's complex gun-handling mechanics are irrelevent in the context of its larger design.
That's a shame, because the larger design has nothing to recommend it. The perfunctory story and low-poly world of Receiver aren't interesting to explore in their own right, much less when one must overcome the game's unforgiving difficulty. The coice to generate the world randomly might add replay value, but it also adds much more to the frustration level while costing the game the ability to present rewarding encounters that highlight its unique mechanics. Receiver has a neat idea at its core, but that didn't translate into an interesting game.

This is probably the most manic game I've ever played. When rush hour hits and you have six meat lasagnes to make your hands FLY. I have PSMCRPSMCRPSCR programmed in my muscle memory forever. After it's over, you know you have another one coming but it still somehow sneaks up on you.

It's a cooking and restaurant management simulation done well. I really like the fact it's based completely around the keyboard, though the mouse is always an option. If only Type To Learn was this fun. And I LOVE that it's a cooking game where I don't have to trace finaky lines across a chicken breast where if I'm one pixel off I'm bumped down to silver. The daily menu design, bad food pairings, and the fact that foods can go stale after a couple days, keeps you on your toes and prevents you from beating the game by spamming the same six recipes. Even expertise can get a bit boring after a while, and the panic of trying to navigate a new recipe in the midst of rush hour is always a fun challenge. This game is excellent. Well-polished software, well-balanced cards, great F2P system, and addicting rewards that keep me coming back every day.
While this game may look like Hearthstone in screenshots, the fundamental mechanics are much closer to Magic. There are 5 factions you can mix and match when building a deck (lots of variety!), the resource cards are similar to lands (although its version of the mana system has been streamlined a bit, making this a much less clunky digital card game than digital versions of Magic itself), and combat is quite similar to Magic in that the attacker simply attacks the other player and the defending player chooses how to block.
The constructed meta is quite fun and balanced at the moment, and DWD fights hard to keep it that way. And with the rewards being as generous as they are, you can have a tier 1 deck after only a few weeks of playing, with $0 spent.
Drafting is super fun and rewards are very generous (including keeping what you draft!); I haven't spent any money on draft and I draft almost daily. Also your packs are passed to you by real players, so you can read signals just like a real life draft. And yet there's no waiting and you can take as long as you like to make picks. It's ingenious how they designed this system.
Please, if you're at all a CCG fan or looking to try them out, give Eternal a download!

Pros:
-Performance: 5760 x 1080 with sliders at Ultra except for traffic at Medium netted an average of about 30 FPS. I think people are forgetting this is CPU dependent code. Running an i7-4930K at 4.5GHz. GPUs are only twin 780 GTX. This is comparable to FPS in P3D and FSX, however, it is much smoother. No jutteres, stutters, or tearing. FPS is consistant, flying rural or urban. Flew out of KPHX during sunset, a lot of 3D lights and shadows, still maintaining 30 FPS.
-Visual: Blurries are mostly gone. Default airports look much better with more buildings and scenery. Colors in general look better, mostly due to the shaders. Shaders are huge improvement over FSX. Landclass is accurate, and roads and bridges look good.
Cons:
-AI traffic is unrealistic, with 4 or 5 Piper Cubs in the air at once. Lack of airline traffic detracts from realism near Class B airports.
-Autogen is wonky in some areas. For example, evergreen trees while flying over mountains in Phoenix.
-ATC is, well it is what it is.
Overall there is a lot of promise here. If you want to fly some fun general aviations flights, its pretty fun. It's easy to quickly create a flight plan, and jump in. It's lacking a lot, but nothing I don't think the developers can deliver overtime.
I would recommend this for someone who wants to get into flight simming general aviation aircraft, or flight sim fans who want to try and help develop this product. My only concern is whether or not Dovetail will listen, and if they will try to make this a money grab. It's early access. Let's see what Dovetail delivers first.

Please understand that if you're buying this (or any Wolfire game, as far as I can tell), you're basically purchasing the privilege to try out a proof of concept. Receiver's proof of concept is micromanaging the various functions of a handgun; one of three you're randomly given at the start of a game. It's a little awkward to get used to what button does what so you can translate your intentions into actions but after you get the hang of it it starts feeling fluid. You feel a real sense of accomplishment at being able to reload quickly. Shooting feels fairly satisfying too. There's recoil but it's not ridiculous. So, yes, the proof of concept works well. Now onto the game.
Almost everything about the game, from enemy and item placement, is random. The only thing that isn't random, as far as I can tell, is the environment you find yourself in. Dull, untextured geometry that almost seems a trademark of Unity games is the only thing you'll be looking at, aside from the enemies.
Which brings me to the enemies. They're... robots, which is disappointing. Maybe it's just me but I don't find shooting machines all that fun. You shoot an animal, it whimpers, it hobbles around, it bleeds, it cries for its mother. There's a lot of feedback there, you know? With robots, they just fizzle out and fall over and stop making such a racket.
There's two types of them. One's an automated turret that spins around in a circle. The other's a drone that floats around and flies at you with a stungun if it sees you. Both beep if they notice you, which is a nice indication that you're probably going to be killed and have to start over in a couple of seconds because there's no health. One hit and you start over. Same three guns. Same two enemies, same old rooftops, over and over and over. Good luck getting those eleven tapes because the time-to-kill for some enemy encounters, especially the drones, can be less than a second. I haven't even mentioned how you have to hit certain parts of the robots to disable/kill them, so yeah, your quarter-second snap shot at the metal blur that's about to zap you better be accurate.
Lore is given through a rather monotonous explanation through the goal; eleven video casettes you find laying around. It's some Matrix-type stuff about how you have special powers that got locked away by being saturated with addictive media or something. To get the full story and figure out what's going on you have to get the eleven tapes, which you're probably not going to do because you're too busy getting electrocuted and shot over and over and trying to remember which key does what. The voice acting is... bad. The way the guy says prounounces the "ch" in mindtech makes my skin crawl.
So, like I said at the start of my review, it's a game that exists solely to provide functional packaging for a novel idea. How's the idea? It's pretty cool. How's the game? It kind of sucks. I'd love to see the gun mechanics in Receiver used in a real, fully fleshed game, but I also really doubt I'll ever see that happen.
I recommend the game, but I also recommend you get it on sale when it's only a dollar or two. That price seems worth what Receiver boils down to; a novelty.

Now this is something interesting.
First of all, there's only 3 weapons in the game (plus other ones that can be added through some kind of file adding) and only 2 different enemy types.
The enemies are flying drones and turrets.
The flying drone is the most annoying thing you have ever seen in your entire life.
The turret is the most frustrating in terms of peeking corners and succesfully landing shots.
About the guns, the ones you can try in the vanilla version are:
M1911
Glock 18
S&W Model 10 (I believe)
I expected something else that operates differently, like a rifle or a shotgun.
The 2 pistols handle pretty much the same except that you have to pull the hammer back on the M1911 (It also has a safety unlike the Glock, which using the safety key changes the firemode to fully automatic)
The revolver is a different story, you actually have to manage better your ammo since you can only carry 6 shots, and to reload it you have to eject all the casings and spam the Z button to fill the cylinder up, and then close it again.
As far as I've played, pulling back the hammer on the revolver doesn't do anything and it should remove the time it takes to manually pulling it back via the trigger.
As someone who has used firearms before, the weapon accuracy is totally messed up.
The revolver becomes useless after being like 5 feet away from your target. You simply won't hit anything unless you spam it and that's not something you should do.
The M1911 has the worst "damage" of them all (I had to shoot the batteries 4 times before they die) and holds 8 bullets if you have one in the chamber.
And the Glock is the most OP thing I've seen compared to every game that also has it.
Instead of being a gun simulator, I was put into a series of randomly generated corridors in search for tapes.
I needed a flashlight but I didn't find one and I had a bad time managing my gun and figuring out where I was due to the time being night. It was all dark.
Plus being all dark, flying drones are spammed and the framerate drops after generating 5 rooms and it gets worse as you continue. You don't have to actually backtrack to search for the tapes since they could spawn again in the next room so why keep the older rooms?
A good idea could have been to have doors between rooms so after you close a door the room behind it gets erased and you can't go back. That way it forces players to explore every room before moving to the next room.
After finally retrying 2-3 times, about 30 minutes each try, I managed to listen to all the tapes.
There's an annoying voice that just won't shut up after picking up some tapes and I don't know if its screaming or singing.
When I picked up the last one I couldn't move. Just hear the tape.
After a while I realized that I wasn't frozen and that the game just crashed.
It literally crashed after completing the game.
The lore was interesting at first but then you realize it's the "robots went crazy" cliché.
Problems aside, the game is fun for around 1 hour if you actually know how to play and you don't keep dying or running out of ammo.
The way you can handle the weapons and the ammo is pretty badass, but that's how guns feel like if you're put on a "conserving ammo while theres enemies on the night" setting too. Just watch John Wick or play SuperHot for a more autentic feel.
It could work better as a VR game for more immersion, but I guess since 2013 we have been limited to 5 keyboard keys.
