Soulsborne games are by now a very beloved and popular series of videogames, and like in all series, there is always a game that is considered to be at the bottom, the gap can be large or it can be really small, but it is there.
Dark Souls II was released in March of 2014, as the sequel to a game that had become unexpectedly popular, it created big expectations, and sadly, for a large part of the fanbase, these were not met, adding to that the fact that this is the only game in the series to not be directed by Hidetaka Miyazaki, it kind of gave it from the start that ugly duckling status.
But hey, no one is perfect, right? so today i'm here to talk about the things that i consider Dark Souls II did right and the ones i even consider it did best than any of the other games in the series, so if you're someone who has tried other souls games but not this one maybe due to its bad reputation, give me please a few minutes of your time.
In Dark Souls II players take on the role of the "Bearer of the Curse" an undead that is slowly feeling their very humanity drifting away, as their memories fade, a dream points towards an ominous portal leading to the faraway land of Drangleic, a place that holds the promise of a cure, and just on its premise we're already straying away from the usual soulsborne formula, we are not some chosen one with a mission or a prophecy to fulfill, we are someone on a personal quest, who will end up in the middle of something far greater than it could be imagined.
The world design in Dark Souls II is not as well thought as that from the first game, and the ways areas connect to each other do not always make sense, but while it lacks that cohesion, i would like to point out how each area does stand out and shines on its own; Drangleic is somewhat of a theme park, one second you're on an ancient manor and the next one you're on a sacred dragon shrine above the world, one moment you're on the most lugubrious forest, walk a bit and now you're on a poison valley, but if this is a theme park, each attraction is sure as fun as they can get.
In the list of things Dark Souls II did right, i have to mention the vast choices for builds and gear this game offers, the number of armor sets is increased so significantly from the first game and probably is the highest in the series, and while the decision to separate certain traits from its former stats was not the most popular, in the end the myriad ways to customize your character is something that overweights the small cons, add to that something DS II did better than any other game in the series, its respec system, which does not have a limit per playthrough as long as you possess the required item.
The next point i'd like to talk about is its NG+ system, as it does again, something no other game in the series did, and went further than just increasing enemy damage but also changing enemy locations and even adding new enemies on each successive playthrough, and on a game like this where knowing where your enemy stands is key to survive, this adds a whole new level of challenge.
As i think i have covered many aspects of what the originally released game brought to the table, it is time now for me to speak of what definitely is the highlight of the game, the Lost Crowns areas, which appeared as three separate pieces of DLC, but are now included altogether for the Scholar of the First Sin release.
Each one of these areas takes back the brilliant level desing from Dark Souls that is missing in the base DS II game, not only they expand far and wide, above and below, but also have that feeling of wholeness, you go back and forth without really noticing due to how finely designed they are, also to mention the boss battles, while some better than the others,  they do not let down, and i want to take some time to specially praise Crown of the Ivory King , probably one of the best areas in the whole soulsborne series, both lore and gameplay wise, i would dare to say just this piece of content justifies playing this game.
And as if the areas themselves were not enough, all three of them also include a special challenge zone, filled with the most unforgiving and defiying enemies, bosses and even the landscapes themselves, that the game can throw at you.
This review has now become very extended, but i hope that you made it to this paragraph and i thank you if you did, Dark Souls II is certainly not its predecessor, but i do not believe it deserves to be looked down upon, it is the least "souls" of the soulsborne games, maybe that is true, but that also gives it an identity of its own and i hope i did shed some light on some of its qualities.
Thank you for your time and i hope you find on this game the challenge and the fun that it offered to me.

I didn't really think the theme of the game was something I would enjoy but the story turned out to be pretty good (It does a great job at creating suspense). I liked the ambience - the amount of detail in the house and the sound direction (probably the backbone of all walking simulators).  But the actual gameplay I think was too monotonous. A lot of reading is involved. They decided to actually scan real life letters and drawings and handwriting in general, so some of the text is actually pretty unreadable. Not that it matters, because most of it is not what you’d call interesting or essential to the story. Also there are a lot of pointless interactive objects in the house. Things that again don't contribute anything to the story or immersion, in my opinion. And whilst the developers made a good job recreating a realistic 90s house in a video game, it’s still just that. One might even describe it as overwhelmingly mundane, but not in a nostalgic, cool kind of way, but just plain boring and predictable. And when you can complete the entire game in under a minute (whilst speedrunning) the 20 euro price tag seems utterly ludicrous. Now, this is the point where I was going to end my review saying ''Don't buy it'', but I went back and played the game once more, but this time with the developer commentary enabled. I mean the creative process of creating a game is very interesting. And building the game from nothing takes huge amount of time and skill, especially if there are only a few people working on it. The developers highlighted some things that I had missed on my first playthrough or rather took for granted. These insights reminded me of the time I made a 10 page newspaper for my english class assignment (smth like 8th grade). It took me roughly 5 months to produce six pages of content I was kind of happy with. It was an enormous chore to think out what was going to be in the newspaper: the attitude of the newspaper, the individual stories, the proportions, the layout, the overall design, the writing style, the pictures, the ads - everything had to be perfect (since it was WAY past the hand in deadline and I wanted to salvage a good grade and of course make the teacher feel bad for ever doubting my abilities). Anyway, after that much effort put into a project, it sure would be nice to be rewarded (*high price tag*). But we still have to look at everything objectively. Yes the teacher was very impressed by my efforts (so much so, that she decided to take it as a keepsake),but I still got an F. And so, while I did enjoy the game, no way should it get away with costing twice the money it’s worth. Snatch it on a sale though.

This game is still reasonably okay, what's with everyone? Let me explain why this CAN be a fun game:
What they have been expecting was this game to be as super as it was marketed; like those people that claim that have never heard of hype-trains before. But the core element of the game is enough. This game has a bunch of minor flaws that e.g.: Microtransactions, and deceptive speed perception.
I can satisfyingly say that as a sim racer (mostly playing Assetto Corsa, GSCE, rFactor, Project Cars, etc.) this game is a decent arcade racer that allows me to use my G27 wheel with good FFB (for an arcade game) in a cockpit camera (yes, the driver is only turning 180° of the steering wheel, but you can use your full 900°; just like in DiRT Rally). 'Been playing this game co-op with a friend, driving for 8 hours STRAIGHT through the U.S. Of A. and we are still not done with discovering, not even at the slightest. AND, bugs are mostly gone... (or reported ones I have not encountered, yet).
What I have been determined to do was:
Let me tell you... it is good at that.
You expected this game to be an ultra realistic driving game with an open world just because you read "simulation" in the tags on the store page? -- Yeah, with expectations like these you are wrong here, entirely. Yes, cars may drive sluggish with a gamepad, but I cannot confirm that entirely. It might have been the assists, an older version, or their own gamepad (again, I don't use a gamepad, I stick to a wheel). BUT, what I can confirm is that driving fast seems to be visually slow (for me only when I drive with the rear camera views). Although, that feeling stops when I change the view to the hood or cockpit camera. Don't think I'm trying to command you to now play the game in cockpit view (because that is personal perspective), but to try it out at least, or accept that the game's visuals are deceptive. You may compare this game with Test Drive Unlimited 2,
I can already hear that you are screaming out loud that TDU 2 was a good. Sure, these two games are extremely similar:
A galore of land to explore (it is not 100% accurate to the USA, but WTF, the game is still HUGE),
Multiplayer that had you roaming with others,
or even competing in challenges with 'em,
it allowed customisation of your car,
cop chases,
Don't compare this to Project Cars (or any other try-hard sim-cade/sim) for example...
Do you smell something fishy here? I do, let me tell you:
The game is not a "10/10 best game ever", but this is a decent game, it has potential that it builds upon. People have to distinguish between this and the "hyped-up version of this game (the one on E3). Yes, Ubisoft has failed at that part; miserably. Bragging with their "revolutionary new MMO racer", though, in the end it just being "vanilla" -- but a good one at that! The game also had huge bad mouthing due to the epic-failing AC Unity and WATCHDOGS.
Adding microtransactions to your game whilst being an AAA is never a good idea, I agree. But the thing is (unless it is a car you really want) you can buy it for about 2 bucks, it is not that much. You are also given 100.000 CP (Premium currency) at level ten to buy yourself a bunch of cars (three at least). There are not that many cars to buy when it comes to cars that have to be bought with real money. With the "Wild Run Expansion" that is to add even more content (Drift cars, Dragsters, and Monster Trucks) there is actually something to enjoy again soon, this may also incentivise portions of the community as well.
Graphics are looking well, the game runs at Ultra settings with 60 FPS (R9 270x Sapphire and i5-3470 @3.20GHz multi-core); only Anti-Aliasing is reduced to FXAA. The sounds of the cars are just as good as they were in TDU 2, might even compare them to DiRT Rally. The Crew should be regarded as a successor to the TDU series, for Atari has faded away due to bankruptcy.
Okay, now let’s talk pro and con:
So, again, if you look for a challenge against AI (like Need For Speed MW, Carbon, Underground), a fantastic story and crews around everyone that battles each other in The Crew this game is not for you. But there is still a thriving PVP mode, an amazing Faction system that keeps you playing after the Story. You will struggle with the AI being just bad at driving and sometimes pushing you off drastically. But if you are looking into a long (sadly cliche) story with nice coop missions, have interest in cop chases, driving about with friends, competing against your friend, aka. "roaming in a racer" You should ONLY get this game on sale, don't pay 60$, it is not as good. This game has just been marketed falsely… But c’mon, how many games offer a demo such as great as this one to showcase its potential? Get the demo and judge it for yourselves.

first of all, don’t play airport simulator 2014 unless you have something else to do while you wait for it to let you do anything.  better yet, don’t play airport simulator 2014 at all.  i thought maybe because i’m a private pilot and probably have an above-average interest in airports i might enjoy it even though it looks like nobody else did, but i only finished it because i wanted to see if anything would happen when i did.  something did, but it was just as underwhelming as the rest of the game.
there were things i liked:  there are airplanes to look at, and i didn’t spend any money on it since i won it on steamgifts.
otherwise it seemed unfinished.  i won’t go into everything that bothered me about it, but let’s go over the biggest problems:
- most of the time in the game there’s nothing to do but wait, and there’s no way to speed up the simulation.  just watch the times tick down for another 5 minutes until there’s something to do again.
- destinations are sometimes all the way across the gate area and are only marked by a floating yellow arrow pointing down to the white arrow circle on the ground.  it’s pretty easy to get lost — even if you spin the camera all the way around you might not actually be able to see the arrows because they’re hiding behind planes or the terminal.
- you progress by automating the various support trucks for each gate (and then upgrading them to drive and work faster), but that leaves you with nothing interesting to do.
- ...except the cargo truck, which is missing from the upgrade list and cannot be automated.  i begat to curse the green, high-wing planes that landed because i knew they were going to need cargo service and there’s only one cargo truck that has to wait for no apparent reason between planes and i just about always had a cargo plane at 3 of the 8 gates.
- the other trucks before you automate them will sometimes get overlapping tasks.  for example, the fuel truck might be at gate 1 fueling it up but a task will come in to bring the fuel truck to gate 3.  if you move it then gate 1 stops getting fueled — you actually have to wait for gate 1 to finish and drive the fuel truck back to the garage before you drive it to gate 3.
- controls aren’t customizable.  it’s mostly a mouse interface, but when you drive the various support trucks you’re stuck with wasd.  at least it used the qwerty wasd even though i use a dvorak layout because otherwise those keys aren’t near each other.
it took me almost 20 hours according to steam to fully upgrade my airport, but most of that time i was doing something else.

I like First Person Shooters with iron sights. Meaning: if you shoot from the hip, you are only able to hit what is directly in front of you; if you want to hit something which is 10m away, you HAVE to aim like with a real gun.
You have to use a button to get the weapon up, pointing towards the enemy and use the sights of the weapon to target.
This is so much better than some cross hairs which show you where your hits will be. It feels better. Much better.
Verdun is such a shooter. There are different weapons from the time of World War 1 and most kill in one hit to the body, pistols need two shots to the body, grenades are brutal and so on.
If you want to run around shooting at everything and killing people like a hero, wrong game.
If you want to move slowly, then climb out of your hole and run zigzag towards the next hole, the whole time praying no sniper and no MG is targeting your area, then jumping into the hole and laying on the ground and preparing for the next run, then this is your game.
If you want to sit somewhere with a rifle and snipe at people who are trying to run zigzag towards your position, then this is your game.
If you want to setup a Machine Gun and spray down people who try to run towards you, this is your game.
Don't expect real good graphics, don't expect smooth moving, don't expect really good weapons.
Even the gameplay is not really good.
Everything is good enough so you can have fun and perhaps this is the kind of game you want to play from time to time.
Just so you know what I think good shooters are:
- Survarium
- Heroes & Generals
- Borderlands
- Call of Duty: World at War
- Call of Duty®: Black Ops II
These are really good shooters. High quality.
Nevertheless, this game is not bad.
It is fun for a while.
I have no idea what engine they are using, but it is not good for this kind of game. Or not used in a good way.
If you want a FPS game with iron sights in WW1, you don't have a lot of games to select one from. I don't know of any others. If you want a game where people have to move the front, where you have to cross a killing field, where nobody is the hero, this could be it for your.
If you want a really good game, don't get this. Sorry.

Absolutely loving the direction that this game appears to be taking. It's definitely FSX under the hood, which is a good thing as far as I'm concerned. If you've spent time in FSX, you'll feel right at home with the keyboard layout and control settings and everything else. I've been playing FSX since it was in beta, and I've probably got hundreds of hours logged in it. FSW seems like a true successor to FSX.
I run a HEAVILY modded version of FSX with tons of addons (scenery, weather, aircraft, etc). FSW looks better than my modded FSX install, and performs FAR better. Very playable framerates, even running the game at 4k with absolutely every setting maxed out and in Southern California during a thunderstorm (if you've played FSX in those conditions, you know how the framerate can plummet...FSW looks gorgeous in 4K, by the way). DTG using ORBx Global for the scenery is a huge plus.
Yea, it has some issues. Aircraft lights do not seem to do anything at night, lighting during the day is a bit washed out due to HDR, and the missions I've attempted so far have no voice overs, which makes following directions a bit difficult when you're trying to fly at the same time.
That said, however, this is the FIRST DAY of an early access title, and these are all things that are easily remedied. It runs smoothly, loads a HELL of a lot faster than FSX does, and looks gorgeous. The screenshots and videos were spot on.
On a side note, I have real world flight time in the DA-40, and the implementation of that aircraft in this game is pretty darn accurate.
I cant wait to see what DTG does with this title years down the road, and I can't wait to see what the third-party addon scene does with the game as well.
Overall, give the game a shot! I'm seeing reviews of people who are bashing the game's graphics and that it doesn't look like the pictures or videos, and then saying that they're running the game at low settings. OF COURSE it doesn't look like the pictures and videos if you're running at low settings! A lot of the reviews talking about low performance and such also seem to be using sub-par hardware, so keep that in mind.
If you like FSX, you've got a decent computer, and you understand that this title is still in early access and will be changed and updated over the coming months and years, then ABSOLUTELY pick this one up.

Note: It's an early access game. Experiences may vary. Mine was positive.
Short Version: For an Early Access Game, I think its enjoyable, smooth as can be and headed in a great direction, I'm ready to say I like it, but we'll see. DEVS DON'T LET US DOWN!!!
Positives: Very smooth, good flight models that didn't make me feel like I was in an arcade but were easy enough to fly simply because it's intuitive[caveat: I have literally thousands of hours with sims so this might not be true for everyone]. Love the graphics. This is not another knock off of a Flight Sim, it's very apparent we're working with a new engine. Its also very apparent we're working in native 64bit, which is exciting on its own, but what this means is a much more detailed experience is possible...ride out a thunderstorm folks! It's like being buffeted by a real storm. The micromovement of the aircraft with swells and drops in air pressure were awesome, the big drops and extreme lifts were like riding a demonic roller coaster that just knocked pack some methamphetamines. Watching the rain gather and streak was almost relaxing. I noted that traffic on highways and freeways seemed very realistic with a few speeders here and there..and oh my gosh, traffic flow was running on both side of a divided freeway! It's a dang miracle. And in the correct directions! I know, I'm so damn picky!
Negatives: The auto scenery(buildings and trees etc) were rather silly most of the time. Pretty to look at, but if you've ever been anywhere on Earth you try to fly here...You'll immediately notice areas you know and while they seem familiar enough for fun, the procedural generation is a bit heavy handed and messy in places. Some roads seemed out of place but the problem was the procedurally generated buildings that couldn't exist. Salt Lake City looked more like a huge city, while New York was underwhelming. Rudder control under "Mouse Yoke" sucks, but I expected so...Didn't have time for controller testing, But I'll get there. Where the [SENSORED] are the [SENSORED] Helicopters???
Finally: For early access, I gotta say...This sim just took 2.5 hours of my time, and I enjoyed every minute of it! From the Mountains of Utah, the Coast of California to Washington DC... I enjoyed the ease of flight, the realistic models; I mean for heck sake Day One plus a few hours - I think we've got a winner. If the dev's stick to it, and build it up in the coming months I think as a community of Virtual Pilots we're going to have a bunch of fun here. I think the physics are in a good place, the flight models seem enjoyable and slightly light hearted but I haven't fully explored the different settings...haven't had time to use my collection of various controllers either so I'll likely be back and freshen this quick review up some.
For the money, this is a good investment. I'm seriously hoping I'll have time to dig deeper, and more so that we'll see continued dev with quick access for Third Party Developers to come in and add to it!

DTG has taken remarkable steps forward in bringing a high-quality next generation flight simulator to the market. The progress they have made in response to feedback is something that should be commended and is testament to their dedication to the flight sim community.  While the road ahead is long and filled with potholes that need to be smoothed over, it is a road that I look forward to traveling with them.
My Top Pros Thusfar:
-  The Flight School lessons are immersive and really make you feel like you're in your first days of flight training (or reliving them in my case). The A.I. instructor gives you voiced feedback, critiques and commendations, making you feel like you're flying with a real instructor. The instructional approach is quite comparable to real life flight training. The fact that you have to put solo hours in to take your check rides is also a nice touch. Having a pilot profile that tracks your progress also aids in the immersive quality of the sim.
- The missions that I've tried so far are fun and each have distinct lessons to teach or skills to test with real-world applications (especially the scenario missions). Like the training missions, each mission includes voice acted performances, making the missions feel more realistic and giving them personality.  I look forward to what the community comes up with since the mission editor is being made available to simmers.
- For VFR training purposes, navigation is made easier thanks to VFR checkpoints you might find on real-world sectionals appearing in the world.
- I have flown several of the GA aircraft that are included in the base product, and I believe that their partnership with A2A simulations was a great choice. Once I messed around with the sensitivities and controls a bit, the aerodynamics and physics of each of the planes I've flown are notably similar to flying their real world counterpart. It is also nice to be able to adjust individual payload regions of the plane and note how it affects performance.
- The audio on the aircrafts is dynamic and sounds pretty realistic.
- The menus, interface and flight planner are user-friendly and easily navigated.
- The environment is the biggest factor for aviators and it is nice to see so much attention paid to this concept. The rain effects are beautifully done. Although there isn't much room for creativity and fine tuning of the weather right now, this is one of the most promising aspects of the simulator.


My Top Cons Thusfar:
- Although they have made improvements, the graphics could still use some work. For the most part, the aircrafts exterior look good, the cockpit/instruments look great and the lighting effects have been greatly improved. However, everything else in the world needs improvement. The scenery is excessively bright and generally lacking in quality when compared to platforms like X-Plane 11.
- The airports could use some work. The graphical representations of the airports I have visited are lacking. The airport lighting hinders the immersive quality of the sim. The lights aren't realistic and don't look like they are even part of the airport, as they hover above the ground. This is definitely something I would like to see fixed.
- ATC is functional, but hasn't improved much since FSX/Flight School and could still use some improvements in order to feel like more realistic radio comms.
- Currently there are a number of bugs and performance hiccups (including random crashes) that I've experienced, but that is to be expected at an Early Access stage of development.
I intend to update this review as I continue using the simulator. I regret having to post this so soon, but felt it necessary to in response to the prematurely negative reviews out there. It's a work in progress guys, give them a chance! Since I purchased Flight School, I received Flight Sim World for free and appreciate the gesture by DTG. A gesture such as this and the fact that DTG brought this work in progress to the public to aid them in the process is even more testament to their relationship with the community. If you are on the fence about purchasing, maybe wait until launch to see if the devs make the improvements they need to make. FSW looks to be shaping into a remarkable next-gen sim with great potential for both veteran and newcomers to the flight simulation community.

Just as tedious as the Old School CRPG™s it's emulating.
Move around on a big empty grid, exploring a world that is so generic you'd assume every art asset was straight off the shelf. One of the most frustratingly linear experiences I've had this year - go in a line, find two routes: one blocked by Gate A, and one with some monsters and Key A. Going through Gate A leads you to Gate B and a similar hunt for Key B. And so on.
"Puzzles" in this game amount to trying to discern what in the game world is a clickable object and what is just a branch or bone on the ground. Prepare to do a lot of clicking. Especially against the monsters, who are HP sponges because the developers realize that their combat system is so laughably awkward (attack, take a step backward so you are invulnerable, wait out the monster's attack, move back, repeat) that they need a huge buffer window to allow chances for the monsters to get a few licks in too.
More than anything else, the UI is what made me give up on LoG2. Click on an item on the ground and then click on the character who has to hold it. Then open the character window. Click on the item. Click on the character. Congratulations, you've equipped a branch. Want to swing that branch at an enemy? Right click on a weapon on a character's portrait to attack with that character - no direct binds for this. Spellcasting is even more clunky. Why?
The reason it's all so awkward is tied back into the combat. Things actually do get legitimately challenging when several monsters are in the area, or you're in a limited space, but only because of the UI. It takes a lot of mouse movement, clicking, and well-timed strafing as you struggle to open and close inventory windows, swap healing potions from who has them to who needs to use them, click the correct weapons for your attacks, draw little spells on a grid, et cetera. I'm not being coy or cute when I say the real monster in this game is the UI.
So, no, the game isn't "too easy", but playing it is boring and awkward and unfun and felt extremely game-y and not at all like an adventure on a strange island. I strongly recommend you play something else. What, exactly, depends on what you wanted to get out of this game.
If you like grid maps and RPG combat, parties, and stats, Atlus makes a phenomenal series called Etrian Odyssey for the Nintendo DS and 3DS that is well worth your time. If you like fantasy action combat, Skyrim is the way to go. If you like exploring a mysterious world and solving puzzles, Myst or, more recently, Machinarium are fine options. Just please don't waste your time on this.

As a fan of sphagetti westerns I love this game. The art direction perfectly captures the sphagetti western, the music (an interesting mix of hip hop and Morricone) is fantatastic, there's plenty of references to the best of the sphagetti western genre, and perhaps most importantly the gameplay is interesting and fun. Gamplay-wise the biggest thing that sets this game apart is the luck meter, you generally get luck by killing enemies which will build up your luck meter, when your luck meter is low you will fall into traps, enemies will burst out of haybales, windmill blades will fall on you and other unlucky things, when your luck is high none of these will happen, your duck companion will find hearts for you, and enemy bullets will sometimes miss you, you can also use half of your luck meter to temporarily make an aura of luck around you, which largely helps in avoiding large amounts of incoming fire.
Previously I had made my review "not recommended" almost completely due to the punishing lives system. I'm now happy to say that the devs added an option that basically gets rid of lives and lets you respawn at the last checkpoint no matter how many times you've died. The game is still extremely challenging, but now there isn't the frustration of having to restart the level if you die three times. I think it's awsome that the devs have listened to feedback and given us difficulty options. As of now the only real negative thing I can think of is the fact that if you change your controls, button prompts don't change which can lead to some confusion.
This is my favorite CCG. If you're looking for a card game that doesn't feel like you need to put money in to have a decent collection, then Eternal might just be the game for you.

I just got into the plane for Flight Sim World. I believe it shows real promise. It's early access, very much in it's infant stage at the moment of public release, as they stated. So, it's best to cut them some serious slack. I've been a Flight Simmer since SubLogic days and earned my real pilot's license with the help of Flight Simulator, designing a few planes for the old FS98 back in the day.
So, here's my thought so far...
I do like the menu system, it's very intuitive and straight forward. I'm sure it's not as deep as some old timers like myself would like, but I prefer the simpler menus. The music is nice too. I do like the straight forward approach to plotting one's flight.
Getting into the simulator, it does have it's graphical glitches. In the heavy rain, there's a stark demarcation line for the atmosphere, looks pretty ugly there, but again, I knew that this was a very early work in progress, so I'm not expecting the whole world to be perfect at this stage.  I do like the rain drops on the window, though it still looks a bit pixelated. I'm running the graphics on ultra high. I get fairly smooth frame rates from medium to high. I have a very powerful (yet slightly older) system, an HP Z820 system with 64 GB of RAM and an older  Dual GeForce GTX 690 with 2GB video RAM.
The outside scenery, well, it's just not the greatest looking at the moment. Again, I figure it's very early WIP, so I'll forgive them for that. I can see the FSX architecture for sure. I'm guessing the simulator is rewritten?
The detail of the aircraft are great! no qualms there. I'm a visual guy, so I nit-pick over graphics.  I would say that the scenery definitely needs to be re-written with more up to date engine, it looks quite old for today's games, it does seem to struggle at times with heavy graphics set ON.
Overall, I do like it. I am not going to be harsh, I totally get this is an early access. Some people just gripe and complain with an entitled attitude. I guess they just had no clue this is an early access version of the simulator.

Eternal is THE game for people frustrated with Hearthstone and looking for a fresh, F2P freindly CCG.  Now typically I'm the kind of person to drop too much money on games like this, but Dire Wolf Digital's F2P friendly purchasing model has enabled me to get almost a full collection of cards WITHOUT going over my budget, meaning I have disposable income to spend on the NEXT SET! It's the player-friendly business model Hearthstone never had.
There's also lenty of opportunity to expand your colelction without spending a dime.  Eternal sports multiple fun, rewarding gamemodes against AI and other players which generate gold for you to spend of packs, and the other gamemodes, forge and draft.  Forge is very similar to Hearthsotne's arena, except you play against AI.  Draft is very similar to MTG's draft format, in which you pass packs around with other players, picking cards from 4 packs until you've formed a deck.  In both formats, you get to keep the cards you've drafted after you're finished playing!
As with any game, there are Tier 1/Tier 2, etc. strategies in Eternal, but overall the meta is very friendly to experimentation and deckbuilding.  New archetypes pop up every week in the Eternal Tournament Series, and when piloted by skilled players these decks can do very well.  Very often, I can play 10 games on ladder and see 9 different decks, including 2 I had never seen before.  The difference from Hearthstone is astounding.  Dire Wolf Digital as a team has also proved that they are willing to make changes when necessary for the health of the meta, and proven a great knowledge of their game far as their nerfs/buffs have had great effect.
In conclusion, if you're a Hearthstone junkie who's tired of the same old RNG, cookie-cutter deck BS (me), or just a longtime CCG fan looking for something fresh, give Eternal a shot!  Once you've gotten through the campaign (which is a tad daunting), the entire game opens up.
-CaptainZachSparrow

A common thread among people coming to Eternal seems to be "I'm tired of Hearthstone, but Magic is too expensive for me". If this describes you, then you'll probably enjoy Eternal.
To elaborate a bit, I picked up Eternal after being somewhat disillusioned with Hearthstone. I hadn't heard much buzz about it, just stumbled across it and decided to give it a go. And it was just what I was looking for. If you feel that Hearthstone is lacking a lot of the complexity that Magic brings to a card game, then Eternal more than makes up for that. While, superficially, it resembles Magic a lot more than many competitors, it has its own spin on many mechanics. And much like Hearthstone, it uses the potential of the digital medium to great effect.
The game is also very generous with earnable in-game currency. Make no mistake, it will take you some time to build up enough of a collection to start playing top-tier decks, but it's very doable without spending a cent.
The game is still young, and it certainly has some growing to do, but it has a lot of potential, and I'm looking forward to see where it goes. If you want to pick up a new digital card game, you could do a lot worse.

Gone Home...where do I start? I'll start with why I bought this game.
Despite already knowing the story of the game from watching YouTubers play it, I got it for one reason: to pick up and throw objects around in a fictional house for fun.
No seriously, that's why I got it. I don't regret getting it either. But word of advice: Get the game during the weekend sales, the Winter Holiday sales, or any type of sale that gets it down to maybe $5. I don't remember how much I got this for, but it was definitely a gift card one. Oh, and try using a Steam gift card while you're trying to find ways to lower the price. It'll make it less of a waste of money if you buy it for less than $20.00 if you don't end up liking the story, but even better if you just want the experience of tossing plates, food boxes, apples, books, papers, pencils, pens, highlighters, pillows, forks, knives, spoons, cups, lids of boxes, or anything else. There have been people who have played the game over hours just trying to pick up and put every pickupable (not a word, but it works) item in the first room. Don't believe me? Check the most popular screenshots of this game in the community. I tried, but there is an ANNOYING GLITCH that happens if you throw items in a specific spot on the floor in many areas of the house: you throw the item and it falls through the floor, never to return again unless you start a new game. It's not with every floor, but it happens on some parts in the greenhouse and on the stairs in the basement. Don't know if they'll fix it, but hopefully they will. Be careful where you throw the items.
TL;DR: Do I like Gone Home? Well, yes and no.
I say "yes" because I like throwing the items around and picking them up and rotating them...I like the INTERACTIVITY of the house. I also like making a mess in a house that's in a video game because I can't do it in real life.
I say "no" because while the main story is a bit interesting, there are other minor stories that aren't told by a narrator around the house that you have to decipher for yourself.
Also, look up in every room. Especially the garage. You wll need to use a "recyclable" item to get an easter egg item. I'm sure you'll figure it out.

What The Crew gets right is its stylised and scaled-down version of the entire continental USA. Cities are shrunken caricatures, but the truly vast sweeping tracts of land between them means traversing it really does capture the spirit of a cross-country, city-to-city road trip better than any driving game before it. Plenty of racing games curate a bunch of different backdrops into their track selections, from urban street races in major American metropolitan centres to icy blasts across snow-swept mountains, flat-out sprints across the baking desert, or muddy expeditions through giant Sequoia forests. The Crew admirably does all this in a single game world you can drive across in one lengthy session.
This girth has come at a cost, though. It’s a world that looks fine whipping by you at speed, but it favours sheer size over the kind of granular detail we now expect in modern open world racers. Cities are smattered with recognisable landmarks but don’t really seem built to stand up to stationary scrutiny. Combined with low-detailed NPC cars (complete with entirely black, opaque glass), some forgettable effects (splashing water is especially dire), no weather, and the fact that the models of the 40-or-so cars are in a league below those of contemporaries like Forza Horizon 2 or Driveclub, The Crew struggles to shake the look of a game several years older than it actually is.

A lot of the critique on Gone Home seems to be that it's 'just walking around picking up stuff'. Which, in essense, is true. You walk around in a forest mansion, picking up notes, letters, cassettes and other objects. A story unfolds through these objects. Simple, but effective.
Rummaging through the house felt 'real' for me. Some things you find form side-stories, or suddenly explain something you saw before. The writing, which covers everything from a child's stories to letters from publishers, is stellar.
If you don't like picking up objects, opening cabinets and looking for clues, this game isn't for you. The more you look in every nook and cranny, the more you'll be rewarded.
I do think Gone Home is really overpriced. Seriously, for a game with punk as one of its main themes, it sure doesn't shy away from capitalisation.

Not worth it. Airport sims are the rare breed, but even with this, there are some more, with so much more content onboard.
For one, this game wasn't working out of the box. I had to do tweaking to start it, which is unbearable in case of game made not so long ago.
Next, it is not really a full airport sim. The procedure goes like this: some plane is boarding, and then you have to drive manually various service cars to this plane. With the speed of a snail. If you'll manage to drive the cars to the plane on time (it's like 2-3 minutes for a distance like half of kilometer, for each car), you'll get some money. When you'll have enough money, you can buy an "upgrade" to you cars. I thought they'll start to run smoother, run faster... no. They just finally hiring some drivers on those upgrade money, so, once you've upgraded all your vehicles, you can just relax and watch the work as a spectacular. And... that't the game! You can't build anything, can't buy anything, you just drive many cars in hope to gather enough to not driving it anymore. Nice, isn't it?
More to it, there are no achievements, no nothing except that point of when you don't driving yourself anymore and just watching as bots doing well, riding across the airport and not bumping into each other...
As of visuals, the picture is tolerable. Not quite good, but appropriate. What is lower than anyone's expectations, is the engine thing. All the game is about riding slooow cars, right? Well, they're not only slow, but also lame at the driving. They are stumbling on a flat surface, out of any apparent reasons... And lacking some slightest touch of reality. Like, you see the bus, which should be full of passengers, going from the plane to the gate... But it's empty! Too many polygons to count, huh? Well, I've played 8bit Nintendo games, where it was made better.
So, the game isn't worth your time - totally. My mark would be 4/10. For it's still better than clickers.

It's a futuristic racer/shooter. Kind of like Crash Team Racing or Mario Kart. Here's the pros & cons:
+ Nicely designed futuristic setting on levels (seriously)
+ Nicely and DEEPLY designed vehicle customization that is consistent with the futuristic theme. What I mean is, your vehicle has multiple parts that affect your racing;
1) Engine: How fast you will go
2) Booster: How good is your situational turbo (press for extra speed)
3) Weapons: How much damage do they inflict
4) Cooler: All of that♥♥♥♥♥♥above creates heat. Gotta cool it all down.
5) Energy: All of that♥♥♥♥♥♥above consume energy. Your energy depot size
6) Armor: How many hits you will take before you explode
7) There is more that I can't remember right now.
^ See all of that, you don't see in every race game. Nice execution there.
+ Diverse weapons types: They are fun to use, I'll give em that.
+ Diverse vehicle types AND the vehicle manufacturers. I mean they might have just created 3 vehicles and released the damn game. No, there is like 15 vehicles.
+ Sound effects and menu music is nice. Didn't like the race music.
+ Diverse race types (elimination, destroy target, destroy all, race, timed, head2head, etc.)
OK... cons:
- THERE IS NO TUTORIAL. Come on. Do I really need to check the damn options screen? The very first time I load the game? Really? To see what button does what in the game? Seriously who does that? I'll tell you who. ME (because I'm a perfectionist maniac) BUT HOW THE HELL AM I SUPPOSED TO KNOW HOW I'M SUPPOSED TO USE THOSE BUTTONS? I may know what the shooting button is. But wtf am I shooting at? What weapon does what? WTF is a booster? When and how am I gonna utilize it for best performance? WTF is going on in general? Serious flaw, no tutorial.
- Uh, opponents are really fast? I mean, maybe I'm doing it wrong (cos I'm still at the exploration period) but as soon as the race starts, everyone except me, vanishes into the horizon with incredible speed. And I'm left at the back, holding my♥♥♥♥♥♥in my hand and pushing the accelerator and the booster and hoping that I'll catch up with them before the race ends. Seriously I haven't been able to win a single race since I started playing. Maybe I'm a retard. My best position was 3, and I was pushing it AND I was extremely lucky too.
- Um, gay music. The race music I mean. The menu was nice but the race music is really bad.
I am going to be able to give this game a sad 6/10. Could have been executed much much better, because the idea and the theme is great. I love racer/shooters, there aren't many good ones around. Well I think you might be better off downloading Crash Team Racing from a PSX iso site, and playing it with your controller. Because this♥♥♥♥♥♥is hard.

I love Final Fantasy and FFX was one of my favorites in the series.  I missed FFX-2 when it came out, so I was happy to try it out on steam... wow was I disappointed.

A mentally unstable ally character "Brother" is basically joking about♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Yuna repeatedly which is played off for laughs. There is very little direction in the game, and you must be very familiar with FFX to get anything out of the story. Depending on how quickly you learn proper control or if you've played a similar game (Surgeon Simulator anyone?) you'll find that even after gaining control over the arm the game will sometimes decide you've broken it. Combined with the utter lack of a story, other than making a stinking cup of tea with about three variations to it infinitely or until the game decides to break your arm whilst simply pushing the button for water or milk. When it comes to Fallout 3 there's many aspects to the game that are unique in retrospect. It's definitely one of the best post-apocalyptic titles out there simply because of the fact that the storyline, gameplay, graphics, dialogue all blend to make a great game. Your character is born into the Capital Wasteland. A very gray, obselete place in post apocalyptic Washington D.C. Survival is harsh and only the strongest endure in this unforgiving wasteland.
Storyline is brilliant with a multitude of quests to take on, each taking you further into the depth of the story and the effects of the nuclear fallout. Whether it is helping different settlements, or murdering and pillaging towns there's always a fun aspect to both. Your actions can influence the wasteland greatly, and that ties directly with your karma which determines certain benefits to each respective side.
Gameplay is fun, and sometimes comical as far as combat goes. I found myself playing through long gaming sessions without boredom which is usually rare for myself. Exploring is entertaining and always keeps you on the lookout for raiders, mutants, and other critters that may try to attack you. The environment is quite grim but surprisingly breathtaking because it makes you appreciate the work the developers put into legitimately giving a certain sense of actually being in the wasteland.
It's price it's currently cheap and it's a definite game to check out and play.
Rate: 9/10

Here's a game that is going to take you back to a time in gaming where we used grid paper to map dungeons and solve puzzles.
It's also a time where puzzle games for some reason had combat and also crazy difficult boss fights.
I really enjoyed the Legend of Grimrock 2, but I feel although it is faithful to the old guard of Dungeon Master and Eye of Beholder... it falls prey to some of the same mistakes those games fell to.
Take for example your party. I believe the game is 'beatable' with fewer than four party members, but I see little reason to do so other than a personal challenge. Your characters can learn all sorts of traits and abilities, but the game becomes so difficult right at the end; you better have built that party extremely well.
Some of the disciplines seem totatlly unbalanced. I can't see anyone playing a game where they do not have someone with 5 in Alchemy because potions and bombs can be really important. Light weapons and firearms do not seem very good... everyone should basically have max heavy weapons, and 2 in accuracy in order to hit from the back row if necessary.
That being said... that ability to customise is there... and I very much appreicated it. The game also comes with a powerful toolbox for building your own "Grimrock". This is excellent, and I am sure people can get many hours out of solving eachothers puzzles and dungeons.
To progress in the game, you have to find these shiny gems... unfortunately although it would have been brilliant to have more gems on the island than you need to beat the game... you in fact have to get "every" gem on the island... this can be very very frusterating if you missed a couple.
Overall, I really enjoyed Legend of Grimrock 2 and would recommend playing it if you can get it on sale or really like a mix between DND, Myst, and Dungeon Master; but it comes with the warning that it does still have all the flaws of those inspirations.

A common thread among people coming to Eternal seems to be "I'm tired of Hearthstone, but Magic is too expensive for me". If this describes you, then you'll probably enjoy Eternal.
To elaborate a bit, I picked up Eternal after being somewhat disillusioned with Hearthstone. I hadn't heard much buzz about it, just stumbled across it and decided to give it a go. And it was just what I was looking for. If you feel that Hearthstone is lacking a lot of the complexity that Magic brings to a card game, then Eternal more than makes up for that. While, superficially, it resembles Magic a lot more than many competitors, it has its own spin on many mechanics. And much like Hearthstone, it uses the potential of the digital medium to great effect.
The game is also very generous with earnable in-game currency. Make no mistake, it will take you some time to build up enough of a collection to start playing top-tier decks, but it's very doable without spending a cent.
The game is still young, and it certainly has some growing to do, but it has a lot of potential, and I'm looking forward to see where it goes. If you want to pick up a new digital card game, you could do a lot worse.

UPDATE FOR 20/08/2015:
Just to say that on the 20th August, the devs made an important update that partly addresses the main criticism in my review. Now from in-game you can change (in the 'Settings' menu) the difficulty from 'Old School' to 'New School'. On the 'New School' difficulty, when you die you only lose half of your luck. In addition you aren't limited to 3 lives, which does lower the difficulty somewhat.
First impressions...
A very challenging sidescrolling platform shootemup in which you play as a 'Man with no Name' silent type. Graphics are reminiscent of C64 era and the difficulty is brutal. The controls are a little tricky to get used to ('D' just doesn't feel right for shooting) but the remapping menu is so offputting I gave up and learnt the defaults.
The game works on a 'luck' system. Enemies you kill drop luck points that can be used to avoid elemental hazards (missed that jump? if you have enough luck you'll land on a roast chicken (?) and survive).
Perhaps my main complaint aside from the controls is the checkpoint system. You accrue luck during a level, the idea being that by the time you get to the area boss you have enough luck to mitigate the difficulty. The trouble is, if that boss then kills you, you go back to the most recent checkpoint with your luck points reset. Given the game likes to put checkpoints just before the boss, it means if a boss kills you, subsequent battles will have to be fought without any luck on your side. My advice is to memorise map layouts and enemy patterns and just try not to ever die.
+ Looks and sounds great (the soundtrack is very good, though can be a bit repetetive)
+ Challenging
+ Luck system is a unique mechanic
+ Lots of Easter Eggs for Western fans
+ Pet duck
- Clunky controls
- Platforming lacks pinpoint precision
- Checkpoints work against the player and the core mechanic
I'm going to keep playing as its a lot of fun. I am happy to recommend the game, but be prepared to tear your hair out!

Not really sure why people are bashing this sim as hard as they are. This sim has been clearly marketed as a pre-alpha level release and is expected to be buggy and lacking a significant amount of what is planned. So let's get in to that:
Pros:
-Flight dynamics feel fairly accurate if not a little exaggerated at times.
-Base ground textures feel a bit more natural than FSX
-Plenty of room for improvement which is fully expected
-Cockpits are very detailed compared to the GA ones of FSX
Cons:
-FPS has been an issue for some but I only got minor studders, should be fixed with future optimizations
-GA only at this moment, no jets (I made an attempt to bring over the base 737 from FSX with no luck, didn't expect it to work anyway). I hope this changes in the future but if the true cost is $25, I'm not sure full jet modeling is in the budget.
-Lightning needs some serious work.
-ATC made me laugh the first time I heard it. The text-to-speech is pretty awful and for some reason, the only voices I got were incredibly British sounding while flying in the US.
Just with my first impressions, I get the feeling this sim is focused towards those interested in casual/GA flying and not to the die-hard jet simulators. You play asLuckslinger, or rather you are Luckslinger. A man in the wild pixelated west. All you have by your side is your trusty sixshooter, a little luck, and a mallard named Duckbridge. He's a badass duck that will fetch your throwing knife or carrying heavy bars of gold. He's super strong apparently.
Luckslinger is a side scrolling action game. You stumble across a dying man who bestows to you his lucky bracelet, with one request, take it to Clover Creek. When you arrive in Clover Creek you meet a drunk sheriff, he tells you that Sean "Boomboy" O'Connor stole the town's six "lckcharmms", which I'm assuming is their lucky charms. (Not the cereal, however, I'd go after him if it were the cereal, it also be fitting because he's Irish)
The major gameplay revolves around the luck mechanic. The bracelet generates luck as you kill enemies. The amount of luck you have has different effects throughout gameplay. It'll make some of the bullets you load head towards your enemy, sometimes save you from falling to your death, and make enemy bullets curve away from you. Your luck also has an effect on the environment, for instance, if you have no luck and you a jump on a platform it may start to fall out from underneath your feet, however, if you have enough luck it'll stay in place. It's a great mechanic to say the least.
Luckslinger will throw all kinds of enemies at you: snakes, armadillos, eagles, bandits. The first boss fight is against ol' O'Connor, where he is throwing different types of dynamite at you while you attempt to shoot him, however, just like you he also has luck and most of your bullets bend around him. It's an interesting and difficult first boss.
You are also responsible for loading you sidearm and waiting for each bullet to chamber, in the words of Shia Labeouf "DO IT!", no seriously, make sure you keep your gun filled with six bullets. Most enemies seem to take between 3-6 shots to kill and reloading during a fight is a skill that you must master if you want to get good at this game.
I can't finish this review without pointing out how amazing the music has been, a combination of chiptune and hip hop. It's amazing how well it fits into the games aesthetics.
Overall, Luckslinger uses a great mechanic to bring to a life a challenging pixelart spaghetti western.

Needless to say, I'm disappointed with what DTG did but from everything I read beforehand, I wasn't surprised either.  They telegraphed early that this was a port of FSX code to 64 bit (which by the way doesn't mean faster, it just means 64 bit pointers that allows them to access more memory).  They also said they would be upgrading the graphics engine to DX11, adding ORBX global scenery and ACCUFeel which they did but that's about it in terms of core product improvements.  The only plus I see at this point is the likely elimination of any OOM errors that plagued FSX with addons and payware aircraft.
Bottom line....if you don't own any other flight sim, sure, pick this one up and evolve with it as it improves but if you already own FSX or P3D or X-Plane and have invested in addons too, let DTG earn your money by first delivering something WORTH abandoning your current investment. Luckslinger is a challening spaghetti western action adventure game which recently released on Steam. In Luckslinger you play as Luckslinger, a luck slinging cowboy who's accompanied at all times by his trusty Duck, Duckbridge. The town of Clovercreek has had its lucky charms stolen by six bandits and the drunk of a sherrif isn't doing anything about it so it falls to you to return the lucky charms to Clovercreek and deliver justice to the bandits.
+Nice, simple graphics which give the game a western feel
+Cool, silent type, protagonist with an even cooler companion, Duckbridge isn't just a pretty beak though, he distracts enemies as well as collects items for you
+Outstanding soundtrack which fits the game excellently
+The game treats luck as a resource which is rather interesting and provides some unique moments in gameplay such as when a bullet bends out of your way at the last second, luck isn't all good though so I'll revist it later on
+Other than the luck mechanic the gameplay consists of shooting/throwing weapons at enemies and dodging their attacks, might not sound too interesting but when you're up against multiple enemies it's really rather challenging
+A few different types of stock enemies which vary slightly depending on the setting you're in
+Chests and gambling tents sometimes provide you with one of several items which add nicely to the gameplay and are also rather handy
+As well as a revolver you also have a throwing knife which is a lot of fun to use
+Challenging boss fights, the bosses are the six bandits you're hunting down and they all have a specific combat style, for example the first bandit loves dynamite so his combat style is based around throwing dynamite
+Great writing and characters
+Good controls (played with an Xbox 360 Controller), everything was very responsive though the platforming did sometimes feel a little forced, i.e. you had to do a lot of little 'fine-tuning' controller movements to successfully land a jump on a platform
-If you die three times (or more depending on if you've collect a life pickup) you have to restart the entire level from the very beginning, this gets rather frustrating very quickly especially when it happens several times
-With luckiness, comes unluckiness and there's a lot of that in this game. I've never really been a fan of luck-based things so perhaps I'm slightly biased here but when you get a few 'unlucky events' in a row, such as a platform collapsing beneath you, it can get tedious. There is such a thing as too much luck in this game also, for example when all of your luck is used up to bend away slow bullets from a regular enemy just before a boss fight

Verdict:
Worth Purchasing (8/10)

DISCLAIMER NOTE: I was gifted a copy of the game by the developers but I will attempt to remain as unbiased as possible for this review. I have also NOT completed this game as I wanted to keep as little story detail out as possible and give you more of a first impressions styled review.
Tell me fellow gamers what does a duck, the wild west, luck and a jazzy hip-hop themed soundtrack have in common?  No?  Well I’ll tell you, it’s a 2D action/adventure by Indie developers Duckbridge and I’m here to tell you all about it!
The plotline for Luckslinger (LS) is fairly simple, 6 dastardly in famous criminal scumbags have stolen the luckcharms of Clovercreek and it’s up to you along with your faithful sidekick to get them back.  So were good right? I can assume you’ll go buy the game now yes? Oh you want me t flesh it out a bit more? Ok but prepare for some gushing because I think I’ve fallen for this charming game…
From the very instant I booted up Luckslinger a smile bigger than Heath Ledgers’ joker appeared upon my face. The charming looks and brilliantly executed soundtrack instantly hit me, and then I started the game, which gave me even more cause to be happy as it was shown to me akin to an old western film with animated introduction credits showing us the hero (anti-hero?) and his epic sidekick Duckbridge, who yes is a duck but comes in very handy!
What really pulled me into LS is the genius “luck mechanic” the developers have implemented in, luck is almost a resource you collect from such things like fallen enemies, chests, etc and builds up on your luck charm.  If you were to for example run under a windmill or jump onto a platform and didn’t have enough luck, the windmill may fall on your head or the platform may drop you into the deep chasm below you. On the other hand if you have enough luck, you will not be crushed or dropped and you can even at times defy long jumps by “creating” your own luck and surviving the fall via mole (yes you heard that right!).
From here on I am also shown how to shoot, roll, reload and even use a knife (didn’t think I needed it but you’d be surprised!) to dodge, kill and stab my way through the first level to reach my end goal…the boss and get that stolen charm back, but first I had to visit the town of Clovercreek, a once happy and busy place turns desolte by these terrible criminals. However you can visit the buildings and buy items like records for playback later, items to assist you on your adventure amongst other novelties that I won’t disclose ;).
From the twon you go off and adventure you way to the end level boss, pretty simple right? Except for the fact that there are many enemies and obsticles in your way to try and stop you doing just that. Let me tell you it isn’t as easy as it sounds and took me a good while just to reach the boss let alone finish him off!  However there is plenty to help you along the way such as Russian roulette and Gambling in a Native Indians’ tent…oh did I not mention that BOTH of those events are affected by your luck meter?  Yes you can alter the outcome and boost your chances of a win by having a full meter!  Brilliant!
It takes me a good hour to get to the level boss (a good 30mins of that spent re-doing the boss!) and it’s a great fight filled with old school tactics and enemy patterns, all this accompanied by a kickass hip-hip themed soundtrack that I’m happy to announce doesn’t make me want to turn off the in-game music (not many games have a good BGM in my opinion). At the end of the level I even get given a choice to either kill the criminal or bring him back alive for trial…of course I blew his head off…naturally ;).
Scoring
Looks: A* – I love the charming look fo the game and it suits the western theme really well.
Gameplay: A* – Xbox 360 controller support that works really well, thumbs up!
Sound: A* – Just…fantastic!
Price: A* – Fair price for a game written by 2 guys with this much polish.
Enjoyment: A* – Smile bigger than the cheshire cats’. Can’t rate it higher!
Overall Score: A* (and I want to give it more!)

Since MS Flight Simulator 5.1, I've been flying in virtual airspace, so I'm very excited there is finally a successor to FSX!
First of all, don't expect to receive a fully polished and stable training environment. The 'game' is still very much in development. I think it's great that Dovetail offers us the opportunity to fly along as they're building this next gen flight sim environment.
First impressions:
- Without any configuration, it looks good straight out of the box. Just don't compare it to FSX with tons of add-ons installed.
- The stock planes have lots of eye candy and the flight dynamics feel accurate, but again, you can't compare them with add-ons like for example the GA aircraft from A2A.
- It FEELS like the Flight Simulator environment we've grown so familiar with in the past decades, and I like this! You will feel right at home.
- I very much like the pilot profile, statistics and the way all of your flights are logged.
Performance:
With everything maxed out, my framerate occasionally drops below 20 FPS in the vicinity of heavy scenery areas with lots of AI traffic. Most of the time my framerate is above 40 FPS. Even with the beautiful raindrop effect, the simulator performs very well.
Intel i5 7600K @ 4,2 GHz
GeForce GTX 1070 8G
16 GB DDR4 @ 2666 MHz
To-dos:
- I would like to see more documentation and manuals for the stock aircraft. Also a kneeboard with general info and checklists would be nice.
- There are much things missing in this version, like a detailed weather engine, detailed flight planning IFR/VFR, (moving) map, ... but then again, it's early access.
Conclusion:
- If you're looking for an instant replacement of your current stable FSX environment, then this is not for you.
- If you want to fly along as Dovetail developpes this great next gen flight sim, then this is very much for you: buy it! It's quite a bang for the buck if you ask me.

The game should run on pretty much any system from 2007 onwards, which makes it suitable for laptop gamers but I would highly recommend using an external mouse.

A amazing city builder which, besides some hiccups plays amazingly well and realisticly. It's less of a game where you build up and watch your city expand, but more a survival game as your population is your most valuble reasorce, and you need to keep them warm, healthy and fed..or they die out, the game being over then. It is very flexable in what strategy you take, there being no wrong or fool-proof tatic..as long as it gets the job done..and thats imporant because one mistake can start a chain reaction..let the popluation grow too fast, you starve everyone as there is not enough food, get too eager building and you run out of wood for fires for the winter. You don't need to worry about combat, as you are fighting the most dangrous thing: Mother Nature. Weather, Sickness and Natural disasters are your enemy, and all you can do is stem the tide, prevent as much damage as you can, and rebuild. It's a fun as hell little time waster, and easier to understand then it looks. My advise is take the time to learn the UI and read the Wiki, as going in blind sets you up for fustrating disaster. Arm yourself with Knowlage, it's your most vital tool, but remeber as I said, there is no wrong or fool proof tatic, just be prepared for what the game throws at you to counter it.

My typical days as of late have revolved around me trying to crunch huge amounts of school work in order to have time to play the games I enjoy without having to worry like a nun who just got caught inviting children into a van. I was in this never ending cycle when I discovered Banished, a strategy game that involves developing a decent society while surviving the natural elements. You start with a small group of citizens who have been banished from their home land and must survive in a climate with no one else around, I like to believe this is how Australia got started. Unfortunately for your citizens winter is coming and you must build houses, collect firewood, and find food quickly if you even want a chance of survival.
Unlike in most strategy games Banished does not make you assign tasks to specific citizens, rather it lets you assign a number of people to do a certain task and the game will sort out who goes where. With a simple game like Banished this system makes sense, and the fact that I do not need to stay constantly involved in every little process allows me to relax while watching my minions slave away. All citizens take their food into stock piles for everyone to use regardless of their job, which works well for the game because this is a game that you are not supposed to get too heavily involved in. Banished, or should I say Socialism Simulator 2014, really shines in it's simplicity and simpleness. There are no goblin armies or dark lords to fight against, the only enemy is mother nature, and my goodness she can be a real b--ch sometimes.
My first town had been living in peace for around 20 years when suddenly a tornado swept through and leveled my town killing all but 4 of my citizens. Things like this make the game interesting because Socialism Simulator is not interesting unless chance decides to make it that way. You will develop a system that will suddenly be ruined by a fire or a harsh winter that ruines your towns resources and weakens the population. How you adjust to these changes is up to you as you will get little help from the game on how you should be running things. It is because of this lack of help that you must use quite a bit of trial and error in order to find an effective way to stay alive. Additionally, I have had my populations fall due to the fact that none of my citizens were having children. The way to fix this is by building more houses because apparently couples refuse to go at it whenever they live with other people. I would think that a couple of lovers that are both in their teens would have no problem with being a little quiet in their business but apparently the threats by the bride's fathers involving pitchforks and fishing rods have made everyone a little less willing to get funky unless they live in their own house.
After playing in several different scenarios I can see why many people would not like this game. The game is very simple and does not feature much variety from town to town. I personally enjoyed the game because it was calm and a nice break from the typical strategy game. I was able to do bits of my schoolwork while playing the game without feeling like I was forced to get involved, this is mainly due to the games very slow pace and constant periods of repitition. If you really enjoy complex gameplay that involves excitement and lots of strategy Banished is probably not right for you. But if you are looking for a game that is simply there to help you relax while doing a side task, I would suggest you give Banished a try.

While by no means a Future Racing pro, I at least hold my own in the majority of Future Racers, good or bad. Quantum Rush Champions, at first, seemed promising, a spiritual successor to Wipeout, on the PC, with some cool ideas. But the game does not want me to like it. It actively resists such attempts.
A heavy chicane series in the third track. Until engines and boosters are upgraded, races are a tedious slog to, at best, a silver. Weapon pickups have a hitbox a third the size of the boost pads, and the same goes for the packages of Courier mode. Weapons, for the most part, rely on either perfect straights, or getting close to other racers (Which is somewhat difficult when said racers have upgrades you do not. Like engines and boosters.) What is worse still, my upgrades in one tier count for... Nothing beyond being able to beat *that* Tier, of *that* campaign, with *that* craft. And Time Trial times require not only those upgrades, but a flawless line.
I want to like Quantum Rush Champions. But it doesn't let me. Needing multiple attempts and specific unlocks to achieve even a silver medal is not fun. Needing to do it every racing class is not fun. In short, though I had high hopes for this game since Quantum Rush Online... This game has too high a difficulty curve, with too much grind, for it to be fun. Which is a shame.

This game takes city building in a different direction. It's not like the Sim City games (The GOOD ones, so definetly not SIm City 2013) or Cities XL, which I do not own but I've soon my friends who love city building games play it and it looks good and they say it's amazing. No Banished is different from traditional city builders where what you build is dependent on the money you have and what poeple want. In those games you're the mayor of your town of >insert name here< and you are there to serve the people that move in because that's government. In Tropico you are the dictator and you have a lot more freedom though the things you do may get you in trouble and it won't take long for you to figure out what to do to succeed (Still a fun game though with a great sence of humor). In Banished, there is no one to please, no income, no hand holding and no dumbing things down just because things should be simple.
Banished adds survival and RTS elements to the city building genre. You start off with a few people, a few resourses and no real instructions (which would be nice for a few things.). It's like Minecraft, there is no shame in going online to look up information on what to do and you may end up failing many times before getting the hang of the game and even then you still need to be careful. What you end up doing is creating farms, houses, tailors, woodcutters and other jobs slowly and allocate the amount of people you want to work that job and you can even adjust the max number of people allowed to work on that location. And if your like me, at least early on, you'll find yourself constently re-allocating people depending on the season. That's another thing that this game has is the seasons which will affect things like crops. For instance, you can't grow crops when there's snow during late Autumn through Winter, so during this time you move people from growing crops to other jobs.
Now one might think that since the player relies that much on the citizen's A.I.'s, if the game is glitchy then they're screwed. And they'd be right. HOWEVER, that is not the case here. Aside from one issue I had with crops that might be due to the A.I., I never had a problem and seem to be someone who gets glitches most gamers don't get. It's so well made that when I fail I have no one to blame but myself. The game did what I asked it to but I should have done something different. This game is so optimized I've never had a problem with frame rate and it takes up such a small amount of hard drive space! I find it amazing that this game was made by one person where games like Day One: Garry's Incedent are made by a group of people and fail on things like collision and even things that can be fixed by simply changing a number. (Seriously, why can't the gun in that game kill people who are wearing nothing but a piece of cloth?) Or even big dev teams with a big name company backing them releasing broken, incomplete games (Looking at you EA).
I would highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys city building. This is a game that can end up taking a lot of time out of you day. I bought it on a Friday and Sunday night I realized that not only have I not reach year 100 yet but it's actually 1 in the morning Monday and I have homework I forgot to do. This is something that has never happened to me with any city building game. Here I really felt incharge and what I say I want my people to do they will and when I fail, it's not to a glitch or poor A.I. but to my own mistake. "I should have had more hunters and less fisherman." or "Should have made my sheep farm bigger." I'm not even really one to play these types of games because I always failed at Sim City as a child. This game has definitly held my interests and I would even say it might be worth getting when it's not on sale. (Which pretty much when I buy all my games)

This game is really hard to recommend as it stands.
To sum up this game simply, it's basically a Wipeout clone. For those unfamiliar, Wipeout is a game originally released for Playstation systems. It's a "futuristic" racer that excelled with strong AI and great mechanics. This game wants to be a spiritual succesor on the PC, but it doesn't quite get there.
That's not to say it's entirely awful. It looks very good. While the tracks lack oomph or big moments, they're fine and the art designers should be proud of the work they did on this game. There's one track that goes into an underwater tunnel and I liked the way the tube was designed. Things like sound effects and music, while not spectacular, do the job and do not take away from the experience. I also liked the weight that the vehicles seemed to feel. Turning was not cumbersome and for the most part bar one key gripe, "driving" was well done.
Where this game truly suffers is in races, which for a racer is obviously a really big problem. AI is bland and the lack of depth really hurts the game. I found myself bored quickly, and considering how high I hold the aforementioned Wipeout, this really sapped my interest in Quantum Rush. The lack of a multiplayer mode hurts replayability as single player races, despite varying modes (i.e. Death Match/Courier/Career etc) just don't feel fleshed out or interesting at all. Another aspect I found really tough to adjust to was I never felt the speed. The odometer reads over 800 km/h and it just doesn't seem like you're going that fast. There's a variety of different weapons you pickup over a course, but they lack any pizazz or help keep the race interesting. It would have also been nice to have an intro/tutorial immediately upon starting the game, but this gripe would've been overlooked if the final product itself was better.
All in all I cannot recommend Quantum Rush for a purchase. If you find it as a part of a bundle, I'd say to go ahead and give it a whirl, but the lack of depth really makes me doubt I'll bother with it ever again.
