Interesting concept, and the dreary and brutal nature of trench warefare is represented really well in this game... visually speaking. It may not be cutting edge pretty, but it's good enough.
This game is basically Frontlines in WWI. For obvious reasons the Frontlines style of territorial progression is ideal for this era of warefare... the actual handling of the game is not.
Movement is clunky. It's not at a horrific, untweakable level, but it's not great. There are times moving through some of the tighter trenches or "over" terrain... it feels weird and... clunky. Clunky is the key word here. Running through the trenches (and there's a lot of running and confused navigation upon respawn) feels, again, clunky when you're amongst other player models.
The leveling up of classes does not help that. On its own the levelling up would be alright as a challenge, but combined with the extended, clunky running (again, not terribly far, but enough considering this is a one hit kill type shooter)  leans this game towards a tedious feeling.
The tweakble issues felt kind of beta-ish to me.
It clearly appeals to a decent enough number of players to populate servers, but if you have a personal standard of FPS movement and handling that you just can't go below, this won't feel fun.
Not a bad game, it just needs more than a little tweaking.

Oh where to start with this game.... Well, first off, it's extremely difficult. VVVVVV is a mind bending puzzler, where you control a little pixelated blue dude who can switch gravity on himself. It's easy at first, but ramps up difficulty very quickly. You have to rescue your crew who got stranded after something horrible happened on the ship. Each person has his own unique level, teaching you a new game nuiance. The game is very hard. First try, it took me about three hours to do. But once you know how to play, it goes much faster. My second playthrough only took 36 minutes, so it is fair. You collect trinkets for bragging rights, and there's one known that goes down as the hardest part of the game... you'll find it easily. Anyway, VVVVVV is a great game, and you should definately buy it if you want rage inducing fun, which will help your reaction time.

If you've ever been envious of the consoles with their fancy AG racing games, well, now you don't have to be. Quantum Rush has some rough spots, but delivers a great AG racing game. Taking heavy inspiration and even improving elements of WipEout, it's a pretty fun racing game, with a great visual look. It's a little like Jax X Combat Racing in that you have a primary weapon and can get pickups on the track, but its AG racing, and best of all, the engine explosions actually are well done. It's also deeper than other racing games, as you have to manage heat and energy and armor, but it never feels overwhelming. $10 isn't a terrible price for this game, and if you see it on sale, definitely go for it.
As for cons, like I said, there are some rough spots. Controller support is fine during races, but bad in the menu. Also, many things aren't explained to you directly, which really should be. Also, the AI is pretty hard, and there's no difficulty settings that I could find, but all of these don't really take too much away from the game.
EDIT: There is actually a manual for this game that explains a lot of the things that I thought should have been explained, however, there is very little indication that there is a manual, and I only thought to check on a hunch.

Homefront the Revolution has potential of being a great game, but ultimately falls short of becoming one as it suffers a bit of idnetity crisis in this saturated FPS market.
The gameplay elements borrow heavily from Far Cry series such as stealth mechanics, hacking the transceiver to reveal surroundings is like hacking the communications tower in Farcry, looting and crafting, interestingly the weapon custimization comes from crysis series.
The opening intro shows an interesting "what if" scenario, but as soon as I got into the game I'm lost with the plot, the game seemed to put me on a linear set of objectives, but I am free to roam the game world however I want.
I don't mind if the gameplay elements are borrowed from other games, the problem is that these elements are poorly implemented in Homefront. The enemy and friendly AI are horrible, the stealth mechanics is near non-existant.
And the game is still littered with bugs and visual issues.
The CryEngine the game is running on is poorly optimised, I am running on a pretty high end machiine that is way over the recommended system requirement, Intel Core i7 7700, Geforce 1060GTX 3GB running on the latest geforce driver with 16GB system RAM and I'm getting  averaging 20-30fps  at near highest setting. Even at medium setting the frame rate I'm getting is 40 and sometimes may dip below 30.
On a positive note, the games visual is fantastic, albeit not always consistant. I particularly love exploring the game world during night time. This is when the CryEngine truly shines when you see the lightings, the shadows and the particle effects. The futuristic dystopian setting of a war torn Philadelphia is well crafted.
Ultimately I would not recommend this game due to bugs, performance issues and poor gameplay mechanics.
There are better games out there such as Far Cry 3&4 if you are wanting similar gameplay.
But if you like the near futuristic dystopian setting then I suggest getting the game during steam sale.

First off, I really WANT to love Verdun, but it's techical issues, lack of polish and clunky gameplay leaves a gaping wound in my heart, as I once again wait for respawn. TLDR: This game is still in beta.  It's unpolished, glitchy, missing key elements of a "tactical shooter" and has overall been poorly executed.
+ Core community despite the low player base, you'll find a game easily
+ World War I setting
+ Great server browser immerses you in the action easily
Unfortunately that's about it. As soon as you join a game that immersion gets cut shorter than the lifespan of a new recruit in the trenches.
- No information on how unlocks, classes or just about anything works (coming from a 20 year FPS player). You'll find yourself staring at the respawn screen with no helpful hints or tips
- Clunky and frustrating controls(in a bad way). It feels nothing like the slow methodical RO2/RS or Squad FPS.   You'll try to run from a grenade, only to crouch or get caught on invisible walls.
- Combat is laughable and frustrating at the same time. You feel like your in control of a mannequin rather than an actual person.  It's neither fluid or easy on the eyes when watching 3rd person.
- Be prepared to get sniped by people hopping up and down over trench walls, or (as mentioned above) the random grenade whose shrapnel/concussion magically goes through trench lines.
- No lean or peek feature, leaving you exposing your WHOLE body when trying to see whats around the corner (hint: it's probably someone camping with a rifle, don't worry you wont have time to react before your insta death)
- All explosions sound and look like a small firework went off, or a dud.  Don't worry though, it'll get you kills through walls.
- Death animations are a good attempt by the devs, but are poorly done, leaving ragdolls glitching everywhere, or dying comrades looking more like "The Thing" than a soldier holding on to their last breath.  I guess it's equally as horrifying to look at.
- Super quiet battlefield. You won't feel like your involved in a massive conflict bigger than yourself.  You'll occasionally hear one of your fellow manniquens say something, or die, very rarely are people on VOIP so it's super noticeable and makes the small server seem even SMALLER.
- unfair spawn system.  There's no base area, it's either on your teamate or NCO, leading to insta deaths on spawn, very frustrating
In the end, it's a valiant effort by the small dev team and I recogize it.  However, I couldn't even recommend this game for $5 when there's much better options out there worth putting that $5 toward.  The only reason this game has a playerbase is that there are no other attempts at a fairly "realistic" WWI shooter.  The game plays like its still in beta, and its community is as loyal as a rabid pitbull (as reflected in the low helpful  review voting).
I would recommend  putting your hard earned money toward the games Squad or RS2: Vietnam (hell i'd even recommend RS/RO2, because it still has a higher player base and better gameplay than this despite being released in 2012)

A platform game where you can't jump?
Running at a surprising speed, your player is in a foreign (to him, or her) landscape, covered in spikes (hence the name VVVV...). How can our hero traverse these areas? By inverting gravity at request, and utilising several platforms whose characteristics change our players direction and gravity.
Designed to simulate games of yesteryear (mostly for our late twenties to early thirties crowds) such as Jet Set Willy, Rad Gravity, and many others, the game is sprite-oriented with simple patrol patterns and basic collision=death gameplay.
A gem of a game, you'll think more than you'll want to to chart this world, and all you need is a left, right and a gravity button to enable our wee hero to do so.

This is a very hesitant recommend vote. The game overall is good, but there's plenty of things about it that are negative as well.
For starters, Eternal is, at it's core, a very solid card game. If you wanted to compare it to something, it's kind of like Hearthstone and Magic The Gathering had a baby, with more of the features resembling MTG.
So if you liked Hearthstone but miss some of the stuff from MTG (and are sick of WOTC's PC/Mobile games), this will probably sit well with you. Mostly.
There's more flexibility here, and more card interactions and things ala MTG, which is a nice change of pace from so many of the more bland CCGs out there. There's also no need to really fork out loads of cash, as you can grind your way into just about anything.
Games are fairly short (usually 4-10 minutes). There's Draft style, Ranked, and a strange pseudo-draft against the AI called forge. You can also challenge your friends to casual games.
The art style is pretty comparable to most CCGs out there, and the sound is at par as well. (Although that splash screen sometimes seems a bit loud)
So where's the bad stuff?
Well, to begin with, the interface is...just bad. It was clearly designed with tablets in mind. It's clunky, (you will open up your options menu screen MANY times just trying to get back out of something) and the chat window? Seriously, I think this game has the single worst in-game chat I've ever seen. It's such a pain to use that you'll be switching out of the game to use just about ANYTHING else. It takes at least 3 button clicks to see the chat window, and then it covers so much of the screen that it's difficult to see what your opponent is doing. You can't resize it or move it, either. Enjoy.
(Seriously, why not just press enter to chat?)
Forge: That AI sorta-draft you can play? It's cool, except for one very rage-inducing problem. The game controls how much mana goes into your deck. You get no control over this. I play a lot of forge as it's one of the best ways to build up your card collection early on, and I can straight tell you the number of losses that have been because of mana issues for me is like 80-90%. Just sitting there either waiting for mana, or drawing nothing BUT mana. (Or energy, or power, or whatever they call it. I'm an MTG player it will always just be mana to me.) This is especially frustrating because it costs you to play Forge. Dropping 250 gems or 2500 coins into a round of forge only to get completely screwed by a system you have no control over is near game-breaking.
Balance: While it's one of the more minor problems, there's still some areas of the game that seem to be a bit out of balance. There's a number of cards I've looked at and just wondered why they bothered? Fair enough, it's hard work balancing a game as big as a collectable card game, but please keep working on it.
PRO TIP: New player? Want to win? Warcry deck. You're welcome.
It feels like there's a lot more versatility and such that could be explored in the game, but certain very strong abilities or aspects kind of drown out potential others. It's something I hope they adjust in the future, but hearing from other players makes it sound unlikely the devs will bother.
Overall I like the game, and I've put plenty of time into it as you can see, but I can't honestly say everyone who likes CCGs will like this.  Those who can overlook the unintuitive interface, minor balance issues, and certain aspects of the game being out of your control (usually to your detriment) will probably enjoy it a lot. If hose kinds of things annoy you, then you might want to move on. Or not. It's free, give it a shot if you're interested.
Overall, it's a pretty good game, but some glaring faults are there; like a supermodel with a giant wart on her nose and a unibrow.

Great digital card game with alot of well respected names behind it. Eternal simply is a solid digital adaptation of Magic: the Gathering. Changes to mana and influence, 75 card decks, varations on the tradition colors, and a different card pool are the major deviations. The game features a leaderboard, multiple PvE and PvP gamemodes including arena style draft and standard pack draft.
The game is generous to new players with most decks being obtainable through only a few weeks of moderate play. Most rewards are handled through chests which appear in bronze, silver, gold, and diamond. Bronze chests award a common and a small handful of gold, which is used to buy packs and drafts. Each higher up chest gives more gold and a higher rarity. There is also the option to grind as much as you want, every 3 ranked wins is a bronze chest, and you can do an infinite amount of a pve gauntlet ala Hex TCG. Overall its an excellent CCG if a bit derivitive, if you are a fan of card games or just interested i would give it a try.

Love this game!
Pros:
- The story (for what there is) was pretty mysterious and intruiging, i found myself looking forward to every letter, trying to decipher who (or what) the "Master of the island" was.
- The graphics are beautiful, and really don't need incredible hardware to function at high settings (i originally played this at max settings with a gt530!)
- Each kill is super satisfying, even killing the little creeps felt really good.
- The difficuly was on point, I played on hard and it wasn't too hard, but wasn't too easy. The difficulty may be dependant on how many secrets you find.  For those of you who like being roughly fondled by video games, there is ironman, no-map, or "farmer" modes for you. This game really does have a difficulty for pretty much anyone.
- There are a TON of secrets in this game, you're bound to accidentally stumble upon some, even if you  don't look for them. They typically contain the best gear and really good survivability tools. Hoewever if you DO put in the effort to look for secrets, it's a fantatic feeling when it finally clicks, it feels just as good as a well constructed puzzle game for some of the secrets in this game.
- Environments are Interesting and varied, I was always looking forward to the next "biome" to explore. This game is far superior to this first, and i mainly give the credit to the enviroments.
enemies are decently varied and i nearly always found completely new enemies for each area, some are just retextures, but there is enough there to satisfy.
Cons:
- some traps are REALLY unforgiving... I'm talking just step into a room, the door closes and out come literally 10 enemies... in a 4X4 room. learn to save early, save often, as there is no autosaving (with the exception of activationg a life crystal) plenty of people have quit because they are cradled by modern autosaving, this game doesn't have it!
- as far as I know there is no respecing, so don't screw it up!
- spells are taught through scrolls, which are pretty much always found in secrets... unless you want to trial and error the spell system all day. This makes playing mages difficult and slow, sometimes impossible based on how many useful scrolls you find. Unless you're using a walkthrough, try not to spec your mages around what you WANT, spec them around what you GET.
- you'll probably be doing a lot of wandering and backtracking if you miss an area or item by accident, sometimes the direction can be unclear or somewhat hidden (main "story" areas and items will NEVER be part of a secret just sometimes really out of the way)
- a couple of the main puzzles required to progress are a little janky, after brute forcing a couple of them i looked it up just to realise I was holding the answer, but that might be because i'm an idiot. (the gravyard puzzle, I still don't understand how i did it the first time)
- As previously mentioned, the secrets contain amazing loot. If you don't get enough secrets, the game may become a gangrape. However I didn't have this problem, and most of the secrets i found were by accident.
- Most of the story is told through the environment and through little snippits from letters and stones. The story isn't hidden on the dark souls level, but it's not super direct either. I personally like it this way, but I can see a lot of people preffering the "story book" type games.
- Hate throwing potions at ♥♥♥♥ing broken feet DAMN IT!
Conclusion/ TL:DR:
Overall, the complaints I have are small and didn't really impede my enjoyment, however I can see them possibly causing problems for others. I thoroughly enjoyed myself all the way through and was always excited to uncover more secrets and get more sweet, sweet loot. Do yourself a favour and pick this up.
And remember, save early, save often.

I cannot recommend this game.
I played the hell out of Eye of the Beholder (all of them) and the other classic D&D games back in the day, and I loved them.
That was a long time ago, gaming has come a long way, and I have obligations and responsibilites beyond your little game. So, when the complete lack of autosave/checkpointing causes me to lose 30 mintues of gameplay...I just walk away.
Picture it: after a few days of work, I finally have a few minutes to sit down at play. I haven't been thinking about this game for those two days, I haven't had time to think about it, but now I get to play it. So, I sit down with it, spend a few minutes getting my bearings, work out a quick plan of attack, and in I go. I play for a bit, stumble around, maybe fight a few battles, find an item or two...and then die from some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Monster got a lucky crit? ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t pressure plate launch a horde of overpowered enemies at me? Item randomly teleports me into a room full of enemies? Great, now I'm dead; last save was...where I started the session.
Look, I understand the *idea* of quicksave (trust me, I lived through it's birth and subsequent abandonment), and I actually fought for it to stay when the checkpoint craze started. But now? There's no excuse for this. Just because you want to pay homage to classic games, this doesn't mean you have to abandon everything we've learned since them.
You make me lose my entire play session due to unforeseen ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t while providing no checkpoint or autosave system to mitigate the lost time, I uninstall your game, regret my purchase, and am very uninclined to buy future produces from you. I've purchased both LoG 1 and 2, but don't expect me to buy anything else unless you learn from the past.
And this doesn't even get into the awkward UI, bags opening over your character's paperdoll, spellcasting being a giant flipping PITA, having to annoyingly spam clicks during combat (even the classic games had an "all attack" button), the poor-fit outdoor environments are to a strict grid layout, "invisible walls" (why can't my characters just walk around that pillar?), pixel-hunting out the wazoo, and just all-around poor decisions.
I wanted to love this game, then I wanted to like it, then I wanted to just power through it, now I want to forget it.

If Amnesia: The Dark Descent and the Penumbra games had a baby, that baby would be Outlast. This is classic survival horror - a creepy setting, no weapons, and no way to survive except to hide. You play as a journalist investigating an abandoned insane asylum, based on an anonymous tip of shady goings-on there. The only tool you have at your disposal is a video camera. The main hook of the game is using the camera's IR (night vision) mode to see just what the hell is going around you. It makes for some very effective moments of terror. Imagine knowing something scary and nasty is out there stalking you, but not being able to see what's 3 feet in front of you... yeah, that's the experience in a nutshell. Those moments are what makes this game effective. But unfortunately the whole game is not just those moments. Some parts I found to be somewhat tedious. For example, in one section, you have to explore an area to collect 3 fuses to restore power to something, all the while being stalked by crazy people. It's tense, to be sure, but also makes you realize that you're playing a game with a lame "collect x things" mechanic. It kind of brings you out of the experience a bit. The final section of the game is also sort of hit or miss, as it changes direction in a big way (reminds me sort of how Amnesia fell apart a little bit towards the end). But it's not necessarily bad... just different (I don't really want to get into spoilers at all), so it's one of those things where you might like it or you might not. But the majority of the game leading up to the end is pretty much consistently good. The environment is creepy as hell, the atmosphere is dark, and the "enemies" (mostly disfigured inmates) serve their purpose well. There are a few jump-scares, and the aforementioned fetch-quest sections where you're being chased, but mostly, the horror of the game comes from the combination of atmosphere and having to rely on a camera (whose batteries drain quickly when using IR) to be able to see. On the downside, you sort of get used to things after a while, so the scare factor wears off a bit towards the end. So it's ultimately a good thing that the game only lasts around 4-5 hours. Any more would have been too much. Despite the flaws, there's still lots of good things to experience here, so if you're a fan of this genre, you pretty much have to play this at some point. I think the price is probably fair, but if you can wait, it's definitely worth picking up in a sale.
Technical notes: I ran into a major bug towards the beginning of the game that prevented any further progress (it involves shaking the mouse during a quick-time event). The issue has supposedly been fixed in a patch, but it didn't work for me. There is a pinned post in the Steam discussions explaining how to work around this if it doesn't work for you either.

This game, a sequal to the popular Five Nights at Freddy's, came out only 3 months after the first game! Now of course what this game does is do what any sequal should, take the formula that made it what it is, and add onto it, and this game does certainly that, adding more animatronics, mechanics and overall more stuff to worry about. What I like about this game is that what I said earlier, it adds onto it's formula. Now I'll admit, the first game had it's sounds and setting to keep you tensed but not alot really happens until you get to Night 4, 5 and 6. The 4/20 mode is the only thing that allows things to be constant, for you to always be on your guard 100% to try and not die. But overtime, the mode is so hard that you just get frustrated overtime, overall losing that feeling of fear to always be on your guard, turning into a feeling of just being tired and wanting to beat it for completion. The second game however, improves on that. By adding more stuff to do, to worry about, it increases the feeling of uneasiness and tenseness, even on the first night! Not to mention how much this game added onto the hidden backstory by adding more easter eggs and details about the company's past. Now, before I end this review, I want to talk about my one complaint..it's jumpscares. The jumpscares in the first game, they were decent, they were alright. It made you feel like they actually were in your face and were somewhat of a threat. But..in the second game..it just feels, well, kinda forced. With most of them just jumping out nowhere onto your face. In the first game, it felt like they were waiting for you to pull down the camera to strike. In the second game, they just, *pop* and go *boo!* But overall, I liked this game and thought it did an ok job of going forward and advancing it's formula. I recommend this game to anyone who liked the first one and are interested.

I have not played this game for very long yet, but I wanted to type in a quick review anyway because the game is on sale now. Simply put, I'm loving this game so far. It feels to me a lot like the original 2005 NFS Most Wanted and considering that was my favorite racing game ever, that's a very good thing if you ask me. It's not quite as heavy on the police chases as that game, for one, police doesn't seem to care much how fast you go, just if you crash into things. And for another, so far I've been able to pull to my top speed and they can't keep up. I've seen others complain that regular patrol cars could keep up with their supercars, but my Mustang had no issues... Maybe it gets harder later in the game, maybe those that complain simply can't drive, I don't know yet but so far I see no problem.
The game is also very big, with different types of country and lots of recognisable landmarks. I spent 2 to 3 hours driving from Detroit to Seattle, LA, then Miami (so about 3/4 around the USA). In Most wanted I used to run a race that went around the entire game area that took I believe 20 or 30 minutes.
Another thing that I think is absolutely awesome is the support for my G27 steering wheel. The game recognises the wheel on its own and all the buttons it tells you to press make sense (although it took me a little while to realise that it used the shape of the buttons to indicate which ones it meant). The force feedback is decent, but gets a lot better with some tweaking (google for the xml file you can make). The game also fully supports the clutch and H shifter. I left it on autoclutch myself because I found that when I use the clutch myself I tend to get too wild at times and my wheelstand pro will not stay in its place (has nothing to do with the game), but I really love using the H shifter.
All in all, to anyone who's looking for a fun arcade racer that still has enough sim-like qualities to enjoy it with a wheel (unlike all recent NFS games), especially if like me you keep hoping that EA will steer the NFS series back to how it played in the NFSU2/MW/C era, I can definitely recommend giving this game a try. And you can download the demo first if you want, it's completely identical to the game, it just limits you to trying it for two hours, so you can safely test it out :)
update july 2016:
Just felt I should update this... The game was really fun at first, but then, it just... fizzled out? It was cool to drive around the USA, but when I actually started doing more races, it just felt boring. I tried getting back into it and I'm just not even sure what to do. There is also NO way to restart your playthrough and Ubi defends this by saying you can replay all events... Yeah, NO! That doesn't help at all when you haven't played the game in a year and want to give it another go. It just drops you right into the middle of things having no clue anymore about what's going on. And with the individual races being so bland, well, I'm permanently abandoning this game and changing my recommendation.

I played this game in 2017; 17 years have passed since the last time I played a Final fantasy game, and while I was very fond of the series at the time, many mechanics that are series hallmarks just feel annoying nowadays. The story, of course, is still great and I feel a casual playthrough of this game would be very satisfying. Unfortunately I'm a completionist and tried to do everything I could in this game, which proved so boring and frustrating I gave up. Trying to kill optional bosses and finding secrets in this game means hours of boring battles, hours of infuriating mini-games and becoming so overpowered that you finish any story battle in one turn.
In summary: I recommend playing this game casually and ignoring optional content.

NEW REVIEW:
With the addition of the "panty panix" casino game (which plays like some old atari and arcade games from WAAAY back...), this game has been elevated to a (barely) passing grade.  With a non-chance related way to gain rep and cash daily (whose cost doesn't make you hide most of your money in the bank), this game is now playable.
This is still a semi-tedious game, however...  (not as much of a grind-fest as Intergalactic Bubbles, though... T_T)
Sadly, there are still no achievements, although there ARE Trading Cards for those SHINY SHINY BADGES!!!  SQUEEE!!!
Some tips tho:
Get the Eye from the fortune-teller girl ASAP, and look everywhere, both day and night.
Talk to the girls on the phone and write down their responses at her beginning, and after each gift!
Write down anything she says about her life, stats, likes or dislikes (you WILL be quizzed later, at the end-game, on whichever girl you choose).
OLD REVIEW:
Ok, this had lots of potential, and the premise is awesome... but not many people will find it fun. Most of it is just gambling at the casino (luck is best, don't hit the skill button or you'll get more awkward reloads) and shoving most of your money in the bank. No real strategy, no consequences of giving the wrong gift to a girl... about the only saving grace to this game imo is the goddess board game. QRC is a nice game in general.
- The graphics are nice (tracks are awsome!!!)
- The gameplay is a bit deeper than Wipeout (you can store up to three weapons to use, you can choose between them, you can use an accelerate button which overheats your engine and there's also a primary weapon you can use even without picking up anything which also heats the racer up).
- The soundtrack is in the same style as Wipeout. Not my favorite in any case but fits the game.
- Another plus I didn't expect is that the game is running very smoothly, eventhough my machine is 8 years old (Core2Duo 2,4 GHz, 3 GB RAM, GeForce 9800 GT 1 GB)
Now the bad parts.
- It has gotten stuck a couple of times during the loading screen.
- The game menu isn't so clear and easy to use from the beginning. You'll need some time to get used to navigating the menu.
- The cursor remains visible always.
- Difficulty of the game is unsensible.
Neutral
- Would be better to have access to more tracks and racers from the beginning.
- I guess it's made for XBOX-like gamepads so my Rumblepad 2 is recognized as an XBOX gamepad, which makes it difficult to set custom controls, but it still works fine after.
To sum it up, having in mind that it costed 5 eu when I bought it, I'd definitely recommend it. Despite the bugs it's much fun!

This game would be really fun if the clipping worked, but sadly items get stuck in themselves and even on your hand with annoying yet inconsistent regularity. The fingers on the hand will also phase through objects randomly, so you're never able to reliably use them. It's all but impossible to place something in a tea cup if you're unsure whether the laws of physics will work this time around. I'm also frustrated by how random the "damage" system is. Sometimes you can pick up a cup with no trouble, other times just brushing it lightly will shatter it.
Finally, for an actual design choice, it suffers from a forced perspective, which makes no sense and adds nothing to the challenge save for frustration. If you bump a cup to the wrong angle, it will take you ages to get the handle aligned to something you can pick up and use. That's not fun, and there's no good reason I can't just step slightly to the side so that I can actually line up on the handle. (Edit: There actually is an alternate camera view. It doesn't work most of the time, but if you push the button enough then it will change your perspective. This does not change the angle of the arm though, so it's of limited use. It is handy if you need to see behind something, but it doesn't work 90% of the time when the button is pushed so it's hard to make any real use of it.)
All told, if they ever patch it so that it actually works then I'd recommend it, but as it is there's simply too much randomness to the laws of reality to be fun. If you pretend that you're a poltergeist learning to use its powers though then it does make it a bit more bearable.

This was originally written on QR:Online, but since that game was removed I'll re-post this.
An excellent Anti-Gravity Racer, QR is well worth picking up. Especially when you consider its indie price tag.
For those who insist on drawing comparisons to other games -
F-Zero focuses more on speed and wide, flowing tracks, WipEout focuses more on technical tracks with tight handling and narrow roadways. QR is a happy middleground. It feels competitive with F-Zero in terms of pace, but has some more technical tracks that feel more remiscent of WipEout.
Gameplay is well paced and deep enough to keep players engaged for a while, without being overly complicated to deter new players. There are plenty of game modes that keep the game varied and interesting. Track variety is still expanding at the time of writting. With over 10 tracks, each of which with a forward and reverse variant, the game is already ahead of most WipEout titles.
Control-wise the Racers feel a bit stiff. Other AG Racers tend to have more ice-like vehicle handling but here the vehicles behave like they were superglued to the road. Hopefully this is something that Game Art Studio will address in the future.
It's also interesting to note that this games Airbrakes cause the vehicles to rapidly decelerate, which is rare for this sort of game.
Racer variety is disappointing. The vehicles are divided by tier, and they plan to have 10 tiers in the finished game, which should be cool. Unfortunately, there are only 3 vehicles per tier to choose from, which just isn't enough variety. Race grids quickly become samey and boring. Compared to any other racing game, 3 Racers is a tiny selection.
Keyboard controls are impossible to use, so I strongly recommend using a controller. The Controller configuration is excellent and as a former WipEout player, I found them instantly recognisable.
Visually the game is very nice. Nothing amazing, but you'd be hard pressed to complain. When you're flying past scenery at 1,000Km/H or more it doesn't really matter.

Pros:

Cons:
1) You will spend hours not playing, but watching the same combinations of deals occur, which, neither allow you or the opponent to play. The game play is hurt to the point I do not recommend anyone attempt this game.
2) They say that with your redraw you will "always get between 2 and 5 Sigles", this would then be that there is a 20% chance of receiving 2 Sigles. In fact this is 80%+ you will receive 2 Sigles on the redraw. If you choose a 2 Sigle draw, 3 out of 4 times you will not see another Sigle for 2 to 4 turns. Meaning you watch yourself fall behind and lose, wasting time and having no fun. There is a lot of no fun in this "game".
3) If a 5 Sigle draw or redraw, (draw can sometimes be 6), 3 out of 4 times you will see nothing but Sigles for the next 2+ turns.
4) If your draw is a combination of unit cards, spell cards and/or items, you will have a playable hand. If your hand is units, you will receive units, if your hand is items/spells and sigles, you will receive items/spells and sigles 3 of 4 times for the preceding 2 to 4 rounds.
3) Regardless of knowledge and deck design you do, you will not be competetive with those, I can only assume, who have paid money and receive a different algorithm in the deck dealing and card drawing.

Nothing to say about this masterpiece of RPG gaming! Till we start to the Vault 101, Bethesda it's being able to bend the gamer into the athmosphere of the story until the end. The Wasteland is the zone around Washingotn D.C. after a nuclear war: all is destroyed, few human survived outside and a little were closed in Vaults, in order to preserve the human beings, and the player, alone, must find his father James to end a mission: make Wasteland's water potable and promote human civilization. The gamer will fight the Enclave, what remains of the old U.S. goverment, with the help of the Brotherhood of Steel, an organization that conserve the wisdom of the old tecnology ( very similar to Isaac Asimov's Foundation).
The choice of Bethesda to do an ending story ( only with a DLC it's possible to continue it) and not a classic no-ending one is a great innovation for RPG games. We can create our carachter like we want with the S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system that characterize our skills and our games abilities. The V.A.T.S.,original innovation that supply an aim problem, will stop the game in order to aim into specific zone of enemies bodies ( ex.: head, arms, legs, chest). In the end, Fallout 3 has revoluzioned the RPG games with his charge of humor, tension and atmosphere by the surreal Washington D.C. zone, begin also a laboratory for Bethesda to develop the fifth capter of TES series Skyrim, but Fallout brought a great message: what we must do as mainkind, to not admit a future like this in the real life.

Truly I believe that Bandai Namco and From Software did an excellent job expanding upon the Dark Souls franchise with Dark Souls II. Scholars of the First Sin adds graphics driver support for better fidelity, framerates, and load times (which you will likely never notice) as well as a slew of DLC content and updates designed to keep the spirit of the game alive.  Dark Souls II:SOTFS is a wonderfully enthralling story that unfolds with you at the center.  The world is rich and atmospheric with a deep history that cannot simply be told, but must be experienced.
To those who are not familiar with Dark souls as a franchise this game and its predecessors/successors are punishing. These games fundamentally add "wind up times" to your actions making combat seem more gritty and realistic. A similar game in this style is Monster Hunter, whose actions are impactful and calculated.  Many might say that its just timed attacks and blocking, but those who do are simplifying a complex system whose creators put much thought into it's design. As for the difficulty, From Software is well known for its difficult games and excellent simulator experiences... This is a company who knows that details matter and it truly shows in their work.
Now that Dark Souls III is out I stand firm in justifying that Dark Souls 2 is still worth playing for its explorable world and challenging fights. This game is not as flighty and twitchy as its 2 descendants Bloodborne or Dark Souls III, but it is still all the better for it as it sticks truer to the original pacing of the classic.  Truly Dark Souls will be remembered as a measure in the gaming world for many years to come, You too can be a part of that history...

Outlast is a picture perfect example of everything done right in a horror game, making the player feel completely helpless and hunted in an environment that makes them feel uncomfortable with a looming sensation of something just around the corner. With 0% of the budget on combat, Outlast has been made completely immersive with subtle and frightening sound effects, disturbing visuals and perfected first-person animations.
The story of Outlast begins with a midnight drive to a supposedly abandoned asylum following a tip from an anonymous lead, the player takes the role of investigative journalist Miles Upshur as he delves to uncover the sinister secrets of Mount Massive Asylum.
Immediately upon entering the asylum the player gets a sensation of being watched, confined and exposed, setting them up for a start at the slightest bump, scratch or shed of movement seen from the corner of your eye. The atmosphere is perfected with high-quality graphics and sound assets, which build up in intensity until exploding in the players face in an intense climax of terror upon their first encounter with one of the asylums mutilated patients.
As with any game, while Outlast is good there are some drawbacks that keep it from being perfect. Outlast's puzzle solving lacks variation, recycling the same old method of rushing to press a button or turn a valve while an enemy chases you. While contributing to the sensation of being hunted, re-using these kinds of encounters over and over with a lack of effective follow-up made the game feel largely repetitive and I felt took a large part out of the experience.
Outlast has also unfortunatly indulged in the cheap shots that are jump scares, which require little-to-no buildup and I feel have no place in a true horror game as they only serve to provide opportunities for talentless hacks like pewdietard to overreact. In comparison with another terrifying game, Amnesia: The Dark Descent, which had no jump scares and instead relied completely on it's atmosphere to scare the player, this comparison proves to me that horror games worth their weight in gold do not need jump scares and should rely on their immersion, which is something that Outlast would have done very well.
Finally, without giving away too much, the story felt rushed and incomplete in some places, which didn't leave a lasting impression on me and failed to avidly explain the reasoning behind the inhumane experiments in Mount Massive.
So while Outlast is a very good game and a welcome addition to the horror genre, it suffered some flaws that kept it from living up to it's full potential.

I like Simcity, thats SimCity Four, after seeing the new one on various YouTubes, I wasn't too impress with Five to where it was a must buy.  But I'm in the mood for a good city builder and started to look around Steam for some decent city building games and I ran into Banished.   I checked out some reviews and it came across mixed, the pro critcs were critical, but the users loved it (mediacritic).   At $20, it was worth a try....so after hours and hours of playing, I came to the conclusion that the pro-critics didn't really try this out to its full extent.  This game is a wonderful and challenging city builder.
First it is easy to pick up, the tutorials are enough to get started in using the the interface, which is very nicely done, but it will take a few trys to see what is going on in this game.  You start with a dozen or so 'banished' settlers with a few resources in early spring.  These few resources are not enough to survive the winter, so the first task is to build food producing buildings and shelters (houses) before the first snow.  If you make it that far, you're not done, you only just begun if you want this village to grow to a large town.
There are various building types that one can build that provide some service to your villagers and each has its importance in surviving a long term play.   In the early years, you will most likely get a fishing hut for fish (food) and a gatherer's hut (again food) and assign a few settlers to these buildings to get the all important food.  You will need to get the resouces (wood, stone, iron) and assign builders to build these.  This is your first introduction to managing the manpower, since out of the twelve or so, only about 8 are adults who are capable of performing assigned tasks.  The others are the children, the future of your soon to be town, that only eat the food.  With the food coming in, you can now get those shelters up, which gives you a  choice - the adequate that takes less resources or the better which takes more resources.  At various stages of the game, you will run into these situations, and naturally in the early stages you go with the adequate just to survive.
With the shelters up, the next important step is to provide fuel for cooking and warmth, and this is provided by the woodcutter who will take logs and chop them down to firewood.   Now one can go and chop every tree there is to provide the logs, but the wise will choose to build the forester hut and assign a forester to manage the forest (cut the trees and replant).   You also find out that the forester also provides a rich forest for the gatherer's to pick the berries and other fruits of the forest.  Little tie ins like this is all though this game, and how one manage these determines how successful one will be in growing the village.  When the essentials are done, you find a new challlenge will start to pop up: tools.  I leave that up to you to figure out.
The interface is well design in helping you manage these settlers, some of which you should always have up: A general status  dialog that shows the current population and the amount of resources stored (I forgot about the storage buildings), second is the professions dialog that shows how many settlers are assigned to what (gatherer's, forester's, fishermand, etc) and provides a way to assign adults to a profession, the third you have to earn it by building the city hall, which provides much needed information about how good you are doing, such as population growth, food production, and a better break down on resources.  A map is provided to allow you to jump around the area at ease by clicking in the map that moves the main view to that area.  All these dialogs are giving you just enough information to suceed at growing, which is the main focus of this game.
Once you are stablized, with children being born, food coming in, and the shelters being heated, one can now go on to provide more to the settlers, such as roads, school houses, and of course the city hall.  Build better food producting items, such as hunters lodge, orchards,  pastures, and crop fields.  Keep the hearts all red and the stars all gold and you know you are doing ok.   Its tough to do, especially as the population begins to grow, people will die of old age and the children will grow to adults to replace them.  Get familar with these cycles that are going on (harvest in autumn, which gets depleted in spring when its time to plant), provide better shelters and better tools and get smarter adults for better everything.
For me the adiction level is high, I have 190 hours in and a village of 1000 laid out on a large map with disasters turn on started in the 'hard' mode, which is just a wagon of goods to survive on for a couple of seasons.  I lost a few times before getting to this stage but I believe that is to be expected.  Its easy to overwhelm the building that soon every settler will die due to starvation, cold, or desease.   Go forth slowly and have patience.  Do the tutorial it is highly recommended.
Getting started for the weak:
1. Build a storage area to store wood/stone/iron
2. Get wood/stone/iron, just enough to build the hut and shelters.
3. Assign two or more builders
4. Build the gatherer's hut for food in a heavy forest area close but not too close to the wagon assign 2 settlers as gatherers.
5. Build the shelters (wood house) for all the settlers.
6. Build a wood cutting hut - assign wood cutter.
7. Build a  barn to store food - after it's built destory the wagon.
8. Build a fishing hut - assign fishermen.
9. Build a Blacksmith hut - assign blacksmith.
10. Build a forester hut next to the gatherer's hut.
11. ?
Note the ring around the gatherer's hut as you place it, this is the area that the assigned worker will use to gather fruits and berries.  The same occurs for the forester hut, fishing hut and various other buildings in the game.   There are some great youtube video's to watch (search 'let's play banish') and good disscussions in the Steam's Banished community.  Do read the topics or search if you have questions.   I hope you enjoy.  Thumbs up.

If Amnesia: The Dark Descent and the Penumbra games had a baby, that baby would be Outlast. This is classic survival horror - a creepy setting, no weapons, and no way to survive except to hide. You play as a journalist investigating an abandoned insane asylum, based on an anonymous tip of shady goings-on there. The only tool you have at your disposal is a video camera. The main hook of the game is using the camera's IR (night vision) mode to see just what the hell is going around you. It makes for some very effective moments of terror. Imagine knowing something scary and nasty is out there stalking you, but not being able to see what's 3 feet in front of you... yeah, that's the experience in a nutshell. Those moments are what makes this game effective. But unfortunately the whole game is not just those moments. Some parts I found to be somewhat tedious. For example, in one section, you have to explore an area to collect 3 fuses to restore power to something, all the while being stalked by crazy people. It's tense, to be sure, but also makes you realize that you're playing a game with a lame "collect x things" mechanic. It kind of brings you out of the experience a bit. The final section of the game is also sort of hit or miss, as it changes direction in a big way (reminds me sort of how Amnesia fell apart a little bit towards the end). But it's not necessarily bad... just different (I don't really want to get into spoilers at all), so it's one of those things where you might like it or you might not. But the majority of the game leading up to the end is pretty much consistently good. The environment is creepy as hell, the atmosphere is dark, and the "enemies" (mostly disfigured inmates) serve their purpose well. There are a few jump-scares, and the aforementioned fetch-quest sections where you're being chased, but mostly, the horror of the game comes from the combination of atmosphere and having to rely on a camera (whose batteries drain quickly when using IR) to be able to see. On the downside, you sort of get used to things after a while, so the scare factor wears off a bit towards the end. So it's ultimately a good thing that the game only lasts around 4-5 hours. Any more would have been too much. Despite the flaws, there's still lots of good things to experience here, so if you're a fan of this genre, you pretty much have to play this at some point. I think the price is probably fair, but if you can wait, it's definitely worth picking up in a sale.
Technical notes: I ran into a major bug towards the beginning of the game that prevented any further progress (it involves shaking the mouse during a quick-time event). The issue has supposedly been fixed in a patch, but it didn't work for me. There is a pinned post in the Steam discussions explaining how to work around this if it doesn't work for you either.

If you like city builders (Sim City, Settlers, Anno, 1701, Tropico, ETC)  you will like this.  I can't stop playing it!  Though outwardly simplistic, Bannished offers suprising depth and challenge. OK, maybe I can recover... not long after a fire broke out and wiped out more of the town... I was done for.
The Good:
-Good, simple UI
-Immersive play
-Graphics are nicely done, detailed where they need to be and simplistic in other areas that don't take away from the game.
-Down right fun and challenging for strategists and city builders alike!
The Bad:
-Sandbox only.  Would be nice to have missions or set goals.  Just building a big town begins to feel a little anti-climactic.
-sometimes things happen and you are not sure what is causing it... IE.  citizens have poor health, but nothing telling you WHY.
Conclusion:
Its nice to have a good old single player game that doesn't push you to buy more in game content... you can just sit down and enjoy building a village and trying to keep your banished citizens alive.
Great game for under $20.

I've got a thing for chilled-out exploration games, and Gone Home certainly ticked that box. You play Katie, a young lady who comes home to a large, empty house to find her sister, Sam, missing, and her parents away on a holiday to rejuvenate their marriage.
The house feels so real, despite the fairly basic graphics. All the notes you find from family members are hand-written, and the bits of information relating to their jobs and personal lives make them feel very believable.
The house is absolutely huge, with hidden compartments scattered around the building for you to stumble upon later. There are moving boxes placed throughout the place, and the very unlived-in state of your mansion gives off a slightly eerie feeling; though this is by no means a horror game.
The game is set in the mid-1990s, and every pamphlet, cassette player, VHS tape and game cartridge you come across conjures childhood memories within a 27-year-old like me.
As you progress through the rooms, meticulously reading every note, school report, book cover and receipt you find, the reason behind Sam's absence becomes apparent. I'll try not to avoid spoiling it, but personally, I didn't find the reveal particularly shocking or scandalous; though I try to remember that her particular situation was still rarely discussed openly, even for the 1990s.
The game ran absolutely fine, but I did encounter one particular, albeit fixable glitch: when going to the basement with the aquired key, the door failed to open despite rigorously clicking on the knob. I saved and quit to desktop, started it up again and the problem was resolved.
Gone Home is an immensely charming game and I enjoyed the three hours I spent with it. To more avid gamers it could be comparable to a virtual house tour than a game, but the experience is memorable.

A futuristic racing game that's inspired by Wipeout\F-zero games. My initial impressions with this game were high but quickly sank soon after as I became bored and frustrated as a result of the game's odd design decisions.
- Beautiful game
- Runs smoothly
- Music is good I guess (nothing for or against it)
- Normal race event is fun
- No Dpad support is a huge oversight. Using RS for the menus is annoying and slow and using it for the hex grid in-game race menu up is a g0ddamn nightmare
- Unskippable race intros, if you have to repeat a race get ready to re-watch the intros for the umpteenth time.
- Unenjoyable and frustrating race events.
- Extremely obtuse item pick ups. Whenever you pick-up an item you'll be left with this exact thought "What did that do?"
- Collision detection feels off at times, I missed quiet a few pick-ups, bumped into walls while on the ceiling exiting a tunnel which reduces your speed and in one event causes your boost timer to restart.
- Boss battles are garbage, boss gets a 3+ second lead and you have to drive through certain rings to send shock blasts until you catch up as pick-up are restricted for bosses.
- Game lacks attention to details making the races feel rather dull. During some races you drive over water or sand and there's not even a particle of water or dust kicking up or spreading out from the base of your vehicle. You might as well be driving over metal.
- AI is the perfect cheater, it takes corners at full speed disregarding the brakes entirely without even bumping into the walls. They sometimes however crash into walls so I don't know.
This game needed more time and play testing to figure out the quirks. Now before anyone says you're only judging it so harshly because you played WipeOut. Let me say this, I never played a Wipeout or F-zero game. The only futuristic racing game I played and loved was Roll Cage, Roll Cage: Stage 2. Those games were the sh!t and this game lacks everything that made those games fun. If you can deal with all the cons then get it, if not then forget it look somewhere else.

My review is 'maybe recommended' but no button for that, as it's quite good for the GFX and sound, but severely lacking in the physics department that this game is trying to clone, there is little sense of gravity or aerodynamics in regards to thrust/turning/sliding/braking/crashing, making it feel a little rigid. so the the game is mediocre but a bit of highspeed fun for fans of the genre, and certainly not the worst clone attempt.
...also, the gamepad steering is too sensitive, rarely if ever do i need to back off on the throttle for turns, let alone use the brakes, using a steering wheel with near 90deg each way turn sense fixes this issue, but an ingame sense option is needed.
it's on a similar level physics-wise to 'hover ace' and that was released in 2002, yet brilliant physics were achieved in 1996 by wipeout 2, since that time the only games that really came close [apart from sequels] was A.I.M Racing on PC in 2007, and Fatal Inertia on ps3. it's a tough genre to crack, with flashy GFX upgrades common, unfortunately the physics may have peaked 2 decades ago...

A triumphant sequel! Looks great, sounds great and plays identical to the first but with more potential build diversity. Some of the secrets and riddles are rather devilish in nature so expect to have your mental capacity stretched as you try to work your way around some of the more obscure puzzles...or just consult a guide for some extra clues/the complete solution. Like the first game, I enjoyed the story for what it facilitated but it generally feels rather redundant in the context of what one would like from such a game.
My only real negative is the skills system - I really think there needed to be more traits in each skill line. There should always be an interesting bonus at the end of each skill line to entice the player to spend more points into single lines at the expense of skill diversity. I generally found there was no difficult choices to make with skill point allocation because you rarely had to max out a skill line to achieve its most important trait.
Other than that, it's a perfect sequel.

Grimrock 2 left a bad taste in my mouth towards the end. The end boss is also very annoying - hard to get to and hard to damage, and I didn't know there was a boss fight coming so couldn't prepare.  I couldn't have beaten him without save scumming.
I would also agree that some of the puzzles (of which there were too many) were often obscure and solved by brute forcing them, rather than by figuring them out, and I think the game might have had too many secrets in it, to the point where you feel compelled to check every wall.
So a solid dungeon crawler but not quite a classic.

I could not reccomend more! A fantastic split between Hearthstone and Magic: The Gathering, urging more towards MTG than any rendition of a CCG I've played.
In summary
Pros:
* Not at all pay to win, surprisingly easy to get into
* Very little RNG, more skill required
* Interactive gameplay that leads to a lot of high moments
* The draft system towers over any CCG I've played
Cons:
* Slower meta at the moment, hopefully future sets flesh this out as it is still early access
* The introduction is slow paced and can take a couple hours to beat (Strongly suggest pushing through it, highly worth it. The game completely changes when you can make your own deck)
Many CCG's tend to focus more on paying in order to aquire cards, and while there are benefits to buying the ingame currency, it's quite easy to make top tier decks without the norms associated with CCG's. (It won't take months, nor would it take much money whatsoever if you decide you don't want to wait the week or two)
After playing for less than a week, I have a fully made Tier 1 deck that I can flex in various options for. I'm on my way to make a second deck, more than halfway there.
The gameplay focuses more on skill than RNG, which I appreciate - you don't feel nearly as screwed over by a lucky roll of the dice as you do in other online CCG's. I can count on one hand (a few fingers) the number of cards that say something along the lines of, "Deal 3 damage to a random enemy". Which, after the resolved play, ends up destroying a 1/1 creature that allows the enemy to draw, rather than the 7/3 towering monstrosity threatening to rampage through your soul.
Another nice thing that I like, in regards to the lack of RNG, is the mulligan system this game has. Rather than traditional mull's, when you mull your hand, your next hand is gauranteed to have at least 2 power (mana) and up to 5 max. Takes away those feast or famine hands you can get.
The mechanics of this game mimic many of MTG, but there are quite a few of its own. It definitely takes advantage of the digital aspect very well. The interactions from card to card are incredibly fun, and more are being found out often.
Even with just one set, drafting in this game feels incredible. Not to mention, it's easy to build up the currency to play drafts. My favorite part? It works like a traditional draft. Everything you draft, you KEEP. That means you can easily greed draft to get the best bang for your buck. So even players that are not too confident in their drafting abilities, can get more than their gold worth from greed drafting. (Always draft, don't buy packs out right)
The only negative I feel I can truly give this game is the restictive meta at the moment. Most every deck in the top tiers are either midrange, a midrange control, or a couple aggro decks. There are very few full control decks, let alone combo decks, that can fair too well against what's currently being played. However, this is common among CCG's that first come out. This is mostly due to card pools, and how many are available. I've found, usually, that as games progres and release more sets, the meta responds well. (Come on aggro decks!)
On that note, they are coming out with patches, and the last one made a direct impact on the meta. Very fun to see and be apart of.
Aside from that, I do dislike the current way they introduce you into the game. It's a long process that is not all that fun. You play through every faction for a number of games, and it can feel slow. It does teach you a bit, and for every faction you beat you get a starter deck (strongly reccomend) That being said, you don't have to do this. You can skip straight to ranked play, drafting, or the other AI matches (One that's a one shot challenge, giving stronger prizes until the end. The other being a AI Draft system that costs less)
Eternal Card Game is one that I suggest for any TCG/CCG player that's looking for a new experience! Extremely fun, with interactive gameplay and an ease of access that I have yet to see in this environment.
Another gem from Almost Human Games. Oldschool gameplay at its best.

What The Developers Say They Are Doing:
"The current flight sim space is a fountain of experience and expertise, and Early Access is our way of drawing upon that knowledge to make Flight Sim World the best it can be."
What They Are Actually Doing:
Locking out all prior content. None of your most beloved FSX-SE content can be used to jumpstart your "best it can be" FSW experience. FSUIPC doesn't work. SimConnect software doesn't work. FSX planes (even though they have the same architecture)  do not show up in the menu (but FSW planes DO at least show up in the menu in FSX-SE - though the model is invisible).
Currently, Dovetail appears to be throwing out every scrap of content you've ever purchased or downloaded for FSX and FSX-SE over the last 12 years, and seem to be pinning their hopes on you patiently waiting to spend over $6000 on DLC, (c.f. Dovetail RailSimulator), from the vendors they have lined up. Freeware (if available) will need to be vetted/approved by Dovetail, and will be channeled through the Workshop - again...IF Dovetail makes Workshop Content available. Otherwise, you can largely kiss Freeware goodbye.
Oh, and between P3D, X-Plane, and the final nail of FSW, the Flight Sim Community is now fully back to the Pay-Full-Price-for-Incremental-Upgrades model that served Microsoft so well from 1996-2006. To be fair, $25 is much more palatable than the $69 that MSFS used to cost every 18-24 months...but when FSW 2019 comes out in 2 years for full price, don't say you weren't warned.
All of this is *before* we even get to how FSW looks or performs.
* Performance:
My performance experience has been largely in line with my FSX experience. Turn detail way down, get closer to 144 FPS, Turn them back up, get closer to 10-20 FPS, depending on how much detail there is. That was normal for every iteration of FS95/98/2000/2002/2004ACOF, so I see it as normal now, too.
* How does FSW look?
It looks like it's built on a 12 year old engine. Picture in your mind what Battlefield 1 (2016) would have looked like if it used the Battlefield 2 (2006) engine... It would look...ok. But dated. I have mixed feelings here - FSW throws some top-tier Payware Planes at us in a 64 bit environment, but uses Landclass data that's even more out of date than the data in FSX. My house was built in 2006. In FSX, my streets exist, but there is no autogen on them. In FSW, there's nothing within a mile of here... Reddit users have pointed out whole sections of Phoenix/Mesa that are missing in FSW - sections that exist in FSX. What's up with that?

"Complex mechanics, barebones game."
That's a short but accurate way of describing the game Receiver. Looking at it in more depth, it's a demo for complex pistol handling mechanics that are surprisingly refreshing and unique considering that one of the most popular genres in gaming are First Person Shooters. Receiver maps this simple process to almost as dozen keys, and after a few minutes of pracice you'll be loading magazines, ejcting spent ones and reloading the pistol, racking the slider, switching off the safety and bringing your pistol up to aim as if you were it were second nature.
However it's biggest flaw is that those gun mechanics are the only fleshed out thing in Receiver.
There's some barebones rooms you'll pass through to collect old tapes and more ammunition, all the while destroying and/or disabling enemy turrets and flying drones that'll attack on sight and kill in one hit, sending you right back to the start. There's real no payoff and no ramp up of difficulty, it's a barebones arena and with some enemies to shoot at.
I enjoyed my short time with it, and I'll probably boot it up every now and then to play around with the pistol mechanics, but don't kid yourself into thinking it's a game in the traditional sense of the word. It's a demo through and through, and thus only really worthwhile on sale or as a free-bee with Overgrowth. You can spend your money on more worthwhile games.

Despite my thumbdown on this title, the game is good and has potential, the thumbdown is due to a few things that makes the game more or less unplayable.
Its not crammed with tons of features, but it holds a few good ones which makes it possible not to lose the overview of things.
However, the gameplay is completely ruined by the starvation bug where ppl suddenly start starving to death and theres nothing you can do about it.
I have approx. 56 fishermen and 44 gatherers in a population of 250, then I also have some livestock, so basically, almost half the population is producing food, but still they all die from starvation.
I was running the town with lots of foods and the stock continuously climbing and with no increase in population, but then suddenly ppl started to starve to death.
I added in xtra gathers huts and a couple of fishing stations, took ppl out of the mines and quarry and put them into the food production units I just created and as those who already died didn't need to be fed, I was actually producing more food for even fewer ppl, still the stock of food were tumbling up and down between 500 and 1200 and ppl kept dropping like flies.
Hopefully the game will become playable beyond a few hrs of progress some day, but until it does, its not worth investing too much time (or money) in as ur town will be doomed the minute u found it, its all a matter of how many hrs before the starvation bug kicks in.
Theres also plenty of room for expanding the AI code to a level where villagers wont make stupid decisions, like one villager I watched, who were grabbing and dropping the same batch of iron in the same spot for 1/4 of an ingame year and when he stopped, he ran out and came back and started over again. :sigh:
Also like some villagers might get stuck between buildings where they walk in to, but for some reason cant find their way out of again.
Villagers will also vanish into the thin air from time to time with no warnings at all.
You wont find out until some production drops massively or is completely halted, due to the fact that whoever worked the given productionunit, has simply vanished.
It means that u have to actively monitor all productionunits by clicking each type continuously (one after another) in order to make sure they are up and running 100% and that part soon becomes VERY annoying, especially as u have to dig up replacement workers all the time.
Implementing some feature that allows u to set automatic job assignments for the villagers by priority, would be a huge advantage here.
Like if u want to have foodproduction set with top priority, so that when a worker within a foodproduction unit vanish, he will automatically be replaced by a worker from a lower priority productionunit e.g. coal mine, stone quarry or whatever u like.
Then add in a notification when it happens, so that u are aware that a worker went from "Mining" to "Fishing".
Combined or made with something like "Automated job assignment" where u can set the minimum and maximum amount of workers u want in any given line of trait, either so u assign a fixed number of workers or by percentage of the population.
The feature shd be free of choice whether to use or not, as some ppl may actually like the micromamangement aspect in clicking single workers and giving them individual assignments.
But if u want to try and grow a village to a more massive scale, that micromanagement may just become too tedious and even overwhelming and in that case, automation shd be a possible choice.

I was hoping for a decently fun game that rewarded you in the same sense as HuniePop. It just feels incomplete and like one of those crap games you bought on the Xbox Live Indie section for $1. Stay away from this unless there is a 90%+ mark off
The main cons of this game:
1. "Reputation" is mainly earned through a single minigame (a 4x4 block puzzle, where you get a different picture every 5 stages). These pictures are usually just pictures of women in underwear/lingerie. This game gets old VERY quickly and the only other method is by working (which is only allowed on Tuesday) that consists of taking random guesses at the answers to questions that you recieve. You also earn rep by gifting items to girls (but this is difficult, which is explained in point 3) Every time you sleep to advance time, it eats away at the reputation you have gained. So you end up sitting there doing nothing for quite a long period of time since you don't want to lose your "rep"
2. There is straight up nothing to do in this game besides go to every area that is currently unlocked and click on "sparkles" that give you $5 at a time.
3. There is no sensible way to make money. You start the game with a whopping $20 from your mom. Like in every dating sim, you need money to buy gifts. The only way to get that money is by going to the casino (which has TERRIBLE luck). Or working your 1 day a week job. Or by going to different areas and clicking on the sparkles that give $5 more at a time. While gifts range from $20 at the cheapest to $200 for the expensive. So, you end up spending most of the time going the casino and losing your money and running back home to mom to beg for $10. If you somehow manage to obtain $100, you can put it in the bank to earn a small interest.
4. The girls that you are supposed to date and go after have next to no personality. Seriously, they just repeat standard lines such as "I like reading about archeology" and the sort. No voice acting. No real dialog. The girls are just cookie cutter stereotypical "smart librarian" and "stuck up rich girl." You do not get to pick which response you give them. You literally stand in silence and give them gifts and clicking on talk gives you lines such "Maybe i will go read about greek history later" No background to any of them.
5. There is no tutorial and you are just thrown into some guy's life and you are expected to know from day one what his daily routines are. No real backstory, you are just thrown in and have to discover along the way. The only real help is an instructions page on the main menu.
6. There is no settings menu, you are forced to be in full screen and can't change the resolution.
I have honestly seen better flash game dating sims on Newgrounds. This still needs A LOT more work to ask for any type of price tag on this.

Pro Tip 2: Ovewhelmed by all the work you have to do? Simply drive a vehicle that is required by 2 or more airplanes to the respective spots on the plane (so that they start doing work on them) then drive the vehicle away. The game will say that the work will occur for a period of time, but the timer will never run down. NOTE: does not apply to taxing or putting vehicles back in garage.
P.S. Ignore the haters, this game is ok and pretty tense; Especially if you (accidentaly) wait for too long.

I don't understand how, but they somehow managed to turn a rather good game ( Quantum Rush Online ) into a boring and flawed single player game. After playing QR online for some time, I immediately bought QR Champions in early access tu support the devs. And as usual, I regret having bought an EA game... Here are some of the obvious flaws I've encountered, I've already listed that on the forum, and other players complained about them too, but it seems that the devs just don't give a damn about user feedback :
- the menus with a gamepad don't work really well, it's OK sometimes, and other times it's a chore, almost impossible to navigate
- the mouse cursor doesn't disappear when using a gamepad
- there is absolutely no damage feedback, most of the time your shield and armor just suddenly disappear and you don't even know who or what hit you
- primary weapon is useless, most if the time you just shoot the ground because the tracks aren't made to use this kind of weapon. Also you have to push the button each time you want to shoot... when it's supposed to be a rapid fire weapon.
- "collisions" problems. And by collision I mean the hit detection of boosters and items. Sometimes you will take a booster even if you miss it by 2 meters, and sometimes you will be exactly on the booster but you're ship doesn't accelerate. Same for the pick-ups, I even saw an enemy behind me get the item I was going to take
- there is absolutely no way to know what an item does, most of the time the icon sucks, and even when you use the item, you don't really know what it did
- there is "that guy". You know "that guy" ? Almost every racing game has it, it's the nearly unbeatable ennemy that is always first, way ahead of the others for no reason because he is supposed to have the same ship, and seems completely cheated. Even when you get ahead of him, he manages to save and use all his energy at the end of the race to overtake you.
- they removed the cash. In QR online, even when you lose a race, you earn some cash, so you didn't play for nothing. It's not the case here, and the game is so difficult that you'll have to restart again, and again, and agin, the exact same race, earning nothing, just to beat "that guy". The game becomes a useless grind really fast, except that there is nothing to grind...
- stupid game modes. For example there is a mode where you have to grab packages on the track. Thing is, the AI doesn't seem programmed to do the same, so they just run a regular race, shooting each others and trying to reach the line first. And, as YOU have to kinda explore the track to find the packages, you will spend the entire race alone. It would be nearly impossible to grab the packages with the other guys around anyway...
- death race sucks. Yup, generally death races in racing games are fun, really fun. Mario Kart, F-Zero, Gas Guzzlers Extreme, it's fun. Not here. Here it's a chore, too. First, for the reasons I already mentionned : primary weapon shooting straight into the ground, bad hitbox on items icons making you miss them all the time, weapons that do nobody-knows-what, and generally useless... you got the picture. But there are even more flaws I didn't talk about. For example I noticied that ennemies don't give a damn about their energy, they generally don't use the  blue tracks to regenerate it, but still they manage to be hard to kill. Also, you never know your position during a race like that : are you first with the most kills ? Where are you on the track compared to others ? Are you far behind and you have to boost to join them ? Generally, the AI manages to go really fast, using their boost like they don't have any energy limit, while happily shooting at each other to have a max of kills, and leting you far behind. They also take almost ALL the items, leaving you with nothing but useless ones, when you are already struggling to keep up with them. This makes the game absolutely not enjoyable, I re-started a death race like 10 times and the best I could do was 7th with 3 kills... IF you manage to got a good weapon that does some damage, it's generally not enough to kill a guy, you will just damage him enough to allow another ennemy to kill him...
- the upgrades we win makes no sense : why do they seem weaker than the base equipement ?
- most of the musics really suck, I deactivated it after 2 or 3 races. But the game is even more boring without it... I have nothing against electro, it's generally the norm for futuristic racing games, but those ones just suck.
Well I could go on and on listing everything wrong with the game, but it takes time and I have better games to play. I've waited for months for them to correct the flaws of early access, and they kinda did nothing ( well at least they corrected the menus with the pads... ). Too bad, QR Online really seemed to have the potential to bring back the old F-Zero and Extreme-G feeling. Seems like we're not gonna play a good like like these on PC for a long time...

Really a great game, especially for the small price. A lot of the negative reviews seem to spawn from having Wipeout-like expectations towards a 10-euro-game. That´s just unrealistic. For its price, the game is really good.
The feeling of speed is great, and while some things tend to be a bit annoying, it makes them feel extra rewarding when you finally manage to win. This would be different if you´d be penaltied for things you have no influence on, but especially boss levels that feel unbeatable and unfair at first become very easy once you figure out the best strategy. For example, if a boss has strong forward-directed weapons, it might best to stay close behind him and overtake him just before the finish line. Or, on tight, twisting tracks, you might be able to get an advantage by using all your boost immediately so you are always one turn ahead and lock-on weapons or straight missiles can´t hit you.
The only thing the game really lacks is motion blur. But that may still come in a future update.
Overall, I´d definitely recommend this game if you look for a rather cheap, fun, futuristic racing game.
