Decent in concept in general except for some flaws.
Bosses rubber band hard. You hit everything and not miss a single boost and eventually get ~3 seconds ahead of them? Haha don't worry, they'll be right up your back-side any second now to smash you from 100% to 0% armour in no time with their overpowered and limitless weapons.
The free/basic weapons every ship has are nigh-useless and a waste of time and distraction. Should limit all weapons to pick-ups only.Destroying pickups should replenish some of your armour--as far as I've seen there isn't any way to replenish your armour aside from being destroyed.
Hard to recommend this game, it really is. It's still in early access but these games rarely fly off well over time. I really want a futuristic racer (anti-grav), I really do. But taking a game like this seriously only slaps your face.
To the devs; play and take note of the WipEout series. The closer to this you'll be, the better.
Update: 10/11/2014
Still no way to replenish armour--again, unless I'm somehow missing something.
Airbreaks are still pointless if you do more than just tap it. If you ever hold it in you'll do much more harm than good.
AI racers seem to never airbreak and seem to turn around every corner at full speed while players need to perfect the track in their mind and muscle-memory to ever come close. High-turn tracks are nigh-impossible to come first place in.
The game seems more and more to be a achieve first-place in the first 10 seconds of the race and maintain it or you'll never get it. So many times I get first place very quickly and hold it with no competition at all. Not a single thing hits me or comes close. Here I am at first place with the second racer ~5 seconds behind with all the other racers fighting eachother and keeping eachother back while I'm boosting ahead and hitting every boost.
There's no come-back mechanic at all. Because once first place has first place and gets a couple second advantage, it's over. Second, third and so on keep fightning and smashing eachother to just keep first place in first place.Not a single weapon/pick-up helps this at all. There are just a handful of close-quarter weapons.
Upgrades for your craft are too few and far inbetween. Especially since each tier has their own set of gear/unlocks. The system should be in points and you get points after every race you complete and you pick what you want to level up. Want more speed? Upgrade your engines. Want a stronger hull? Upgrade your hull. So on and so on. Not this random, rare drops that don't even seem to change much to begin with. By the time you finish a tier you have a few unlocks where some things are still stock-standard.
The basic/free weapons that every ship has all the time are awful and very distracting. Again, these really should be removed. They do very little damage and if you ever plan on hitting something, you'll be focusing mostly on aiming and shooting rather than racing. These are a really bad idea and I struggle to think of any good idea (let alone concept) as to why people would this this is a good idea, then add it in and then actually keep it in. It'd baffle me if anybody actually likes these.
The vehicles release a constant black smoke when they're low in hull/armour which constantly fills out ~90% of the track with black smoke. Makes it impossible to properly race if you're anywhere behind them since the smoke trail is very long and lasts a long time. Covers most of the width of your average track.
There's no minimap either which is another con.
Conclusion: Game is still very frustrating and painful to play. It isn't a casual game and seems as if the devs don't want for it to be. This just makes the game extremely more annoying to take seriously at all. So, game still sucks at this date. Game is riddled with cons with very few pros. Don't buy it.
There was some content patch recently. Didn't seem to do much but add some content (ie ships and tracks) I've noticed the main menu mid-race actually pauses now. Prior the race would still go on.

oh boy oh boy, as my Legend of Grimrock review made it abundantly clear
LoG1 is one of my favorite indie games, and Legend of Grimrock 2 is one of my favorite games EVER period.
the best way to describe this game is "Legend of Grimrock... but BETTER", more Legendary, more Grim, more Rocky, all the base mechanics from the 1st game remain in place so i wont waste much time explaining it
the Legend of Grimrock series is a grind based dungeon crawler RPG series in which you control a group of 4 characters, you fight monsters and solve puzzles, thats the short verion. what makes LoG2 even superior to its predessesor is content, variety and the expansion of the core mechanics, instead of exploring a single big dungeon in the game, you explore an island filled with multiple dungeons and secrets, to returning players of the series this game truthly changes things up with the addition of these open environments and the classic dungeon gameplay is still there, you only have to enter the numerous caves, temples and dungeons to experience it again
the basic combat has also been expanded, the game now has a new type of weapon, guns as well as 5 new character classes and a new race, the ratling, also the devs have made other classes besides the mage a little more fun to use (the mage remains just as fun to use dont worry), certain weapons now have special attacks that add versatility to each character and you unlock new perks and abilities as you level up your class skills
puzzles, a major feature of the last game are back and with force, this game has some very incredible puzzles, almost all of them are hard but fair, i can really count 1 or 2 puzzles AT MOST in the entire game that followed a very weird logic, for almost everything else, you just need to use yer brains, im actually very proud of the fact i didnt need to use a guide for any of the puzzles in this game, unlike the first game
enemies also received an overhaul, the main strategy of the first game, running in circles around them, is much less effective now since the enemies turn faster and many have moves that make it very hard for the player to circle strafe, and hell the game now has more than 1 boss and they are all great and challenging
if theres one thing i wasnt a fan of in this game, is the new limb injury system, basically, some enemies/traps/enemy attacks have a chance of crippling your head/legs/feet/right arm/left arm, each crippled limb applies a different debuff, these can only be removed by either consuming a red potion or touching a save crystal, now this on itself is not bad, except for the fact that FALLING DOWN PITS CAN CRIPPLE YOUR LEGS AND/OR FEET, those who played the first game should be able to see the problem with this, the LoG series often hides secrets or alternate routes down pits, there are no "bottomless pits" in these games, every pit leads to a lower level you can explore, usually you will want to use the stairs tough, because in the first game, falling down these pits hurt you, in LoG2 however, it hurts you and CAN cripple you, this is made worse by the fact some puzzle and obstacles send you down pits if you fail them, adding to the frustration. now to be fair LoG2 added a new item, the rope, which allows you to descent pits without taking any damage, still, until you manage to find a rope, your LoG1 habits might lead you to a nasty experience
i suggest anybody interested in LoG2 plays LoG1 first for two reasons:
1) its a great introduction to LoG2, since the game doesnt have a particularly good tutorial, those who played LoG1 should be able to get around LoG2's mechanics more easily
2) this game is such an upgrade over the first game that is almost impossible to go back once you finish LoG2, is just so much better than a game that was already great
i cannot recommend Legend of Grimrock 2 enough, its my 9th favorite game of all time, a goddamn masterpiece

With Sigil-Screws & Floods happening very commonly in Eternal it is something you should be completely aware off. Its not just a game out of 100, 50 or 30 - It is common. Counting it up of all games i played, and making every 5th Game a Flood or a Screw it would be around this:
Roughly 20% of Games were compromised by a bad behavior of the drawing-mechanics, be it either a sigil-flood (Getting one Sigil after another) or a screw (Getting no Sigils for 3 or more rounds)
When can we call it a Screw or Flood? I am not sure on the real numbers, but i am sure that, within a 75 Card Deck you have 25 Sigils. Most Meta-Decks are 2 or 3 Colors, which means you have 4 Diplomatic Seals and at least 4-Sigil Searchers in the Deck, closing in total 8 Slots where other Cards can be.
Drawing 1 card out of 25 has a pretty high chance at first and then a decreasing one after another one (Making Sigils appear less and less probably if you draw one after another)
I played now around 16 Years of Magic the Gathering and as far as i remember,  i never experienced so many 7 Sigil-Hands, 5 Sigil-Hands, Mana-Floods or Screws as it is in Eternal Card Game.
Which is also very Strange is the 'God Like'-Draw by your enemy. Some may say its a negative influence of being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥salty/angry already when having a big loosing streak, but i must say that i saw a godlike or even a good-hand from my enemy's very often.
You may say "Yes, but everyone has this problems" - Well, in MTG you have mostly even out matches and i have played over a thousand games with a lot of different decks, be it type 1, 1.5, or 2. Booster-Drafts as well.
If everyone would stand up and boycott Eternal for a bit, the Programmers have to intervene and change things.
And i dont even started out on telling you how extremely good and often very overpowered cards are, while a bunch of other Cards arent even worth playing - be it Draft and/or Constructed. Example?
Warcry. If you dont have an early-game answer you face a lot of cheap high-buffed creatures in mid/late game. Why is that? Warcry has just to be attacking (No matter what happens. As soon you order the attack, the warcry-effect [next creature/weapon gets +1/+1] triggers).
If warcry would be a one-time use effect it would be still a great effect, like Infiltration, but not that extremely overpowered as it is now. Play a cheap warcry deck and you will win most of your games. Craft Icaria (A legendary 7 Drop with way too much abilitys for just 3200 Dust) as soon as possible and you will have a stable winning deck.
Yes, some others may say "But my control.../But the meta-control deck.../But some decks...." beat that. Not many and not often. A friend of mine craftet such an overpowered warcry Deck he went Masters right at the start of a season, 2 days after, loosing games that you can count on two hands. In short: Fun, beautiful and a bit difficult old school challenge.
Like it's predecessor it's a tip of the hat to the classic grid based fantasy roleplaying games back in the 90's, like Eye of the Beholder. It's a good mix of tough monsters and tricky puzzles, and there's a lot of variety in level design and theme for the different areas. Legend of Grimrock 2 adds outdoor areas, height differences (and ladders), underwater areas amongst other things, as well as new character options and both new and old familiar monsters. Some areas have quite impressive visuals that made me stop and savour it. And on top of it, it has multiple endings too. Well done, devs.
A few puzzles were pretty much impossible for me to solve (or rather, realise what they wanted me to do), despite being attentive to a lot of details and finding most secrets without help. Thankfully there are a lot of online resources if you get stuck (always try a lot first yourself) but at the end of it, the puzzle part is good but there's room for improvement.
Combat is mean, in the sense that you can't straight up fight anything. If you do, you're dead. Square circling or sidestepping is a must for surviving any encounter. This is just how LoG works but I think I would prefer a more straight on approach. On the good side, a lot of monsters have abilities that work against the circling, so it's still a fun challenge. The monsters are varied and fresh but if I should be building new maps with the ingame level editor I would like some of the more classical fantasy monsters as well.
If you liked LoG1 or other games of the genre, it's definitely worth a buy.

This game isn't worth $5. Maybe $1 or $2, but not $5.
The game is just using the principle from Surgeon Simulator: you have specific control over a hand, and you must perform a task while trying to get a hold of the odd control method. Except in Ampu-tea, the goal is to just make a cup of tea rather than performing various surgeries.
One of the problems with Ampu-tea is that the (supposedly prosthetic) hand isn't attached to anything. You can just make it fly around the room like some sort of... I dunno. Helicopter? Flying Insect? Anyway, the game doesn't have any proper limits on where the arm can be moved.
Another issue is the lack of any sort of menu. You have a text box in the top right corner of the screen telling what certain keybings are (changing difficulty, disabling music, etc.), and a menu that pops up when you first start the game asking what language you want. Other than that there are no menus, and even then, the language select menu doesn't have mouse control, and is operated through pressing keys such as F1, F2, F3, and so on and so forth. There are also no performance options, you can't even change the screen resolution, leaving you with some pre-determined resolution rather than what your monitor actually uses. Another thing: people are saying that the translations are terrible for the different languages. I only speak english, so I can't tell for sure..
The game assets are weird too. There's a bunch of stuff on the table that has no reason to be there that could harm game performance on slower machines. Examples of these things are: random cloth rags with the words 'keep calm and make tea' on them, an 'out of order' tea kettle, and one of those horse head masks that are so popular on the internet (seriously? putting in an irrelevant internet meme just for a giggle?
). Also, the devs supposedly had to increase the gravity in the game just because everything in the game wasn't scaled properly (as in, everything is smaller than it should be).
The scenery consists of a terribly-made room with bad texturing (seriously,
) and way more free space than you need.
The overall game lacks content and isn't executed very well. This shouldn't be on steam, this should be on a website like kongregate or something.

Please read the whole review before flagging as helpful/not helpful. It's at times like these that I wish Steam had the option for a neutral review.
Paying homage to fan favourite and viral classic
, Ampu-Tea (LOL VERY PUNNY) is a tea-making simulator. Like SS2013, you need to use both your hands to control a solitary left arm. (Which, in this case, is robotic, and unlike SS2013, it can be VERY fragile. Don't hit it too much on stuff or it will break and you will have to restart the level.) The control schemes for both games are roughly very similar, and this review will be littered with a lot of comparisons between the two games.
Unfortunately, while SS2013's controls, though awkward, still had reasonable control, this game practically throws all semblance of control out of the window. You'll be in for a torrid time if you try to grab anything with your hand's fingers. I've tried quite a lot of times and I have to say that I've NEVER, in my 2.5 hours of playing this, successfully gripped or picked up the cup. Or anything else for that matter. I've had to resort to pushing the cup around with my arm then pushing the tea ingredients into/near the cup.
Also unlike SS2013, you can only do one thing in this game, and that is to make tea. This makes the game potentially frightfully short, depending on how skilled or lucky you are. All you can change is whether or not you add milk or sugar. There are 2 achievements where you need to add milk and sugar, but after those are done, there's not much point to playing on the harder difficulties.
Why did I give this game a barely passing grade though? Because, like SS2013, there is this sense of hilarious illogicality, only this time, it's more subtle. Remember what I said about pushing the cup and the ingredients into each other, with the cup on its side? Well, it turns out that you can complete the game this way if you can really find no way to lift the cup and ingredients properly. Just imagine: your hot water and cold milk exist as orbs. You nudge the cup along and miraculously the liquid orbs somehow land up in your cup. And when you imagine that if this was an actual tea simulator, the tea would have long spilt by now! Oh well, glad to see that it's at least forgiving in that regard.
And, unlike SS2013, you can flip the whole damn table if you screw up your tea in epic fashion.
(╯°□°）╯︵ ┻━┻)
It's enough for me, at least, to overlook its massive shortcomings. But only barely so.
When to buy: I'd recommend picking this up as part of a bundle. Depending on your tolerance, skill and/or luck, this game will either have you ragequit after the first hour, or finish it within 2 and a half (like I did), which means very short gameplay time on average.
Actually, scratch that.
You'll have a lot less frustration (and a lot more laughs).
5.5/10

The sequel to the hit First-Person Dungeon-Crawl RPG, The Legend of Grimrock II improves on the previous game in so many ways! The gameplay, the music, the graphics, the dungeon layouts! Everything! So, let’s go into one of my trademark reviews and see just how much was improved!
Gameplay: If you’ve played the first Legend of Grimrock, then the gameplay is going to feel extremely familiar. It’s the same as in the first game, but with a few minor tweaks that make playing the game so much more enjoyable. Firstly, you’ll notice that instead of being in a dungeon throughout the entire game like you were in the first game, in LoG 2 you spend most of your time outside with only needing to go into the dungeons (you read that right, in this game, there’s not just one dungeon, but a whole bunch of them!) whenever you need to solve some puzzles. The monster AI has been improved and multiple heights in dungeons were added, which kind of takes power away from the whole attack, sidestep/back away from enemies that worked throughout much of the previous game, although still doable to some degree. There’s more weapons and armor and skills and spells to learn, and new classes were added, as was a new race, meaning you have even more customization than you did in the previous game with your party generation. I also like how there are pools of water in the game and you can dive in and explore as if you were still on land but just slower moving. As I said, Almost Human has improved the Grimrock experience in many ways!
Graphics: While the graphics look the same, they’re still really friggin’ beautiful! You have the same graphics engine that was used in the original Legend of Grimrock, but with more enviroments, more monsters, more weapons and armor, and more other stuff but I haven’t exactly beaten the game yet so I can’t tell you about all of the new graphics in the game.
Music: The only music that I really know for a fact was new was the Grimrock II Title Theme, in addition to the new ambient sounds for forests, but that’s all I know of that changed.
Story: I saved the best for last this time! In Legend of Grimrock II, as with the first Legend of Grimrock, your party is a group of prisoners who are accused of some unknown crime and are being transported somewhere (where, I don’t know, I don’t think the game exactly tells you) but during your “trip”, a storm brews and casts the ship your on into the Island of Nex (the game’s setting) and you have to find out why the Island Master has summoned you here so that you can leave. The story is a much better one than the one found in Legend of Grimrock I and, without spoiling the story too much, there’s a twist ending in the game! Even the old-school Dungeon Crawler RPGs that I’ve played couldn’t pull that off! Mind you, I’ve only truly played and beaten the Eye of the Beholder Trilogy (if you can call it that) and they didn’t have any twist endings.
Overall, this is a game that shows just what a game company, no matter how large or how small, can do, especially when they’re this dedicated to improving their games’ experiences and I should hope that, should Legend of Grimrock III ever come to light (and I’m really hoping it does), then may Almost Human improve upon this game’s strengths, and make an even better one. Really, this is the classic story of a game company that could’ve used the Legend of Grimrock I Dungeon Editor to make another dungeon similar to what was in the first game, but they didn’t, they took it a step further than that and completely re-tooled their old Dungeon Editor and make a similar, yet very different, Legend of Grimrock game. Hopefully, other game devs will follow in Almost Human’s footsteps.

Eternal Card Game Review - Raymond KT
Summary: Six-guns and sorcery collide in Eternal, the new strategy card game of unlimited choices and unbelievable fun. Eternal brings AAA pace and polish to the the infinite possibilities of a deep strategy card game. The only limits are your own creativity
With spells and swords, six-guns and subterfuge, heroes collide in the struggle for the Eternal Throne. Where will you stand? Join the battle in Eternal, the new strategy card game of unlimited choices and unbelievable fun.
Variance. A lot of people will say "variance is in all card games, it's part of the game", and I will agree with them. However, when playing Eternal in any of its formats, there are far too many "non-games" - games where you have drawn too many sigils (lands), or too few, or are missing a colour entirely; games where you have drawn poorly and/or the opponent has drawn perfectly; games that are not really games, because either you, or your opponent, did not really participate.
Eternal is very much a 'value' game rather than a 'combo' game, 2-for-1'ing your opponent is always what you play to, and often what you lose to. While out-valuing your opponent can be fun, often a single 'out-value' moment can snowball into victory. Why? Deck size requirements are too high (45 for sealed, 75 for draft), you can only mulligan once, and games are a 'best of 1', which means that consistency is regularly quite low. With this, even the best decks can easily lose repeatedly to lower tier decks, even if the match-up is favourable.
Also, this issue of variance practically doubles in draft. The limited format is decent, and the card design makes it clear that MtG professionals have assisted with creating the set. However, the drafting stage takes place with AI bots (draft with bots, play against live players), and the AI often make strange choices that lead into odd drafting signals. Packs also have extremely poor variance, often only containing one card of a particular colour. Due to this, it's quite often that you will be passed a pack where there are literally no good picks for your colour(s) (even at pick 2), and even pack-1-pick-1 can be extremely poor. These issues exacerbate the previously mentioned variance issues, often leading to a bad draft experience.

Three guns. Two enemy types. Eleven tapes. An entire keyboard of reload procedures. This is Receiver, and it wants you dead. Good luck.
If you have no idea what this game is, the best way I can summarize it for you is this: you have a Gun. Not one of those handy dandy point n shoot gunz that you see in every shooter ever, but an iron and gunpowder Gun, that requires you to understand exactly how to use it. Is the hammer cocked? Magazine full? Safety off? Get along well with your Gun; it's the only thing keeping you safe against the opposition.
The setting is graphically bare, for the most part. Apartments and rooftops and giant stairwells. The randomly generated nature of the layout leads to some strange combinations, but it's all perfectly traversable... so long as you keep an eye out for drones. Did I mention that you're a one-hit wonder? No regenerating health for you; you're a fleshy ball of important parts, and a hit from anything can and will be your end.
But where the game excels, and why I like it so much, is the parts in-between deaths, where you crawl from vantage point to vantage point, pressing your ear against the wall to listen for the whirring of blades from a shock drone, or a motor hum from some turrets. The shock that runs through you as you hear the crystal clear "beep" of something seeing you, and the momentary scramble back to cover. The satisfaction of seeing a drone fall out of the sky, or putting out a turret's camera in a single shot. And as you clear each apartment, each cluster of furniture and pipes, you gather the tapes. You listen to the voice's teachings. And you learn what it is you're doing here.
Other better reviewers than me have said it before, and I'll way it again: you don't feel invincible in Receiver. You feel all too delicate. You feel like you, with a gun. And that's pretty much the best way to put it. It's a gun simulator that somehow manages to actually wring a sense of danger out of the whole thing. So yeah, it's good. Maybe you don't want to spend $10 for as small a package as it is, but put it on your wishlist anyway. It's worth whatever you pay for it.

An excellent game, though I'd argue it's worse than its predecessor.
The pros (compared to Dark Souls 1):
-Graphic fidelity is much higher
-Allows summoning and invasions even with dead bosses
-A jump key
-More weapon types
-In general more fluid magic system
-Character creation (as in the visual part) was massively improved
-Online play actually works all the time without third party applications.
-Online play actually blocks people who DC constantly.
What still is an issue:
-vertical hitboxes. Good luck hitting enemies slightly below you with a horizontal swing weapon.
-generally occasionally wonky hitboxes. Got hit more than once while actively blocking and facing the enemy.
-Online play still has massive lag, although I doubt anything will ever fix that so I can't really blame them for that.
What actually got worse:
-Art style. While graphics fidelity improved, the general tone of the areas is much less dark than in dark souls. Dark souls felt like you were intruding on something old, something much bigger than you. Dark souls 2 just feels like you're wandering about some ruins that happen to have undead in them.
-Soul Memory. While it might seem good, it has a number of issues. First, it punishes players who lose a lot of bloodstains or just don't know what to buy. Meaning, exactly the players who are actually worse at the game and less skilled, get matched with players who are both more skilled and have objectively stronger characters. Secondly, It means that you can't coop continously within one area, unless you use an Agape ring.
-Blood stains. Dark souls placed bloodstains a few steps before you died. Dark souls 2 places it where you died. On the surface all fine and dandy, but it also means if you die say, on lava, it means you're never getting those souls back. Of course, that wouldn't be much of an issue (it's just increased difficulty) if it weren't for soul memory.
-less impressive bosses. Dark souls bosses were massive, and always initially first felt like you could never beat them. Dark souls 2 bosses, while actually not really easier, just don't feel at imposing, due to both how they look, their animations, and their surrounding.
All in all though, it's still another dark souls game. If you liked dark souls, it's more of what is mostly the same. It's not as good in my opinion, but it's still good.

I'm reminded of how I felt when I played Splinter Cell: Double Agent, which had me wondering whether the design supervisor was just lazy on the day of presentations and approved everyone's ideas on the spot. Most of these minigames are unintuitive and tend to be stacked in the aggressor's favor. This is especially evident in matches against the computer, whose reflexes and grasp of game mechanics I cannot possibly hope to match.
Everything else feels sluggish. A CaW with 100 Agility still runs like a cancer patient and slugs like a blind kindergartener. Load times seem unreasonably long. Control response is frustratingly delayed on both keyboard and controller (an X-Box 360 Wireless, if it matters), which when coupled with the afore♥♥♥♥♥edabout minigames leads to so much anger I nearly put my fist through my monitor.
Finally, the game is riddled with glitches even this long after release - guess they had to get to work on their next failure. They range from the minor annoyance of pyrotechnics failing to go off during an entrance, to wrestlers outright missing with their punches for no obvious reason.
This is a huge step back from what I remember. If I do not get a refund, it will not be from lack of trying.

An incredibly fun game that I clocked more hours into due to losing internet for a few months(steam won't track hours this way), and the DRM free version I had before buying the Steam Version.
Basically, you run a restaurant and serve food day by day. You can buy various food and drinks, each can be upgraded to not only sell for more money, but get more ingredients so you can do more recipes. Each food/drink(which I'll be calling 'menu items' from now on) has a practice area where you can make that menu item over and over, and you can even select the various recipes available to you. This is perfect for those difficult menu items so you can practice them.
As for the actual restaurant mechanic, you start the day at 9am and end at 10pm. The game moves at an accelerated time frame, so the entire in-game day takes about 10-15 minutes irl, though I've never actually timed it myself. Various customers will come in and order something off the menu items you choose for the day. Up to 4(in the beginning) orders can be placed at once, so you'll need to pick up the speed if you fall behind.
For the actual cooking, if something requires some preparation, like a burger or pizza, then you do so. Using the Burger for example, the customer orders a BLT with 3 patties. First you slap the 3 patties on the grill and press enter, they'll start cooking and you'll be free to continue/prep other orders. When the patties are done, you can continue it. You'll start by slamming the patties on the burger with the "M"(for meat) button, then the "B", "L", "T" buttons to put on the Bacon, Lettuce, and Cheese respectively. Then press enter and your done.  For something like the pizza, where Prep is basically putting on the Customers ingredients and tossing it in the oven, you just have to wait for it to finish cooking and then bam, you're done.
The Pizza and Burger are some of the easier menu items, the rest, like the Lasagna and Soup, can become quite difficult, though they're worth more in proportion.
There are also chores like dish washing, mouse trap setting up, and garbage throwing that needs to be done during the work day. They can be difficult when they happen during peak hours(way more customers). Some menu items increase the amount of some chores, so look into the various menu items to see if they have the negative if you really don't like them.
There are a list of goals you can accomplish to proceed in the 'story' and upgrade you resturant. Stuff like serve X amount of customers or buy X amount of menu items. Also pass a few safety inspections, where an inspector stands around and you cant fail too many chores.
Along with buying food you can buy upgrades that reduce chores, increase waiting time of customers, etc.
This game is definitely worth the price and comes by it's 'Overwhelmingly Positive" rating honestly. Also, there's a 'Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2' in the works, though it's still quite a ways off and looks promising. That shouldn't stop you from purchasing this game at all.

So first off, I played Dark Souls for the first time last year, with DS2 being my only other taste of the series. With that out of the way, it's basically Dark Souls: Now with More Dark Souls edition, with some differences.
Gameplay works much the same way as the first game. Enemies are almost everywhere, you spend much of your time killing them and you being killed. And like the first game, you will die a lot, sometimes because you made mistakes and sometimes because the game just hates you.
A few things are different, mostly the hollowing mechanic, where your max health bar slowly shrinks down the 50% until you use a consumable to become human again(which resets it back to 100%). This is quite irritating until you find the ring early on that caps your max health loss to 75%. Weapons degrade faster but bonfires restore them. However, bonfires are a lot more plentiful in DS2 and repair powder is available. Oh, and bonfire warping works from the start in this game, which is good because you have to go back to the hub town to level up.
One of the biggest differences is that after you kill an enemy like 12 or so times, they stop respawning, which is bad for grinding(but honestly killing each enemy 12 times is gonna grant you a decent number of souls as long as you don't lose them all the time) but does grant you the small mercy of not having to painstakingly fight your way to the boss door every single time(which is quite a pain in some areas). And you can revvive all enemies(including the boss) if you like.
Level design is a mixed bag. Some levels are really interesting and well designed, while others feel very artificial and "video gamey". There's a much better variety but the transition between them feels bizzare and off. The best example is taking an elevator up from the top of a windmill(built into a hill) and ending up in a lava field castle.
There are a lot more areas and bosses, but there are a fair number of bosses and areas that are completely optional. The bosses themselves range from pretty awesome to fairly lazy, with a fair number of them being some varient of "a big dude wearing armor" and one of them literally being a swarm of rats(with the "boss rat" looking almost exactly like all the other rats in the small room).
There are more covenants, if that's what you're like, but most of them are PVP and if you don't like PVP you're pretty much stuck with the Sunbros, which luckily this time doesn't have a faith requirement to join(but you don't find it until a bit later then in DS1). This probably explaisn why invaders, both NPC and PVP seem to happen a lot more often in this game, especially since you can be invaded when hollow now and some areas(Belfy Luna) are designed to spam you with invasions. Luckily, most of the high invasion spots are optional.
The lore and story are weaker then DS, mostly due to being disconnected from the first game and rather vague to start with. It's own lore isn't bad, but none of it really stands out like the unfolding tragedy invovled in keeping the first flame going from the first game.
Oh, and finally, it does feel like the game designers spent a lot of time bringing back stuff from DS, as if at times desperately trying to recapture the magic of the first game, but often feels like imitation, when it doesn't feel like they looked for all the parts of DS people hated and brought them back. Remember Blightown and Tomb of the Giants? Welcome to the Gutter! Enjoy the SIF Fight? Meet the Royal Rat Authority! Think ladies with spiders for an♥♥♥♥♥are sexy? Here's a lady with a Scorpian with TWO tales this time. Hate the Anor Londo Archers? Well, have fun, because there's an open space with a bunch of those guys trying to murder you from afar while their melee buddies rush you. Like Poison areas? There's 3 of them now!
Oh, and if you are creeped out by spiders.....you're gonna have a bad time in Brightstone cove.
OTOH, I've played for 36 hours so far and I'm enjoying it most of the time, but it feels flawed in many ways, like it's a game that wants to be Dark Souls but isn't quite Dark Souls. I feel like once I'm done with it, I'll likely never come back to it.

I do not like this game. That is a matter of opinion. In my opinion, this game is not fun, bar the PVP encounters, which at this point consist of twinks and hackers (That is when you can actually find anyone to play with at all). The tight, fast gameplay and controls of the first game have vanished, in their wake is a combat system that is incredibly slow and weighted. Weight in combat is not a bad thing most of the time, in The Witcher 3, the weight of the characters and enemies feel correct for the type of game that it is. In Shadow of the Collosus, the weight of the game was very well done, because it is a game that is meant to feel weighted. Dark Souls, in my opinion, is good because it doesn't have a lot of weight, most of the time. Enemies jump about and throw themsleves at you from all directions, and it's up to your quick reactions to get you out of those situations. Dark Souls 2 makes most encounters feel monotonous. There are good encounters, but most of the time, it's just boring. The story in Dark Souls 2, is very well done, like the first. The PVP in Dark Souls 2 is vastly improved from the first game. The game that you're forced to sit through in order to experience both of those aspects, is tedious. I'd recommend this game to people who prefer slower paced gameplay from the first game.

Man I really wanted to like this game, despite the negative reviews. I really did. It's got a lot of good things going for  it, but...I just can't.
Let's get the most obvious stuff out of the way first--the game looks ♥♥♥♥ing beautiful. The graphics are great, the environments look fantastic; characters, vehicles and enemy designs look really cool. The sound design is awesome, and the musical score is intense; and all of these positives lead to a very immersive experience. My first half hour of the game was absolutely incredible. The cutscenes were well rendered and amazingly choreographed. The attention to detail was over the top; ♥♥♥♥in hell, you can even see your legs when you walk or crouch! Gimmicks such as the addition of a smartphone as a vehicle for portraying menus, collectables, and logs were nice, as were the addition of weapons that you can modify on the fly.
But that's where the positives really end. At the end of your introductory mission, you're plopped down in the middle of a firefight. Where the game felt like it was gently guiding you through tutorials and on-rails sections, you're suddenly plopped down into an open world. It's as if that guiding hand decided to drop you into a puddle of freezing water, and it's as jarring as it is overwhelming. There are tutorials sure, but I found they didn't really help alleviate the general sense of confusion and overwhelmingness that comes with being thrust into the middle of a combat zone after an incredibly scripted starting section. If that was intentional though, well, they certainly nailed that part of the game. To make things worse, there is no quicksave function, something that I believe is vital in an open world game that wants you to traverse entire maps to reach objectives.
Moving on, I feel the game lacks in the options department. It's got a large plethora of video and HUD options, but it misses out on a few essentials, FOV sliders being my largest gripe with that.
The rest of the things I have problems with are mostly quality of life issues, and while small, they really add up. Stuff like  atrocious vehicle controls and handling, clunky shooting mechanics, substandard plot writing (including how NK was able to occupy the US so easily and quickly), terrible AI, unskippable cutscenes, NO ♥♥♥♥ING STEAM CLOUD SUPPORT DESPITE BEING A FULL BUDGET AAA GAME, etcetera etcetera.
I'd say it's worth picking up on sale though; don't waste your money on a full price copy. Despite everything, I hope they'll be another Homefront title; one better than the last two. Perhaps in the far future.

Those F-Zero and Wipeout fans looking for a decent PC fix should look elsewhere at this point in development. Though the engine is stable, nice-looking, and generally very functional, there is little depth or challenge to the movement physics, leaving even casual fans I've introduced the game to playing dull, easy races. Though I certainly applaud the developers for trying something new, the addition of heat tracking, a permanent rapid-fire weapon, and the ability to pick up and store three weapons instead the traditional one adds little to the game as they are currently implemented, instead cluttering what has proven to be a very focused and effective formula in other series.
My experience playing a number of Wipeout and F-Zero games has colored my opinion, without question, but the fact of the matter is GameArt Studio are making a game in a subgenre that has produced some of the best racing games ever created, and that's hard to live up to, no matter who you are. Unfortunately, the current state of the game, though technically solid, lacks a focused enough design to make an impression, not only in the hovercraft-racing subgenre, but the racing genre as a whole. I would be more than willing to give future builds a second chance if the design moves toward expanding unexplored elements of the genre, instead of the current design, which seems little more than "What was done before, but with more stuff tacked on."

The Crew has quickly become my favorite racing game ever. Let me first qualify by saying that I am not a racing sim fan but prefer arcade-style racers. Previous favorites have been Burnout: Paradise and Flatout: Ultimate Carnage. I also enjoy the DIRT and Forza series of games. With that said The Crew has an engaging story with a cinematic feel. I was able to play through the story at a casual pace in about 15 hours. The cut scenes are very well done and really draw you in. Once you finish the story there really isn't much that ties the campaign to the rest of the game however. I hope Ivory Tower (the developer) finds a way to create new missions which allow you to see what Alex and the 5-10s are doing instead of the player just running around the US doing races that don't connect with the story.
Other than the disconnect from the story, once you make it to "V8" status then the open world really affords you many choices. In addition to the option to go back and re-race any of the campaign missions (to win better car parts) you can also run skill events. You must do wither of these to get better parts for your car(s) before you will have a chance in the PvP section. You can also race in Faction events which earn bucks that you can use to repurchase parts you have already won for cars you haven't yet upgraded or to buy entirely new cars.
Speaking of cars, The Crew actually uses licensed cars from a wide variety of car makers including domestic and foriegn. Most of the cars are available to purchase with the bucks you earn in the game but others are only available if you pay real cash. The cost is relatively low and the season pass can make them even more affordable to buy all together. Each car has a variety of "spec" ratings from Full-stock, Street, Performance, Dirt, Raid and Circuit. Not all cars support all specs such as a Ferrari wouldn't have Dirt or Raid but many such as the Mustang GT have all so you can get really crazy with your builds. You can also customize the exterior and interior appearance of your rides and with the daily and monthly challenges you are encouraged to enhance your cars to earn more bucks. The variety of car looks and builds is pretty amazing. I rarely see the same configurations more than once when playing PvP.
I could go on and on about this game but one of the things I like the most is that the developer, Ivory Tower, keeps enhancing and updating the game to make it better. Recently that added a league rating system and they routinely release new cars, tracks and events. The fact that this game continues to grow really makes it a great value. Unlike my past favorites I am always able to discover new things in this vast vehicular playground. Whether you buy The Crew on sale or at regular price you won't be dissappointed. This is one of the most fun and engaging racing games ever.
Oh and did I say that there is a huge expansion coming in the fall: Monster Trucks, Motorcycles and Dragsters!!!!

I recently read about this game in a random forum post and now 2 weeks later im more then sold. This is pretty much exactly what ive been looking for in a digital ccg.
It is very similar to MTG which is a good thing. The f2p model seems really fair so far, you can endlessly grind against the AI if you want but the really cool thing is that their version of "arena" lets you keep the cards you draft.
Also just playing ranked basicly gives you half a pack to a pack evry 3 wins, daily quests are half a pack to 2 packs and overall it just seems reasonable. i can already play 3-4 different decks on ladder (budget versions tho) and do fine and got like 5 legendaries just in the last 3 days.
The high end decks can get very expensive tho since you can run up to 4 copies of a legendary in a deck and some are just that good. id like to see a higher "luck" ceiling on the packs tho since in each pack there is only 1 slot for a rare/legendary card. having the ocasional double rare or even legendary+rare would make opening packs more exciting.
Deckbuilding seems way more open and creative then most of the other games out there and in general there is very little RNG and much more strategy compared to the competition. Also since there is always value in playing the AI it is great to play on the phone (even tho the client isnt optimized for phones yet and text can be a bit small) since you can just pause and resume mid match.
If you like magic, are looking for a more complex ccg or just are tired of Hearthstone then you have to check this game out.
p.s. i got low time on steam cause i mostly play on my tablet. mainly have it on steam for more convenient deckbuilding.

There are plenty of PvE modes that really help you undestand how to play the game in Eternal before you play already well versed players in PvP; something Magic Online could also take a note from. I was turned on to this game watching Brian Kibler stream it; if anyone is interested in learning draft strategy check him out. There are a number of decent players on twitch streaming if anyone is having trouble with their play.
The one issue I hope to see addressed further in the digital space is abilites to fix power. A little too often I feel I open with two power after a mulligan and do not see another power to progress the game for an entire game! That MUST be addressed; it is an outdated function of random shuffling in physical card games. To perserve the rng of the cards drawn I suggest something akin to Heathstone's coin, but each player is allowed once per game to draw a power. This power could be colorless, if not too broken it could be of power color already played. Being stuck on 2 power is a helpless feeling; it does not allow for interactivity, instead leaving even the best player helpless to do anything but essentially watch his opponent play a quick game of solitaire ;) please use your creative powers to bring an end to this archaic issue of the physical world! :) Thank-you for an overall amazing game. 10/10

Man, I'm really trying to like it, and I'm going to keep trying, but I just can't bring myself to enjoy this.
The combat is similar to LoG 1, but enemies are much tougher. Not in a difficult way, but in a tedious way. It takes way too many hits to kill even the most basic of enemies and it gets boring after a few hours.
The above-ground island portion isn't really that great. I think they were going for an open world kind feel, but it doesn't work. I only find myself having fun when I go underground to the dungeons, but those parts don't last nearly as long as I'd like.
The Puzzles aren't great. They're either too simple, have a stupid solution involving searching the walls for a hidden button, or require an item you don't have yet. Or maybe you missed it all the way back, you have no way of knowing.
There's no real sense of doom like in Grimrock 1. Then, I had no idea how far down I was or what was next. Now I just find a puzzle, see if I can solve it, and if I can't I look for a dungeon.
They try to replicate the mysterious story of Grimrock 1 by adding the Island Master, but it's not as interesting or thrilling. "Ooh some dude brought you to his spooky island with monsters and traps, scary..." Reminds me of the first live action Scooby Doo movie.
Like I said, I'm going to keep trying because I loved Grimrock 1 so much, but I'm having a lot of trouble enjoying this one and I can't give it a positive review.

Despite the obscure name, VVVVVV is 2D Platformer with simple graphics, simple gameplay and a simple story. When your ship crash's and your crew is scattered out in space, it's your job as the captain to round them up in order to get the ship flying again. The game's layout is in the same style as Metroid, as the map is huge and it's easy to get lost. You basically move around while defying and re-defying gravity to navigate through levels. Checkpoints are scattered everywhere and your going to need them from all of the times you die. There are 20 trinkets to find in order to unlock the jukebox or something as the music in this game is epic with its catchy tunes. Graphics are simple classic 8-bit style with bizarre looking enemies, almost feels like something out of a Commodore 64 or ZX Spectrum game. If there's one thing this game is known for, it's challenge, there is a lot of tricks and puzzles in navigating through the place and you really have to be quick on your feet and plan ahead on what to do. Overall VVVVVV is a great challenging game that feels like a throw back to the old PC games.

There are many things about this game that I consider to contribute toward a positive experience.  I must give a brief preview of the game before I proceed.
You are on a grass farm that grows grass.  Your job is to mow grass. You have to mow the grass with a lawnmower, which is a fairly large gasoline-fueled motor-driven machine that uses blades to cut grass.  The one the character uses in this game is ridable, so you have to drive it around like a car.  The driving in this game reminds me of GTA V.
Duties: do not run out of gas and mow all of the grass.
As you lawnmow the grass farm you will be paid in a currency known as "Score."  Be careful because the higher your score will get, the sweatier you will become, and you might find yourself beginning to become irritated as well.  Just take it out on the grass.  Remember, you have a job to do.
The grass farm grows grass in two large fenced-in areas.  They are known as Grass Yard Alpha and Grass Yard Beta.
Grass Yard Alpha is a special grass-growing area because the farmers have planted grass in the shape of massive letters spelling out "LAWNMOWER."  Yes, you can even mow the grass letters as well!  Grass Yard Beta is just full of grass, but you will learn to appreciate that for what it is.
I was at first in awe when I launched the game because of the amazing graphics.  The motion blur alone is astonishing, and I almost wet my pants when I realized the game features a unique first-person-view mode that will completely change gameplay.  When the "first person experience", as I like to call it, is activated, a truly realistic law mowing experience begins to unfold.  You'll have to master the art of switching between first and third person view to get the full experience of this game.
It took a good hour or two, but I have personally mowed every single grass unit there is to mow.  There were times when I thought I would give up, but I knew deep down that I had to complete the job.  I had to mow the lawn.
I have witnessed the secret surprise that occurs when all of the grass has been mowed.  Trust me, the experience is rewarding, and the "end game content" will make you want to play through the entire game again!!
Tips:
1. NEVER RUN OUT OF GAS!
2. Don't try to mow two rows of grass at once.  That's foolishness.  Get the job done one row at a time.
3. Don't go into town.  That's foolishness.  It's a waste of time and gas.  You have a job to do.
4. Don't ask questions... the grass will tell you what you need to know.

Receiver is an engaging premise, a shooter game that saddles you with many of the hassles of operating an actual handgun.
The experience is a bit like Dark Souls, in that it involves repetetively venturing into a challenging environment until it kills you, at which point you reset and try again. Like Dark Souls, the story is largely ignorable (delivered in a drone over the set of cassette tapes it is your goal to collect). Unlike Dark Souls, your equipment, environment and enemy placement are randomized, demanding adaptability and caution from players.
You'll develop an algorithm of sorts for survival: find cover, check and consolidate ammo, load your weapon, flashlight on or off, carefully approach and survey a nearby room, try to determine the threats inside, and how you'll dispatch them. Mess it up, pull multiple enemies, panic fire a few times and probably die.
The enemy design isn't flashy, but the fact that there are many ways to disable them makes for some tactical uncertainty. Destroy just a drone's weapon and it's harmless but will still valiantly try to track you. Blind it and it will still patrol (and perhaps could still kill you). Immobilize it and it may still kill you if you walk within range of its weapon but could be safely avoided.
I'd really like to see the developers return to this project, perhaps adding new enemies room templates, tweaking ammo spawns, or even just improving the draw distance. That seems unlikey, but that's fine: I've more than gotten my cup-of-coffee's worth out of this program.

Receiver is a unique FPS game by it's mechanics. It has downsides about which I'll talk in a bit, but I personally love it. In order to play it successfully you have to pass a learning curve and it worth it. It has been years since I’ve played it the first time and I still remember how to play it. It’s like a bike – when you learned it, it’s hard to unlearn it.
Now, about the downsides. The game was developed in 7-day FPS challenge, keep that in mind. It means that developers didn't have time to write a story or to create many interesting levels. What they did is made solid building blocks, which can be combined together in any way, so the engine generates level while you’re wondering through it. Also, there are two types of enemies and, believe me, that’s more than enough. Standing turrets and flying electrocuting drones are deadly but fair.
With that been said I want to tell you about why all the ruckus - gun mechanics. Oh dear, this is just amazing. Every new game you get one gun from three: Glock 17, Colt M1911 and S&M Revolver. All three have different characteristics which are: magazine capacity, fire-mode and damage. Glock can burst-fire and has biggest magazine but has low damage. Colt is a middle ground – does decent damage but has comparatively small magazine. Revolver is the most powerful but it’s hard to reload and it doesn’t have a magazine at all.
The amazing part comes when you decide to reload your handgun. Using specific keys you have to manually load every piece of ammo into magazine or cylinder. It feels so good when you do it fast and accurate. You can put ammo into different magazines if you find ones, so you can swap faster. With revolver it’s not the case – you have to unload the cylinder and point gun up while waiting for empty cases or ammo left to fall down, and only after that you should start putting new ammo inside.
Enemies, ammo and flashlights are randomly placed on the map and the important part is that every bullet counts. Burst-fire mode is good and reliable but it will leave you with no ammo in a heartbeat. The best way to do it is precise one shots into vital parts of the enemy’s bodies. You see, drones and turrets are mindless and do exactly what they are programmed for – idle until their sensor notices you, make a beep while waiting a fracture of a second and after that engage. Turrets engage by simple shooting at your direction when drones are flying to you and trying to electrocute you with their lethal tasers. The thing is enemies has their modules open so you can disable them with the precise shot. Damaged battery? Enemy immediately is shut down. Shot their gun or taser? They will actively beep and look or fly at you whitout the ability to hurt you. When you destroy their sensors they just idle never realizing you near them. Also you can disable drone’s blades so it will fall to the ground beeping at you and if you come close trying to tase you.
So, what are you doing in this odd empty building? You can find not only ammo and flashlights but audio tapes. In order to win you need to gather and listen to all 11 tapes while there are more and more enemies in every new part of the building generated. Tapes play automatically when you pick them up. Nice voice will tell you what’s going on.
Now, I strongly recommend to turn music and voice sounds off, so you can focus on idle sound of enemies. Since tapes are random you can listen to every one of them in multiple playing sessions.
In conclusion I want say that I never gathered all 11 tapes in one session but I still try from time to time.

So first off, I played Dark Souls for the first time last year, with DS2 being my only other taste of the series. With that out of the way, it's basically Dark Souls: Now with More Dark Souls edition, with some differences.
Gameplay works much the same way as the first game. Enemies are almost everywhere, you spend much of your time killing them and you being killed. And like the first game, you will die a lot, sometimes because you made mistakes and sometimes because the game just hates you.
A few things are different, mostly the hollowing mechanic, where your max health bar slowly shrinks down the 50% until you use a consumable to become human again(which resets it back to 100%). This is quite irritating until you find the ring early on that caps your max health loss to 75%. Weapons degrade faster but bonfires restore them. However, bonfires are a lot more plentiful in DS2 and repair powder is available. Oh, and bonfire warping works from the start in this game, which is good because you have to go back to the hub town to level up.
One of the biggest differences is that after you kill an enemy like 12 or so times, they stop respawning, which is bad for grinding(but honestly killing each enemy 12 times is gonna grant you a decent number of souls as long as you don't lose them all the time) but does grant you the small mercy of not having to painstakingly fight your way to the boss door every single time(which is quite a pain in some areas). And you can revvive all enemies(including the boss) if you like.
Level design is a mixed bag. Some levels are really interesting and well designed, while others feel very artificial and "video gamey". There's a much better variety but the transition between them feels bizzare and off. The best example is taking an elevator up from the top of a windmill(built into a hill) and ending up in a lava field castle.
There are a lot more areas and bosses, but there are a fair number of bosses and areas that are completely optional. The bosses themselves range from pretty awesome to fairly lazy, with a fair number of them being some varient of "a big dude wearing armor" and one of them literally being a swarm of rats(with the "boss rat" looking almost exactly like all the other rats in the small room).
There are more covenants, if that's what you're like, but most of them are PVP and if you don't like PVP you're pretty much stuck with the Sunbros, which luckily this time doesn't have a faith requirement to join(but you don't find it until a bit later then in DS1). This probably explaisn why invaders, both NPC and PVP seem to happen a lot more often in this game, especially since you can be invaded when hollow now and some areas(Belfy Luna) are designed to spam you with invasions. Luckily, most of the high invasion spots are optional.
The lore and story are weaker then DS, mostly due to being disconnected from the first game and rather vague to start with. It's own lore isn't bad, but none of it really stands out like the unfolding tragedy invovled in keeping the first flame going from the first game.
Oh, and finally, it does feel like the game designers spent a lot of time bringing back stuff from DS, as if at times desperately trying to recapture the magic of the first game, but often feels like imitation, when it doesn't feel like they looked for all the parts of DS people hated and brought them back. Remember Blightown and Tomb of the Giants? Welcome to the Gutter! Enjoy the SIF Fight? Meet the Royal Rat Authority! Think ladies with spiders for an♥♥♥♥♥are sexy? Here's a lady with a Scorpian with TWO tales this time. Hate the Anor Londo Archers? Well, have fun, because there's an open space with a bunch of those guys trying to murder you from afar while their melee buddies rush you. Like Poison areas? There's 3 of them now!
Oh, and if you are creeped out by spiders.....you're gonna have a bad time in Brightstone cove.
OTOH, I've played for 36 hours so far and I'm enjoying it most of the time, but it feels flawed in many ways, like it's a game that wants to be Dark Souls but isn't quite Dark Souls. I feel like once I'm done with it, I'll likely never come back to it.

I will say all in all I enjoyed this game. As a long time fan, who recently returned to the show I haven't touched a WWE branded game in a long time. In fact the last game I touched was still titled WWF. From what I can tell the game has more or less what would be expected from a WWE title. Such as a creature your own wrestler, entrance, and so on. You also have online modes which was kind of a new thing in the older games and adds for a nice feature to play with friends, or those who want to prove they are the best at the game.
The Showcase is pretty good as well, it was awesome going back and reliving Stone Colds career mixed in with live footage, and hearing JR once again brought back a lot of good memories..
I will say the only thing that seems to be lacking is the career mode. I really enjoyed the moments from the WWF smackdown career modes where it played out more like a television show full of drama and backstage scene's no matter who you picked, even if you used a custom wrestler. Now you just wrestle, and then just wrestle some more with the occasional interview here, or run in there. Just gets boring real fast and lacks any story what so ever. Which makes sense with the amount of work they put into Showcase mode, but there is just so many times you can play that before it gets boring as well.
The game also seems more of a simulation then it does a arcady game. Which is not a bad thing, but isn't everyones cup of tea.

I like playing it in short bursts, around 15 minutes per day. Any more than that and I get tired / bored.
But those 15 minutes per day are a lot of fun. I enjoy using the keyboard to quickly and efficiently put together the various food items, and I like that each item has its own quirks and method of preparation.
The gameplay is mainly this sort of frantic mix of speed and accuracy. The management side of the game is secondary, I think, but also well developed with enough room for you to decide your own menu and upgrades.
The game is playable with mouse or keyboard or controller or even touchscreen, but I highly recommend playing it with a keyboard - nothing else will give you the same edge as keyboard shortcuts.

This thumbs down comes with a few caveats and is yet another reason why a binary yes/no rating system is simply flawed.
The long and short of it is that the game needs more options and modes. I bought it specifically because I was thrilled with the sim-level detail that it goes into with gun handling, but without a "free mode", you're left hoping you spawn near no enemies and are able to pick up the right stuff. As a game, it's lacking much in the way of meaningful visual assets or level design, so I'm not exactly sure why the game couldn't just take place at an actual firing range or something. Maybe I'm missing the point.
I got it for one dollar and don't regret it at all, but saying that I "recommend this game" just isn't quite accurate. Good proof of concept that deserves to be fleshed out with more guns, actual gameplay objectives, and a free-play mode.

Dark Souls 2 isn’t Dark Souls 1. It shares a lot of the broader strokes and some things that are basically unchanged, even down to its name and story, but it differs in the finer details, which is what matters if you are expecting to find more Dark Souls. And while Dark Souls 2 is different, the majority of the changes made vastly improved upon the gameplay, while the storytelling and world cohesion suffered. Dark Souls 2 is also a lot bigger than Dark Souls 1, though a huge amount of the content is optional. This means the experience isn’t as tight and focused as Dark Souls 1 (well, as the first half of Dark Souls 1), but on the other hand, it’s a lot more replayable (as if my playtime didn’t already clue you in on that). I do not like this game. That is a matter of opinion. In my opinion, this game is not fun, bar the PVP encounters, which at this point consist of twinks and hackers (That is when you can actually find anyone to play with at all). The tight, fast gameplay and controls of the first game have vanished, in their wake is a combat system that is incredibly slow and weighted. Weight in combat is not a bad thing most of the time, in The Witcher 3, the weight of the characters and enemies feel correct for the type of game that it is. In Shadow of the Collosus, the weight of the game was very well done, because it is a game that is meant to feel weighted. Dark Souls, in my opinion, is good because it doesn't have a lot of weight, most of the time. Enemies jump about and throw themsleves at you from all directions, and it's up to your quick reactions to get you out of those situations. Dark Souls 2 makes most encounters feel monotonous. There are good encounters, but most of the time, it's just boring. The story in Dark Souls 2, is very well done, like the first. The PVP in Dark Souls 2 is vastly improved from the first game. The game that you're forced to sit through in order to experience both of those aspects, is tedious. I'd recommend this game to people who prefer slower paced gameplay from the first game.

I imagine the original Dark Souls as the first born of Miyazaki and Dark Souls 2 as the middle child.  Miyazaki poured a ton of love and effort into making Dark Souls a thoroughly connected and well designed world, but when Dark Souls 2 happened the novelty of kids wore off and he lost interest.  So the middle child did his best to imitate the elder son, but he emphasized the wrong things (difficulty) over the right things (level design, enemy designs) and Miyazaki was too busy with the newborn (Bloodborne) to give a sh*t.  So when Dark Souls 2 grew enough to be released it was alright but compared to the rest of the family is just a disappointment, and everytime you go to his house you say "hey where's your brother Dark Souls?" and the poor kid feels insecure and inadequate.  And then he kills himself and you shrug and go replay Dark Souls.
It's not bad though.

To start with, I would like to say that this is not a bad game exactly. Really, the main problem is that there is not much to it. As of now, I have earned 100% of the achievements, and the absurd one for launching the game 500 times easily accounted for the bulk of the time involved. The one really good part is that it's my first perfect game. All that is left to do at this point as far as the game is concerned is to endlessly try my hand at making cups of tea in the tea cups using any combo of milk and sugar along with the teabags and hot water. There are no other levels, tasks, or challenges. You're only given the one set-up to work with, with various levels of difficulty only coming into play via the complexity of the cup of tea being requested.
Like other games of the sort, every movement required to actually achieve a task is absolutely painstaking, which is where the fine line between fun and frustration comes into play. Unfortunately, the glitches within the game do make things weigh slightly in favor of frustration, as the arm has a habit of going through things and getting stuck, plus other issues, along with the other intended quirks common in games like this, where it refuses to truly grab things, instead often flipping, dropping, or even breaking them.
Having gotten the game in a bundle, I certainly wouldn't complain, as there is definitely some amount of fun to be had here. Nor would I dismiss the possibility of getting future games from the creators in the future, especially if they do something a bit bigger in scope. Yet, still, for what it currently is I cannot recommend buying it, unless you find it in a bundle with other games you want.

Featuring a cast of colourful characters and a complex, deeply philosophical story that delves into religion/spirituality, existentialism and the power of knowledge and truth, Final Fantasy X has only one weak point and that is the voice acting. This doesn't take away from the game but it is a glaring downside to what is otherwise a 10/10 game

I got Legend of Grimrock 2 as a gift around two years ago, played it until I killed the Viper Roots, put it down, and didn't touch it for another two years.
After resolving to pick it up again and not set it down until I was finished, I can say that LoGII does everything from LoGI, and more.
While LoGI was entirely set in the claustrophobic confines of Grimrock, a giant dungeon built in the mountains, LoGII takes place on the Isle of Nex, with over 10 unique environments, 5 bosses, and more of the fun rune-based magic, hunting for rare items, and secrets that made LoGI so great. The level design and puzzles are on point, reminescent of classic dungeon crawlers like Dungeon Master. Many old enemies return from LoGI, with a few new ones to mix up the joyful shuffle-foot slice and cast combat routine of the original.
My only real complaint about Grimrock II is the difficulty: either I don't recall how difficult LoGI was, or this game is on steroids. Enemies deal insane amounts of damage and are bulky as hell, making combat difficult if you get pinned between two enemies or a wall. Nostalgic enemies as well, while great, seem to be added in as sort of a fanservice thing (the Herder's Den comes to mind as such, as well as the Crowverns that only appear in one area.)
Despite that, Legends of Grimrock II is more of the same greatness that made LoGI so fun, now with added plot outside of "escape the Dungeon." Would heartily reccomend, if you're a fan of the original or looking for a good Dungeon Crawler.
Just remember to plan your characters properly, or else you'll be in for a bad time.

But, once you learn the very basics of the game, skill doesn't matter.
In Magic the Gathering, and other games, there is a lot of choice involved. Do I use my kill spell on a creature on the board, or do I hold on to it for a potentially bigger threat? Do I sacrifice my creatures to kill a current attacker, or save them for later? Not here. Once you learn the basics and the cards that are out there, there is always a clear, objectively best choice.  The majority of the cards have insanely powerful effects, even for 1 mana. Most of these effects snowball. Most cards that see play can win the game by themselves, including cards for 3, 2, or even ONE mana,  if you can't stop them asap. Your hand is forced, since if the card survives for more than a turn or two, the game is over. And of course, if you don't happen to draw the card you need to stop it, you lose.
There are also tons of incredibly powerful "win more" effects. In any game like this, you want to control the board and have the strongest presence. That's what you have to do in order to push through and deal damage, or prevent it. That's fine, but the "win more" effects allow insane bonuses for controlling the board. So, if you're already winning, you get insane bonuses. There's infiltrate, which gives you a bonus for getting one hit on the opponent. For 3 mana, you can get a creature that lets you draw three cards AND gain life. Or a 3 mana card that creates 2 5/5's. Or a 2 mana card that gets the equivalent of first strike and death touch. There's warcry, which gives the top creature of your deck between as many as 5 1/1 counters whenever the warcry creature attacks. These effects, and similar ones, are seen on creatures of all costs, not just big ones.
The end result is that you MUST kill anything you can as soon as you possibly can. You can't try to hold out and overcome in the late game. It is never in your interest to plan for the future.

At first you'll feel like a total fool trying to manage all the mechanics and steps of reloading. You'll be dropping half your equipment on the first few attempts just to reload a simple mag. But every time you die you become more skilled with handling the gun, and eventually you become a gun wielding expert. It's super satisfying to do all the steps when handling a gun in combat in a few seconds.
From doing quick reloads by dropping the mag on the floor to grab a spare in the span of half a second. To actually being able to♥♥♥♥♥♥the gun slightly to see that there's a bullet in the chamber before bursting into a room full of foes. To reloading while a drone flies towards you and shoot it down at the last second. To becoming such a crack shot that you can target specific parts of the turrets and drones so they can't fire, no matter how angrily they beep and shine red lights at you. You will feel like a badass when you finally get the hang of the gun. And considering how complicated the gun is, it is a well deserved feeling.
Note that this game mechanic is very unlikely to be taken up again by another game company as this in depth level of weapon handling is impracticale for people who, at the end of the day, just want to shoot stuff. So if you were ever interested in handling a gun realistically in a videogame, this is the absolute best game you'll ever get to settle that curiosity.
Tip, pressing e twice completely drops the mag from the weapon. Some people find this weird but it's actually super useful when trying to reload as fast as you can.

Review is specifically on the MyCareer part of the game.
Cons
- Not allowed to hold multiple titles (singles/tag-team) at the same time.
- Sluggish mechanics. (not a stamina issue) Control pathing from running to picking up grounded opponents can sometimes get caught by the environment. Inability to get out of the ring while the player is near the turnbuckles etc. Problematic controling due to simplistic nature of the game's intended layout.
- Unresponsive controls. (again, not a stamina issue) Submission, chain wrestling minigame mechanics are sloppy, and slippery. Pressing a button a second too fast causes the action not to register at all. This happens during striking, grappling, and reversals.
- Match rating system is a poor attempt at prolonging matches. Game only registers one grappling, striking, and running move per match. Players will have to utilize about 3-4 signature and finishing moves to gain a five star match rating. 6-8 special moves per match counteracts the game's intentions to make the game realistic.
- MyCareer match booking system will often pit the same wrestlers against players even when no rivarly is in place.
- Rivarly system feels stale at times. Not varied enough to provide storyline tension.
- No create-a-move option
- No mycareer rematch option.
- Manager relationship system not explained.
Pros
- Decent variety of wrestling moves to choose from. This should always be improved.
Score: 4/10

All I have to say about OUTLAST is WOW!
I haven't played a scary game like this since Silent Hill back on Playstation 1.
The devs of this game obviously made it with one purpose, and that was to scare the heck out of anyone who plays it.
First off, the graphics are really good. The lighting effects are amazing. Even the small details are just mind blowing. Like the attention to detail on the rain and even the detail when the rain hits a window and you can see the water lines dripping down. On top of that, the sound effects and soundtrack is top notch giving you that feeling of true horror. If you ever seen a horror movie where you would hear the music score pick up and get tense when a character was running for their life and about to die then you should expect the same with OUTLAST. The more your life is in danger the more the soundtrack gets tense.
Also, the sound detail put into your characters' level of fear is some of the best I have ever heard. His breathing changes according to the level of fear he has. Like hearing him breathing heaving from nose and mouth to the point of dry mouth you can hear him close his mouth to swallow and continue breathing heavy again.
The controls are very smooth and responsive. Like running for you life, feeling the enemy breathing down your neck, you manage to get away and slamming a door open and turning quickly to shut it, then do a running slide under a bed to hide hoping you won't get found.
Yea, this game is scary and tense. I hope they make a second part to OUTLAST because I would definitely play it. :)

Banished, a city building game that not only makes you want to build a city and have it self-sufficient, but to push the boundaries with labourers. This game tests your managing skills and your ability to work out what you need and when you need it, to keep the city going. Banished is based in an era where technology is not around, so farming, tree cutting, tool making and other similar jobs are done by hand/humans. This make the game simple by there being no upgrades, however for your city to grow, you need to build more houses so the people of your town can reproduce growing your adults population which in turn creates labourers which you can use to set a direct task i.e. farmer or blacksmith, or simply leaving him/her as a labourer to collect stock from the areas around your town coal/iron etc. By evolving and building up your town, you need to make sure that it has sufficient food wood/coal to survive the winter. This game is based on seasons (Summer, Autumn, Winter, Spring) which is broken up into 3 sections early middle late. Surviving before during and after winter is one thing, but to survive with enough food for your town during all seasons, or being able to help the sick, or even put out fires is a constant battle. This game make take an hour or two to understand, and you may wipe out a town in a process. But this is the Banished experience. Every person play this game differently, and it is great to see how people setup their towns if you buy the game as it is only $20 and play a few hours you too will enjoy this game.
