Since I noticed many of the people who are reviewing this title have less than 10 hours played, I will write from the perspective of my hours playing it.
The good?
-The main attraction to this game is the ability to do everything like engaging the safety, racking the slide, an extra round in the chamber, and other stuff.
-While the base game only has 3 guns(m1911, glock, model 10 revolver) there is a mod on the wolfire forum that adds new guns like a shotgun, Thompson, C96, and more.
-VR. Not built-in though. On the Receiver steam forum someone just added a VR mod that works with oculus and vive. As of writing this review, the extra weapons mod doesn't work with VR just the base 3 guns.
The bad stuff?
-The main thing that this game suffers from is the lack of different rooms/environments. Even though they are generated, the game chooses from a list of different rooms and puts them together.
-Lack of guns. If your not into modding then this is a deal-breaker.
-Gets repetitive. This relates to the two points above.
-Complex controls. I noticed that many of the people who wrote negative reviews are ones that didn't like the controls. Plus, they have low hours. But if you have played for a while , they become second nature.
-When entering rooms it always freezes for a couple frames to load them up. This has gotten me killed plenty of times!
Extra thoughts:
I think that if your willing to mod it, get it on sale($1.50), and don't expect to play for hours at a time, this title will be a pretty fun game to come back to every once in a while. This is one of those games that is good to play for 10-20 minute bursts. It's easy to jump in and jump out of.

Gone Home is a beginner's lesson in implied storytelling. The "mystery" that shrouds the game at first quickly disapates but is welcomed back by a few surprises. There are no jumpscares, but the atmosphere/random background noises can be frightening at times. I had to play with music because it seemed they were trying too hard to scare me with random thudding noises in the background that just became annoying after a while. Unfortunately, the game kinda slowly gives up on implied story telling by letting the girl in subject (your sister) pretty much straight up tell you the events that unfolded. But by that point it's almost obvious what the "surprise" is. There's a lot of symbolism and irony hidden into certain aspects of the story which is refreshing to see in a video game. I did find myself getting emotional towards the end, but any further info would spoil. I don't think Gone Home is neccessarily worth 20$ (you can beat this pretty fast, depending on your goals) so I reccomend picking it up on sale if you have a few extra bucks and are just trying to quence that bad thirst that "life is strange" left in your mouth.

That said, I enjoyed it quite a lot.  The questions I had at the beginning of the game were all answered through the course of playing.  I loved all the attention to detail ... even the most mundane things like a cereal box or a magazine were fully detailed.  That helped establish the setting as a realistic 1990's house (especially things like the distinctly mid-90's electronics & appliances).  It made the oddities in the house more rewarding to find. There were also a couple funny things to discover.
In summary, it is an engaging interactive story that has you walking around in a 90's house. You eventually figure out what happened to the people living in the house. Exactly as advertised.

Ah, what to say about this game.
First off, Gone Home is not a game in the usual sense.  There's no monsters to kill, no levels to gain, no achievements, no fantasy world to conquer.

I rarely, RARELY, ever say the following:
The sequel was even better than the original.
I can't put my finger on just one thing that makes it so much better, but I really enjoyed the entire experience.  If you like dungeon crawlers on a grid, like (and I'm going back to the 80's here) Bard's Tale, Wizardry, Dragon Wars (Amiga 500), Heroes of Might & Magic Series, etc, you should try this game.
The one adjustment to get used to is combat is in real-time, so it is not turn-based like many games in this genre.  You'll need to get good at moving your party to a dead-end to prevent being attacked on multiple sides or become quick with the WASD keys to keep moving so you don't get hit much.
Going back to why I think this game is better than the original Legend of Grimrock: I like that this game had environments that took place on the surface.  You explore forests, deserts, even underwater at times.  This was a fun change from the first game where you are underground traveling floor to floor deeper into your prison/dungeon.  It also means you will frequently revisit areas and as time goes by some of the monsters will respawn giving you an opportunity to pickup some extra xp and food.  This helps make food an easier resource to obtain unlike the first game where I was stressing about running out more frequently.
Inventory management was easier for a loot hoarder like me because there is an area called the Hub which you can revisit.  There are no creatures there, just a small chamber where you can drop off the extra things you may wish to save for later.
I hope there is eventually a Legend of Grimrock 3 as I really enjoy the series and look forward to whatever else the developer may come up with to keep the series fresh and entertaining.

This company knows how to make a horror game. Though it was incredibly short (took me about 6 hours to complete), it can create amazing amounts of sheer terror and tension. The setting of a shut down mental asylum is something I've never seen in a game - something i've wanted for a long time. It touches on many "mature" themes such as human experimentation, personality disorders, sadism, torture, and the decay of the human mind, but it didn't go deep into them (I wanted to be perturbed and disturbed after I played, not only during).
The quality of the game is surprising, with relatively good looking graphics, amazing design, and a fantastic use of light. The main interactive feature, the camcorder, is nothing short of surprisingly fantastic. The night-vision is very similar to the tiny bits i've seen of Grave Encounters (utter garbage minus the nightvision shots). The game encourages you to use it even when not in dark places, because whatever is recorded gets a note in your journal.
I have always enjoyed reading chunks of lore in a game (Myst, Amnesia, Fallout) and this game does have some pretty awesome backstory-content conveyed through documents, but they aren't all that great (considering this is a screwed up asylum).
Scares range from dead bodies falling from the ceiling, disturbing "scenes" centered around patients (completely missed the body shagging in my playthrough thankfully), and utterly genius chase sequences. Movement is reminiscent of Mirror's Edge and the frantic feeling of trying to escape and elude patients is something that has always gotten to me. That being said, this needs Oculus Rift support. AI is pretty screwy at times. Sometimes the main enemy is looking straight at you but it doesn't chase or follow you, making it real easy to exploit them. One thing however that was amazing was when at point where you've completely avoided one enemy, you run into another that stands still, simply staring at you, and the cognitive dissonance created by this is absolutely amazing. One of them even follows a little ways behind you and it's something you only realize if you happen to look back. Final thing I have to mention is the presence of lockers. They are the main thing you hide in (other than darkness) and when come across one, there will always be an enemy up ahead, behind you, or hiding in a room, making a potentially unexpected encounter turn into something you immediately predict.
The sound design is phenomenal. Fantastic incidental music. Though there aren't any iconic tunes (see: Amnesia's "Panic and Paranoia") but that is the tradeoff for non-repeated incidental music. I need this soundtrack.
Some peope don't like the ending and that's understandable. Without spoiling anything, something big happens completely out of the blue with no fanfare, but there is one line that doesn't make it completely terrible (it's pretty easy to miss).
And while this has some faults, the overall experience was fantastic and Outlast is the one of the best horror games out there.

Eternal is essentially a hybrid between Magic the Gathering and Hearthstone. It takes more inspiration from Magic than Hearthstone.
What you can expect are fairly quick matches based on deck building, strategy, and obviously card draw.
This game has the fundamental flaw of being as luck-based as any card game however, so expect to get regularly screwed over by bad luck. Keep in mind though that sometimes you can get insanely good luck as well.
One of the best things about this game are the plethora of modes available to the player, both against the AI and against human players. There's plenty of content here, even for people who don't enjoy PVP.
The learning curve for this one is much higher than any other card game I've played. People who aren't veterans of online card games are probably going to get crushed a lot on ladder against real people, but fortunately there are the tons of other options against AI as well. Technically you would never have to play against a real person in order to unlock all the cards, but it would take longer.
If you know what you're doing, this game is extremely generous. I've probably done about 8 hours of research total, but this is combined with my hundreds of hours of experience in similar games. However I haven't had to spend a dime and likely never will have to in order to create competitive decks while keeping my own style. There are plenty of sites online to help new players get started.
On a final note, check out Dire Wolf Digital's other card game, Elder Scrolls Legends, which is just as amazing in its own way. If you're willing to invest the time (in either game), the payoff is incredible.

This is a painful platformer that is really simple to play. You can move left and right, but instead of jumping you reverse your own gravity. So instead of having your feet pointed toward the bottom, you push the space bar to have your feet pointed to the top and you float to the top. Its a great mechanic.
The game consists of a small open world that lets you go anywhere you'd like all to rescue your crew members. The screen doesn't scroll. When you touch a side of the screen, it brings you to the next screen like Zelda. The game mostly feels like challenge rooms, dodging spikes. Hence the name VVVVVV. There are checkpoints everywhere, so when you get spiked, you'll always go back to the last checkpoint. Later in the game it makes use of the single screen mechanic where if you exit the left, you'll appear on the right side of the same screen. It is a distraction and several 'challenges' span more than one screen. The trippy moving backgrounds don't help either.
The music is happy 8-Bit chip tunes. The simple art style is good, its just not that fun to play. There isn't just precision platforming, but diving down pits and precision platforming, shifting your character in mid air to avoid spikes.
It can all be completed in 90 minutes or less. The game has a few extra modes like time trials and flip where the world is flipped. Its all extra challenge.
If you're the type to enjoy a steep challenge where your only reward is more challenge, then this is the game for you. It has also been in a few bundles for a cheap price, so I'd recommend waiting for a bundle.

Forget Battlefield 1, this is the game that gives you a real insight to the
. Weapons are very authentic and you can tell that the developers really did their research for this game. Trench warfare at it's best.
And that really is what this game is all about:
. Your team either defends a trench, or storms one (and/or dies in No Man's Land) and that is it. It doesn't sound too appealing perhaps, but once you get into it, it is actually great gameplay. That feeling of finally getting into the enemy trench and working to clear it out is exhilarating, especially when you take them by surprise and help your entire team getting into it!
is simple and just right. You can run around and do your own thing if you want, but you'll score so much more if you stay with your squad leader. Also, playing SL is easy to get used to and will be a great advantage once you get the hang of it (you've basically got two things to keep track of: a special ability (such as mortar rounds, gas or recon planes) and a position order to place, in which all squad members will score more than double points for taking down enemies (should they choose to follow that order).
The only negative aspects are relatively small bugs such as dead people's limbs flailing about or going inside their bodies, even if the death animations including them writhing in pain is a great touch (and for the picky, the reloading animations are not always top-notch).
Also I have to mention that you shouldn't be able to jump and fire your gun with accuracy. Luckily though, people don't do it (mostly because it clearly reveals your position and begs for a mortar shell). I did it once and just felt dirty doing it. Hopefully it will be changed.
There are no drivable vehicles, but considering it's trench warfare it would be hard to implement.
Don't expect running around with machine guns playing Rambo or fast sniping. There are a several machine guns but they're made for support, and sniper rifles are made for
, as they should be! You can always switch to the rifles main sight though (and rifles is the main type of weapon you'll use apart from pistols).
It might be hard to tell the difference between friend and foe in the field, but luckily there is no friendly fire (otherwise every new player would be crushed by accidentally killing teammates over and over).
This one is important:
. If you've played Red Orchestra / Rising Storm, you'll be familiar to the type of gameplay. You'll struggle to stay alive, but that's World War One for you. In the real war people did not willingly jump into No Man's Land without worries, and that for a damn good reason. If you want fast-paced action and rushing, you've got Battlefield 1. This game focuses on realism, which becomes it's charm. Often when I play, I can't help but think how it must have been a hundred years ago, fighting in the trenches...
The best game about the Great War and the trench warfare. Even if you don't have any real interest in history, chances are that you will have after playing this (especially since the loading screens contain information about the battles).
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who cares for realism and some wonderful weapon sounds.

I've had to put this game aside for a while because I started playing it the other day and put in over 8 hours without even realizing it. I'd really like to put some more time into it, but overall accomplishments come slowly in this game.
Cook, Serve, Delicious! is a restaurant sim, but the focus of the game is on the individual preparation of dishes, all of which are delivered in deceptively simple minigames which you have to complete in rapid fire succession over the course of each day of running the restaurant.
It's a great concept that they can get a lot of mileage out of. There's a surprising amount of depth in this game, especially since I picked it up for just 5 dollars.
There's a high number of dishes you can buy to serve in the restaurant, as well as uprgrades to all those dishes. There's a number of upgrades you can buy for your restaurant as well. There's random events that can occur during the day, and if you want your restaurant to be successful you have to manage your menu in such a way as to maximize appeal, taking various factors into account. These factors include your own abilities at the game as well.
Perhaps there's going to be a safety inspection that day, and you don't want to miss out on any chores, so you stack the menu with dishes you know you can prepare quickly and easily, so you have more opportunity to focus on things the safety inspector will pay attention to.
In addition, there's multiple modes available in the game, catering requires you to prepare a smaller number of dishes, but in faster succession and with less room for error. There's also a battle kitchen minigame, and other content that I have yet to experience because I'm only a 2 star restaurant right now.
There's competitive and co-op multiplayer as well. Including a mode that can be played with two people on the same mouse and keyboard, which is nice to see.
Like I said, a surprising amount of depth.
I understand a sequel is coming out soon, and I'm already excited for it.
There are however, some things that frustrate me about this game.
First I feel like the progression is a little slow, but that's understandable, as it encourages you to hone your skills on certain dishes before moving on. It also means that this is a game you can get a lot of mileage out of.
Also, I feel like some of the upgrades on food items are unneccesary and break the flow of the game. Lasagna, for example,  was already a difficult dish because it's slow to prepare and cook. The minigame associated with it required you to press 4 buttons in a specific sequence three times. It got easier after you memorized the sequence and I eventually got better at it. With the upgrades though, lasagna orders have more ingredients, and become randomized, completely  changing the nature of the minigame associated with it, and making it much more difficult.
I think there should be more options to customize the look and feel of my restaurant, and perhaps a chance to specialize in certain types of food rather than having a menu that changes every two days (I don't know of any restaurants that do this). I mean, I really enjoyed preparing the seafood items in the game and I would enjoy having an in-game restaurant that specialized in this, and showcased it through decor or something similar, but there are no options to do so.

Receiver is an odd mix of brilliant idea and incomplete design. Essentially, it's more of a proof of concept than a finished game.
Reloading, managing bullets, switching switches and all the various bits of micromanagement that we take for granted when playing most FPS games all add up to making for a fun experience that give an awesome feeling of knowing you've done the whole process yourself. It's thoroughly satisfying when you first figure out how to unload, drop mag, reload new mag and unlock the slider all in a second. That's the game's main selling point and it does it well. What you might not expect is that this is a very tense, almost horror game that gives off a creepy, lonely atmosphere. I've not felt like that since playing Amnesia.
All this creates a great game but there are major problems that mean I simply cannot recommend it (but only just). Firstly, it's buggy, unoptimized, void of any real detail, has dull scenery, there's no choice which gun you start with, there are only two enemies and it often feels very unfair when you spend ages looking for cassettes without finding a single one or start with only 3 bullets and finding no more around. As I said, it's a great proof of concept but it's not a finished game. For that reason, I can't recommend it. If you happen to have it free then give it a go and feel like a champ in a cardboard world.

TL;DR: Easily my least favorite of the 5 souls games. DLC almost saves it, multiplayer is good but everything else isn't. I only enjoyed this game Co-oping with friends.
(Played through 3 times: One hexer build, one dexterity build, one strength build)
Dark Souls 2 is a game that has no one fatal flaw, but has so many small issues that they weigh on the experience and kind of ruin it for me. It's strange considering that taken as a face value, this game is almost identical to Dark Souls 1. It's a semi-linear RPG with stamina management risk/reward based gameplay with large sprawling levels featuring lots of small side paths to explore that include items capable of building many different playstyles along the way.
But it's in the fine details where Dark Souls 2 fails. Gone is the beautiful, consistent art style of the first game to be replaced with dull, empty rooms and an awful lighting engine. Gone is the grim, oppressive atmosphere to be replaced with one that feels closer to the high fantasy of Oblivion. The soundtack, while mainly subjective, I enjoyed far less than the first games in both composition and implimentation. The voice acting and writing have both taken a severe dip in quality too, with every character feeling lifeless aside from maybe Maughlin.
Even the core gameplay has changed for the worse. The overall speed of the combat has been slowed down in favor of a more combo heavy style with frankly ridiculous hitstun on most attacks on both the player and enemy side, which wouldn't be a bad thing on its own, but this game's level design and the way they changed how enemy agression works means that you're often fighting multiple enemies at once, and Dark Souls' combat system clearly works better for one on one fights.
Which makes it abundantly clear that the B team at From Software had a clear goal in mind: Base the entirety of Dark Souls 2 on the multiplayer element (Mainly PVP). The netcode is much better this time around, and other small multiplayer improvements have been introduced such as being able to roll cancel gesture, white soapstones avaliable sooner that have a timer on phantoms, more AOE spells, etc.
Unfortunately, PVP isn't what me or most people are here for, and the single player experience is painfully mediocre, especially considering how excellent Demon's Souls and Dark Souls were. And it's not just in the set dressing elements like sound design or atmosphere, there's a very noticeable lack in level design creativity and quality compared to the first game. It all feels very odd to have blandly designed levels that mostly play the same be stretched out for the ~55 hours it took me for my first playthrough, counting DLC. Which, I might add, is a longer game than Dark Souls 1 or Demons Souls by a pretty large margin. At least for my first playthroughs.
Much of this could be forgiven, however, if Dark Souls 2 had an interesting story to work with. And it doesn't. The flavor text on all the items seems to be much lazier written this time around, and the lore just isn't as interesting as the first game, and often contradicts it. The NPC questlines are much more obtuce and unrewarding compared to Demon's Souls or Dark Souls, and again, the writing and voice acting are both worse.
Now let me take one moment to discuss something pretty important to the Souls games, difficulty. Remember how good Dark Souls 1 implimented high difficulty by making the level conditions the same no matter how many times you attempted it in order to force you to be skilled enough to beat the level with the circumstances given? It was brilliant, and one of the best parts of the game's core design philosiphy. Dark Souls 2 however goes the Demon's Souls route of having buyable healing items, but this time around, there's no item weight so you can carry basically as much as you could ever possibly need. This makes it feel like it's focusing on making the individual enemy encounters more difficult but the overal levels easier, but there's a catch. Because of the previously mentioned hitstun issue, and because most enemies seemingly have infinite poise, the fight outcome is really only determined who hits first with many builds. Whenever more than one enemy is involved, it ends up being circling the enemies looking for an opening, taking it, and running far away to heal if you get hit. Repeat as necessary, and you have the entire Dark Souls 2 experience.
However, this isn't to say that Dark Souls 2 is necessarily easier than Demon's Souls or Dark Souls. Being in hitstun from some of the harder hitting enemies can result in an easy death, and many of the bosses focus on having multiple enemies in the arena, none of which are fun to fight. Another thing that Dark Souls 2 does bafflingly awful is the difficulty curve. The entire game ranges from being incredibly punishing to being flat out easy depending on your build and the situation. Take for example the Iron Keep area, which in its first area, has well over a dozen enemies that are required to fight to get to an optional boss which ends up unlocking an optional bonfire to finish the rest of the level easier. This wouldn't be that bad, but the boss happens to be one of the hardest bosses in the game, and half of the run up to the boss itself is platforms over instant death pits that you can be easily knocked into by the areas 5 enemies with greatbows. And to add insult to injury, the boss following this optional one is one of the easiest in the game.
Something also needs to be said about the world consistency in this game, as it's totally immersion ruining. Remember how Dark Souls 1 had the entire world fit together perfectly with levels visible from other levels? That's gone, and it makes each level feel like it's taking place inside a totally different universe. For example, there's a poison swamp area in Dark Souls 2 where you work your way up to the top of a windmill on the top of a hill. When you beat the boss inside, you take an elevator upwards to a ♥♥♥♥ING LAVA LAKE. Legit burst out laughing, it almost seemed like a joke on the developers part.
The DLC is a significant step up in quality in every way, mostly in level design and lore. The story finally starts to be interesting in the DLC, and the levels finally take advantage of using a central bonfire with shortcuts leading back to it, unlike the linear collection of bonfires throughout the rest of the base game.
Taken as it's own experience, Dark Souls 2 is merely a high concept but low execution, ultimately mediocre game. When compared to Dark Souls and Demon's Souls, it feels like a bad Chinese bootleg that had the base game figured out but has none of the subtleties. Your time is better spent with literally any other souls game.

This "game" is, for starters, pretty much a rip-off of
, so what little novelty and interest as a curiosity it might have had, will be pretty much null and void if you own, or even seen, that.
What sets this one apart from the original, besides the difference in setting - making tea in a kitchen instead of performing surgery in an ambulance - is the execution. Where
is hard to control, this one adds another obstacle - bugs. I have, for example, literally turned my hand into an endlessly spinning propeller by trying to turn it. While this may at first sound mildly amusing, it unfortunately isn't, since the graphics craps out as well.
Oh, yes - the graphics. Not only does it look really poor, even if you crank the settings to max, but it lags and stutters so much most of the time, that it would have been unplayable, had there been any play to be had. And mind you, I'm running it on a Core i7 4820K running at 4.6GHz, with 16GB RAM and an AMD R9-290 GPU. I'd hate to try it out on a less powerful system.
So my only advice is to stay away. There is little fun to be had here, even if you missed
.

Story:
This game has a predictable, boring, long, and just outright bad story.  The concept has been used to death. On top of that, all the missions are boring, hard, repetitive, and long. There is a significant lack of character development on every character you encounter in the story. Even the main one. All of the missions are either 'Chase X', 'Run X off the road', 'Escape the Cops!', and mostly 'Win this race!'. In each race you can't get third place, or second place. You have to win each one in first place in order to pass the mission.
Gameplay:
(Note: I use a Keyboard.) The gameplay is buggy, and aggregating. If you have driven a boat in GTA5, then you've driven a car in The Crew. It feels like plain luck if you spin out on a corner, barely turn, or make it. Breaking is laughably bad. As in, you have to hold down both the brake, and handbrake to come to a complete stop. Changing from 6th gear to reverse using a manual transmission, you should just restart the mission. You must cycle down to reverse. This will cause the loss of at least one race. The camera is legitimately one of the worst cameras in any game I've played. It locks you onto a certain position, and if your car is moving and you try to move the camera to see the front end, each time you get a bit out of that locked on position, it will snap back to it. Meaning in order to look at the front of your car, you must come to a complete stop.
Environment:
The game is gorgeous. The cars are stunning, and the environment is fantastic. It may be one of the best looking games of 2015. (Yes, it came out in December of 2014, but I'm counting it as a title from 2015.) Sadly, this is really the only pro I can find in this game. It's nice to just drive around and enjoy how nice the game looks.
Economy:
Getting IGC (In-game currency) in The Crew is a boring, and repetitive grind. Unless of course you cave, and just buy it. Yes, this game is loaded with micro transactions. On top of costing $60, having an optional yearly subscription ($25 I think), and some cars that can only be bought with IRL currency, you can also buy ICG. It seems like Ubisoft is trying to become EA.
Playerbase:
I haven't really encountered with the MMO aspect of this game. I played through most of the missions single player, thus it feels like a singleplayer game to me. The small amount I have experienced has been people running my down in free roam, and crashing me off the road for about 30 minutes.
In conclusion, this game is nice if you just want a pretty game to drive around in. But if you want a serious racer with realistic controls, it is not for you.

Given that I enjoy flight simulators a lot, I figured giving the airport management side of the story a try. This was a very bad idea. If you still for some reason are considering buying this game, spoilers are ahead.
The game consists of the following features:
1. Wating for planes to arrive at your airport, which occurs somewhere on the order of once every 15-20 minutes. No, you cannot speed up time until the next flight arrives. No, there is nothing even remotely entertaining to do while you wait.
2. Driving various airport vehicles from their respective parking spots to the airplane and back. Cargo trucks, maintenance vehicles, cleaning services, and even your own personal truck! Honestly, the game makes it seem like it's going to be incredibly difficult to fulfill all the airport roles by yourself but it takes only a few minutes to move around vehicles that then take ten minutes to complete their respective jobs. On top of that, you can't even do anything fun with the vehicles because most of them are incredibly slow at max speed.
3. Waiting for planes to mysteriously decide to leave the gate after an arbitrarily decided amount of time that you have no notification of whatsoever. After you finish "servicing" the plane, it waits in the gate for some time before randomly departing.
This game is easily the most disappointing title in my entire library. Please do not buy this game.

Alright if you already play Terra Mystica, yes, this is way better than what we have currently for online gaming.  The interface is solid, although things are a little clumped and you need to do some clicking and open some menus.  But since it's terra mystica, that's like a given.
As a big time terra mystica lover, I am trilled to find this game.
If you DON"T know what Terra mystica is, it's one of the most heavy borad games out there.  It is praised for it's depth and complexity, a boardgame that incorporate a lot of boardgames mechanics such as worker placement, resource management, terrtorial dispute, timing, etc.  It's a really well done board game.
Problem: if you don't enjoy heavy and in depth board games, don't bother with this.  Please leave.  This♥♥♥♥♥♥ain't Settlers of Catan, although it may look like it at first glance.  My friends complained to me that this is worse than doing taxes when I tried to teach them this.  One of them rather do his CS homework than play it.
Explanation: Terra mystica isn't so much as complicated than it is dense.  There is a lot of mechanic and stuff that you have to know about.  None of them is difficult to understand, it's jsut that there is a lot.  The real issue is that every turn your action seems compleatly arbitrary.  You will start off not knowing what you are suppose to do.  There seems to be so many ways to get points, so many ways to make reasources, etc etc.  But that's the whole strategy of it.  The entire game is based aroudn coming up with a plan during the set up, and know how you can maximize your points while growing your economy.  Knowing where to compete and where to spend reasource in order to disrupt opponent.  It is a really well made game in the sense the strategies are truely fun to solve.  Again, this is meant for people who love games because they enjoy learning as part of the process and solving the startegies.
Lastly, you know what is really amazing.  This game has zero luck factor.  Okay well maybe 5%.  It is all in the set up.  You see what the tiles for points and passing bonuses are, and the rest is all up to playe decisions.  No dice, no RNG, no bulls*it, ALL SKILL.

The big challenge in Eternal is the very poor system governing resource draw. Resource cards are included and then drawn from your deck (like Magic, Hex, etc.), and there seems to be something wrong with Eternal's deck randomization system. It is common to encounter resource glut, sometimes drawing nothing but resource cards during a single match. While a hand redraw guarantees two resource cards, resource drought is also common. While I understand the wish of the design team to stay true to their Magic roots, the competitive, digital CCG space demands design systems that optimize the player experience. And while Hearthstone's steady resource gain system seems to take some of the life out of the CCG experience, it balances the competitive experience in a critical way. Imagine, for example, if Eternal had a steady resource gain mechanic with a 'random' color draw that could determine the type of the resource drawn. This random draw could still be based on a number of resources included during deck building while helping mitigate the game-breaking randomness of resource draw.
While the resource issue is enough to keep me from spending a ton of money on Eternal, I have enjoyed the rest of the game. If you're looking for a game with a strong MtG feel but with a mostly modern design approach to the digital CCG genre, I think Eternal is a good choice.

Verdun is probably the most realistic depiction of WW1 in a video game ever, multiplied by the fact that it's in first person which allows for a more immersive experience. Squad variation is good although it really doesn't matter as long as there aren't four sniper squads on one team. Gameplay is pretty clunky and the graphics aren't anything special but it gets the job done. While most games have an active autobalance script in place to allow for a more balanced experience, this game uses a passive method that politely asks the overpopped team if some could join the other team while lengthening respawn times for the offending team. This can be a double-edged sword because sometimes people won't listen and you'll be stuck with an unbalanced team.
Unfortunately this game is mostly dead at this point ~500 players on average isn't a whole lot when you account for the huge split between regions and the smaller splits between game modes. Speaking of which, there's really only one active game mode and the rest rarely have enough players to warrant a prolonged session. It was a whole different story when this game first came out and was alive and well.
Overall, if you have or find a dedicated group of friends to play with, I'd give it a shot on sale but don't buy this at full price and expect an active game. Most similar realistic military shooters are more active players than this one so take that as you will.

Whelp, what started as a hopeful replacement for the terrible current meta in hearthstone, i have put enough hours into this game's ranked play to conclude it's even more poorly balanced than yugioh, and even very low ranks are infiltrated with decks and players far in excess of what their "rank" belies. I'm strongly familiar with MTG as i have decades of experience playing it and am no slouch with strategy, timing, counterplay, bluffing, etc.
While i credit this game for having the kind of depth that hearthstone lacks, it is a shame that the game is otherwise wrecked by awful balancing and match making. There are some absurdly powerful decks and combinations, and wouldn't you know it, 5/6 players you meet are playing cookie cutter top meta builds. This is identical in nature to hearthstone where players with 52+% win rate decks intentionally concede their way to lower ranks for the purposes of easier grinding of in game currency and quest completions off potentially lesser skilled players YET should they be interested in players of comporable decks and skill they need not procede up the ranks, as everyone is right there with them at the bottom.
This game continues to suffer from the usual issues you can expect from a MTG knock-off (mana-flood/drought) happening way more often than one would think possible, and utterly avoidable considering the digital formating, the games quickly devolve into whom can be first to inact their imbalanced strategy or who is last to fail to achieve the power resources they need. This game's design philosophy seems mired in a swamp of developer ideas of "what would happen if we made late game strategies possible by turn 2?' Genius.
Also, Pay2win in the extreme. Not recommended for casuals and non-whales.

I got this on sale for two bucks. Definitely worth that price, and probably worth $5. It deserves a Superhot treatment, though. It's a must-have for people who like interesting shooter concepts (for example, those like me who played the Superhot alpha in 2011).
Pros:
- Great use of atmosphere, the enemies are legitimately imposing
- The core mechanic, where you have to manage inventory and your gun, is compelling
- Disabling enemies isn't just a matter of shooting them enough, you need to aim for the right place (like the camera on a sentry turret)
Cons:
- The point is to listen to 11 casettes, but your progress resets every time you die. There should be some way to progress after a run - when you get to like 5 and then die it's discouraging.
- It could use a bit more variety in terms of enemies and weapons. I'll expand on this at the bottom.
- It really needs some form of progress between levels.
- Death from bullets is slightly delayed so sometimes you can't tell if you got hit for a few seconds
In terms of variety, there are three weapons in the game, which are randomly given at the beginning. The revolver is weak and slow, the 1911 is good, and the Glock is very good. You can't to my knowledge find new weapons in-game. I feel it would be interesting to find, say, a shotgun or a rifle when you advance pretty far, not to mention having to manage 2 weapons and their ammo would increase the core mechanic's longevity. Also, there are two enemy types in the game: stationary turrets and melee drones. It feels like there should be one more, perhaps a humanoid ranged enemy, to increase interest later in a run.

Overall, I really enjoyed it, and if you go in expecting more of a player controlled narrative than an actual story based game, you will too.

You have a map, that you can annotate more clearly and write on easily. You have a spell list to automatically remember your spells with. There are a variety of skills that create a pretty diverse set of viable teams which don't require gimmicky cheesing to function well. There's inside and outside, so you get a change of scenery much more often. And so far the puzzles are less obscure guessing and finding small buttons, more careful thought.
All this is quite good, except for the one randomly almost unkillable monster that shows up without any warning in a large number of the areas of the game and requires a specific item/spell (which you don't get until an indeterminate mid-game point) to kill. This monster is probably the worst design decision in any otherwise good game I've played in years, and is actually a serious detriment to my enjoyment, especially since I had to go look up how to kill it or basically stop playing. I still recommend the game but I'm really rather disappointed.

I initially got this game for free from some kind of promotion, but I came back to Steam and paid €5 for it because A) I think it deserves it and B) I wanted to write a review. My only criticism of the game is that I don't think I would pay €20 for it, so if you're currently eyeing the fact that it's on sale, I'd suggest you go for it. (Personally, by the way, I'd say I would pay up to €10 for it.)
I've been reading some of the reviews on here, and I want to clarify a couple aspects of the game that made people leave it a negative review. No, it is not a horror game. Yes, it is a simple point-and-click game. No, it is not an especially surprising or innovative storyline.
But yes, it is a great game.
Do not buy this game if you are looking for something that puts emphasis on gameplay. I think you have to imagine that you are buying a book that allows you to engage with its world slightly more than you normally would. It is 100% story- and atmosphere-oriented. Buy this game if you want to spend an hour or so delving into a beautifully-crafted storyline. If you're looking for anything else, do not buy this game.
Anyway, as for my actual review -- it's great. I'm going to echo Polygon's review by saying that I never expected to find a character in a game that I related to so strongly, and I think THAT is what makes Gone Home such a pleasant surprise. I predicted all the story beats before they came, but I could not in any way predict the intense sense of validation that certain moments in the story would bring me. This is a beautiful, incredibly necessary game, and I fully recommend that you buy it with the full knowledge of what it is, and nothing more.

The Legend of Grimrock 2 is a throwback to the time of Ultima: Underworld, but with better graphics and deliciously enjoyable puzzles and secrets.
The 40+ hours I spent on this game were enjoyable, nostalgic, and satisfying in equal parts. The puzzles are not designed to be extremely difficult, PROVIDED you find the proper clues for them. Backtracking is a necessity in this game, which focuses in a more messhed approach where the entire map offers secrets in the early, middle, and late game.  In fact, there are TWO endings, which I found very interesting.
Though the game allows for a playthrough with any character class, I observed that a mage/wizard/spellcaster of some kind makes the game a lot more playable and, more importantly ---> you MUST have someone with the ability to cast spells (or at least invested 1 point into Concentration, the main spell casting requirement and have a low requirement wand) if you want to find the 2nd ending.
That I didn't enjoy, the fact that if I had chosen all non-casters that I wouldn't have been able to get to the 2nd end.
Also, the last 3 boss fights are monumentally more survivable with long range attacks.
These are not reasons to avoid the title. It is such a rewarding experience for the genre. If you love puzzles, secrets, and old school dungeon crawling remniscent of table-top maps, this is the game for you.
Buy it. Play it. It is a darn satisfying game.

United Independent Entertainment GmbH must be one of the most dishonest software companies in existence. This "Airport Simulator" is all about driving airport vehicles, and nothing else. The description of the game is completely misleading (see later). It should have been called "Airport Dogsbody" instead. Passengers need to get off a plane? Drive the stairs to the side of the aircraft. Luggage needs to be unloaded? Drive the luggage trolley to the side of the plane. Passengers need to get to the terminal building? Drive a bus to the side of the plane. Plane needs to be cleaned? Drive the cleaning truck to the side of the plane. The description on the Steam store page says "Many management and business options for the expansion of terminals and extension of runways". That's a lie. You can't expand the terminal buildings or runways, and there are no business decisions to take. The description also says "Countless missions and tasks that the player has to fulfill in order to guarantee a successful airport". That's a lie too. There's only ONE job at this airport, and it's driving vehicles backwards and forwards to and from the aircraft all day long. Admittedly there is a "profit" figure which goes up with each driving job you complete, and this money can then be used to automate the driving tasks. But that simply leaves you with nothing to do but twiddle your thumbs waiting for something to happen at the airport. There's no "accelerate time" button to speed things up. And there are bugs galore too. I was given a task to push-taxi an airliner to the runway, ready for departure. But no matter where I stopped the plane, the task would never end. I was left with arriving aircraft queueing up on the taxiway, trying to get into terminal gates which were blocked by aircraft that I couldn't taxi! It was a nightmare. Steam should remove this game from the Steam store, and UIE GmbH should be prosecuted for obtaining money by deception. My only solace is that I bought this game in a Humble Bundle sale for a small price, so at least I didn't waste much cash, and some of my money went to charity. Don't make the same mistake I did.

The Crew is a multiplayer always-online arcade-racer set in a huge open world which is a condensed version of the United States. It was designed by many of the same people who created Test Drive Unlimited, so it can effectively be thought of as TDU 3. It contains many of the same features, but not all (no houses or shops).
I think many people are unfairly critical of this game, and are failing to appreciate the best feature, the huge open world. In reality, the world area is only around 5000 sq km (about a quarter of the size of Wales), yet that's still a huge size for a game world, possibly the second largest open world racing game (Fuel is over twice as big). Road wise, there's 10,000 km of roads, 10 times as much as in the first TDU game, so that will take a long time to explore properly. But it's not just the size of the world that's impressive, it's the attention to detail and the huge number of landmarks. It's extremely well designed.
The USA is not only condensed, but distorted, some areas are much larger than others. This is necessary since if everything was to scale, every city would be a tiny village. Instead, the biggest cities are made much larger, as well as features like the Grand Canyon, while less interesting areas are shrunk in size. The result is greatly distorted, but it feels really good to drive around, and I believe it does a good job of representing the "highlights" of the USA in a way which suits a computer game very well.
Many people have complained about the horrible car physics. I was a bit shocked at this too in the beginning, but it turns out that the early cars handle badly by design, and get much better as you upgrade them with parts. The few cars I've tried from the DLCs handle much better. It also takes a little while to tweak your wheel or controller settings to get it to feel good, but it's worth the effort.
Apparently rubber banding is also a problem in the game, although I did read someone say it's been fixed. I've noticed it a few times with police chases, but it doesn't seem to be much of a problem to me. Speaking of police chases, I find them to be a lot of fun, while others seem to hate them. Similarly, the raid challenges can be quite frustrating, but are also fun to me. Depends on your point of view I suppose.
The GPS tends to provide the shortest route between two points, which is often not the best way to get to where you want quickly (taking you through backstreets instead of sticking to main roads), but hey, SatNav does that in real life too! Just think of it as a guide that you don't have to stick to. Learning the main roads and using your "local knowledge" instead can save time! Also it tends to suggest offroad shortcuts, which can be annoying if you want to stick to roads, but on the other hand, it gives you a route through difficult scenery which you might otherwise get stuck in.
One annoying thing I have noticed is graphical glitches during the cut scene intros to most missions. Don't know what's causing this, but it's only a minor irritation, it doesn't happen when I'm driving.
Another slight peeve is that much of the terrain is too destructible, you can drive straight through lamp posts and other features as if they weren't even there, yet some are rock solid. It's sometimes hard to know which is which. Okay, so it's just an arcade game so you could say it's excusable, but it does lead to bad driving habits, driving through obstacles that you'd normally avoid. In fact, to win certain missions it's often a good idea to crash through things.
Same goes for crashing into other cars, often (not always) this has little or no effect, barely slowing you down in most instances. Again, I don't like this because it encourages bad driving habits, not caring about hitting other cars when normally you should try to avoid them at all costs. But again, it's an arcade game, so I can live with it.
Sure, there are a few faults with this game, but most of them hardly matter to me. The game world is so large, with so many places to go, so many things to see (there's educational info on historical landmarks) and so many cars to drive (not a huge selection, but there are many variants of each, and who needs hundreds of cars anyway?) that I'm having too much fun cruising and exploring to take much notice of the faults. I think if people focused less on the faults and concentrated more on the fun aspects of the game, they'd enjoy it a lot more.
For me the FreeDrive mode is the real game, going on road trips solo or with friends. I dont' really care about the missions and the story that much (although they do add a nice bit of character to the game), I just want to explore America!
Having said that, the game gets more interesting the deeper you get into it. As you level up you unlock factions and faction missions, and that adds a lot more fun to the game, not to mention money! Some say that money is hard to come by and there's a lot of grinding, but they're wrong, money is easy to make. It's not a "pay to win" game, you can pay if you're lazy, but you can make it easily enough by simply playing the game.
I'm really enjoying The Crew and I highly recommend it to positive gamers who enjoy exploring a huge open world, who don't mind the arcadey gameplay and can live with a few faults. Be sure to get the Gold Edition or buy the Season Pass to get a bunch of good cars that unlock fairly early in the game, to give you a decent variety of cars to go free roaming in, otherwise you'll be stuck with the early cars for a while.
Negative focused nit-pickers need not apply!

I confess - the visual appearance of this game put me off for a very long time. In fact, I think I bought this almost two years ago and have never played it.
Sometimes though, you get to a point where everything else you've been playing either frustrates or bores you and you look for something which is so vastly different, that you might just install that game that looked kinda bad to you.
I don't think I've been
wrong about something in a very long time... Yes, the graphics are extremely basic (but by no means bad - they convey exactly what they need to, basically minimalist perfection) - I mean pre-Mario level platformer graphics with minimal colours and basically no visual effects except an almost fit-inducing colour-switching sprite here and there (actually on that note, this game probably
safe for epilepsy sufferers).
But the most important thing, the thing that I was
wrong about, is how much fun this game is. In fact, I'd say this is
I've had playing a game in more than a year (possibly even longer). VVVVVV reminds you what gaming can be, even if you strip all of the fancy, big-budget AAA treatments out of it. The storyline is quite basic too, but the gameplay... wow, the gameplay... Starting with the interesting idea to leave the ability to jump out of a platformer, then the even more interesting decision to give you the ability to reverse gravity for your character. (although I guess it does make sense within the context of something that happens on a spaceship/in outer space. Sort of...) It's pretty original though.
The characters are completely lovable (my heart just broke each time their little smiley faces turned upside down). The overall message you get from the game is also overwhelmingly positive, from the first "Everything will be okay" to each confirmation thereafter that you're on the right track, you're helping your friends, etc. Furthermore, the music in the game (of which more can be unlocked by finding hidden "trinkets") is absolutely fantastic. Next to how much fun the game actually is to play, I'd say the music is its strongest point.
In the first 5 minutes of playing, I wasn't quite sold yet, but I had nothing better to do, so I played for another 5 minutes. And then it hooked me. After about 45 minutes, I thought that the puzzles/levels were clever, but nowhere near impossible to figure out. So I played on. And found out that the puzzles got
difficult later on (but still not impossible).
I finished the main game in just under four hours, but there's more game modes unlocked now and further exploration that can be done. To reiterate, VVVVVV was the most fun I've had gaming in a very long time. In short, this game made me happy - it gave me pure, childlike bliss. I don't think there's a lot of games that can make that claim.
And if you're still wondering what on Earth the strange title (VVVVVV) refers to, you'll just have to play it to see... ;)

I purchased Verdun several months ago, hoping for a realistic-feeling game.  One where your opponents weren't "bullet sponges".  Verdun does not dissappoint.  It has some aspects that I find a bit annoying which I will discuss in a moment, but overall, I find the game very enjoyable.  So much so, that I play it almost daily.
The GOOD:  Very realistic as games go. One shot equals one kill.  THIS I LOVE.  You are rewarded for good, accurate shooting.  Spraying bullets will not help you.  The weapons feel right.  Pistols fire as quickly as you can hit your mouse button, whereas rifles require rechambering of reach bullet with your rifel bolt.  Grenades feel right as well.  The various maps are each very different, from trenches to fields to fortresses. The graphics are quite good.  Gas attacks are another addition to the game that changes things up a bit...fail to get your mask on in time and you DIE!
THE BAD:  Nothing really game killing, just personal preferences here.  When engaged in a battle, you are suddenly ordered to retreat to a designated area..identified as green on your mini map.  Too many times, I have advanced far from my lines only to have to rush back to my lines in a timed limit, only to "commit suicide" by not making it back in time, or getting shot in the back as I rush to the authorized fighting area.  I really HATE that.  A major pet peeve for me is the barbed wire.  If you are unfortunate enough to run into some you just didn't see, you get a warning that your are entangled in the wire.  You attempt to break free, usually by jumping or retreating.  MOST times, after two or three attempts you die from blood loss.  Must be pretty sharp wire that causes artery severing.   Finally, I feel that respawning times can run a bit long.  Though many times respawns are in 10 secs or less, most times it is more like 18 to 24 secs..  This can be quite frustrating, especially if you die just before the enemy is attacking, or you are ordered to attack.  Nevertheless, I find Verdun to be VERY ENJOYABLE!  It is a game where you find yourself trying to better your last kill total for each match.  I RECOMMEND ANYONE WHO ENJOYS FPS WAR BATTLES TO CHECK THIS ONE OUT!

Really great game, although not perfect on many points.
PROS :
_Amazing job on weapons / uniforms / languages / landscapes, it feels extremely realistic and historically accurate.
_A whole lot of rifles, pistols, grenades, melee weapons, and each faction has got its own weaponry.
_Many different nations playable with their own abilities
_Fun gameplay (ironsight aiming, NCO's abilities, squad-based games, intuitive trench-warfare gameplay)
_Squad leveling system encourages us to play with friends
_Maps are both beautiful and huge, and the level design is great. Also a great variety from map to map.
_Some intense trench chaos where you stab people with baionettes in the middle of a confusing mustard gas attack, really fun and definitely boosts your adrenaline !
CONS :
_We could definitely use more maps
_Really frustrating at times, when you get indefinitely chain-killed and you can't do anything about it
_When you play with a lvl 1 squad and there's a lvl 100 squad in front of you, you feel like it's pretty unbalanced (artillery strikes, I mean come on)
_Artillery strikes are really fast to reload, but gas-attacks take for ever and don't really do much
_It can be frustrating for new players to be confronted to experienced ones who seem to never miss a shot, so you end up dying 30 times in a row and you end up being fed up with this game
_It's not the game's fault, but the community is really small, there are hardly more than 100 players playing at the same time
Overall 7/10, sometimes it's great fun, sometimes it couldn't be more frustrating, but you can definitely feel the atmosphere of World War 1

An exhilarating journey through a war-torn Philadelphia, Homefront: The Revolution not only lives up to its IP's potential - it downright sets a new milestone for open world games for years to come.
You play as Ethan Brady, a Resistance Agent whose goal is to liberate Philadelphia from the yoke of the KPA - the Korean People's Army, which in an alternate timeline occupies the United States, Your tasks are at first a tad mundane - as with all sandbox games - but after leaving the first area (which amounts to a war ravaged industrial district) only then do you get a taste of the finest the game has to offer: it plays very much like a modern day, first-person Assassin's Creed, as you have to liberate the downtrodden neighbourhood which makes up the second area using stealth and guile, instead of fighting it out as in the previous one. You achieve this by completing radiant assignments such as helping out civilians and tacking out APCs and by taking over strongholds and checkpoints being held by the enemy. As in Assassin's Creed, hit and run tactics are essential in order not to be overwhelmed by the enemy's sheer numbers. Trash containers, public restrooms and a myriad of other hiding spots are there for you to hide in and evade the KPA's ominous leer as they pursue you through the various streets and alleys that make up the city.
Of course, ideally you will not have to resort to such means if you do your utmost in remaining hidden in the first place - evading security cameras, flying face-scanning drones, soldiers, APCs, etc. Since all of these know how you look like - courtesy of your actions in the first area - you need to blend among the civilians, climb out of sight, or delve deep into houses and apartments to escape their line of sight. There are three civilian areas such as the above-mentioned (called Yellow Zones) to explore in-game, and four war-torn areas (called Red Zones), so there are plenty of areas in which to experience both all-out war and sneaky tactics alike.
For a game that places such emphasis on stealth, the combat is simply FANTASTIC. You can customise every single weapon you own (a la Crysis), making your pistol an SMG or your Crossbow a flamethrower on the fly. This makes the restriction of only carrying two guns and a sidearm completely bearable, while retaining some sense of logic to the quandary in which multiple-gun bearing characters put us. The shootouts have this "ooomph" that makes them so enthralling, as you plough through hordes of KPA soldiers with only a yearning for more. Some have deemed this game repetitive, and that it may be, though it excels in delivering every single bit of its experience, much like Far Cry 3 did - and much like Far Cry 4 did NOT.
Even the crafting system - which I hated in games such as Dying Light, due to the ridiculous amount of ingredients available - works perfectly well here, having just a handful of ingredients with which to craft makeup pipe bombs, molotovs and the like. You can also craft hacking darts, which allow you to hack doors open and make drones fight for you. You can also laying traps to blow up unsuspecting soldiers, which is (needless to say) especially fun.
Performance-wise, the game is top notch. I am running it on a GTX 660, Phenom II x6 1100t Black Edition with 8gb RAM DDR2, and it pretty much never runs below 30 FPS on high settings, 1920x1080, AA and Vsync enabled. CryEngine, with its solid performance and beautiful graphics, delivers . as it always has.
My only qualm would be the story, which is downright cheesy and boring. It does see a bit of a revamp in the DLC, being far more fleshed out - even if at the expense of the sandbox nature of the base game - in the character and story department. The arc ends in a neat note that lays the foundation for what will likely be a future Homefront installment. Even the base game's lacklustre story makes no difference in so beautiful a game, which excels in every other department. It may very well be the one of the best sandbox games I have ever played, and without doubt 2016's finest.
9/10. Would free Philadelphia again.

First of all, yeah. This is a parody of Five Nights at Freddy's. A parody, not a rip-off. If you think someone was trying to pull a fast one here, you're a moron. You haven't noticed something that's escaped the notice of everyone else. You've noticed the most obvious thing in the entire collected history of obvious things.
As parodies go... it's one of those parodies that's better than the original product. You know, the kind of parody that ALMOST NEVER HAPPENS. And I really like the games it's based on, don't get me wrong. The production values here are well in advance of even the last Freddy's game, as its developers can boast decades of combined experience in making awesome games. It's got indie soul plus triple-A quality.
This game was made by the Two Guys from Andromeda, who made Sierra's famous sci-fi parody adventure game series Space Quest. It's in the same vein. In fact, it's been released to get a bit more funding for their new project, SpaceVenture, a spiritual successor. So buy this cheap-as-heck game, enjoy it, and know you're making an even better product possible. I grew up playing Space Quest, and I can't think of a better way to pay these guys back for the hours of fun and frustration they provided than helping them provide even more.
Be assured, this is a full game in its own right. It's a bit longer than the games it parodies, in fact.
This game has terrific visuals, excellent gameplay, and a great mixture of goofy and nerve-wracking moments.
Seriously, play this game. FIve Nights at Freddy's is awesome. This is awesome plus decades of talent and a lot of Kickstarter money, and it'll pay for even more awesome later on. PLAY THIS GAME.

Receiver is hard to rate, because it's an example of very abstract, unordered storytelling. I personally enjoyed it and enjoy doing run throughs of it occasionally, but I wouldn't recommend this to someone who either doesn't appreciate realistic gun mechanics or OHD (one-hit-death) games.
Receiver is a game that was programmed from scratch in a mere 7 days for an FPS challenge, and it shows. Level geometry has nearly zero detail, levels are simple, and there's essentially no post-processing. However, the game works surprisingly well; everything is (weirdly) easy to tell apart, including enemies, and weapons make satisfying firing, chambering, and reloading sounds. The game's emphasis on survival and conserving bullet by bullet makes every miss on enemies all the more punishing, and by the end of a playthrough you'll wind up being a crack shot.
The story isn't much to explain because it's unordered, on audio tapes, and abstract. It's a neat concept and it meshes well with the abstract nature the game exemplifies.
The drawback to Receiver, which is less so a flaw and more a mechanic, are OHDs. Getting hit by any enemy in any form will instantly kill your character, and there's no kind of saving or checkpoints; you either gun it and get all 13 tapes, or you die. This isn't a big deal on its own, but falling a certain distance will also instantly kill your character, and unfortunately there are tons of chances for this to happen on accident.
This isn't really a flaw since lots of games do this (like rogue-style games) but because of its fickle nature and difficulty, those looking for a stroll in the park won't find it.
Ultimately, Receiver is a cool project that any shooter fan would
enjoy experiencing. It's only real drawback, its simplicity, is also its greatest strength, and as a result I can't really recommend paying full price for it unless you seriously need to play it or you want to help the dev.
Otherwise, goodluck beating the Mindkill. You'll need it.

Anyway, this is still Counter-Strike and it will be a good buy if you are a huge CS player.

In some ways it is a sequel better than the first Dark Souls game, in others it is worse. I think the situation is similliar to the KOTOR games, where both games had some features that were better in one instalment.
DS2:SotFS definetly is a better conversion to a pc even though it's still pretty bad... playing with controller is in most cases way better.
DS2 Does has improved fighting system with more acurate hitbox system (ds3 has even more better)  and just a nicer feeling to the fight, both PvP and PvE (personal opinion). This is obviously big part of the game, but the improvment is not hugh mungus, both games have a great fighting feeling to it.
DS1 has a better story. There are a lot of interesting storylines in DS2 specially in expansions, but in overall DS1 has a story with more thick atmosphere, story that is more interesting, compeling. Again it's not a huge diffrence, and possibly a matter of preference.
DS1 has better bosses. More hard ones and with interesting lore, while DS2 has some forgettable and too easy boss fights, with uninteresting lore behind it.
DS2 has better looking locations, but DS1 has better world design (even though it lacks fast travel, but some see this as an advantage). Some places in DS2 just look beutiful, specially put together with music, both Majula and Firelink Shrine have great feeling of safety and peace, while Anor Londo for example hits you with its beauty, but also emptiness, presenting you this magnificent place in full glory, but also in decay cause of the lack of inhabitants. DS2 has great locations like Heides Tower of Flame, beatiful and full of nice, lore details and hints, Dragon Aerie and Shrine are also great.
Graphics are obviously on the side of DS2 cause its newer game.
Anyway I don't really like reviewing the game by comparing it to its previous installment, but they both work so great in pair, cause of how lore beetwen them works (a very mysterious way, that requires to you give it your own interpretation).
What i value most in Souls games is three things:
1 Smart game design (locations, fights, game progress)
2 Interesting, involving, thought-provoking lore
3 Compeling gameplay that sucks you in with its system
Both games have it, both have moments where some of those things are lacking (Lost Izalith locations in DS1 for example, Grave of Saints in DS2) except the lore I think, even the gameplay has it flaws with fights and their system (lazy boss design of infamous tree fight in DS1 and recycle bossess in DS2). But when in their prime, both games are just the absolute best you can possibly get.

I really tried to like Dark Souls 2, since I loved the first Dark Souls.
Yesterday I finally gave it a shot, even though I've always had a bad feeling about this game...
Unfortunatly the bad feeling I had was right and I had no fun during the nearly 4h I've played.
The ambience was still Dark Souls like, but visually I find Dark Souls 1 still more appealing... I don't know how they didn't manage to improve, but it was still good.
I guess one good thing to note is that I didn't experience any frame drops, which I half expected since I was playing on high graphical settings.
There was no interesting story and all NPC's you meet are quite shallow and boring...
I also didn't experience any bossfights, while in Dark Souls 1 I'd have at least beaten 2 if not 3 within these 4h...
These are the things that just made Dark Souls amazing and I see no point in waiting for any of that to come if it's just annoying to play the game.
It has really broken controls... at least with my 360 controller, that I've been using for countless other games, including DS1, without getting any of these problems...
The input delay is already a bother, but sometimes they don't work at all.
I've had moments where my character just stopped raising his shield even if the button was held and sometimes I pressed the trigger to attack and had no response from my character until it was too late... so when I wanted to roll out of the way, he finally attacked and well... got slaughtered... by the way, I did have full stamina in there moments.
Aside the controls, the hitboxes are also quite annoying as in you have to visibly hit the enemy to deal damage and the same doesn't apply to you.
I experienced moments where I was clearly away from any threat and I was still hit?
The environmental hitboxes are also quite annoying, since any obstacle that is in your way can be a deathtrap and somehow a little bit of rubble can count as a complete obstacle for no realistic reason...
At last I come to the camera, which I couldn't seem to fix, but I always had a tunnelvision and sometimes the camera moved automatically upwards in some places so I could only see my character and less than a meter ahead... (this seemingly didn't have anything to do with the controler)
In conclusion I had too much trouble playing this game and that's why I don't recommend it, but it's not really a bad game.
It has it's flaws that were unbearable to me personally, but there are people who clearly love this game somehow.
I'm going to start Dark Souls 3 soon, since I had a good feeling about it... let's hope I'm right again this time...

Good attention to detail, lots of depth, and adding the commentary helps more than hurts. Watching it over, it's funny how the whole story happens right before the main character leaves. I was at first afraid there was going to be lots of jump scare or horror or chase scenes (like the red herring about the note about the lights going out), but as the story progressed I became more afraid that there would be one because then it would be cheesy. Fortunately, the director's knew it, and even admitted to the one jump scare being stupid. I like how the designers worked like they know what they games are like from a player's view, and thus tried to incorporate that into their own game. There is the easter egg (and the 4th wall-bending admonishment about leaving the lights on), the set design influenced by limitations on coding, how sometimes the prompt isn't to pick things up but of the character's thoughts about that item.
Turns out the horror is of less supernatural, as is first implied, or even less psychotic murderers, but of the more mundane and yet no less horrifying implications of child abuse and love-rending discrimination. I am happy that the ending didn't put a body in the end, as the last note had seemed to imply, by either the main story character either killing herself or killing both her and her lover. The beret in the garage really set me off.
I praise the director's for designing the game in a way that the exploration is fully possible because nothing is really locked, but also linear by the scattering of the clues, even though technically it is more or less an open world.
Story wise, I found the story to be oddly compelling and...touching. Part of it is the whole coming-of-age story. Part of it is seeing Sam find a fellow soulmate. Part of me is ...why did I write part of me? Anyways, part of it is the whole awkwardness of Sam's exploration with Lonnie, with the classic elements of finding someone with a compatibility, the halo around a person, the first meetings, the excitement, the moment when there's a moment, then the first advances of vulnerability, the fear, Sam's awkward foray, the reassurance, the turn, the buildup, the confrontation, and the climax. I've always thought of DADT as a detached observer, seeing it as a good compromise for the time. But this story made it personal, and like I   said, oddly compelling. I was rooting for the two near the end, something I'm not sure I would do for a real-life couple. Does this make any sense? Maybe I see some of myself in Sam. Or maybe the story was well written and had emotional impact, with voice delivery being well.
Beyond the game itself, I am especially pleased that such a narrative can cause such differing reactions. The interpretation of people being happy for Sam that it all worked out, especially in the world of 1995 (vastly different political climate compared to 2008+), is as valid as her being a selfish, impulsive teenager, that noticed nothing of her family's festering problems and stole VCRs to be with her lover. The requests for more background on the family to be elaborated is fun, in that it inadvertently shows people wanted more from the story because they had an interest in that kind of thing. And the fact is that there are no other physical characters besides the player character, who is almost an empty shell.
All in all, an excellent game/story that I would've gladly paid $10 for. It's an interesting story that could easily be made into a compelling movie or OVA.

This is a frustratingly uneven game. It starts off painstakingly slow: An aircraft comes in and you, apparently being the only person at the airport with a driver’s license, have to drive various vehicles to and from the plane: a passenger bus, a rolling staircase, a fuel truck, two types of cleaning trucks, a luggage trolley, etc.  It’s very tedious, but eventually multiple planes start arriving and you have to juggle various tasks among them. The plane at gate 5 is fueling now, the plane at gate 6 wants fuel next. A plane that just landed is waiting for a parking spot and you’re trying to push back a plane at gate 3 to make room for it. At this point the game isn’t exactly *fun*, but it’s at least involving. Get those tasks done to get the planes off the ground!
But then you earn money and hire help and once you hire enough employees to handle every vehicle at every gate the game becomes nothing more than a slightly interactive screen saver: A plane lands, you assign it a gate and everything is taken care of. You just sit there and wait for it to take off again.
There is one maddening exception: The pallet loader for cargo aircraft. You can’t hire anyone to drive this. It’s all you, and it's buggy and annoying. For starters, only one cargo plane can be serviced at a time. If you have 3 cargo planes parked at gates you'll only get loading/unloading instructions for one of them. You can entirely finish loading up the first plane but you won't be able to start loading and unloading the second plane until the first plane is on its way to the runway. It can sometimes take 10-20 minutes between the plane being loaded up and actually pushing back, during which time your pallet loader gathers dust and other cargo planes take up gate space waiting to unload. Additionally if you make the mistake of parking a cargo plane at gate 6, 7 or 8 you need to make ridiculous round trips back and forth across the tarmac between unloading a pallet on the south end, going to a parking spot on the north end, and returning to the cargo area on the south end again to pick the next pallet up (for gates 1-5 the parking spot is thankfully right next door to the cargo area so moving the pallet loader from the cargo area to the parking spot takes about 5 seconds).
There are other frustrations too:
+ Wonky physics that allow you to flip a plane nearly upside down with a nudge from a luggage cart
+ Tasks that appear and disappear from your task list
+ A non-intuitive interface
+ An inability to move vehicles to a gate prior to a plane being assigned to it
+ Awkward vehicle/gate rules. An aircraft can't push back until all of the vehicles servicing it have returned to their parking spots. It's not enough to simply clear the gate area. This makes multitasking difficult. For instance, say you're fueling a plane at gate 1 and when finished drive the fuel truck to gate 2 to service that aircraft. Even though the fuel truck is no longer at gate 1, that aircraft won't push back until the fuel truck has actually parked in the fuel truck area.
For that small percentage of people who *really* like airports, there are bits and pieces of this game that are slightly interesting, but the bugs & game logic & freakin’ pallet loader make it nearly impossible to recommend.

Airport Simulator 2014 is a mixed bag as far as simulators go. I'll give you the negative points first; The video settings, no matter what aspect ratio and/or resolution I set the game to I could not for the life of me get it to show me the full game screen in fullscreen mode. Instead, I was forced to play in windowed mode, which was irritating. The game crashed a total of 3 times in the span on 4 hours. The fixed view from the control tower has blind spots due to where it is located, and if you preselect units which are almost completed with their tasks, you run the risk of the game bugging out and being made to sit and wait a long, long time before the next objective becomes available. I should also mention there is no tutorial, you are thrown in head first to figure it out as you go.
Sounds like a lot of negative right? It is, but this game for some weird reason was also very addictive. Once I got over the initial shock of not having a tutorial, I got into a nice rhythm and within about 4 or 5 hours I had upgraded all 8 gates at least once and was working on the second level upgrades. My airport was essentially running itself by that point. I had a lot of fun with it and while it does have it's negative drawbacks, it can still be a lot of fun to play. I would recommend this game to someone, only after they have reviewed each of the negative points I made and went into this game cognizant of what to expect.
