I've always been a fan of grand strategy games, especially covering World War II, and especially covering the Western Front. I've dumped hundreds of hours into Europa Universalis, Crusader Kings, Hearts of Iron, Victoria, and so on.
There is no other game that goes so far into detail as Gary Grigsby's War in the West. If you want to get into the operational minutaie of logistics, support units, assignment of individual aircraft to airfields, and even the freaking names of the individual pilots that are attached to your fighter wings then WitW is something you need to get into. Ultimately though, it's still a war game. In spite of the detailed minutaie you've still got to organize your ground units into the right hexes and attack the weak points in your opposing army's line.
It's definitely a little overwhelming at times and even after playing War in the East awhile ago there's still a learning curve. Ultimately, however, it's definitely something you want to pick up if you're looking for the most grognard of grognard wargames.
I would also recommend picking up War in the East if you can spare the $80.

This is my first ever review of a game in Steam. That must be an indication that i really like the game. I am going to tell you why:
In Verdun you're thrown into the trench warfare of WW I. In my opinion the game does a great job in creating a tight atmosphere and tension.
Your goal is to defend your trench or attack the enemies trench. For defending you are not allowed to move out of your trench, so you're just sitting there and waiting for the opponent to come. For attacking you have to cross the dangerous Niemandsland.
Quite phases where you just wait for the inevitable attack mix with fast paced close combat in the trenches.
You are dying quickly, which makes a tactical and cautious approach neccesary. I really like the way the game unfolds on most maps, i hate some other maps.
Other issues i have is the imbalance you have when one team is not filled up while the other is. Even the penalty for it does not kill the advantage.
The technical side may not be the best, but therefore you don't have to have a high-end machine to play it.
So if you're into WW I and a more realistic approach than BF 1, than this might be worth a try!

Eternal Card Game initially comes across as being quite a solid redo of Magic the Gathering. It has some very interesting mechanics that build upon previous concepts from other card games, and has made some effort to reduce the common issue of variance. Eternal uses a number of mechanics seen in MtG and hearthstone (such as trample, flying, death-touch etc), as well as a very similar mana system and turn structure. Eternal moves on from there though with a slightly different take on hearthstones weapon system, and some interesting mechanics that make good use of the digital format.
Unfortunately I cannot recommend this game, and instead recommend 'Magic Duels' instead. There are some flaws that hinder Eternals current potential, and 'Magic Duels' is simply a more balanced and newcomer-friendly environment. To explain, I will list the pros and cons below.
Pros:
- Eternal makes good use of being a digital card game. There are a number of mechanics and unique card abilities (namely 'echo' and 'crown of possibilities') that are fun, reasonably powerful, and also very difficult to replicate in a paper format.
- Eternal is somewhat balanced. Some cards are great, some are not, and no cards (from what I have seen at any rate) are game-breakingly poweful. Ranked (Standard) definitely has tiered deck lists (ie, some decks are better than others), but budget or janky decks can still participate with an expectation to pull off a few wins
- Eternal is free to play, paying simply speeds up the process. All formats can be played with the in-game currency (gold), and all of the cards can be obtained through earning and using gold. Gold is also not too difficult to obtain, as you can complete quests, battle players, or battle AI to earn gold. Participating in drafts or sealed formats also awards gold and cards/packs, and doing well in draft will either cover the entire cost (winning 6 games and losing 3) or will earn more gold than what you paid (7 wins, 2 or fewer losses)
- Eternal is reasonably solid with very few bugs or systematic issues. It doesn't play well with certain GFX settings or GFX cards, but the only real issue I encountered was that certain parts of the UI might black out (while still being usable).
Cons:
- Biggest first: variance. A lot of people will say "variance is in all card games, it's part of the game", and I will agree with them. However, when playing Eternal in any of its formats, there are far too many "non-games" - games where you have drawn too many sigils (lands), or too few, or are missing a colour entirely; games where you have drawn poorly and/or the opponent has drawn perfectly; games that are not really games, because either you, or your opponent, did not really participate.
Eternal is very much a 'value' game rather than a 'combo' game, 2-for-1'ing your opponent is always what you play to, and often what you lose to. While out-valuing your opponent can be fun, often a single 'out-value' moment can snowball into victory. Why? Deck size requirements are too high (45 for sealed, 75 for draft), you can only mulligan once, and games are a 'best of 1', which means that consistency is regularly quite low. With this, even the best decks can easily lose repeatedly to lower tier decks, even if the match-up is favourable.
Also, this issue of variance practically doubles in draft. The limited format is decent, and the card design makes it clear that MtG professionals have assisted with creating the set. However, the drafting stage takes place with AI bots (draft with bots, play against live players), and the AI often make strange choices that lead into odd drafting signals. Packs also have extremely poor variance, often only containing one card of a particular colour. Due to this, it's quite often that you will be passed a pack where there are literally no good picks for your colour(s) (even at pick 2), and even pack-1-pick-1 can be extremely poor. These issues exacerbate the previously mentioned variance issues, often leading to a bad draft experience.
In all, there are an alarmingly high number of "non-game"s, and be rare to experience actual games. Non-games are less likely in ranked, but even then the rate seems (purely based on experience, not at all researched) to be approximately 50-50.
- Eternal is not newcomer friendly. There is a tutorial, and you do get to play a relatively easy and straightforward campaign. 'Forge' (sealed) is also relatively easy, and can be a good way for new players to spend gold and learn pick order basics. However, there are a few mechanics that are not explained well, and a number of interactions that are not particularly intuitive. Good examples of this are 'Aegis' and 'Exhaust', as neither are explained fully by the in-game rules description. Thankfully this issue isn't too uncommon, but (without some prior research) you will likely lose a few games (some of which you may have paid for, like draft) due to not fully understanding a particular mechanic.
- Certain cards and mechanics are unbalanced. Anything that provides card advantage, and any mechanic that provides an easy and/or immediate 2-for-1 (eg. warcry and echo) are notably more powerful than other effects. While this would be fine normally (as you do need certain cards/effects to be pushed), the issue of consistency and variance makes this a bit more unbalanced.
I did say earlier that Eternal is "somewhat balanced" as a 'pro', and overall the game is good in that regard. The colours all do fine in limited, and nothing is game-breakingly powerful. However, you will experience more 'non-game's the moment you don't run some form of deck-thinning/card advantage/inherent 2-for-1s, as variance will simply punish you more often.
To conclude, variance is painful, and "non-game"s are the worst. The game is fun in a lot of ways, but sadly the sheer number of "non-game"s detract a little too much from the overall experience.
The game is still in development, and it still holds a lot of potential, and hopefully the developers will work toward some better solutions for the current issues. For now though, I suggest finding another game.

Escape From The Planet of The Poultroid, developed by Guys From Andromeda, is, to put it lightly, a Five Night’s at Freddy’s clone. Only this time, you’re not the night watchmen at a children’s pizzeria, but a Space Ranger by the name of Cluck Yegger. Crash landed on the industrial planet of his arch nemesis, Colonel Zanderz, Cluck must remain on the planet for seven days before his ship’s engines can reach full capacity. Each night, however, he must survive the constant threat of Zanderz’s mutated chicken monsters.
As mentioned before, Escape From The Planet of The Poultroid is an FNAF clone. You’ll have a variety of security cameras to monitor, doors to open and close and lights to flicker on and off, all the while maintaining battery power… sound familiar? So, gameplay is pretty much identical between both titles.
However, Escape From The Planet of The Poultroid is clearly aimed towards a younger audience. The scenery and monsters aren’t nearly as sinister as other horror titles and the game has a humorous tinge to it. Thing is… it’s not very funny. The voice actor behind Cluck is trying WAY too hard to be Patrick Warburton, who some of you may know as Joe from Family Guy, and his audio logs between nights may crack a smile outta your kid, if anything.
The game’s managed to get me with a few jump scares, and I’ll give it credit for that, but there’s such a lack of dread to it. There’s no nail-biting tension or crazy build up, they just seem to happen without rhyme or reason.
Gameplay is solid for the most part, but one thing is seriously hindering the experience: Almost every ten seconds or so, your monitors will be bombarded by static. This happens so often and so frequently, that I don’t have time to spot the monster before the screen goes white. It’s stupidly annoying. Apart from a minor mechanic where you can stun the monsters with high-powered lights, there’s nothing new to see here.
As of this review’s posting, I’m only on night five, but I still plan on beating the game. Seeing as how they’re only asking for 3 bucks, feel free to give it a shot if you're a fan of FNAF or games like it. But don’t expect anything too special from Escape From The Planet of The Poultroid.

War in the West provides the most complete portrayal of the Western Front during WWII of any game on the market. If you're not prepared to devote hundreds of hours delving into its intricacies then look for another game.
The air war is a complete game on its own. You can play it with large amounts of AI assistance and automation and just devote yourself to types of missions and targets. You can also go into much greater detail such as where a squadron is based, what type of aircraft they have, how many aircraft, how they are armed, what's their bombload, will they have drop tanks, what type of missions they will fly, their targets, what days of the week they will fly, what altitude they will fly at, what weather conditions they will fly in, what priority they have for supplies, what is the minimum aircraft needed for a sortie, what level of training the pilots need to fly, and who their commanders are at their higher headquarters. There are other factors you can adjust that I haven't mentioned.
And then there is the ground war which has its own intricacies. Unfortunately, the naval war is highly abstracted; however, the commanders' stats currently in the game indicate that the developers have the capability, if not the intent, to introduce a more complex naval version.

Eternal would be such a great game if it wasn't for the constant issues with resources and draws in general, I often find myself holding duplicated cards in hand regardless of how many I use in the deck and no matter what deck I'm playing, no matter how many utility cards, fillers, or whatever it takes to try and create a balanced list.
After trying several decks, some of my own, others made by better deckbuilders than myself, I get the feeling that nothing really ever works at it should, or not as often as it's supposed to anyway. The matches become repetitive and boring, way too often the game comes down to you getting power flooded/starved, or the opponent, or both. If by any chance none of that happens, it's a very fun experience otherwise.
But right now it's frustrating more than anything, I just really wish Eternal will get in a better state and make me change my mind.
Edit: 3 months after first reviewing the game, I came back to see if anything changed/improved in light of the new mulligan rules, but despite that the game feels exactly the same as before.
I'm no math genius, but whatever mechanism is responsible of shuffling the deck is clearly not working properly.
Playing a deck of 75 cards composed by 1/3 units, 1/3 spells/attachments, 1/3 sigils, it doesn't make any sense to draw 8 sigils in a row or none at all, or only units, or only spells, or all copies of the same card turn after turn, game after game. It's not even fun to win while watching the opponent in that situation.
I understand that being a card game there's a chance of that happening, and it would be fine if the game wasn't so "consistent at being inconsistent".
I don't care much about winning or climbing ladder, it's just that it feels unreal, there's no way an actual deck of cards would be shuffled that badly and that often.

For all of these reasons, I 100% recommend this to you.

An improvement over first LoG which was a solid game as well.

While puzzle freaks may find it appealing i certainly didnt because they rarely deliver great items.Only on two such occasions i found strikingly better gear and both of them were 2-handed weapons.
-Classes are ok but could be more intresting.
-Characters can now recieve permanent wounds(debuffs) when they take damage that can only be healed by potions and healing crystals.While it was good to see a new mechanic at start, it grew to be an annoyance as i invested more hours into game.Given that fights in LoG 2 became more brutal we certainly didnt need them to be punishing forcing us to either struggle through inventories to brew some more potions or backtrack to nearest crystal of life.

In some ways it is a sequel better than the first Dark Souls game, in others it is worse. I think the situation is similliar to the KOTOR games, where both games had some features that were better in one instalment.
DS2:SotFS definetly is a better conversion to a pc even though it's still pretty bad... playing with controller is in most cases way better.
DS2 Does has improved fighting system with more acurate hitbox system (ds3 has even more better)  and just a nicer feeling to the fight, both PvP and PvE (personal opinion). This is obviously big part of the game, but the improvment is not hugh mungus, both games have a great fighting feeling to it.
DS1 has a better story. There are a lot of interesting storylines in DS2 specially in expansions, but in overall DS1 has a story with more thick atmosphere, story that is more interesting, compeling. Again it's not a huge diffrence, and possibly a matter of preference.
DS1 has better bosses. More hard ones and with interesting lore, while DS2 has some forgettable and too easy boss fights, with uninteresting lore behind it.
DS2 has better looking locations, but DS1 has better world design (even though it lacks fast travel, but some see this as an advantage). Some places in DS2 just look beutiful, specially put together with music, both Majula and Firelink Shrine have great feeling of safety and peace, while Anor Londo for example hits you with its beauty, but also emptiness, presenting you this magnificent place in full glory, but also in decay cause of the lack of inhabitants. DS2 has great locations like Heides Tower of Flame, beatiful and full of nice, lore details and hints, Dragon Aerie and Shrine are also great.
Graphics are obviously on the side of DS2 cause its newer game.
Anyway I don't really like reviewing the game by comparing it to its previous installment, but they both work so great in pair, cause of how lore beetwen them works (a very mysterious way, that requires to you give it your own interpretation).
What i value most in Souls games is three things:
1 Smart game design (locations, fights, game progress)
2 Interesting, involving, thought-provoking lore
3 Compeling gameplay that sucks you in with its system
Both games have it, both have moments where some of those things are lacking (Lost Izalith locations in DS1 for example, Grave of Saints in DS2) except the lore I think, even the gameplay has it flaws with fights and their system (lazy boss design of infamous tree fight in DS1 and recycle bossess in DS2). But when in their prime, both games are just the absolute best you can possibly get.

I really tried to like Dark Souls 2, since I loved the first Dark Souls.
Yesterday I finally gave it a shot, even though I've always had a bad feeling about this game...
Unfortunatly the bad feeling I had was right and I had no fun during the nearly 4h I've played.
The ambience was still Dark Souls like, but visually I find Dark Souls 1 still more appealing... I don't know how they didn't manage to improve, but it was still good.
I guess one good thing to note is that I didn't experience any frame drops, which I half expected since I was playing on high graphical settings.
There was no interesting story and all NPC's you meet are quite shallow and boring...
I also didn't experience any bossfights, while in Dark Souls 1 I'd have at least beaten 2 if not 3 within these 4h...
These are the things that just made Dark Souls amazing and I see no point in waiting for any of that to come if it's just annoying to play the game.
It has really broken controls... at least with my 360 controller, that I've been using for countless other games, including DS1, without getting any of these problems...
The input delay is already a bother, but sometimes they don't work at all.
I've had moments where my character just stopped raising his shield even if the button was held and sometimes I pressed the trigger to attack and had no response from my character until it was too late... so when I wanted to roll out of the way, he finally attacked and well... got slaughtered... by the way, I did have full stamina in there moments.
Aside the controls, the hitboxes are also quite annoying as in you have to visibly hit the enemy to deal damage and the same doesn't apply to you.
I experienced moments where I was clearly away from any threat and I was still hit?
The environmental hitboxes are also quite annoying, since any obstacle that is in your way can be a deathtrap and somehow a little bit of rubble can count as a complete obstacle for no realistic reason...
At last I come to the camera, which I couldn't seem to fix, but I always had a tunnelvision and sometimes the camera moved automatically upwards in some places so I could only see my character and less than a meter ahead... (this seemingly didn't have anything to do with the controler)
In conclusion I had too much trouble playing this game and that's why I don't recommend it, but it's not really a bad game.
It has it's flaws that were unbearable to me personally, but there are people who clearly love this game somehow.
I'm going to start Dark Souls 3 soon, since I had a good feeling about it... let's hope I'm right again this time...

In no way do you control the layout of the airport or budget - it's not a "tycoon" game.   It's someone's 3D model of an airport with planes that land and take off, and all you really do is watch them do it. Some people may enjoy this... but most people probably expected a lot more.
The second reason this "game" should be avoided - technical reasons.  There's no 1080p or higher support (for a 2014 game!).   The game will run at 1050p... but it's just 720p upscaled to 1050!  Jaggies everywhere!  Console players may enjoy this kind of treatment but PC gamers don't.  Textures are low res, but you can't change the graphics fidelity much anyway, the options are too basic.
I picked this up in a bundle in one of my crazed bundle buying sprees, so have only myself to blame.

Even more than most games, whether or not I'd recommend
depends upon your taste and preferences.
Mostly that's because of the kind of game this is.
reminds me of some of the adventure games of my youth.  (Yes, I'm old.)  You're dropped into a situation that is quite unexpected for your character and left to explore your environment (the titular home) while slowly uncovering the story of what happened to lead to the current situation.
There are no enemies or combat.  The puzzles you encounter, if they can even be called puzzles, revolve entirely around gaining access to more areas of the house.  They're "solved" through simple exploration and really serve as a device to keep the story discovery in order rather than as any kind of challenge.  And that story, as you'll quickly realize, is mainly a coming of age story.  Whether any or all of that is good, bad, or indifferent is completely in the eye of the beholder.
Which leads to the other part of why I would or wouldn't recommend
.  In the interest of avoiding spoilers I'll simply say that the main story involves a topic that has been one of the primary fronts for the past decade or two in the ongoing culture war in the US.  If you strongly identify as either progressive or conservative on social issues you may be either elated or disgusted, respectively, by that aspect of the story.  On the other hand, if you're somewhere between those two extremes your enjoyment of the game probably won't hinge on the matter.
Personally I enjoyed
.  The environment is just a little bit creepy, which befits the situation perfectly and helped highlight the inflection points in the story where I genuinely feared what I was going to find next.  And I don't mean feared in the horror movie sense.  I mean the story drew me in enough that I was concerned about the fate of the characters.  To call the game a "walking simulator" sells it short.  While there may be exploration involved in taking a walk, there usually isn't much of a story to be revealed, at least in my experience.  I suppose your milage may vary if you commonly take walks in your friends' or family's homes when you arrive and unexpectely find them gone, with a cryptic note addressed to you tacked on the front door.
If you choose to play
I would recommend doing so at a time when you have several hours available, so you can play through in a single session.  I would also recommend taking your time and exploring the house throughly rather than trying to rush through.  Much of
is in the details and I imagine it would be something of a thin experience if you bypass most of that in favor of pushing to reach the story's conclusion as swiftly as possible.  Case in point, in reading through some of the discussion threads here on Steam after playing the game through, I saw reference to some things I didn't find even though I thought I had explored completely.  So I'm looking forward to playing through again at some point with an eye toward figuring out where I missed those bits.
Finally, to address a point that is commonly mentioned in reviews, I have to agree that the regular price feels a bit steep for the amount of content
offers and its fairly limited replayability, especially this long after release.  But it goes on sale fairly often and is a decent to very good value at the common sale prices.
So, can you enjoy a game that's about exploration and story, without any guns, explosions, platforming, crafting, or zombies involved?  If you are socially/religously conservative, can you still enjoy a story even though it casts a generally positive light on a topic with which you may personally disagree?  Then yes, I do indeed recommend
.

This game let's you take command of the combine air and land powers of the western allies or/and the axis powers in the western European theater of operations from the invasion of Sicily in 1943 to the summer of 1945. This game is turn-based and each turn represents a week in the historical timeline.
You will constantly face the same historical  dilemmas as the commanders of the time, both on a tactical and a strategic level.
As the allies; how can you speed up the collapse of the axis military and reach berlin before the soviets? You can for example limit your commitment in the Mediterranean and launch D-day earlier. You can focus your bomber campaign on the bottle necks in axis production and infrastructure much more effectively with historical hindsight. Or perhaps a pure tactical deployment of the air forces will be a better idea? What ever your strategy you will have superior numbers and be much more well equipped but have the time against you.
As the axis you need to household with every resources at your hand. What can you afford to lose? Letting yourself be bait into a battle of attrition on the periphery is almost suicidal. Heavy commitment in Italy will almost certainly hurt you more than your opponent. Just as bad is perhaps to defend every factory you have with the Luftwaffe. Each trained pilot you lose will hurt. And sooner or later you will have to send novice pilots against the allied veterans.
Perhaps the most strategic part is handling the eastern front box. You don't control the actual fighting but as the axis you decide which forces you send to the slaughter in Russia and what forces you keep in the west for defence. When the fighting calms down during the mud season you can shift forces from the east to try to throw back an allied invasion. But when the soviets attack again you must send every formation  you can spare east.
If you want a grand strategy game focused on force management and fighting but with minimal resource gathering, this is together with Gary Grigsby's War in the East probably the best game on steam! The ai is great, and the historical feel is superb.
However I know this game isn't for everyone. Just the time to learn all aspects of this massive game will take longer time than to play through most other games. If you are new to the genre I recommend you to begin with Gary Grigsby's War in the East instead. That game has much more simplified logistics and air war which is the hardest things to learn.
This game is extremely time consuming but if you are interested in history you will be rewarded for time spent with an amazing experience. I recommend this to all historical strategy gamers on steam!

Eternal would be such a great game if it wasn't for the constant issues with resources and draws in general, I often find myself holding duplicated cards in hand regardless of how many I use in the deck and no matter what deck I'm playing, no matter how many utility cards, fillers, or whatever it takes to try and create a balanced list.
After trying several decks, some of my own, others made by better deckbuilders than myself, I get the feeling that nothing really ever works at it should, or not as often as it's supposed to anyway. The matches become repetitive and boring, way too often the game comes down to you getting power flooded/starved, or the opponent, or both. If by any chance none of that happens, it's a very fun experience otherwise.
But right now it's frustrating more than anything, I just really wish Eternal will get in a better state and make me change my mind.
Edit: 3 months after first reviewing the game, I came back to see if anything changed/improved in light of the new mulligan rules, but despite that the game feels exactly the same as before.
I'm no math genius, but whatever mechanism is responsible of shuffling the deck is clearly not working properly.
Playing a deck of 75 cards composed by 1/3 units, 1/3 spells/attachments, 1/3 sigils, it doesn't make any sense to draw 8 sigils in a row or none at all, or only units, or only spells, or all copies of the same card turn after turn, game after game. It's not even fun to win while watching the opponent in that situation.
I understand that being a card game there's a chance of that happening, and it would be fine if the game wasn't so "consistent at being inconsistent".
I don't care much about winning or climbing ladder, it's just that it feels unreal, there's no way an actual deck of cards would be shuffled that badly and that often.

A hardcore World War 2 strategy game where you take on the role of high command of either the Axis or the Allied on the Western front.
During gameplay the turns are broken up in phases. Among other, there are the air and ground phase. In the air phase you have command over all of the Air HQ's. You can let the AI take control over this and it will formulate directives for each of the wings and it does quite a good job of it. Yet you can also take direct control and plan out every combat sortie of every squadron. The options at your disposal are quite intricate as you can not only set its priority targets, but also at what altitude the missions will be flown at and even change the loadouts of all the planes. Awesome...
The groud phase follows the air phase and this one is a bit more straightforward. You have all of your combat units, its HQ's and loads of other support units at you command. It is up to you to break through, defend, take victory points and generally overcome the enemy towards victory. With this it is important to break the enemy units, but it is equally important to disrupt its supply lines and ability to repair and replenish its units. Bombing and capturing industrial hubs for instance is a quite crucial element in any long range planning.
Scenarios range from '43 to '45, including a grand campaign style scenario in which the whole theater is opened up. Even with its scope this game is incredibly detailed. It keeps tabs on just about all of the materials and its production (like tanks, planes, trucks, etc) and manpower. The game simulates weather, levels of interdiction, damaged railway lines and industry and so much more. It is just mind-boggling to think of it.
All in all a must have for any serious wargamer.

GG's War in the West is a 10/10 complexity wargame covering the main allied operations in the west from 43-45. These include an invasion of southern france, DDay, Market Garden, Bulge, etc. While the mechanics are similar to War in the East, WitW has completely revamped the air system, for the better in my opinion.
By trading off learning the complex air doctrine rules, you save yourself time dictating every single air operation like you do in WitE. The air campaign is unbelieveably well modled and fascinating to play on its own. If you have experience with WitE, it's still reccommended by me to check out tutorials on how to work out air combat.
Some people may argue this is a boring campaign but I disagree, logistically it was ambitious as all hell and unprecedented in human history in terms of amphbious invasions. Logistics takes a lead role in WiTW (as it should have in WitE) where players have more control over their depots and how they stock/send out supply.
Overall, this is worth 80$ if you can afford it, automatic buy on sale.  It's about the price of a newer board wargame but enforces all the rules for you and keeps track of otherwise miniscule details. While the game can still be enjoyed without learning all of the complexities and nuances to the system, you are depriving yourself of gaining any insight as to the operational difficulties of the campaign.

This is an indie FPS where you shoot at robots.  you only have limited ammo, so you have to make your shots count. One hit from anything kills you. The goal is to find all the tapes scattered around the game before you die.  Graphics are simple.
This game does some interesting things:
- The game is procedural.  Every time you die, everything resets and you start over from scratch.
- The guns have way more detail than most games.  There are separate buttons for ejecting cartridges, reloading bullets, removing spent cartridges, pulling the slide, toggling the safety, etc.  The only game I've seen with more detail in it's guns is Horseshoes, Hotdogs, and Hand Grenades for the Vive.
- There is no story or explanation aside from what you find on the tapes. When you find a tape, it has strange scientology stuff on it.
I was really really bad at this game, so I doubt I'll ever play it again. I'd recommend playing it until you get frustrated, then watch a Lets Play on youtube to get the rest of the story.

Perhaps this is better alleviated with experience and a larger card set, but 15 hours of play later and it's something i've come to accept.
Overall the Pros heavily outweigh the cons. If you like TCG's, Eternal has much to offer over the competition.

A "look-up-the-puzzle-solution-on-the-internet" simulator, at its finest.  This is an RPG with almost zero "role-playing," as there is not a single character throughout the game with which your party will interact with in any way, other than to kill.  No dialogue.  No choices.  No plot.  No NPCs.  Nothing.  Just enemies and puzzles.  And those puzzles?  Almost impossible to solve.  Many have no clues at all, so you must flip levers and press buttons and step on plates and walk through teleporters randomly, hoping you get lucky and "solve" the puzzle.  Other puzzles have clues half-way across the game world that you may or may not ever find.  I'm no stranger to puzzle-solving in RPGs, but I had to look up the answer to almost all of the puzzles in this game.  Half the game involves walking sideways along walls looking for switches...like a giant "hidden object" game.  And the charcters classes?  Make sure you look up the "correct' way to build a party, because the "wrong" choices are devestating (i.e. your characters will not be able to survive later in the game).
Summary:  This is not an RPG--it is a puzzle game, and the puzzles are awful.

This is a bizarre mix of great and awful elements. The Showcase mode is stellar, the editor is remarkably detailed, there is an exceptional amount of content and it all runs beautifully.
Unfortunately, this is let down by other aspects of the game.
The commentary is so far short of the NBA series as to be embarassing. It's buggy (incorrect lines are often spoken, and sometimes the same line is repeated several times in a row) and there are times when the commentator is clearly reading from a script (particularly Cole). Some lines are recorded at a different volume, and sound like they were literally phoned in.
The AI is wonky at best, and when combined with the awkward hit detection and inconsistent ability to interrupt animations, multi-man matches become an absolute trainwreck where AI teammates constantly interfere with each other.
Several of the achievements do not trigger properly.
Game concepts are explained poorly, no effort is made for a manual or tutorial. Not ideal when the series is new to PC.
The career mode is built around grinding; even though this version comes with DLC to at least boost your character (albeit buried away in a menu - I wasted plenty of time before noticing it), it is still a painful slog through match after match against the same opponent - aggravated by the nonsense Authority objectives, some of which are rendered impossible by circumstances out of your control.
Oh, and on career mode, it baffles me how an otherwise great-looking game reduced Renee Young to a plastic, Uncanny Valley resident.
It's frustrating because this could be a great game, and elements of it are outstanding, but it's just let down by so many needless flaws.
Oh, and I didn't miss 2K's continued gouging of Australians, either - a 30% mark-up is a disgrace.

I have a rule that I will only write reviews for games I've beaten.  I've been waiting to write this review for a long goddamn time.  I got this game for a dollar or something on a sale a long time ago.  I thought I'd be done sooner.
You'll spend day 1 giggling and feeling silly playing around with the guns.  When you don't have the help menu open you do silly things.  Pull the slide back and eject a bullet then have to pick it up.  Eject your magazine from your your gun and grop it on the ground like an idiot.  Use the glock on full automatic mode, wasting bullets like a madman, it's silly, it's fun.
Then that starts to wear off.  You start feeling like a badass, working your way around the gun like a pro.  You'll use the help menu less and less.  First you'll master the revolver, in the end you'll finally know what side of the gun the glock's semi automatic mode sits in.  You're like James friggin' Bond.
Then that starts to wear off.  You start your game and begin mechanically checking your gun from memory.  Eject magazine, check to see how many bullets, holster gun, top it off, draw gun, unsert magazine, pull slide if there's not one in the chamber.  You've heard every tape by now and understand the story about how 11 tapes will set you free from this reality, you've also learned there's a pause button on the tapes so you don't have to hear them anymore.  It's not fun now, it's personal. You don't just hit your enemies, you target cameras and loading mechanisms.  Every death you swear, grit your teeth, and prepare to check your gun.
You become paranoid and start checking every corner like the world is filled with snipers who exist solely to kill you....and it is.  You learn the turrets actually have limited ammo, if you're low you might even exploit that.  You sneak up on flying tazers and catch them off guard.  When you hear a tazer spot you there is no fight anymore, you run, run far and fast.  You'll come back and shoot it in the back but there's too much riding on this.  The route you choose becomes entirely based on how many tazers you need to fight.  It's so simple, just finsh 11 tapes and don't die, you could finish it in five minutes but I've been at it for 40 hours.
Then you finish, you slide tape 11 in and you sit back in stunned silence.  The game finishes and shuts down and you drop it into your finished games folder.  You never need to play that game again, you're done.  Somehow, the game was right.  Tape 11 set you free.
I regret nothing.

In some ways it is a sequel better than the first Dark Souls game, in others it is worse. I think the situation is similliar to the KOTOR games, where both games had some features that were better in one instalment.
DS2:SotFS definetly is a better conversion to a pc even though it's still pretty bad... playing with controller is in most cases way better.
DS2 Does has improved fighting system with more acurate hitbox system (ds3 has even more better)  and just a nicer feeling to the fight, both PvP and PvE (personal opinion). This is obviously big part of the game, but the improvment is not hugh mungus, both games have a great fighting feeling to it.
DS1 has a better story. There are a lot of interesting storylines in DS2 specially in expansions, but in overall DS1 has a story with more thick atmosphere, story that is more interesting, compeling. Again it's not a huge diffrence, and possibly a matter of preference.
DS1 has better bosses. More hard ones and with interesting lore, while DS2 has some forgettable and too easy boss fights, with uninteresting lore behind it.
DS2 has better looking locations, but DS1 has better world design (even though it lacks fast travel, but some see this as an advantage). Some places in DS2 just look beutiful, specially put together with music, both Majula and Firelink Shrine have great feeling of safety and peace, while Anor Londo for example hits you with its beauty, but also emptiness, presenting you this magnificent place in full glory, but also in decay cause of the lack of inhabitants. DS2 has great locations like Heides Tower of Flame, beatiful and full of nice, lore details and hints, Dragon Aerie and Shrine are also great.
Graphics are obviously on the side of DS2 cause its newer game.
Anyway I don't really like reviewing the game by comparing it to its previous installment, but they both work so great in pair, cause of how lore beetwen them works (a very mysterious way, that requires to you give it your own interpretation).
What i value most in Souls games is three things:
1 Smart game design (locations, fights, game progress)
2 Interesting, involving, thought-provoking lore
3 Compeling gameplay that sucks you in with its system
Both games have it, both have moments where some of those things are lacking (Lost Izalith locations in DS1 for example, Grave of Saints in DS2) except the lore I think, even the gameplay has it flaws with fights and their system (lazy boss design of infamous tree fight in DS1 and recycle bossess in DS2). But when in their prime, both games are just the absolute best you can possibly get.
Hmmm, not bad.

I really tried to like Dark Souls 2, since I loved the first Dark Souls.
Yesterday I finally gave it a shot, even though I've always had a bad feeling about this game...
Unfortunatly the bad feeling I had was right and I had no fun during the nearly 4h I've played.
The ambience was still Dark Souls like, but visually I find Dark Souls 1 still more appealing... I don't know how they didn't manage to improve, but it was still good.
I guess one good thing to note is that I didn't experience any frame drops, which I half expected since I was playing on high graphical settings.
There was no interesting story and all NPC's you meet are quite shallow and boring...
I also didn't experience any bossfights, while in Dark Souls 1 I'd have at least beaten 2 if not 3 within these 4h...
These are the things that just made Dark Souls amazing and I see no point in waiting for any of that to come if it's just annoying to play the game.
It has really broken controls... at least with my 360 controller, that I've been using for countless other games, including DS1, without getting any of these problems...
The input delay is already a bother, but sometimes they don't work at all.
I've had moments where my character just stopped raising his shield even if the button was held and sometimes I pressed the trigger to attack and had no response from my character until it was too late... so when I wanted to roll out of the way, he finally attacked and well... got slaughtered... by the way, I did have full stamina in there moments.
Aside the controls, the hitboxes are also quite annoying as in you have to visibly hit the enemy to deal damage and the same doesn't apply to you.
I experienced moments where I was clearly away from any threat and I was still hit?
The environmental hitboxes are also quite annoying, since any obstacle that is in your way can be a deathtrap and somehow a little bit of rubble can count as a complete obstacle for no realistic reason...
At last I come to the camera, which I couldn't seem to fix, but I always had a tunnelvision and sometimes the camera moved automatically upwards in some places so I could only see my character and less than a meter ahead... (this seemingly didn't have anything to do with the controler)
In conclusion I had too much trouble playing this game and that's why I don't recommend it, but it's not really a bad game.
It has it's flaws that were unbearable to me personally, but there are people who clearly love this game somehow.
I'm going to start Dark Souls 3 soon, since I had a good feeling about it... let's hope I'm right again this time...

Homefront: The Revolution is not revolutionary, but I've found it provides numerous small objectives and activities that are fun and quick to play.
Moment-to-moment, it is very similar to Far Cry and Dying Light, but whereas those games have large open areas and more involved objectives, H:TR places them in a smaller, denser urban space and makes them achieveable in about half the time. I find myself playing for anywhere between 20 to 90 minutes, taking over occupied Philadelphia block by block. Given that the level of challenge starts low and increases slowly, and that most of the objectives and enemies are quite similar, I feel that the game is perhaps best played in these smaller sessions—a few objectives over lunch.
The story moves along whenever I'm ready to move it, but it's not what keeps me returning to the game. I like finding and eliminating the five snipers in an area, sabotaging enemy electronics along the way, looting the corpses I made when running past a patrol, quickly hacking a comms tower or reclaiming a guerilla safehouse.

Wow, what a really fun game.
The Legend of Grimrock games are great, though it caters to an audience with a specific taste. If you ever played the old Eye of the Beholder gameboy game or something like it, you'll appreciate this. Grimrock takes the classic dungeon crawl scheme and modernizes it.
This just doesn't mean better graphics and game mechanics though--the developers of this game really thought about these and spent time putting in intricate, yet very solvable puzzles and riddle-like passive narratives into the game. Meaning, you will be challenged, but you will also feel very rewarded when you figure something out. This perfect balance along with some nice, classic RPG elements make for some great fun.
Legend of Grimrock 2 is better than the first, but this is only because of the graphics upgrade and the much more diverse environments you get to explore instead of being cooped up in a tower all day!
On my top games list--a must for lovers of the genre!

The main problem I have with this game:
It's not fun. Never. Period.
Because of the sheer number of enemies, always, everywhere, every action you do - even supposedly 'stealthy' ones - result in enemies alerted. From that point, every action draws even more enemies, etc.
And I mean even shooting a surveillance cam, with a silenced weapon, crouched, from cover, alerts all enemies in that zone because of the sound of the exploding camera.
While the gunplay is solid, there's not much more to do than constantly unlocking safepoints, many times the challenge only is finding the way to climb up to the third floor or so, without being seen by one of the guards. Because you often need to sneak around the house first to figure out where to begin and many times you get killed, it's particularly frustrating that the save system is crap, you can't manually save, only inside safepoints.
Problem is the variety the game offers you, is not for choice, but rather a necessity for most of the objectives. Which in turn means that the only way to play this game is how THEY intended. To open that door you MUST use this game mechanic, to reach that spot you MUST use that other mechanic. There's no freedom of choice.
So summarized, I found there's no room for your unique way of playing:
Guns blazing? You get overwhelmed within 10 seconds.
Stealth? Only if you never, ever draw a weapon and walk crouched all the time.
And for me the main bummer:
It has infinite respawn of enemies, the cheapest game mechanic known to man. Which means that you can't pick off enemies from afar to make sure the area is clear. Also there's no point in trying to fight yourself out once cornered. You can always run away and hide in a trash container (which magically makes all alerts fade away within 20 seconds), but come on, that's sooo chicken...
This game is not complete crap; it has very nice graphics, the performance problems it had on launch have been fixed and it deserves at least a proper review. But I can't recommend this game except when you are extremely bored and have played every other major shooter/stealth/open world title on this planet.

slides into a confident first place lead for best games I played in 2015. It is atmospheric, fun, and challenging - providing enough modern influence to keep me interested while also staying true to staples of the dungeon crawl genre of old.
The story is simple enough: you control four prisoners who have shipwrecked on a mysterious island called Grimrock. Here, you must wield powerful weapons and utilize ancient tools in order to progress through the island.
At first, since I was unfamiliar to the concepts of the genre, I found the combat strange, confusing and even awkward. But I quickly adapted and the gamplay became second nature soon enough. The heart of the game, however, is the puzzles. They are oftentimes relatively complex logical puzzles, a few of which border the lines of non-sequitor, but for the most part are very satisfying to complete. The dungeons are a blast to explore and there are enough modern tweaks to the system that elimate most uncessary hardships (fast-travel, saving without needing save points). If you want an added challenge, you can choose to disable all in game maps which forces you to draw your own on paper.
It was clear that my computer was not up to snuff to run this game to its full potential. However, I enjoyed even the minimalist graphical settings and felt completely absorbed into the dark, gritty world. In fact, I found it more and more difficult to play as I progressed in the game due to the feeling of paranoia and solipsism. The deeper dungeons left me exhausted from stress. From a technical point of view, the sound effects are fantastic: swords swing with a satisfying crunch when you score hits, and monsters are terrifyingly ferocious. The musical score is subdued and only provides a backdrop, which is perfectly appropriate for this game (the title menu music is amazing, by the way).
If you are looking for a rpg with a focus on extraordinary gameplay, this would be a fantastic journey for you. The story is open-ended enough for the player to fill in the lines , which I think allows the focus to stay on the gameplay. You will be bewildered, frustrated and ultimately extremely satisfied should you brave the mysterious island of Grimrock...

Overall, I was incredibly dissapointed by this game, but would still recommend it. I have heard a lot about it being challenging and unforgiving, but this wasn't my experience. I can still see why it might be, but if you expand methodically along with your birthrate, you should be fine. Food is incredibly easy to come by. For example, when going for the Mountain Men achievement (basically you have very little room to build), I had a point where despite limited food production capabilities I could comfortably give my entire town a year off and would still have food to spare. Pretty much any resource is easy to get in abundance. The only ones I had trouble with were the non-renewables (coal, metal, stone). Quarries/mines have a lot of resources in them, but it is finite and with the pace of hte game/intended length, you will run out, and therefore are essentially trading a large chunk of land forever for a sum of the resources. Metal isn't that bad because you don't need much, but stone is very important for growth, particularly optimizing. This is somewhat mitigated by the trade system. While the trade system is pretty interesting and unique, merchants are too unreliable and bring too few goods to really base an economy off of. Most of your purchases will be extortionately priced seeds, though even then, you surplus so much it is easy to afford after the early game. Nor can you specialize in a trade good, as each merchant has its own set of very limited acceptable goods.
With those critiques out of the way, on to what is good. First: the UI. RPS' review almost scared me off of this game with its talk of the UI. The reviewer's complaints were unfounded. I had no trouble with the UI, deaths were easily noticed via alerts, and overall I found it made managing my little economy pleasant. Where this game really excells is the whole circle of life aspect. Watching your town grow and change over the generations, the forests grow, be cut down, and replanted anew is very beautiful. Putting the game on 2-5x and watching your peasants scurry about town can be immensely calming and immersive. I'm going to have to fall in to the 'this game can totally be zen' camp on that issue. (Though the first year can be pretty intense to get everything in place for winter, particularly on a harder start.) Through in the variability of the weather (some winters are harder than others), and you get a very organic and lively game.
In conclusion, it is not necissarily a groundbreaking city-sim, nor a compelling survival game, but it does have a beautiful organic fluidity to it. If you tap in to that - growing at the same rate your people do, rather than playing it as an intense buildfest like the early stages of a 4x - you will find life's resillience overcomes nature's challenges.

F1 2016 is, uh, that year's officially sponsored Formula 1 game, if that didn't come across.
Starting the career mode, you can make your own in-game driver avatar from pre-set models and helmet designs, then give them a name and a shorthand nickname. From past Codemasters games I miss the option to be called by a set nickname, personally, but that's a negligible downside.
The career itself is
, it spans 10 seasons of some 21 tracks, and on 25% race length you're looking at some 2 hours per circuit if you don't mess up too much - that's three 30 minute-long Practice sessions, one 20 minute long Qualifying run, and one 20 minute long race on average. There's a rivalry feature, which tracks and compares your accomplishments across the Qualifying and Race stages of the weekend, and if you do well you get bumped to a greater rival. Practice sessions have a point beyond mere track memorization, as you can opt to complete practice programmes to get you acclimatized to the track, manage your tyres and set qualifying runs, in order to get research points that will be used to gradually perfect your car over the career.
Visually, not much to complain about here, except for the facial animations not
looking right. Other animations are rather basic but you really have to look hard to find flaws. Great level of detail even on low graphical settings, and Ultra looks damn good.
Car sounds are pretty good, and especially from the cockpit cams you get the full symphony of turbo whistle and high-revving V6 notes for the whole time spent on the track. The rest of the sound effects are done nicely too. Music only plays in the Main Menu, career lounge, while fast-forwarding in the pit garage, and on results screens - and it's rather good as well! No complaints about the voice acting either, it does the job to both immerse you into the race event (with the presenters) and to communicate your status (with your engineers).
I probably won't stand a chance at driving F1 cars anytime soon, but they feel pretty close to what I think are the real deal. On a gamepad you need careful throttle, brake and steering management to keep the beast in check, and then further management to ease up tyre wear, heat and fuel consumption. A huge host of assistance and difficulty levels let you tailor your experience just the way you want it - from the shortest possible races with full assists and limited wear and tear, to 60 minute long, gruelling races where one wrong move can ruin your day (if you don't rewind, that is). Safety cars step in whenever things get rougher than wanted on the track, and the AI seems to put up a good challenge on Hard and above. I'm pretty sure it follows the rules, regulations, track and driver lists of the actual 2016 F1 Championship, which is neat.
For F1 nuts I think this is a good package, and for racing game enthusiasts it is an equally attractive choice for its current asking price. Others may find it more palatable on a discount. This is Codemasters level of quality, detail and fun.

King of Fighters XIV, the latest game in the long running franchise, is a very challenging and fun entry, with devilish quick and precise attacks, as well as tough to pull-off and powerful combo moves that feel extremely satisfying. It also represents the series' first entry into a full 3D, with combatants fighting in two dimensions. You fight in tag teams with three fighters that pitch into the fight as soon as the previous one loses.
Armed with a new and beefy 3D engine, awesome visual design of its fighters and stages, and coupled with 54 fighters (including the DLC), KOF XIV looks pleasing to the eyes and provides a lot of content. You have standard game modes: story, versus, missions, training and online fight. Story is decent and it will take you between 2-3 hours to finish, versus is a standard you versus another player or a computer where you can fight solo or with tag teams. Missions provide a bit of variety: there's survival that pits you against exceedingly powerful fighters as you try to last as much as possible, time attack where you fight with 10 opponents for the best time and trial as the hardest one that focuses on pulling of powerful and demanding combos. Training modes can be offline or online where other players can communicate with you as you train with them, which is a very cool add-on other fighting games should definitely have. Finally there’s a standard online brawl and a ranked mode, where you’ll usually find someone to play, mostly from Asia and South America. Oh, and there is a gallery mode, with artwork, movies and sounds from the game, but they kind of pale in comparison to the Tekken 7.
Fights themselves are fast with quick standard attacks, and combos that can be chained to super combos for greater damage, and you can easily rank up 20-50 hits at once, which is amazing. Controls are super-responsive, and animations short so you can block or dodge 95% of all attacks. When you take damage, only a small portion of your health is restored as you go into another round. In tag team battles, you can’t switch in the middle of the fight among your three chosen fighters, but you can decide in which order they’ll participate. The only wat to get better in KOF XIV is to play aggressively, leaving an enemy with little time to recuperate as you chain you combo and super-combo moves before you pin the player to the wall and finish the fight.  Knowing combos and mastering them is the way to master this game, as standard moves, though quick, dish out a small amount of damage. Enemy AI is competent but I advice on playing the toughest or one step below the toughest difficulty to have a decent challenge.
There are some bug-bears with this game: texture work on all fighters is basic and low-poly at best, which makes graphics feel a bit last-gen, but on the other hand, most of computers will have a steady framerate while playing. Menu is clunky and ugly looking, difficult to manage and get to where you wanted to be. But most of all, waiting times for online games are long, since this game has a small but dedicated community of players that are all better than you but also surprisingly polite, compared to the online community for Tekken 7.  People only play tag matches, and if you were hoping to enjoy ranked matches, good luck since I haven’t managed to find a single player there. Lastly, controller support is not all-encompassing; it didn’t manage to recognize my Cyborg Rumblepad 3/excellent PlayStation knock-off controller, and playing on a keyboard is a stuff of nightmares. So getting a steam or an XBOX controller is a must.
Overall, KOF XIV is like a good vine, it’s an acquired taste for dedicated lovers of old-fashioned, fast and brutal fighting games similar to older Street Fighter series. Latest King of Fighters is tough but fair game, more demanding than Tekken 7, but easier than BlazBlue series, and as such gets my two-thumbs-up recommendation.

I've played Magic on and off my whole life and spent at least 1000 hours playing Hearthstone. I had MTGO since the very beginning, and Hearthstone since late 2013 near the end of the open beta. Eternal is the best online card game I've ever played. It combines the best aspects of Magic's strategic depth and Hearthstone's fast-paced accessibility while avoiding their flaws.
F2P
Magic will always be expensive because it's a tradable CCG with a reserve list of cards that can't be reprinted and expensive booster packs. Most cards lose tons of value when they rotate out of standard. MTGO is less expensive and more liquid than physical cards, but still expensive. Recently, Wizards have added features similar to other digital CCGs like treasure chests.
Hearthstone is "F2P" in name only. New players need to spend lots of money or time to earn a viable deck. Otherwise, enjoy scraping out wins with a crappy pile at rank 17. Rewards for winning games are meager. You can get big payoffs in Arena (where you don't get to keep the cards you draft)...if you're already an experienced player and/or lucky. Arena costs 1.5 packs to play with cards you don't own and win at least 1 pack of value. You don't keep the cards. New Arena players get trashed.
Eternal is truly F2P. The spoils of victory are frequent and generous. Each win either gives a treasure chest with gold and a card, or more gold and a better card, or even more gold holy♥♥♥♥♥♥and a booster pack. Each treasure chest has a chance of becoming a better treasure chest full of even better rewards. Single-player Gauntlet mode lets you face the AI for free to win big rewards. Forge and Draft are more expensive than HS Arena (2.5 and 5x pack price vs. 1.5x pack price), but you get to keep all the cards you draft in Forge and Draft modes while still winning big payoffs for playing well.
Magic is pay to play, try to recoup your losses later. Hearthstone is an evil slot machine that reluctantly hands out the goods. Eternal is a slot machine that always gives you something, but sometimes gives you something better, and occasionally gives you an all-expenses-paid trip to Hawaii.
Winner: Eternal
Gameplay and RNG
Magic is the deepest, most complicated, most strategically interesting CCG ever. Almost every type of card, zone and resource can be interacted with, during both players' turns. The mana system rewards intelligent deck building and decision making skills. However, the mana system has also been a constant thorn in its side. Mana screw and flood as well as color screw are a necessary evil of the game's design, and consistently ruin the experience and decide high-level matches. The mulligan system punishes you further for the crime of being unlucky. Magic Online makes no use of any digital-only design space (except Momir Basic) and the relief from shuffling physical cards. The metagame gets patched several times a year whenever the physical Banned and Restricted list is updated.
Hearthstone sidesteps resource problems with its mana system, but has different issues instead. It's a simplistic "My turn, your turn" game with a hard limit to how interesting and interactive it can be. The mana system means that instead of getting mana-screwed, you get tempo-screwed if you don't draw a 2 on turn 2, a 3 on turn 3, and so on. It's called Curvestone for a reason. Being able to attack anything directly means that losing the board first usually means losing the game. The mulligan system is good. Hearthstone explores digital design space, but leans overwhelmingly on random effects. The RNG is so hilariously pervasive that even top-level players meme about it on a constant basis. Omnipresent powerful random effects make situations that are impossible to play around. It's one thing to get outplayed, but it feels awful to get outlucked. HS is the game of getting outlucked. Also, the meta is prone to getting extremely stale as Team 5 moves very slowly to nerf problem cards and very rarely buffs weaker ones.
Eternal simplifies the essence of Magic's strategic, interactive gameplay. You can still interact on your opponents' turns and there's plenty of powerful spot and mass removal (at common and uncommon, even!) to deal with tall and wide boards. The mana and combat systems are similar to Magic's. Eternal mitigates bad opening hands by allowing you to redraw a 7 card hand with between 2-5 mana cards, guaranteed. Flood and screw are still possible, but not nearly as frequently as in Magic. The combat system is much more interesting less blatantly aggressive than Hearthstone's, with different advantages given for attackers and defenders. Eternal makes excellent use of digital design space. You can affect cards in any zone, some cards make copies of themselves when drawn, and card attributes will persist across different zones, resulting in creative combos. As far as the metagame, in the last few months Dire Wolf Digital has shown a willingness to alter cards and tune up the meta in a timely manner when certain strategies are revealed to be too oppressive or lacking in counterplay.
Winner: Magic for overall depth, Eternal for elegance and creativity with digital space.
Polish and Features
Magic Online is the laughingstock of the digital games world. However, it has many more features than HS, with a huge variety of formats available, a full-featured collection and deck manager, and the ability to trade tickets cards with bots other players.
Hearthstone is a beautiful experience with compelling graphics, music, animations and voice acting. However, it possesses a few game modes (casual, ranked, arena, tavern brawl) with only two formats for now (wild and tavern brawl). It possesses extremely few features despite its obscene profitability and years post-release. There is no tournament mode and the deck and collection managers are very weak.
Eternal's art direction, sound design and graphical effects are better than Magic Online (like every other game) and worse than Hearthstone's (like every other game), but far closer to Hearthstone than to Magic Online. It only has two single player and two multiplayer modes. It has an intuitive, full-featured collection manager and deckbuilder with analytic tools to help guide deckbuilding.
Winner: Hearthstone for polish, Eternal for features.
Verdict
On the whole, Eternal refines and simplifies Magic's gameplay and creatively explores new design space while avoiding the egregious errors of Hearthstone. The gameplay finely balances a majority focus on skill with a pinch of luck. There is a wealth of interactions and strategies to explore. The online experience is elegant, enjoyable and full-featured. The game is generous with its rewards. You should stop reading this and install it right now. Why are you still reading this? Go away. Go play Eternal

I'm an ex MTG player.  I played hearthstone for quite some time before moving onto other ccgs and I'm currently enjoying shadowverse.  This review may come off extremely critical, but with so many f2p online ccgs to choose from, I feel it's warrented.
Your power (resource) cards are drawn from the same pile as your other cards.  This leads to flooding and not getting enough power far too frequently.  Since this is a digital card game there are several better options and there is no need for this serious problem to occur.  If they wanted to have players draw the power cards, they could have just made two seperate draw piles for resources and non-power cards and let the player choose what they want to draw to avoid this.
Going first has a large advantage.  The only thing you get for going second is you draw first (firs player skips their initial draw).  That's not enough to make up for being the player that's constantly reacting to your opponent's plays since you're basically a turn behind.
Some cards are obviously "pushed" too far.  Some cards have stats and abilities well above what they should have at their cost and are often put at higher rarity which makes them harder to obtain for new players.  While some colors need these to be balanced compaired to the other colors, this is still at the very least a poor and lazy way to balance.
Eternal currently has no casual play, only ranked.  Why would it take so long to implament this very basic game mode?  If you're fine with only playing ranked as I am, then it's a non-issue, however I know other players get anxiety when they play in ranked modes or just want a place to test things out and mess around when they don't feel up to playing ranked so I thought others should at least be aware.
These next couple are just things I didn't like about eternal, but wouldn't call inherantly negative parts of the game.
Defender decides what is blocked and how the blocks occur.  This leads to too many board stalls.
Damage is wiped from units at the end of the turn.  Again this leads to board stalls since you can't just chip down a big minion over time and you often won't want to attack with it either since your opponent can assign multiple blockers and kill it if it attacks.
This game isn't all bad though, I did like being able to play against the AI to earn some chests (which contain cards).  The drafting process was also well done.  UI and art are decent enough.
If you have no fast spells (cards that can be played on your opponent's turn) the game doesn't require an "ok" to progress the game which does help speed things up a bit.  However if a player does have a fast spell, then the game requires you to push a button in between plays to progress.  Players should be able to quickly tell the time difference in between plays and know that you have a fast spell.  This information can/will cause different plays vs. if the player didn't have that information.
TL;DR There are better f2p ccgs for me.  If you're looking for something closer to MTG than hearthstone, and the above issues don't bother you, then it's worth a shot.

The mana and combat systems are similar to Magic's. Eternal mitigates bad opening hands by allowing you to redraw a 7 card hand with between 2-5 mana cards, guaranteed. Flood and screw are still possible, but not nearly as frequently as in Magic. The combat system is much more interesting less blatantly aggressive than Hearthstone's, with different advantages given for attackers and defenders. Eternal makes excellent use of digital design space. You can affect cards in any zone, some cards make copies of themselves when drawn, and card attributes will persist across different zones, resulting in creative combos. As far as the metagame, in the last few months Dire Wolf Digital has shown a willingness to alter cards and tune up the meta in a timely manner when certain strategies are revealed to be too oppressive or lacking in counterplay.
Winner: Magic for overall depth, Eternal for elegance and creativity with digital space.
Magic Online is the laughingstock of the digital games world. However, it has many more features than HS, with a huge variety of formats available, a full-featured collection and deck manager, and the ability to trade tickets cards with bots other players.
Hearthstone is a beautiful experience with compelling graphics, music, animations and voice acting. However, it possesses a few game modes (casual, ranked, arena, tavern brawl) with only two formats for now (wild and tavern brawl). It possesses extremely few features despite its obscene profitability and years post-release. There is no tournament mode and the deck and collection managers are very weak.
Eternal's art direction, sound design and graphical effects are better than Magic Online (like every other game) and worse than Hearthstone's (like every other game), but far closer to Hearthstone than to Magic Online. It only has two single player and two multiplayer modes. It has an intuitive, full-featured collection manager and deckbuilder with analytic tools to help guide deckbuilding.
Winner: Hearthstone for polish, Eternal for features.
On the whole, Eternal refines and simplifies Magic's gameplay and creatively explores new design space while avoiding the egregious errors of Hearthstone. The gameplay finely balances a majority focus on skill with a pinch of luck. There is a wealth of interactions and strategies to explore. The online experience is elegant, enjoyable and full-featured. The game is generous with its rewards. You should stop reading this and install it right now. Why are you still reading this? Go away. Go play Eternal.

Bought the game and subsequently returned it.
Pros -
- Customization is great. I spent a lot of time making a cool superstar with an awesome intro. I liked him. He was gonna go far.

- Music selections didn't make me want to jam a screwdriver in my ear. Well, not the first few times through the rotation, anyway.
Cons -
- Music gets repetitive real quick.
- Controls are incomprehensible. There are so many layers of abstraction between me and the moves I want to do that it ends up being a series of mind-numbing mini-games rather than something that even resembles a fight. "Rotate the controller until the blue dot turns red and fills up the gauge." "Rotate the controller until the red triangle is under the blue triangle." "Press A when the bar fills up to the tapout button."  etc., etc., etc.
Not to mention, of course, the ridiculousness of attempting to counter a move, wherein you may only succeed in doing so if you press R2 at the exact right moment, not before, not after, but if you wait until you receive the prompt on-screen, it's already too late.
- Tutorials teach you very little, while simultaneously penalizing your long-term progress for not yet knowing the rules or controls.  It honestly took me 5 minutes to figure out how to leave the ring after tagging in my partner because the game never explained it, but sure as hell was happy to have me lose the match to disqualification.
- Kayefabe.    Call me a romantic, but I'm not at all interested in seeing how the sausage gets made. I don't ever want to see my supernaturally themed, giant death-man of badassery smiling and high-fiving people while back-stage at the NXT performance center, or looking at Triple H with a wide-eyed stare and a "put me in, Coach!" attitude. None of my fantasies about wrestling, none of the things I've ever enjoyed about it, have come from the idea of getting in the ring and seeing it all from the other side. What I want to see is that Randy Orton lives in a straight jacket, that John Cena salutes himself in the mirror every morning, that Bray Wyatt holds strange rituals down on his farm and that The New Day wake up every morning and eat a big 'ol bowl of Booty-o's. I want the fantasy. I want the stories and the characters. The Undertaker isn't very cool if he's just some guy named Mark.
- Loadscreens upon loadscreens, upon loadscreens! For a 20 gig game, you'd think they could have smoothed this out a bit, but instead every other menu requires a minute-long load screen just to change an option or select the next match. WHY?!  (well, I know why, but I didn't want this to just be a rant about crummy console porting)
- - Overall - -
Nah.  Unless you're a SUPER-HARDCORE-ULTRA-UBER-MEGA-FAN of the series already, this isn't really worth the time it takes to make it worthwhile. Just go watch the 900+ hours of content on the WWE Network ("For only 9.99!") and give this mess a pass.

Receiver is an experimental First Person Shooter, developed in just 7 days to partake in a Game Jam challenge.
The plot is told via cassette tapes, that you must collect 11 of in a single playthrough.
Almost every surface is untextured and there's minimal, if any, post processing. Surprisingly good lighting effects. The most detailed models in the game are the firearms, conspicuously floating in front of your invisible player avatar as part of the developers' conscious decision to not obstruct the weapon models with your mortal
arms.
The soundtrack is only one dynamic, tense and somewhat electro track which changes in intensity depending on your proximity to enemies and certain items. Weapons sound distinct and accurate to life. You'll quickly learn to dread that
It has elements of the roguelike genre: the levels are generated by stringing together rooms in a random order and randomly placing enemies, items and even leaving your firearm in a random condition every time - means you are just as likely to spawn with two full mags as you are to spawn with nothing but a single round in your magazine. Death is swift, taking just one bullet or one zap from any enemy to start generating a new level.
It stands out from other games through its incredibly detailed portrayal of the firearms. Every weapon has keys associated with different functions that are part of an intricate reloading and readying process. The standard M1911A1 handgun has you: ejecting the magazine, holstering the pistol, loading live rounds into the magazine, drawing back out the pistol, loading the magazine, then, if necessary, racking the slide to chamber a round from the magazine.
The two other handguns in the standard game, the Glock 17 with a fire selector and the S&W Model 10 revolver, have their own unique functions as well: the G17 foregoes an external hammer and traditional safety toggle in exchange for a larger magazine capacity, reduced individual shot power, and a full auto toggle that should really only be used in emergencies. The Model 10 revolver, meanwhile, lacks a traditional magazine; you must open the cylinder, eject all rounds that may or may not be spent from the cylinder, insert up to 6 fresh bullets, then close it back and optionally pull back the hammer for the fastest trigger response. Ballistics overall are highly detailed, with bullet drop-off over distance, muzzle velocity, impact penetration and even ricochet chance depending on surface and angle of firing - be careful of shooting yourself in the foot!
The gameplay is part first person shooter, part horror (limited resources all around, and attacking poses a significant risk of wasting precious ammunition; running is a risky option) and part stealth (the two enemies featured require line of sight to engage and can be detected early by an attentive player via their projected lights and buzzing/droning sounds). The stationary turrets spin in a 360 degree angle and are easier, relatively speaking, to avoid or to disable, while the hoverbots... are absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. A huge part of their bodies are not vulnerable to being disabled, while the weak points are much more difficult to hit on a small, constantly moving and especially zipping-towards-you target.
The control scheme is such that you will fumble with it the first dozen or so lives, but an in-game help menu can provide guidance on quickly getting your gun ready to fire at a moment's notice, so it becomes a matter of muscle memory - just like real life reloading, in fact.
It's a $5 game but it's most likely worth your investment if you're any shade of gun nut or if you enjoy first person shooters. For anyone else, you should grab it as part of a bundle.
