VVVVVV takes its name from the game's main objective, which I shall not touch upon in order to leave the discovery to you. The first aspect of the game that took me by surprise is the superb 8-bit chiptune music. The only problem with that is that it does get repetitive only because it replays one single track for about 30 minutes at a time, until you complete each level. The graphics are imitating the general style of the Commodore 64, including its startup screen. VVVVVV's main platforming mechanic is the player's ability to flip the character's screen position vertically, going from bottom to top and vice versa. This makes for some complicated platforming in general, as well as some challenging and entertaining rooms. Because of the game's incredible difficulty, the developers have cleverly implemented checkpoints liberally throughout the game world, which cuts down on rage and frustration. With that said, VVVVVV still manages to be extremely difficult, and you should expect to die hundreds of times, if not one thousand times by the time you complete the game. The platforming and controls are not badly designed, as in Super Meat Boy, so do not confuse this well crafted, yet simplistic game with that developmental disaster. Younger generations of gamers may find the overall presentation of VVVVVV to be unique and hip, but as we all know, these graphics have been done before, about 30 years ago. One serious flaw is that there are no audio options for volume. The in-game default is quite higher than usual, and requires turning down in Windows. While the majority of the levels' rooms are a lot of fun, and well designed, some are simply unreasonable and require too much luck as opposed to actual precision and skill. Because of this, you will die many times and spend far too long attempting single rooms. Which also means being forced to listen to a single song on a loop, for the entire duration of your trials. This is something of a shortcoming and should have been avoided completely by the developers, as these uncalled-for rooms only add negatively to the experience. Even though you get unlimited lives and unlimited continues, having to repeat a single room hundreds of times in order to pass it gets boring, repetitive, annoying, and only serves the purpose of replacing actual content with limited and mundane game play. While the music is once again, excellent, there are only a few that repeat over and over, as the rest must be unlocked by finding and collecting certain orbs within the game world. There are also a few more game modes for the player to experiment with once the campaign has been completed. The storyline and ending are endearing and delightful, and once you complete the game, there is an overall feeling of satisfaction. VVVVVV is short but perfectly sweet.

A very fun CCG with mechanics in line with Magic (5 colors of mana, mana cards have to be drawn, defender chooses blockers, instant cast spells usable on opponent's turn, etc). The initial intro with the starter decks is a little tedious, but once you get past that the game is shockingly fair for a free to play game.
For single player content, you have the Gauntlet and the Forge. The Gauntlet is free and pits your constructed deck against up to 7 AI in a row (one loss and you start over) for progressively better rewards (gold, cards, card packs if you win all 7). The Forge lets you draft cards to play 7 games against the AI and ends if you lose twice. You keep ALL the cards you draft and can also win 3-4 card packs and a chunk of gold (buy in is 2.5 packs worth of gold), making this a great way to build your collection while learning the game.
Multiplayer currently has Ranked and Draft, with each ranked win giving gold / cards (sometimes a pack with a lucky roll) and Draft is like the Forge on steroids, with you drafting (and keeping!) a larger number of cards to create your deck.
I've been collecting cards so fast I felt obligated to send some money the dev's way, which is a hell of a contrast from many other games in this genre.

Okay, first of all, I would like to say that this is a great game, despite some of the criticisms that I have for it. I would recommend that anyone who likes this genre get this game. I can't really imagine anything better for what it is.
I'm going to focus on a comparison between this game and the first, and I would, in fact, recommend that you play the first before you play this one. It's a little bit simpler and gives you a better idea of what this game is all about.
First of all, some things that this game introduces that I consider positive:
--A wide array of different environments:
The original was basically limited to three environments, and they were all dark and dungeony. This game has a huge number of unique ones, all with different themes, including outdoor areas, which give the game a much brighter feel than the original.
--A better skill leveling system:
In the original, there were a lot of incentives to run hard in a single direction and level up all of a single skill without touching anything else. This did take away from the excitement of leveling a bit, since almost regardless of the situation, you would be leveling "throwing weapons" or whatever. In this one, it's important to level up a little bit in a lot of different skills, since there are plenty of items that want you to have 1 skill point in air magic or something, and almost every skill gives you a neat perk if you level it up to a certain level. Certainly, the way it is now is much cleaner than it was before, and it's all laid out much more plainly.
--Way more items:
Obviously, the second edition was going to have more things, and it does. The wide variety of items makes finding secrets and just generally progressing through the game more exciting, and also lets modded maps take a wider variety of directions.
--Multi-layer map structure:
In addition to the classic multi-floor structure of the original game, maps in the sequel have access to ladders and pits, which just generally lets the designers jam more things into smaller spaces. This is another feature that should make map modding a little more interesting.
--New race:
This isn't the sort of thing that makes me all that excited, but I know some people will be super into the character creation element of the game, so this is certainly a positive.
--Better special attacks:
The combat system has just generally been revamped, and the most noticeable thing to me was that, rather than getting special attacks by leveling the weapon type and just doing it randomly in a fight, you trigger it actively by holding the attack button. A nice touch that make combat a little more interesting.
--Better story:
The first Grimrock had a story, but it was fairly secondary to the game itself. Basicaly, you're some adventurers in a mountain trying to find your way out, and that's pretty much the gist of it. In Grimrock 2, you truly feel like there is a goal most of the time, and I'm not going to spoil it, but it certainly adds to the ambiance.
And now for the things that are worse than the original:
--Open(ish) world:
Don't hate me for putting this in the negative camp, but for this particular game, the world just felt far too big, and in order to do things in the "right" order, players sort of have to get lucky. The problem is that the various areas and dungeons across the map have varying difficulties, and the player has no way to know which are hard and which are easy, so it's fairly easy to poke your head a little bit too deep, and try to take on dungeons which are far too difficult. Another problem with this design is that the game sometimes makes reference to clues hidden in completely different areas, which means that if you encounter the puzzle first, you don't really know what to do, and if you encounter it second, sometimes you've forgotten about the hint that you might have read literally hours ago.
--Inaccessible puzzles:
Everyone loves a good puzzle, and for the most part, these were really good, but, like in the last one, there were a few puzzles which you just can't expect for a reasonable human being to be able to figure out, so it's almost impossible to finish the game without cheating and looking on the internet for answers, unless you're a genius.
--Really annoying new enemies:
You will notice that for most of the other new content, they were clear upsides. They make modded maps better and spice up the game with new material. It's great to have new monsters to face in your adventures, but in this game, more often than not, I felt that the added enemies were just annoying. From the mosquito swarms that are very hard to hit, to the toads that steal your weapons, to the ice guardians which just generally feel too difficult, to the xeloroids that paralyze your party members, to the medusas that petrify you until you can get to a healing crystal, to the Eyctopusses that blind you, to the Trickster, who seems intentionally annoying, to the air elementals that you can't kill, and finally, to all of the things that poison you and give you diseases. Fighting a lot of the enemies in this game just isn't very fun, and that's linked to the next point.
--Injuries really suck
LoG 2 introduces us to a very frustrating combat mechanic: injuries. In battle, your adventurers will sometimes injure some part of their body, which might keep them from casting spells, stop health or energy regen, slow movement speed, or keep you from using your left or right hands. The game honestly didn't need this, and since the only way to fix it is to use healing potions, you basically need someone on hand at all times to make them. By the end of the game, this, combined with the next point, made me use probably more than 100 healing potions.
--Boss battles:
Boss battles are a cool idea, but LoG is more of a puzzle dungeon crawler game than an action game, and these just made me feel like there was too much empahsis in that direction. Some of the boss battles were also quite difficult, even on the easiest difficulty, and usually required that I take several healing potions and try several times to beat. The fights should not be the challenging parts of this game in my opinion, but in retrospect, they were. These are the reason that I recommend having someone leveled up all the way in alchemy as quickly as possible, since having resurrection potions and greater healing potions on hand can tend to make the bosses more manageable.
Overall, this game was great, and while I did have a lot of negative things to say about it, remember, I was just comparing it the the first, which is a tough thing to beat, and one of my favorite games of all time, so even if I might have sounded a bit harsh, I'm not saying that this game deserves any less than the 92% positive community rating that it currently boasts.

First be warned that Receiver is more of a short demo than a full game. Personally, i love its concepts, and i would love it to become a full game. Here is why.
It mixes in two of my favourite things in gaming: survival horror and attention to detail.
You start off with either of the three handguns: M1911 Colt, a double action revolver, or a Glock, and random amount of ammo with you. The point of the game is to wander around in search of the cassette tapes, and there are eight of them. The levels are random generated, and have enemies, ammo and/or cassette tapes scattered inside.
The trick is that you can manipulate your gun. You can manipulate the slide, the hammer, take the magazine out, safety switch, and each gun works differently. For the colt and the glock, you have to check whether the bullet is in the chamber. Or for example, the colt requires you to pull the hammer to be able to shoot it. The revolver also has a hammer, but it is a double action, so it does not require you to pull it back, but you can still do it and it makes it more accurate that way.
I also want to mention the enemies in this game - turrets and flying drones. The turret is stationary and it rotates. It has a camera and if it spots you, it starts shooting from its machine gun. The flying drone is a mobile version, with a tazer. One hit from either of them takes you down. Each enemy is made up of some parts: motor, battery, camera, weapon, and depending on where you shoot, you can either partially or fully take them down.
You shoot a turret or a drone in the motor, it will stop spinning or flying, but its camera and weapon are still active, and if you get into its line of sight (turret) or close enough (drone), it will kill you.
If you shoot its camera off, it will still fly around or spin, but it will be harmless.
Also, the turret's machine gun has an ammo box, which you can shoot preventing its machine gun from shooting, but there is still one round in the chamber.
Here is for the visual representation:
As for the survival horror part, i think you have already guessed it. You start off with a pretty low ammo count. You must carefully use what you have, and try to actively find more ammo.
The game is pretty hard to complete though, but what matters is not the ending, but the experience. That said, there are cheats to provide unlimited ammo, invulnerability and slow motion. I highly suggest using the slow motion cheat - just type "slowmo" and use to tab to switch back and forth in speed.

Short and Simple - Good Game.  In the midst of buying games that are so/so for $60, I can justify spending $30 for this game and here is why...
Pros:
- Quality game. All of the components are there.  From graphics, gameplay, UI, AI (as far as AI goes) and story, I think it is easy to see that the developers put a lot of work into the game to earn the Quality mark.
- RPG element adds to this FPS.  Throughout the game, you can customize your overall equipment and upgrade by spending cash and “skill” points.  I think they are called “hearts and something” but anyway, you can modify your loadout for your character to spice up the gameplay.
- Stable.  I list this because a lot of games out there are buggy and require patching prior to play.  Nice to know the game doesn’t crash and is playable right away.  A few graphic glitches here and there but very minor ... no real glitches that caused issues for me.
Cons:
- Initially Slow.  When I first bought the game, I put a few hours in and it was just slow for me.  It was only until recently where I found myself searching for some pre-Christmas gaming and gave it another chance and glad I did.
- Repetitive Parts.  Sometimes location finding can be a little annoying and repetitive.  I appreciate the clues (scaffolding and blue-colored hints for climbing) but I found it to be a little bit too much of rinse and repeat.
- Gear Bonus?  Sorry, I just don't see where the knee pads helped me in anyway.  Not only was there not enough gear but I felt it barely mattered.
- Loot the enemy gear but not the Gun!  What?  So, I like being able to loot the dead guys but their guns are right there and I can't pick them up?  Annoying.  It would also be nice to grab some armor too.
Overall
If you like FPS and a little bit of RPG then I think you will enjoy this game.  I enjoyed the story and characters and felt it to be better than the average FPS.  This is a plus in my book.
Ideas for the next Homefront (developers read)
- Keep the same staff :) - You have a quality game and for the most part, all the elements are there.  Sure, there are things to work out but I see plenty of reusable code!
- Add some parkour to get into the buildings.  Don't go crazy.  I am not talking another Assassin's Creed but allow us to get a little creative to get into the locations.  You can keep the scaffolding but I am fairly sure my special-ops player who has killed hundreds of KPA can figure out how to get into that window that is a few feet above his head. ;)
- Motorcycles are nice but what about the other vehicles I can't hijack?  I understand about the big tanks but spice-it-up with a few other vehicles (oh, and allow me to switch to 3rd person on the vehicle - didn't spend too much time on it but I couldn't see how to change that).
Again, good game and worth the buy.

If you liked the first Dark Souls, then great! This is more of the same. If you didn't like the first game, there aren't any substantial changes here that will sway your opinion.
As before, the enemies and levels are interesting and varied (and sometimes incredibly frustrating). A few minor annoyances from the first Dark Souls have been smoothed away: for example, weapons auto-repair unless they're fully broken, and you can eat multiple souls at once from your inventory. The levels don't have the interconnectedness they used to, but the game makes up for it by giving you fast travel between bonfires from the beginning. I particularly appreciated that some modifications to the equipment-weight mechanics made it so that medium or heavy armor can actually be fun this time around (it no longer affects your movement speed, just stamina recovery and roll distance).
On the negative side, collision detection with the environment is still awkward, so you'll see plenty of arrows get stuck on invisible walls. You're once again heavily incentivized to not try out new equipment because it isn't yet upgraded, which feels like a missed opportunity. There are also a couple of places near the end where you may have to look up what to do next unless you have a very good memory for the locked doors you found earlier in the game.

A worthy successor to the board-like dungeon crawler known as Grimrock I. Both of them seem to hit that sweet spot between making a game look good and leaving things to your imagination. It's tough to describe, but there's just this feeling of charm to it few games have nowadays. Combining old-school gameplay with graphics on par with the Trine series does work out for this one.
While the core mechanics remain the same, pretty much every aspect of the game has been expanded upon. No longer are you limited to dungeons, you actually get to explore some outside environments for once. They look daaaamn good too, especially the beach. The new campaign only starts out linear to ease you into things, but after the first two areas you end up in a hub-world from where you choose to go next. There are new puzzles that aren't limited to "put rock on pressure plate", new items, more monsters, more classes, etc. Speaking of items, weapons have special moves now. Also day-and-night cycle.
However, I don't think this game would be the same without the editor, which alone is enough to make cool maps. It doesn't take much at all to create your own levels, the editor's fairly simple to use for a 3d game. To make it even better, you can use lua scripts and custom assets to make your dungeon even more interesting. You could create some intricate puzzles, boss fights, or even add your own tiles, objects, and enemies if you have a bit of know-how.
What else can I say, I highly recommend LoG2. It's a very solid upgrade from the first game, and even though I'm not even a quarter through, this game satiates my thirst for a chill video game sesh better than Skyrim ever has. It doesn't seem to go on sale very often though.

The story is extremely cliched and even despite this, it will manage to hold your interest for a while until you realize it doesn't go anywhere. The ending that they build up to the whole game (it's heavily implied that something very bad happens to Sam, your sister in the game) does not even come to fruition, the side story with the father and mother is interesting for a while as well until that also turns out that it doesn't go anywhere. The journey is somewhat engaging for a little while, but there is no conclusion whatsoever. I suppose it's somewhat like real life in this sense, that the events just sort of happen and keep happening, and keep happening, but eventually you look back on the whole game and ask yourself: what the hell is the point? If the story went in an interesting direction and had a meaningful conclusion, I would have enjoyed this game so much more, as then the several hours you spend playing would actually lead to something.
In terms of gameplay, there's nothing here. It's very much like Dear Esther in the sense that you sort of just walk around and the story is revealed to you. Yes you have to look for clues and hints to move the story along, but this mostly just consists of opening up drawers to find letters and diaries and such. There is nothing challenging whatsoever about this game, and the gameplay does not change or evolve one iota during the entire playthrough.
TL;DR - Bad game, meh story that goes nowhere, good soundtrack (the score, not the in game music). Very short and unrewarding. Even if you enjoy coming of age stories about homosexuality (the game's main theme), don't spend money on this, just watch a playthrough on youtube. You will get the exact same level of enjoyment out of just watching.

So I've been thinking for a while on how I feel about this game, and honestly my answer is just kind of...meh.
I mean, what I like about it most is the gameplay itself.  This sort of going around, gradually uncovering a story and some mysteries, that's something I love in a game.  I love it when the world itself is interactive.  It's introspective, it's got just the right amount of cookie crumbs in the trail of plot discovery.  I'll probably replay it some time to see if I missed anything.
The main problem I have is that it wasn't what it was advertised to be.  It was spun as a horror game, something seriously and deliciously spooky, with a romantic side plot.  But as I played the game, I realized the "spookiness" wasn't really anywhere to be found, and what had originally been made to seem as a *side* plot, was really the *main* plot.  It had set me up as expecting something entirely different to be focused on, and that just sort of soured the milk when I got to the real ending.  Where are the ghosts?  Why are there so many spooky passages and whatnot in the house?  All the threads I wanted to be tied up were left unravelled, and the one I really wasn't emotionally invested in was the only one that got resolved.
But maybe that's just me.  Regardless, I really don't think it's worth the price.  Luckily for me, I got it on sale, and if you'd like to play a cute little walking sim with some nicely fleshed out teen romance, I suggest you do the same.  But as it stands, I really don't feel comfortable recommending something incorrectly advertised at such a steep price.

In short, King of Fighters XIV is a solid game.
+ Large cast with a good mix of old and new characters.
+ Good mix of mechanics from previous games and some new ideas.
+ Pretty decent character balance. (Based on tournament results.)
+ Solid "netcode".
+ Easier execution than KoFXIII.
- Very poor at explaining itself to newcomers. The training mode is decent but the trial mode is very poor and barely teaches you anything useful.
- Single player content in general is limited.
- It's not a looker, even after the improvements SNK made to the visuals.
- Some technical annoyances such as limited default arcade stick support, requiring users to have to create their own mapping.
All in all I am quite pleased with how this one turned out, and SNK is still supporting it as well with a new fan created character coming in the (near) future.
My main gripe is how bad it is at teaching the player how to get good at the game. In a world where Skullgirls, UNIST and Guilty Gear have made great strides to help newcomers get good at the game it's very much lagging behind.
I recommend getting in touch with the online (Discord) communities to learn the ropes.
I also wish it had a better story mode but I understand I might be in the minority when it comes to caring about that stuff.

Personally I think this is a really interesting game. Yes, the whole dungeon crawl premise is being over done, but I feel like this game captures it pretty well without making it overly difficult. A bit complex, yes, but it balances everything out with the equipment you can get and if you have the mind for it you will overcome any challenge thrown at you.
The game randomly generates the floors of a dungeon, with certain things being certain per floor, such as shops so you can spend the hard earned gold from killing monsters. Each class starts with two skills, and earns more from shops, searching bookshelves, and possible monster drops. The hunger system is actually a really interesting mechanic that adds that extra layer and helps to seperate it from other games of the genre. If your character gets to the point you are starving (I say if because food is quite generous in the game, unless you get really unlucky) your health regen stops entirely, making your only way to gain health potions and leveling up (which will become a lot more difficult even with great gear). You generally find the food on the floor or in boxes, and you can find rotten food for those times when you are real desperate and NEED your health regen back to get back into the fight.
The level up system is interesting as well. It's not your typical "Level up your skills and base stats" even though it uses some of those aspects. You get the choice of what you want to do with the points. You get 2 points to spend on your base stats, which I enjoy because the other games generally give you 4 or 5 making it rather easy to make a tank, DPS, or just impossible to hit character, and every other level up (I believe it's the odd number ones, if you prefer to keep track that way) give you one point for traits and one point for skills (HOWEVER you must keep in mind that in order to level up your skill you need to find a book for a skill first and waste your skill point learning it). The traits are interesting and vary from skills that increase your hunger so you won't have to worry about food to trap detection/disarming (Both from same trait/feat) so you can alter your character each run. OH, right, once a character is dead, that's it. So that means no "Oh, I'll run in, level up, die and start with him again" nope, none of that, it's on the spot thinking to keep you on your toes and make you think about what you level up before you jump right in.
All that being said, if you like the sound of that this game, I absolutely recommend it and think you should pick it up because you will have hours of fun playing it and seeing how well you end up doing. If not, well, I'm sure you'll find something that you will enjoy. After all, Steam has plenty of games for everyone.

VVVVVV takes its name from the game's main objective, which I shall not touch upon in order to leave the discovery to you. The first aspect of the game that took me by surprise is the superb 8-bit chiptune music. The only problem with that is that it does get repetitive only because it replays one single track for about 30 minutes at a time, until you complete each level. The graphics are imitating the general style of the Commodore 64, including its startup screen. VVVVVV's main platforming mechanic is the player's ability to flip the character's screen position vertically, going from bottom to top and vice versa. This makes for some complicated platforming in general, as well as some challenging and entertaining rooms. Because of the game's incredible difficulty, the developers have cleverly implemented checkpoints liberally throughout the game world, which cuts down on rage and frustration. With that said, VVVVVV still manages to be extremely difficult, and you should expect to die hundreds of times, if not one thousand times by the time you complete the game. The platforming and controls are not badly designed, as in Super Meat Boy, so do not confuse this well crafted, yet simplistic game with that developmental disaster. Younger generations of gamers may find the overall presentation of VVVVVV to be unique and hip, but as we all know, these graphics have been done before, about 30 years ago. One serious flaw is that there are no audio options for volume. The in-game default is quite higher than usual, and requires turning down in Windows. While the majority of the levels' rooms are a lot of fun, and well designed, some are simply unreasonable and require too much luck as opposed to actual precision and skill. Because of this, you will die many times and spend far too long attempting single rooms. Which also means being forced to listen to a single song on a loop, for the entire duration of your trials. This is something of a shortcoming and should have been avoided completely by the developers, as these uncalled-for rooms only add negatively to the experience. Even though you get unlimited lives and unlimited continues, having to repeat a single room hundreds of times in order to pass it gets boring, repetitive, annoying, and only serves the purpose of replacing actual content with limited and mundane game play. While the music is once again, excellent, there are only a few that repeat over and over, as the rest must be unlocked by finding and collecting certain orbs within the game world. There are also a few more game modes for the player to experiment with once the campaign has been completed. The storyline and ending are endearing and delightful, and once you complete the game, there is an overall feeling of satisfaction. VVVVVV is short but perfectly sweet.

Secondly, the game is poor - it's difficult to see players, combat isn't very enjoyable and the attempts at realism are ineffective due to both the small playerbase and the combat balance.
Bolt action rifles are the most common gun, which is historically accurate, but it isn't very fun to basically have entire teams of snipers. The scope you can attach to them is disorienting at best, ugly and unusable at worst.
Machine guns are largely ineffective. The sights make seeing enemies even more difficult than normal and you can't take cover while they're deployed, making you a sniper's (read: The whole enemy team) wet dream.
Barbed wire is interesting, if completely horrible. If you spend too long in it, you "succumb to your wounds" and die.
Fair enough.
However, the way it is implemented restricts your movement so much, that you can only leave and enter trenches from very specific points and going off track grinds you to a halt and kills you after a few seconds.
I believe the developers designed the attrition game mode (The proper trench warfare game mode) to have players running across no mans land in an attempt to take the enemy trench - as might be done in a real WW1 battle. Unfortunately, due to the tiny playerbase, the result currently is one trench being sniped by one guy lying on top of a crater in the middle of the battlefield. The little experience I did have with a large playerbase (I think some online group arranged a Verdun event or something) showed me that the normal gameplay isn't much better, with crowds of players in each piece of cover, as standing up or moving leads to being instantly shot by a swarm of snipers.
In conclusion, avoid this game - I haven't even touched upon the other 2 game modes, the redundancy of the gun variety, the poor gun balance, the technical issues (Your antivirus blocks the multiplayer!!!!!), or the cool but ultimately unused gas mask mechanic.

Getting lost in this huge and varied world is so great. Even in the age of Witcher 3, this game shows that grid-based movement can still be fun. I have a hard time explaining why but here are some possible factors:
- Enemies feel more menacing because you can't circle-strafe them, play with aggro range or exploit pathfinding bugs against them like in most free movement rpgs/fpss. So the dungeon feels more claustrophobic and menacing... I definitely don't feel that in Skyrim dungeons.
- Mapping out the dungeon square by square and paying close attention to your environment for secret buttons and switches feels great, and it's not the typical modern RPG experience. A free movement game can hardly hide a button somewhere on a wall and expect you to find it, here with the constrained views it works.
- The grid system allows for some very smart puzzles, I have to admit I sometimes give up and consult a walkthrough, but I enjoy their presence nonetheless!
And you get to control (read: juggle) 4 characters, so four times the RPG goodness!
All in all, you'll like it if you liked old-school RPGs like Dungeon Master, Eye of the Beholder and Lands of Lore: Throne of Chaos. But if you haven't played those games you should try it anyways! You might very well find that grid-based movement is a bit like pixel art: originally born of technical limitations, it can still bring a unique and interesting twist to a game.

An excellent strategy survival town-building simulator. It's like medieval SimCity, but without the bullcrap. There is no money, so you never have to worry about depts, markets, or any money related issues you find in building games. Rather, the game challenges you through the core components of the game like resources, citizen health, population, food, and space. You have to find a balance between all these components; that's the challenge, because achieving balance is hard as balls. Expand too quick, you might not have enough food to feed your people. Expand too slowly, and your people might age and die. It's a simple but extremely deep game.

Do I recommend this game? For the most part, but with some caveats. Let's start with the good:
- Great story with great writing. Though not all trhat original, the story still tugs at the heartstrings throughout.
- Outstanding voice acting. The two characters which are voice acted sound like natural, relatable human beings.
- Great sound design, which includes the original music.
-Lots of items to pick up and examine. Really helped flesh out the characters and make the world feel alive.
Now that that's out of the way, what about the not-so-great? Well..
- It takes two hours to beat. Two. And that was with me taking my time. Now that's not to say it doesn't tell a good story in that timeframe, it's just that I wouldn't pay the full $20 for it (which luckily, I didn't). Definitely get it while on sale or with a bundle.
- Very little replay value. As is standard with "walking simulators" (at least the ones I've played) there's very little that would bring me back. No alternate or secret endings or anything like that. I suppose I might pick it up again just to hear the story one more time or find items I hadn't discovered before.
- Runs poorly on my R9 290x with i5 6600 and 16GB ddr4 RAM. It was usually somewhere between 35-50 fps, and that's with some of the options turned down. I can run DOOM at max settings with no lag. This game doesn't have an excuse.
And that's about it. Hopefully this helps you know what you're getting into. If you're into these types of games, you'd enjoy it. JUst know what you're getting into first.

But I'm confident this will be looking great in th next year or two when they finished polishing the title and giv eit its final form.

Death is an extremely complex theme, with a lot of meanings depending on your cultural background. But in Verdun, it becomes almost meaningless, and given that its objective is to loyally represent the memory of World War 1, I'd say mission very well accomplished.
I won't lie, you will die A LOT, especially in the beggining. And even that is an understatement: if you poke your head out of the trench for more than 2 seconds, you'll promptly be sniped by a top level guy; if you charge the enemy trench, you either get sniped by said guy, or get stuck in barbed wire only to be sniped by said guy; and if you lie down in your trench, trying not to get sniped, an enemy will breach your trench and stab you in the back while you were trying to counter-snipe the original guy.
That said, it is still very cathartic, especially when, after dying A LOT, your team manages to grind its way into taking the enemy trench, which depicts the memory of the war it's trying to represent a whole lot better than many triple A games out there (no finger pointing).
And from time to time, you'll get one of those breakthrough moments when you save the entire team from being flanked because you threw a grenade that killed 5 guys trying to force their way into the trench. And those moments are so satisfying that you'll spend the entire conclusion of your review of this game bragging about it.
But if you tire of dying, you can always flee in the opposite direction to hear your Scottish officer angrily telling you to "GET BACK IN LINE, LAD!" and be executed for desertion.

The King of Fighters XIV is SNK fixing exactly what a lot of people complained about in KoF XIII: No more infinites everywhere, a bigger roster, and an easier excecution (maybe a bit too much?). One of the biggest positive point to me is also how the tier list isn't as important as in other fighting games (if you every watch competition, you'll see that a lot of different characters are played, and the characters thought to be "top tier" are far from being mandatory to win).
If you've ever dreamed of playing a KoF but always found it too be too hard, it's the perfect KoF to start with. The game is really easiest KoF to play, and there's some tutorial to get you started and learn some cool basic combo. There's also a tutorial to expain the basic mechanics of the game like small jumps, fast jumps etc ...
The only complain could be the graphics, but it's understandable: SNK was nearly bankrupt, and using an old engine allowed them to put a lot of characters quickly which is why this game has such a big roster from day one.
Also we should have at least 1 more update, and unlike a lot of gaming compagnies they don't shove DLC every week to milk you.

VVVVVV is quite fun, colourful, and quite an interesting experience to say the least. It has a very decent progression of difficulty, starting out easy as it shows you the tricks and mechanics, then it gets harder as it steps it up creatively with what you've been taught. It's pretty short, I clocked in around 2 hours, but it offers plenty of side challenges and bonus levels to keep going when you're done. Many other people state that this game is very difficult, excluding the final stretch of the game, I felt it was actually kind of easy to beat....
.....UNLESS YOU'RE GOING FOR A COMPLETIONIST RUN. For the sake of your sanity, do NOT do an completionist run. There are trinkets collectables that some require some tricky searching, others that require insane platforming and timing and abuse of checkpoints (Veni, Vidi, Vici, I'm looking at you) and then there's the trophies to collect which require beating the game in limited time, only dying a certain amount of times (The games easy by itself it's just that checkpoints are common, so Death is cheap, VERY often, but cheap.) beating the game WITHOUT dying....
I do recommend this game, but know what you're getting into if you go for 100% completion.

Roguelikes are characterized by a list of gameplay mechanics, such as procedural level generation, permadeath, turn-based gameplay, and randomized loot. The latter includes random stat generation for equipment and unidentified potions and scrolls. This game includes all of them, but unfortunately not much else. As it stands right now, the game is a barebones roguelike in terms of gameplay. Compared to its competition in terms of gameplay, the game is running far behind. If Claustrophobia wants to stand out - even while in early access - it should have gameplay elements unique to it. Be it a fusion of gameplay elements from different genres, or simply a new set of mechanics not seen before.
The gameplay is fairly simple. You start your character by picking a class, and (if desired) you can do some very minor modifications. You are subsequently dropped in a dungeon where you get to fight a very small variety of standard mobs. Think of the rats, zombies, skeletons, and spiders kind. Your character has a set of abilities that cost 'mana/stamina' to use, but at the very start you will not have access to many of them. You defeat the aforementioned enemies, pick up whatever gear you find and wear it if its an upgrade or sell it if it's a downgrade if you encounter a shop.
The game controls pretty well. The animations and UI are very indicative of the commands you give, and that's pretty much all that can be said about it. WIth turn-based gameplay in the standard roguelike fashion there is not much to controls. While the game has fairly little 'meat' to it as of yet, the controls are not convoluted. What I like is that you can bring out the map and click on locations to auto-walk there. Skill use and target selection is also very intuitive with a nice layout indicating range.
So far the difficulty of the game is lacking. While there are traps around, I have yet to step on one by accident. My juggernaut without any trapfinding skill is pretty much capable of seeing and disarming every trap so far encountered. While disarming a trap can still fail (and deal damage in the process), the game's health regeneration mechanics make this trivial.
Every turn you automatically recover health as long as you are not starving (in which case there is simply no health recovery). While enemies don't seem to roam through the dungeons (they stay nicely put in their enclosed rooms) waiting and healing is not dangerous at all. With the common availability of food, it is even possible to easily kill bosses simply by beelining to the entrance stairs and safely recovering your health on the previous dungeon floor, before you can resume killing the boss again.
As is common with roguelikes, positioning is key. You don't want enemies to surround you. Instead, enemies should be funneled through so only one enemy at a time can engage you. With the dungeon level design this is fairly easy to do. There is (so far, as I have discovered) only one enemy type with a ranged attack who can foul this tactic.
Gold seems to be too common in the game, especially since you can sell the gear you don't use. So far I have been able to purchase any gear I wanted from the shops, which means your character is more often than not well supplied with equipment of fairly high strength.
With the aforementioned ease of getting equipment, I often even forget to level because the 2 points I can add to my stats makes barely an impact based on the gear upgrades I'm getting. This makes the attribute system rather pointless. Even worse, item requirements are not tied to the base score of an attribute, but to the total score. Thus, you could wear +strength items to sufficiently increase you strength in order to wear the gear you want. This often makes me forget 2 attribute scores are given every time you level.
Every odd level you also get 2 further points to level in a skill tree and a specific ability. This system is really too convoluted. First you will need to find a skillbook of the ability you would like to use. Then you have to read it, but reading it requires a minimum amount of points in a certain skill (e.g., defense skill, or assassination skill). If you have enough points in that, you can read the book but haven't learned the skill yet. You then have to spent one point into the ability in order to learn and use it.
This system should be reworked, because it makes you require 3 things before you can use an ability, while abilities should be fairly important as they diversify combat.
Graphically, the game reminds me a lot of Pixel Dungeon (free mobile game for android devices), which actually does a much better job gameplay wise. It is nice that this game changes the looks of your character based on the gear being worn. The graphical style is good, and makes also for a clear UI. Unfortunately so far there is fairly little variation in the graphics, but this is not a point I will stress too much since it is still in early access, and graphics aren't the most important factor in roguelikes.
The game does what all other roguelikes do, but nothing extra. It currently lacks a lot of content and doesn't stand out among its peers. This is basically the harshest criticism of the game there is, because making a roguelike (or roguelite) nowadays seems common practice among indie developers. For now it is "just another roguelike", and despite its early access status nothing has been added that hints at interesting new mechanics. Its lack of content furthermore makes it lack much replay value aside from trying out the different classes.
If you want to satisfy your hunger for rogue-likes, try out Pixel Dungeon (mobile game, great controls, good graphics, and currently better gameplay than this game while also being fairly bare-bones) or Tales of Maj'Eyal, which is a difficult and full-featured roguelike.

An excellent strategy survival town-building simulator. It's like medieval SimCity, but without the bullcrap. There is no money, so you never have to worry about depts, markets, or any money related issues you find in building games. Rather, the game challenges you through the core components of the game like resources, citizen health, population, food, and space. You have to find a balance between all these components; that's the challenge, because achieving balance is hard as balls. Expand too quick, you might not have enough food to feed your people. Expand too slowly, and your people might age and die. It's a simple but extremely deep game.

This game is exactly what I'm looking for.
I love games where you get to build a town, manage resources, grow your population -- but all the other games inevitably lead to war. Either I "have" to attack someone else to get their resources, or someone else attacks me, even if I'm being peaceful. Those games are fun too, but sometimes I just want to build and create and grow.
This game does that.
And it's HARD.
I'm still fairly new at it. Each time I play, I get better. Definitely go through the tutorials first. I tried jumping right in and had no idea what I was doing. The tutorials are quick and easy, enough to get you started. But you'll still be doing a lot more experimenting and problem solving as you go.
One thing I miss about this game, that I wish it had, was some kind of "tech research" that could upgrade my buildings and resource effectiveness. One thing the game prides itself on is letting you build "anything" right from the start. That makes it both fun and hard at the same time. So many ways to start. So many temptations to grow too fast. But -- I'd still like to be able to upgrade my existing buildings (make them bigger/higher on the same plot of land, use resources more effectively, produce tools faster, etc). It'd be cool to "unlock" a few special/unique buildings as a reward for your progress and research so far too.
But I *LOVE* that you're not at war with any other town or nation. This is a game about planning, survival, strategy, and resource management. And there's a lot to keep track of -- just when you've got it all balanced and everybody working their jobs, someone dies of old age. You're constantly juggling and balancing a lot of things -- food, resources, the weather, population growth, everything. A great challenge. But fun and addicting too.
It's my understanding that one guy developed the whole game too. Kudos to you, sir. Job well done. This is a great game. Somehow it's both relaxing and stressful at the same time. lol. A worthy challenge. Yet a simple, enjoyable, peaceful, relaxing fun game.
I recommend this game.

Not because he kills me, but once you realise you can literally just roll under every attack he has, and parry almost all of them, he's basically just another regular Hollow.

My cousin and I preordered this game and started playing it as soon as it was released. I'll be honest, it's not what I expected at all. I was hoping for another Test Drive Unlimited, so for the first while playing it I didn't like it much. We ended up stopping for three months before picking it up again and now it is one of my favorite games. They've made a lot of changes and fixed a lot of things, but I also like the game for what it is now, not what I wanted it to be.
I've spent hours just driving aimlessly to see what I can find, more than half the time I'm not even on a road, I'm using a RAID spec vehicle (think offroad racing truck type of vehicle) to drive where there aren't even roads because the team even put detail into those parts of the map.
Speaking of Specs, that's what makes this game so cool. Currently, I am using a 1969 Camaro for all races. I have a version that is basically an offroad buggy meant for driving where there aren't roads, another that is a high-performance circuit racer, a street racing version, a dirt track version, and a NFS-type high-performance street race version. The same car becomes 5 VASTLY different cars, each handling differently and meant for different types of races and terrains. You simply can't drive a Circuit car in a RAID race, that'd be like driving a formula one car in a rally, it just doesn't work. The same is true vice versa. But you can use the same car as both specs if you want.
The story mode is pointless, I won't disagree with that, but this game is meant to be an MMO, the story doesn't really matter. It's only there to introduce you to the different specs for PVP events. It is still fun with a crew of course, but pretty boring by yourself. My cousin and I never even finished it. We got as far as unlocking the last SPEC and then focused on PVP events and faction events. PVP events and faction events are what's the most fun. They are races of all types across the US. My favorite race is a RAID race going down the side of a snowy mountain, it's high speed and there are no roads. Faction events can vary in length between less than 10 minutes to over an hour. That seems crazy at first but with a crew it is fun.
The entire map is covered with challenges like speed, escape, jump, raceline, etc. to get upgrades for your car like loot drops in an MMO. It's a great way to keep just driving interesting as well. But most of the time you will probably avoid them if you're just driving because really, this game makes just driving feel great.
I'm looking forward to what is planned to be added to this game, they said they will support it for a long time and I really hope so. This is the kind of game you can drive for hours without even doing anything and still enjoy yourself, whether or not there is even a road in visible distance of you.

Thismay not be a good thing if you're a roguelike veteran who makes very few mistakes. Great CCG. Can be thought of as a Hearthstone++.
Major differences from Hearthstone:
- Combat happens in a similar way to Magic: you choose the attackers and then your opponent chooses which creatures blocks which.
- Damage from combat is NOT permanent.
- Uses the concept of lands (called sigils in this game)
- Multicolor decks
- Less focus on RNG
- Fast spells (spells that you can cast when your opponent declares an attack / ends the turn)
They took Hearthstone and then tried to make it feel a little bit more like Magic. While the changes may look small, they truly improve the gameplay.

If you can't tell from the number of hours I've played it, I really love this game.  If I were to design my own roguelike, it would pretty much start out like this one.
As a fan of roguelikes, Claustrophobia really hits the spot when I feel hungry for some beatdown, both given and taken.  I'll be cruising along, crushing little monsters, looting some neat gear, until I hit a room full of monsters looking at me funny.  I died to many such rooms until I learned a few tricks that made it easier, and even then I would still die, mainly from making "stupid" mistakes.  An unforgiving roguelike?  Now there's a tautology if I ever saw one.
About the Early Access status...  I've given feedback for many games in the past (not only on Steam) but I've never seen a developer be so receptive to his players' comments.  The interaction is timely and courteous; the developer is a real professional in every sense of the word.  This tells me this little gem of a game will grow to become something quite extraordinary.  With a 5$ pricetag, it is a steal.

Quick Overlook: 8/10
Though never playing the first Homefront game, I found it easy to dive head first in to this one. There's a compelling story, and the game stays true to it's atmosphere. It performs well, and has many fun gameplay elements. It's a semi-open world experience with minor parkour mechanics that give off a wonderful feeling of freedom and exploration. Other than a few visual bugs, and story ruts, this is a great game that I suggest anyone to buy. If you're on the edge about the price, then it's worth it to wait for a sale.
Homefront: Revolution takes place after the first game, but even if you haven't played the first game you'll have no trouble diving in to this one. The story goes through multiple dull spots, but is overall compelling and enjoyable. I felt a near constant insentive to move to the next objective, or a sense of urgency when things were going downhill and people were relying on me. This game does a wonderful job at selling just how brutal and oppresive the North Korean forces are within the story. With every few small victories, it feels like you have one big defeat. It's a constant uphill and downhill story that will really make the player have a sense of whats going on in this world. The characters are somewhat forgettable through the first bit of the story. You only really start having connections with the main characters as far as halfway through the game, but by them you'll have developed a certain sense of care and feeling.
This game looks incredible, and I expect no less from the Cryengine. Even beyond the superior engine, the game looks quite realistic, and with relativley no performance cost. I played through the game at all high settings with a GTX 970, 8gb RAM, and an i5, and I only experianced a few frame drops here and there. The lighting and weather is another stunning factor of this game. The lighting looks realistic, across all the weathers and times of day. I was specifically surprised to see how realistically dark the night time got. The days and nights cycle which is a nice touch in an open world game, and theres even a chance for overcast or raint weather. The architecture varies from district to disctrict, and sometimes I found myself just stopping to look at the crumbling skylines in war torn areas, or the prestine white concrete nearer to the heart of the NK stronghold. This does apocalyptic ruin like no other that I've seen before, it's simply breathtaking. On the contrary, the North Korean stronghold structures contrast very nice with the jagged un-even ruin. The dark gray metal and uniform look make it easy to tell when you're entering a heavily fortified area, even in the more put together areas. The character design is stunning, and gritty. Same applies to the weapons, which have plenty of character simply due to all of the things attatched to and hanging off of them.
The open world gameplay though reptitive at time, never failed to make me bored. The cycle of liberating areas and slowly taking over chunks of the map, to see the resistence move in and occupy it remaind appealing through the whole game. I even went back before completing the story to ensure I'd captured all the zones.The gunplay is smooth and accurate, and the animations that go along with the guns and movement feel fluid and natural. There are actually only a handfull of guns in the game, but for each base weapon, a modified version can be created on the fly. You can go from an assault rifle with an ACOG and muzzle brake to an LMG with a EOtech and a laser sight within a matter of seconds and a few clicks. This system, and the fact that you can carry up to two weapons of your choice (You always have to carry the base pistol which can be modified too) makes gunplay that much better, and truly prepares you for any scenario. On top of the extensive gunplay, theres also 4 grenade types, each coming with 4 different ways to use them, be it by drone, proximity, stuck to surfaces, or simply thrown, I found myself using all of the functions for different purposes throughout the game. The traversal of the world in this game is quite appealing, especially with the parkour mechanics. The parkour mechanics are nothing to right home about, simple climbing, jumping, and running, but it makes for some fun vantage points and stealth tactics. Speaking of stealth, there are many ways you can go about things when it comes to taking down enemies. On top of the extensive guns and grenades, theres traps set around the map for you to use, as well as motobikes, and the ability to recruit fellow fighters. Though run and gun seemed to be my most popular method, there is definately different ways you can go about taking down the moderatley sized roster of enemies.

Let me just tell you first, Legend of Grimrock 1 was a game I really enjoyed, simply because it was fun and not too complicated. It didn`t cater to challenge the titans of the genre and I never expected it to, so I had a blast. I counted on Legend of Grimrock 2 to be of the same caliber, maybe a bit longer, maybe a bit more fancy looking.

I counted wrong.

Shortly into my first game (on normal difficulty) there was this plant-boss. It could not be just danced around mindlessly. I certainly couldn`t just tank it with my four-human party. Already on the first level I had to learn to play this game not as the next easy-money follow-up, but as a new game. I was really caught off guard, but I still had no idea what was waiting up ahead. Next, I went through a phase of irritation as the game was wrong. Certainly you have been challenged as well, but when were you actually proven to be the one wrong? I wasn`t wrong, of course, at least not for a long time. Then I realized I was. The irritating game gas fun. A lot of fun.

Now, for a breakdown of the goods and the bads of this game. Let`s do the bads first.

BAD:

How do I put this gently? The game has (almost) no story. There. Put. Not gently. There are no NPCs to interact with and the story, told through a few scrolls and wall-writings, is thin, very thin.

Then there are the new mechanic of injury to bodyparts. Now this is one unnecessary annoyance added to the game that really is nothing other than a new condition (poison, disease, etc), that can hit any of your party members almost anytime throughout the game. Oh, there are plenty of ways to avoid it and cure it but FOCL, THIS is not fun, nor does it add to the experience. (Okay, I can see it have an impact on ironman and the number of potions available, but at least for me, this is a direct drawback.)

The game is surprisingly hard even on normal mode. For me, this was overcomeable. However, if you do have a lot of trouble with the Viper-Roots, and the things beyond, there is no shame in starting over on Easy. You should ENJOY the game, not SUFFER through.

The game is extremely puzzle oriented. Even on the main…uh…”story”. (I know what I said about story above, thank you!) Yep, puzzles are heavily a part of the main “story”-line. So much so that you may end up stuck on puzzles, unable to progress the game. As a former AD&D DM I do not quite like this approach. Puzzles (mostly) are for side-quests and bonus objectives, not for progressing the game. At the very least, answers or hints should be present for completing the main “story” line puzzles.

GOOD:

The graphics are great. The outdoors are great. The underwaters are great. The beaches and forests are great and so on. Music and sound effects are also very good. Nice balance and composition. Take Medusa (or is it Gorgon) as an example. The scream that accompanies her petrifying attack is frightening enough to create a chill (thrill, even) without having the real Medusa in the living-room also cry out…. (I`m gonna be in a lotta trouble for this if she ever creates a Steam account….)

The game is actually quite non-linear. And it works pretty well. It may be limited a bit by your play style, but really, this is a feature that is rather impressive in this genre of games.
The game has a fantastic old-time grid-based game atmosphere. In LoG 1 you were meant to dodge and dance around your enemy to be able to overcome them. A great way to evolve the mechanics from the old-time grid-based games where this was often an exploit. In Log 2, the monsters have evolved to counter (partly) this strategy forcing YOU to evolve also. This also probably means LoG 2 isn`t the best starting point for newcomers to grid-based RPGs.

I above claimed the puzzle-heavyness of this game to be a bad thing. I still mean that within the boundries set above. But after having consolidated myself with the fact that this game IS puzzle-heavy and that puzzles ARE a part of the main “story”-line, I learned to appreciate them. The designers of the puzzles of Legend of Grimrock 2 are geniuses. The depths of some of the puzzles are amazing. I mean, it`s one thing to appreciate the puzzle itself, but if you look at the process it must have been to PLAN these puzzles, your jaw should drop. If it doesn`t, well, if you can`t see it, just open your mouth and sit still until drool comes out and know that this is the right thing to do.

There are some epic battles in this game, ones that really make you feel you`ve accomplished something when you overcome them. There are also some (nice? Hehe, lol) surprises that may or may not be avoided, depending on how well you explore.

The game most certainly has a replayable value. I`ve done three runs (132 hours) so far and I may do another one, on easy, to breeze through. I love the game and there are some race/class combinations I still want to try.

CONCLUSION:

Is it the best game I`ve played? Is it the best grid-based RPG I`ve played?

No and no.

But the competition isn`t really fair. I`m a long-time fan of the Might & Magic series and I really doubt that any game will ever topple Might & Magic III - The Isle of Terra from my throne. The Might & Magic series has a long-running story that (imho) is really good. These are complicated games in vast worlds. So any one (or two) new games (in an old genre) can hardly ever compete with that for me. (NOTE that Might & Magix X is not included in my praise. I do not currently recommend that game.)

However, Legend of Grimrock has at the very least made me make the comparison. Had LoG had the same depth of story, it would have had the last element (pun intended) to challenge the best grid-based RPGs of old.

It will still go down in history as one of the obelisks of the genre.

In my humble opinion, it is an 7/10, compared to ALL the grid-based games I`ve played (this includes the MMs, the Eye of the Beholder series, Lands of Lore, Ultima Underworld, Elder Scrolls, etc). Lack of story is the main reason it does not quite reach the top, but the annoyance of bodypart injuries also pull down a bit. All in all puzzle-design is so good it actually gives a plus to the game, even though I think there are too many puzzles in the main storyline. Non-linearity, nostalgia, atmosphere and replayability are also all good factors. The skill system is a bit simple and could certainly be improved, but it works and does not lower the quality of the game.

I wholeheartedly recommend this game (and LoG 1). It`s a lot of game for the money. It is truly well designed. If you take it for what it is, you will have many hours of fun gameplay to look forward to.

Highly addicting game. Your main goal is to serve as many customers as you can during the workday by pressing correct button combinations for each order. You're single worker in restaurant which means you'll serve several customers at once and doing catering jobs at the same time. Customers will not wait for you forever, if you're too late serving them or not giving them exactly what they wanted, they'll leave unsatisfied, giving your restaurant negative buzz for next day, which means - less customers. Basically, your restaurant's success depends on your speed, accuracy and multitasking skills (serving 5+ orders at the same time). There's also a "manager" part of the game (between workdays) where you organize menu list for next day, responding to mails, buying upgrades, etc. Take note that this game is not a manager simulation, success depends of your skills as a cook.
This is not a game for relaxation - it's very tense from the start, the more successful you are it will be more difficult for you in later game (more complex orders, more customers) and again, you'll feel more accomplished as the game progresses. Game comes packed with many challenges and goals, including multiplayer/co-op - enough to give you dozens of playing hours. Recommended!

Through simplicity comes complexity with Banished.  Banished is perhaps one of the more difficult city building games I've ever played, and it's not the difficulty of the AI or the scaricity of the resources, it's your own doing that will result in your downfall.  Banished is a "teeter-tooter" type of game where success is determined on how well you can balance all factors of the game.  Any resource overlooked can result in your town becoming a ghost town.  It is a fun game and I highly recommend it.  Though the structures you can build and the resources you start with are essentially the same, no two games will ever be the same.  Pick up this game and test your own patience and attention to detail.

First off, I'm not saying that this is a bad game. As it is, Claustrophobia is a fully fuctional roguelike dungeon crawler that certainly captures overly unforgiving nature of the genre. However, this is not to say that the game is all that great either, especially when compared to other (very) similar games.
While most roguelikes tend to follow a similar gameplay regime, Claustrophobia does very little to make itself stand out from other games, namely Dungeons of Dredmor. Aesthetically, it uses the same 3D top-down dungeon view as Dredmor, and the cartoony style of the sprites is very similar as well. Even the title screen appears to have taken influence with the logos using almost matching fonts and the backdrop depicting a very similar scene. And while Dungeons of Dredmor implemented an extensive skill system and an imaginative cast of baddies, Claustrophobia seriously lacks in the character customization department. And the enemies? Zombies, rats, spiders; Bland, bland, bland.
They even reused the same tileset across different floors. The game just seems to lack any creativity whatsoever.
Again, I'm not saying that this is a terrible game, but I don't understand why anyone would choose to play it when there are far better games elsewhere. Maybe it's still to early to judge since it's still in early access, but seriously, if you're going to spend $5 then you may as well just buy Dungeons of Dredmor (it's the same price by the way).

This is a first and foremost a really great game. It has taken obvious inspiration from Dungeons of Dredmor, and in many ways I think it personally succeeds and being superior. The animations, the moving, the combat is so lovely and clean compared to D&D which I find jittery and sometimes buggy.
At the moment though, C:TDS is very much an unfinished game. Once you get the hang of it, and it will take you several new characters, and once you have descended through each floor and fought the final "boss" you have then reached the end of the current version (I think this is about 5 floors?). You are told how the game is in alpha stage and that there are plans for much more content, which I think will truely make this game fly. But for now, you are sent back to the beginning of the (randomly generated) dungeon to face harder and meaner foes.
As I mentioned before, when/ if this game is fully finished, I believe it will be very successful. Much like D&D.
The loot system is superb. I found myself grinning with glee everytime I stumbled upon a new weapon/ piece of armour/ piece of jewellery with awesome stats and felt very satisfied as these improved stats worked their magic quite visibly so.
The combat is beautiful, and so... Idk, clean! It has nice sound effects which makes killing enemies very satisfying.
The hunger system is a nice little added tidbit which makes it very challenging. You will be very pleased to find a big slab of meat lying on the ground, even if it is green and potentially unsafe to eat, as long as if satisfies your hunger, you're happy!
One final note/ plea: Please devs! Please complete this game! I love it so much and it would be even more perfect if it were complete with the features hinted in the final message at the end of the dungeon.
Overall I give this game an 8.5/10. I will happily update my review once the game has more content.

I wish the reviews had a neutral option. The game has so much potential and with a few tweaks could be the top CCG. It by far has the best single player & AI of any game in the genre. There is a very fun and free single player mode vs the ai that gives you lots of cards / gold. They are very generous and make the collection building much easier than other games. The ranked system is actually very well done. You need 100 points to rank up and every win gives you some points and a loss takes some away. You gain more points for wins than points loss for losing.
I have a few key issues with this game which is the main reason I only really play to do daily quest now and instead play Elder Scrolls Legends with most of my time. Elder Scrolls Legends is by far the bes CCG available and it's a shame nobody has heard of. It's kind of funny that Dire Wolf is also doing Elder Scrolls, but yet that game blows away Eternal. Anyway, let's get into the actual problem.
The decks are just too large with 70 cards, but they do allow for up to 4 copies of each card. Carrying 4 copies of each with 70 cards is NOT the same as having a 35 card deck with 2 copies of each. Your extra copies or even all of the copies of 1 card can and often do end up in the latter 2/3rds of the deck which never see play. There are just too many total cards to be able to have very consistent gameplay. I have spent a little over half of my time playing ranked matches and I have had only a couple of games that actually felt like good solid games on both sides. Just for a comparison, Elder Scrolls has almost every game feel like a good close game with the winner being determined based on skill more than rng. The other 99% of games were just blowout wins or losses. Too often the game is decided in the opening hand. Whoever wins or loses is more often a question of which player gets a better distribution of their sigils rather than who actually played better or had a better constructed deck.
You put 50 cards into the deck and then you are forced to put at least 25 Sigil cards. If you want to play a 1 cost unit then you must first play 1 sigil. To play a 2 cost unit requires you to have played 2 total sigils and you can only play 1 sigil per turn. In theory this is a good idea, but their system needs some serious tweaking to make the gameplay feel balanced. 90% of the games end with 50+ cards left into the deck. Too often you will have cards in your hand, but then can't play them because you draw a sigil for 6 turns in a row. The other thing that happens is that you only draw minions / spells, but no sigils. I hate winning a game for no reason other than my opponent drew sigils for 6 straight turns while I bashed his face in. I also equally hate losing for this same reason.  The mulligan system will allow you to either keep or replace all of your cards which does not help these things from happening.
If the developers will fix the sigil issue and cut the size of the deck by about 10 cards then would be a perfect game.  The way the game is right now I would recommend it if you like Magic as it's really close in gameplay or hate the other CCGs you're currently playing. You would be better off checking out Elder Scrolls Legends because until this game is more balanced, ESL is just a better game all around.

Like many others I grew up as a typical teenage Magic nerd and naturally I am interested in any digital version that could capture me the same way. Other than the timeless and amazing Shandalar, I have yet too find a really decent and accessible digital competitor, until now!
Eternal is far from archaic and has happily and correctly snapped up all the best things about Hearthstone, while also integrating the best of the more advanced mechanics from Magic the Gathering.
Pros:
+ Clear and inviting interface. Smooth graphics and decent art for an indy title. Performance is very good and I have yet to encounter any disconnects or crashes. The cards and their actions are all very nicely and satisfyingly animated. It is very reminiscent of Heartstone in this regard. Lots of attention to details, like high power creatures having an extra 'oomph' when they do damage
+ The card-playing mechanics are significantly improved and much more in-depth than Hearthstone. One of the key factors here is the way blocking works. Just like Magic, you can't just attack whatever creature you want. Rather you declare your attackers and the opponent can then choose to block them (or not) and assign his blockers as seems best. This is a fundamental change from HS and it makes the game feel much more strategic. You also have interaction with the graveyard, interrupt spells, artifacts, attachments (enchantments) and plenty of dimensions you can build your decks around, including new ones not seen in classic MtG or HS.
+ Similarly, the game uses a mix between hearthstone and Magic when it comes to mana. You need to budget for mana cards and there are many variants of them. This adds an extra dimension to deck-building as many creatures and spells directly interact with them. It can result in some dead hands although this is very rare (the game secretly ensure you get two power cards should you decide to mulligan)
+ Despite offering more depth, the game is far more accessible and generous than HS. The devs have correctly understood that for a game like this to gain traction when HS is so dominant on the scene, you need to let players get a lof of cards quickly so you can open up the choices. Almost anything you can do in the game results in a constant flow of cards, be it Ranked, Gauntlet, Forge or Draft. You also get lots of crafting dust so you can get those key cards to make your deck work and there are plenty of quest rewards and themed decks coming your way.
+ The four game types mentioned above are likewise very well designed. Ranked is your standard ladder. Forge is very similar to Arena in HS. You pick from three options at a time until you have 25 cards, then you play against a gauntlet of AIs, each win upping your reward. Draft is a direct derivative of Magic's drafting format. You and other players take turns picking cards from 4 random booster packs, and then you craft a 45-card deck. You then have a gauntlet of 7 real players to beat. Did I mention that in both forge and draft you get to keep ALL cards?
+ Balance is on-point to the extent that it can be for the moment. So far I haven't seen any outrageous or unfair cards that cannot be countered. Some deck types will lose to others more often than not, but that's just card games for you. There is of course a meta and I'm sure the deck types narrow as you go further up the ranks.
Cons:
- I honestly don't have any serious complaints to mention. The game is still early access but it certainly feels like a full game. The casual mode is not yet active, and that is a bit annoying. When you try out new decks, Gauntled mode against the AI won't really give you a good benchmark and you are going to be hesitant to take it straight to ranked. Luckily you can still play against your friends as much as you like, as if it were casual.
- I would like to see a tournament mode added into the game as well. It would be a lot of fun to participate in elimination-style competitions against other players and of course your friends on a daily basis, with rewards for finishing in the top 2 or 3. Larger seasonal tournaments would be really cool as well.
EDIT:
- One serious issue with the game currently is the mandatory campaign tutorial. You have to play 4 games for each color, for a total of 21 games, one of which can take a good few tries. You are limited to really poor starter decks that are very boring to play. This can really turn off a lot of players and it takes a good 2-3 hours to get through. If I hadn't already known this going in, I might not have continued playing and that would have been a great shame. I really hope the devs revisit and shortens this soon. 5 mandatory games would've been plenty. Gauntlet mode is already a great way to learn the game.
In summary: a great free-to-play title with a complete lack of paywalls or pay-to-win mechanics. It combines the best of Magic and HS into a brilliant mix and you will get addicted.

Im writing this because this series doesnt get anywhere near enough recognition. I bought bouth games on a whim during a sale, because I like old school PC stuff, love RPG's, and remember seeing Notch (yes creator of Minecraft Notch) rave about these on twitter, and saw a video done by LGR.

If you enjoy RPG's at all, then do not hesitate and buy both of these games, they are worth any price and you will not be disapointed. This series deserves to be regarded as some of the best games of all time, with other greats, but instead it seems they fly just beneath the radar for far too many.
