Homefront: The Revolution is a surprisingly good shooter. In terms of gameplay it plays very similar to a toned-down Far Cry 3 and 4, being a (semi) open world shooter with a lot of weapon customization.
-	First and foremost, the
The fighting, the shooting, the sneaking and stabbing all works very well in the game. Apart from the few linear mission, the objectives in the game can be approached from (literally) any angle. Want to enter a stronghold? Blow it open, sneak through the sewers or jump over the wall with a bike. It all works. You can go in alone or recruit other resistance fighters for backup. A respectable difficulty makes it necessary to plan actions ahead, as even on “medium”, a few well-placed bullets can kill you and med packs are always in short supply. On the other hand, the game features the so called “yellow zones”, which are under stricter control and require a very stealthy approach, were you must hide your weapons and avoid patrols. This provides a very nice change in pacing in the game.

-
The game has a very well implemented (if not entirely realistic) weapon modification element. Guns can be modified quite extensively and, a very nice detail, are modified on screen, with parts being added or removed by the character.
-
That is really were the game really takes the cake. While the visuals of a war-torn city are bleak, it does fit very well into the overall game. Especially the depressing looks of the yellow zones, with the propaganda loudspeakers, public arrests and seemingly omnipresent cameras is very atmospheric. A nice detail is how the environment slowly changes with your actions. As the resistance becomes more and more bold and successful, so change the streets. Soldiers are becoming less visible, only appearing in groups or with armored escorts, resistance members moving more open and even whole blocks coming under resistance control. This subtly changes during gameplay and is a very nice detail.
-
While the story is nothing special by itself, it works. A very basic story, with no failed grandeur or big deconstruction efforts. Which is somewhat refreshing these days. Voice acting is good across the board and the characters are mostly likeable. (Those who should be anyway).
-	All this is rounded up by an
. Were a group of up to four resistance fighters must fulfill a series of objectives in the city. Again, a very open approach (for the most part) to the mission objectives and excellent immersive voice overs. Alas, it is somewhat dead now, which is a pity.
-	The game feels somewhat short and rushed in parts. There are clear drops in quality and sometimes the open world clashes with the story progression (which is hardly noticeable even then, as it works very well on other occasions).
-	The visuals can be very bleak and depressing. Some areas being outright ugly. It does fit in the game, but a dot of green would have been nice here and there.
-	The graphics are on (very few) occasions downright ugly, and there are also some glitches here and there. Additionally, the player sometimes can get a bit stuck in the rubble, if exploring too vigorously.
-	Some of the (completely optional) “job” objectives are a bit difficult if you are too thoroughly in clearing the zones, as the required enemies don’t show up as much. Which is only a nitpick for completionists, as getting all jobs done doesn’t even net an achievement.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Quick Review: Great Magic: The Gathering inspired digital CCG. Amazing UI, loads of features, brilliant draft system, and some truly awesome cards. But... as an MTG derivative, you have to be able to accept mana flooding/screwing.
Long Review:
I wanted to put some good hours into the game before reviewing (18 as of this post). I've completed the Tutorial Quests, four Forges, one draft and a ton of ranked games. Oh, and I've been playing Magic since Arabian Nights and Hearthstone since Beta.
To start, this is NOT Hearthstone. It is Magic the Gathering. Everything you know from Hearthstone doesn't apply here. You have to play "power" cards (mana/lands), so you need to know how to balance a deck. The system will try to do it for you and they start you out with a full set of 40 "dual stones", but to be good at the game you'll need to understand how to get the proper ratios. You also don't choose how you attack. You choose WHO attacks, and the opponent chooses blocks.
Once you accept that this is Magic on digitial steroids, you can really enjoy the game. Note: the initial tutorial quests are drudgery. Your decks suck and the mana ratios aren't great. They should really let you skip parts of this, but they don't. JUST PLAY THROUGH. It's worth it. You'll get a free Forge, which will net you a solid amount of packs and get you going.
The UI is AMAZING. You can get through games in 5 minutes and there is almost no waiting. Everything just works like you expect it to. WotC should hang its head in shame after seeing this.
There are a ton of cards for a first launch and lots of interesting deck ideas to build around. You could say that there are some balance issues - Black has a ridiculous suite of creature removal for a core set - but overall it does feel like every color have something truly special that it can do, and there are solid Aggro, Control and Combo strategies.
While I still love Hearthstone, I've been finding myself coming back to Eternal again and again, excited to play more. It's awesome and will be enjoyed by anyone who has played and enjoyed Magic at any time in their life.

This is the best kind of sequel. It takes what the original Grimrock did- filling the niche that classic first person grid-based dungeon crawling RPGs dug out- and improving almost every aspect of it, while giving it an original spin on the structure of the world and its story. It's full of secrets, surprises, and challenge in a world that's a blast to explore with a fine-toothed comb.
There's a lot to this game from the very beginning. Creating an effective party of four members, whose choice of race, class, attributes, traits, and skills for each can deeply affect your experience per playthrough. And it's all quite well-balanced, as damage output depends a lot more on equipment you find, and your ability to use them, more than base stats. The party creation opens a ton of avenues for unique challenges. You could for example try having less than four party members or having a team of farmers (who can only gain experience from eating food.)
One of the most obvious changes from Grimrock 1 is the world's structure. While in the first game it was a massive downward slog through floors of an endless dark, gray dungeon, the game takes place in an overworld "dungeon" with several variously sized traditional dungeons scattered around. The seven distinct environments of the world provide a much-needed and somewhat literal breath of fresh air, especially when coming above ground after traversing through one of the larger dungeons. At the start, you travel linearly between the first three areas, giving you time to establish an effective party through the simpler challenges. In the third area is where the game's structure really shines, letting you choose between four potential paths. The road ahead to your eventual goal needs to be unlocked by finding gems through exploration, combat, and puzzle solving throughout the world, which make for good gauges of progress as you make your path. Even if you skip over a few, you shouldn't face much backtracking thanks to the tight level design and the teleportation hub.
There is a distinct 'Treasure Island' feel to the setting. Your party beings the adventure shipwrecked on an Island, there's a shovel to unbury treasure (and graves, naturally), as well as the addition of firearms, which have distinct advantages and disadvantages to the usual throwing weapons. Your exploration of the world and eye for secrets will not go unrewarded, even if sometimes the 'reward' is a miniboss, another new addition to Grimrock. One of the things I love about both Grimrock games is that you're never instantly killed. Falling down a pit will never kill you, however whatever is IN that pit just might. Regardless it's almost always worth taking the plunge to potentially find items than to play it safe for the sake of your party's ankles. There are ways that YOU can instantly kill enemies by falling on top of one or telefragging them, but I have not seen if they can do the same to you.
As for the enemies themselves, there is a fair bit of variety, including flying leech-squid things, rat pirates, and a complete♥♥♥♥♥♥of a leprechaun. Even the more generic themed enemies typically have unique movement and attack AI. Your success against these enemies require a lot of thinking ahead. You typically can't risk full-frontal assault if you want to keep your health. The combat is mostly movement-based, meaning you have to essentially dance around your enemies. In the original Grimrock, this would typically lead to what fans came to call "square-dancing," where you and your opponent would be locked in a 2x2 square as you move laterally, turn, hit the enemy as it takes your place, and just as they turn to face you, repeat. This problem rarely occurs in Grimrock 2, as the enemy AI typically isn't willing to move ahead to give you a free hit, and often have certain tricks to confound you (ie. quickly cartwheeling to your flank, leaping into the air to land in a nearby space, lightning-fast sideswipe attacks). This makes the combat generally full of suspense, necessitating precise footwork and planning as to not get yourself cornered or caught between multiple enemies, often whose tactics complement one another to your disadvantage, particularily in the boss battles. The enemies, after they die, only respawn after a certain amount of time and progress. Sometimes they may even become tougher versions or new kinds altogether. I don't know how exactly it is designed, but it seems to scale well with your party's power, always providing a decent challenge.
As far as story goes, there's nothing too groundbreaking, but what is there is handled well. Other than the intro, your experience through the game is never interrupted by cutscenes, and everything is told through notes and lore that typically leads more into puzzles than just for its own sake, which is something to be appreciated. There's just the right amount, from the notes directly from "The Island Master" that give you plenty of reason to want to go fight him (if you needed more than all the traps and♥♥♥♥♥♥he left around), to the rest that adds flavor while at the same time interacting with gameplay.
If you're interested in a challenging, fun, and fair RPG with a fair level of depth, with a balanced blend of old and new, this is a phenomenally good choice. With great replayability from the base campaign alone, the dungeon editor and workshop support should give you plenty of extra mileage from this game.

This is a game that is surprisingly better than what I expected (or that reviews, in general indicate).
First off, the bad parts.
The game is glitchy in same places, but mostly fine. There are, however, one or two frustrating mission glitches that can be a pain to work around.
Lack of vehicle options. Thematically, I get this limitation in some of the areas where it's much just ruined city. But, even in the areas where there's plenty of healthy vehicles to go around? Come on. This is a relatively minor gripe given what they were going for, but still would like to have a little more variety beyond just a dirt bike.
The story. This is my biggest gripe. Every time a cut scene came up, my thought invariably was, "If these are the people running the revolution, we are screwed." Again, I kind of get what the devs were going for, but these people seemed genuinely stupid. I mean to the point where I couldn't see them organizing a bake sale, much less an uprising. And I'm pretty sure their approach to the bake sale would be to eschew any baking and just shake down anyone that walks by. I eventually had to just give up trying to make sense of the characters' actions and just go with the flow to enjoy the other parts of the game. Some of the DLC content is better in this regard (the Walker prequel especially), but overall...ugh.
Those complaints aside, there's a lot to love here. The "limited resources" feel was refreshing for an open world game, though I do think ammo should have been more scarce. The fact that you can get killed pretty damn quick by even a signle enemy definitely keeps you on your toes. I also loved that the enemy retaliated on occasion, even driving the rebel forces out of an area. Further expansion on this concept would have made this even better; having said that, I can see where having to constantly re-take an area might get frustrating. The AI can be kinda dumb at times, but still posed a decent threat. Alternating between stealth and full-on combat added a layer of tactics that you don't always see.
The game itself is beautiful. Some weird facial animations aside, the environments and character models are gorgeous. They had a very clear idea of what they wanted and an almost OCD level of detail when it came to the visuals.
Weapon crafting was pretty cool. I loved the idea of swapping weapon capabilities on the fly. The fact that they had so many combinations, but still made most of them still feel unique is impressive. A few extra (and clever) weapon add-ons would have pushed this into greatness territory.

It's not as bad as most made it out to be. It's actually quite fun and educational if you take the time to read the infos on why you drive the vehicles around the airport. To be fair, this is a simulation of airport operations not driving experience so it's to be expected that vehicle handling is only an approximation. That said, vehicle handling is quite distinct between vehicle types. The cute baggage transporter is a little skittish compared to its bigger sibling the cargo transporter for example and this is compounded with the fact that it uses a swivel junction point. OK enough about vehicle handling as this is not a driving simulator but suffice to say the overall handling is quite pleasant and the zoomable rotational camera makes it easy to look around to see where you need to go.
As the name imply, this game depicts quite well the scope of ground operations needed to support aircraft servicing requirements. Having said that, the representation of airport operations are somewhat simplified ; not that i know anything about it in real life. Simplification is both good and bad. IMO this level of simulation could be called basic to intermediate.
Example
You drive the refuelling vehicle from parking bay to aircraft. Refuelling is fully automated. You drive the vehicle back to the bay on completion of refuelling.
You manually start & stop the refuelling operation waiting for the tank to fill-up. Close valves and drive the vehicle back to parking bay. Tanker needs to refuel ballast from either ground storage or wait for scheduled fuel suppliers to replenish fuel stocks.
The same goes for other operations like transporting catering supplies to & from aircraft. No provision is made for stock resupply or cost. Especially cost. Nowhere in this simulator is cost a concern. You crash a vehicle, no repair cost, you tip a plane no penalty or fine. Like i said this is both good and bad. To fully simulate airport operations in fine detail would probably need a 6 core, 12 threads CPU with 32 GB RAM at least.
Back to what is at hand. There is no human traffic anywhere within the boundary of operations save the drivers. Passengers embarking and disembarking are not shown for example but this is alright unless the game simulate congestion or delays. In a nutshell Airport Simulator 2014 only focuses on ancillary vehicle operations in relation to aircraft needs. No other aspects of airport management are simulated like operational costs, resource cost, commercial income, stocks resupply schedule and other staffing requirements besides ground handling crew. I've not put sufficient hours into this game to comment on execution bugs if any but 2 things clearly indicate lack of completion. One is the lack of graphic customizations; you're only given 5 levels of general settings, 5 being the highest. Two is the inability to pull the aircraft across the tarmac using the taxi / towing behemoth; not sure if this is the case in real life but i would expect at least a coupling and de-coupling function before & after taxiing manoeuvres. But this is minor, it should be possible to complete the game if savegames can be backed-up.

In short: FFX is my favorite game of all time. Everything related to FFX that is not FFX is really bad.
Longer version:
First of all, i really dont like FFX-2, all i will say about it is that i don't think it respects its source material, however there seems to be a good amout of people that like it, so maybe it is for you, try it at least.
The HD version of this game does not do enough that i can recomend someone who owns the original game to buy this because of HD, but if you have not played the game or lost your old copy, then this is a great buy.
You get to chose between the original and remixed music, wich is always a plus. The faces of most major characters have been updated, some work really well, some not so well. For example to me Tidus looks a little to "cute" and Yunas hair got a darker tone for some reason that really does not fit her while Auron still looks awesome.
Now, lets leave the HD part of the review and focus on FFX.
To start of with, the game is not perfect, it actually have some of the strangest design decisions i have seen.
The combat is quite simple, and have a really annoying thing where everyone in the party have to participate in each combat in order to recive exp wich means you'll want to switch every character into each fight to maximise the power of the team. They should have made it so everyone get exp.
There are quite a few mini-games. So what can be bad about that? Its optional right? Well kinda. But if you want to get everyones best weapons you have to do them. The worst of them is Chocobo riding in calmlands almost made me wanna tear my hair out. Then we got dodging 200 lightning strikes wich is beyond me how they could put it in there (luckily there is a trick to it if you are a completionist). And then there is the Blitzball game, wich is not bad, but the amount of time you have to sink into the game is waaaaay to much to be worth it.
So how can I say this is my favorite game of all time? Becuase everything else is absolutly amazing.
The music is some of the best in the entire series, and also have my favorite piece (FFX Ending Theme). Graphics are still holding up today imo, and were for its time mindblowing. The world design is a uniqe and extremly beautiful. Great character design overall. The story strikes the perfect balance between being intresting while not becoming overly complex.
But what stands out in a sea of greatness is the characters themselfs. As a group they work soooo well it feels completley natural. The characters become alive, they are so relatable, their realations are handled masterfully to the smallest details.
During the game the characters worries are played out beutifully, and how they handle them. It is never to slowly paced nor rushed. There is a great deal of character development especially for our main characters. It all builds up to be the most heartfelt story i have ever experienced, wich is why this game is so great.

Final Fantasy X is, simply put, the best Final Fantasy entry in the series. The characters are all memorable without certain ones being annoying, as tends to be the case with other Final Fantasy games. Its hard to create a cast of 7-9 playable characters and make all of them relatable and/or tragically interesting. Yet Final Fantasy X manages to do so.
The Sphere Grid is an ingenuous leveling system that suits all styles of play. Do you want to customize all your party members from the get go? The HD Remaster allows you to do this by starting all of your characters in the same place on the Sphere Grid. Or do you want to the more linear route, where each character's early/mid game progression is locked to a certain type of job or class (For example, Yuna being a healing White Mage or Tidus being a quick Thief), then you just play classic mode and enjoy!
The turn-based combat is very well done, probably the best iteration of it in any RPG to date, and for graphics that were created in 2000, somehow still hold up to this day.
The story is absolutely phenomenal, with twists and turns, heartbreak, sadness, joy; every emotion will come through on Tidus' journey with you. The ending will make you cry. And that's a good thing!
As for FFX-2, the dresssphere job system is arguably the best adaptation of the "job change" one in Final Fantasy's history. The combat is more action-packed, and all of the different jobs/classes are extremely varied, with even MORE having been added in the HD Remaster.
The story of FFX-2 is decent, although nowhere near as close as FFX, however I found it a quirky, fun, adventure that quickly turns into a serious, "save the world" scenario in its second half. The emotional devotion I had to helping Yuna reunite with her beloved spurred me through the game twice, since you need to do so to get the perfect ending. Hooo boy, I regret buying this game! I like Rogue like games. Every encounter is tense, you never know when or where more supplies are going to turn up from, you are kept on your toes and if you get overconfident, you die.
It really is a thrill and many of us would agree that you feel crushed when you die in a Rogue-like game, but from the ashes you rise again!
Hell, even games that aren't rogue-like in nature may feature an ironman mode or a hardcore mode such is the legacy of the rogue-like.
Enter this game.
For me, I've played a lot of rogue-likes or games with perma-death and without a doubt the one recurring theme is that you take the safest build possible. This obsoletes most of the other things in the game. Build health, build just enough damage to kill things respectabley and not an iota more. Build defensive stats and evasion. Horde food.
Playing through this game was just me going through the motions. It didn't bring anything new or "challenging but fair" it was just another rogue game, designed like it was painting by numbers.
But wait! You can customize your own class! That's what the promotional blurb said anyway.
I won't critique the interface for not being clear on this aspect, that is subjective. However how can I customize my class when there are no classes to customize with! We have warrior, shieldbearer, ranger, thief and hex-caster/warlock. With the exception of pairing up Warrior and Shieldbearer,
An arguement can at least be made for ranger/thief since thief gets stealth but what on earth are you going to combine warlock with?
Doesn't matter anyway because here is the golden rule.
.
Rules every game that it is in and this is no exception. Shieldbearer and Warlock get stun, you may combine the two classes if you want but regardless you will want shieldbearer since he has the longest stun, no matter how you build your class, get that stun or you are going to get annihilated.
Ultimately the game is not good. It is drowned out by a sea of games that do what this is trying to do but better, much better. The music is good, the art direction is very good, but the game is just paint by numbers. Traps you can't see? Check. There is a perk for that by the way and it is the ONLY perk worth your while. Hunger? Check. An outdated relic but hey, Rogue did it so we'll be damned if we don't! Monsters that outscale you horribly? Oh yes, got to have that, so playing Melee is a huge waste of your time. I could go on but you get the idea and really the only question worth a damn is; is it good? To which my answer is no, it is too tedious and too boring because that is the only playstyle that will keep you alive. Stun, hit a few times, run away. If Ranger, place a trap, run away. If thief, you are already dead. If Warlock, cast poison, run away.

The rewards for Draft are also very generous (beyond even just keeping the deck you make).
The only significant warning/con for people looking into the game is this: The Campaign is a slog. A semi-action RPG in the vein of the old Dungeon Master games, Legend of Grimrock 2 improves quite a bit on the original's already strong performance. With secrets abound, hidden alcoves, and a mysterious story with more depth than it appears to have, Grimrock 2 keeps much of what was good about the first game of the series.
However, Grimrock 2 improves the game in several ways. First of all, the game takes place in the over and underworld of the Isle of Nex, a land with varied terrain and many foes. The overworld segments are interesting, holding shortcuts to dungeons, their own secrets, buried treasure, and several puzzles. The overworlds also have respawning foes and food supplies, allowing the beleaguered adventurer to get their resources back and grind if truly necessary. The main goal of the game centers around collecting various items from the world, and thanks to the overworld is very freeform-- besides a fairly linear intro area, you are free to go wherever you please. However, some areas are gated by their difficulty, so progression still exists.
Dungeons are entertaining as always, with a mix of combat-heavy areas, boss battles (another new feature, and one that's quite well-executed), exploration challenges, and difficult puzzles. Traps and ambushes are still common, as with Grimrock 1, but they felt less frustrating, perhaps because there was typically at least one place to run to if things got difficult.
Graphically, the options are good enough to make the game very pretty, or ugly enough to run on computers without high-tier GPUs. On middling settings, the game ran very smoothly on a Surface Pro 3 in every case, and the game ran smoothly in less intense areas when on higher settings on the same device.
As far as negatives, there were a couple things that I noticed. The food system makes a return from Grimrock 1, and while it remains as unintrusive as always, it's definitely nothing more than a way to put weight in the party's packs. While there were one or two times where I took breaks from dungeoneering to secure more food, it was never a huge concern because of the overworld. As long as you're progressing at a good pace through the game, the food mechanics only show up when you forget to do the inventory dance every half-hour of gameplay or so.
Also somewhat disappointing was the spell system, which felt like it had some wasted potential. While there was one unique spell per spell tree, some elements are outright better than others, and spells range from uncreative (a multi-rune ranged bolt and single-rune damage spell of every element, as well as element-resistance shields for each element) to somewhat interesting but already done (the utility spells in Air and Water trees), with one notable exception: the Force Field spell, which creates a block on a tile of choice that no projectiles or foes can enter, attack from, or exit. I would have appreciated the following:
-A utility spell for Earth (Air and Water have one, and Fire's is replaced with a unique damaging spell)
-An Underwater breathing/Underwater action spell (Typically, underwater action is impossible, and time underwater is limited)
-A transmutation spell, to make junk more useful
-The arrow enchanting spells from Grimrock 1, or a similar sort of spell
-Some sort of knockback or pushback spell (maybe make that the Earth utility, with damage?)
-A "Detect Secrets" spell, but perhaps with a high cost or skill requirement and very short duration. Something to highlight secret buttons, basically, even if it just used a sound indicator to show if one was close.
-Something unique to the Wizard class so that it isn't hilariously useless
-More unique, varied spells that I didn't think of
The casting system was improved from Grimrock 1 in terms of useability, as it's now much faster to cast well, but the lack of spells really was disappointing.
Third, due to the freeform progression, it's possible to barely scrape by in a difficult area and then return to an easy one, kicking yourself for not going there first. Your mileage may vary on this one-- it's pretty fun to just blast through areas, after all. Also, inventory management can become cumbersome-- in the late game especially. However, as everything is in real time, this could be considered part of the challenge.
Finally, some of the required puzzles felt somewhat esoteric. However, I've never been good at those sorts of things, and many would consider brain-bending puzzles to be a pro, so take this with a grain of salt.
Overall worth the purchase. And I'm not even including the custom dungeons, which have full scripting and great potential! Seriously consider buying this game.
Of course, caveat: This game is very casual-unfriendly. If you don't find at least some of the secrets, you're gonna be in trouble. Also, those with poor eyesight won't appreciate small, difficult-to-find secret buttons.

This game... is very unique.
Don't try it if you don't like trying new gimmic-esque things.
If you do enjoy things like that, get Receiver on sale.
I first got this game a while back after remembering the gameplay from a random youtube video.
I thought it was pretty basic ingameplay, in graphics, and story. I went in with fairly standard thoughts, ones you'd make yourself if you just took a couple minutes too look at this very storepage of the game.
Ever play QWOP?
You know, that weird relay racing game that was severely hard to control? Receiver is that, "With guns".
Guns are very tricky and keybinding to use- that's the point of the game- to be very close to the real life counterparts. Press V to load bullets, holding a flashlight under your gun, turning off the safety, aiming down your sights, sprinting, all of that. Each key press feels impactfull and refreshing, and this game has a lot of keypressing - the good kind.
You start with one gun, such as a Glock-18, Colt 1911, and a revolver, with a random selection of equipment. Such as extra magazines, bullets, and a flashlight. Using these guns, you must find more bullets, to fight more enemies (which I'll delve into later) which makes finding cassette tapes easier which are needed to finish the game.
Each gun behaves differently.
The revolver is a single cylinder based pistol, forcing you to reload every bullet (in total of 6)  that shoots fairly slowly. Enemies only take a few shots to kill making this weapon completely inferior to the others. The revolver still behaves differently with how it fires, and the keys you need to press to use it, which makes it fun to use.
The Glock-18 can be used in automatic fire mode as-well as single fire, has a big magazine
You'll find yourself emptying a entire magazine into one enemy that scared you.
The Colt 1911 is the standard point 'n shoot, no gimmicks here. Great to use when you start with it.
The enemies are 2 types of robots throw about in the fairly big map (The only map) you are on.
Turrets and Drones. Each has their own unique sounds and lines of sight.
The line of sight the two robots share add an element of stealth. Don't have ammo but see a turret perched up on a ledge?
Try to sneak past it when it's not looking.
Turrets are exactly as they seem. A rotating sentry that has an ammunition box that feeds bullets into a barrel, that goes straight into your body. Spawning in bathtubs, on stairs, sitting on a dinning room table, you know one is near due to it's very specific beeping, and sounds of the turret's motors rotating.
Shooting it on the tripod it is on, immobilizes it. The turret can still shoot you if you are in line of sight but it can't rotate.
Shooting the sensor will turn off the turret completely.
The drones are much different. They are high up in the area, either in the sky or banging around near the ceiling. These bots will follow you in-till you successfully escape their line of sight. they are equipped with a tazing rod that forces the drone to charge at you from the sky. You'll either be running away hastily or pumping bullets into the poor machine hoping it will fall. Shooting the fans that power it's flight will result in the drone falling, though still being  able to taze your ankles, killing you. Shooting the light sensor (the line of sight) will make it blind and fall instantly.
This robot however, if shot enough will eventually fall. It does have some significant armor though.
You will find more ammo, (maybe another gun or flashlight too if you're lucky.) magazines and most importantly, cassete tapes while exploring. Each cassette tape enables a voice over explaining a part of the games overall story. Getting the required amount of these will take you a few times, either dying by a robot our clumsily falling off a ledge. Getting closer and closer to finding all the cassettes is very fun and rewarding.
Story is the standard "Ooh, reflect on yourself!" type story. pretty much all I can say without spoiling.

At first I thought that it's only a bit better browser cooking game. I was only partially right.
If you have ever played any cooking flash games, you know what is it all about. You run low tier restaurant, earn money to buy new food, more equipment ect. in order to create renowned restaurat. You do it by preparing food and selling it to customers. Preparing itself seems to be pretty easy - you have customers' order at the bottom of the screen, and you have to press buttons corresponding to requested adds. Where it gets tricky are rush hours - they occur twice a day, and result in huge amount of customers - so you need to be fast not to make bad food. There are of course rewards for your effort - it's marked in three ways: perfect - exactly what asked; good - small mistake; bad -... pretty obvious. Good and perfect orders result in +0.5% of buzz, wile bad ones result in -0.5% of buzz (buzz is meter of popularity, the bigger the buzz, the more customers next day). Plus, perfect days result in additional money. Besides of cooking, you have also sanitary duties, like cleaning toilet, tossing garbage and so on.
After day of cooking, you go to main menu, where you check your emails (they contain spam, random events yelling in more money or higher buzz, notify you about sanitary inspection or else), spend money on new food types or their upgrades (ugraded foods *might* be a little harder, but they are a bit more profitable) or change your active menu. You can't have all your food available every day - you have to change it once per some days (with some exceptions, most of foods are affected by so called "menu root" - it was too long in your menu, and people got bored, resulting in negative buzz). Also you can buy equipment, which will make your job easier, by for example cutting amount of dishes nneded to cean by two, or making customers wait a little longer.  After some time, in main menu you will be able to acess special events - like eg. catering events. Theese are a way for you to earn nice money in 2-3 minutes. There are also bets - if you take them and complete, you get more money.
All of modern games must have some kind of multiplayer - CSD has Battle Kitchen, with plenty of game modes, like weekly game, with your score posted on the leaderboard. It also includes local coop.
Simple as it is, CSD is pretty enjoyable game. I became victiom of "one more day" within first few hours of playing. If you don't mind managing restaurant, this is a game for you. My only question - why are people in this game so depresed?

When I consider playing an online CCG, my natural reaction is "too much Pay2Win", as the access to rare (and powerful) cards is usually hidden behind a paywall. Driven by the positive feedback, I ultimately decided to give the game a try, despite my concerns regarding its business model.
After only a few days of playtime I already realized that Eternal has one of the most generous F2P models I've seen. The game hands out so many packs for pushing your progress in various AI modes that building a decent constructed deck is no problem.
One could argue that the deck variety on the ladder is currently quite limited, however I think that this is mainly caused by the fact that only one set has been released as well as due to the popularity of a certain budget deck amongst players that still need to grow their collection.
I can recommend Eternal as a true F2P game that combines gameplay elements of MTG with the presentation style of HS.

Cook, Serve, Delicious! is a restaurant simulator, or perhaps a line cook simulator, that is ambitious in its reach but somewhat failed in its execution. I'm not talking about the gameplay, which is fun; I'm talking about the bugs. The gameplay reminds me of old coin op serving games with modern twists; instead of pouring mugs of beer or root beer to satisfy customers, each menu item has its own recipe to be followed, many times with multiple steps. The game takes into account time of day (some people get turned off at the smell of fish cooking at breakfast) and weather conditions (rainy days mean comfort food will be popular) as you work to make the money to upgrade your kitchen and buy new appliances.
Unfortunately, the game menus are terribly coded so that I could only read roughly a third of the buttons. This includes options menus, food selection, item purchases, upgrades, you name it. If you're not behind the counter making food for customers, there's a two to one chance you won't be able to tell what you're doing. At some point, my control scheme was changed to that for a PS controller without any indication of what key I hit or how to change it back.
I really want to like this game. Someday, with proper developer support, it might be worth buying.

The power flooding/screwing, how you mulligan, and how inconsistent your decks play ruins what is a competent online CCG.
Magic the Gathering is already an exercise in frustration with its 60 card decks. Eternal has 75 card decks -- Why?! This just increases the odds of drawing a streak of cards you can't utilize resulting in many games where you literally lose the game without playing a unit. This, combined with the game's harsh mulliganing where you can only mulligan once to which you have to dump your whole hand, results in a crap shoot that often ends up with these wildly polarizing hands.
If you somehow manage to make a game more inconsistent than Magic the Gathering, then you're doing something very wrong. It's really fun when you get a reasonably balanced hand, but too often your options are to draw power for 10 turns in a row or not draw power for 10 turns in a row.

This is an interesting sort of game that at first glance might seem like another city builder. It's rather a simulation of the struggle to survive.There's a couple ways to play the game and one is to read a guide and spoil the entire process or simply endure a lot of failure so that you better understand it. Given that I rather enjoy games that thrive on the later, I've been quite content with the purchase of this game.
I saw a lot of complaints from people that suggest they "figure it out" and then become bored, but now I realize that realistically that would require them to reroll the map to get better conditions for themselves and I'm glad I didn't listen to them. I've failed a half dozen times , learned from my mistakes and adjusted only to realize my strategy was being formed around being able to place fish immediatly or some similar "best way to start" scenario which I suppose is a possibility towards a better way to ease you into learning, but for a long term solution on playing the game as it's presented to you, not so much.
I've noticed a few issues with roads and pathfinding (they will ignore roads and take a straight path in a lot of cases), but it's intended to fixed in a later patch. Also was  times where I feel like I had to be a bit too explicit with commands and often people still might not do exactly as I tell them, but once I learned how the game wanted you to go about this, it became less stressful. That's kind of the point of this game though. You have a lot of control and freedom, but it's very evident this game knows what it wants from the player and you will have to give it that attention. It also takes a ton of preimpetive planning and not understanding the result of what you just set in place may bring the learning curve up a bit until it all sinks in. I welcome that kind of thing though.
Given most building games are meant to be some kind of peaceful endevour where you stack blocks and watch plants grow, it's nice to finally see one that embraces a bit of a harder-edged attitude. It's slightly rough around the edges in a few areas, and I feel like the UI is working against certain aspects, but for it's price and considering ONE person developed this, it's a solid recommendation from me if you are looking for a builder game that has a bit of roguelike curve to it.

F1 2016 is a good game with a few rough edges, it is good for anyone not wanting to but F1 2017 until it is on sale,

Background, I've ~120 hours in DS1, and atm ~70 hours in DS3, +60 (console)in  DS2:SotFS
tl;dr: HIGHLY recommended Game is lots of fun, very well done with only few and relatively minor shortcomings. Feels just like DS1 and 3 in a good way. Buy it, play it, enjoy it
tl;dr first because I'm a nice guy. In-depth review:
What I like
- Combat is really fun
- a LOT of weapon diversity (many viable options)
- The world is beautiful (gorgeous view ahead) and there are lots of connections, the map layout is smart. Not as   connected as ds1 but still.
- Some boss soul weapons are very cool, as are the boss fights to get them
- Lots of secrets to discover in multiple playthroughs; illusory walls, which pharros contraptions are useful to activate, etc
- The torch mechanic is smart, simple, and useful
- Power Stance is a really cool feature (look it up)
- Long game (my first playthrough took ~45 hours, 220 deaths)
- 'voluntary invasions' via the red soapstone = PvP without cracked orbs (which are finite/farmable)
- Item to re-allocate your stats
- NPC invasions are cool, and can be challenging
- Co-op is far easier than DS1 (with Name-engraved ring)
- NPCs have their own stories and some can follow you throughout the whole game, either as shades (temporary summons) or regular phantoms, in addition to appearing physically for you to talk to and uncover some secrets of their past
- Satisfying to overcome challenges
What I don't like
- Select few enemies (Ogres, some giants) are difficult solely because their size in combination with uncanny speed
- PvP hitboxes/hit detection (or perhaps more likely latency-->server side) is absolute trash, you'll regularly get hit or backstabbed a second or so after you've moved from that position, katanas have the range of whips, etc.
- You can get trolled by online players' messages (you accidentally hit them during combat or when trying to activate something else)
- A few bosses are forgettable, as are their boss soul weapons
- Power stance is not explained in-game, you can easily play through the game many times without figuring out that it exists at all
- Death counter in the 'town' area shows global deaths of all players ingame, neat but not particularly useful. If you play the game ENTIRELY in offline mode however, this will show only your deaths, which is cool
- You can get chain cc'd by certain enemies (only 2 that come to mind) which is infuriating, though you can do the same to some enemies as well.

This dumb idea had potential. I'm somewhat a fan of both boring games and games that progress in real time, but Airport Simulator 2014 takes it to a new level. The game lands one plane, you drive a few vehicles around to deal with the plane, and then... Nothing. Waiting real time for the next plane to land with NOTHING to do. When it lands it takes a solid 5 minutes to taxi before you even get to select a gate for it, then another 2 minutes for it to drive to the gate. Planes are not THIS slow! I would be fine driving slow vehicles around a crappy looking airport wasting my life away, and you won't even give it to me.
After playing a couple hours to really give this a shot... vehicle positioning is a HUGE problem!! Your vehicles can get unfixably stuck under moving planes, forcing you to reload your save. Additionally, your automated vehicles can be blocked by parked vehicles... and there's no way to get into them to move them unless there is an active task for the parked vehicle. A very large portion of this game is running working vehicles into stuck automated vehicles to fix them. Frustrating.
The game does pick up... an hour or two into it. And "pick up" is a real stretch considering the pace of this game. The most management you'll do in this game is managing AI controlled vehicles that get stuck. EVEN THEN, just as it's picking up, you have enough money to automate most tasks and you're back to doing almost nothing. Large portions of this game are spent waiting for ground crews to complete tasks and waiting for new planes to land. The game is in "full swing" about 6 hours in where you'll have a lot to do, and might actually have to think about the order you tackle tasks in. Good luck holding out that long. A couple hours later you'll have literally everything but cargo automated and the rest of the game until you win is waiting. That said, it does almost, barely, in a very small way scratch the tedious pointless game itch I have for some reason.
I'm not going to give a BS review, this game was salvagable, especially to someone who enjoys crappy simulators. Here's a list of things to fix for Airport Simulator 2015:
1. Stuck vehicles. People who want to play this game barely want to play a game at all, let alone have to actually fiddle with something.
2. I can't figure out how this game handles multiple vehicles, but I do know that sometimes the same vehicle will be assigned to two or three tasks (putting the inactive tasks on hold). This is nonsense, I'm at an airport, the other vehicles are even modelled but you can't drive them.
3. Clear, sensible goals. Since the game can assign the same vehicle to multiple tasks you might have to drive the luggage car to Gate 4, Gate 8, and the Terminal. You can do this in any order. That doesn't make sense. The timer for each task is either a time limit to complete the task or the time remaining until the task is complete. These are not the same thing! Why are these in the same column!?
4. Faster vehicles. No vehicles in an airport are this slow.

So I've played Verdun for at least a hundred hours now, so I reckon that I can give a fairly solid review on just what it has to offer, especially when it's competing in the same war/timeframe as a big title like Battlefield 1.
Verdun is a realism-based multiplayer-only match game that places you into the trenches of WWI. As a soldier, you're certain to use any number of weapons from machine-guns, to flame-throwers, to pistols. Even clubs and shovels play a role. The ruler of the battlefield however, is ultimately the bolt-action rifle. All squads have different makes and models, and these are the standard weapon for the forces of both the Entente (USA, France, Britain, Canada) and the Central Powers (Germany, Austria).
If your looking for an awe-inspiring, stunning visual masterpiece, your looking in the wrong place. That's not to say that it's bad, it's definitely a solid Unity engine experience and it's not really noticeable, but it won't compare to something that runs on the Unreal or Frostbite engine.
Sound design is good with careful matching to each weapon, allowing you to pick out individual weapons simply by hearing them. The rapid
of machineguns and the whistling of incoming shells will put fear in your heart.
As mentioned in the overview, Verdun is a realistic multiplayer match game, where you will join a round based on it's map. After the timer of roughly twenty-five minutes is up, the match is over, and you move on to a different map. Each map is fairly large so you won't feel too cramped but at the same time it's not so large that you have to walk for five minutes to even find the enemy. Variety is also good, with rolling hills, pent-up trenches, thick bushes, and tight tunnels.
There's one game mode, with one objective. Take the enemy trenches. Each side takes a three-minute turn to charge the other side across No Man's Land, and seize their trenches, though that time is often extended with what's known as a "foothold overtime". If the enemy is still in your trench and has a 'foothold', you have to wipe them all out, before you can counterattack.
When you join in, you'll have a choice of different squads to join on both sides, with an additional choice of your role in that squad. There's four people in one squad and each has a different role which can change based on the squad type. They all have the same format though.
-One squad-leader which can call down artillery, poisonous gas, recon planes, bombers, and mortar fire; as well as giving orders. You usually have the choice to arm him with a pistol, a revolver, or a rifle.
-One rifleman, who's equipped with a variety of options. Oftentimes you'll have the choice of a bayonet, and sometimes a sniper's scope.
-One specialist, which depending on the squad's type, could be armed with a machinegun, shotgun, flamethrower, or just a rifle.
-One trench raider/grenadier type. He's almost always armed with grenades, melee weapons like a shovel, knife or club, and usually has the option of using either a pistol or rifle.
All weapons are very dangerous, with most if not all rifles killing in one shot to the chest, shoulders, upper legs, or (Most obviously) the head. A revolver might do the same, but it's range and fire-rate is terrible, with pistols usually taking two or three shots to take down an opponent. Machine-guns are likewise two shots. Explosions are also extremely deadly, with artillery fire being a constant threat.
Verdun is a solid war game set in WWI that any History buff or old-fashioned weapon lover is bound to enjoy, mostly because it really captures the horror of war; especially if you have Gore turned on. When you see the guy next to you have his arm blown off by artillery, and he's screaming on the ground, it's a chilling reminder as to the events of the past. However, for those that would prefer to go without that experience, it's turned off by default.
That's not to say that all is sunshine and rainbows in Verdun, there can be some things that would really dissuade people from playing this game and what turns it into more of a niche attraction. First off, your going to die. Alot. Between the constant bullets going back and forth, the artillery raining down, and the gas shells landing all around, it will take a miracle for you to go through a round without dying at least ten times, usually more. As time goes on and you become a more accomplished player, you'll work out ways to limit your deaths but you will still die quite a bit. If this will be a problem for you, stay away.
Second, explosions in Verdun have been complained as being a bit... Overpowered. Grenades and artillery are perhaps one of the most deadly weapons on the battlefield, simply because their radius is huge and if even one of your limbs is in the area of effect, your dead. Realistically, this is entirely correct to the time period. Artillery killed far more people than rifles ever did in WWI, and grenades were likewise very dangerous. However, this may also be a turn-off to people.
As a recap, or for those that didn't fancy reading those walls of text up there and so they came to the end... Verdun is an excellent game,
, you do not mind dying many times, and if you hold a profound interest in WWI's setting, or in a realism-based shooter. A more casual audience may also find interest in it just so long as they understand that this is not a game in which you can 'run-and-gun' in, otherwise you will be gunned down like a turkey on Thanksgiving.

I dont care aboyt this game but heres a lemon bar recipe
2 cups sifted flour
1⁄2 cup powdered sugar
1 cup butter
For top
4 large beaten eggs
2 cups white sugar
1⁄3 cup lemon juice
1⁄4 cup flour
1⁄2 teaspoon baking powder
1⁄2 teaspoon fresh lemon rind (optional)
For the base mix the butter into the flour and sugar.
Mix with hands until it clings together.
Press into a 13 x 9 x 2-inch pan.
Bake at 350°F for 20-25 minutes or until lightly browned.
For the filling, beat together eggs, sugar and lemon juice.
Sift together flour and baking powder.
Stir into egg mixture.
Pour over baked, cooled crust.
Bake at 350°F for 25 minutes.
Cool and sprinkle with powdered sugar.
Cut into bars.

I had a massive text block describing my history with fighting games from before even Street Fighter 1 and how only the true fighting game fans stayed around for the drought of 99-2007 (which The King of Fighters series stayed true, releasing games that whole time).  But decided to say, fighting games, have never been about graphics, its has always been about the soul, technicality, depth and fun.
Firstly if you know you fighting games, then you'll know Garou: Mark of the Wolves battle designer, Yasuyuki Oda.  He is the Director os KOF XIV.
Garou: Mark of the Wolves is arguably the best fighting game of all time (Yes, even compared to SF3:TS).
The King of Fighters roster is incredible and KOF XIV is one of the best rocking 50 (unique) characters old and new (with 4 legendary extra characters in the DLC), you won't find ONLY Charge characters or Shotos, etc.  You'll find a fireball character that has charge moves, command grabs and 2 "supers" with two levels of power and a final third CLIMAX super, making up 5 total (Options).  You have many different jumps, from hops to long leaps, meaning you can start with normal jumps but end up being able to plan moves with a tiny little overheap hop.  There's no catchup gimmick and there's no learning other characters special life or abilities above their movelist.  It really is everything a 2.5D game could have to let you feel in control of your fighter.
Before my final words, The King of Fighters XIV has;
- Arcade Mode (with ending)
- Auto combo system for newbies, that allows casual fighting game fans a great stepping stone to true combos
- Team specific endings (pick the people from a team and get a canon ending), over 50!
- Online Training mode (train with your friends/enemies/teachers)
- Online Ranked / UnRanked modes (with great netcode)
- Basic Systems Training mode (Character neutral)
- Mission Mode for Character Trials (Combo examples)
- Survival Mode
- Time Attack Mode
- Unlockable gallery (Pictures, movies etc)
- Great PC Port with minimal requirements (Which is updated all the time).
NOTE: Please take the Negative reviews with a grain of salt as the game is updated all the time and as PC gamers we realise
you need a certain level of hardware for modern games. (Sorry it probably won't work on a business Dell from 2008, but it will work on a minimal gaming rig from 2012).
I'll leave you with this, take a chance on The King of Fighters XIV!  It has over 26 years of history, characters and story development. (The King of Fighters Universe, includes but not limited to Psycho Soldier games, Athena Games, Ikari Warriors, Fatal Fury/Garou Series, Art of Fighting Series, Metal Slug Series, and the list goes on).  All mixed in a pot with superior & more varied characters than any of fighting game out there.
Come visit Southtown, if you give it a chance, it might just change your view of Fighting games!
And as the Lone Hungry Wolf himself, Terry Bogard would say;
"Get Ready!  A Storm is coming!"

At first I thought that it's only a bit better browser cooking game. I was only partially right.
If you have ever played any cooking flash games, you know what is it all about. You run low tier restaurant, earn money to buy new food, more equipment ect. in order to create renowned restaurat. You do it by preparing food and selling it to customers. Preparing itself seems to be pretty easy - you have customers' order at the bottom of the screen, and you have to press buttons corresponding to requested adds. Where it gets tricky are rush hours - they occur twice a day, and result in huge amount of customers - so you need to be fast not to make bad food. There are of course rewards for your effort - it's marked in three ways: perfect - exactly what asked; good - small mistake; bad -... pretty obvious. Good and perfect orders result in +0.5% of buzz, wile bad ones result in -0.5% of buzz (buzz is meter of popularity, the bigger the buzz, the more customers next day). Plus, perfect days result in additional money. Besides of cooking, you have also sanitary duties, like cleaning toilet, tossing garbage and so on.
After day of cooking, you go to main menu, where you check your emails (they contain spam, random events yelling in more money or higher buzz, notify you about sanitary inspection or else), spend money on new food types or their upgrades (ugraded foods *might* be a little harder, but they are a bit more profitable) or change your active menu. You can't have all your food available every day - you have to change it once per some days (with some exceptions, most of foods are affected by so called "menu root" - it was too long in your menu, and people got bored, resulting in negative buzz). Also you can buy equipment, which will make your job easier, by for example cutting amount of dishes nneded to cean by two, or making customers wait a little longer.  After some time, in main menu you will be able to acess special events - like eg. catering events. Theese are a way for you to earn nice money in 2-3 minutes. There are also bets - if you take them and complete, you get more money.
All of modern games must have some kind of multiplayer - CSD has Battle Kitchen, with plenty of game modes, like weekly game, with your score posted on the leaderboard. It also includes local coop.
Simple as it is, CSD is pretty enjoyable game. I became victiom of "one more day" within first few hours of playing. If you don't mind managing restaurant, this is a game for you. My only question - why are people in this game so depresed?

Cook, Serve, Delicious! is a restaurant simulator, or perhaps a line cook simulator, that is ambitious in its reach but somewhat failed in its execution. I'm not talking about the gameplay, which is fun; I'm talking about the bugs. The gameplay reminds me of old coin op serving games with modern twists; instead of pouring mugs of beer or root beer to satisfy customers, each menu item has its own recipe to be followed, many times with multiple steps. The game takes into account time of day (some people get turned off at the smell of fish cooking at breakfast) and weather conditions (rainy days mean comfort food will be popular) as you work to make the money to upgrade your kitchen and buy new appliances.
Unfortunately, the game menus are terribly coded so that I could only read roughly a third of the buttons. This includes options menus, food selection, item purchases, upgrades, you name it. If you're not behind the counter making food for customers, there's a two to one chance you won't be able to tell what you're doing. At some point, my control scheme was changed to that for a PS controller without any indication of what key I hit or how to change it back.
I really want to like this game. Someday, with proper developer support, it might be worth buying.

Nothing needs to be said more then this:  Don't judge this game by the simple graphics you see.

This is a great game. As a gun nut, I feel it's a clever idea for a game, subverting the usual trope of firearms in games being the simplest thing in the world; this novel idea is really what makes the game shine, yet there are a few places it falls down or is just incorrect. It's complicated to a point where it's not a really easy arcade shooter but not too complicated to where you need a degree in astrophysics to play the game! It is so unforgiving that one bullet will mean game over, starting again with a random weapon, random amount of ammo and in a random location; yet this for me just added to the fun, as way too many games will let you be a bullet sponge, taking away any risk resulting in no reward upon completion (i.e. Call of Duty). The difficulty increases as you go along, which is an essential part of an arcade game, but the difficulty spikes very fast, which isn't awful but might put some off. The enemies, while varying few in  types, yet can become overwelming in number quickly, take trial, error and thought in order to efficiently take them down.
The atmosphere is very good. The story goes (as far as I can remember) that
The procedural rooms with multiple layers is a good concept and the designs for the levels are varied and look cool, yet the way the game loads each room means there will be lag when walking through some doorways (even with a high-end R9 390 graphics card and the game being on an SSD), leading to unfair kills and thrown headsets. The music is very eerie and fits well, but can inhibit gameplay from not being able to hear the enemy. The voice which gives you advice works for what it does very well but after 5 hours of gameplay, you will want to turn him off.
There will be a few thing I'm missing out but the game is definitely worth buying for $5!

See a recommendation below depending on if you've played Magic, Hearthstone, Both, or Neither:
MAGIC ONLY:
MTG is obviously the foundation of Eternal. The rules are virtually identical. But the game gains two very important qualities over magic: One is the ability to use effects that would be impossible with physical cards. For example, cards in the graveyard (called the "void") keep any stats changes applied to them on the battlefield. Some cards affect give permanent +1/+1 to the next unit you draw, etc. Second is the ability to balance these cards if they get out of hand. There won't be a Jace, the Mind Sculptor incident, because these cards aren't in print. They just get patched, and if you don't like the patch changes you can swap it in for any other equivalent rarity card you'd like within a few days. You also don't have to spend money, though you probably used to spending if you're a magic player. It has only one set as of right now, but this one set is a lot more fun and diverse than MTG vanilla was.
HEARTHSTONE ONLY:
If you've only played Hearthstone, you'll have more cause to hate this game than any of these other groups. Hearthstone uses a system by which you get one mana each turn, with some cards (mostly druid) that let you get more. In this game, you have to draw your mana and play it, max one per turn, as a card from your deck. So what happens if you don't draw any? You get rekt. You lose for no good reason. It's a mechanic pulled over from MTG and it is absolutely infuriating if you haven't built a tolerance to it. Carrying the mana system over from magic without modifying it is probably the biggest mistake the devs made in designing this game. If you sort by negative reviews, this is the theme of almost all of them.
On the upside, this game is waaaaay more generous than hearthstone when it comes to earning gold. You can even just play the "gauntlet" mode and earn tons of free gold by playing against the AI if you're afraid of your performance vs humans. You know how in HS every three multiplayer wins gets you a tenth of a pack? It's closer to half a pack, plus some cards, in this one. That's not even counting the arena-style modes, which unlike HS let you KEEP the cards you draft and give much nicer rewards without having to win 7+ games in a single run. It really puts the rewards system of hearthstone to shame.
BOTH:
As someone who put hundreds of hours into both MTG and Hearthstone, I am seriously convinced that Eternal will overtake both of them when it leaves beta. The developers of this game understood some of the core mechanical weaknesses of both of those games (overly complex rules and inability to act on your opponent's turn, respectively) while incorporating many of their strengths. If you enjoy both of these games or have in the past, this might replace both of them. I can't imagine you not liking it.
NEITHER:
CCGs are a different kind of beast for someone who hasn't played one. They have a lot of variance, which is to say the winner is sometimes a little "random." But part of the joy of mastering these games is learning to play within that variance and maximize your chances of winning as many games as possible. It's fun to predict what cards your opponent will likely have in their deck based on what you know about the cards they've played so far, then make plays to counter them. The tutorial ("campaign") is very long and will help you learn all the basics of games like this. If you're afraid of going up against players with expensive decks, the AI matches are very rewarding and let you build up your own stuff quickly. This is not a simple pay2win iphone-style game where you get clobbered by people with better stuff. I mean, you WILL get clobbered by people with better stuff at first, but you don't have to spend money to ascend to where they are. If this sort of thing sounds up your alley, Eternal is a great first combat card game for you.

This game was a technical mess at launch but provides an amazing variation from the standard FPS. Instead of being a superhero who can take on enemies with guns blazing, it really captures the feeling of being an insurgent in enemy-occupied territory. Setting up ambushes, using the environment to your advantage, and running away are the tactics you'll need to rely on rather than just trying to soak damage and wait for your health to regenerate. It really makes you fight differently than almost any other FPS on the market.
And that's just in some of the game's zones. In the more controlled environments, Homefront becomes a stealth game where you need to carry out assasinations and acts of sabotage to turn the populace against the invaders controlling them before going loud to drive the Norks out of the district.
Add on to it an underappreciated but creative co-op campaign separate from the main game and this is a hidden gem that a lot of people overlooked due to difficulties during launch. Pick it up on sale and you won't regret it.

They say more of a good thing is still a good thing.  I can attest to that, it's true.  Legend of Grimrock was basically an Eye of the Beholder clone, even down to its puzzles and annoying spiders, i.e. a dungeon that started out rather bland and simple, but got progressively more difficult and challenging, as well as varied, as you descended towards the boss fight.  Eye of the Beholder II had expanded on that formula by allowing you to experience a greater variety of locations, monsters and puzzles.  Legend of Grimrock does the same - it's basically the same game with a large and expansive outdoor hub, multiple dungeons and buildings to explore, the ability to have multiple floors in a single level, a broader selection of monsters and even more mind bending puzzles.  There are changes to the game as well: a new race and some new classes have been added, the leveling system has been tweaked to be less all or nothing, skill branches are less deep, weapons and armor have been categorized into broad proficiencies, alchemy has been added and magic has been reworked.  But ultimately, it's the same game, just bigger and better.   Get it.  It's great.

The only downside to this game is how focused you get. You are so into it that the time just melts away and suddenly two ours are gone in what feels like ten minutes. At first you just cant wait for more people to be born you are sitting there half yelling at them to just bang out more kids, but when things start rolling and the population is growing much mroe quickly, you start running out of places to put them all. Im doing pretty freaking well on my first time through, so I know with a little forthought you can go far without too much difficulty. My advice, make sure you have alot of storage space and just stockpile tons of resorces. food doesnt go bad to having extra cant hurt. start building stone houses soon after your first few wooden. Keep your people in school and building them a church is a decent investment for its little effort required after construction. farms will do you wonders, and try to get sheep early. sheep = wool = warm clothing. Hope to get lucky from the trader, because often the prices are just too dang high to try to order livestock or seeds. Keeping at least 1 forester, quarry, and mine functioning at all times will be nice to have. A constant steady supply or iron and coal means plenty of valuable tools for trade, and stone is used so much that a quarry is pretty much a need. Its slower than just harvesting from around you, but being renewable, its a good way to keep stone stocks up and have the stuff out there in nature for when you need to dig deep for the big building projects.

I got this on sale for $7, and an extra $5 for all the DLC. The game certianly was bashed when it released, and with good reason, as it was horribly buggy. Looking at it now, it is a competetant open-world shooter that looks pretty nice graphics-wise. Gameplay-wise, it does not do anything special other than weapon customization, which is excellent. Gameplay is fluid if a bit repetitive, but is ultimately satisfying to take down strike point after strike point. There is very little to do other than get the hearts and minds of each zone to 100%, clear all strike zones, and of course do the story. The story itself is a bit boring, and really is missing any strong narrative or thematic elements. The DLC I actually found to be quite fun, if a bit short, especially "Beyond the Walls", which is a nice change of pace and color compared to the rest of the game. Overall, if you can get the base game and the DLC all for under $20, I'd say for for it. It's a decent, and at times derivative, open world shooter that is an easy 20+ hour experience.

After hearing about Gone Home topping many game of the year lists I was interested, but the review that had me hooked was one that simply stated “I can’t tell you anything about the game, just play it!” Two days later, I can honestly say, they were absolutely right!
I preface this post by saying that I will not give away anything about the game, because that will only take away from the beautiful experience that the first play through is.  The story takes place in 1995 where you, a college student after spending a year abroad in Europe, returns to your family home. You get to the new house your family just moved into in the middle of a stormy night to find no one there.  This is where your story begins.  Where is everyone? What has been up to for the past year? What’s the story behind this old house?
The developers manage to tell an amazing story strictly through the environment of the world around you.  You learn things through pictures and notes.  Every item you find has its own history, and does it’s part to shed some light on the history of a particular person or event in the world.   The fact that they devs made gamble to not hold the player’s hand allow them to piece things together on their own was not just refreshing, but impressive.  2 – 3 hours in, I completed the game. At that point, as the final credits rolled, I smiled, slid my chair back away from my desk, and actually said “Well done, guys”.
Truth be told, I cannot tell you what the game was about.  Well I could, but I would be doing you a great disservice.  The feeling you get when the pieces start to come together is incredibly satisfying to say the least.  So perhaps I should say I will not tell you what the game is about, it’s something that each person should experience for themselves.
After completing the story, I was left with several things running through my mind.  First of all, the story was not only very well told, but the story in and of itself is one that will stay with me for years to come.  There was a good deal of mid 90’s nostalgia that hit me, what can I say, I’m in my early 30’s…  I was there… They managed to nail it…
The last thought I had was about the story itself.  Not so much the content of the story, but the whole story telling method.  For a game with limited character interactions, there were plenty of characters involved.   For game with no puzzles in it, there were several lifetimes worth of pieces to put together. For a game that was developed by an indie studio with a limited budget, there was a better experience put together then any of the triple A studios have done in years.
This game is proof that the adventure game genre is alive and well.  It shows that a little imagination goes a long way, and it proves that a solid story wins out against gimmicky gameplay mechanics or shiny graphics on any day of the week.
If there was any doubt by this point, I was a huge fan of the game, and  I highly recommend everyone plays it.  Though not the longest or toughest of games, I promise those few hours you spend playing it will be special.   The guys over at Fullbright did an amazing job with this one, and I’m looking forward to what’s next from them.  As far as I’m concerned, they have my money the next time around,  I just need to know where and when.
Check this one out, guys…  …And you’re welcome…

Do NOT waste your money on this hollow shell of a game.
It's titles like this that move the title of "greediest gaming company" to other people than EA. Your initial $60 gets you a whopping 40 models of car, with somewhere between 1 and 5 tuning settings each. Then, you're forced to pay for any additional content they provide past "updates" for those first 40 cars. Now that wouldn't be so bad if they didn't waft all these extra rides in front of your face on every vehicle select screen, including the new car lot, making every completionist out there cringe. Oh, and the icing on the car cake? Your vinyls/liveries for your car are limited to whatever presets are available in the game, and some cost as much as a new car. Talk about limited customization!
On top of all their swindling of your cash, the map is far from fleshed-out, with vast expanses of nothingness where only one relatively small subset of the vehicles in the game can get above 60mph. This makes the game feel very empty, and it's only compounded by only being able to see 7 other players (in an MMO, haha!) at a time in-world. The rest of the "life" in the game are NPC cars with little to no driving skill who will inevitable get in your way more often than not, NPC pedestrians with whom your only interaction is "spooking" them out of the way, and random furry critters that act suspiciously like the people.
The story is short and will only take a day or two to finish for a decent player. The endgame content is lacking and the leaderboards are dominated by trainer-using cheaters, so you can give up your dream of being e-famous in this game.
It really feels like I paid $60 for a very pretty but very empty tech demo. Despite desperately needing some games to play with new PC friends, I'd never recommend this thing to anyone.

VVVVVV is an extremely fun and challenging little puzzle platformer from Terry Cavanagh, the maker of Super Hexagon. I beat it after playing for about 3 hours. In that time, I died over a thousand times and collected 13 of the game's 20 collectables, which serve as optional side challenges (one in particular seems damn near impossible). The game is very difficult at times, and it can get frustrating if you let it, but it's profoundly rewarding to succeed after struggling with it a bit - as any puzzle game should be.
The soundtrack is perfectly suited to its retro/simplistic graphics. It feels like a game that I would have played and loved on an NES when I was a kid. I loved it, and I'm even more of a fan of Terry Cavanagh now after playing it.

I really recommend this game, the visuals are stunning, the gameplay can be fast or slow (depending on which mode you pick) and there are many playable teams. Also the dev's are really good and they listen to community feedback.
