PERSONAL OPINION
Well, I'm going to tell you that this game needs a friend. Unfortunately, it doesn't come with one guaranteed.
When I played this game/ both alone and with a friend, it is the absolute best racing/driving game I have ever played.
No, I don't understand why there's so much hate. What do all those haters play, Need for Speed Rivals?
All jokes aside; this game is definitely better than its competitors at its gen.
I enjoyed this game thoroughly, and would rate it 98/100 (1 point minus for minor connectivity issues, 1 point minus for bad ending)
Let me start with the goddamn map. Yes, the freaking huge map. And its not just 90% emptiness, no no no no....
Its probably one of the largest maps in gaming history. I'm pretty sure it could go par against Guild Wars 2 in map size.
Next up is the main story sequence. Overall, the story was NeedForSpeedMostWanted(2005)-ish and really pushes you to want to know more. Its not shakespeare but hey, I found it to fit okay.
The cars in the game are well modeled (except their bottom; but who the hell looks there), and there is a pretty good level of car-modding. Okay, not Need For Speed Carbon/UG2 level, but at least around NFSMostWanted(2005) level. The paints choices are great, and the vinyl choices are not bad. They should make more though.
I don't think there is alot of cars in the game, and before people start chirping the game because you can purchase cars; you can finish the game and get the best car without paying a single extra dollar. Just don't pay heed to purchasable cars and you're good. I personally liked their car choices; despite the low car count.
The AI in the game (which some saw glitching) was actually flawless for me. They are pretty smart, and I'm pretty sure they are much better AI than that of older racing games. This is because the AI will not let you grind onto them or use them as "padding" as you make a sharp turn with them. They will speed up or slow down to make you screw up. It makes the game have a level of challenging in it.
Okay, you got me here. The handling. Its not great is it? Well, I'm going to tell you that to each his own because me and my friend both just got used to it. I know, its kinda annoying, but it makes it a tad bit more challenging. It kinda forces you to learn how to properly turn and drift. Not sure if its realistic, but that doesn't matter for me anyway, it wasn't the end of the game.
The graphics. This stuff is not your Driveclub or Forza graphics. But its definitely the right gen. I can barely run it with my computer but it looks amazing. Although there are some blotchy textures in shady places, the surrounding game has some good texturing.
The Audio is good, but could use a little bit more bass/could sound more heavy.
All the different specs you can get for your car, these are what fill in the "not enough customization" and "not enough cars" gap. The specs and their upgrades are well done, and they give the cars more specialization in what they do.
The performance parts in the game are acquired by the means of completing mini-challenges or buying them at high levels. Of course, I didn't mind this as much but I could see why people would prefer buying them. Plus the model of the vehicle's inside does not change, no matter which performance part you pick.
I did not have this game crash too many times, only twice from my many hours of playing and also once because my Eyefinity is not really compatible. I didn't find any bugs so far (minus my friend apparently being able do drive underwater once).
The PVP in this game was decent, and the MMO-thing is not the biggest thing about the game. I played with a friend; as I said before, and we both really enjoyed this game.
The challenges are a bit silly, but they are great in the case that someone wants to get some quick cash. The game's economy isn't that bad.
Worth every dime of my 40$.
TLDR; 98/100, huge map, get a friend, ending sucks, but overall an enjoyable game.

People say a lot about the Crew. That is good and fun and others swear that it is next to terrible. For me the Crew has been a lot of fun, but I have no interest in being with a group of people tearing up the country-side. I personally like the idea of the crew and the changing of car styles and it forces you to play with all of the spec's (Street, Dirt, Performance, Raid, and Circuit) through the Campaign. Overall if you like driving around a massive open world in any car you like doing random skills, races and occasional pvp it is a lot of fun and worth the cash.
---->The campaign in general is alright, it is enough to keep you interested in how the characters work as a whole, but it nothing compared to Ubisoft's other story lines. It was written by the same writer of Red Dead Redemption, but was given a limited window in which to write it. The story feels rushed and a little bit like the fast and Furious, but it is a racing game and the Fast and Furious franchise really set the cliche and standard for many years to come. It is best to think of the Campaign as an interesting Tutorial rather than any form of story.
---->The game play is very fun in my opinion. In the open world you can drive anywhere you want with ease and have a multitude of things to do along the road trip. With five different types of cars you can go anywhere. The races are fairly easy in solo, but can pose a challenge in Co-op. The servers are lacking players though, because of the recent political and social mishaps that Ubisof has had, but I have had no problem getting into races in PVP. There is a large gripe about the handling model with this game. *IMPORTANT* It is a little difficult to understand, but this is an arcade racer with a logical handling model. The handling is actually quite realistic; its clunky, difficult, and sometimes very difficult to control, but this is how real cars work at high speeds. (I have two performance muscle cars and race them on the weekends, so trust me when I say they can turn at speed worth anything. One is a 1970 Camaro SS Z28 and the other is a 1970 Dodge Charger R/T) Use the brake and don't just slam on the gas the while time is the key to racing effectively.
---->The Customization is more than extensive (except on the Circuit cars but they are supposed to be race cars so I get that.) I have had a lot of fun personalizing my cars to be something that I like and find attractive. I can happily say that they have attempted to find looks and styles that suit everyone's interests. The visual parts can all be bought so you roll out of the tuner with a badass looking Mustang, Camaro, or whatever else. Althought, the performance parts are sometimes frustrating to acquire, but are rewarding after a challenge.
---->My frustrations;
-The occasional lack of players in the open world
-The tiny chance of level 50 parts
-The traffic spawn distance is very short sometimes giving you no chance to dodge them when you are ripping along the desert at 250+ mph.
-The expense of some of the parts. (Now this is a little bit more specific. Because it is so easy to make money it doesn't really matter anyway.)
-The fact that there isn't a circuit spec for the Agera R.
---->My Joys;
-The customization for the cars
-The little things, like overheating brakes and over-spin.
-The graphics for the cars and damage models.
-The auto-repair for the exterior of the car so you aren't forced to look at a car the is half destroyed.
-The Performance tweaks to the driving models that are a little difficult to notice.
-The Spec differences and play style choices.
-The ease at which you can make money.
All in all it is very good. Not perfect by any means, but enjoyable. Worth the money, you ask? There isn't an easy way to answer that. For me I have played a lot and plan to play more so it was for me, but for others who knows. It is really one of those; "I love it" or "I hate it" games. The hype it got really hurt it. I like it better than GTA five, way more. So if you want it, get it and play with it. Take the challenges with pride and just at least give it a try before judging. My friends and I love it.

Wonderful game that writes rouge-lite mechanics into it's lore beautifully. Gameplay loop is that you travel similar locations that generate procedurally, being reordered and shuffled around.
The great part about the game is it's gun mechanics. You have to operate the gun that you have. Not only shoot it, but use hammers, revolver's cylinder, and load bullets individually into magazines you carry around. You might get lucky with amount of ammo or have need to rush through locations to save your ammunition, as it might be lean. And you can hit ricochet shoots(realistic ones, not 180 degrees).
Although there are only two types of enemies(turrets and flying drones) there are multiple parts of hitboxes that can be hit and affect enemies differently. You can shoot their camera, weapon, engine or battery.
As engaging and rewarding a platformer as you'll ever play, I've been driven to both madness and elation. A must-play.

I really enjoyed Homefront 1, despite everyone around me hating it. I was warned of this game as well, and again I ignored what others were saying and gave the game a good honest try.
I have never been more frustrated to play a game in my entire life. Here's why:
1. Endless NPC Spawning
Stealth games or shooter that requires a little bit of thinking or tactics shouldnt have endless spawning. Especially ones that know exactly where you are, which seems to happen for every single enemy in the game. Oh seen for 1ms longer than expected, well now the entire fort knows your exact position until you run away and hide in a dumpster for 5 seconds and then they magically forget of your existence
2. Enemies are bullet sponges. I go for the head whenever I can but the Assault Rifle in this game is so inaccurate anything past the first shot is useless if aiming for the head. Sure its fun having the AR when against the weakest of enemies but as soon as they start getting tougher that fun fades fast. Along with the infinite spawning of enemies, you run out of ammo way too quickly
3. Weapons are godawful inaccurate. Want to go completely stealth (lol good luck), oh neato they give a weird silenced pistol type thing, well apparently whenever your character holds this they decide to have a seizure cause they cant hold this tiny little pistol steady. oh neato, they have a hold breathe mechanic...... that does next to nothing, especially with the pistol, still having a seizure.
4. Missions require equipment with little/no warning. The mission I quit on was where I broke into a fort and after failing to stealth because the alarm automatically signals I spend the next 10 minutes fighting off endless spawning enemies and looting them hoping that one of them will drop some damn batteries so I can build a bomb. NOPE. Batteries are either really well hidden/rare or have to be bought in the shop, completely ruining the whole idea of a crafting system.
5. Promotes stealth, then throws it out the window. Like I mentioned in point 4, tried to go into a fort undetected and the alarm automatically signalled. Sure im about to blow open a vault and the fort will be alerted anyway but I should at least be able to take out the surrounding guards without everyone in the entire complex knowing my exact location. Related: the escape mechanic is also dumb as hell. Easily one of my favorite games, and deserving of my first review. Well-designed levels, fluid controls, incredible weapon feedback, and the game oozes with visceral polish everywhere you look.
The campaign took me around 6 hours as promised, granted I tend to take my time with them. The setpieces and challenges were imaginative and frantic throughout. A story is there, though thankfully it isn't the focus; I enjoyed some of the characters' comradery towards the second half, but a lot of the pop-culture references admittedly went right over me. I played on hard difficulty (originally 'normal' difficulty when the game released), and didn't encounter any moments that felt too unfair. A couple sections in particular took me a good half-hour each, but after a second playthrough (on the updated hard-mode), I think both of those areas have been adjusted to fit the difficulty curve better.
If I had to name it's biggest flaw, it's that the game struggles to stand out in areas beyond its core gameplay elements. While the environments are pretty, and the
setpieces are great, the
setpieces aren't especially interesting to look at -- well-drawn backgrounds and vague machinery all about, but no strong aesthetic that draws interest to it all. The spider-mech you spend the whole game looking at isn't the most appealing thing either, although it sounds great and gets the job done.  For all the fun that this game's bosses were, they were also incredibly plain-looking -- one of them is aptly named "Mega Smashbot", to give you some idea.
RIVE includes three survival modes, gutted from the most intense 'arena' sections of the campaign, and the latter two are great for the adrenaline factor. The 'Challenges' feel a little more tacked on, with a couple that feel outright daunting to score above a Bronze award for -- hell for achievement hunters, but welcome as extra content.  Its soundtrack suits its levels perfectly, and changes dynamically as you progress through; this along with its sfx is almost flawless, and it made several sections of the game far more tense and impactful as a result. But in line with the issue mentioned above, very few of them are songs with interesting melodies, and I didn't find them as great to listen to outside of the game. It's an old-fashioned way of doing things, but it didn't take away my appreciation of the title as a whole.
All in all, RIVE is a swan-song title that delivers hard-as-nails explosive gameplay in spades. It feels old-school, not just old-school-inspired. I bought it on release day, and felt it was worth the purchase. I recommend this game to anyone looking for a solid challenge, and those with a passing interest in twin-stick shooters should certainly take a look.

Now I first want to say I have some things I'd like to compliment the game on, but before that the main reason I'm giving this a no is because the game is still a beta, IE incomplete. You don't pay for a movie that isn't fully edited, so you shouldn't accept the same for video games, even with Homefront's troubled past. It's a very toxic move to release games that aren't reasonably bug tested and fixed up. I've had MANY bug run-ins and a couple times I've had to restart the game due to a broken respawn in a scripted mission. On a side note, including DLC that should have been a part of the game, like tying up plot points cost cash, which is wrong in my books. Finish your plot points and don't make people pay to wrap things up.
Now with that out of the way, here's some things I liked about the game.
1: The game wasn't as predictable as I expected. I won't spoil anything but there was some genuinely tense monents in the game that were quite fun!
2: I like how they did the head of Philledelphia resistance, Jack Parish. He reminds me of Rocky Balboa and I love the job the voice actor did. My one critisism is he seems a bit too flawed and for his position, has a bit too much self doubt. Other than that I always enjoyed seeing him in cutscenes and around the game.
3: The open world nature of the game might be restricted to different sections of the city, but I always dig an open world shooter and this reminded me quite a bit of farcry.
4: The weapons are fun to switch up, though I find there is a very big lack of balance. Things like the flamethrower are garbage up close (fine for a couple of weak enemies, but it doesn't do burning damage and just stuns them for a bit), but others like the upgraded Automatic Shotgun are COMPELTELY OP!
5: Upgrade system: Some people find these the bane of shooters but I love the feeling of earning rewards and getting to upgrade my character with them. It's a good feeling of progression and growth, and the upgrades don't make you super powered. They help a bit but it still comes down to skill.
I'm not going to list any critisisms of the game because there are plenty around this post (and I agree with most of them), so I'll just leave what I liked.
If the game was finished: 7.2/10. Mostly because the game is very repetitive and doesn't change much across the campaign. Writing was half decent and I respect some of the changes they tried out, for better or for worse.
Buy it on a big sale, don't pay full price. Don't steal it either though, that's just a♥♥♥♥♥♥move.

This game received a lot of flak when it first came out, mostly for not very good reasons.  Often it was lambasted for not being a type of game it had never professed to be, or for telling a story aimed at people the critics didn't want the story to be aimed at.  So I think it's worth looking at what Gone Home tries to do, and how well it lives up to it.
Gone Home, on a gameplay level, is all about exploration.  It's not rewarded in the typical ways exploration in a game tends to be -- you won't find power-ups for completing jumping puzzles or get an achievement for completing the map.  Instead, you're rewarded with pieces of the puzzle that is the story of the game.  Sometimes these are explicit -- voiceover diary entries for reaching certain places, or letters and notes to read.  Others are more implicit, often looking like just parts of the background -- a TV with cables hanging out underneath it, for instance, implies that there once was a VCR there, and it's gone.  Put this together with clues from other areas in the game, and you can figure out the story behind the VCR -- and where it went.  There's not a room in the game without something that expands on the picture the game is painting.
And on a story level, that picture is the entire point.  The game is really a portrait of a family, both its surface and its secrets.  The main story of the game, the one conveyed through voiced diaries, is all about the protagonist's younger sister, but the smaller clues lead to a surprisingly detailed pair of stories about their mother and father, intersecting at points and diverging at others.  The protagonist herself ends up less well-defined, but that's not uncommon for player avatars, and we still get a sense of her broad personality.  The game doesn't focus on a linear narrative so much as the exploration of a family, its history, and its strengths and flaws.
That's what the game is.  It's also important to know what it's not.  It's not an action game of any type.  It's not a traditional horror game -- if you're enjoying the game, you'll certainly feel tension and apprehension at certain points, but it starts out as the nervousness you'd feel about exploring a strange empty house where some of the lights don't work and you don't know what's around the next corner, and moves on to a quiet dread about how the stories of the family wind up, and whether things ended well for them or took a turn to the worst-case scenario.  It's not really a puzzle game -- there are some secret passages to find and locked doors to open, but the solutions are usually pretty simple and obvious.  You won't be rearranging soup cans in the pantry to spell out a secret password -- more likely you'll just be trying to figure out where Mom would have put the spare key.  It's not a game that sets out to challenge the player with its gameplay -- the real challenge is piecing together the story, and if that doesn't entertain you, you'll have less fun with this.
I think, overall, this is a very good game, if you're willing to engage with it on the level it's meant to be engaged with.  Of course, it's not perfect -- what game is?  You're meant to explore the various sections of the house in a certain general order, but it's possible to access them out of order, especially if you're hunting for easter eggs or just lucky enough to stumble on something before you're pointed to it.  This will confuse the narrative significantly, and possibly abbreviate it.  There's not much replay value -- once you've understood the family's story, the only reason to come back is to experience it all again, or if you missed something your first time through.  (The safe in the basement seems to be the most commonly-overlooked thing -- the combination is very close by, but you might not recognize it the first time around.)  And, of course, a game like this relies on you getting engaged with the characters and wanting to unravel their stories and what happened to them.  If for whatever reason they don't click with you, the whole thing will be uninteresting.
Overall, though, I highly recommend this game.  If you're very concerned about the value you're getting for a short, low-replay-value game, you may want to wait for a sale, but if you love exploration and piecing together a mystery (as I do), it may very well be worth full price.

This game is an arcade-y game, maybe like Blaster Master coupled with a SHMUP. You play as a dude looking for space loot, but ends up needing to explore a decrepit space freighter and blowing up lots of robots. I like that the game feels really slick, fresh, and has a light narrative with some clever ideas sprinkled in. The encounter design, however, feels a bit lazy, with just about every enemy or enemy projectile having homing. It just adds tedium when everything can zero-point turn on a dime and then run into you; multiplied by as many enemies as are clustered around you at the time. Fortunately, there is a fairly generous auto-save between encounters and phases of long encounters that helps temper this problem. So, the game wants to be really hard, but doesn't quite have the foundation to support itself. The controls on K+M are also WAAAY WAAAY too sensitive, as your ship will be flying disproportionately far for how long a key is pressed. Once I switched to my controller, I noticed a dramatic improvement in handling. Overall, there is enough here to recommend this game, despite some of the frustrating elements of the game's design. I justify the recommendation by mentioning that I got this as part of a Humble Bundle, so I likely paid $5/$1 to get this and several other games. Use that as your measuring stick to determine what is a fair price for this indie game.

Cook, Serve, Delicious! is a fairly innocent looking game, which is very easy to pick up and play, but hard to master. As the manager of an up-and-coming restaurant (more like a greasy spoon at first), you'll purchase food, devise a menu, and quickly whip up tasty food for the many impatient and particular customers who enter through your doors.
In CSD, you'll do everything. Yes, you're the manager, and when you're not "in the restaurant", where the bulk of the game takes place, you'll have to take the meagre funds that you start with and buy equipment and food to sell, in the hopes of turning a profit. However, your job doesn't stop there. This business is your life.
When the restaurant opens, you'll be the waiter taking the orders, the cook slaving away over the stove, and the janitor setting traps and throwing out the trash, amongst other things. How this works is extremely simple.
Customers come in, and a picture of what they want appears next to a number at the left of the screen. Let's say it's salad. Press that number and you now have to prepare the food. A bowl of greens appears in the middle, and on the right are other options tied to buttons on the keyboard, "G" for "Green and Carrots", "C" for "Cheese" etc. At the bottom of the screen it says "I want just greens and carrots", so you press G and with a tap of enter, send it out. If you don't like the keyboard, you also have the option to use the mouse and just click the icons, or even a gamepad but I can't say if that's a good way to play or not.
That took time to type out, but you'll grasp this in about 5 seconds, guaranteed. Speed and accuracy are extremely important. Speed is important because people are impatient. Once you're preparing their food, it's okay, they'll wait as long as it takes. But then other customers come in, wanting other things, so you'd better do this one quickly or they'll leave. No money for you, and even worse: you get negative buzz.
Buzz is basically a measure of your popularity. It will increase if you're doing well, and decrease if you're doing badly. Not in the same day, mind you, but a poor performance one day (missed or inaccurate orders) will mean less buzz on the next day. Other factors affect it too, such as what foods are on your menu. Each type of food has positive and negative values, which you can view before you purchase them to put on your menu, or at any time after you've done that. Some foods are Fatty foods, and if you have too many on your menu, people start to have a negative idea of your restaurant and your buzz will go down by 5% or more. Some increase buzz, by being healthy, or by being considered to be "worthy". Aspirational foods, like fine wines and lobster. A good player will take a little time to balance their menu around foods which have lots of positive values but are perhaps difficult and time-consuming to make, and easy ones which are fatty foods or come served on a stick, like something you'd get at a noisy, smelly carnival for poor people UGH
So, you have a game of two halves. You have this calm, thoughtful management aspect of the game. No customers and no need to rush, just make sensible business decisions and try not to run out of cash. And then, when you click "open restaurant", you have this frantic button-mashing, so simple it could be a minigame on Newgrounds, and you're flinging food at impatient customers and cleaning up their mess as you go. Did I just serve that customer some raw chicken? ♥♥♥♥ IT MOVE ON. *wipes sweat off brow* The game actually balances the two sides very well. There is just enough meat to the management part that you can make good decisions (or bad ones) and this will affect the other side of the game, which works wonderfully because it's simple and just plain fun. You press the buttons and serve the food, and you do it FAST.
There are a couple of issues I have with the game which I fully expect to be resolved in the sequel. Firstly, you start off with a one star restaurant, which is fine, but in order to move up to two stars and start making more money, you have to do a full 20 days of service. There's no way around that, and it doesn't matter if it's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ 20 days of terrible service where your buzz is awful, or if you got a perfect day every time. Essentially this kind of "gating off" of the second star is to prevent the difficult from getting too much too fast, but it also limits your income and your choices. I feel it would work much better as a sliding scale. Do really badly, and you have to do the full 20 days. Do really well, and you'll bag that second star after just 10 days of service. I believe this 20 days of service applies for every star level, by the way.
Another thing, and it's super petty but I have to say it. You can practice making foods before you buy them, which is AMAZING. You don't have to spend $2000 on wine only to find that it's really tricky to make and means you get it wrong or do it really slowly. BUT, you also HAVE to do chores like washing the dishes and setting traps, and there's no way to practice doing these. You have to learn on the job, and this could ♥♥♥♥ you up in the heat of the moment. Doesn't seem  fair to have one but not the other.
My final complaint is that customer orders are written in prose. "I'll have a salad with ranch, cheese, greens and carrots and mushrooms and onions", or whatever. I'm a good reader and can parse this all dead quick, which you absolutely need to do, so that's okay. But what about people who struggle to read? Wouldn't it better just to have bullet points:
*Cheese
*Mushrooms
Like that? None of the connectives, just what you need to know.
Anyway, ♥♥♥♥ all that. This game is awesome.♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's nearly Rush Hour, I'd better get my apron on.

I can only recommend this game within a specific set of paramters. If you're interested, read below:
1) Bought complete edition for under $15 (I got it for $7.20).
2) Play only on deathwish (hardest difficulty)
3) All hud removed
If you like a challenge AND want to have fun with this game, then I here's how I recommend going about it.
First try the game on easy with all the hud features, that way you're familiar with the mechanics. Take as much time as you need. I took about 5-6 hours, but I could have taken a lot less. I wouldn't recommend any more than 3.
Once you've got the hang of the gameplay and mechanics, START YOUR GAME OVER. (you don't have to, but I think it's worth it).
Play Voice of Freedom first on deathwish, then start the main campaign on deathwish. Remove all HUD elements and set music volume to zero.
By doing what I've suggested, you feel like you're actually fighting for your life against a massive, opressive force (namely the KPA). You have no HUD, no suggestions, no mini-map, no direction. Just you, your phone, and your pistol/whatever else, to take the USA back. I think that's the kind of experience the developers were going for, but made it too easy with all the hud elements. The game just felt so....bleh...on easy. The game provides a much more enjoyable, realistic experience with no HUD on the hardest difficulty.
I hope this was helpful to you!

I love this game, Banished is medieval city building game that puts you in control of small group of settlers that have been banished from their homeland, trying to start fresh in the wilderness. While most games have you gathering resources and technology to advance , in banished the people are the most important resource. You want to protect them because once they die the only way for new people to come about, is for them to be born and it takes years for them to mature and be able to contribute to the community.
Graphics: The game feels like a living and breathing creature, from the movement of the citizens, to the smooth flow of the water, you can almost feel the wind blowing in the trees as they sway back and forth. The bounding wildlife looks alive as you watch them search for food, in this utopia.
Is it Addictive and challenging? This game will challenge you in a multiple aspects, from the way you deal with everyday issues such as feeding, housing and clothing your population. By far one of the hardest challenges you will face is the survival of winter. Other challenges include making sure your population is kept warm as a supply of firewood can burn up quickly. As the population ages they also die, soon you run into unique problems such as natural disasters like twisters, lighting starting fires and lack of  population growth. If that happens jobs go unfilled and soon you find yourself in a nose dive filled with starving people, lack of firewood and gravestones.
Repetitive: Over all banished has a lot of great qualities, the amazing price. beautiful wilderness, and the challenge. however the game gets very repetitive rather quickly. Once you survive your first couple of winters and have built up a few farms and your population has grown enough to staff all the jobs, you can almost let the game go on autopilot, the day to day concerns become year to year concerns with you doing very little to improve the quality of life of your citizens. That the only thing you care about during summer is o please god winter is coming, i need more time, i need more food, i need more firewood.
Lack of winning: If you're looking for a game that will offer fulfillment this isn't it, there is no winning only losing. It just keeps going until you get bored or run out of space on the map for farms and houses. One of the few things that can make the game end is if you get unlucky enough to have a smallpox virus outbreak that kills all your people or running out of firewood in the beginning of winter. Which then causes everyone to freeze to death. However an even worse fate is still in store for the poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that you control and that is running out of food in a harsh winter and slowly watching all your hard work starve to death, as one lonely tear trickles down your face. The only thing you know is failure because no matter how hard you try, all this game wants is to see you cry.
Price:  Dont let me, persuade you from purchasing this great game, its well worth every penny of the 20$ price tag. The god like complex you develop is worth well more than 20$ you spend. there has been many an afternoon i have heard my wife telling her subjects to work harder or she will not plant enough crops for them all to survive the winter. Over all banished offers a very unique set of circumstances and lets you go wild in the pursuit of the utopia you wish to create.

When this game was released, it became one of the most polarizing games in recent memory. Much of the negativity regarding this game arose from the game's themes and subject matter, which if you're unfamiliar with at the time of reading this review, worry not, you'll find no spoilers here.
In my honest opinion, this game is a must-play. It's not quite the game that people were expecting, many of whom expected it to be a horror game of some description. While I can say that this is definitely not the case, it is most certainly not lacking in atmosphere and eeriness at many points throughout, a tone that I still felt during my time playing the game, even knowing what not to expect from it, and even the second time that I eventually came back to play it.
More than anything however, the story of this game is a truly beautiful one, and is neither pandering nor politically correct, it is simply a story that I'm sure has been an experience of many people in our own world, past, present and future. Regardless of whether this kind of story has been heard before, there has been no such story to my knowledge, represented in gaming form, a medium that can contain a great deal more immersion when executed correctly, making this kind of story highly suitable to the platform.
I will admit that this game is what some people might describe as a "walking simulator", in the sense that you have an entire mansion-sized house to yourself to explore. The potential for tediousness wth this however, is quickly avoided through both the aforemetnioned atmosphere to the game, as well the promise for more tidbits of story, which lead you from room to room through the game. This can be a short game, though the experience of playing it can very easily be drawn out to a few hours, so long as you do not rush through the story, and play the game as intended.

This review will probably be lost in the sands of other reviews, but I thought I'd put my thoughts out here anyway.
Overall, the game is a little more difficult to learn if you aren't using a controller. It isn't because controllers are convenient, but because quite literally all of the tutorials are showing you how to play- using the controller format. Come to think of it, it isn't limited to the tutorials, it's true for everything. If you want to learn everything for yourself, you can just skip this next part.
Luckily, the first area is kind of like a "safe haven" where you can try to learn these controls on your own.
The game itself rewards the cautious and alert. I've saved myself dozens of times because I looked both ways before crossing a room, or realized that item next to a corner is probably a trap. Of course, to learn "that item is probably a trap", I had to die or nearly die to a similar situation. This is where the next paragraph comes in.
The game also gives you many chances to learn the area around you, learn the AI of an enemy, or notice patterns. If you die or rest at a bonfire, all enemies respawn in the exact same area, in the exact same state. Things technically don't get easier, but because of this it feels like it does once you go through the same area enough times.
Anyway, aside from the game expecting you to use a controller, I really don't mind. I know it looks like I haven't played this very long, but that's because I typically play offline at this point in time. Not sure if that'll change in the near future, but it won't matter because this review will be lost in the sea of other reviews.

Dark Souls II is what you get when the guys at From Software wants you really, really dead. Several things that they did better than DaS:
+ They fixed how the PvP works (at least it's fun in low-mid SM tier, before every player you came across is basically a Sentier-swinging Havel). Covenant feels a bit "grind-ish" but gives different rewards for every rank. Limited means to invade discourages people from invading thougtlessly. Lagsouls and phantom range still exist though, which is a bit annoying but can be prevented with region lock matchmaking.
+ Game gets harder the more you die. Enemy despawns after so many tries means souls are a finite resource and should be used with careful planning. Also lowering HP as the hollowing takes place is a nice reason to not die, should you need another.
However there are several areas were DaS II failed to deliver:
- Level design is a total immersion breaker. In DaS you can go anywhere, each areas are basically connected to one another and makes a logical transition. Meanwhile in DaS II you'd be forced to warp back to Majula eventually, and the transition is terrible. Take the Old King path, for example: you go through an abandoned royal hunting ground, arrived in an abandoned mining facility filled with poisonous gas, which leads to a giant windmill. When you finally arrived at the top of the windmill, you take another elevator going up and you'd arrive to a sinking fortress made from iron, in the middle of an active volcano.
- Boss fights (and the boss itself) are badly designed. DaS have some of the most memorable boss fights. Take Sif: a giant wolf swinging a giant greatsword and you'd actually understand how the sword came to the wolf's possession. Or the intimidation you felt when you go into Anor Londo royal hall and had to face the Ornstein and Smough duo. Here in DaS II we have a giant boss, the last of his race, ripping his own arm in an attempt to club you to death.
- Badly written lore/story that doesn't even compare to DaS. Who was the Lost Sinner? What sin did she commit? How did she came to posses a fragment of the old witch soul? The lore in Souls Series is always obscure, but in the original game they actually had a story about the great lords and bosses.
Despite all that this is a game that I enjoy thoroughly (60+ hrs in now, can see myself investing another 100 into this game). This is a good game by itself, although not a worthy successor of the original Dark Souls.

Much like 50% of the people who bought this remaster I played this game as a kid and I liked it a lot as a kid. As an adult I'm wiser and I've learned to notice wild and blatant flaws. I'm going to be ignoring ffx-2 for the sake of brevity (it's the better game of the two) and hone in on FFX since it's sort of the starting point and generally considered more culturally relevant.
I'm going to start by praising that the HD remaster has a few built in cheats and more importantly an option to speed up gameplay (sort of) and an option to automatically fight thru battles. These are good additions but poorly implemented. The speed up of the gameplay doesn't speed up animations during overdrives, which are the lengthiest animations in a battle and therefor what you'll spend half your time seeing as a result of having to wait thru them and the automatic fight in battle just has your characters use the regular attack function every turn. This remake was brought to us after FFXII provided players with a "gambit system" which allowed them to set up automatic actions for the characters to perform that weren't ♥♥♥♥ing completely asinine. I don't expect the HD remaster to have a full gambit system but maybe making people with low strength and high magic cast spells would be like an obvious little inclusion or failing that, it could just auto confirm the last selected option in the battle menu so your characters perform the same action every battle. That would be really easy to implement and instead they chose an inferior option where they basically give your team the berserk status. Furthermore this game is sorely in need of a skip cutscene. People complained when this game was released about how you'd sit thru a 6 minute cutscene, maybe lose to a somewhat overpowered boss that you couldn't possibly be prepared for the first time around due to jenkiness and instant kills on the boss' part and then have to sit thru the 6 minute cutscene again.
It comes with an arranged version of the soundtrack and I guess the graphics look nicer kind of sure whatever.
Too bad the animations still look like♥♥♥♥♥♥sometimes.
Which is amazing cause I mean damn the graphics are nice. But then you go thru the nightmare that is any of the cloister of trials where you if you're lucky you can completely turn your brain off and then come to 5 minutes later with the trial complete. Realistically tho you probably shouldn't be able to ignore terrible things and you'll be stuck with very slow and very terrible repetitive animations of you putting spheres into things wherein a confirmation window pops up and the only option is to do the thing or not do the thing but there is never a penalty for doing the thing so why is there a confirmation window? Cause FF games waste your idiot time and you're stupid for playing them. Then when you're watching these animations of you pushing a pillar into a slope you can't help but notice that the pillar clips thru the floor or the ice or the wall during its agonizingly slow journey and you wonder why the developers would shove that in your face. Like they really want to waste your time by making you watch the least impressive thing they could provide you with.
In battle gameplay is almost not worth talking about. Easier enemies you beat by hitting confirm until the battle is over and there's no thought involved but hey you have to fight them again and again and again anyway. Slightly stronger enemies might require you to heal once or twice in battle and you still go thru the same rinse repeat motions so that's terrible. Actually strong enemies are stupidly non interactive. I've wondered why poison, sleep, blind, etc etc etc status effects are in final fantasy games since I was a child because against weaker enemies you have no impetus to inflict these statuses on your opponents and against stronger enemies they're useless because your enemy is pointlessly immune to things. So boss fights and the like might occasionally contain one gimmick where the boss can actually be negatively effected by a status thing but much more often they can't be. The design of the superbosses is even worse. Dark Ixion's thunder spell isn't actually thunder aligned so you'll go into the fight with a lightning ward on or something thinking oh hey maybe this ♥♥♥♥ing ability is useful for the first time in the game but no you get killed because of this nonintuitive thing the designers added to waste your time that you shouldn't have had to anticipate because you shouldn't be playing a game wondering what idiot thing the developer is going to force you thru next.
Blitzball is like a faux sports/sports management type game but it's so overly simple and so poorly introduced (you go thru your first game without any introduction to having played the game and the first game is a tournament in story) that after the first time playing it you should be hoping it will never be forced upon you again.
Levelling up with the sphere grid is a horrible nightmare and nobody thinks it isn't. It's a poor system that's intentionally bogged down to give the illusion of complexity but for even the quickest level ups it takes you choosing to take an action moving, then confirming the move, then you watch an animation of your little sphere moving, then you click confirm, choose a sphere to use, confirm using it and then repeat that another 2 more times. If you're somehow under the illusion that it's actually complex I highly recommend looking up "Straightening Out Final Fantasy X's Sphere Grid".
If I really wanted to break down more of why and how this game is terrible it would take another 5 pages of writing about bits of nuance but I'm going to leave it at what I've written so far and hope that I can have saved at least a couple curious people from wasting 16 dollars. If you really want to play something turn based go play Banner Saga or Xcom or something. Or if you really really need the FFX experience just watch the 10 hour marathon video on youtube.

Great port of a great game. Runs like an absolute dream on my mid-level rig and it has all the features you've seen on the PS4 version on top of the configuration options you'd expect a PC game to have.
However, SNK's curse of poor netcode remains. Online is absolutely TERRIBLE. It's about as choppy as the PS4 version if not worse in most instances. I could barely play a match without stutter or high input delay and this was with people who were as close as possible to me.
Netcode issues aside, King of Fighters XIV is an outstanding game. Loaded with a huge variety of both returning and brand new characters, a renewed MAX system that combines elements from KOF13's HD/Super meter into one, all the while maintaining the series mainstay mechanics such as rolling and blowback attacks. It's a fantastic experience and there is a lot to dive into that can keep you busy.
I highly recommend this game for local play as it's one of the best fighting games out there right now and a must own for anyone who is a fighting game fan. However, in regards to online play, do not put money down for this if you're planning to play online until a patch comes out to optimize the netcode.

The protagonist and his video game references can be a little grating at times.  But that's mostly forgivable, because the game plays like a love letter to all the shooters he references.  The beautifully machine you pilot has modes that make it more or less mimic every genre of side-scrolling shooter ever.  (I've not finished the game, as it is pretty challenging, but I haven't seen Bullet Hell yet.)  What you have here is basically an anthology game, with a seamless framing narrative.  The framing story itself is full of elements you'll recognize from elsewhere.  (The ship AI is equal parts GLADOS and Wheatley, for instance.)  But the way the homages to old shooters are presented within that story is original and enjoyable enough it doesn't matter.
The game auto-saves, so it's pretty easy to play 5 or 10 minutes at a time.  I wouldn't really call this casual, though.  This game can be brutally difficult at times.

I bought this game as a part of the last humble-bundle after seeing it at GC 2016 and being pretty impressed by it. The game plays as a combination of twin-stick shooter and a metroidvania game. However the enemies the game presents are another story. Often times, the screen is filled by enemies, which approach you quickly and no clear pattern is describable. You just have to jam your gun and hope you make it out fine - if not- reset! Which you will do quite often.
The main character and his antagonist are immediately endearing and well written, the story is charming but the pacing feels maybe a bit plodding and a bit slow at times. The writing is fourth-wall breaking, but not in a awkward way and makes the whole game more enjoyable. The whole presentation is fitting, with nice menus and flavorful in-between-mission title cards.
The game is challenging, with fast enemies, environmental hazards and platforming sections. After my first hour I started to feel kind off frustrated after failing many sections of the levels, only to realize the game was designed that way. You have to memorize the patterns of lasers, buzz saws and flaming pits and then execute your movements perfectly in order to advance. Personally, I don't enjoy execution as much as exploration and system-building, but people who are seeking this kind of challenge, will find it here. My main gripe with this game is, that it builds a character that is maneuverable but time and time again it builds smallish battle-areas, where you have fight wave after wave of enemies. Several times, I was not sure if I should progress but can't find my way or if I am stuck there for some arbitrary time. In addition to this, there is no indicator for how long more you are required to fight, which proved somewhat frustrating (at least to me.)
Overall, the game is enjoyable, with a fun little story and challenging gameplay.

Very slick card game that sits in complexity between Hearthstone and Spellweaver. What I appreciate most about it is the refined interface that allows you to play quickly without waiting for animations to finish, and to have access to all info you need about the various card effects.
The MTG-inspired battle mechanics are pretty good, as is the Instant system which allows you to react to enemy instants, stacking effects until one player stops replying - the only thing I sometimes wish for in Spellweaver, though that's definitely a tradeoff that will slow the game down when facing some players.
The number of game modes available is also laudable, everything from gauntlet vs the AI to Ranked, to Draft.
This said compared to Spellweaver or Hex I find browsing the card collection quite yawn-inducing. The effects on most cards are not very inspiring to say the least, they don't fire my imagination about potential synergies and combos like the former games do.
In the end I'm recommending it as "fast food": it's easy to get into, they even give you pre-made decks regularly so you can just jump in without knowing a thing about deckbuilding, and you'll already be playing something more interesting than starter decks.

Eternal Card Game follows the “traditional” CCG model that Hearthstone popularized of “dusting” and “crafting” cards. It is a collectible game only as there is no trading system. Eternal is currently in open beta at the time I am writing this, so you should take all my thoughts here with a grain of salt as I am sure anything I talk about here is very much subject to change between when I post this and when the game is marked as a finished product.
To date I have logged a few dozen hours playing the game in open beta and have spent probably an equal amount of time playing it during closed beta. I am going to focus on three areas when talking about the game today: Game Play, Software Quality, and Formats (Limited / Constructed / Single Player).
Game Play
The core of Eternal’s gameplay is similar to other modern card games today. There are five “factions” that require different “influences” to play cards from. The resource system Eternal utilizes is identical to that of Hex: Shards of Fate, which is a good thing in my opinion. It is a modern take on the resource system that Magic introduced two decades ago.
The game play in Eternal strikes a very interesting balance between the slightly clunky priority system Magic utilizes and the fast pace, little interaction, game play of something like Hearthstone. In general I am a fan of the pacing of the games in Eternal. I get some interaction on my opponent’s turn via “fast” spells, but I do not need to manually pass priority or configure different “stops” to play the game properly.
The fast game play does come slightly at the cost of strategic gameplay though. Eternal only pauses to give your opponent a chance to respond to things when they have the ability to actually respond. This means that if your opponent passes the turn with resources up you can often play a “test card” to see if there is a pause for them to respond before playing out the card you actually want to do something with.
The mulligan system in Eternal is worth commenting on a well. Each player is allowed exactly one mulligan per-game, but the mulligan you take is guaranteed to have between 2 and 5 resources in it. While I think this system does a good job of creating less non-games than something like Magic’s mulligan system does, you do still have some non-games where your second hand is nonfunctional due to the curve or types of influences it requires.
To prevent abuse of this mulligan system there is a deck building requirement that all of your decks must be at least ⅓ resources.
Software Quality
Direwolf Digital is a software company and the quality of their product shows it. The Eternal client is fairly slick in almost every aspect. It is fairly attractive and runs smoothly on everything from my Linux / Windows PCs to my Android phone. Even though the software comes with a beta tag it has been nothing but stable for me throughout my dozens of hours of game play.
My only two complaints about the current client are fairly minor and could easily change before the stable release. The first is that the “end turn” button is located in the same place as every other button in the game. This leads to accidently skipping turns when you do not intend to. The button for passing your turn should likely be in a different location or have a confirmation that you intended to press it.
The second is that it can often be hard to distinguish between cards that are “exhausted”, or used, and those that are not when looking at the game board. Cards that are used are simply a faded color as opposed to changing direction / size / something that makes them clearly used.
Formats
There are four primary methods of playing games of Eternal. Gauntlet (single player constructed), Forge (single player limited), Ranked (PvP constructed), and Draft (PvP limited).
The limited in Eternal is hands down the best I have played in any digital card game to date. Forge does a good job of introducing new people to limited. Each pick gives you three cards to choose from and once you have two different factions of cards you will only see cards from those factions for the remainder of your picks.
The draft format is where the innovation really is though. The draft is fully asynchronous, which means you can draft on your own without ever waiting for other players. You can always pause mid draft and pick back up later on. There is no timer on your picks so you have plenty of time to make important decisions. You draft from four, twelve card packs until you have 48 cards and you get to keep the cards you draft. You then build a 45 card deck with 48 cards you have drafted plus resources.
People who follow me from other games know that constructed is my true passion. I enjoy tuning new ideas and working on things that are traditionally outside the box. It is fairly expensive to get all of the cards you need to be able to play a variety of decks in Eternal’s constructed due to many of the better cards being legendary and being four ofs in the better decks. While most card games come with a large price tag to own everything, Eternal’s lack of trading means any money you put in can never be cashed out.
I put $40 into Eternal to buy some packs and do some extra drafts, not only because I wanted to support Direwolf, but also so I could play some constructed. I was able to battle to Masters (the highest rank) with a budget deck that did not contain any legendaries, but my interest in the game started to wander when I realized I need to spend a good deal of time grinding or dump in a pile of money to get all of the cards I wanted to experiment with.
For reference if you want to craft a specific legendary card it would cost you approximately 8 USD worth of product to do so assuming you were not lucky enough to open that specific card.
Wrapping Up
All in all Eternal is a very reasonable digital offering. It does a good job of offering faster game play, while still having many of the tactical decisions generally only present in longer games like Magic. The technology support is there, so the main thing that will be the driving force to determine if Eternal can become and stay popular is the strength of their card design team. We currently only have one set released, so time will tell if they excel in this area or not.

I have two main problems with this game that ruin it for me. The setting, and the difficulty, or rather the nature of the difficulty.
The setting is really just boring. Extremely samely with little variety for enviroments. Basically, it's all just dark decrepit space station with a few element variations such as the lava and water levels, but basically it still very much the same. It doesn't help that enemies are equally limited in variety, with most common ones being flying bomb robots that just rush you, or torpedo like bots that fly in a fixed pattern. However, given the game's length, this isn't too bad of a problem, and by itself wouldn't really bring the game down for me. What does do so is the challenge, not that it's too hard, but that it relies on trial and error to beat, and a lot of repetition.
That's the only thing I can call a significant amount of the challenge of this game, trail and error. Many times, the game hits you with hard to, if not impossible to forsee threats and obstacles that can easily kill you very quickly. The obstacles themselves aren't all that hard to avoid/defeat, but it's in seeing them coming where the annoyence starts. One good example would be the escape sections where you need to outrun a certain threat, such as lava or crushing mechanisms. You're field of view is limited to what's just in front of you, and without forknowledge of what happens next during the chase, you'll likely get surprise killed by something you couldn't see coming and/or aren't given enough time to react to unless you're already doing the specific thing they section wanted you to do beforehand.
This happens in other aspects. You can get killed by things outside of you're field of view, you can literally fall into situations that demand instant reaction such as dropping onto a conveyer belt that speeds you toward an instant death saw that you have 2 seconds to react to, and enemy swarms that can pop out fast with little warning and destroy you if you happen to be near their spawn point. But, after you know what's coming and can plan ahead, the game isn't toooooo hard, but that brings me to the second aspect of the difficulty I don't like, the repetitive combat.
As I said before, enemy units severly lack variety, which is made even worse by the fact that the game mostly throws the basic, common enemies at you through the entire game, with no evolution from what they are in the beginning. Worse than that, the enemies don't have a varied attack method even counting all the types. Most are some form of contact damage flying bot that rushes you and damages on touch. There's turrents which shoot homing missiles which basically function that same as the first type of enemies, or beams which act as movement restricters. Then there's some squid like bot that fly close and shoot missiles, and flamethrower spider bots, but they're are far in the minority of enemies you face. Add to this, is that the game's approach to game length is by having segments where wave after wave of the same enemies come at you, in the same numbers, over, and over, and over, and over.........and over and over.....................................................................and over again, maybe increasing the number by 1 or 2 after a few intervals. This is where the repetition becomes most prevalent as I redid the same strategy again and again until the waves stopped. Maybe this wouldn't be a problem if it happened every once in a while, but it's a far too frequent method of game length padding that gets boring fast. Maybe this is common for games of this genre, but I'd like to think standards and game potential have risen so that having more complex combat and enemy variety in a combat focused game should be expected.
Outside of all this, there are a few minor gripes I have. There's a few situations where certain objects bugged out and didn't work properly such as a flaming rock getting stuck in place when it's supposed to roll out of the way. I doubt it's common though and that other players will experience the same ones I did, but the possibility is there. Also, the story isn't all too interesting, at least for me. It's a simple plot that's primerily a meta classic video game homage, with references to video gaming, game genres, and specific famous games like Tetris. Some people might like it, but I found it more on the obnoxious side of referential joking and allusion.
Long story short, The game isn't bad. It's perfectly functional aside from the few minor glitches I experienced, and the core gameplay is solid, but it does so little in terms of content variety and expansion, Has such a limied amount of variety in setting and styles, and relies too much on trial and error as a substitute for more entertaining forms of challenge that I can't find any great joy from it. I beat the game once, and have no interest in beating it again. It might be worth it for some fans of the genre, but for me, it's just a plain sidescrolling shooter, of whic hthere are better alternatives.

I love this game, Banished is medieval city building game that puts you in control of small group of settlers that have been banished from their homeland, trying to start fresh in the wilderness. While most games have you gathering resources and technology to advance , in banished the people are the most important resource. You want to protect them because once they die the only way for new people to come about, is for them to be born and it takes years for them to mature and be able to contribute to the community.
Graphics: The game feels like a living and breathing creature, from the movement of the citizens, to the smooth flow of the water, you can almost feel the wind blowing in the trees as they sway back and forth. The bounding wildlife looks alive as you watch them search for food, in this utopia.
Is it Addictive and challenging? This game will challenge you in a multiple aspects, from the way you deal with everyday issues such as feeding, housing and clothing your population. By far one of the hardest challenges you will face is the survival of winter. Other challenges include making sure your population is kept warm as a supply of firewood can burn up quickly. As the population ages they also die, soon you run into unique problems such as natural disasters like twisters, lighting starting fires and lack of  population growth. If that happens jobs go unfilled and soon you find yourself in a nose dive filled with starving people, lack of firewood and gravestones.
Repetitive: Over all banished has a lot of great qualities, the amazing price. beautiful wilderness, and the challenge. however the game gets very repetitive rather quickly. Once you survive your first couple of winters and have built up a few farms and your population has grown enough to staff all the jobs, you can almost let the game go on autopilot, the day to day concerns become year to year concerns with you doing very little to improve the quality of life of your citizens. That the only thing you care about during summer is o please god winter is coming, i need more time, i need more food, i need more firewood.
Lack of winning: If you're looking for a game that will offer fulfillment this isn't it, there is no winning only losing. It just keeps going until you get bored or run out of space on the map for farms and houses. One of the few things that can make the game end is if you get unlucky enough to have a smallpox virus outbreak that kills all your people or running out of firewood in the beginning of winter. Which then causes everyone to freeze to death. However an even worse fate is still in store for the poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that you control and that is running out of food in a harsh winter and slowly watching all your hard work starve to death, as one lonely tear trickles down your face. The only thing you know is failure because no matter how hard you try, all this game wants is to see you cry.
Price:  Dont let me, persuade you from purchasing this great game, its well worth every penny of the 20$ price tag. The god like complex you develop is worth well more than 20$ you spend. there has been many an afternoon i have heard my wife telling her subjects to work harder or she will not plant enough crops for them all to survive the winter. Over all banished offers a very unique set of circumstances and lets you go wild in the pursuit of the utopia you wish to create.

For the first time in a long time, I was properly scared while playing a game!
Atmosphere is everything in Outlast. The sound design is superb, with little sounds indicating the presence of nearby enemies and tense ambient music when something significant happens in the game world. The attention to detail is another factor that creates such an effective atmosphere. The walls look real, lighting has a full spectrum of dark to light, and animations are realistic.
The camera is a nice gameplay element. The night vision is the most realistic I’ve seen in games and extremely creepy when navigating pitch black environments (plenty of those).
What I enjoyed most about Outlast was the disturbing story. I won’t spoil anything, but it’s very well done and there are certain moments that really shine. The only problem was how quickly it finished and left me wanting more.
Buy this game. It’s short, but very well made.

King of fighters 14 is a breath of fresh life into a venerated series with their first foray into 3d. Sadly, this is a bit hit and miss to an overall excellent fighter.
Video:
Text:
The video, as always provides much more depth than a few paragraphs can.
First, lets talk about the visuals - the switch to 3D is a welcome one in my eyes, but the implementation isn't the greatest. I wont disparate the animation or combat interaction quality, those are absolutely fantastic. Combat feels great with each punch and kick and magical ice-blast feeling exactly as you would imagine and reactive and instant actions being very responsive. Again: KoF 14 is a fantastic fighting game.
But it does look like a game from 3 or 4 years ago visually. While 60FPS without any dips is great (and important for fighting games more than almost any other genre), the visual fidelity (including options) is very lackluster, which is a damn shame. It looks closer to Street fighter 4, than it does to any modern competitor, even when it it can trade them blow for blow on the technical implementation.
So, onward to other parts of the game, i (mostly) have praise. The tutorial is extensive and mostly good, the training mode is excellent and a very solid addition. the local multiplayer is amazing to have and all in all this is a very complete product. Especially taking the solid online component into account.
But its not perfect, and the issues here are twofold: Find online matches isn't as smooth as i'd like with especially unranked games being hit and miss on matchmaking quality (getting curb stomped 9/10 games isn't that fun to me). The Second issue does tie directly into this..."getting good" requires an immense number of hours and with a roster of 54 characters, a lot of grinding. The game does to try create more accessibility / forgiveness for newer players, but even then its a very steep learning curve before you can stand on two feet, which is not that great.
That said, Once you get on your two feet, or if you want to face the AI / Friends, you really cant do wrong in looking in the direction of this game for your Face smashing fun.

Before you move on to read me say how I feel about the game the most anyone casually passing this review is to answer the question of is the port good. Tl;Dr: The game port is good and it is a quality fighting game.
KOF XIV breaks tradition in a lot of ways. Tons of new characters, as in fresh characters to the SNK universe as well as some older SNK faces unexpected in KOF, a very home focus on marketing the game and a new 3D animation style that is pretty in some places and rubbish in others. I am a massive weeb so I prefer 2D animated fighters. I can appreciate a good looking 3D art style like Guilty Gear Xrd. KOF XIV does not look anywhere as awful as it did in it's debut trailer and certainly does what it is trying to do at least. It just visually very shiny but a bit bland and while some characters like Yamazaki show so much energy and prove SNK was trying hard to make the best of their 3D it still comes off as bland looking.
Gameplay wise obviously it is good. SNK have dumbed down the game a bit but have not sunk as low as some developers go and that is nice. Years and playing and I still have a tough time really getting down the more advanced stuff of KOF even in this easier game but that is entirely my fault. The game remains very fun and shows that some games can go on for fourteen damn games and still be good. The auto-combo system is stupid. A stupid choice made for stupid people. Not that I mind folk enjoy fighting games on a casual level, fighting games can be fun for all, but I dislike auto-combos as a concept and this game does nothing to change that.

The King of Fighters XIV quickly became my favourite fighting game even when it was still in beta (I played it for 40 hours in total). It features a fast-paced and well-balanced gameplay, with tons of cool characters to choose from. The Combo Rush system (new combos which are relatively weak but very easy to use) is an excellent addition to the series, as it allows you to competitively play as characters which you haven't mastered yet, which is especially useful in Story mode, but it also gives newcomers a little advantage in Online mode without ruining the game for veteran players. The graphics are nice and the stages are beautifully crafted, with background characters cheering the fighters and reacting to various combat moves in a natural way. KoF XIV also features a classic arcade-like Story mode, which is becoming rare these days. Good online experience so far. TOTALLY WORTH THE PRICE! Keep up the good work, SNK!

Cook, Serve, Delicious is a restauarnt management game where you have to set up you restaurant and prepare a whole bunch of meals for your customers. The art style of this game drew me in, but it was the game play that hooked me and kept me playing for a very long time.
Most dishes are somewhat simple to prepare. Click a few buttons, try to replicate what the customer asked for, let it cook, and send it. The difficulty is in perfecting the dish so that you can serve it many times over the course of the day, and do it quickly and correctly. Choose your menu items carefully, because some dishes might really trip you up when you're presse for time. The farther you get through the game, the harder it gets, and New Game+ mode is pure insanity. Insanely tough and insanely fun.
There's really not much to complain about with this game. The controls are pretty solid (I recommend a game controller), the music is very nice, and the art is stylish and pleasant. This game is surprisingly well polished for an indie game.
Cook, Serve, Delicious is absolutely worth buying, and I could recommend it to just about anybody. It's honestly among the best games I've played in recent years.

Receiver is a fun little FPS game which focuses on some pretty advanced and realistic gun control mechanics.
You control every aspect of using whichever firearm you randomly spawn with from manually loading bullets into the magazine to removing the magazine and pulling the slide.
You roam around the randomly generated map collecting bullets, flashlights and tapes which give you the insight into Receiver's background story. You win once you have collected all 11 tapes.
In my opinion, the price of £4 is well worth the experience of originally trying to work out the weapon mechanics to roaming around taking out the hostile drones like a professional.
There are also mods for Receiver which expand upon the original three firearms and include bug fixes and optimisations which I highly recommend.

Although there are microtransactions, I would not consider this game "pay-to-win" since I never feel I was killed by someone because of the cool shiny weapon they were using with a $50 price tag on it.

Fun game; I got vibes of a lot of games playing this; from Call of Duty (3 or whatever)'s grungy tones in some areas and near-future warfare, to Far Cry's capturing strongholds and open world (the game is more like Far Cry 2, 3 or 4 than any other game I mention here), to Half Life 2's overtones (some levels feel like occupied City 17 at times) and some puzzle mechanics, to Assassin's Creed's verticality and stealth gameplay. According to Wikipedia this game got a bunch of 4s and 5s out of 10; with a lot of that being due to technical issues. Having bought it and played it a year after launch and after various patches / DLC were released, I'd happily give it an 8/10.
As far as bugs go (because this game was notorious for them when it came out), playing in November 2017, I only encountered 2; in one shipyard level there's a bug with scripted NPCs getting freezing and blocking a walkway I needed to get through; I googled the issue and the solution was easy; just wait in an overhead area you just came from and it doesn't occur. The other issue was that alt-tabbing could sometimes cause the game to behave as if it were borderless, with the mouse being able to click outside the game (or through it) and pull you out of the game. My solution was to just restart the game; not great, but the game loads quickly and lets you skip through the initialising screen, so getting back to the action is quite quick.
Gun gameplay is weird in that it seems to have mouse acceleration or something, but it's acceptable. I ended up only really using 2 of the ~15 or so possible weapons (SMG and battle rifle). One negative is that it's too easy to unlock / buy everything.
Without spoiling anything, the story isn't great, but at least the voice acting, facial animations, etc aren't bad. One negative is that the game goes a little unnecessarily excessive with scripted camera / player movement. Sometimes you can wander a room during a cutscene, othertimes you're on rails; it's a bit inconsistent in that way. Haven't played the DLC yet but the main campaign, while playing reasonably quickly / without trying to be a completionist at all, took about 11 hours.
Graphics are great; the game capped its framerate at my monitor's max refresh rate, but with an i5 3570k, 16GB RAM and GTX1080 it ran smoothly at max settings.

Rating: 7/10
Genre: Open world FPS
The Good:
+ Great graphics and plenty of graphical options
+ I really love the atmosphere; a derelict city, airships, enemies patrolling the streets etc. I feel like it’s a mixture of deus ex, half life 2, Stalker. I know that’s a lofty claim to make but it’s the one aspect of the game that really held everything together.
+ The gun play is solid, often requiring some strategy, standing out in the open even on normal difficulty will get you killed quickly. You will have to hide behind cover, strafe and sometimes run away to survive.
+ Completing missions earns you money and xp allowing you to buy more weapons/upgrades, gear, attachments etc.
+ Customize guns with different scopes, muzzles, grips etc.
+ Like most open world games there is plenty to do, most of them revolving around taking over districts by navigating the level design and hacking a computer while killing enemies along the way. After doing so, your faction takes over that part of the city making it easier to traverse the open area. I found most of them fun to complete as each one felt like a little puzzle to solve.
+ Sound Effects
The Average:
+/- Multiplayer is long dead.
The Bad:
- Respawning enemies, resulting in some frustrating missions.
- lack of save option in an open world game.
- Some really annoying bugs/glitches that bring the entire game down.
Conclusion:
I can only assume this was a bug-ridden, unplayable mess upon launch given all the low scores and I can believe it. Even after the game was patched I still encountered some annoying bugs, I almost ended up getting a game breaking bug as well. It does nothing new it terms of gameplay, if you ever played an open world FPS game then this game provides no surprises but what you do have here is a solid FPS game worthy of your time.

This game isn't great at one particular thing, but rather competent in most areas. As a package, it's not a bad game at all! But picking apart one aspect and analyzing it, you will find that it's "good" or "alright" in most cases. The graphics are quite decent, and allow a passable amount of customization for a game more catered towards those on console. With max graphics settings the game ran very smoothly on my gtx980 + i5 4690k, something very important for consistency while hotlapping, or when racing other drivers.
The sounds are nice and reflect the sounds of the 2016 spec cars, however, the seem to be missing something I can't quite put my finger on. Their sound doesn't seem to reflect how powerful they are (lets keep the vacuum cleaner jokes to yourself), almost as if they are slightly muffled
. Onboard videos give you a sense that these cars/engines are indeed incredibly powerful, but it's hard to get that across in this game, even with max volume. That being said, I believe they are all unique to each car. The Mercedes sounds more raw than the Ferrari, which is indeed the case in real life.
It is very, very, very nice having all of the circuits from the calendar, however, they aren't particularly special, and in my opinion, feel quite weird to drive around in after spending some time on the laser scanned tracks from Assetto Corsa. Perhaps it is the lighting or general desaturated feeling this game has, but some corners just feel alien to me after driving them in other titles.
Each car from each team is uniquely modeled, including the chassis, power unit, driver's helmets, gloves, unique steering wheels, and liveries. This is no doubt
, and something you simply can't get in Assetto Corsa.
The behavior of the cars is enjoyable enough-the cars will, and do, spin out if you get on the throttle too early, and the brakes will lock up- provided you play without assists :). Gameplay on a controller is
, so it's hard for me to reccommend this to someone playing on a controller (which is indeed a great deal of players). That's not saying you can't have fun with the game, but it will be hard to race at a higher level with the amount of input lag.
The controls outside of turning the wheel are slightly confusing, and took a little getting used to. Navigating radio menus was quite difficult, and I could never seem to do what I wanted to in the menus while driving. This is something I personally had trouble with, however, with a little work I'm sure it's not a big deal.
The net code seemed to be rather bad as well when comparted to other games that require several updates per second to register small movements. Again, could by something on my end, but I'm just throwing anything else I could think of in this review at this point.
All in all, it can be a fun game to play, however, it does fall in that boundary category between something like Assetto Corsa and the Forza series.
