I bought this game, and the others from the trilogy-pack because I hoped that it might be a cheaper alternative to Codename: Panzers, which I have on cd but can't play anymore, because the old, outdated copyright-protection software causes a conflict with win10 (at least that's what I think is going on). I was a bit disappointed. Of course, in this game you also have to work with limited troops, but there is one thing about Codename: Panzers that I really liked: You get some money after each mission, and then between the missions you can use that money to add units to your army (or replace the ones that died). also, units get xp when they're in battle and become stronger if you manage to keep them alive for long enough. It makes you really care about all your soldiers. And, contrary to my assumptions, this does not seem to be possible in Sudden Strike.
However, I do still recommend the game, because even though I was disappointed because of wrong assumptions, it is still a very nice and interesting strategy game. If you are not bothered by outdated graphics and other things that are normal for very old games, you will probably enjoy this game. But don't make the same mistake that I made and assume it is completely like Codename: Panzers just because a few things are similar. If you do that, you will probably be a bit disappointed, at least until you have played long enough to be able to appreciate this game without making any comparisons.
Just to clarify, I don't think one of the two is better or worse. They simply do a few things in a very similar way but are ultimately two entirely different games, therefore I do not want to compare them. This is just meant to be a warning for anyone who might have the same wrong assumptions that I got from reading the store page and a few forum-threads and reviews.

Sudden Strike defines the Real Time Tactics genre, as there is no base-building to be done. There are no resources to collect, no units that the player has any ability to spawn, and no technologies that must be researched. Therefore, it is not a race to any technology, special unit, or army size, like a typical RTS. In Sudden Strike, you are given a fixed amount of units to order around at the beginning of the mission. Often you will receive reinforcements, but rarely do you have any intentional influence on when they will arrive. You simply cannot beat your enemy by mobbing them, or by spamming them. Instead, you have to figure out how to flank the machine gunners, how to keep the armored cars away from your foot-soldiers, which building to hide your sniper in, and even who to re-supply in the heat of the fight. Each of your units has experience. Ones that have survived more fights can see further, react faster, and hit more often. That being said, they are still not super-human, and two enemies at once will take them down. Each unit feels real. When you send three men to a front-line AT gun, you root for them. You try your best to preserve every single person, including those that jump out of your burning tanks. You come to care for your little guys, because you can't just spawn a thousand more. There are hundreds of unit-types, and things seem to be less restricted by balance and focused on what sorts of weapons and machinery was available to each side in WWII. The missions are well-varied. Some are to defend a front, and some are to attack a front. Some give you just a small group of men, and some give you an army. Some missions are long (don't worry, you can save any time), while others are over in minutes. Many RTT games never make the transition from several squads to an army, while Sudden Strike plays both. It even comes with the scenario editor used by the creators themselves. Sudden Strike is difficult and realistic, but a lot of fun.

You *will* need the auto save just to ensure that your controller, mouse and keyboard doesn't become a permanent dent against your wall.
My PC could play FFXIII and Dishonored 2 without much issue but this port is a disaster. The thing is it can crash as odd times, when you move from one screen to another, during battle, an odd spell or two. If I am able to play this game for two hours straight without crashing, I considering it a good session.
Two hours. For a game that averages 40. Yes, hairs were pulled and teeth gritted. Which is why the Auto-Save feature was practically a boon.
There are countless discussions as to what is exactly causing this unpredictable crashes  but it is something that Square-Enix has no interest in fixing, which is a goddamn shame cause otherwise the game is quite amazing. If you're looking for a good PC port update, this is not for you. Not unless you have a great deal of patience. If you want to buy wait for a sale.

The game is good. At first it seemed like a Magic: The Gathering clone, but I soon found it was more than that. The designers effectively use the digital medium to differentiate itself from the game that most clearly inspired it. Developing a sizeable collection through F2P means is relatively fast whether through single player grinding or against other players.
Some card interactions take getting use to (all buffs/debuffs persist through zone changes), but it is a nice option for enfranchised card game players who don't like the randomness (other than which cards you draw) other digital-only card games incorporate.
[End of my review]
Some tips to get you started if you do try this game out:
-The hotkey 'A' to attack with all your minions. Many people miss this.
-The best way to develop your collection is to play the single-player modes (gauntlet and forge) until you get to 'master' in both. Once you get master, the rank-up chest you get after each full run is replaced with a less valuable silver chest.
-Only spend gold on forge (until getting master) or draft. If you go 2-3 or better in draft, you get a better value than buying packs. (A 2-3 record is essentially 5 packs for less than the price of 4 packs. Plus, you can "rare draft" or pick cards you want for your collection)
-Currently the only faction pairs with dual-faction cards are the ones that correspond to the colors of the "ally-colored" pairs in Magic the Gathering. If you don't know those, you will just have to look through the cards and learn what they are.

Well, I never thought I would say this but Homefront : The Revolution is a sucky game. It is a repetitive system with a most unrealistic storyline and world. The premise of the game is that in 2029, North Korea has become the manufacturing hub of the world causing the USA to buy weapons and goods from it. This results in the US owing money to North Korea and when the USA defaults on its debts, there is a casus belli for North Korea to attack the USA. Since they make all of the USA's vehicles and weaponry, they use their electronic backdoor and turn off all of the USA's vehicles and weaponry. It is a parody of the real world, where North Korea plays China. I am seeing a trend of multiple game developers simply mimicking the GTA-styled zone control method and procedurally generating the map. I believe it's just a simple cash grab and it's bad for the game industry. It will result in multiple clones being created with no innovation or great leaps forward in gameplay.
Gameplay-wise, it's like a first person Grand Theft Auto/Mad Max/MiddleEarth:Shadow of Mordor/Batman : Arhkham City. Basically, you conquer one zone after another while doing jump puzzles and killing enemies. Once the zone turns blue from red, you move onto the next zone. Rinse and repeat. The enemies are not even anything special. They are just foot soldiers, heavy soldiers, flying drone, moving turret and Goliath. You have a giant blimp but all it does is follow you around and its AI is stupid. If you are spotted by enemies, you get to run away but hiding in a dumpster. Wow (sarcasm).
Conclusion, it's a very cheap knockoff of multiple games. You can feel like Dambuster simply copied from others and didn't really bother to create an exciting game or their own style. Rather, they decided to repeat the same gameplay over and over again. By using the Unreal engine, you can easily procedurally generate multiple instances of the same gameplay without a storytelling. You will see that it resembles Middle-Earth Shadow of War a lot. You would be better off with the Deus Ex series.
Note: The game was developed by Deep Silver Dambuster Studios (Owned by Crytek and Koch Media GmBH) and published by Deep Silver.

It's one of those games that is pretty simple to learn, but takes a long time to master. This game revolves around using hotkeys to perform tasks that involve making food and doing chores in your restaurant. On top of the main gameplay, you use the money generated from sales to buy new food items and equipment. This is a constant component because the items on your menu will "rot" over time. This means that the items that have been on your menu for more than two days will become boring to customers, and your rating will suffer. This requires you to constantly buy new items and equipment even later in the game. Even though this is all in career mode, there is a competitive "Battle Kitchen" mode that allows you to face off against others. On the technical side, the game is very minimal, which is to the game's benefit. Because of the very low system requirements, the game allows you to render 4K textures, which make the game look really good. Overall, this is a fun game to have on any system since the requirements are insanely low.

This game is one of those games that had an interesting premise but just slowly accumulated lots of little issues and generally subpar aspects where you have to wonder why you're playing it all.
Homefront: The Revolution was trying to do the hip and cool thing to do about a year or two ago, and that was open world shooter a la Far Cry. And that's what it is - a Far Cry clone with an interesting premise but utterly mediocre execution.
Graphics/Sound wise, can't complain too much. I have a mid-range system, and I only experience infrequent slowdowns and graphical bugs while playing on high settings. Gun sounds were fine, so was minor NPC voice acting. I'll leave my choice words about the major NPCs for the story section. The one thing I do have to complain about is hitboxes - especially on scenery, it was not uncommon to appear to have good LoS on an enemy, but instead put my bullets into the invisible wall between them.
Gameplay-wise, it's hit and miss. Gunplay does not feel very smooth. I appreciate the fact that I cannot crawl behind a rock and eat some dirt to regrow my limbs, but the health kit system really should have taken the full Far Cry approach rather only allowing a little regeneration when I'm bleeding all over the place. The climbing was fun, but especially toward the end of the game it's increasingly difficult to figure out how to climb into side objectives. As others have said, it's not uncommon to experience glitches and falling through the bottom of the map.
Story. So much potential, squandered! So many questions left unanswered! You could have had a really interesting game about the political implications and costs of occupying a country - instead, we have fake instability and a misplace sense of patriotism. The voice acting for major character ranges from acceptable to cringe-worthy, and the game basically goes out of its way to bring up interesting problems and choices one has to make while running an insurgency, and then totally ignores them in favor of shooting anything that moves. Other times, questions are raised but never answered. Minor spoiler: Chemical weapons are used by North Korea in game. Why is this okay? Why has the rest of the world rolled over and said "OK, North Korea, you can gas those Americans. They're an international pariah anyway" when in the real world, they would be under intense scrutiny and criticism for doing so. And maybe they are, who knows, but the game gives you absolutely no information on this. You might say "Why are you looking for geopolitical realism in a mindless first-person shooter" but I think a little bit of complication and character complexity would have gone a long way in making the game a little less bad.

Eternal Card Game is like Magic the Gathering (MTG) with a Hearthstone mix. The gameplay and mechanics are the same but the cards are named differently. As much as I like the graphics, I don't support the idea of copying MTG wholesale and pay to win. Try to come up with something unique and original if you want my vote. I'm basically seeing this as MTG with a reskin. As for copying of Hearthstone, there are a few abilities that are copied. If you know how to play Magic the Gathering, you know how to play Eternal.
Conclusion, Dire Wolf Digital really copied too much of Magic the Gathering to be able to stand on its own. At least ensure that most of the gameplay is different. It does not bode well when a game designer like Scott Martins, copies wholesale from other games.
1. Some Abilities Based on MTG Spells but with a Twist
Killer - One Time Attack Creature Directly
Infiltrate - Do Something When Creature Attacks
Warcry - If you attack the enemy player, the top card on your deck get +1/+1
Destiny
2. Artwork
Nice to look at and well-named.
1. Pay To Win
Sigh. The Eternal problem. Buy Gems at 7000 Gems for $60 USD. Buy 2 Boxes (64 Packs) with 6 Guaranteed Legendaries for 5800 Gems.
2. Crafting
Want that card you need to fill up your deck? Make Shiftstone, the crafting essence. 3200 for a Legendary card and 9600 for an animated Legendary card.
3. Similiarities and their MTG Counterpart
Influence - Mana
Endurance - Vigilance
Overwhelm - Trample
Charge - Haste
Flying - Flying
Aegis - Hexproof (Slightly weaker as Aegis only works once)
Quickdraw - First Strike
Lifesteal - Lifelink
Shadow Sigil - Swamp
Primal Sigil - Island
Time Sigil - Forest
Justice Sigil - Plain
Fire Sigil - Mountain
4. Similarities Magic the Gathering : Full Mulligan
Seriously? It's such a bad rule that they copied it wholesale.
5. Similarities Magic the Gathing : No Targeting of Creatures
You have to use a special ability, weapon or spell to get creatures to attack one another
6. Similarities Magic the Gathing : End of Turn Creature Healing
At the end of any player's turn, creatures that are not killed, heal back to full.
7. Similarities Hearthstone : Equipping Weapons to Hero
Equipping weapons to yourself and directly attacking creatures
8. Similarities Hearthstone : Abilities
Summon - Battlecry
Entomb - Deathrattle
9. No Tradeability or Secondary Market
The cards cannot be traded so there isn't perceived "value" in the cards and you make it way harder to form optimal decks since there is no trading. To get a specific card is pure gambling on the packs and crafting.
10. Similarity Magic the Gathering : Strangers Deck
If my guess is correct, Strangers mimic the Sliver decks from Magic the Gathering. Strangers basically only affect other Stranger cards and their effects stack on one another.

So I just played through this one, and the first thing to strike me is that it reminds me alot of Amnesia, but is nowhere near as scary.
Don't get me wrong, this one truly has it's moments, but it's not as easy as one might think to get frightened by a human retard inmate who can't check in more than one closet in his hostile pursuit for my soon-to-be dismembered limbs.
After about half into the game the "scary" moments just become tedious, having to run around in the dark with my night-vision camera for that one single half-invisible exit, constantly jumping out of the way of my brutish pursuer's swings with his favourite rusty pipe "Linda".
The story though, is one that only makes ANY sense what-so-ever at the very end of the game, and even then the dramatic twist is not very satisfying, and I usualy do like that way of story-telling, BUT IT NEEDS TO BE DONE RIGHT.
I will give the game a big plus for it's great graphics, incredibly tense music, brilliant animations and realistic blood-textures, but putting completely meaningless jumpscares here and there for me to jump into kind of kills it for me over time, since most of them also serve absolutely zero purpose to the story-telling and completely slaughters the re-occuring, short-lived suspense that the game try to maintain for most of it's sequences.
It's not the best, but it's far from being actually "bad", and even when it probably sounds like I just want to take a♥♥♥♥♥♥all over it, I highly enjoyed this one in the long-run, because it really does have it's moments of originality and horror, and for it's price it's still a decent length of gameplay (depending on your set of gamma and/or liking/disliking for orientating dark hallways while being chased by some lard fatso without an assessment of either lips or nose.
But I'd still recommend Amnesia over this any time.

This review will not be talking about the game's story wise as I believe that it's a pretty solid entry for the PS2 era Final Fantasy. The voice acting might not be up to par with XII or XIII but it's still workable. The main issue I have with the VA lay mostly with the acting, not with the voice itself as I believe they are quite suited.
This review, however will focus on FFX/X-2 as a PC port.
It's not very good. Graphic wise, it's quite beautiful and worthy of the title HD. However, in terms of technical slickness, this game is a buggy, crashy, mess. If you're the sort to enjoy a long, immersive gameplay then this port is not for you. One of the main advantages this game has is the Auto-Save function. You *will* need the auto save just to ensure that your controller, mouse and keyboard doesn't become a permanent dent against your wall.
My PC could play FFXIII and Dishonored 2 without much issue but this port is a disaster. The thing is it can crash as odd times, when you move from one screen to another, during battle, an odd spell or two. If I am able to play this game for two hours straight without crashing, I considering it a good session.
Two hours. For a game that averages 40. Yes, hairs were pulled and teeth gritted. Which is why the Auto-Save feature was practically a boon.
There are countless discussions as to what is exactly causing this unpredictable crashes  but it is something that Square-Enix has no interest in fixing, which is a goddamn shame cause otherwise the game is quite amazing. If you're looking for a good PC port update, this is not for you. Not unless you have a great deal of patience. If you want to buy wait for a sale.

This is a game that rewards your empathy rather than your reflexes. It is a lovely and lovingly told story in the form of a open plot game and is for persons who enjoy emotionally investing in settings and characters. For the classic adventure gamer (myself dating back to the original "ADVENT" when I was a youngster), it will at first seem like old hat: Explore a mysterious place, picking up clues to find what the story is, etc.... but, where are the monsters, antagonists, treasures? In this story, it's all in your head and in your heart. In hearing evocatively recorded bits and pieces of the story from one main character we feel teen angst, discovery of love, discovery and rediscovery of dreams, chasing risk, endings and beginnings. Because it is intended to be an emotionally resonating experience, it is a game for mature gamers, not for persons looking for simulated thrills. It is more of a game for book readers than the mainstream gaming community. As you read others' reviews of this game, keep that in mind.

Studio "Red Barrels" combines three key features in it's fear inducing game "Outlast":
The first is "Atmosphere" - our hero is placed in a mental asylum, which is located far away from the rest of the world. As you progress through this terrifying building, you won't be able to escape the feeling of being lost and clueless as you make your way through ventilation shafts and creepy corridors!
The second is "Helplesness" - our protagonist, Miles Upshur, is your ordinary run-of-the-mill investigative reporter, looking into uncovering the truth behind Mount Massive Asylum. And that is it - you are an ordinary person, just a simple mortal man, who can easily get crushed by the insanity, which is hiding behind each and every corner of the asylum.
And the third feature is the "Darkness" - the dark is the canvas, on which our imagination brings our greatest fears to life! Most of Outlast will be spent in darkness. When engulfed by it, we won't be able to differentiate what's really happaning and what's in our head.
Outlast sticks to these features and slightly alters them at the same time - even though Miles can't physically defend himself from the horrors, he can run pretty fast and squeeze through tight spots. These abilities make the player feel like he has only one option to survive and that is to swallow one's pride and haul♥♥♥♥♥in the opposite direction!
The Atmosphere reminds us that we are alone in a giant asylum, where the first feeling we get is of misdirection - we don't know which corridor leads twords salvation, but on the other hand we are forced to traverse both ways so we can get something that will lead us to the right direction!
Darkness is what it is - it's darkness! And it is the unexplainable, but our mild-mannered reporter has come prepared - he has his trusty camera, with which he documents all the gruesome things he encounters. And it is equipped with a night vision option! It helps us see in the dark, but only for some time, because the batteries will eventually die on us. So when the camera's battery indicator starts blinking, you know it's time to replace them, but that might be hard, because you'll be forced to scavenge for new ones! What I think is truly unique with this mechanic are the green glowing eyes whenever you encounter a patient of the Asylum - as you walk in the dark, you'll first see the deranged stare of a shirtless maniac, as he slowly walks infront of you and suddenly starts to run and yell at you. These moments really managed to make me jump off my seat a huge amount of times!
Outlast tries to play it safe and not stray too far from the beaten path made by previous horror titles, and for the most part it works fine, but at a cirtain point it gets slightly predictable - as you walk down a flight of stairs or exit another ventilation shaft, you'll know that there's a baddy waiting for you just a phew steps ahead. This prepares you for the inevitable jump scare.
Outlast by "Red Barrels" Studio dosen't reinvent the horror ganre, but it ads it's own unique spin to the concept and it works flawlessly. This is a indie title that should belong in every horror fan's game library! And if you're a newcomer to spooky games, this will satisfy your gaming palette!

The game is best in small doses, like no more than a couple of hours maximum. Any longer and you really do start to feel shell shocked.
The guns are hard to aim, but when your squad levels up it really makes you appricate it because finally you'll have some decent sights. Of course the guns still aren't that accurate until the next squad level. Which is kind of the breaking point for the game. Always look to advance the entire squad and work as a team, otherwise the game will completely suck. However once you get that down it becomes a really fun game.
If you want a game where you can just run, juke, and jump in without getting killed then play something else. This game forces you to choose your cover and use it. Advance on the enemy trench wisely and hold your own at all costs because every inch you crawl across no mans land is like running a mile up hill.
I really can't give this game enough praise for capturing WWI, but I also feel like I have to warn potential buyers that it really isn't made for everyone. However if you want an FPS where you spend more time thinking about how to advance your goals (which are more often than not smaller ones like "Make it to the next fox hole.") then this is your type of game.

Bought this game a few months back for Remembrance Day, conveniently that happened to also be around the time of the Black Friday sale so I got a pretty good deal.
Being from Canada the first world war is kind of a big deal here, not that it isn't in other places, but this was really when we made a name for ourselves, Vimy Ridge for example was the first major victory of a colonial power over an empire, in which we captured a sector that had been previously untouchable by the allies.
This game really captures the feel of trench warfare, while it would be cool to see things like more factions, tanks or planes, it would detract from the overall experience.
The game focuses around a four man squad dynamic, each unit has different roles and playstyles but usually the format consists of a: Squad Leader who calls mortar strikes and gives commands to the unit, a rifleman or marksman who acts as a grunt and support troop, a gunner or otherwise support unit equipped with the heavy munitions of the squad, and a specialist who usually has some kind of special role such as recon, trench raiding, or throwing grenades.
The units are varied, some units have lots of rifles but not much specialists, other units have a specific purpose in the battle, but don't do much good in a static fight.
The allied forces have units from all range of nations with loosely based on history squad structure, the French for example do a lot of recon and sabotage, the Canadians do a lot of trench raiding and brutal close range brawling, the British rely more on their rifles and the cooperation of the team, and the Belgians tend to catch you off guard with the tricks up their sleeves.
On the other side of the coin, instead of basing the squads of the Central Powers off countries, because it was all Germany on the western front, they base the squads off individual units, some are defensive rifles, some are balanced support, while others are brutal raiders armed with submachine guns or flamethrowers.
No two battles are the same, because any combination of units can come up against one another, and the squads themselves will change as the squad ranks up, or as the individual people in the squad choose different perks for their role.
Machine guns and snipers can cause an amazing amount of terror, and while it's frustrating to not be able to shoot the enemies because a sniper has a bead on you, it's very close to how real snipers worked in trench warfare.
It's really satisfying to thwart an attack on your trench with a well-placed machine gun, and on the other side it can be absolutely devastating to see your team get cut down by a few experienced gunners.
They don't force any of this either, they just give the players the tools and the ability, and people just naturally do what they're supposed to, gunners just seem drawn to choke points, snipers seem drawn to empty flanks with good line of sight to the enemy trench.
And for people who have looked this stuff up, it's really fascinating to see this stuff happen in real time on a virtual battlefield.
I would recommend to any history nut, or fan of shooters who wants to change it up, it's not that intense, it's just a really well made FPS game.. although if you're coming from Battlefield 1 you might be surprised to find the machine guns are pretty hard to master, and there is a total lack of any semi-automatic rifles.

(This is Final Fantasy X's review only)
Final Fantasy X is a role-playing game from Square and the tenth installment of the series. It was originally released in 2001 for Sony Playstation 2, and re-released as Final Fantasy X/X-2 HD Remastered in 2013. The story follows a group in their quest to defeat Sin, a rampaging monster, from destroying Spira, their homeworld.

The basic plot of Final Fantasy X is actually really interesting. Unfortunately, the execution leaves a lot to be desired. Bad script, bad acting (it's kinda goofy) really hampered the enjoyment. It's still interesting enough that you would want to know the rest of the story. But it's just could be better. It has a wonderful but sad ending, though.
Square has done a quite good job in this part. Updated textures, remodeled characters model are a really nice touch in this version. It's still not perfect, since characters like npc still has it's old and blocky models. Main characters also suffered from more stiff facial animations. Overall it's a decent effort from Square.
The game lets you choose from the original music or the arranged version. Can't give any recommendation since I've only ever used the original version. The music itself is fantastic, you will not be disappointed. The game also features a song, performed by RIKKI. Unlike its predecessors, Final Fantasy VIII and Final Fantasy IX, the song is still performed in japanese.
The strongest part of this game. It's no longer use Active Time Battle system (first introduced in Final Fantasy IV), instead, it uses Turn Based Battle System. Characters growth no longer use traditional leveling system, which uses predetermined stats when your character leveled up. It now uses a new system called Sphere Grid. The sphere grid system allows player to customize character to a role that difference than it is intended to be. Although, in the end, if you max the sphere grid, most of it will be pointless, since the differences between characters mostly come from their Overdrives aka Limit Break.
The game is mostly linear, in fact, it's the most linear Final Fantasy game that I've ever played (have not played Final Fantasy XIII series, yet). It doesn't has traditional overworld, and you can't go back to the old place, except at the late part of the game.
The game has so many side quests and mini games. From the most annoying, the chocobo catcher, to a good but too easy Blitzball. It has also monster arena, where you can fight monsters that even more powerfull than the final boss.
Specifically, for this remastered version, player can use its built in cheat, such as no encounter and auto battle, which is really useful, especially later in the game when you want to grind your character to the max.
Overall, the gameplay of Final Fantasy X is really its best part.

Another great iteration from the legendary, historically-rich KOF series. This game does not cease to provide players fast-paced, execution-heavy gameplay, and with the tweaked system drawing familiarities from 2K2UM and XIII (such as MAX Mode and CLIMAX DMs), this game proves to be more friendly for newcomers to the series and less arcane for veteran KOFers. The game is also a lot more balanced compared to its predecessor, along with a larger roster of 54, allowing for more creativity and variety on a player's part.
Pros:
+ Fast-paced gameplay that rewards high-execution mastery
+ Large, balanced roster
+ Team Battles, 3v3, and 1v1 are all available
+ Solid netcode and input reading
+ More beginner friendly than XIII with auto-combos and removal of Drive Cancel
+ Not just an SF clone
+ Gallery and DLC artwork are actually
nice without just being a 'fanservice corner' (I look at you, BB)
Cons:
- Absolutely poor visuals all across the board (and yes, this game was rushed in development due to some large changes occurring with the company itself, but don't let this discourage you unless you have legitimate reason; I myself say that the XIII 2D visuals were beautiful compared to this)
- Quite pricy to most, especially with all the other games on the market
- So-so story (the stories in the KOF series have really never been that 'great', per se)
- Primarily built for people who are already fans of the series (so not as newcomer-friendly as, let's say, GG, but still more so than XIII)
- ...that's actually it.
Overall a solid 9/10, there have been some reporrted issues and bugs so far so there is no rush to by this game unless you are just a fan of the KOF series, play competitively/are a pro, or any other reasonable motive to do so. But do I recommend it still? Yes, it is a good, solid fighting game that should not be neglected just because of GGXrdR2, or Tekken 7, or I2, or anything else in the future (I'm looking at you, MVCI).
If you need any help or have questions, just leave a comment, PM me, or check the forums to see if someone else had a similar question (you probably want to do this first).
*EDIT* (16 June 2017, 14:44) - A patch was announced earlier today that addresses the reported issues and bugs of which I spoke. Just wanted to make sure that this was accurate :)

Receiver teaches the player about the mechanics of a pistol as they traverse in a concrete jungle full of threats and danger, finding audio tapes and completing the game.
The player is randomly given one of the following pistols when they spawn. (They may also be given extra ammunition and a flashlight, should chance allow.)
1. Colt M1911A1 single-action semi-automatic pistol
2. Glock 17 automatic
3. Smith & Wesson Model 10 revolver
Despite the confusing controls some new players may feel, The game has a very good idea of how each firearm works. The firearms all function in a variety of ways. For example, The Colt may not fire when the hammer is lowered as it is in single-action. The S&W Model 10 is a double-action, meaning that a pull of the trigger will♥♥♥♥♥♥and slam the hammer, firing the gun. Thus the players will find out the the S&W has a longer trigger pull, causing a slower firing rate.
The game is very informative, thus I enjoyed it. But there is only one thing I have to add. the Model 10 should also be able to fire single-action as long as the hammer is half-cocked. The game doesn't allow that to happen, however. (Or is it because I haven't found that feature?) This would make the Model 10 fire faster.

Nowhere on this store page does it say the game requires to be online at all times. I assumed there would be a single player mode of some description as listed along the side, so I didn't have to deal with laggy servers or anything like that. Unfortunately, that's not the case. Unless you live in America or Europe you're going to lag horribly. And I don't mean other people rubber banding everywhere in multiplayer races or anything isolated like that. I mean the game's handling model is directly linked to your connection to the server. So that 300ms ping means there's 300ms before any of your inputs register on screen. Not only that, but I had to spend several hours troubleshooting to get this game to even run at all, only to find out this always online mode renders the game entirely unplayable to me. Thanks Ubisoft.
Note: The error I was receiving was essentially that "The Crew has stopped working", after looking up all of the fixes online, the only thing that worked was completely removing all traces of my original up to date graphics driver, including going into the registry to remove files, then reinstalling it. The game doesn't crash or anything for me now but it's something to consider if you have trouble getting the game to run. It's only configured for purely default drivers.

I had a surprisingly good time with RIVE!
The glorious soundtrack suits calmer, airduct intervals and transitions itself into skillfully kickin’ combat encounters. Levels, although revisited, host unique tracks that pertain well and add to the atmosphere of the area.
Game feel is remarkable. It feels great to rip and tear through enemies. Checkpoints are abundant, making the game feel less rage-inducing (although I did play through on normal mode). Levels frequently introduce and then entertaining mechanics and the game never ceases to stale.
The game ran surprisingly well on my old and dying laptop, a feat many other semi-hardware-intensive games still failed to deal with.
Something I found initially disconcerting was the seemingly unnecessary Brooklynn pilot. I’ve played a few games where the whole, “We know that you’re a real gamer” attitude coupled with throwaway lines referencing all sorts of nonsense just didn’t fly. But RIVE managed to pull it off, although its presence was still shaky in the beginning. Just enough happened to give the characters a tangible personality and connection. I had a surprisingly good time with RIVE!
I played the WiiU Nindies demo a while ago and don’t remember there being any characters in there, but I guess that would’ve been confusing, having the demo take place in a level a decent way through the game.
Alternatively, having no characters would’ve made the game feel a bit more mysterious. Coupled unlocking abilities, it would just feel like a linear Metroid. Revisiting areas also would’ve made less sense and being about to immediately mention the next way to head help retained the game’s flow. I was actually happy to hear the pilot chime in when I was about to give up on a jump that seemed to hard and look elsewhere to advance.
Going in almost blind (except for that demo more than a year ago), I found myself pleasantly surprised by RIVE. I fully recommend it for its campaign.

I really really really like this game. it's got a really cool gameplay concept (the gun handling) every function has a different button (slide, hammer, eject magazine, insert magazine, slide lock, safety, etc) and it is pretty unforgiving in its difficulty. first, every run is different. the map is randomly generated and you spawn with 1/3 possible guns, each of which have their own inherent strengths and weaknesses. second, movement is key! you can be running along and make a simple mistake like not checking a corner (or more than likely not looking up) and you're dead. the more you play the better you get though. it's not a pretty game, the graphics are pretty bare bones, but that isnt meant to be the focus of the game. neither is the story, but it's still an interesting weird sci-fi that I kind of enjoy.
some people have complained about it "not being optimized well" but the only time I've ever experienced any kind of stuttering is occasionally when I move into a new room. the easiest way to handle this is to just not charge into a room and instead ease your way in. this is a tactical game! you shouldnt be sprinting at all unless you're 100% positive that you cleared that area. I say that because there have been plenty of times when I used to just run into a room and (lag or not) I wound up right in front of a turret with no cover to save me because of my own fault. or that I ran into an open area and got tazed by a flying drone before I even knew where they came from.
yes, this game was made for a game jam in a very short amount of time, it's far from AAA. but it is still an awesomely fun game for me. it's so simple but it has this strange kind of depth to it that I really cant explain. I highly recommend it.

CONs:

Magic : the Gathering is known as a definition of TCG, but at some point with all those expansions and new mechanics it became incredibly complicated and unfriendly to new players. Soon after that Blizzard released Hearthstone, the renown digital CCG, which quickly got well deserved popularity as a casual and easy-to-get-in f2p game.
But few years later Hearthstone now comes alongside with some issues. Mostly its RNG based mechanics and debatable balance of some cards, coming with new expansions and adventures. So the story kinda repeats itself and Hearthstone gets more and more complicated and hard for a new player, just like Magic did.
At this point people that were hooked in by HS start looking for something else, with less RNG and more skill-based( or rather prediction-based) gameplay. And here we are, looking at this beautiful game called Eternal, with great art-style, Magic-like mechanics and casual feeling of Hearthstone. The game is evenly interesting, fun and complex.
The game is fresh and worth at least checking it out. Beautiful graphics, interesting mechanics, but still casual enough to enjoy even small sessions of game.

I'm going to sum this game up like this:  If you like F1, or racing in general, BUY IT.  There are a few issues, but the overall experience more than makes up for it.
Honestly I am writing this to cover the main two issues I have, both of which deal with the back field AI.  I've only had these problems with the Manor MRT and Sauber cars.
Problem 1:  When these cars start their out lap in any practice session at Barcelona, they will hit the brakes between turns 2 and 3 on the racing line.  If you know this track, it should be flat out.  I've been running qualy pace programs and ran directly into the back of them when they do this.  The same issue is present at Monaco, this time they exit the pits, move to the center of the track and hesitiate to accelerate by probably around .5s.  Once again this resulted in a crash, as there is no room to pass on either side at that point.
Problem 2:  They don't understand blue flags.  The mid field cars behave fine, giving plenty of room in good overtaking sections.  The back field cars like to give you space in non-DRS straights but don't slow down, and then proceed to clog the racing line in the corners while slowing to a crawl.  Monaco makes this unbearable.  I was leading the race with Verstappen 8s back.  I came across a Sauber in front of me and by the time I was able to safely pass, Verstappen was a mere .7s back.  This was in 2 laps.  As a point of reference, I was lapping around 4s faster than the Sauber with a clear track.
All this being said the game is fantastic and I will probably sink way too many hours into it :)
Pros:
Excellent career mode structure.  100% length race weekends are amazing
Physics are very good, not simulation level, but also not forgiving
Dynamic weather is very well done
Tire and Fuel management is very in depth
Cons:
The AI issue listed above
Frame drops.  It's a problem.  Make sure Steam isn't downloading anything, but the game drops on its own as well

Fallout 3 is a RPG in a post apocalyptic scenario. It also includes a pinch of FPS elements.
It brings you into a post-nuclear war Washington DC in the (former) United States of America in some alternate 50ties in which you try to find your father. You will meet different factions, monsters, allies and tons of quests.
While the main quests leads you (more or less) straight to the end of the game (approx. 20-30h, depending in your style) the side quests add at least another 20 more.
The game has a rather high re-playability as your decisions on an action or in a conversation have direct influence how other entities behave towards you and how certain elements in the (side as well as main) quest change.
The game is highly moddable and even though the graphics may seem somewhat outdated they match very nicely into the scenario and time. They can be enhanced by the mods as well.
If you are into RPGs and into post apocalyptic scearios...this game is actually a MUST.

can literally instantly warp to any location/event on the map (assuming you've driven to the area before)

to have any chance at winning multiplayer matches, you'll need to grind a lot to upgrade your car (which can only done in solo-mode). If you don't improve your car level, you'll lose the race so bad you won't even see your oponent for 90% of the race.
This means you will basically NEED to spend 6+ hours (on top of completing the story mode) trying to improve your cars doing repetitive tasks (hit the targets, drive as fast as possible, jump as far as possible, etc) until your cars are leveeld up) just to enjoy multiplayer races. I really dislike the car leveling system (at least as far as the multiplayer is concerned) and it's for this reason, I haven't had a chance to enjoy multiplayer and probably never will (I refuse to play X hours completing mundane tasks just as a prerequisite to compete against others in multiplayer.)
All-in-all, it's a great game, especaially if you're into arcade racing. They really setup a nice framework and allow a lot of flexibility to encourage people to play in groups. If you hope to race against others in multiplayer, be prepared to do 6+ hours of grinding first.

The King Of Fighters XIV is the newest installmet of the KOF franchise of fighting games, which I am a avid fan of. I've played all the KOF games growing up and XIV has honestly surppased my expectations. Seeing the trailers when it was announced for the PS4 almost made my buy the system just for this game. When hearing the PC port announcement, I was so excited and pre-ordered it straight away. This was definetly worth it as KOF XIV has definelty lived up to it's expectations in my opinion compared to other KOF titles
The gameplay of KOF XIV is where it shines the brightest; it's smooth, consistent and solid making it both welcoming to newcomers (with the Rush system) as well as catering for the hardcore fans like myself. The mechanics are also a new welcoming change, with the return of the MAX mode and the cancelling into Climax moves which opens opportunities to land some real damage. The moves of most of the characters have translated very well from the previous titles as well as throwing in some new ones. Apart from some balance issues here and there, the charcaters play really well and complement the gameplay
Performace-wise, KOF XIV is a worthy port with the game mostly running a smooth 60 FPS, save for the 30 FPS drops here and there and the special character interaction sequences in-match. Other than that. it runs beautifully and there are plently of graphics options to tweak to your preference.
In terms of graphics, KOF XIV has taken a drastically different art-style with 3D models as opposed to the majority of previous titles being 2D pixellated sprites as well as the hand-drawn visuals seen in XII and XIII. Personally, I liked the new 3D models despite them looking a bit out-dated as many people have voiced concerns about. I can understand SNK's reasoning behind the graphics because they wanted performance to be smooth, but at the same time they could be a touch better. That being said, it was very good of SNK to release the patch on the PS4 which improved the visuals and shading quite a bit. Compared to the previous graphics, they are much improved and better looking than before. The backgrounds are also amazing to fight on, with a wide range of beautiful landscapes as well as reimagined versions of old favorites (such as the Transcontinental Railroad from Fatal Fury 2/Special) being added via free updates.
The character roster in KOF XIV is outstanding, offering a total of 50 chartacters consisting of the original cast (Kyo Kusanagi, Terry Bogard, Ryo Sakazaki, Mai Shiranui etc.) and newcomers alike (Shun'ei, Sylvia, Meitekun, Xanadu, Mian etc.) which all play very nicely and all give a unique way to play the game. The 4 DLC characters are also a nice addition with the likes of Rock Howard, Yamazaki, Whip and Vannessa being very fun characters to play as and I do hope SNK continue to support the game like so with faces new and old being added to the roster and at a reasonable price compared to other fighters on the market.
The music, like in all KOF titles, is amazing and an absolute treat to listen to. SNK's talented composers have once again outdid themselves with the soundtrack of this game and are continuly adding more wonderful tunes via free updates
All in all, KOF XIV is an amazing installment to the franchise which stacks up very well against previous KOF titles. Although it doesn't stand out to some, it's a very solid fighter with amazing gameplay and definetly worth your time for newcomers and veterans alike

This is an first look-initial impression only. The isn't an in-depth analysis of the gameplay.
Good:
Gameplay is engaging. The true-to-history trench style warfare is brutal and fun. Well, if you call, poking your head up over the parapet and getting it blown off, fun. Which I do think that's fun. Another reviewer pointed this out and I can confirm, that this game makes all the fighting over meters of ground feel pointless. The screams of my teammates that dragged on and on after game "death" filled me with despair which added to the realism.
Bad:
UI is rough and not very intuitive. The problem for the developers is that the upgrade/rank up system is complex. However, the UI kind vomits it on the user. My biggest issue was the UI and the explanation of the upgrade system.
The weapon sound effects need some updates. Specifically, my rank 2 machine gun sounded like a pistol on repeat.
My overall opinion:
History buffs and realism proponents, like me, will love this game. If you want a late model realistic WW1 shooter this is it.  It's definitely not worth the $25 I paid for it, simply because of the lack of polish, sound effects, and seizure-like animations. I have seen free mods of similar quality for HL2. It's almost there though. I feel like with some more revisions and TLC this game could be a bargain at $25.

TL:DR

Detailed review
Receiver is a rather interesting game for a few reasons. The main attraction here is how guns handle. Compared to pretty much every other FPS, the gun mechanics are not simple. To reload, you have to press certian buttons for each function such as mag ejection, loading mags, cocking hammers, ect. At first it feels rather clunky but with practice you will be able to reload your weapon much more quickly.
In terms of enemies there is really only two. A taser drone and a turret. Both have weak spots and the ability to only have certain functions such as flying or the gun being disabled. Now this is where the flaws of the game start to show. On occasions when you walk into a room, you can be shot immediatly. Making the game rather difficult at times. Death will almost always be unexpected. There will also be moments where you will run out of ammo due to missing an enemies weakspot several times.
The story is kinda interesting and unexpectedly deep for this kind of game. Its experianced best going in blind.

Magic : the Gathering is known as a definition of TCG, but at some point with all those expansions and new mechanics it became incredibly complicated and unfriendly to new players. Soon after that Blizzard released Hearthstone, the renown digital CCG, which quickly got well deserved popularity as a casual and easy-to-get-in f2p game.
But few years later Hearthstone now comes alongside with some issues. Mostly its RNG based mechanics and debatable balance of some cards, coming with new expansions and adventures. So the story kinda repeats itself and Hearthstone gets more and more complicated and hard for a new player, just like Magic did.
At this point people that were hooked in by HS start looking for something else, with less RNG and more skill-based( or rather prediction-based) gameplay. And here we are, looking at this beautiful game called Eternal, with great art-style, Magic-like mechanics and casual feeling of Hearthstone. The game is evenly interesting, fun and complex.
The game is fresh and worth at least checking it out. Beautiful graphics, interesting mechanics, but still casual enough to enjoy even small sessions of game.

YES ! A perfect city builder at last. No foreign invaders, and disasters can be toggled off if you want. Literally is just you versus nature.
The basic idea is to expand your village/culture but it isnt as simple as just placing the correct buildings - weather needs to be taken in to account for example should you push your workers to complete that new stone quarry before winter sets in or, if times are hard food wise do you sacrifice some sheep for meat resources which could otherwise help to make warmer clothes for your hunters and farmers?
Trade routes can be established with outsiders, but this can increase the risk of diseases that a basic herbalist isnt really up to curing.
Another common resource in these kind of games -Wood- here becomes not just a resource. Its good to strip swathes of forest down for building and firewood, but as herbalists and apothecary types like to gather in the forests this can have negative effects on the health of your people. Trees can be replanted and there are many wyas to get food.
Its all a zen like balance, especially in the sand box mode but may take a few tries to get a feel of what be wise in the early game and what isnt as a poor choice early on could literally cripple your population as they grow years later.
It can also be paused in real time or time sped up or slowed by degrees if you re waitin on a construction and charts can be accessed during the game to help with your grand designs on food needed for population growth, most efficient paths taken so you can built the best roads n all that jazz. Its a sweet distraction for sure.

If you've ever played Hearthstone or Magic: The Gathering, this is the real digital experience for you. Magic is a fantastic game, but it's old and doesn't translate well to online play. Hearthstone is quick and easy but lacks a lot of interaction with your opponent and always felt a bit flat to me. Eternal is the best of both worlds, with some extras. The game is silky smooth like Hearthstone, with some cool extra modes like Forge (AI controlled draft/Arena) and easy "grinding" (You will get cards at a *much* faster rate than in Hearthstone and have more choices in how to grind). On top of that it has stellar game play like I've come to expect from a much deeper game like Magic: The Gathering. It's hard to recommend this game highly enough. I went from playing Magic Online 30hrs or more a week to playing Eternal for 40 or more and it's swiftly looking to become my main stream game as well as something I actually enjoy playing off-stream as well. AAA quality here.

For starters, if you like to experience gameplay, puzzles, cutscenes and what-not, then this game is not for you. This is pretty much a visual novel. Scratch that, it's more like an audio novel but with some walking around in between. It has basically zero degrees of replayability. Once you find all story elements, the game's finished.
Despite all that, this game, or rather the story it tells, is fantastic. If you choose to follow through, and if you have a shred of empathy, you will love this story and hate the fact that it made you cry. This is largely contributed to the excellent voice-over.
Finding the story is mostly linear with the option to skip large parts of the story. Also included are many smaller side stories. Although not voiced, they are still interesting additions.
In conclusion, if you like games with a great story, and you hate grinding for it, then this is your kind of game.

22hr review:  I REALLY like this game! There is a LOT to do between you and your main objective.  You can take over a critical location, activate a location to empower the resistance, save the people who are being abused in the street, free the prisoners from their captors, stop a house raid where they use charges on the door and go in blasting everyone, activate radios broadcasting the resistance station so the citizens become more emboldened to fight back, sabatoge enemy generators and vehicles.. there's a ton of stuff to do!  The AI reacts to being shot like you would expect.  They stumble and may fall down and get back up If you don't take them out with the first few shots. If you use a silenced weapon, they will look around frantically while going for cover.  If they spot you, they will call for help and try to work their way to you.  If you are scanned by the bots, they will sound the alarm and usually a 5 to 10 man squad will come running and execute a search. You can stealth kill, use the boobytraps placed all over the environment or just gun them down!  You take the city back block by block by taking over critical locations by killing the enemy and sabatoging their equipment or by reactivating key resistance locations thru various means.  These key locations serve as respawn points, weapons and equipment purchase points as well as a place to sell valuables that you scavenge along the way and you do this all at a weapons locker that is available immediately after you capture the location.  Using the weapons locker also saves your progress! So having one close by is really good for respawning and for getting paid for the loot you collect.   As you navigate the world, you come across opportunities to create a sense of hope in the people to fight back while building your rep as someone they can follow.  The shanty town feeling of the city is really cool with multiple ways in and out of most structures.  There are motorcycles you can ride or use to start generators, weapons and ammo caches scattered around and loot is pretty much everywhere you turn.  When you kill the enemy soldiers and bots, you can loot their remains as well to get ammo, valuables and money. The Ai is surprisingly smart in comparison to some reviews.  I have been overwhelmed,  flanked, and grenaded  by the enemy because I underestimated the AI.  They will climb ladders, cross over the many makeshift walkways between buildings, execute searches and seek out high points to gain an advantage over you.   I find the game engaging and very fun to play with a bit of realism that makes it that much better.  You can shoot enemy soldiers from a window or hole int he wall to lure them into the building to bomb them, shoot them, or so you can run out the back and get passed them without being seen. You can throw bricks to destract them, or try to blend in with the people scattered throughout to get past them. As you progress thru the missions the people, who start out as depressed and defeated, start to become more and more vocal to protesting the enemy in the streets to picking up arms and fighting back with you.   The many weapons in the game are cool!  You have different guns and a bow that can be modified and converted into other cool weapons!   Like the shotgun can be converted into an auto-shotgun with a drum magazine,  the assault rifle can be converted into an AMG (automatic machine gun) and a grenade launcher for instance.   You can also add  upgrades to your weapons, like forward grips, scopes, muzzle brakes, silencers, etc, to increase their effectiveness. However,  the game doesn't tell you what upgrade fits what weapon, so its helpful early on to go into the upgrade process and see what you can put on the weapon you want to upgrade before you make a purchase.   For instance, I bought the silencer thinking I could fit it to the assault rifle, but it only fits the pistol. Which, by the way, can be converted into a silenced automatic rifle.  Some of the upgrades  are interchangeable and some are not.  Like the forward grip and one of the scopes will fit both the shot gun and assult rifle.  Once you get your weapons setup the way you want, with your upgrades, you can switch back and forth between them and the weapon will be converted just as you configured it.  The weapons conversions can be done on the fly, in the field,  in a matter of seconds thru a pretty cool animation sequence where the character unlocks the action, snatches it off and mounts your requested conversion! Really cool!  In this game you have access to a bunch of cool weapons and equipment. Like a battle rifle, remote control cars with explosives, molotove cocktails, throwable bombs and proximity bombs, just  to name a few.  I haven't bought them all yet. With the pistol, assault rifle and shotgun, I have 7 weapons already. You can also craft things in the field like molotoves and bombs for instance in seconds if you have the ingredients.   I have found nothing about this game that I dislike... unless you count being killed by the AI.. but hey.. it happens.
I highly recommend this game and honestly, I don't get the negative reviews. I run this game on the highest level of graphics it will go and In my 22+ hrs, I have not had a single crash or problem.  I cannot rate multiplayer as I have not played multi or co-op yet.  Im having too much fun playing single player. Besides, I dont much care for multiplayer because, no matter the game,  there seems to always be A_holes who cheat with mods in multiplayer.
Bottom line: if you like FPS games, GET THIS! Its cool, it's fun and the replay value is definitely there.

Spoiler Free Thoughts
So much of this game, this interactive short story, is in the things you discover as the player. To put it simply and hopefully without ruining anything, you take control of Katie Greenbriar, a 20-year-old girl who is returning from a year abroad. During her time abroad, her family, consisting of her parents and younger sister, have moved into a new home. You show up after a late flight to find no one home and a note on the door from your sister begging you not to snoop around and find out where she went. Obviously, you’re not going to take this weirdness laying down, so you investigate.
The gameplay is simple. You use arrow keys or WASD to move, the mouse to look and interact with objects and 1/2/3 for Items, Map, and Journal. That’s it. The game will take anywhere from 2-4 hours to experience the story and mystery of where your family is, what’s with this house and how they came to be there.
I know some people have a hard time calling this a game, or say that what the player does isn’t actually ‘playing’; but to me, that’s just semantics. If we wanted to give in, we could call it an interactive story, something much more involved than a TV show, but less controlled than a standard video game experience. I may be wrong on this, but I’m not here to argue its classification.
If this has at all made you interested in trying the game I urge you to go do so without reading further. Don’t look at any other spoilers, nothing. If you have ever felt lost, in love, rejected, confused by yourself or your own family, if you’re at all empathetic for fictional characters, you owe it to yourself to check it out.

Solid fighter containing staple features such as arcade,survival, time trials, versus, etc. The roster is huge and there is a huge variety of characters to choose from. The roster goes to 50 characters (54 when deluxe is purchased) so you have no shortage of fighters to pick.
Traditional KoF matches are 3v3 where you pick a team 3 fighters and a round ends when one fighter is knocked out. You can't tag in like other games rather the fighter you picked in order will replace the fallen one and the round resets. HP of the surviving fighter will be carried over to the next round only recovering a bit depending on the remaining time from the previous round. The meters are carried over from round to round and shared between your team. This is what made KoF great. You need to put careful consideration in picking your fighters and the order that they will be fighting. You can use canon teams or just mix and match.
Mechanics-wise KoF is deep and satisfying. You got emergency escapes (rolls), varying jumps, and the super/advance/climax cancels. It is hard for me to explain these since I am fairly new in terms of really analyzing the mechanics in KoF despite playing for some time but the game does a good job in teaching you the basics of these mechanics.
One of the biggest "issue" that most people seem to have is the jump from sprites to 3D. I personally prefer the sprites and still find ones from Garou or 2002UM, heck even 98UM still looks beautiful.I am a bit biased but that doesn't necessarily mean the graphics are horrible. By today's standards it doesn't look like Tekken 7 or Injustice 2 but it is still good. What I do love about the visuals though is how smooth the moves translated from sprites to this. I was amazed when doing the same moves across 98UM,2002UM, and XIV and they look very well in 3D.
I can't review the online part due to my internet connection not really the best. I leave that to other more competitive people to do.
All in all this game is a must-buy for fighting game enthusiast. You get a good solid package and a great entry in to the series. Hopefully if this succeeds we will be seeing XIII UM or more cool SNK fighters (we desperately need a new Garou, Last Blade, or something like the good old battle Coliseum!)

Basics of fighting: press down diagonally then up diagonally in the reverse direction to long jump quick. Release the jump fast to long short hop; do it without the down press to hop shorter or jump shorter. Hold X/B  and press the dpad in the direction of your opponents when close to opponent to throw and if being thrown press the heavy punch or kick button of the throw quick enough and you can escape it. Press Y/B to do a power (knockback) attack and it even works while airborne.  To block press away from your opponent and to block low press away and down at the same time (diagonal).  For max mode press all four buttons at the same time (A,B,Y,X) and you can rush attack (usually hit X four times but not too quickly for all characters). Oh and A is light kick, B is heavy kick, X is light punch and Y is heavy punch. Now go and rip it up!

Popular criticisms include; "handling too much for an arcade game" Because it's not an arcade game
"wheelspin is too much" because you're using a 250 horsepower shot of nitrous in a car with a 10:3 power-to-weight ratio
Unfortunately because Ubisoft has listened to what they're hearing (ie; game hate faries on the forums) the AI has been brought down to a minimum.
Game has a huge map, probably the biggest of any open world game so far, the car handling is amazing, physics are pretty much bang-on, the in-game community is great, the car customization could use some work but it's a very small kink in an otherwise well-oiled machine.
As a veteran racing-game enthusiast (weird guy that 100%s gran turismo games) it took me almost 20 hours to get through the story mode watching every cutscene, the story is even good although somewhat generic, it's well done.
If you're an open-world racing game fan this game will probably give you a weird feeling, traditionally we saw games where you could see it, but not necessarily go to it. With this that simply isn't the case, if you can see it in The Crew, you can almost always go there.
6 levels of customization put the game's huge map to use, they are fullstock, street, dirt, Perf (performance), raid (trophy trucks), and circuit (full-blown race cars) each with it's own merits and downfalls that add an unmatched level of diversity to the game.
The options menu is even pretty comprehensive with toggles for anti-aliasing, even types of anti-aliasing. individual performance impactors with their own toggles, and full wheel support with multiple ways of customizing so you can tune it to your driving style.
All in all a fantastic game, even after the career mode there's plenty to do and fun to be had. 9/10

WWE 2K16 does its darndest to provide whatever it can for the fans to enjoy out of the game, but its gameplay and pace restrict it to a certain demographic.
When it comes to gameplay and controls, the pace may feel a little slow for an audience that comes from a twitch-timing lineup of games. Regardless, it matches very well to the way we normally see pro wrestling matches and doesn't falter from the unrealistic side of things by far except for physics which barely matters and how much of an impact it would have to set the outcome of a match. Mini games at the start and end of a match fairly tell in comparison on what superstars can do against each other, and it works well. Realistically, the game does its darndest to keep the competition from going one-sided way too quickly without limiting a player's capabilities.
Online multiplayer is a subjective matter, and performance may vary depending on which player faces which along with their Internet connection.
As far as features go, you can go pretty far with creating things of your own. There are limits, though, as there's only so much you can build out of your superstar, logo, show and arena when you wish to share them with the online community. If you want, you can also make an alternate attire out of other WWE superstars. I can finally dress up John Cena in his generic green trunks since his first debut in the WWE.
In addition, you get to relive some of WWE's history back in the early years of the World Wrestling Federation with "Macho Man" Randy Savage and Jake "The Snake" Roberts. Various conditions and seeing the outcome of each match as is recorded in history is eye-catching. But the commentary from today's announcers disconnects the legendary vibe some. You never hear Mr. McMahon's angsty dialogue at ringside apart from replays and historic vignettes. Plus, performing these feats as accurately as possible is a way to unlock content. Austin 3:16, which is the staple of the game, demonstrates the evolution of Steve Austin and the franchise as a whole as he turns the tides to his favor with his new face and attitude since his first appearance and pains in his career. This shows that not everything in the franchise is all sunshine and bunnies, and is an appropriate chapter to show in the midst of the franchise's history.
The roster is definitely plentiful, but selective as usual, with the lineup consisting majorly from NXT and this era's superstars from SmackDown! and RAW. DLC also has a fairly impressive amount of selections, from legends to new bloods to Arnold "The Terminator" Schwarzenegger.
The pace of the game is much slower compared to previous games, but relates a lot more to pro wrestling in real life. There are limits to what a superstar can do before they are worn out, and to keep things an a more level playing field, reversal opportunities are limited. You are fated to take the pain if you exert too much from the start. It's up to you if you want to set momentum, but how you adapt to the superstar you are playing as is more important than ever. At least nobody feels like a cardboard cut-out in that regard. A five-star rating will not be as easy as before.
As I said before, there is a limit with how much you can make with your superstars, shows, and arenas. It saves bandwidth and server space when sharing content with other players. You'd have to improvise with what you can to make the most accurate appearance of what you're going for as possible with little resources. While it's convenient to access other players' creations in-game, the limit with what you can create in order to share and play online with them is disappointing. If I had a suggestion, it'd be to remove the limits and advise me that I can't share them until I lighten the loads. That way, it's more universal and less stressful for both the creators and the WWE Creations server.
One presentation name I used in previous WWE games was "The Vampire". But it wasn't available from a few games back and I had to settle with "The Monster" instead. Presentation names are plentiful and there's quite a variety. But the pot gets stirred more often than not between each WWE game released. If you've been maining with the same created superstar and presentation name, you might be disappointed.
I'm quite happy with the roster selection this game, and even happier that we are able to design alternate attires for our WWE superstars, something that had been missing for many generations. But don't expect all alumni to make an appearance in this game. Sorry, Hulkamaniacs.
The only reason I would recommend this game is because it's been many, MANY years since a WWE game has been released on PC. But that isn't saying much. If you're new to the franchise and want to get your feet wet, this would be the best place to start before getting acquainted with previous pro wrestling games on consoles from two decades ago (some of which are better). But if you just care about gameplay and creativity, skip this one out-right.

I really wanted to like this game. But in the end, the gun mechanics just dont work that well. Sure, it's cool when you do something right, like grab the magazine with bullets in it, push the hammer forward, put the cylinder back inside the revolver... I think you might see the problem. I ecentually got to the point where I could reload my gun without looking at the help menu but even with the satisfaction that comes with that, the gun mechanics are, in my mind, simply not very good. There are enemy turrets in the game. They are one of the obastacles that you have to deal with, and you deal with them by either shooting a camera attached to them, effectively blinding them or, shooting their battery pack, a brown box at its base, which will completely diable them. Shooting them in the camera is generaly a bad idea, since you must stand directly in front of them in order to do so. However, shooting them in the battery pack is incredibly inconsistent. I put an entire magazine into it to no effect. I eventually killed it, only to discover that almost all of my bullets, including the one that killed it, had landed in the exact same place. Also one bullet kills you and you respawn at the beginning of a completely new randomized map. I actually found turrets to be far easier than tazer drones. Tazer drones have weak spots but they incredibly difficult to hit due to their speed. They do have weaknesses, such as their slow turning or their inability to see you if you just duck behind a corner, and if you keep your distance, than they aren't normally that hard to kill. But when they are charging at you in a hallway, you pretty much just fire as much as you can and pray that you hit something vital.
In addition to the random map, it seems that your ammo count is also random. I respawned several times to discover that I had no ammo at all. Once I respawned with a tazer drone facing me.
Maybe this appeals to some people but It absolutely does not appeal to me. Even after I tried to learn how to play and was encouraged to try again by other Steam users, I still found no enjoyment in this title.

I bought this because Monster Slayers was so enjoyable. I really liked this too! Pretty impressive portfolio from a one-person studio.
I have to agree with another reviewer in one aspect though - I am not sure why the tag line is that "YOU are the dungeon". The tagline and name of the game seem to come from an entirely different game. But that doesn't stop this game from being fun in its own right.
This game allows you to pick from up to 3 missions between dungeons. Depending on which you choose, you will unlock different gear, minions, or powers. You will probably get a couple chances at the major players, but for the most part the choices matter and your party will greatly change based off what you do. And the choices aren't dross - you can choose to abandon compatriots (leading to permanent skill loss)or trigger "bad endings".
It did take me a pretty long time to figure out the different power options. Each character has a vanilla attack as well as a "power" that can be used in the same term and is subject to cooldown. There is also a team-wide "Threat" meter - which you use to trigger other (sometimes quite powerful) powers. The lines between these powers blur and I was nearly to the end of the game before I finally figured out which powers had a cost and which were essentially free.
But the writing is sharp and funny and the gameplay is interesting. I was really charmed, as a whole. I will be looking for the next Nerdook game and buying on release. Thanks for your work, the effort really shines through.

A very good RPG, kind of in the same vein as Wizardry 8 but not as amazing as that game. You might also say it's like if Might and Magic X was good. The exploration is by far Grimrock 2's strongest point, with a sprawling open-ended world to explore and tons of secrets to find. It can be tense too, as you come to expect horrible things to happen when picking up items, etc. Multiple times I got jumpscared by unexpected enemies. The graphics are even pretty great, especially for an indie studio. Character building and progression isn't bad, though there's some useless skills and it starts to not matter what you level towards the end. Music is great on the menu and in boss battles, but nonexistent otherwise. It works for Myst and Demon's Souls, but I would've preferred some more traditional music to the ambience in this case.
The one thing that really threatens to spoil it is the combat system, which is carried over from the previous game where it also was a problem. Positioning determines roughly 90% of your success, or should I say, whether or not you can find four open squares to move around on. People cheesed enemies in Grimrock 1 with squaredancing, and instead of revamping it, the developers just made skillful squaredancing 100% necessary to have any success in combat. There are more nuances in enemy movement to make it interesting, but if you ever get cornered at the end of a hallway, even the god damn mosquitoes will tear your party apart. I don't care if it's old school, It's fundamentally broken, and anyone who stuck up for it after the first game is wrong. It also sucks that you have to click small icons and make complex actions with the mouse while doing all this movement, when even the 90s RPGs allowed you to attack with hotkeys for your characters. However, combat isn't the majority of the game, and in MOST cases it's manageable without much frustration. It's only when they throw enemies at you in cramped hallways that it stops working well. There were a lot of times where I got gameovers and then easily overcame them the next time because now I knew where I could safely fight.
Anyway, whatever, good game overall.

Cook, Serve, Delicious is a game I never quite anticipated enjoying. It's a game about running a restraunt. It's a very simplified version of running a restraunt, but it is every second intense, entertaining, and fulfilling, surprisingly so. Is this Cooking Mama, PC? No. This is Quickly Prepare Food For Hundreds of Starving Customers In A Twenty Minute Sitting.
Each meal has a specific recipe, one you get to know by heart. For example, a Chicken Breast is, as follows: tenderize six times, season, cook, serve, delicious. Sounds simple, right? Now cook six in ten seconds flat. It's a bit heart racing (hard to believe, I know).
The variety of recipes is vast. There are dozens of different foods, and hundreds of ways to prepare them each. They also each have there plusses and minuses- for example, there are staple foods which always have a high demand, and there are other foods, like steak and chicken which lose demand and must be replaced on your menu every few days (No worries, this change is not permanent). You're given a liberal variety in your menu- you can design it as you please with up to six items, change them between each day, and feature a meal of the day. Each food has dozens of alternative recipes, and you can upgrade each food to make more recipes available and increase the profit of your meals.
The art and soundtrack for this game are not to be ignored. They are each terrific, and fit one another like a nice hug, and fit the genre like a puzzle piece. The music consists of smooth, jazzy tunes I enjoy listening to outside of the game on a nice rainy day, and the art is complemented by it. The art has a wonderfully individual, indie feel that you'd expect, and is very warm and homey.
Altogether, this game is not a waste, and a game I'd wholeheartedly recommend. I was surprised how much I enjoyed it-surprise yourself too.
