The basic idea is to expand your village/culture but it isnt as simple as just placing the correct buildings - weather needs to be taken in to account for example should you push your workers to complete that new stone quarry before winter sets in or, if times are hard food wise do you sacrifice some sheep for meat resources which could otherwise help to make warmer clothes for your hunters and farmers?
Trade routes can be established with outsiders, but this can increase the risk of diseases that a basic herbalist isnt really up to curing.
Another common resource in these kind of games -Wood- here becomes not just a resource. Its good to strip swathes of forest down for building and firewood, but as herbalists and apothecary types like to gather in the forests this can have negative effects on the health of your people. Trees can be replanted and there are many wyas to get food.
Its all a zen like balance, especially in the sand box mode but may take a few tries to get a feel of what be wise in the early game and what isnt as a poor choice early on could literally cripple your population as they grow years later.
It can also be paused in real time or time sped up or slowed by degrees if you re waitin on a construction and charts can be accessed during the game to help with your grand designs on food needed for population growth, most efficient paths taken so you can built the best roads n all that jazz. Its a sweet distraction for sure.

First off, do note that my playtime is not much, but I've managed to get a lot of cards through draft, already going 7, 5 and 6 wins respectively.
I played HS and Duelyst in the past, and I must say this game blows them out of the water. I'll give you pros and cons (might update this in the future).
Pros:
- game is generous as hell, you can easily earn gold and shiftstone (equivalent of dust in HS), contains achievements which give gold and sense of accomplishment, and overall data collection for us nerds. You will get gold quickly. You even get 100 shiftstone every time you open a pack, which is amazing
- client is optimized amazingly, runs crisp, animations are gorgeous and everything feels polished. I have an older laptop and game runs great on it. A big plus!
- all of the 5 factions are very unique and cool to play, and you can build decks around any of them, even all 5 at once, or any combination you want
- gameplay is amazing. You can interact with graveyard (discard pile), resurrect units, steal them, there are quick spells to use in the middle of attack phase or enemy turn
- even in the first set, there are a lot of cards to collect
- a lot of modes are available which I'll cover later, you wont get bored or stay without something to do in game, you can always earn gold and cards, even against AI opponent
- community is nice, discord is here to help us newbies, you can ask anybody to answer your questions, or help you in some way
- you can play it on mobile! That's right, big plus if I'm not at home, I can play during job breaks or when I'm travelling to work
Cons:
- Legendary cards are a bit expensive to craft (3200), and since maximum number is 4 in a deck, decks can become expensive. Not to say there aren't great budget or mid tier priced decks, there are.
- You can't monitor your total match history. For example, Duelyst lets you do that, you can see all the games you played since the beginning of time
- no replay function, could be good to learn from your replays, what you did wrong etc.
Some other explanations, read below:
Do note that gold prices may seem higher that in HS/Duelyst, but you earn it that much faster.
You can enter Gauntlet for free, for any amount of times you want, you play against AI opponents, and you earn chests every time you win, giving you gold and cards or even packs. Great for learning the game and getting some gold for it. Make sure you play this till Master, since every time you go 7 wins, your rank upgrades and you get a chest. Bronze>SIlver>Gold etc. After Master you don't get those chest, but you get regular ones.
Forge is also great place to be till Master. 2500 gold to enter, all the cards you draft are YOURS after completion, AND you get packs/gold for how many wins you had. Amazing.
Draft is 5000 gold, you also keep all the cards you drafted. Drafting is a bit complicated, I'm still learning quite a bit, but can proudly say I went 7-1 in my first one (7 wins is maximum). If you get 7 wins you earn over 6000 gold, premium cards, free packs and also you keep all the cards you crafted. I hated draft in HS and Duelyst, I love it here.
All in all, I could write here all day, but fact remains that this is the best CCG currently on the market, and I tried a lot of them.
Now if you will excuse me, there is Draft awaiting for me. Cheers!

These restaurant-managing sims are a guilty pleasure of mine, and I think this one will keep that part of my brain satisfied indefinitely.  Smoothly polished gameplay, good variety of items to make (all with their own quirks; like having to fry or chop ingredients, and whether you cook at the start, middle, or end of preparation), and a decent amount of fluff around the edges to round out the game.  Also it actually gets seriously challenging.
You know how these games work; if not go google "Papa's Burgeria", play for ten minutes, and then come back.  It is a big pile of minigames, and you go through a game-day worth of them at a time.
* Includes non-food chores (dishes, trash, etc) that carry special penalties if you fail them
* Health inspections, which make the chores harder for a game day
* Optional dating minigame; where a special customer shows up, and if you do well on their order they'll text you during work (reading comprehension time trial)
* Optional betting minigames, where you take on extra challenges to make more income in a day
* At-your-liesure speed/accuracy trials, guised as catering jobs, iron chef competitions, and something hilarious
* Upgrade your recipes and restaurant over time, adding new complexities to recipes
* Weekly leaderboard challenges
* Amusing tidbits to read (fake spam emails, food and event descriptions)

Wow the review I spend an hour typing didn't post after I hit post review...
Anyways short version because I don't want to type that much again: first mission/quest you get is to complete the campaign which is horribly RNG coming from an experienced player of card games and you will spend a long time just completing that. You have to win 17 matches (4 for each of the remaining factions and unique deck style boss) against the AI after playing the 4 matches forced on you. The boss alone took me 10 re-tries because it is pure RNG since he has a Sliver deck if you've played MtG and although a lot of the slivers don't have useful abilities once the useful ones come out you lose unless you can counter.
The game has the same issues as MtG which means mana drought/ mana flood/ creature and/or spell flood which just means you lose unless your opponent is also experiencing difficulties. This also means that those initial 17 wins tooks me close to 50 matches becasuse I had horrible RNG and the starter decks are not very good.
PvP matchmaking does not exist as of the moment! You will need to spend time/money to get decks able to consistently win in ranked PvP matches since casual ones don't exist... In addition the daily quest is to win in PvP so you are forced to play ranked unless you have 5 spare boosters so you can play draft which I didn't have. Proceeded to go 0/5 in my placement matches because there is no matchmaking and my starter deck was pitted against multi-legendary decks.
I don't recommend this game unless you are a masochist, willing to invest the time to grind out a good/decent deck, or willing to spend money.
The good thing about this game is that the factions or whatever they're called system is very versatile like MtG because you're not limited to 1 or 2 of them which means you can make some crazy multi-faction deck or at least theorycraft one.

This game is brutal, but awesome.
Usually with a game like this you will find yourself in the swing of things once your poplation gets bigger. Your new disposable workforce will be able to switch around to make non-essential goods as needed. But not this game!
at a population of around 300, I was "lucky" enough to experience a population surge of around 150 new people in just one year. That spring, 250 people starved to death since I now couldn't support everyone.
Suddenly I don't have enough workers to get in the necessary food to keep the remaining people alive, so I promtly shut down the production of all non-essential materials, I got low on tools, alcohol, clothing and firewood. My graveyards all filled up over the winter, my teachers, doctors and clerics all died. Town morale was at an all time low.
The game saw I was down and decided to kick me. A fire broke out in a concentration of my stone houses, burning down around 1/3 of my town. I was left with a huge population of starving homeless people who froze to death as soon as winter arrived.
...I think I'm going to start again at this point. I'm not in a great position in my devastated land of the now-ironically named Paradise Falls. But if you, like me, enjoy a city builder that's a real challenge then this game is you. Only don't get complacant just because you're established. You'll only end up hurt.

It relies on lack of information and having to gather and interpet information yourself to gather and  understand the story. Seriously, buy this game. Otherwise, 11/10, best horror game in YEARS.

Myst-like in that you must figure out what's going on, but unlike in that there aren't any puzzles to solve - you just walk through and explore the station.  Your actions/choices do not make a difference in what you experience.  You can only "play" the game once.

Is the game worth the asking price?
I bought it for 10$ with the DLCs in a sale. I don't think it's worth that price.
It might not be as buggy as it was at release ( I saw the reviews and videos and just gave it a skip). I've waited over a year now and figured they'd fixed the bugs... Yeah, no.
A lot has obviously been fixed, but I've been having extreme issues with the game crashing. Sometimes to desktop, most of the time I am forced to use a secondary monitor to kill the task.
When it first happened I just ignored it and jumped back in, really wanting to like the game. I passed the 2 hours played - Then I wanted to know what happened with the story, and kept on pushing through the crashes. Today I tried playing the DLCs after the game completed. I've crashed around 12 times in 3 hours and 30 minutes. It's a complete immersion breaker, and having to redo everything since the last savepoint becomes a chore after a while.
That said; The game itself is "ok". If I could play for half an hour without a crash I would probably give it a positive review, but the way the game is today - it is just more frustrating than it is worth.
The default setting gunplay is horrible with mouse acceleration and smooting. With a few config fixes (check the forums), you get decent gunplay again.
The story is perhaps far fetched. You play as a terrorist, using insurgence tactics agains an established military force that has invaded your country. Putting the disbelief on the sideline the story is good enough. Nothing to write home about, for sure, but ok.
The world is pretty generic. Reminds me a lot of an urban Farcry. You take over "outposts" and eventually control the whole map.
All in all, it's a big fat NO from me. As I said, I wanted to like it, but with all the crashes it's just frustrating.

It's a great display of art that I can't recommend. I say art instead of game because this is truly the closest thing you will get to a true WW1 experience, for the most part.
The gameplay itself isn't what lacks, it's the development and the skeleton that makes it. Hitboxes are all over the place. I find that when I'm down in a pit with reasonable ping, I still somehow die to a bullet that in reality, went right over me. Either this game is a zero tolerance with ping, meaing you need 10 or less to actually play it, or the 'fixes' they've implemented aren't doing anything. The prone animation and hitbox are completely broken as well, often It seems that you rest on your toes while your body goes to a 45 degree angle upward. Often I find that when I shoot at their body, it's only their head poking up and not their entire torso. This makes me quite weary to even use prone as the enemy probably knows exactly where I am, even when I'm in cover.
There's also an issue with people exploiting the hitboxes and not-so-great shooting mechanics. You can get perfect rifle accuracy while jumping and aiming. This shouldn't be the case by any means, as I find it difficult to be accurate in reality if I'm even as much moving at a slow pace, let alone flying through the air. This is one of the few things that break the immersion which keeps me coming back to this God-awful 'game' that I own. I love the Stahlhelms and tornister packs, the Brody helms and laughably bad Adriene helm, but when a Stoßtrupp in the early uniform is using an MP18(i), I feel like walking away and uninstalling, but this is the only game that actually does WW1 without being an arcade game.
So, if you want to see what it's like the crawl through the trenches and have someone who is completely imcompentent with a rifle constantly drop mortars on your head as opposed to using them tactically, see people in incorrect period uniforms for their weapons, and actually see the Chauchat actually function, then this is for you. If you're looking for a fun tactical game to play after work or school, don't bother. It isn't worth your money.

Side characters introduced like Nooj, Gippal, and Baralai extend the Spira world, but lack enough substance or connection that would allow the player to care for their problems. Dark Souls 1 was a game with its flaws that kept you playing it, giving you a sense of achievement as a result alongside all the frustrations it caused. It had a realistic feeling with weapons that had weight to them and had a really good level design and enemy placement. Not many things were out of place and you were able to, most of the time, get pretty satisfying progress if you took your time and not rushed through areas.
Dark Souls 2 on the other hand, kills most of the positives of its sequal.
-Enemies are doing jerky and unpredictable and unfair movements such as target locking on to you, striking at a 270 degree arc, doing unexpected combos, jumping from ledges, playing dead and the worst of all their weapons have no weight to them. I believe this was done to create the illusion that the AI was stronger but it not only fails to give that impression, also manages to look very stupid while doing it.
-Level design is not coherent and do not connect to each other for the most part. They laid out the map laterally and resorted to cheap tricks such as carrying you with an eagle when you reach a dead end. That is lazy.
-The environments look uninspired and the textures and models for the most part are out of place. This game got a huge graphical downgrade after its E3 demo. Most environments now look bland and empty, the developers tried to compensate for this by adding thousands of breakable barrels everywhere. Lazy.
-The enemy placement does not make much sense. The strategical aspect of the first game is gone here, for the most part you try to lure enemies out 1 by 1 because when they are in groups, their jerky movements do not give you an opportune moment to strike. They also spawn in abundance from places you do not expect. Combine the overpopulation of your enemies with the sub-par level design, it becomes a chore rather than a challenge. Boring.
-Boss fights have less of a challenge to them and they are not as memorable. It is really hard to follow the lore of a souls game but we all understood why SIF had a big sword in the first one. No special moments like that here, just more bosses with cheap mechanics and jerky, unpredictable movement. I don't consider a giant that has a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for a face ripping his own arm and trying to beat me with it special.
-Character movement, animations and weapon balance is a downgrade. Most weapons that are the same class behave the same, your attacks feel just as artificial as the critters you kill and the animations look like lego bricks rolling around. Weapons get damaged by half after you kill 10-15 enemies and get automatically repaired when you rest at a bonfire. Enough said.
If I think about it I can find more faults with this game but I will not bother because I think I made my point. So what does this game have over its predecessor as a positive? It runs better and smoother. That's about it.
It is quite clear that the developers tried to appear like they were "innovating" with this game but since they actually did not have a clue what made Dark Souls special and appealing, they messed up big time. So, after all this time, you get this cheap, bland, not exciting game that is actively trying to sell itself by giving the message "I'm hard, I'm hardcore", "You will die!" and making you die due to its poor movement, mechanics, enemy placements etc. If it had the quality and feel of its predecessor, I could overlook its flaws and maybe keep playing for more than an hour or be excited when i started it again. But as it is, I sometimes even forget that I have it installed and can not stand it for more than an hour. As a result;
NOT RECOMMENDED

Despite being 3-D, it plays like a true KOF game, as opposed to Maximum Impact. The speed of every move feels just right for KOF veterans. It uses the classic Advanced groove, with 3-on-3 fights.
Every single special introduction is now a mini-cutscene. If you loved keeping track of all the special relationships that existed between KOF characters, this game takes it to the next level. It's like SvC's battle intros, except voiced, and without the horrendous flatness of SvC. There are a few unfortunate ones missing, due to the fact that they never brought back voice actors to help with DLC character intros (e.g. no special Vanessa versus Ramon intro).
The main story itself is not much, but it still makes more sense than the entire Ash Crimson saga, and it promises a lot more in the future. It does not rely on yet another evil person running the KOF tournament but secretly trying to take over the world, which is a welcome change from past KOF story formulas.
Not as good as KOF 1998, 2002, or XI, but the most iconic hero teams have all returned. There are also lots of new characters who are far better than Ash Crimson, and many of them could easily become iconic in their own right. Unlike a certain other fighting game, it never feels like some character is just the evil version of another one. Hopefully, more fan favorites will get added in later seasons of DLC.

tl:dr There are probably better alternatives, both for time killers and turn based games. If there existed a neutral option on steam, I would certainly make use of it here. Unfortunately there isn’t, and since I cannot wholeheartedly recommend the game, it is not recommended. As a cheap, quick time killer, the game is serviceable, but its poor design drags it down too much.
Despite its low asking price, and even buying on a sale for just over 3 dollars, it’s hard to decide if Reverse Crawl is a good purchase. It was fine for the 6.3 hours I spent playing it, but not great. Having played several flash games of the developer’s, all of Nerdook’s games have a simple, if rough, charm to it. Those flash games were free however.
While there were some funny lines in the game, like its characters and plot, they were ultimately forgettable. They weren’t bad by any stretch, but not memorable either.
The real issue comes with Reverse Crawl’s design, which is clunkier than it needs to be, and lack of Quality of Life features. A lack of shortcuts for spells and abilities, a cluttered interface that doesn’t provide useful information about the statuses and attributes of the characters on the field, a poorly organised upgrade list, an inability to see all available monster groups on the world map, the list goes on.
The base gameplay loop of choosing which squad to deploy against the enemy’s was fine, the flanking and status effects adding some variety to it. Having some variation with traits was fun too.
Despite having a foundation to support different playstyles, the random nature of rewards, lack of useful explanation for some mission rewards, as well as brief campaign prevented any really meaningful specialisation.
Overall, Reverse Crawl is just serviceable. While not frustrating to play, and I certainly don’t hate or dislike the game, I probably won’t remember it after some time which is a pity. I wanted the game to be more.

This is, without a doubt, one of the hardest games I have ever played. No, it isn't like Dark Souls hard where the game punishes you for every mistake you make, but is rewarding in the end. No, receiver is the kind of hard where if the game doesn't like your face, you're f*cked.
Basically, the goal is to find all 11 tapes that are randomly placed within a randomly generated map. You start off with one of three guns, a random number of bullets, and maybe a flashlight. You then have to stealth your way throughout the map taking out turrets and drones as you go, praying you don't run out of bullets. What makes receiver unique, is the implementation of complete gun control. That is to say, everything about your firearm is done manually. In most games, you just have to press 'r' and your character inserts a new clip. In receiver, to reload a 9mm, press 'e' to remove magazine, press '~' to holster your weapon, press 'z' a few times to load bullets into the magazine, press '~' to hold your weapon, and press 'z' to put your newly loaded magazine into your gun. Then you may have to press 't' to release the slidelock. Sound complicated? It is. But it's still cool.
*IMPORTANT NOTE: Everything kills you in one hit*
Since everything about the game is randomly generated, the game varies in levels of generosity. There will be sections that give you four tapes in one room and sections that give you seven turrets in one room. This is why the game is hard. The majority of the challenges you face (No ammo, stupid f*cking flying drones, etc.) are because you're unlucky.
For an overall rating, I'd give this game an 8/10, for its awesome concept. No other game has made me feel so bad*ss and so desperate at the same time.
Oh, by the way, please comment your record for number of tapes acquired on one life. Currently mine is 7.

RIVE – Wreck! Hack! Die! Retry!
PUBLISHER – Two Tribes
DEVELOPER – Two Tribes
GENRE – Twin-Stick SHMUP/Action-platformer
LET'S DO THIS! (GENERAL):
2-D twin-stick SHMUP/action-platformer hybrid. Yer a rough-and-tumble kinda guy (with clean teeth!) named Roughneck who pilots a little spider tank of destruction. Most of your time is spent within the bowels of a starship nearly bereft of life, and in artificial gravity. Some areas turn off the gravity entirely, some have anti-gravity bubbles, some have water that blocks your shots entirely, etc.
SHAKESPEARE, SHMAKESPEARE (THE FLOW AND THE STORY):
After passing through a meteor swarm, you end up stuck inside a robot-infested space hauler run by a persistent AI who really doesn't want you to leave. You progress through new areas, seeking out new Hacks (which the AI isn't to happy about) to take over bots and activate control nodes, upgrading as you go. You'll also find Warp stations along the way, and utilize them after each stage is complete. You will also be able to afford a weapon, shield, or loot magnet upgrade after every mission or two, provided you make sure to grab the bolts the enemies drop when they go pop. Four special weapons (kill stuff faster, but you can only hold one ammo unit at a time), two armor upgrades (live a little longer), and two loot magnet upgrades (draw loot in from further away) are available. When you die – and you will die – during the main part of a stage, you'll respawn at a nearby checkpoint. When you die during a boss battle, you'll just get kicked back to the start of the most recent phase the boss entered; generally, you will lose ten seconds at the most, so you get right back into the thick of things.
PEW! PEW! PEW! (CONTROLS):
Four control setups; by default: Control your tiny spider-tank with the left stick, fire with the right stick (endless rapid-fire ammo), L2 to jump/doublejump, L1 or L2 to hack nodes and specific AI bots such as healers and turrets, face buttons to select a special attack, and R2 to fire them. Controls are responsive, your tank turns on a dime, and jumping is reasonably precise; it benefits from momentum. Movement speed is nice and zippy. You can fire in 360 degrees, at will, for most of the game.
OOOOO, PRETTY....(GRAPHICS):
Really impressive. Lots of background detail in the decrepit ship, and the dark color scheme of the foreground elements (most of the time) makes it easy to keep track of your ship in all of the chaos. Has just a taste of bullet hell, but not with actual bullets. Most enemies prefer to ram you at high speed, or loose missiles in your general direction. Enemy bots are widely varied – from the swarming blue orb bots to the pink saucers that try to cut you up like Wolverine – and each type has different tactics they use to do you in.
BOOM! (SOUND):
Great soundtrack, solid voice acting. Explosions feel meaty and “explodey,” very satisfying.
THE TOTAL PACKAGE (OVERALL):
A wild ride, if not a terribly long one. Well worth the money for the experience. Has multiple challenge modes, such as one-credit mode and survival mode, to extend the lifespan.
SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS: Minimal/moderate (Dual Core 2.5ghz, 4GB RAM)
STORY: 80
GAMEPLAY: 95
GRAPHICS: 95
SOUND: 85
FUN FACTOR: 95
ATMOSPHERE: 85
Pros:
Fast and furious action
Easy-to-use controls
Dying during boss fights (generally) only sets you back a few seconds
Good voice acting; clever script; great sense of humor from a bunch of veteran gamers (when's the last time YOU saw a game make a Parodius reference?)
Attention paid to many tiny details
Vibrant graphics; beefy explosions
You can blow up the plot exposition fairy – er, bot and his endless supply of replacements – if you don't wanna be bothered with the story. At least, until he wises up and turns on his energy shield...
Cons:
Prepare to die a lot on bosses until you GIT GUD. No mercy given.
Tends to railroad you – in an area with seemingly multiple paths, only the one you need to progress will actually be available for use.

An action packed balls to the wall platformer shooter hybrid.
RIVE's subtitle perfectly describes the game in 4 words. I could atone its gameplay sparingly as the "Metal Slug of this Generation" wherein destroying stuff actually feels amazing and moving on to the next segment makes for quite a relief and satisfaction. The twin stick mechanic mixed with precise platforming, complete with the classic double jump allows for great maneuvering of your ship to dance around the onslaught of bullets and enemies.
At its core it follows the "destroy waves of enemies, go to next room, repeat" formula but fortunately, it had enough bells and whistles that every level feels fresh with some introduction to some kind of gimmick. The constant switch of genres; making you control flying sections  with 360 scope, into precise platforming, and then back again, and even pure avoidance swimming sections wherein there is no shooting,  all makes the game free from feeling monotonous. In fact, some of these segments are highlights of the game. Mix in along the hacking abilty (used for opening doors,  anti-gravity switches, recruiting enemies, trains, and healing aids) makes for little gameplay stagnation. The story is passable and the dialogue is pretty meta. (not even necessary but it is welcomed) I only started being amused by them towards the end.
Mind you it is a very challenging game. There is little downtime and there are parts where it can be deemed frustrating and borderline unfair wherein you can't rely on just reflex alone when hoards of enemies just suddenly start diving towards you in one direction without warning. The challenge is there, but not to the point where it starts becoming a troll. There is still reliance on anticipation and predicting where the enemies will spawn in order to not get instagibbed out of nowhere. Luckily , respawns are quick and it brings you back almost instantly to the moment you were in before you died, and yes you will die a lot; In fact, the necessity for familiarity in order to move on actually demands for it.
There are moments that make you go "Okay, the screen is about 80 percent filled with lasers now, there is no way they are going to continue upping up the ante, I just need to survive a little lo....." ,and along with more lasers the game spawns flying discs that start hurling toward you. It is these HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥ moments (and there are plenty of them) that make the game all the more satisfying to accomplish. That partnered with the stunning visuals and the "I can't believe I just survived that" triumphant feeling, overall circumvent all the frustrations and makes this title worth at least a  playthrough.

For a free to play FPS, Warface is an actually decent game- especially when you compare it to most other F2P shooters that have enroached onto the modern day gaming market like a plague straight out of a horror movie. Warface also holds up surprisingly well against P2P shooters, such as CoD.
The Story is set around two forces fighting each other- the special operations force known as "Warface", and the sinister corporation known as "Blackwood". Both have access to near-future technology, and are fighting in pursuit of different goals.
The gameplay consists of choosing between four classes- Rifleman, Medic, Sniper, and Engineer. Each has their own playstyle and unique set of weaponry, as well as different roles to play in the scheme of things. Combat is relatively fast paced, with engagements going down fast and furious- especially in CQC. In Warface, teamwork is also an extremely crucial facet of gameplay, with certain locations on the map being inaccessible without the aid of an ally. Combat is also very team-oriented, as usually a lone gunman will be quickly taken out by a disciplined squad.
In terms of content, Warface is pretty deep. It has a leveling system that rewards you with new pieces of equipment (There's a VERY large variety to equip your soldier with, all of which do give certain benefits. I.E. Being able to see enemy mines.), and has a crate system that is used to purchase new pieces of equipment. However, something that bothers me is the fact that the game can be P2W with the inclusion of Kredits, which allow access to the best weapons and equipment. Aesthetic equipment is also Kredit-bought.
All in All
is a really nice FPS Game!

Especially coming from someone who has not played a WWE game since WWE '12 and not watched a second of it since 2008... I do, however have a few problems with it:
- The Jukebox is annoying, with only a few songs on it (by default), that just repeat over and over again, this, however can be fixed by allowing the Jukebox to play Superstar's songs, but, again, as I only know about 1/3 of the roster, I still hear repeats very often, especially as the songs that play are not the full songs, they only run for the time it takes for a SuperStar to perform an entrance.

In an industry riddled with companies releasing buggy unfinished games, milking their customers with shallow dlc and indie developers making nostalgia pandering shlock, Legend of Grimrock 2 stands as a shining example of the game done right. Ready out of the gate, working, polished product that knows its strengths and weaknesses, it manages to present an old school dungeon crawling experience made with modern standards and excel at it. For a fair price of 24 dollars you going to get a fulfilling product that provides around 30 hours of gameplay, with free dungeon editor and a bunch of well done community made maps.
Compared to its predecessor Legend of Grimrock 2 is doing well to learn on past mistakes and improves itself in many areas: boss fights are now more varied and interesting, level design isn't as convoluted but still contains many secret areas, leveling and class systems provide more room for experimentation, and the whole open world twist is just a great finishing touch.
As with the previous title, each area contains many puzzles and secret areas, so if you're really into treasure hunting you gonna have a good time.
Overall all, I give Legend of Grimrock 2 a heavy recommendation and Almost Human Games deserve some applause for doing so many things right, where others have failed.

An organic 'village/town' builder. This is what Sim City 5/6 should have been like. Steadily advance your fledgling village, one building at a time. Build what you need, when you need it. You can't just plonk buildings down like a mayor on steroids.
I've always been a big Sim City fan and, like many people, I've been bitterly disappointed by the recent reincarnations of Sim City and I was pleased to find Banished. In essence, the game is all about resource management, both in materials and labour. Keep your food stores up and only take from the environment what you can afford to lose in the short and long term. Delegate your work force to the ultimate objective - continuous, sustainable growth.
Its a challenging game that requires you to think about what you want to build, when you should build it, and most importantly, why you should build it. It takes a little time to get used to the game mechanics, but it is incredibly satisfying to build that local school or get that chapel up and running. A great and well thought out game, especially considering it was only made by one guy.
9/10 - Get it if you enjoy your old fashioned Sim City games!

Outlast is a very good game! If you are into Survival Horror this game is for you, it combineds al the aspects required to make a Survival Horror game.
Some of these key points are:
1. Savenging for fact sheets to understand why this is happening
2. No combat, you can only run and hide.
3. Enemies are belivebly insane people, with genuine voice acting to make this seem real.
4. Items are sarces so you're never feel 100% comfortable, if you're careless with your Battery supply this can be made doubly worse.
5. Your best friend is your Flashlight, in this case it's a Video Camera which has nightvision and requires batteries to fuction (Of course if you run out you're not left completely in the dark just harder to find where to go)
6. Not only does your best friend light the way it records key moments so you can find secret infomation while recording (So long as you're holding your camera at the correct sections).
For an Indie Developer (thats not so Indie but more ex gamedevs) to make something very close to a AAA Title this game is very impressive.
The graphics are amasing and make you feel like you are actually living the horror, the sound design is spot on everything sounds scary whether it's distant or close, screams of agony in the background and rattling chains, patients screaming weird profanities at you while they're trying to kill you or alerting the enemies of your presense.
I have enjoyed every minute of this game & hope that this little review will give people an idea of what games of this genre should be made like.
It's gotta be a 10/10 from me but remember that i'm a Horror fan.
Red Barrels new Downloadable Content for Outlast is known as Whistleblower, this DLC gives you the story of an inside man, the man who sent the Email letter to Miles Upersure & told him to go and check out Mount Massive Asylum and shut down the whole conspiracy project they had going there.
Whistleblower starts off with you learning who the snitch was you're name is "Weyland Park" you're a Computer Specialist on hire & you're job is to keep the computers function for the company so they can keep on testing,
After a brief intro of your peers you learn that they're all completely willing to kill you in order to stop you spreading the word about what they were really doing & so begins your decent into hell.
This DLC was very enjoyable for it's Story, it helped you understand what was going on in the building before the main game & you got to feel what it would have been like for someone who was working with the Corporation from the inside, you got to see the sick twisted minds of the workers & of the "Big Cheese" who was a complete "AZZ" right off the bat.
There was new enemies to see & also a return of some of the classic enemies we saw in the main game, there was new area's of the Asylum to witness.
This DLC featured some REALLY sick and very twisted moments in it (which i wouldn't say are bad), especially with 1 of the more insane enemies, who has a very deep & sad story that kind of explains why he's so twisted.
Keep this in mind because if you plan on getting this DLC you're going to see some really deranged crap, so don't get this if you're queezy or one of those easily offended types.
The Enemy Charcters in this peice of DLC have very interesting and unique stories that you can find out by reading the documents and this will help you learn why they're being submitted to this facility.
As much as i enjoyed most of this DLC there were some really frustrating things that just made me hate it at times.
Getting stuck on props & walls while an enemy is chasing you is god aweful and it takes you out of experience of the game which then just gets you very frustrated.
THIS ENTIRE GAME LACKS PHYSICS PROPS,
(The props don't move which makes it so god damn easy to get stuck on stuff & that is very annoying.)
On several of the sections in this game i got stuck wondering where the hell i was meant to be going & most of the damn time i died many times trying to outrun an enemy that was chasing me while i was trying to work out where i needed to go next.
Although the fact that this game doesn't hold your hand and point out obviously where you need to go, (Which is not a bad thing by the way) it really seriously needed to be a little bit easier to tell where you needed to go sometimes, because getting chased endlessly in circles whilest trying to find the correct path to get to the next objective it's just not fun.
The scares in the DLC feel very much the same as the original game, i didn't really get that scared in this DLC as i did in the original game. (This is not all that bad but it was a bit disappointing.)
With all these things in mind my final rating for the "Whistleblower" DLC would have to be a 7/10.
It's a very solid peice of DLC, it's not just a reskin of the same old place we played in the main game but it has new area's and some new enemies with unique & interesting characteristics which make them that more facinating when you listen to their mental rambling both while they're searching for you & while they chase you.
The places that you explore in this DLC feel new even though there are a few area's from the original game they're not all that common until the end of the game & at which point you're not spending a great deal of time in them anyway.
The downsides of this game weren't too common except for i spent a whole lot of time dying because of getting stuck on props or because i was stuck wandering in circles alot of the time because i couldn't find the exit to the next section.
All in all this DLC is worth a purchase if you enjoyed the Main Game, if you didn't enjoy the main game then this DLC probably won't do you justice and you will probably want to give it a miss,

As writing this review, I only have 51 minutes clocked in, but that's because I just bought it on Steam. I have actually completed the story and done most side missions in this game and can thoroughly recommend it to anyone who likes over the top action and mayhem reminicent of 80's and 90's action movies. The grappling hook is such an awesome gameplay mechanic.
The story is pretty bad and even with it's campy humour and self-mockery, it is very uninteresting. Games like this however, aren't about story - the only thing that you need to know about the story is that you are an American special agent who has been dropped onto an asian island which has just suffered a coup. Your goal is to destabilise the new dictator's government by causing as much destruction as possible to his facilities.
It plays like Grand Theft Auto games or Saint's Row games - you know the type. Open world, story if you want it, side missions and other things if you don't. You steal cars, you fight the authorities or run from them, etc etc etc. What makes this game different is the gratuitous level of destruction and mayhem. Sure, that happens in the other titles that I mentioned too, but this game has it's own style of doing it and it's all down to the amazing grappling hook and the havoc it and the physics can cause.
At the price this game is nowadays and the constant sales, I can't recommend it enough.
Verdict: Great fun though somewhat lacking in interesting story telling, atmosphere or voice acting. If you enjoy blowing things up and messing around with physics, this game is a great laugh. I picked it up for $2.50 on sale and for that price, it's one of the best bargains that I have ever had on Steam. 7/10

After playing FINAL FANTASY X/X-2 for the first time ever in my life, I can safely write a review about these games and give my thoughts about them. But since this includes 2 games, I believe I need to review them separately so here goes!
FINAL FANTASY X was the first game I played and I suppose it should be everyone's first game to play when one buys this.
The game is a turn-based JRPG where enemies and your characters take turns of action. I feel this system is a very good one and it's ultimately sad that there aren't so many games with this system nowadays. You can have up to 3 characters on the field, but can call out any reserves you have and replace one of the field characters at any time you wish as long as it's your turn. Another thing that's very good about this system is that there is no rush in deciding what to do on your characters' turns. You could just never insert any commands and nothing would happen. Of course there are other elements to the combat, such as Overdrives and Summons but I feel they are best experienced individually.
Leveling up in this game is different from most other "standard" JRPG games since when you level up you usually gain instantaneous stat gains. In this game, however, you don't just gain levels. You gain
. You use these sphere levels to move around in this massive menu called the
. Moving around in this sphere grid requires sphere levels and to move one step you require one sphere level. The point of moving in this sphere grid is to find nodes with stat increases on them. You then use spheres to unlock these nodes and get the stat increase. There are multiple different spheres which essentially unlock specific nodes. The good thing about this whole sphere grid is that you can level up your characters the way you want to. You can make your healer the best physical damage dealer, and likewise. Or just make a hybrid. Whichever suits you best.
The story and characters in it are some of the best I have ever had the chance to experience. The characters have actual development and all of the characters feel like individuals. Many get turned off because of the game's main character for some reason.
The story itself is a very enjoyable part of this game. It has so many plot twists and it surely keeps you on your toes all the time. I for one was waiting in anticipation what would happen next. Then again, I haven't played any other FINAL FANTASY games (other than FINAL FANTASY VIII) so I wouldn't know what else they have to offer.
Then there's the music, which fits all the moods and environments perfectly. When something dramatic is going on, the music will make sure that you feel it as well. I cannot stop listening to the music after beating the game, it's so good.
FINAL FANTASY X alone is worth the price.
After experiencing the greatness of FINAL FANTASY X I couldn't even imagine how good the sequel would be. I'm afraid I was disappointed horribly.
I have read what other people had to say about this game. So many people claim the story and characters to be trash and the only redeeming factor for this game to be it's combat system. I guess different strokes for different people, but here's what I think:
At the end of the day, the story was the only thing in this game that kept me going. It was the only thing that made me force myself to finish and see how the game ends. So what was so bad that made me want to stop half way through?
The characters in the game were - if not enjoyable - atleast bearable. The real problem hides in the battle system. Now don't get me wrong, I have nothing against ATB (Active time battle system) based battle systems. Quite the opposite actually. I have played FINAL FANTASY VIII in addition to these games in the FINAL FANTASY series. That game had ATB system as well, but that was well made. This game's system has atleast 3 major problems:
1. When your characters' ATB bar fills up and you decide to attack with a character, the character may MISS. I don't mean that the enemy evades your attacks. I mean that your character does the attack animation, but doesn't actually hit the enemy. After the animation is done your character tries to attack again.
2. Everything in this game has some form of a wait time, aside from the basic attack (or the equivalent) command. Want to heal your character quick before the enemy gets its turn? Too bad, you have to wait for a while so your character can pick the item from her♥♥♥♥♥first. Want to cast a quick Thundara spell? Too bad, you have to wait for a while so your character can stand still for a while first. This makes especially healing a bloody nightmare.
3. This problem is related to the first problem. Whenever your character goes out to attack, the game won't stop. It will go on just like it normally would. The problem is, your character is attacking, while your other characters get to fill up their ATB bar and so does the enemy. The frustration grows when your character misses the first 3 times and then the enemy gets to KO your character BECAUSE IT CAN'T BLOODY HIT THE ♥♥♥♥♥♥. Meanwhile your other characters are already ready for action.
Then there is the "Job" system or Dress spheres how they like to call it. Basically all your characters can specialize in different classes for example Black Mage, Warrior, Thief etc. each plays differently, but there are way too many of them. At first I was very into the idea of different playstyles, but then it just became too much effort. I ended up sticking with 1 class for each character, because I just wouldn't want to spend the rest of the game tinkering with the dress spheres.
I already said before that the story was the only thing that kept me playing didn't I? Well even for that you need to go out of your way to get the story bits in the game, because they're hidden IN SIDE QUESTS!! Can you even believe that? When has a game hidden important story elements behind side quests? Of course you don't need to complete these to beat the game, but you'll be missing out on A LOT of the story. You won't get even 50% of the story completed if you complete none of the side quests.
This game has also a lot of minigames, most notable of them being spherebreak and blitzball. The other minigames I just couldn't be bothered with. Spherebreak is a bit too complicated to explain, therefore I'll just explain blitzball. It's a mess of stats and an adrenaline meter. You don't even get to control the players yourself. You get to watch as the AI just stupidly throws the ball all over the place. The adrenaline determines wether the players perform 4 times better at the cost of losing morale and gaining fatigue. No fun. Spherebreak I could at least see some people finding it interesting, but I couldn't be bothered to win even 1 game.
I wouldn't recommend buying this just for FINAL FANTASY X-2. I believe it alone isn't worth the price, but considering you get FINAL FANTASY X which is an extremely exquisite game you might as well try this if you dare.
Well that was a long review wasn't it? I highly recommend buying this, because it's just something you need to experience before your life on this planet ends. I wouldn't personally recommend playing X-2, but as I said earlier in the review: different strokes for different people.

Disclosure:
I have completed this game many times on all platforms, both the original (100%) and the Remastered versions. I have yet to get 100% in the PC version, but I most definitely will get around to it!
TL;DR at the end of this review!
Setting:
Spira is the world in which Tidus - a young athlete is thrown forward, a thousand years in to the future. Lost, scared and homesick, he meets some unlikely friends and a summoner - Yuna. He quickly learns of Sin, a huge mysterious creature that terrorizes Spira and also learns that Spira no longer seeks to further technology but instead casts it asside in favor of the worldwide religion of Yevon. Tidus has two objectives, the first to rid Spira of Sin and second to find a way back to his Spira.
Spira is a lush beautiful world, from colorful seaside resorts to deserts to snowy mountains and thunderous plains. While there is a lot to explore in Spira, the main story will take you on a fairly linear path. There are occasions where you can explore and backtrack at will but most of that will come in the second half of the game. Overall the general design and setting of Spira is unique and beautiful and more importantly - memorable. 9/10.
Gameplay:
The gameplay in Final Fantasy X is reminiscent of the older Final Fantasy ATB turn-based system in which your party and your enemy take it in turns to pick an ability and then execute said ability. Each enemy has it's weakness and its strengths, for instance: some enemies are weak to fire, some to lightning, while others might be strong against standard weapons but weak to piercing weapons.
The game is tactical by design and a lot of success in battle comes down to simply knowing your enemy.
Final Fantasy X comes with some unique changes from previous entries. For instance, summons or "Aeons" are very powerful creatures that are summoned by, you guessed it; Summoner Yuna, they come with a great deal of depth and the game allows you to eventually increase their stats or teach them new abilities. Each Aeon is acquired by completing the "Cloister of Trials" A unique puzzle dungeon at each Temple you visit in your travels through Spira.
Another addition to the series is the "Turn Bar". A unique bar on the top-right of the screen that gives you a clear indication of the order that each character and enemy will execute their turn.
Outside of combat the progression system is fairly easy to understand. It uses the "Sphere Grid" in which you combine "AP" or "Sphere Levels" and "Spheres" to fill the Sphere Grid up and become more powerful. There are several different types of "Spheres", some increase basica stats while others give you abilities or magic. Thankfully the "Sphere Grid" is fairly non-linear and will allow some freedom to progress as you will. When you start a new game you can chose a "Standard" or "Expert" Sphere Grid, the latter makes the game slightly harder by making some abilities harder to get to.
Overall the combat and gameplay in Final Fantasy X is easily one of the best and very rewarding 9/10.
Sound and Voice:
You've probably already heard or seen videos and for the most part they're true. Yes, the voice-acting is ....hit and miss (mostly miss) but it's what they say that really matters for me. Some voice acting actually stands out to me as being well done, specifically the voice acting of "Wakka", "Seymour", "Auron" and "Lady Yunalesca".
Sound effects come as you would expect from a Final Fantasy game with nothing really standing out as extraordinary or bad.
Music is absolutely stellar, with memorable soundtracks throughout. This is Final Fantasy - expect amazing music. Overall, music stands out and carries the sound through and in the end, it will be the thing you remember the most. In addition, the PC port comes with 2 options for music, the original version and the enhanced version. Both are amazing but having the option to choose between both is even more amazing 8/10
Graphics:
A lot of people forget that this game was developed in the late 90s and finished in 2001. That is a good 17 years ago. The world is artistically stunning and it really shows in the PC port. While the game is capped at a drab 30FPS - as long as you aren't playing on a PC made of wood and sadness, you should have no issues with performance. The only noteable difference between this Remastered version and the PS4 version is more variation on graphical settings (via a launcher), an increased texture resolution and higher draw-distance. Simply put, this is the prettiest version there is. The CGI has also been remastered and looks absolutely incredible. The lack of variable framerates really bugs me however so I'm gonna give this a score of 8/10.
Replay Value:
The main story should take around 40-50 hours to complete. If you want to explore, get the Celestial Weapons, fill the Sphere Grid, grab all the treasures, defeat the super bosses and dungeons AND do the mini-games you're going to want to add another 100 hours on to that. You are getting a phenomenal amount of content for your money in this game, 10/10.
TL;DR:
Setting: 9/10
Gameplay: 9/10
Sound & Voice: 8/10
Graphics: 8/10
Value: 10/10
Overall: 9/10 - Must-have for any JRPG or RPG fan!

If you are new to Final Fantasy then this is as good as any game to start with. It has a classic turn based battle system, fantastic artwork, even more fantastic music, beautiful cutscenes, a grand epic story to tell, and a vibrant main cast. I guarantee you will grow attached to at least one of the main cast. There are a few minor flaws such as time-consuming and poorly designed minigames (like the Chocobo ride or collecting butterflies), but all of that is strictly optional.
10/10 Port: Runs smoothly at high framerate, no crashes in 30+ hours, no glitches to be seen. The updated HD art makes the 2001 game look like a 2008 game. The high quality cutscenes haven't aged a day. They hold up extremely well.
The art has very slight issues, notably the main cast is updated to high resolution textures but many of the side characters stay at low polygon count and low res. This leads to side characters looking a bit out of place standing next to the main cast, an issue which wasn't a problem on the original PS2 game where everyone was low res. The same is true for some backgrounds. 2D background art is still gorgeous, but some 3D background items (like trees) look notably poor in HD where they would be too distant and pixelated to pick out flaws on a PS2. Other than that the HD update to the classic is superb, retaining the art style while sharpening it up.
Music is 10/10. Listen for yourself. I recommend the classic soundtrack for new players and the arranged soundtrack for returning veterans since it's fun to hear the same soundtrack done by a different composer.
Gameplay is 10/10. It has the best fight system of all the Final Fantasies IMO. There is no real flaw and the pacing of the fights are also superb. You can have a decent challenge throughout the game if you choose not to grind, and if you want the game to be easier you simply have to spend a bit of extra time in each area overleveling your characters.
You can choose two leveling systems. The Expert Grid gives you the option to fully customize each of your characters, however I high recommend the Classic Grid because it gives each character a role within the party which matches their personalities and backstory (Auron the hard-hitter, Waka the ball sniper, Yuna the white mage, Lulu the black mage). Though it might be fun to spec Lulu into being able to one-shot armored opponents with her doll, it significantly impacts immersion.
If you're just in it for the story there are also built-in cheats that give infinite money, infinite items, etc.
For returning players who are doing multiple play-throughs or grinding to 100% the game, there is also a x4 option which is much appreciated. It speeds up animation for x4 and also speeds up walking by x4, dramatically reducing the time it takes to play the game. You can also choose to set No Encounters, which speeds up walking through.

An incredibly clever hybrid twin-stick shooter and platformer, Rive is good fun. This isn't an arena shooter, it's a decent length campaign with some good level variety, almost always throwing some new gimmick at you. The levels play decently quick, shuffling you from shootout to platforming setpiece to platforming/shootout hybrid easily, and gives the game a decent length with not a lot of downtime. When Rive is working, you'll be swinging from platforming to zero grav classic twin-stick shooting and back and again multiple times in a single segment.
There is nothing to the plot. It feels like a parody that parodied too hard. It is too self-conscious and basically ensures there are no stakes to anything you are doing. Not offensive, and kinda charming at times, but mostly it is off-putting.
Rive in a lot of ways feels like a traditional linear action game than many of the twin-stick games you have probably played recently, focusing on either arcade score chasing or arenas. Score is a factor here, but Rive has a different, more substantial feel than the average twin-stick game.
Rive's platforming is good and the gunplay is strong. It is a fun ride. The fact that Nex Machina has front page hype and Rive is relatively ignored is an utter crime.

Some of the foods are just a little TOO complex, sometimes detracting from the experience a bit. Aside from that though, Cook, Serve, Delicious is a "delicious" little strategy-slash-management simulator which will keep you entertained for a long time.

Right now F1 2017 is just about a month away from release so it'd be better to wait for that.
As for this game it's currently the best in the series AS A GAME. It's got a nice career mode and the practice programmes are really helpful. Not that the programmes give you a good direction on setting up the car or something but they help one in learning the track, practice making consistent laps while saving the tires and the other sets the car up for qualifying. It has a track acclimatization on Baku though.
Technically it's the best looking in the series and it's also a lot more optimized than F1 2015. It fails on the audio department though. OK, the real cars don't sound loud too but in F1 2016 everything sounds so weak and distorted. Raising the engine volume to 10 helps but then it's impossible to understand what the engineer is saying even if the game automatically lowers the engine sound volume whenever he speaks (even with voice volume to 10). I could also raise the volume of the speakers but playing another game afterwards makes my ears blow up. I don't know why the max volume of F1 2016 seems like it's just 1/3 of other games' volumes yet it has the most distorted sound.
For the driving part, I might be alone here but with a T300RS steering wheel I really don't like it. I really prefer how F1 2015 handles over this. In this game the tracks feel like super smooth glass with invisible banana peels all over. The torque of the cars is so unpredictable. The cars don't feel like open wheel cars, they feel more like old muscle cars with turbochargers. F1 must be the most expensive motorsport in the world yet in this game it feels like all teams are too cheap to hire engineers that make driveable engine maps.
Still on the handling, adding more downforce feels like just adding a limit on how fast a car goes. I really couldn't feel the benefit of more downforce on the corners for this game. It's like all corners are always taken at a certain speed regardless of downforce level. Add the terrible feel of the throttle and you've got, without doubt, the best driving simulator if you ascribe to the notion that difficult = simulation. The Formula RaceRoom X-17 car without traction control is easier to drive than this game's cars.
For me F1 2015, IMHO, is a lot better in the physics department.
Again, wait for F1 2017 but if you're deciding if you want to get this game it's just a matter of what you're looking for. If you like gamey elements then F1 2016 is a really good buy. If you're after a Codies F1 game of the turbocharged small wings era that feels good to drive then get F1 2015 instead.

I wanted to love this game. I was all about the gameplay and graphical style. I was excited about the game genres the makers said this fit into. However this game suffers from some creative choices that cause the controls to be needlessly frustrating. As with many games that have 360 degree free shooting and platforming you might find yourself stuck between two control schemes that are at war with eachother. The platforming is very precise except for when it's not, your character almost has too much mobility. That might sound like a silly criticism but what I mean by that is that there is some very punishing "you will die if you don't do this perfectly" platforming like you might find in a Mega Man game. While I certainly did die a lot in battles with the various enemies, which is incredibly fun, but it's the in-between stuff that requires pixel perfect jumping skills with a robot that moves so quickly it's very easy to overshoot and I was never able to get the correct rhythm down. The slightest mistake is punished brutally. There is one particular section that involves killing enemies while hopping on the top of fast-moving trains and it is just straight-up ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Then you finally beat it and then the game immeditately throws more enemies than you can ever hope to kill and they'll knock you back down again or just straight up kill you. It felt like the game just gave me a huge middle finger and I'd just had it. Challenging is one thing but this game is hard for the sake of being hard with endless blind drops of doom, barrages of enemies you can't possibly see coming, it's just too much.
Then I know this is picky but does the protagonist have to talk SO MUCH? Thankfully they have a volume level for the voices because his endless talking to himself starts off as a him pointless saying "I gotta go here, I gotta go there" in a game that is TOTALLY LINEAR. Then later he's making references to Parodius and other classic schmup references, we get it guys YOU LOVE SCHMUPS. But for all of the claims that this game plays like those schumps they're referencing, it really doesn't. This is Megaman with parts that play like micro-versions of levels from Geometry Wars.  Maybe a lot of this frustration could have been alleviated by having couch co-op like Gunstar Heroes or similar but nope, this is a purely single player experience and I think that was a gigantic mistake. If they ever made another game like this which wasn't quite so frustrating and allowed you to play with a friend I would most likely buy it. RIVE has so much going for it but I just can't recommend it.
However you say it a reView for this game will always haVe a V in it

I first bought it directly from steam, and despite having a more than optimal hardware configuration for playing it, an error would appear every time I tried to launch the game. It has really good graphics, nice animations, a challenging AI, and an impressive roster!

An organic 'village/town' builder. This is what Sim City 5/6 should have been like. Steadily advance your fledgling village, one building at a time. Build what you need, when you need it. You can't just plonk buildings down like a mayor on steroids.
I've always been a big Sim City fan and, like many people, I've been bitterly disappointed by the recent reincarnations of Sim City and I was pleased to find Banished. In essence, the game is all about resource management, both in materials and labour. Keep your food stores up and only take from the environment what you can afford to lose in the short and long term. Delegate your work force to the ultimate objective - continuous, sustainable growth.
Its a challenging game that requires you to think about what you want to build, when you should build it, and most importantly, why you should build it. It takes a little time to get used to the game mechanics, but it is incredibly satisfying to build that local school or get that chapel up and running. A great and well thought out game, especially considering it was only made by one guy.
9/10 - Get it if you enjoy your old fashioned Sim City games!

Average story, decent voice acting, repetitive and uninteresting missions and yet I can't not recommend this game.
Why? Two words: Grappling hook.
The fun in this game, primarily, comes from the grappling hook. The grappling hook allows you to quickly traverse terrain, hook on to a vehicle to then hijack it or even use it to tow a vehicle around. You can even jump from vehicle to vehicle and add parachutes to the combo so that you can either hook on to another vehicle or use the momentum from your grappling to parachute higher and further.
The open world of this game is set in the fictional island paradise of Panau and a very large paradise at that. The graphics are quite impressive, particularly in the large mountainous areas or high above the world in an aircraft the view really is great. The range of vehicles is large from cars, motorcycles to various aircraft and boats; using these vehicles to explore the world and wreak havoc is incredibly satisfying.
That brings me to my next point. The destruction. The explosions. The weaponry. Whether it be a handheld gun or one attached to a vehicle, you're going to be causing a lot of damage to Panau. Causing a lot of explosions is satisfying and (other than grappling hooks) is what this game is all about.

If you are new to Final Fantasy then this is as good as any game to start with. It has a classic turn based battle system, fantastic artwork, even more fantastic music, beautiful cutscenes, a grand epic story to tell, and a vibrant main cast. I guarantee you will grow attached to at least one of the main cast. There are a few minor flaws such as time-consuming and poorly designed minigames (like the Chocobo ride or collecting butterflies), but all of that is strictly optional.
10/10 Port: Runs smoothly at high framerate, no crashes in 30+ hours, no glitches to be seen. The updated HD art makes the 2001 game look like a 2008 game. The high quality cutscenes haven't aged a day. They hold up extremely well.
The art has very slight issues, notably the main cast is updated to high resolution textures but many of the side characters stay at low polygon count and low res. This leads to side characters looking a bit out of place standing next to the main cast, an issue which wasn't a problem on the original PS2 game where everyone was low res. The same is true for some backgrounds. 2D background art is still gorgeous, but some 3D background items (like trees) look notably poor in HD where they would be too distant and pixelated to pick out flaws on a PS2. Other than that the HD update to the classic is superb, retaining the art style while sharpening it up.
Music is 10/10. Listen for yourself. I recommend the classic soundtrack for new players and the arranged soundtrack for returning veterans since it's fun to hear the same soundtrack done by a different composer.
Gameplay is 10/10. It has the best fight system of all the Final Fantasies IMO. There is no real flaw and the pacing of the fights are also superb. You can have a decent challenge throughout the game if you choose not to grind, and if you want the game to be easier you simply have to spend a bit of extra time in each area overleveling your characters.
You can choose two leveling systems. The Expert Grid gives you the option to fully customize each of your characters, however I high recommend the Classic Grid because it gives each character a role within the party which matches their personalities and backstory (Auron the hard-hitter, Waka the ball sniper, Yuna the white mage, Lulu the black mage). Though it might be fun to spec Lulu into being able to one-shot armored opponents with her doll, it significantly impacts immersion.
If you're just in it for the story there are also built-in cheats that give infinite money, infinite items, etc.
For returning players who are doing multiple play-throughs or grinding to 100% the game, there is also a x4 option which is much appreciated. It speeds up animation for x4 and also speeds up walking by x4, dramatically reducing the time it takes to play the game. You can also choose to set No Encounters, which speeds up walking through.

Fantastic level design, tons of armor and weapons along with a solid combat system. Dark Souls II doesn't really live up to its predecessor, however it's currently my most-played Steam game and is a must have for anyone who enjoys open-world games or players looking for a challenge. After playing through every game in the Souls series and getting every achievement in DSI and DSII, I don't really understand all the hate for Dark Souls II...
Pros:
- Game runs at a solid 60 FPS on my GTX 960, haven't enountered any crashes or oddly timed lag-spikes in my 200 hours of playtime.
- Massive variety of viable armor and weapons to chose from, different stat builds keep the game refreshing after each play through.
- Tons of people still play it; I have an easy time finding people to summon until I reach level 125 - 150.

Cons:
- Most players you encounter in PVP tend to forget they're not playing Metroid and roll nonstop.

I have compared this game with Battlefield and would like to address why I favour Verdun, should I get a choice of which to play with a friend (and why I think you should pick it ;D)
The main point is realism.
Verdun and Battlefield 1 are both set in WW1, both with varying levels of realism. The better of the two in this case is Verdun. Verdun provides not only a more realistic array of weapons, but also sets up a more authentic atmosphere over all with the anxiety and discomfort everywhere within a trench (while BF1 uses hardly as many trenches as Verdun). The recently added gore and gibs and blood (lovely sights in battle) further add to this effect of the feeling that the player feels like they're actually in the war. In Battlefield 1, there is no such dismemberment and huge amounts of blood anywhere. Battlefield 1 also generally feels way too technologically advanced on part of any country at that time to actually fit it with the authentic WW1 experience.
Bonus points go for:
The price of this game (cheaper than BF1 for sure).
A very "historical" community (a lot of people naming squads after those of their relatives etc.)
An actual trench layout with No Man's Land guaranteed (and little cover for maximum decimation.
Pretty darn good devs and community members in terms of helping you with bugs, for example.
I hope this review helped YOU in making a decision on whether or not to buy this game :)

i've been playing the kof series since it's inception, back in 94. i've always been a fan, and i bought all the games, through the playstation(s) era, all the way up to kofxiii; and i've spent hundreds of hours on kofxiii alone on my ps3.
kof has always been known for it's nice 2d art, and it was epitomised in kofxii, with a reset in the art department; big characters, all beautifully hand drawn. while i did play kofxii a bit (not much to be honest), it felt like an incomplete game. still, the new system was fun, and had me looking forward to kofxiii ... and snk delivered. kofxiii was not only beautiful, it was a great game too.
fast forward to kofxiv. when kofxiv launched on the ps4, i was almost tempted to buy a ps4, and a new stick, just for that ... but i stopped short right there. why? the graphics, was a bit of a turn off. snk had decided to shift to 3d instead, and those who have played the maximum impact series would know, snk isnt really all that great at 3d. that stopped me dead in my tracks, and for a long while, i had kept contemplating if i should actually splurge on a ps4+stick+kof because that would cost me a chunk of money.
so eventually, snk released kofxiv, here, on steam and i thought ... ok, now i have a stick that works fine on pc, and i dont need to buy a new console, so why not~ and thus i plonked down the money for the pre-order/closed beta session ... and ended up spending a ton of time on it as well.
what i'm trying to say really, is that while kof have (regretably) shifted from 2d to 3d in the latest reiteration in the series, it's still a really great fighter. of course, the change of system almost necessitated a change of the combat (albeit, only slightly), but it plays and feels very much like the kof of old (not old old, but the advent of the 'max mode' first introduced in kof99, evolved to much of what we know now in kof2k2, leading into the more elaborate combo strings of kofxiii). over time, it's easy to overlook and forget about the 3d-ness of the game. in fact, comparitively, since snk released the new shaders, kofxiv has looked much better since the launch back then.
more importantly, i've tested online play (primarily in closed beta), i guess it goes almost without saying that it's smooth and without problems when playing with people nearby (e.g. same country), but gets bit laggier for longer distances. you would have to keep in mind that the latency where i'm from isnt all that great, so it's probably much harder for me to call this aspect accurately; although when i was playing it with my friends (within the same country), it was all fine and dandy, went smoothly without any hitches at all.
so yea, as a summary of sorts, graphically, it's not too shabby afterall; but the main ingredients of the game, which is the battles, and the system, is still a great joy, and still brings great fun. not as tough to pick up as a newcomer (as opposed to the guilty gear series), and plenty to learn and master if you want to be competitive. online play is also fairly good for me at least, and being the latest iteration of the game (as of posting at least), there'd be plenty of fights to pick online too.
do pick it up, especially if you're an old kof fan, who was skeptical about the graphical direction of this. you wont even notice it as much once the battles heat up.

Reverse Crawl's title and description don't really create a good representation of what the game is about.  I suppose that's the first thing to say.  Don't buy it if you expect some really unique take on the standard tactical RPG universe.  The narrative quite literally has you going to places that are in the generic sense 'dungeons' and fighting through them for and end goal such as new spells, units, or upgrades.  You aren't “the dungeon” and you're not fighting back against heroes.  The only place you can sort of get that perspective from is that you are most often on the right side of the screen going left rather than the old RPG style that was often the other way around... and perhaps that your characters are sometimes undead while the enemy is usually living.
With that out of the way, I want to move forward saying that Reverse Crawl did appeal to me in a number of ways.  It is a turn based (with initiative) tactical battle system that would quickly be familiar to fans of tactical RPGs worked really well.  On top of that there's a bit of a strategy layer in that you have to pick reasonable counters to the waves of enemies you face in each 'dungeon.'  For instance, if you see that the first wave features magic wielding enemies, you'd want to select from your collection of minion groups (each containing a preset assortment of specific units) one that has a resistance to magic.  Given that you have a set limit each battle for the number of groups you get to place, it's very important that you're aware of this strategic layer.
This is where one of the issues I had with the game presented itself.  It throws you right in to combat and spends the majority of the game explaining some of the mechanics and rulesets as you approach them.  This generally isn't a problem, but it seems to fall short in explaining all of the elements of the game.  It doesn't really tell you what the benefit of picking one particular dungeon in each chapter is over another, or how it will affect what you can do going forward – which leaves me picking each one based on just whatever sounds mildly interesting and hoping the reward is actually something I wanted.  I don't find myself wondering if I missed anything or if I would have had a different experience as much as I'm just curious why there's a selection at all if my random choices didn't seem to have an impact on the gameplay or story.  Also, I still have no idea what the Hall of Champions is or does.
Reverse Crawl doesn't have a lot that makes it stand out visually, but the music is actually pretty solid and I found it, at times, getting me pretty amped up for some battles.  Not a lot of indie games do that, so I will commend the developer for his choice in soundtrack. The sound effects are truly baseline, but I don't think they are a detriment to the overall experience.
What you end up with here is a game that, while flawed in a few areas, still made a positive impression on me.  Even with a simple story and fairly easy gameplay to master, I found it enjoyable throughout my four hours of gameplay.  Though, while it does offer replayability and perhaps different endings from the 'paths' you can take, I don't believe I'll get back in to it.  But for its small base price tag and extremely small sale price tag, it's a great value.  It's another proven instance of Gamemaker letting people contribute in a positive way to game development.
