First things first, most of the poor reviews for this game are from hardcore racing game fans. this review is from the point of view of someone who has almost never played a racing game before. with that said, i can safely say that the crew is actually a pretty good game.
The story is a little short with me having beat the campaign in a little under 18 hours (over the cource of about 5 days with ocasional side quests to level up my cars a bit before the next race), however the game offers some replay value in that you can go back to any mission you have done and replay it, though the rewards dont change for beating it at a higher level unless you've reached level 50 and unlocked platinum parts, in which case its worth going back and re-doing some missions.
The "skills" are a touch annoying in that if you accidentaly trigger one while driving about you either need to open your phone and choose abort, open the map to auto abort it, or just let it time out.
The game also claims to be MMO, but i played the entire campaign in solo mode because i couldnt find anyone to coop with, instead just getting an error that coop failed because there is no one in my session and in general only actually passing other players on the road a coupple of times every so often.
In general, i did enjoy the story and the game as a whole and ill continue to play it to complete the challenges, skills and the factions missions you unlock after reaching new york. If you havnt played any racing games before, this is quite a good one to start with, BUT i would not reccomend buying this at full price. wait for a sale and get it then.
i will say that i haven't noticed any problems with "rubber banding AI" or undestructable cops, but thats just me and i also haven't had the game crash on me (yet)

[Warning: Long Review]
Seeing as Grimrock 1 is my favourite dungeon crawler, I got very excited when this sequel was announced. Unfortunately, my graphics card was kinda broken, so the game kept crashing when I attempted to play it. Booo. Now though, I have finally found a graphics card and the time needed to play it. So I booted the game, put the game on old-school hard difficulty, brought out my notebook with chequered paper and crashed my ship.
With that said, a party of adventurers washed up upon the Isle of Nex. They were:
In the top left: "Goat C", the minotaur barbarian. She smashes things with the heaviest weapons available and is being kept alive by carrying the heaviest armour available. Does a lot of damage to everything, but is slow and prone to missing enemies right in front of her.
In the bottom left: "Harry", the insectoid wizard. She casts spells that, if elemental weaknesses apply, wreck enemies dead in no time - until she runs out of mana. Unfortunately, Harry decided to put one point in each magic school to test all low-level spells, so she can't use the more powerful ones until later, which requires a LOT of skill points. If she could start over again, she would wait with assigning skill points until said powerful spells were found.
In the bottom right: "Elizabeth", the lizardman alchemist. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ alchemist is so stronk! The whole party would have died many times over if not for Elizabeth. Apparently her backpack is magical, because inside of it potion ingredients multiply! Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥that is so broken. So, Lizzy keeps the party alive and fuels Harry's destructive powers. Also she slings rocks and darts at the enemies basically dealing zero damage.
...and in the top right I have inserted myself into my fantasy journey: "Brunkuhrskrunkuhr II", son of "Brunkuhrshkrunkuhr   I", one of the survivours of Grimrock I. I am a ratling farmer. When I read the description for the farmer class (no xp from kills, only xp from picking locks and eating food, starts with no skills) I thought; "damn! This is the definition of a joke class! And since it's a joke class, it'll probably be insanely powerful late-game!" One thing I remembered from Grimrock 1 was that I never ever was in any shortage for food, ever, so I would probably reach level cap in no time!  And it seemed I was right; "Brunkuhrskrunkuhr II" soon leveled far beyond his companions, mastering light weapons and light armours. But then something happened while I was deep inside a dark, damp dungeon with dastardly demons delivering deadly deliveries... I ran out of food.
Grimrock II is substantially more difficult than the first game. Enemies are faster, have more health, deal more damage and above all else are smarter = exploiting the square grids on which the game is based is harder. So one has to think more strategically, observe enemy patterns and weaknesses, then deliver the hurt. To exemplify: there is an insanely fast mosqito swarm you can't outrun that deals unholy amounts of damage, but it dies in one hit to the first fire spell you find. There's sentient rocks that take pathetic amounts of damage from physical attacks...unless you get a critical hit. Overall, the enemies are well-designed and challenging.
Grimrock II lacks one thing from it's predecessor - cohesivness. Where in Grimrock 1 you finish everything on one floor, then move to the next, solve the puzzles there, slay the giant trolls, then move to the next floor, etc. while always being in the same, huge dungeon, here the maps are more of a patchwork of different enviroments, with some puzzles extending over several maps and the maps having several exits in all three dimensions. So while in the first game you always knew where you were heading, this game requires a lot more exploration. It's kind of like a Metroidvania game. I want to get to the big castle. To do that I require 4 keys. One is on Sleet Island. How do I get onto sleet Island? I get a hint that the answer is in the cemetery. How do I get into the cemetary? I get a hint that the answer is in the archives. How do I get in the archives? I need to cast a long-range spell to extend a bridge that isn't ice spikes, like fireball! Where do I find fireball? In the dungeon you get to by extending said bridge! FUUUUU- So while I like Grimrock II for trying a different approach, I feel that much of the wholeness of the original game goes lost. And the farmer class would be much more OP if I knew where I was going and didn't waste food by walking everywhere.
While Grimrock 1 had deliberately extremely minimal graphics, with every wall looking the same, Grimrock 2 is substantially more diverse and at times beautiful. So +1 to graphics. However, it does lead to ridiculous circumstances as where I cannot cross a small patch of grass because in gameplay it's the same as a solid rock wall.
The puzzles are still decent, basically more of the same. Some are bad, like the aforementioned bridge-extnding that requires you to put points into skills you don't want. Some are dull, like looking for hidden buttons on the identical walls. Some are decent, like trying to time dropping a giant spider so it stays trapped at the right spot and doesn't come out to kill you. Some are good, like attempting to decipher treasure maps and codes. ...and some are traps. Allow me to quote my notes: "This is a trap if I've ever seen one." "Itsatrap! Jumpscurz" and one that made me smirk: An alcove in the wall containing a powerful magical book placed over a closed trapdoor with a sign next to it reading: "I dare you."
I'm writing this review inside a dark dungeon where I have repeatedly died trying to kill the same enemies in order to get the coode to the archives, where my provisions have run dry (because I ate all the food) and Harry is starving. I'm torn between continuing to push forward or to shamefully backtrack to the surface to catch some fish. As we sit in the flickering light of our single, failing torch and not even Goats stoic expression can hide her despair, when our legs be broken from jumping into pits, when my hand-dawn maps are incomplete and we hear the monsters endlessly crawling around us I gush and exclaim: "I Love Grimrock!"
Then we're off to die again.
-
Edit: I have now finished the game, finally. Both endings. It took a long time, since I tried to find most secrets (but failed, ♥♥♥♥ing pixel hunts) and, you know, drew my own maps. I just have to say it's a shame games this good aren't being made as often. The feeling of adventure, the atmosphere of exploration, the intense battles... 10/10 would recommend, "like dungeon crawling meets the Myst series."

This game is very crafty and all of the spawns, from rooms to what you spawn with, are randomized. The game very quickly teaches you to be cautious, ranging from punishing you for running into a room without looking into it first, to immediately being rammed in the side with a drone with no way to counter against it.
How enemies spawn is randomized, and sometimes a bunch of turrets will be spawned in such a way that you'll need to tactfully take out each one before you can move on, and sometimes it'll cluster 5 turrets in one room.
To keep you on your toes, how quickly you can react to turrets seeing you varies, ranging from being able to be seen by a turret for a full second and not die, to being shot the instant you enter their field of vision.
Additionally, it seems how durable the robots are is also randomized. For example, sometime's you'll take out 4 enemies with one shot each, and sometimes you'll have to dump 10 bullets into a turret's weakpoint before it stops moving.
What you spawn with is randomized, which means sometimes you can spawn with a revolver and 30 bullets, and sometimes you'll spawn with a M1911A1 and 4 bullets.
Where you spawn is also randomized. Sometimes you'll spawn in a room full of ammo and maybe a tape and/or flashlight, and sometimes you'll spawn in direct view of a turret.
Don't get me wrong, this is a great game, it's just that if you're purchasing this, prepare for RNGesus to kick you in the butt. A lot.

I love this game.  I love it very much.  Not everyone will love it, but it's not the sort of game that cares about those folks.  It's a reasonably challenging game with some of the most respectable riddles of any RPG I've ever played.  The combat is great, definitely more polished over the first game and strikes a nice balance between rewarding strategy, improvisation, and speed.  The world is nicely fleshed out with lots of attention to detail.  The designs are not extravagent or particularly novel, but they're not meant to be.  This is a classic fantasy game in many respects.
But the core of why I love Legend of Grimrock is really how much it respects the intelligence of the player.  It expects you to use your brain, and it rewards you for paying attention.  It has some flaws with minor mechanics - but nothing that will plague your game experience.  As a whole, it's just a satisfying 20 hours.

I think what we have here is a well designed sim game that is more of a precise button mashing extravaganza than an actual game. There are plenty of features, but it comes off as rather tedious and at times frustrating.

You set your menu, make some food (which is basically intense button mashing on a timer), then you get the happy hour rush and button mash faster, and then eventually the day ends. You feel tired, you feel bored, and you feel annoyed. Having worked in the service industry before, I can tell you, this delivers a true-to-life experience. The only way it could be more real is if you were sweaty, covered in food, and sleep deprived... Maybe we have to wait for the Oculus Rift version...
Anyways, you have to hit each food order's buttons precisely and it turns out to be a rather frustrating experience. The game looks like a tough casual game, but it's far from it. Eternal is a game unlike any other before, combining elements from the classical trading card game Magic: The Gathering, as well as some elements from the rapidly popular Hearthstone, Eternal is a wonderful fusion of classic TCG gameplay brought into the new digital age. Unlike HS, Eternal generally leans away from RNG elements, prefering to use the online platform to implement mechanics that would be impossible to track in a paper card game. Eternal stays true to the formulaic gameplay of MtG, having five colours of resource, and needing to have colored resource cards in your deck, as well as limiting cards based on said resource. All in all, if you enjoyed any TCG or OCG, Eternal is a wonderful unique experience and it absolutel is one for you!

I rarely write reviews for games, but I felt I had to for this one.
As a TCG/CCG junkie, I have never been this hooked on a digital card game before. This game has just enough MtG in it to feel familar with enough new mechanics to feel new. The balance between interruption/stack is very well done, allowing smooth gameplay like Heathstone with meaningful controlled choices. Deck building is top notch and allows for a lot of creativity. For new players, there is a lot of free cards to be had and the game does a great job of making you feel like you get cards at a fast pace. Eventually the dwindles out, but in doing so it is gently pushing you towards drafting (which is the most efficient use of your gold).
No game is perfect mind you, but these downsides are not a big enough deal to stop me from coming back day after day. The most glaring ones are that the power system still needs some tweaks (think mana from MtG) and there are too few options when it comes to competative decks. Hopefully both of these will be fully or parially solved with the introduction of set 2.

I used to play wrestling games on the N64 and I haven't liked any of the newer ones I had tried, but I heard 2k16 was supposed to go back to the roots and try to make a better experience.  I personally didn't have any good experiences with it. First, when it is in full screen I still have a bar visible on the top and one side of the screen, it is annoying, but not a big deal.  For me the worst part of the game is the wrestling. It feels like the entire combat is based on reversals. The reversal system requires you to press a button at exactly the right time to reverse the move. It sounds ok, but by the time the indicator shows up to press the button it is too late if you try to anticipate it coming up it will say you pressed it too early.  This makes it very hard to successfully get a reversal and can mean you spend the entire fight trying to get a reversal or lose. My first match I only got one or two hits in the entire fight. Which, leads me to another issue there is no tutorial or training mode. Well, there is a tutorial, but you need to use a create a wrestler to do it, and there is no way (that I know of) to go through it again other than creating another new campaign. While you can make your own matches to practice with there is no dedicated training room like other fighting games have.  The pinning system is also very annoying. A wheel will pop up and start filling up you have to press a button to stop it while it is in a specific zone to kick out it sounds easy, but it goes so fast it is very hard. Now I've read a lot about the reversal and pinning issues online and most people seem to think you just need to keep playing to get used to the timing, well I didn't get to that point when I had a (for me) game breaking bug.
I made a create a hero started doing the campaign and very shortly after I had an issue where it failed to save or let me load a save.  I tried every suggestion I found online except completely reinstalling (because if it happened once whats to stop it from happening again?) with no luck.  While looking online I saw someone lost a save with over a hundred hours on it. Fortunately, I only lost about an hour or so, but if this is happening to other people and with far more time invested than me, why should I or anyone else put time into it when we could lose it all to a bug that there is no known way to fix or prevent? Even if I could get adjusted to the reversal and pin system I cannot recommend a game that can randomly corrupt a save that people have put hours into.

I originally saw this on sale and had the words "walking simulator" and "adventure" and "sci-fi" jump out at me, all things which I'm a fan of, so I figured at 99c I probably couldn't complain either way no matter how it turned out. I didn't read any further on it beyond the general positive score, and, boy, am I glad that's as much digging as I did. This really is a game that benefits from some blissful ignorance before going into it, save for maybe the fact that it's pretty much completely devoid of conflict of any kind and is instead based mostly on "purpose". At least in as much as you have a role to play and a function to fulfil and that will pretty much be the extent of the gameplay.
You awake on the titular station and are immediately given a test on your mental state and told to perform it again every 30 days. You are then given the task of maintaining the station's plant and tree life for future endeavours and to also check them every 30 days. What follows is the strange juxtaposition of tasks of tedium among a spectacular setting... basically a janitor in space. There's more to it than that, as you'll explore the handful of rooms that make up the station and read various log entries, but all that is best left to your own discovery.
I know it sounds like a total non-event, but I promise you there's more to it than that.
It kind of reminded me of the classic '60s TV show The Prisoner. It was weird and never really explained itself and by the end you probably had more questions about everything than answers, but still thoroughly enjoyed your time with it the whole way. That was definitely my experience with it.
The only complaint I'd probably have is I was left wanting more. Sniffing around every inch of the station to try finding new things to see or possibly interact with took up the lion's share of my hour or two with this title, and I do wish it could have been eked out to something longer and the concept expanded upon. But otherwise, the brief time I spent is something that still managed to have great impact and will stay with me for a while, and I strongly recommend you take the time with it, too.
Oh, I just remembered... the safe word is Verde Station.

Gone Home is a game that, at first, resembles a modern mediocre horror game. While it's not horror, it sure struggles to go beyond mediocre.
It's pure exploration and nothing else. You walk around a house, look at stuff, examine some things more closely and occasionally hear voices. It's these voice-overs, that tell the story, with other examinable things fleshing some things out a bit, but are not necessary to understand what's going on.
And that's the entire game. As such, the quality of the game mainly depends on the story. And... it's not very good. The story itself is short, pretty lacking and feels undeveloped. The characters are uninteresting and not very sympathetic. And then there are certain themes it deals with, which is what Gone Home made so popular. And it's rather puzzling why. The way it deals with them is pretty shallow and unremarkable. Terrible fanfiction I read over ten years ago had deeper exploration of these themes than this game.
There's also a subplot, that's actually kinda interesting, but of course it's even more underdeveloped than the main story and as such ultimately unsatisfying.
The portrayal of a home in the 90's is pretty good and if you have fond memories of the 90's, it can give you nice dose of nostalgia. But that's not enough to carry the game.
The presentation is pretty okay. The graphics are nothing to write home about, but are certainly not bad. And the music is pretty nice.
Gone Home asks for a lot and gives very little in return. Even with the reasons why it got so famous in mind, it's hard to see how it ever became so popular. It can be interesting, but not enough to pay lots of money for it. I'd say $5 at most and even that is pretty high for it.

In all honesty, I didn’t know what to expect going into this game. I knew it was a first-person exploration game from the trailer on steam, but that was all I could expect from it.  I have played quite a few first person shooter games in my time as well as horror games.  The entire game had me on edge, I was expecting something to pop out at me the whole time.  On the contrary, nothing popped out.  In fact, nothing happened at all, ever.  All I did was walk around the house and picking up stuff to fill in the story.  I did enjoy this aspect of the story.  However, when I opened a secret room off the front room and found the Ouija board I was quite surprised.  That for me was probably the scariest part of the game.  I was also surprised when I found the secret passages in the house, that was a twist for me.  Though it was convenient for navigation because there was no run mechanic.
I did think that the game was a good method/ strong example of diegetic storytelling.  I felt that the revelation of the story through objects was great and something that could be utilized in more games.  I felt a sense of accomplishment when I would pick up certain objects and it would trigger vocal responses letting me know I was progressing in the story.  I thought it was a nice break being able to listen to my sister’s voice as I continued exploring.  However, I was confused at the end when the journal opened, I was confused why I wasn’t able to see what was in the journal.  It wasn’t until class that I figured out the voice I was hearing were entries in the journal I opened at the end. I’ve been playing Bloodborne and practically all of that games story is revealed through reading object description and speculating about what things mean.  So I did think this way of storytelling was great.  It really made me feel immersed in the world.  I also enjoyed the different type of object descriptions.  How when the curser was over my sister’s pornographic magazine displayed “Gosh, Sam” rather than “Magazine”.  I felt that it portrayed more emotion rather than just stating a verb.

I have spent 18 hours to finish this game. It is a boring game. Especially at the begining and then in the middle and aproaching the end.
Why?
Because it is a real-time simulator, so if fueling up the plane takes 15 minutes and it's an only plane in your airport, you have to wait 15 minutes doing almost nothing else.
It is an Airport ground worker simulator. You drive a set of vehicles around - to the plane, and back to the garage (or rather a spot where you leave the vehicle).
The problem is when you have to use the same vehicle on two planes, apparently you can't have another one (despite loads of them on the airport), you have to use the same one, so either you will be late to the second plane or cheating.
As you progress, you automate the gate operations. Soon you will realize that there is a growing queue of planes. Don't worry there can't be more than five waiting. Annoyingly, that queue of planes has the engines on all the time so whizz of jet engines will be constant till the end of the game.
An annoying thing is that the cargo vehicle is not automated. Or maybe it was intentional. Cargo is the only skill/arcade part of this game that requires youy to accurately position the vehicle. Also the cargo carrier is the only vehicle that has some moving parts (apart from passenger tunnel but that's not really a vehicle).
Also, bugs! Lot's of them. Planes without shadows. Especially one cargo plane where you see the cargo moving inside as cargo container has shadow, but plane doesn't. One of the planes catches the stair vehicle. (use the cargo one to free it up).
Automation, once automated, you cannot help the workers but only watch them drive to the planes at snail's pace.
Really, the only 'fun' part of the game are dad jokes in the description of vehicles used on service the gates.
I finished it, so you don't have to.

I would like to start off with the biggest reason I even recommend this game is because it is the closest thing we PC gamers have to Midnight Club L.A.
I love and hate this game!
What is does right, it does right! What is does wrong, it really does it wrong!
I will only list the things wrong and missing in the game. It has everything else in my opinion!
1. This is possibly the biggest one for me and I don’t really know why! The side and rearview mirrors don’t work! WHAT THE HELL WERE THEY THINKING! Almost every racing game has working mirrors!
Racing games on mobile, last gen systems even the PS2 AND PS1 racing games had working mirrors!
This seriously needs to be fixed!
2. Not enough races or race types! There are plenty of street challenges… -_-
There are so few races that I forget I’m playing a RACING GAME sometimes!
3. Damage on cars are overdone in some places and underdone in others!
If I hit a leaf, my whole front end looks like I hit a tree at 200mph! But glass wont break or even crack even if I roll my car! This just seems lazy!
4. Textures look good on your cars and most of the environments. It’s not what you would expect from a next gen graphics game, but they look good. And with the size and scope of the game I would think they look amazing! Where is the bad? EVERY SINGLE PEDESTRIAN CAR AND THE PEDESTRIANS WALKING DOWN THE STREET! I have seen better textures on the PS2! I swear I am not exaggerating! They look horrible!!!
I can’t even begin to figure out why they thought this was OK!
5. Now on to the little things. No neon lights. Why is this a big deal? It is and isn’t. I like neon’s, what can I say? But in a game that is supposed to be an MMO, you need to have more customization!
6. No window tints.
7. Very limited on body parts.
8. The game has a lot of rims to choose from, but 90% of them all look the same!
9. Cant paint parts different colors.
10. The performance parts system is kind of wack! Look it up on YouTube.
11. Not a lot of cars to choose from. But at least they had my Skyline!
12. Its structured as a F2P type game. Now that wouldn’t be such a problem if it weren’t for the fact that they are selling it for $60. Plus I have played some F2P racing games that felt more complete than this game that had WORKING MIRRORS! (Sorry, but I’m not going to ever let that go till they fix it).
At any rate, the game is fun, not worth what I paid, but fun.
Buy it on a sale, a BIG sale! Anything over $20 is way too much! But if you really want to play a game that kind of reminds you of Midnight Club L.A. then this is the game for you….Kind of.. -_-
So yes I recommend it, even though is sucks!

While I do recommend this game please understand that most of the bad reviews are true and should be taken into consideration when purchasing.  I bought this game knowing what I was getting into and wow was some of it terrible.
Setup:
It took me 40 minutes to even get the game to let me map my wired Xbox 360 controller.  It required me to restart after every key otherwise it wouldn't save the key mapping.  That isn't the worst part about the controls though.
Controls:
The worst part is the fact that the game doesn't take an analog reading for the joystick.  What this means is any direction you turn no matter how little it jumps 100% in that direction making this game a fishtailing mess.  In game menus require you to use the keyboard because the make the 4 different menus in the game require different buttons and a controller only has one D-pad.
Cops:
The cops are pretty dumb, if you drive in a straight line the cops will magically be able to drive as fast as you and you will never lose them.  As soon as you make a few quick turns they are lost.  The chopper is the same way as the cop cars.  I wish they used spike strips and strategic placements in the cities rather than the boring same way every time to get rid of the cops.
Civilians:
There is a decent amount of traffic (sometimes on a rare occasion I can't find a car for miles) and it is randomly generated.  The only problem is it is randomly generated in groups.  So rather than a car here and there it will be 20 cars taking up all the lanes then a 1/4 mile of no cars.  This gets annoying with the controls as mentioned earlier.
Audio:
I am using a high end sound card with a nice Sennheiser headphones in this game and all I have to say is the cars do sound different from one another but they sound boring; with the exception of a few cars.  All the cars sound like they run really poor when at idle.  They make horrible ping noises and run rough it is kind of funny.  The tires make the same screeching noise whether they are on asphalt or dirt.  I will say the pedestrians have very good placement and freak me out every time because I think someone is sitting next to me.
Graphics:
This game looks like it’s from and Xbox 360.  Seriously it looks pretty poor and the attention to detail on things like no functioning review mirror or side mirrors is just sad.  I play in 4k on ultra-settings on two 660 FTW and an i5 @ 4.4 GHz and I will say both GPU's are pinned at 100% and CPU is around 70%.  So it's not very efficient, BF4 runs better on the same ultra-settings.  With that said I don't ever have any dips below 30 FPS it is always running smooth so I guess that is good.  Just realize this game is only around 14 GB which is incredibly small for a game with such a large map.  This goes to show you how low res the textures in the game are.
Map:
Everyone talks about how awesome the map is; this is the reason I bought the game.  Let me say the map is larger than any game I've played.  With that said there are only a few cities and the rest is just a highway attaching states so it is much smaller than I anticipated.  With that said I have much to see with 30+ hours of playing at the time of writing this.  I put this game on an SSD and it was the best game you could ever put on an SSD.  After seeing complaints about how slow all the constant loading screens are and moving in the map I have not had this problem.  Everything happens within a second or so.
Racing:
Look the story line may be terrible but it is definitely bearable and I enjoy it being there.  There just isn't much motivation to complete it other than to unlock tuning shops that are only useful once.  Leveling up is done much faster on PVP races even if you come in last every race.  The parts you win are no different than any other short challenge scattered across the map.  Speaking of skill challenges, there are about 5 different challenges and you just do the same thing over and over but in a different area.  It's the exact same problem with the main story as well.  Yet I still find myself going back and completing them in between story missions.    The biggest problem I have with this game is when you hit level 50.  That is the top level you can reach and it unlocks the ability to get special parts in any skill challenge.  The problem is I can go back to a skill level 1 challenge and win the same part on a skill level 50 challenges that is way harder.
Conclusion:
Look this review has been super negative about the game yet I still recommend it.  The reason is because I am playing it about 8 hours a day since I got it.  Even with all of these issues I still enjoy seeing all of the ugly scenery and driving around in all of the terrible driving cars.  So if you can live with all of the issues mentioned above I recommend the game on a sale like the way I got it.  I do not recommend it at $60.  I wish they would have split the US into 3 sections and charged $60 per-section.  It sounds crazy but with a higher budget and a year in between each section the game could have been so much more.  The map would be the same size but California wouldn't have been cut off at Sacramento and the “Mountain States” wouldn’t be empty along with all of the problems plaguing the game would be fixed.

Yupp, the same problem most people dropped MtG - either you have no resources, or you have only resources. i have easily had a game where I draw 3 sigils (resource cards), 1 creature and 4 sigils. And that's playing 45 card deck :D So yeah, there you have it - it's pretty cool, until all your progress gets wiped away, because you draw 10 sigils.  Therefore this is also easily the most frustrating card game I have EVER played. You can take a "mulligan", but even with that it gets ridiculously, insanely, epicly frustrating, when you just keep drawing those sigils. OR play 15 turns (yes, 15) with 3 resources. even when playing mtg online I didn't get such mana floods I'm seeing here. THIS IS WHY PEOPLE LEFT MTG AND WENT TO HEARTSTONE! Come on, guys!!! I'd Still recommend this game, but I'm a TCG fan and i doubt average player would enjoy it.

Let me start off by saying that Eternal is a great game. Any criticisms I have about it should be taken with the consideration that I love this game.
Eternal takes the aesthetics and game speed of Hearthstone and combines it with the strategic depth and mana systems of Magic and Hex. It may be bias because I play and love paper Magic but I feel like I am more often in control of the outcome of a game in Eternal than I am with Hearthstone.
There are a couple things I'd change to make this game even better, however:
1) If not all modes, at least one game mode should have a best-of-3 with sideboard match. A lot of the cards seem like they were made with this in mind, and it would allow certain deck archetypes to flourish as they would be able to sideboard for bad match ups. Perhaps a BO3 game mode with gold buy-in and gold pay-outs or something similar.
2) I think if you're going to enforce the 1/3 deck power rule in order to allow for the mulligan always getting 2-5 power, your starting hand should also always get 2-5 power. Sometimes mulligans don't feel like a choice (as they should) and when you're forced to mulligan due to 0 power and you mulligan into a hand that is terrible for a different reason (too MUCH power?), and then play out a game that was decided because of that garbage mulligan, it's a real feel bad moment.
3) I'd also like to see an option to bluff instant speed responses at all times, rather than only when you have them. I understand this was a shortcut taken to speed up games, so I can accept that this might not happen. Being able to respond to attachments would be cool, too, but I know that was a step taken to make them playable vs removal.
4) The ranking system should be tweaked. As it is now, I believe there's a hidden MMR rating that matchmaking uses in lieu of using your ladder rank. This means that even if you're in silver rank on the ladder, if your MMR (which carries from previous seasons) is high you'll get paired with diamond/master players. This means it gets progressively harder each season to ladder. Additionally, end-of-season rewards are based on where you ended, not your peak--so if you made it to diamond but then dropped back to gold because of a bad streak, too bad. This actually DISCOURAGES continuing to play if you've reached diamond and are a borderline gold/diamond player.
Overall, great work from the folks at Direwolf. I know and love a lot of the names involved with development from my Magic life, and it's good to see that those players are able to translate their skills into a solid, strategic game.

Alright kiddies, lets talk about Receiver.  This is a gun porn game. You get bullets, you get a gun.  That's it. One hit, and you die.  You've got two enemies, stationary turrets and flying tazers. You're dropped in this tower complex and have to find eleven cassettes to unleash your mind powers and finish the game.
The plot doesn't matter.  This is a gun porn roguelite with gunporn and swat gameplay.  Its simple and low overhead, but high concept.  You're going to check corners, sprint erratically (none of that 360 no scope ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t), and will start praying that the next set of rooms you encounter will have more bullets or clips. You can die from fall damage, you will risk falling to make a running leap for those bullets. You will crouch around corners to kill those turrets with three shots to their base. You will dip around corners to try and take out their sensors to save those precious rounds for later.  Those bullets are all that stand between you and oblivion at the hands of the enemy. Your psychic powers will make them glow like manna from heaven. You will take every spare second to load every spare bullet into a clip. After every engagement, you will check your gun and your ammo and make sure you don't spend the last free moments of your miserable existence frantically trying to load bullets in a clip while a hovedrone closes in for the kill on your enormous head.
You are also going to fail, a lot.  But many of you like that, and it can be very satisfying to clear half a level only to fail in a hail of gun fire or miss that ledge for those precious shiny bullets.

Coming from Hearthstone, which was my first true CCG. I have no Magic background, but holy hell, this game is amazingly fun. I have not been this sucked into a CCG since, well, Hearthstone's early days, since now it's just aggro/pirate nonsense all the time over there. I'm not a great draft player, but I do really enjoy Gauntlet as a way to test new decks and Forge I've had more success with than Draft, probably because of the more limited options.
Although I've dropped some money on the game, if you plan on playing completely F2P it doesn't take that long to build a decent budget list, and there are tons of resources out there online (NumotGaming and RNG Eternal are probably the best right now). Keep at Gauntlet and Forge to get new cards/packs before attempting Ranked and Draft, and it shouldn't take that long to start climbing if that's what you're aiming for (solely based on experience, but you can play however you like!). There are already a huge variety of deck options ranging from
aggro/control/midrange/combo/burn, and each deck really feels quite unique (even the aggro decks don't always feel like pure aggro, there are lots of decisions to be made), and cards can always be substituted or replaced as necessary depending on your collection.
I do think the blocking system can be worked on a bit more, especially in terms of explaining it to new players coming from games such as Hearthstone where this isn't actually a thing. The game has a bit more of a learning curve than HS, unless you are coming from an MTG background.
That being said, I plan on continuing to support this game throughout the rest of the open beta and into release, and already its numbers are on the rise. You should do the same!

In Rive you explore an abandoned spaceship full of robots that want to kill you. There are multiple areas that change as you go back to them.
In between areas you return to a room with a teleporter and an upgrade station where you can spend the credits you earned to upgrade your tank. There are two direct upgrades, armor and pickup range, and four different special attacks that are more side-grades than upgrades. The teleporter brings you to the area you are supposed to do next; you don't get to chose.
Each area has a few more parts: Exploring the area with a bit of platforming and the occasional robot wave, A huge battle, and a boss, Some of them have platforming segments where you are running from lava or something.
The battles are where the game shines. They each take place in a very distinct environment that keeps them fresh. For example, one is on a high-speed train. One is in a Tetris game where you can get crushed by falling pieces, one is in a collapsing arena.
The bosses are decent, but it seems like they are in the game just because every other game has bosses.
Overall, if you enjoy twin-stick shooters this is a great one.
EDIT: Beat the game, went to try the "battle arenas". It says "To access battle arenas hit the follow button on the community hub" The feels really scummy to me, locking part of the game behind a follow. It left a bad taste in my mouth, but not enough to not recommend the game.

My love for F1 has sort of died recently. I used to watch Formula 1 every damn time it was on until around about 2012. I still occasionally watch F1. But what I do more? Play F1 games. Sure, they are the same most of the time, with the major differences being graphics or functions you can change around in your car.
I have played F1 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2016. I decided to skip 2013-2015 as I haven't heard great things about those. But I can honestly say F1 2016 is the BEST game out of all F1 games. It does more than improve the formula of the series, it adds much more stuff, for instance career is back after not being in 2015 (possibly 2014 and 2013 idk) and it's superb, you now have agents to help you with certain stuff, and it really gives F1 2016 a realistic feel to it, even better so is the superb graphics and use of mo-cap. The graphics are brilliant, and you can see the emotes of people in what really feels like the true next-gen F1 game.
The controls are smooth, you can communicate with your engineers (You can also tell them to ♥♥♥♥ off, which is hillarious). The rival system is a nice addition. The tests you take in Practice really feel like they do good for your vehicle, as you get results and points which you can use for Research and Development in which you improve the engine, the traction, controls, and others. It's great.
I cannot say much for multiplayer as I have decided to skip it, though I have heard great things about it.
Overall I recommend if you want a F1 game then get F1 2016, or wait for F1 2017 and see what they have done with that as that releases very soon. Though if you want a F1 game right now, then buy F1 2016, you won't regret it. Heck if you just want a racing game then buy this, it's extremely fun, though is a bit more limited compared to other racing games, but also remember this is a game that sticks true to Formula 1, not trying to be it's own thing completely.

I must be one of the few people in the world to have gotten all the way to 2016 without playing Gone Home - or really being spoiled about it. I'm glad I was. This is a unique experience.
Being the cheapskate I am, I'll admit I didn't pick up Gone Home at full price. I can't remember what sale or bundle I got it in, but I never got around to even installing it, which isn't unusual for me. One day, bored of the usual, I installed it to see 'what the fuss was about'. It probably sat on my desktop, unclicked, for about two or three months. Last night, even more bored of the usual, I launched it.
What I'd heard - or rather, vaguely remembered - about the game was that it was a favorite of LGBTQ community members and friends; that it involved a house and exploring it... and that was about it. What I expected was a game, I guess perhaps an adventure game, which isn't my preferred genre - what I found was a heartening, moving, beautifully created interactive experience.
I won't spoil, but this may not be the game you're expecting. It projects a feeling of mystery and potential fear, but that anxiety, that expectation, may be from within you. Gaming has conditioned us to feel a certain way about darkened houses, loud thunderstorms, and vaguely creepy settings. What gaming hasn't done much - but Gone Home illustrates this beautifully - is create human, emotional stories that draw you in, take you on a journey, and perhaps even change you by the end. I was captivated by Gone Home. Explore every nook and cranny and the house will take you somewhere very special.

So far I love this game! It is absolutely something I've wanted for a long time, a sequel-like game to one of my childhood favorites Freedom Fighters. The main premesis and even the whole atmosphere of the game screams FF while still giving new breath to the whole setting by making it more of an open world version that allows you to do make decisions more thoughtfully rather than linearly. I am 100% certain that unless something out of the ordinary happens, I will 100% Full Complete this game just because I like it that much. This game seems like The Division but with more meaningful story driven direction. Rather than just stumbling upon events and participating, you can choose to finish missions/quests in an order that may help the make doing another mission/quest easier which provides incentive to prioritize in order to be most effective/efficient. I also like the mixture of the typical FPS shooter gameplay that also fits seemlessly into a hide&sneek as I like to call it (think Splinter Cell). I should also not forget to mention that just like FF, you can recruit people to fight with you, albiet only 3 others to make a 4 person squad including you, but still, it's a really cool feature to have! By having all these attributes and I'm sure there are others as well, this game really gives you an impressively immersive experience and I do reccommend it based on those.
However even though it is a great game so far, the game is not without faults too. One of said faults is a weird issue where sometimes enemies will spawn right near you without any warning which can cause a bit of confusion when you're not in a position to fight. Another issue is mouse delay which is primarily noticable when below 60fps and around 60fps. Once you pass 70fps, the mouse delay becomes minimal enough that it's hardly noticable, but under that mark, it will take some getting used to. The only other thing I can consider a con is that sometimes AI that you recruit can block your way and sometimes get you stuck which can be a little annoying, but the best way to avoid this is just to recruit when you're about to fight that way you can explore solo free of worries.

Verdun is a blast to play. It's not like most games where you just run and gun and those with the quickest reflexes win every time. Each kill is a thrill because you spend time sneaking up into a good position with cover and fire support. Half the time, the enemy doesn't know what hit them. Or you don't know what hit you.
The game mechanics sound a bit limiting at first but they channel you into the type of warfare that Verdun is supposed to model -- gritty, dirty, muddy, freezing cold trench warfare. You feel the helpless vulnerability while slogging through open muddy land, and it's a relief to drop into the relative safety of a sodden trench. Most matches are quite evenly played, too, so the auto-balancing system is well developed.
The only downsides are that there is an occasional crash and it's a little confusing for the first couple matches. Once you get the hang of it, though, this is a solid game to have in your Steam library and play regularly.

So, The Crew:
Basically they took the idea of NFS Rivals and improved it, added a storyline, and optimized it better. The idea is that the game is always online. Any time you play it you will be able to see other people and even CO-OP with them.

Some people are complaining that the map is not big enough. Well think about it - Fitting thousnds of miles/kilometers of roads and hundreds of cities into a game is pretty damn hard. Not to mention that if they did so, you'll probably get a game that will weigh over 100 GB's, and probably won't run on most PC's. So they took the best of what there is, and put it in the game.
My only complain is that the game lacks some cars, for exmaple: Subaru Impreza WRX STI, or Toyota Supra. I expected to have those cars in a street racing game. I truely hope they add these cars sometime.
And another thing, and this is aimed towards people, not the game itself: You complain about unrealistic physics in an ARCADE RACING game?! Are you serious?! An Arcade Racing game is supposed to have unrealstic physics.
If you're looking for sims: Go for something like Assetto Corsa. Because this is not a Sim. This is an ARCADE RACING game.

Absolutely a worthy follow-up to the amazing reboot of the old style dungeon crawler that was Grimrock I. A few new elements, some new functions with alchemy and optional use of guns. They've made it work both in dungeons and outside which is really cool. The square-walking fighting system has been enhanced a bit so that it isn't just enough to sidestep and hit over and over anymore. Some monsters will jump behind you, some will hit to the side if you sidestep them to their sword-arm side. Little things like that. Still, the main objective remains the same: don't ever get surrounded.
Only negative point at all is that a few of the puzzles sometimes seem a bit too far out, so to speak. And they can be a bit annoying more than clever but it's very rare. Usually, you can work the solution out from clues and all together the balance between too difficult and difficult enough is accurately struck.
The game ending seems to lead to the next game in the series and so it can feel a bit unfinished, perhaps. The final boss fight comes a bit out of nowhere, it feels, but it's actually a good boss fight. It's tough, sure, but it's not just about learning all the mechanics from replaying it 100 times, it's actually just about fighting well. So all in all, a very nice game. Into RPG? Buy it, simple as that.

Legend of Grimrock was a remake of the old Dungeon Master series of video games, where four of the unluckiest people on whatever fantasy world you care to name slugged it out in a first-person viewpoint through a never-ending dungeon solving puzzles, killing monsters, and reloading saved games a lot. Grimrock is a fantastic revival, updating the format with a new-school look and filling the dungeons with enough monsters to cover every possible phobia that human beings have. Creepy spiders? Got them. Horrible zombie monsters? Got those too. Starving to death in a dungeon because the puzzle for a solution eludes you? That's you. It turns out you are the monster who ate all the cakes and now have no more cakes. Way to go, Chompy McFoodie.
Legend of Grimrock II is largely the same thing, but massively improved and even more difficult than the first game. I get the feeling the developers didn't have a good direction to take the Grimrock series, so they went the BIGGER AND BETTERER route. This is not a bad thing at all - the first Grimrock left me vaguely unsatisfied after I reached the bottom, because I realized all we were doing was running around narrow corridors in a goddamn mountain. Well, Grimrock II is for picky-picky pants who thought along the same lines, because this time you get to GO OUTSIDE AND GET KILLED BY HORRIBLE MONSTERS. Seriously - the game has you start out fighting for your life on the beach with scraps and rocks, and every fight feels like a goddamn do-or-die frantic clawing at each others' throats. The game is able to keep this crazy amount of tension going with each and every new area - fights become intense and terrifying with every new monster because it has this little quirk or trick up its sleeve that it's going to use to ♥♥♥♥ your party over and kill you dead.
It works out a lot of the quirks from the first game's puzzles - mostly. The puzzles are difficult, but not too brain bending - they don't quite reach the Portal sweet spot, but they come close and solving them made me feel like a champion. There's still a couple that require moon logic and sent me towards a walkthrough guide.
The plot is a bunch of accented nothing. The first game's story had a bunch of information on the world, but not a whole bunch as to why the King sent four poor suckers into a mountain cave to find out what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on. The second game doesn't have much more than that. It has lots of beautiful details about the world that the game exists in, but there's not much else to it other than "Gotta get the ♥♥♥♥ off of this crazy death island full of crazy death monsters, gotta go!"
I can't really say much more about this game other than it's a bigger and better sequel and you don't need to play the first game to understand it. I will say that whenever people talk♥♥♥♥♥♥about beating hard bosses in Dark Souls or Bloodborne, I'll talk about the time I got jumped by cobras and crazy undead Medusa archers just to get a longsword that I didn't even end up wanting to keep.

This is a digital card game with the depth of Magic and the polish of Hearthstone. Direwolf has hired on some of Magic's best pros to help out with the card design and it really shows.
This game uses MTG attacking and blocking, meaning it is easier to get a stalled board than Hearthstone, but so far I've not had too many issues with it because there are lots of way to break stalls with combat tricks and other cards. You can play instants in this game, though they are called Fast Spells, and can only be played in response to a card being used on your units, during combat, and at the end of turn. This is actually very nice because it means you aren't f2ing through your opponent's turn. There are a few RNG cards, though nothing nearly obscene as in Hearthstone.
This game has you put your mana, which is called power in this game, in your deck, like in Magic. However colors are done through Influence. Once you get 1 of an influence of color, you can play any card that only has that influence requirement. So you don't have to worry about using the right color power. For players coming from Hearthstone, the power system can be a sore point because you will come across times where you either draw too much power, or not enough power. You get a free Mulligan each game. When you take a Mulligan, you are stuck with what hand you draw. However after you mulligan, you are guaranteed to get at least two power in your hand.
The free-to-play model is very generous. It follows the same pattern of Hearthstone, but since each pack contains 12 cards, rather than 5, it makes it easier to get all the common and uncommon cards. Also, drafting and forge let you keep the cards you choose, which let you build up your collection that way.
All-in-all, I would say this is an excellent game and highly recommend that anyone try it.

Definitely helps to shift the mood back to the lost / isolated / tragic ambiance of the first game.

Most reviews have already said it: FF X is a great classic everyone should have played at least once. Nothing more to add here.
I am however writing this review for FF X-2 (giving a thumbs up regardless because this is a bundle, and FF X is a good game.)
I am not sure why FF X-2 is so terrible compared to FF X. The combat is mindnumbingly awful - it is supposed to be real time combat, except actions don't always play when your ATB bar is full, sometimes only play after an endlessly repeating insignificant voiceline, or only play after an enemy has done a special attack which somehow stops all your ATB bars from filling until it is done (nice "active battle system") If you wanna change your classes during battle, cool, you can! Except you have to sit through the same 30 second animation every single time with no way to skip them.
But the battle system is the least of the games problem. The story is nonexistent, only barely there while you complete set after set of mindnumbing repetitive missions with cringeworthy dialogue. Every character that was in FF X apparently lost at least 90 % of their braincells in the 2 years between FF X and FF X 2 because no character behaves the way it should and almost everyone is so incredibly irritating.
The gameplay is, do this mission in one of the 90 % of recycled maps from FF X, and maybe if you're lucky you will get a main mission while you massage someone (which funny enough was part of a main mission), run a Gunners Gauntlet with terrible controls, or interrupt a TV broadcast to squabble some ****.
Seriously, I know I am ranting, but I did not have one tiny bit of fun while playing FF X-2. It has nothing to do with FF X, nothing to do with fun, and nothing to do with intelligence or innovation. It is a giant mess. So please buy this bundle for FF X but stay far away from FF X-2. It will save you a lot of frustration.

The game's pretty metal.  Disease will kill plebs.  Pestilence will♥♥♥♥♥♥and murder their wives.  Tornado's will smear their buildings across the landscape like so much wet paper bag.
Between the natural disasters, not-so-natural disasters, or otherwise by your own inept hand in managing your tea-cup humans, you WILL lose.  In fact, there is no winning. That's not a joke.  At no point will the game say "Congratulations."  There's no campaign.  No set goals.  Just the start of your town, and its inevitable end.  It's what happens in between, with the goals you set for yourself, in which the gameplay resides.
Will your little pathetic village survive the first winter?  Did you think your villagers could survive on a diet of ale?  Dead.  All of them, dead.
My first 4 towns all died within a couple of in-game years (in all, about 20 minutes each).  My current town, however, is thriving.  If "thriving" means 36 plebs, 12 successfully disaster-free winters later.
You know the game is hard when having 36 villagers and a working market makes you want to climb to the highest roof and shout "I AM THE MASTER OF TINY PEOPLE!  FOR IN MY GUIDANCE ALONE, THEY WILL SURVIVE!"  But they'll be dead soon.
10/10.  Will play for days.

This is a really enjoyable game if you like Stanley Parable-esque "walking simulators" and games that mess with your head from start to finish.
I would highly recommend not reading too much about it first, as any kind of information about the later parts of the game especially will really skew and possibly ruin the experience.
This takes a couple hours total to get all achievements; your playtime will vary based on how much you explore and experience.  You could probably blow through it in half an hour but you will miss the majority of the pieces of the puzzle of what's going on.  As it is, the game leaves a lot for you to think about and connect the dots on yourself.  If you don't want to think much or want the whole story 100% explained in black-and-white by the end, you're not going to be happy.
I will mention, without spoilers, that several of the achievements require you to enter DOS-style .cmd commands into a terminal.  The terminal that's required is the MAIN MENU terminal before you even launch the game itself.  This has been confusing to a lot of people so I wanted to throw that out there for anyone who is, like me, obsessed with achievements.
Give it a shot if you like these exploration/story-driven games.  It is 100% worth the $4.99 asking price for the immersive experience and story.

Couple other random notes that annoyed me about this game:

The short form:
If you think “Dear Esther” is an awful and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game do not buy this one. It is the same over expensive♥♥♥♥♥♥by the same publisher.
The objective form:
Gone Home is a good “walk around in an abounded mansion simulator“, but it is really bad in being an adventure game. Of course at some point it is questionable what really makes a game a game. For me a game has to offer a player some kind of challenge.  This challenge can be a test of certain skills like reflexes or strategic thinking, the ability to solve puzzles or recognize connections; sometimes the goal is to overcome fears, sometimes to build empires. There are endless possibilities for games but they have all on thing in common.  They offer some kind of interaction for the player which has an impact of what happens. Gone Home does not offer this at all. Walking around in it feels linear like reading a book, which can be exiting too, of course, but again not as an adventure game.  A lot of people like this game as it gives them a nostalgic feeling. But honestly, this walking around simulation will take 2 hours of your time for a price of 20$ which is way too expensive for what it offers.
The spoiling form:
The whole game and all of its content can be explained in one sentence:
You walk around in a left 90s house and collect parts of a diary for 2 hours.
That’s all what happens here… for the price of just twenty bucks…

Gone home has a great atmosphere which gets increasingly darker and more mysterious as you play. This game also has a really cool and detailed 1990’s setting. There is a sense of humour here too with some unexpected jokes and ‘Easter eggs’ to be discovered.
The game ran fine for me at max settings on a GTX980 running Windows 10. A cool feature that the developers included is a ‘Modifiers Menu’. Whenever you start a new game, you can modify your experience, in some fun and useful ways. The ‘Game Options’ menu also contains some nice features. Which allow you to turn off various ‘in-game prompts’ for an even more immersive experience. There is also the option to turn on ‘in-game developer commentaries’ which is always nice.
The house in which this game takes place is very well designed. Providing an eerie sense of realism with mysterious and creepy undertones. The house is also filled with interesting, interactive content including good music and other cultural references. There is a nice little story here too which unravels as you explore.
I would highly recommend ‘Gone Home’, I really enjoyed my time spent in this creepy, cool, house from the past.

Amazing! This is an instant favorite. Beautiful introduction, simple and classic controls, and an absolutely frightening experience. To those looking for a thrilling and memorable game, I recommend Outlast without reservation.
Pros: Elegant game-play with surprisingly high production value. The trailer gives an excellent feel for this game. The experience has been a delight, and I'm sure other horror genre fans will agree.
Cons: Can't close doors quietly (unless I'm missing something). I don't like being forced to slam doors shut as I sneak around... but this is only a minor complaint, and it doesn't seem to effect the gameplay.

Pros:
1. Massive open world map with very nice scenery and different track types (Mountains, Valleys, Plains, Cities, etc...)
2. Side missions and extra stuff to do (Skill ,missions, exploration, hidden cars, etc...) if the story starts to get stale.
3. Decent driving controls, not too realistic, but not over the top arcade style either, over all very fun just driving around.
4. A lot of potential to grow into an even better game.
Cons:
1. Networking issues: (Booted out of the game at the end races with a friend on multiple occasions, and lag tends to be a constant issue when playing with friends)
2. Limited car selections, especially from the asian market (Honda, Toyota, Subaru, etc...)
3. Customization/progression feels very linear, less like you choose how to improve the car, more like you take whatever the game gives you that isnt worse than what you currently have (At least in the beginning of the game).
Conclusion:
I am happy with my purchase, and hope to see this game get even better.

"where YOU are the dungeon": no, you're not, we need more games like that on steam but this isn't one of them. It's a super-simple fire emblemy deal where you play as the "evil" characters and level yourself rather than individual units. The dialogue is plenty entertaining and the gameplay kinda scrapes by, working as well as it has to. Two points of note there:
Both the player and the enemy bring in their units in "waves" and the next wave only shows up when the previous is cleared. This allows for situations like "you get 3 waves and they get one, so go ham" or "they get 3 waves and you get one so play scared", and since you have a variety of wave types to choose from, there's a strong incentive to make sure you're picking into a fresh wave, not the remnants of the previous one. The counterpicking comes at the cost of gameplay depth though; once you're actually in a matchup there's nowhere near as much outplay potential as there is in any other fire emblem clone I've seen (units take turns on an "initiative" system so you don't get to choose who goes in what order, don't get a ton of manueverability, and are never numerous enough to really set up a wall around a ranged unit). The matchups are pretty stat-checky, but I never found myself on the wrong side of a stat-check. A lot of the mechanics were clearly put in place to curb the dominance of ranged units that usually happens in these games, but everyone does so much damage that despite everything, "burn through everything with unlimited-range attacks" is basically always a valid plan. The fights are a cheesefest where the only defense is to melt everything before it melts you, which I suppose is a logical result of both sides getting the fodder units typical to this genre. All in all this variation of the genre works decently if you aren't looking for a deep experience.
A more specific thing that stuck out to me is that right from the beginning you get a "command" that reads "attack with less accuracy but an ensured crit". This is on everyone, always. Has a 3 turn cooldown sure, but given that you can upgrade it, using this skill is the main strategic aspect of the game (spoiler: you almost always want to use it when it's up).
So yeah, it's a fire emblem clone you can blaze through in a couple hours without problems. Get it if you don't want to commit to a long epic quest and nothing I mentioned above turns you off.

Don't let the somewhat flashgame-esque art style fool you, this is an incredibly satisfying experience as a person who really enjoys tactics and strategy games but doesn't have time for the plodding pace of many entries in that space.
The game is sort of like playing a Heroes of Might and Magic game but instead of spending tons of time building up armies and traveling around occasionally having a big battle (which is rarely evenly matched as if you lose too many of your troops you might as well quit), you take part in a number of smaller battles with smaller but tactically relevant squads of minions.  The interesting decision making on how you will choose to build up your army and what you'll specialize in is still there however, as you have a number of missions to choose one from between each mission and each gives you a choice of multiple relevant (and meaty) rewards.
It took me about 4 hours to clear the game for the first time, but I consider that a pro rather than a con as in that time I probably had 20 or so fun and satisfying battles with enough interesting choices to keep me thoroughly engaged.  The fact that you don't have time to try all the missions (or what they unlock) the first time around also gives a lot of replayability to the experience if that's your cup of tea with the usual new game+ and endless modes available after you complete the game.
The humorous style and fairly light-hearted plot fits this time window nicely as well, and it's a nice game to finish in a single sitting on a day off.
Overall, it’s definitely worth a purchase and playthrough.  Give it a shot!

I was expecting a Cooking Mama clone but it actually seperates itself out by using a series of key presses to complete your orders rather than physically prepeating the food yourself. This is good or bad depending on your tastes but it does make for a special kind of manic gaming that captures your complete attention.
The game is difficult, there's no denying that, but after a bit of practice muscle memory will take over and you'll be serving pizzas and salads at super human speeds. One thing that I would suggest is to map the key bindings for each individual meal as if it doesn't make sense to you it will slow you down massively. For example, for some reason unbeknownst to me, to add sausage to a pizza, you must hit the "M" key - I changed it to "S"... you know, for "Sausage"...
There's money management, food menu management and time management at play here with lots to think about before you even start your day cooking. Buying new equipment and foods, upgrading them and perhaps most importantly, making sure you select the right menu to get the most out of the day are all key to your success.
A lot of fun can be had here but as mentioned the prework (which is equally is fun) is also required.

RIVE felt, to me, incredibly generic. There's a thin line between 'homage' and 'retread', and I certainly felt that RIVE crossed it in its attempt to modernize the shoot'em ups of yesteryear.
That's not to say RIVE is a bad game. Despite some persistent control problems (I was using a Steam controller), I managed to breeze through the game in 2/3 of the time suggested (3.9 hours vs. 6), and it was consistently well-polished in terms of graphics, music, and sound-effects. The issue is that it is consistently, almost painfully, mediocre in terms of level design and gameplay, as well as storyline.
Otherwise competent or innovative levels are often dragged down by enemies popping in from offscreen too quickly for you to react, necessitating that you always be firing your weapons in the most likely path of intercepting enemies, just in case. This creates problems when the player needs to hack enemy machines and ends up destroying them, or when you have a hacked sentry turret that is set to expire after a certain number of shots fired.
There's also situations where the game's own bombastic graphics get in its way; the bright explosions and overlapping enemies can easily create situations where the player can't actually see what's going on in a given sector of the screen, forcing them to fire blind and hope for the best. In one particularly memorable and egregious example of this, I slew the final boss, only to be so blinded by its explosion as to not see that it had opened a lava vent near me (something which it had done inconsistently up to that point), causing me to stand still and die right after slaying it (and forcing me to refight the latter portion of the battle). This was only a minor inconvenience, but it's an example of how questionable level and game design dragged down what should have been a triumphant moment.
As for story and character interaction, RIVE went for a very Borderlands-esque feel, right down to the character designs and voice-acting sounding like they were out of that franchise. Whereas Borderlands uses humor to set up a storyline, however, RIVE never evolves beyond low-key goofing-off, so don't expect anything revelatory or original in that department. To be honest, it wasn't even funny to me, aside from a single comment a character makes about how one of his attempts at a joke failed to even be a pun, complete with apology.
So you probably shouldn't play it for the story, and you shouldn't expect a bump-free ride in terms of controls (if you're using the Steam controller), level design, or general gameplay. What does RIVE have to offer? Well, as I said before, it's very well-polished. "Generic" also doesn't mean "worthless"; while RIVE can be summed up as "Shoot'em Up 2017", the whole purpose of the game was to make a modernized shoot'em up with good production values, and it did succeed at that. To those unfamiliar with the genre especially, it may come off as more innovative or fun than to those of us who have played dozens of such games. If it weren't for the level-design issues (I'm not counting the controls against it), I'd give it a recommendation as a bit of harmless high-intensity fun, but the occasional cringe-inducing cheap-shot or dull yet-another-robot-grind made this game overstay its welcome at even the brief mark I played, so it gets the thumbs down.

Legend of Grimrock 1 was a GREAT puzzle game. It had a certain amount of combat in it, but it was kept to a minimum, and generally you were rarely outnumbered. You could take your time with the combat.
Legend of Grimrock 2 seems to have forgotten it's puzzle roots and provide puzzles that are far too easy to solve even for someone who is generally not that into puzzle games, and adds a HEAPLOAD of combat to the game, and also against far more dangerous enemies. Enemies are also much more numerous in this game compared to its predecessor, leading to you being surrounded and slaughtered sometimes in seconds, leading to multiple frustrating reloads in order to handle random battles that you had no chance preparing for.
In fact, the random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t battles is what, in the end, caused me to give up and say good bye to Grimrock 2. I wanted a puzzle game, and was given a dungeon crawler with a subpar combat system instead. After I had finished Crystal Mines and ended up outside with 10+ rat patrols and the rat boss (which I'd already beaten) AGAIN I just had enough. There are so many ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t moments where enemies will spawn out of nowhere or just give you the middle finger saying "Oh, you solved that puzzle did you? Here, have a near impossible battle!"
It's just the fact that you have no chance to prepare for these that make it overly annoying and leading to multiple deaths and reloads just to try and get that one "perfect" battle that you actually survive.
I was NOT looking for a combat game. I do not recommend Grimrock, in spite of it's graphics, atmosphere and puzzles. It's not worth it.

Your field of view is too small to see them and they are just way too fast and maneuverable. I think they were supposed to be an enemy who would force you to rapid reload under pressure, but in practice they either don't detect you and drop with one shot, or you empty your mag on one while the other one zaps you from behind. I really do like playing this, but its not developed to a stage where you'd really want to try and "play through" to the end (believe me I've tried). I had a positive review of this game before, but honestly, I have to rescind it.
There's so many problems with this game that become apparent over time, and it just does horrible things to the types of decks you can play.
For one the 75 card deck size just ruins reliability and grossly increases variance. In a recent blog post the devs made about the redraw rule, they mentioned keeping the deck size so there could be more ways a deck can play out. Honestly, all it does is increase the chance in which you don't draw lands (power, whatever, too used to mtg) after the new redraw rule lands you a 2 power hand.
And because of this, the meta is so heavily in favour of aggressive crature decks right now. That or 3-4 colour control decks. There's nothing competitive in between. Hell, I was comandeering an agressive deck called Burn Queen for a while, then the devs decide to nerf one of the star creatures in my deck. For what reason, I have no idea. There's a reason why  'dies to bolt' exists in magic the gathering; and nerfing a creature so it dies to Lighting Bolt/Torch happens to be more than enough to kick a good deck off its pedestal.
Honestly I'm writing this because I just uninstalled the game after running 5+ games in a row where I got to do nothing. NOTHING. Just sit back and watch my opponent win because I got land starved/mana screwed every single time. I've been trying hard to construct decks that lie outside the meta, from more value oriented decks, to mid range decks not unlike MTG's Jund decks. But to be honest, if you're not aggressive, there's no point in being played. If you can't live of a 2 land hand and miss a land drop, again no point.
Go play something like Faeria where the mere odds at play when drawing a hand don't lose you the game.

I got this on the cheap and by surprise from February 2017's Humble Bundle Monthly pack, and played it beginning to end in about 2 days (4 hours playtime altogether for the basic campaign, not counting extras like speedrun mode, single credit mode, and challenges).
I'm altogether pleased. The art and animations are altogether a treat. It's a nice adventure for anyone who's the slightest fan of shoot-em-ups and gaming pop culture. The music is a pleasant and well-composed blend of electronica with some throwback to older (8- & 16-bit) video game music, but not to the degree of something like Shovel Knight. I found the storyline and dialogue amusing as well. Think of this as an adventure, like going to a movie theater. The $15 price right now is fair, but even better if you spot a sub-$10 sale.
Downsides?
This is a very difficult game. Expect to die many times, and unfairly. Normal enemies don't do much damage, but often one slip-up can send you into near-instakill lava or sawblades. And that's in Normal mode. Luckily, you have infinite lives and checkpoints are fairly frequent.
There are only a handful of enemy types, but they do attack in varied enough formations and arenas for most big setpiece battles to feel unique.
I had one instance of a setpiece battle being much harder than it should have been due a bug (debris was falling at a time when it long should have stopped). I was forced to retry the whole chapter. I also had a few instances of it being unclear as to where to go next. At least in the latter you can go track down a longplay to see what they do, but there should be in-game hints to point you in the right direction if you go nowhere for a minute.
I would not call this 10 out of 10. Nor 9 out of 10. Nor even 8 out of 10. But it's more deserving of a thumbs-up than not.

One-man studio Duelboot knows how to engineer a big payoff from a minimum of means. Verde Station abounds with mind tricks predicated on the player's expectations and imagination. These conspire with pacy, competent writing to keep you on your toes for the entirety of the ride. The game simmers like a fine sci-fi short story, a disquieting experience that leaves many issues unresolved and rewards a couple of replays.
It's been compared, aptly I'd say, to the movie Moon; another obvious parent would be video game Consortium for its spaceship setting, its puzzling structure and focus on minute exploration.
This is the rare game that manages to present itself in such a mysterious guise that even the achievement guide on the community hub takes the form of hints and questions rather than straight-up instructions.
In fact there is so much dramatic flair on offer here that it begs the question of what could be achieved with greater means. If I had a regret regarding Verde Station it's that there isn't more of it - I don't mean hours of useless to-and-froing or shooting sequences, but hidden narrative depths to tangibly explore, not just muse about. The game feels like it's brimming with fascinating secrets but I guess there is only so much actual scope you can reach for as a single dev.
Kudos for evoking so much. I strongly hope down the line these fascinating intuitions and conceits will mature and yield an even more coherent whole, and this promising short story will blossom into a full-blown novel.
