I've played around 30% of the game's content at the time of this review.
Please not that this game was purchased during a sale.
This does not include any input on the COOP in this game.
Not
revolutionary,
. It boasts nothing too fancy and borrows some ideas from other games. Graphically great to sometimes sub-sucky. Looking at you, environment textures. The story is dragged down by the somewhat repititious nature of the gameplay, lacking in variety of mission choice.
One of the biggest offenses this game has to offer is the alarm mechanic. One of the triggers of the alarm mechanic is having your weapon out. There is no bindable key to holster your weapon. The only way to holster (your weapons) is to go into a "hiding" spot.
There have been a few bugs that I have encountered. I am surprised they have not been fixed to this day, despite 3 DLC's being released. You will often see enemies running into walls, into eachother and sometimes morphing into eachother. There are a few spots that will glitch you through the map, such as transition areas that you have not unlocked.
The artistic direction in this game gets a pass. It feel believable, but lazy. You don't really feel like an inspired revolutionary because you play a character that is silent. Hearing some of the same dialogue from civilians happens way too fast, especially for a 60gb+ game.
Some people like to think that there is a lack of weapons in this game. This is not the case. Each weapon offers upto 3 distinct firing modes. The pistol,
the assault rifle,
the battle rifle,
and rocket launcher all serve their purpose. The pistol in it's most basic form, is surprisingly powerful. It's downside is the damage drop-off at range. In CQC-close ranges, it is between a 1-5 shot kill for most units. I've mostly used this gun in the game.
The sound design in this game is nothing special. If you're using a 7.1 surround headset (which you should if you have the option) there are a few audio bugs. Like when using a takedown on enemies, the sound rapidly switches between the left and right channels. It's somewhat disorienting. Apart from that, weapons sound like what they should, but could have a little bit more grit added to them.
The recoil is very under developed. It seems that weapons have 1-3 animations for the recoil. They either go straight up,  slightly to the left and up or slightly to the right and up. The recoil animation also cancels on each shot for the automatic weapons, making it look choopy. Also some of the reload animations look absolutely goofy when you get reload speed increases.
The upgrade system is fairly barebones and lacks anything unique. They often just unlock something passive that lets you modify your playstyle slightly or moderately. They could have added an upgrade that makes you loot faster, as that is the main way you recover ammunition. Another good upgrade that should have been added is one that improves your mantling and climbing speed. Mantling ranges from fluidly fast to annoyingly slow. I try to avoid ladders as much as possible, as they take a while to climb. This is mostly due to the animation that attaches you to the ladder and the animation of you getting off of the ladder.
Having more medkits on your person is nice and all, but if you're a smart player, you could probably go through most of the game without using one.
The combat is pretty similiar in all aspects. Engaging enemies from CQC-mid ranges. They often have someone fire at you while others seek routes to flank you. This would work, if the "flanking" enemies would not sit in cover for 2-5 seconds before popping out to fire at you. You can just takeout the one guy shooting at you and wait for "flankers" to pop out of cover. If they enemy is out in the open and there are at least 3 of them, one of them will just open fire. An interesting design choice because it probably sounded good on paper but does nothing for the game in reality.
The stealth mechanic in this game sucks. As far as I can tell, visible light barely changes the time it takes for you to be detected.
, apart from footstep sounds and line of sight. Being detected isn't a problem, as I can usually take out the infinite number of reinforcements with the standard pistol until I get bored of it. Mind you this is very early into the game and I could imagine later that is might be worse, but most likely manageable.
I have not played enough of the game to give a good point of the story. I imagine it needs to be played in it's entirety to have an idea of what the story is going to be and if it will be satisfying.
It's a solid experince at a reduced price. I could not jusitfy owning this game and it's DLC's for more than $25 (CAD) or $20 USD

A hidden gem of a top-down puzzle game. You'll definitely enjoy this if you enjoy puzzle games, especially if you like top-down ones like chuck's/chip's challenge. There's even a competetitive aspect if you're into that - every stage has a speedrun leaderboard for any% and 100%. It took me about 14 hours to get gold on every original stage (but I didn't do any of the bonus worlds).
The premise of this game is, for each level, to burn up and explode everything that can be burnt/exploded, collect all the stars, and to do so in as short of a time as possible. However, this isn't like Bomberman where you have an unlimited supply of bombs - every bomb is something that has to be picked up in the stage and is consumed when used. The time, stars, and burn percentage are flexible, too - you don't need to collect everything or come in under the par time for the level in order to advance. However, if you want to "gold" a level, you'll need to get 100% stars and burn rate and finish under the par time (but you don't have to do that all in a single run, so you can go for 100% one time and go for any% but under par in a subsequent run and you'll still earn a gold for that level).
While you CAN simply play to just beat each stage, I think this game is the most fun if you shoot for getting gold on every stage. You could probably blow through this game in a few hours if you didn't try to get gold. Adding speed and finding ways to optimize your run for a given level is one of the key aspects of the fun of this game, IMO.
So, the first time you play through a stage you'll probably take it slow and figure out what you need to do to get 100%, then later try to build speed and optimize in future replays. Towards the later stages, I found most of my time being spent optimizing and attempting to achieve the par time (after I had already figured out how to beat it with 100%).
The gameplay of burning stuff is unique and satisfying. Since things take time to burn and explode, a key aspect of going fast is to figure out what to burn first so you can maximize the amount of things you have burning at once. But when you start to burn more things, you can open yourself up to getting killed and having to restart.
Each character has different abilities, meaning there's multiple ways to complete stages, some faster than others. If you're creative you might even discover routes the designers never thought of.
The level/puzzle design is excellent. It increases in difficulty and complexity as you get further into the game. New mechanics are introduced at a satisfying rate.
My one suggestion would be to provide some sort of global leaderboard that takes into account your position on every stage, so you can see who is the overall top player or something like that.
Overall, if you're a fan of puzzle games, I'd say this is a must-have. It can get very heavily discounted and there's plenty of hours of playtime as well as an aspect of competition and replayability if you're interested in climbing leaderboards. There's plenty of content, too. Even after getting gold on the main game you can still play the bonus worlds and collect the hidden saplings. I highly recommended this unless you're not a big fan of puzzle games. This game deserves a lot more attention than it's received, IMO, but I think that puzzle games in general tend to be less popular these days.

Just to add more opinion in case you still need/want help. I just got this a few weeks ago without even having heard about it before I just randomly saw it on steam. The game is damn fun. It's basically just a city builder placed in a harsh medieval setting. There's no military, combat, or RTS-like elements. It's a pure village management sim. It blends a pretty good and informative UI with strong default controls to allow the player to focus more on learning game systems than learning how to do things or find information. The game has a short (took me about 30 minutes to go through all 5 scenarios) tutorial section which does a pretty good job of setting up the player with the tools required to dive right in. Once the player is acclimated the game is revealed to possess a depth of micro-management options and choices, even if the building roster can become a bit small once you reach late-game. The game probably tends more towards being punishing than forgiving, although I hesitate to call it flat-out difficult; it simply punishes mistakes a bit more severely than other current games might.
Now those are just my initial thoughts/impressions. I'll give a go at a super cliche, but informative, categorized list.
Graphics: Good!
The game looks good enough, but I've got a decent enough gaming rig and I haven't had any difficulty playing the game on max settings while having a few windows and a music player open in the background. I've heard through the grapevine that if you play a village up to 1000 population that the game will start to suffer some performance issues, regardless of the quality of your machine. I would expect that with maybe some tweaking of settings that just about any relatively current laptop or "work" machine would be able to play the game, albeit at reduced settings probably. Bottom line for the graphics: The game looks good enough that you won't sit there calling it ugly, but it's not exactly going to blow you away, and it certainly hasn't set any new benchmarks or anything.
Sound: Okay.....
The game has decent music and the ambient sounds for things like the blacksmith hammer and animals are good enough. I knock points off here for the blatantly ridiculous rain noise. When it rains it sounds exactly like someone turned on the faucet in a bathtub and just stuck a mic close enough to get a few "water" noises and that's what gets played whenever it rains. Bottom line for the sound: Good music, good ambient noise, rain sounds awful.
Controls/UI: Good!
If you know how to open and pin the information boxes to your UI, which is explained and/or revealed in the tutorials, then the game does a great job of revealing to you all of your relevant data. The absolute base UI that you start each new map with, before you open any additional windows, is pretty poor and would force you into a lot of guesswork, but it's an easily correctable issue for the player to have, and in my opinion doesn't warrant any sort of addressing by the developer, things are fine. The default controls are very nice and the options panel to tweak them is a thing that exists, which is good. The game defaults to a WASD/Edge scroll camera control that can have its scroll speed adjusted, with an interesting submenu hotkey setup. Each submenu is accessed through either clicking or pressing the assigned F key (F1 for information graphs, F2 for storage buildings, F3 for housing, etc.) and then each option in the submenu can be used by hitting the assigned key 1-9. Bottom line for controls/UI: Things work well and are basically intuitive, if you've played other games on PC then things will make sense at default, and the customization options are more than enough.
Just a note on the controls I specifically listed: those are not the actual key assignments, just an example
Gameplay/Game systems: Good!
Gameplay: It's a medieval city/tribe management simulation. The name of the game is to provide food, shelter, warmth, space, and health for an ever-expanding population. The challenge comes from doing it all efficiently, while still managing to bear the brunt of bad weather, disease, and flatout god damn fires. It's challenging without being "cheap", and the game will absolutely punish you if you make a mistake or expand too quickly without taking time to thoroughly establish sufficient infrastructure. There are also enough customization options that if you reach a certain base level of skill, you can setup just about any sort of special challenge play-through that you could possibly imagine.
Game systems: Arguably the single most important element of any management sim. All it takes in this genre is for one particular bit of game flow to be improperly designed or implemented and the whole thing can go to hell. Happily, in this particular case everything is handled quite well. Most systems are quite clearly illuminated through the tutorial scenarios, and even ones that aren't covered specifically will still make sense when the player discovers them. Everything flows nicely and can be independently managed and manipulated, while still being interdependent enough to force players to consider their macro-level strategy even while micro-managing something as small as figuring out storage for your new row of fields. But! And this is a big BUT!! There are two specific things that probably aren't balanced quite to satisfaction. The first one is what I would refer to as "The Firewood Racket". It's really simple, when you build a trading post you can trade for logs, which you can then quickly and efficiently turn into firewood via a woodcutter (or several woodcutters), then when you return the now-processed firewood to your trading post, the firewood is worth a ridiculous markup of 700%!! That's just a little bit broken right now. The second game system issue is with quarries and mines. Both are horribly inefficient methods of gathering their respective resources (stone and iron), while being an overbearing drain on manpower and tools. Right now the community is clamoring for something to be done about mines and quarries, they're both considered to be the one BIG black mark on the game in its current state. My particular issue with the firewood racket is that once you reach midgame, you can actually manipulate that market enough to ** completely** negate the need for certain other resource endeavors. It's so bad that you can trade foodstuffs for wood, turn the wood into firewood, and then trade the firewood for however much stone or iron you need, at a very player-friendly exchange rate. Most players probably don't really mind how imbalanced firewood is right now in terms of trade value, but it really does have the potential to completely throw off the amount of challenge presented in mid and late portions of the game. Bottom line for Gameplay/Game systems: Everything here is pretty good, there's really only one or two weird little balance issues that tarnish an otherwise very well-polished and well-done game. It's engaging and challenging, while still being very player friendly and possessing a decent amount of quality of life features. It's also replayable as all heck and has a good list of challenging achievements that will take numerous files to complete.
tl;dr The game is fun and well-done. If you're hankering for a city management sim then this game is absolutely for you. At the price of $20 I would say its a must-buy for fans of the genre or anyone who feels even the slightest of tug when checking the game out. Otherwise, I'd recommend to penny pinchers and casual genre fans to be patient and wait it out for a steam sale or some other discount, it's absolutely worth the wait and it will probably only continue to get better.

On normal difficulty, this game is brutal. Not for the faint of heart.
For me, the challenge was welcome. I have been gaming for many years, probably longer than many of the people reading this review have been alive. And, these days it's hard to find a hard game that's still fair.
Well, I would definitely say that Banished is fair. It's fair in the way that forgetting to switch your farmers over to fishing during the winter, then everyone starves to death two years later due to food deficit is fair. Or, fair the way that running out of coats and firewood during the winter causes all the young children to die off very quickly is fair. You get the idea.
In other words, if you lose in this game, it's your fault. And, it will be your fault often, particularly if you are not used to playing this type of game.
If you're looking for dragons, magic, or gory violence, look elsewhere. Gone Home is either a bare-bones adventure game or a walking simulator which included a very small number of puzzle elements. I would suggest it is really more like the latter from a cladistics point of view; its attraction lies in that direction, and if you’re looking for really cerebral gameplay, this isn’t the place to look.
Gone Home is really a story that happens to be presented in a video game format. The game consists of you (a early 20s woman who lives as an independent adult – you were in the military) coming home after a vacation in Europe to an empty house; your parents and your sister are all absent, and as you explore the house, it becomes increasingly clear that it is a bit disheveled. You find some notes from your sister scattered around, as well as various notes and scraps of life left by your sister and parents. Some of these trigger audio logs from your sister, which are really journal entries that you are listening to. These tell the story about what your sister has been going through over the last year, and the story of her relationship with Lonnie, a girl she knows.
There are other stories interwoven into that one – your father, who is a failed writer who is trying to climb back on the horse while working a real job, and your mother, who is struggling with her relationship with your father and who might or might not be having an affair, or at least contemplating one, as well as the story of the former owner of the house that your family moved into while you were in the military.
These stories all come together to create a picture of a family that is troubled, but not broken, and of people who are people. Your sister is an immature high school student, but she is mostly immature like rebels without a cause are. Lonnie seems to be simultaneously more and less mature; she’s a bad influence on your sister in some ways, but also seems to have a more realistic and grounded view of the world in other ways.
I liked the story of the lives presented here; it is sort of everyday drama, with people struggling with real problems rather than contrived situations (much as the game likes to pretend at one point that there might be supernatural elements involved).
What I didn’t like, however, was the ending; when you get to the end, it seems to sort of throw away Lonnie’s character to force a “happy ending” which, if you think about it, isn’t actually really a happy ending at all. And this sort of ruins the story to an extent, because the whole story had been about growing up and trying to accept reality and find happiness through it, and then the end has Lonnie and your sister throw all that away while making a very stupid decision which flies in the face of Lonnie’s prior characterization, as well as the general theme of the piece.
I’ll also note that it is possible to sequence skip in this game; as I assumed it was more gamey than it really was, I managed to find some secret passages, including the one that lead to the very final area of the game, far before I was supposed to. This partially spoiled a major aspect of the story to me from quite early on. The worst of it is, finding these secret passages isn’t even very hard if you are familiar with floor plans and realize that there are empty spaces which, in a real house, would have rooms in them.
In the end, I’m left feeling ambivalent about this game. I wouldn’t not recommend it – I thought it was a decent enough use of two hours of my time, and I was reasonably immersed in the experience – but simultaneously, I feel bad about recommending it, because in the end, the story doesn’t really feel like it actually came together thematically and tossed its build-up away for an ending that the game thinks is a happy one, but which the rest of the story (and plain logic) suggests wouldn’t be. Also, it feels overpriced for its length; I got this as part of a bundle, but throwing down $20 for a 2 hour game that you're only going to play once seems like a kind of poor deal (and, as a side note, the developer commentary, which seems like it might provide additional content, wasn't worth listening to).
If you want something with actual gameplay and puzzles, you should definitely steer clear; this is one of those games which is only debatably a “game” in the first place, and while it is more of a game than something like Dear Esther, it is not as much of a game as something like The Stanley Parable.

I definitely found it compelling to learn about a family by looking at the different artifacts around their house. And it was ultimately interesting to learn why nobody was home. All this involved me going through and opening up every last drawer and cabinet in the house, which was occasionally boring but which was mostly interesting because how often do you get to snoop around a normal family's home like that in real life. The game also reminded me of the quaint old days when we used landlines and answering machines, which was fun.
I think what bothered me was that things weren't realistic, which didn't actually bother me that much while playing the game, but which bothered me in retrospect. I was left with questions like: Why are there so many conveniently useful scraps of paper everywhere? Why am I spending all this time looking at background information I should already know (given that  I've lived with these people for years)? Even more so because right now the house is creeping me out a little. What about my sister's situation required her to be so drastic? It also seemed debateable whether it was a good storytelling choice to have my sister read her diary entries before I actually found her diary. (It probably made the story more compelling, but it's a bit lacking in temporal realism.)

I've seen some negative reviews for this game, but mine won't be one. Those saying that the walking&touching game is a waste of money are just missing out a new trend in game industry, which is the walking simulator. In "Dear Esther" you take in the gorgeous island landscape with its ocean, sunset, hidden caves and waterfalls. In "Gone Home" you have a grand old house all for yourself to explore, really creepy and squeaky at times, and at some points you almost expect the old uncle ghost to jump out at you. This is not a puzzle game, nor an action or a scaretale. There's no dialogue. It's all a story, threading from room to room while you're collecting dots and trying to find where your parents and sister have gone. The story is more about the sister, though, who we get to know through her notes, books and schoolbooks, horrid music tapes, tales she wrote, her photos and feminist brochures. It's a game to relax and think, reflect on the characters' fates and the issues they raise, deduct their past and present and accept it. It's like visiting a friend's home when he or she is away and only things can tell stories. So yes, I do recommend this game, and I thank the developers for a beautiful, very 90s, Twin Peaks-ish, Walt Whitman-ish and Life Is Strange-ish ride. I got this game during a promotion, so no regrets here either. We do pay to go watch a movie, don't we? So here's a good one!

It seems there is a lot of people who did not like this game and, honestly, I can understand why. Gone Home is rather short and the asking price of 20 pounds seems much for any game of barely two hours of play time.
Also, this game is the apotheosis of the walking simulator: All you do in Gone Home is walk around, open some doors or drawers, turn the lights on and off and explore a seemingly abandoned house. And if that was all there was to it, i could not for the life of me recommend it.
However, the minimalism of gameplay has a purpose: Gone Home is all about story and atmosphere.
The story is told through countless audio logs, notes, letters, postcards and documents -- if you despise reading, this game is not for you. And although you have to piece the story together bit by bit on your own, it is sublimely written and unfolds into a very sweet narrative.
The atmosphere is one of the richest and most immersive I have encountered. While the minimalism mentioned above also stretches into the graphical presentation, it does not break immersion and serves to focus on the important things the house you are in has to offer. But Gone Home does not rely on graphics alone to build its atmosphere: The soundscape is brilliantly crafted and plays a key role in the game.
All in all, I personally can only recommend this jewel of a game, though it might not be everyone's cup of tea.

The worst soulsborne game by a huge margin, does not even come close to quality and consistency of DS1, DS3, or Bloodborne. This game is worse on every level imaginable, except for the scope of the game. Despite the creators attempting to make evrything better with the addition of SotFS, I did not notice any difference in fun or interest between my playthrough of vanilla and SotFS. Souls games cannot be fun without responsive combat, so I focus on combat in this review.
Everything put into this game seems to directly contrast some other design of this game, creating a huge mess of conflicting ways it seems that FromSoftware wants you to play this game. In DS2, there is wave after wave of gank sqaud enemies mixing in ranged attackers and melee opponents. In DS1, this could be handled using a good parry i-frame or a backstab fishing. Some people may call this cheap, but for me it was fun getting a clutch parry, rolling away to avoid attacks, and repeating. DS2 tries to fix this by removing i-frames for parrry and backstab which is not so bad by itself. However, they compounded that by adding a new stat, adaptibility. Leveling this stat gives you agility, basically an i-frame and action stat. Without sufficiently levelling this, rolls are basically useless and chugging an estus flask takes around 3 seconds before you can move again, and like other people may point out, this is now a heal over time. From the time you hit heal to you rhealth fully gaining, it may be 5 seconds. In a game where gank sqauds are common this is a huge problem that yes, makes it challenging, but at the expense of fun.
Adding to this problem are the horrendous hitboxes in DS2, and the 360 degree enemy tracking. Nowhere is safe with a circle strafe in DS2, all must be dodged with a shield or a roll, but oh wait rolls are terrible now and shields don't block until one second after you hold block. What is the right way to play this game? Parry king? No, the timing is stupid and it doesn't work on most bosses or gank squads. Tanking? Good luck healing without getting slammed by the enemies. Magic? Enemies will run you down, or you could be an OP mage and trivialize the game, making it not challenging or fun.
Thus, you are forced to level ADP if you want any semblance of a respnsive roll or estus use, leading to pumping a stat that does nothing for your attack power, making you forced to grind for some levels. This next bit is more of a PvP problem, but any souls gained increase your total sould memory, limiting who you can PvP with. This is not resettable so to have a fun PvE playthrough means forgetting about any PvP.
The biggest problem with this game is the lack of fun. In my experience, I have fun 5% of the time I play DS2. The rest is either frustration from terrible combat or boredom from running around the terribly designed levels. Dark Souls 1 and 3 are way better buys than this game. I got this for $10 on sale and I would not say it's worth much more than that.

I just got the entire Homefront 1+TR bundle for 19 pounds on a sale. I finished the first game a couple of years back. I liked it. It was CoD with a pseudo-futuristic approach driven by a vastly fictional world.
This game? I would say this is totally underappreciated.
As someone who greatly enjoyed FarCry 2. The, 'Here you have a world. Here you have missions. Mess around', vibe is really strong and similar to that very game. I can clearly say this game is an uncut gem, just like FC2.
Reading about the crap this game went through, switching developers and such. It really shows how much time they have put into Homefont The Revolution.
The setting and the art direction in itself are astounding. It flawlessly blends the hyper-futuristic KPA tech with the post-apocalyptic like run down buildings of Philadelphia. It sticks out like a sore thumb. And not in a cliche manner like you seen in most modern games.
The enemies, especially the damn vehicles they have in their arsenal are outright menacing. The visuals mixed with the sound effects really make you stay the hell away from them. Avoiding them like the plague.
The gun mechanics are nothing amazing. They're typical, with additional kick added in requiring a little bit of skill. The kit system is really cool in my opinion. It basically grants you the ability to switch the upper receiver in mid-battle, enabling you to adapt your playstyle.
The only quite major critique I have are regarding the AI, the spawn system for NPCs and minor bugs. It really feels like the programmers just sat with their fingers up their back sides at this stage of developement. Everything is nicely polished until some of your enemies dissapear. Which is in itself a slight immersion-killer. In some corners you will get stuck and will have to load from last checkpoint. It's annoying.
The sound design in this game is really good. It feels like the guns have a punch and the ambient sounds of people talking, screaming and rioting really is the cherry on top when it comes to immersion.
Music wise, it's nice. But after the 5 hour mark I found myself turning it off as it started to take off the immersion. It was just too up-beat for me for such a serious and depressing setting.
The story is interesting. Nothing amazing but it's definitely something. It's quite cool seeing how the KPA grew in the Homefront universe. You are playing as the revolutionaries, which are no better than the KPA themselves as you drag defenceless civilians into your conflict. Very well knowing they will get killed on spot. It isn't by mistake though, as the writer acknowledges this fact with a quite vocal character you meet really early on.
Overall, this might be one of my favourite sandbox shooters to date.
I really like it.
It's definitely worth a buy.
EDIT: I just flew through the game to finish the campaign and story DLCs. I take it back. The writing is pretty damn good.
Starting the game again on the hardest difficulty with all UI turned off, Music at 0% and going through the game fully. Doing all side missions, capturing all strongholds and exploring the world, put me in in a position where I can confidently say that this game trumps all other open world shooters in the category of FarCry and Just Cause. The immersion is just ridiculous. With not many games I can just put my headset on and sit back to immerse myself in a world, and this game does just that. It's a true gem.

Legend of Grimrock 2 is a solid iteration of the first game, offering largely the same kind of gameplay but also boasting a bigger world, more content, and improved game mechanics. While it's not without some flaws, and there are parts of the game that I feel were done better in the original - overall it's still an enjoyable experience.
.
Thanks to a nice mix of dungeons and newly added outdoor areas, environments are a lot more interesting and diverse. Characters are more interesting to develop with the revamped skill system, and chargeable special attacks add an extra level of depth to combat. Progression is less linear and you'll often find yourself backtracking to different parts of the world, gaining access to previously inaccessible areas or secrets (though it can also be frustrating when you don't know where to go and wander into a higher-level area).
On the other hand, I found dungeon design to be somewhat weaker - most fun and memorable battles I've experienced were during boss encounters where there's more open space, cover, and bigger and more interesting enemy combinations. Less can be said about normal dungeon areas, which often put you into narrow corridors or otherwise linear paths or even dead ends. This leaves little to no room for strategy, often causing fights to boil down to "attack with all characters, step backwards, repeat".

Grabbed this game as a value title to take a chance of a turn-based indie strat game -- could NOT be happier. A lot of games have mechanics like this, and a lot of them play the same. This one is full of strategy and meanful and sometimes tough choices. The Rock/Paper/Scissors mechanic with units in games like this is a common trope -- but in this game it shines because there are plenty of different options, certain things trump others for obvious reasons and others for not so obvious, the choice of powers and upgrades over the course of a campaign is meaningful... I always wanted to fight one more battle. A single playthrough won't reveal every power, or even every unit -- there is depth and replayability here. I'll also say, that subjectively -- the anime art style is not my favorite... and that was NOT an obstacle to me enjoying the game a whole lot. If you actually LIKE the chibi/anime/whatever japanime style that comes with the narrative it could only be a better buy. The story is also very interesting and compelling -- for what it is, the characters are fun and relatable and you'll start to have favorites. Almost every battle can introduce new allies or enemies, which was constantly satisfying. I have seen games like this that fall flat on their faces... this one does a friggin' HEADSTAND. RECOMMENDED.

One of my favorite things to do in a video game is blowing stuff up, and I’m sure there are a lot of you who feel the same way. Bomberman used to be a good option to scratch that particular itch, but after more than 40 entries in the franchise, they became rather stale. Enter Burnstar, an attempt to fuse the classic Bomberman gameplay with the elements of a puzzle game. And luckily for all of us pyromaniacs, this mix works surprisingly well.
As I mentioned before, Burnstar is heavily inspired by the Bomberman franchise. So much in fact, that you immediately become familiar with the controls: You run around while placing bombs that create new routes through the level. There is one main difference: the goal of each level is not to blow up your enemy, but to blow up the level itself. Each mission has two progress bars. You fill the first with blowing up crates, and the second with collecting stars that are dropped by the objects you blow up.
The most important aspect of Burnstar is strategically placing those bombs. You see, there is a certain hierarchy behind the crates. Three different sizes of crates, red, orange and yellow respectively, are scattered around the level. If a crate is set on fire, it blows up and burns smaller crates around them. This doesn’t work in reverse: a red crate can burn the orange and yellow ones, but yellow crates can’t set the red and orange ones on fire. This is an essential part of Burnstar, and mastering this mechanic is the key to completing the game.
The percentage of burned crates isn’t the only victory requirement. You also have to collect a certain number of stars, that are hidden behind purple goo or underneath the level. Blow these up via the bombs or crates and the stars will appear. If you’ve played Bomberman before, you’re probably thinking that this all sounds pretty easy. Well, it isn’t. In Burnstar, you only get a certain amount of bombs. Make one mistake and you  have to restart the level. Add that to the many times you’ll die because of an exploded crate or an enemy that appears out of nowhere, and you have the recipe for a challenging puzzler.
Most of the difficulty won’t come from merely completing the levels. Completing Burnstar is no cakewalk, but finishing the 60 levels is definitely doable and will only take you a couple of hours. The meat of the game is perfecting every stage by blowing everything up and doing so in time. This  requires  a certain amount of trial & error, a mechanic that will appeal to some people but one that I’m not particularly fond of. What I like more are the various secrets you can collect. Based on the location you have to choose the right character, each with its own unique ability like dashing and teleporting, and then figure out how you have to reach the collectable in the first place. It’s basically a puzzle within a puzzle.
As you can probably tell from this review, I like Burnstar a lot. It takes the best parts of Bomberman and puzzle games and combines them into one great whole. Even though perfecting the game isn’t for me, I had a lot of fun figuring out the puzzles and of course blowing stuff up. Whether you’re looking for a new puzzle game or a solid Bomberman alternative, you can’t go wrong with Burnstar.

I know the term "hidden gem" is cliched, but it's a perfect descriptor for Rive.
Practically unknown, huge quality, fun to play, good voice acting, silly and self referential humor, and great level design.
I got it in the most recent Humble Bundle and went in, not knowing anything about it and having never heard anything about it.
Played it from start to finish. I don't do that often.
As for a quick description of the game - you're piloting a tank through an abandoned ship controlled by a seemingly homicidal video-game loving AI. It's a side-scroller, for the most part, but the gameplay changes in various sections as the games progresses.
The game is short, clocking in at a bit under 6 hours for my first fulll playthrough with no extras, but it's the perfect length, I think, because I had just enough time to upgrade my tank fully and experience everything that the game had to offer in the "ship" setting.
Controls are tight. I never felt like I was out of control of my tank. I used KB/M, but it seems as if it'd fit controller play just as well.
Difficulty is up and down. I played it on the hard setting and was certainly challenged. Many areas I breezed through, although a few spots I was so hung up on that I retried them nearly a hundred times. It was never really *too* difficult, although in one particular section, I felt like lucky drops were more important than actual skill in completing it. That said, I still always felt incredibly accomplished when I cleared them.
Overall, I'd absolutely suggest a play. This game needs more recognition and I'd like nothing more than to see a sequel of some sort one day down the line.

Haven't regularly played a wrestling game since Smackdown! 2 on the Playstation. Saw a good deal on WWE2k16, figured what the heck, I'll try it.
There's a lot to like in the game, but matches can often go from fun to absolutely infuriating based on the dumbest things. I get that handicap matches are supposed to put the player at a disadvantage, but there should not be the *added* disadvantage of having the game ignore you when you're trying to target a specific opponent. For example, in the Showcase, there's a Stone Cold vs. Vince and Shane McMahon ladder match. I can't even count how many times I would turn Austin towards Shane and try to strike or grapple, only to have Austin magically spin around and flail in Vince's direction. The game's decision for when you can or can't target someone seems completely arbitrary.
Similarly, attempting to grapple an opponent standing right in front of me works 90% of the time, but 10% of the time, inexplicably, my character just sits there doing nothing, allowing the opponent to recover, often costing me the match. This is inexcusable.
On top of that is the counter system, which basically turns every match into a game of chicken to see who's going to blink first. If I have four counters, and my opponent has four counters, the first one to use a counter is at an *immediate* disadvantage for the remainder of the match. For example, let's say Austin vs. Rock, each with four counters. If I'm Austin and I counterattack to get out of a bad situation, Rock has 4, and I have 3. That means my BEST CASE SCENARIO is Rock counters (3,3), I counter (2,3), Rock counters (2,2), I counter (1,2), Rock counters, (1,1), I counter (0,1), Rock counters (0,0). We're now both empty, but because he got the last counter, he has absolute control of the match, and I can basically just put my controller down and walk away for a minute or two, because I can't do ANYTHING. Counters recharge over time, but as soon as I've regenerated one, he's regenerated one too, and he's still controlling the match, which means I HAVE to use mine first, but as soon as I do, he'll use his, and he's back in control again.
There's actually some strategy into how this can work in a tag team match or triple threat (though those come with the targeting/nonsense mentioned above), but in a singles match, the counter system effectively punishes whoever uses it first.
On top of all that, the game either has no real tutorial, or has hidden it well. The NXT career and Showcase modes offer some tips, but leave others out, and there seems to be no rhyme or reason to what is and isn't taught. For example, the game teaches you the submission minigame, but never teaches you how to actually start a submission on an opponent. It teaches you the collar-and-elbow tie-up minigame, but never teaches you how to initiate a collar-and-elbow tie-up. Never tells you how to climb ladders or cages. Never tells you how to target another opponent.
It's frustrating, because when the game isn't being super goddamn annoying, it can actually be fun! But the moment your character randomly decides not to grapple when you're telling him to, or decides to target someone outside the ring instead of the opponent standing next to him in the ring, the fun instantly stops; all that's left is yelling at your monitor.

TL;DR 8.5/10 - Great game. Highly recommend, especially to Magic players who were left disappointed by Hearthstone.
This game brings Magic: The Gathering into the modern era. With the quick game time, balance patches, and fun but not over-the-top interface, this game is everything I hoped it would be. The card design is fantastic, and taking the blocking and instant ("fast spell") rules from Magic makes the game far more dynamic than Hearthstone.
Furthermore, the "Free to Play" onboarding experience is great! Right from the beginning, the game starts throwing cards at you and doesn't stop. I have not yet felt the need to spend money to buy cards, and it feels like grinding and playing will actually be a decent way to build a collection up towards viable Tier 1 decks. (I did, however, make a small gem purchase to support the development.) It also doesn't feel like I'm missing out by not having a complete collection. Opening packs brings me back to the early days of MtG when each new card was exciting and fun.
The one flaw at the moment is the limited card pool. Although it is an impressive quantity and quality for the first set, I cannot wait until more sets are released. I would also like to see a game chat to talk with opponents, but I understand why that might not be desirable.

During my first foray into the Steam sale over Christmas, a friend of mine alerted me to a game on sale for 50 cents. How could I say "no" to that opporunity? I didn't care what it was. Much to my happiness, the game turned out to be quite fun and a lookback into the 1980s.
is a 2010 flash game from developer Terry Cavanagh, known for his retro-style, 2D games.
The story of
is easy to dismiss since the game's main feature is it's puzzle platforming gameplay rather than storytelling. You play Captain Viridian, commander of a science space vessel that gets caught in "dimensional interference" forcing evacuation through a trans-dimensional portal. You quickly discover that your crew has been scattered across multiple dimensions and are tasked with their individual rescue.
Controls are very simplistic. If you were to rank a game's control complexity on a scale of "Dive Kick" to "Steel Battalion",
would rank just above Dive Kick.  Left and right directionals plus an action key are all there is. The most notable limitation is you cannot jump. Instead, the action key reverses your character's direction of gravity from the floor to the ceiling and vice versa.  This, combined with the various puzzles of the different levels, defines the gameplay. You use your lone ability to traverse the map avoiding enemies and, most notably, the endless plethora of death spikes, the appearance of which one could argue contributes to the game's namesake (the game's title is actually named for the dimension your ship is stuck in).
The is no health meter and, thankfully, no limit to the number of lives, for you will be dying a lot. However, I surprisingly found myself not being at all frustrated with this for a few reasons. There's no death sequence; respawns are near instantaneous and checkpoints are rather frequent. Also, the simple joy I got from trying to figure out how to safely traverse a section using the unique controls deterred "rage quitting" at least for me. There is a death counter in the pause menu if you like to see how many times you've died since starting the game.
The game is rather fast paced, but for those whose eyes have a terrible time keeping up, the game's speed can be dialed back. A time trial mode, no death run, and flipped mode are also unlockable for the truly hardcore.
Visuals are textbook Commodore 64 era.  If you're a spoiled child of 3D visuals, bright bloom, and HDR lighting, you will find none of it here.
is classic 8-bit, 2D display with nothing entirely special about it. It's a simple thowback to gaming days of yore. All characters are the same model, differentiated by solid color alone, with only two facial expressions (happy and sad) while legs move about a pixel width back and forth during movement. Enemies appear in forms ranging from squares of garbaled mess to seemingly arbitrary words and numbers flying across the screen.
I was instantly in love with the soundtrack scored by chiptune artist Magnus Palsson. The tunes are incredibly catchy, upbeat, triumphant at times, and you'll find yourself having many of the songs stuck in your head for days on end.  If I wasn't too into the game itself, I'd play the game simply for it's scoring. I wouldn't put it past myself to turning the game on and pausing it at a certain level just to listen to the music although that's easily accomplised by YouTube.  The songs are also available for purchase through the composer's website.
is a great puzzle platformer anyone is sure to enjoy. The programming is solid and simple.  I never came across a single glitch.  System requirements are not worth mentioning as any 10-year-old PC could probably handle this game. Nothing hampered my enjoyment short of dying 100 times on one obstacle. Your patience will be tested, your eyes will work a little harder, and your ears will be singing praises.   Check out
on Steam and Nintendo 3DS.  An iOS, Android, Ouya, and PS Vita release are slated for 2014.

So I finally bought it during the summer sale. I was interested since the first appearance because of the positive reviews, but the reports on the overaggressive AI were quite disappointing. I am the hardcore simmer type, but at the same time, I love F1 and wanted to love the official video game. But couldn't, even though I tried with what was celebrated as one of the best installments in the series, F1 2013. It just couldn't draw me in.
F1 2016 did draw me in, however. 5.6 hours on the very first day, though I only wanted to give it the "2hrs before refund" go. I have spent some fun hours in Dirt Rally, which made me suspicious. And now my suspicion has been reinforced. I'm not sure, but
So many aspects of F1 (rivalry, R&D, high life etc) have been perfectly nailed, and now the driving experience is much better, too. Difference between tyre compounds and the impact of physical damage on the car feels nice. And meanwhile, the visuals are mindblowing - just run a race in Bahrain with the setting sun, and you'll have no doubts in that regards.
My greatest concern, besides the driving feel was the AI, and I think this is one of the final issues that CM must somehow resolve as soon as possible (too bad that they are not going to mend it in this title ever). It is so bad that I almost asked for a refund after the first two hours. I later realised that you can get used to SOME of the aspects of their driving. But be prepared: you will want to run several championships with this game, and whenever you'll be racing, you will feel genuine terror because of the opponents. Their sudden slow downs in unexpected places (places which you'll have to learn to succeed), their train-like lane changes, their overall insane agressivity will make you feel like you are being hunted out there. But if you somehow survive the carnage (it's not entirely impossible), then you will have the best F1 gaming experience since Geoff Grammond's GP series and and F1 Challenge.
Since I have restarted my simracing hobby almost three years ago, F1 2016 is one of the biggest and most unexpected positive disappointments for me. In many areas, the best hardcore sims could learn from it (like the fixed tyre collection for the weekend instead of use as many tires as you wishe, timed repairs taking away from total session time instead of have as many brand new cars as you wish etc), whereas the official F1 content and the perfect career mode makes it one of the most immersive games I have raced with. Learn to live with the AI, and you will have much fun. Definitely worth 15 bucks.

i look back on this game after seeing the ridiculous $24.99 pricetag of SUPERHOT to comment on receiver's incredibly low price /and/ innovative design.  for a production time of seven days, this is a substantial gaming experience.  (excuse my hour and a half gameplay time on this comment, but believe me.)
basics of the game is your now-classic indie survival collectathon.  start out in a randomly generated map, with randomly generated inventory consisting of one of two possible guns (m1911 and what looks like a .32 revolver), and your mission is to A) survive and B) collect tapes.
realistic handling of a firearm in a video game is what should pull you to buy this game, because that's what it guarantees.  the survival aspect and the tapes are literally just dressing around this mechanic.  bullets can be acquired loosely or in magazines.  loose bullets can be immediately loaded into the revolver, and must be loaded into a magazine with available capacity for the m1911.
the only conflict you'll encounter in this eerie cyberpunk polygonathon are turrets and drones.  turrets scan horizontally around a room from a fixed location and drones fly around, general♥♥♥♥♥♥  but neither of these enemies, nor yourself, are bullet sponges.  for a kill: one to two bullets per drone, a minimum of one per turret, and around two for you.
the story is negligible.  literally.  while the gameplay is actually super immersive and really does give you a feel for what you would do when confronted with a situation like this, the story is vague and lacks substance.
receiver is a game that you should play if you are interested in game design or enjoy firearms and realistic representations of them in games.  is it game of the year for its year?  no.  is it an 8 hour AAA title with side quests and an engaging story?  definitely not.  it IS a very interesting novelty, and worth $4.99 USD price.
getting back to the point though, SUPERHOT is extremely comparable to receiver.  very entertaining concepts and fairly short, novelty experiences.  save your money and buy this game, play it for a bit, and wait for SUPERHOT to get a price cut.
rating: 8 / 10  --  impressive and concise.  nothing is wasted, if anything, receiver leaves you wanting more.
Overall, great game, brilliant story line, fun, interesting and unique gameplay and world, I definitely recommend this game for all who love FPS' and RPG's.

Well, From Software, you really screwed this up, didn't you.
Before you read this, you gotta know that I started with DSI, then DS3 (which I played before the 2 because it was one of the rare occasion where I could have a more expensive game). I loved them both, and DS1 made the Dark Souls series immediatly one of my favorites. However, I've heard a lot of people bashing DS2. I thought: "Why? Seems quite like the others. I gotta play it too."
And, my bad. I realized why people didn't like the poor Dark Souls 2.
I'll start with the pros, first.
Graphically, the game is pretty good. Its optimization, however, is absolutely amazing. I can run the thing in maximum settings on an Nvidia GT740 (this GPU is quite a pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥. So, the graphic argument is 20/20. Too bad they didn't keep that kind of godlike optimization on DS3, however.
The emerald herald. It's the firekeeper lady in Majula. Yeah, you can guess that I was desperate to find another good point to the game. Well, let's go with the ugly then...
And let's start by the essence of frustration itself: the gameplay. It looks like DS1, in theory, except that everything is slower. Rolling takes at least three times the stamina it used to (stamina which regenerates as slow as a snail under the grip of acid), and it's been nerfed (you gotta increase your AGL stat to gain some few frames of invulnerability while rolling, but that doesn't change that much imo). The character takes literaly hours to get his estus flask, and the regeneration it provides goes very slowly (unlike the other episodes where it just instantly filled the health bar). That, my friend, will cost you many, many deaths. Pretty much everything in the damn game became slower and incredibly frustrating. And there's also the soul memory, aka a perfectly useless system which only purpose is to prevent you from playing in coop with your friends. I mean honestly, this system has no need to exist.
But what about the bosses then? Easy. They just die so quick that you can't even focus on their theme (which are pretty meh anyway). But then, why is the game frustrating then?
Mobs. It's not that the mobs are particularly hard to beat. They're all pretty simple, to be honest. Either ranged or melee. But the thing is that the difficulty was made by number. Have fun trying to slay three knights in front of you while being assaulted by four different archers in four different, remote locations. Instead of "Scholar of the first sin", the edition could have been called "Prepare to throw your controller at the screen" or something. The game is just that frustrating: Horde of ennemies who continually staggers you, giving you no time to drink estus, and when you beat them or run past them, all you encounter is a lame boss with meh lore and a meh theme.
It's honestly a shame, since the lore over Vendrick was interesting. The passage with the memories was possibly one of my favorite concept from the game. But sadly, the rest of the game is just average/bad. Where DS1 and 3 made practically all of their bosses epic, those in DS2 are just merely a soul farming tool.
Well, back to an important point of the DS series: The music. Well, the few I've heard of the boss themes was rather dull. The only tracks I do remember in this game are Majula (the game lobby, equivalent to the other game's Firelink Shrine) and the credit song, which was in my opinion far too pretty for the dissapointment this game was.
Now I've just finished the main story, going through as much side stories as I could. I've heard that "The DLCs of DSII were actually better than the game itself" so I gave a quick try to Crown of the Iron King. What did I meet? Tons of ennemies without much characteristics, only their strenght was their number, and that is honestly a poor move to add difficulty. So after all the♥♥♥♥♥♥I went through in this game, I thought it was time to stop it; I choose not to give the DLCs a try. Maybe later on, if I'm really bored; but for now, I just don't feel like doing this. The game is too much of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to play. Perhaps if the combat wasn't so lame and clunky, the spam of ennemies wouldn't have been a problem. Perhaps...
Seeing Dark Souls 2, I feel glad that From Software went back in the right direction with Bloodborne and Dark Souls 3. I've finished Dark souls 1 with all achievements, and I'm currently trying to 100% Dark Souls 3 as well, while waiting for the next DLC to come out.
This is something I will not do with Dark Souls 2. I didn't feel the same eagerness to complete it that DS1 and 3 gave me. I feel sad, for I really hate to♥♥♥♥♥♥on this game. But a credit song and the emerald herald aren't a justification to such lame game mechanics, particularly when you had excellent bases with Dark Souls 1. Yeah, perhaps the game runs like a charm on a lesser computer. But remember that the most important point in a game is the gameplay... which, in Dark Souls 2, became the fatal flaw of the game.

This is by far the best WW1 representation on the market, but be wary, no matter how hard you try to look at it, this is still an FPS.
Breakdown:
Why I love this game:
-The maps are fanastic. Good mix of trench warfare and no man's land shootouts. Some maps reward some forms of play more than others, though. Some maps are a real royal rumble of close quarters firefights, some are snipefests, but most are balanced and allow both front-line and back-line roles to enjoy themselves.
-Weapons are so incredibly satisfying. Never has a bolt-action rifle felt so good. Rifles feel nice and meaty, pistols have a good kickback to them. Sniping is an art; ballistics and depth of field exist, as does the light loss from magnification, so distinguishing targets at extreme range is harder than first expected. I can't talk about MGs as I have never used one in battle.
-Squad variety is good, with a mix of recon, standard and defensive specialties, and you can swap roles (assuming the other player consents) and squad types (assuming 2 other squadmates consent) to suit the state of the battle. Sticking together is also rewarded as each squad's Officer has a command aura that grants certain bonuses depending on the squad specialty.
My problems with it:
-I'm bad at FPS. And this is a problem if you are too, because no matter how you look at it, this is still an FPS. If you and a Jerry come round a corner at the same time and he has better reflexes, he's still going to shoot first.
-There is also a certain frustration in looking at the enemy team and seeing someone with a better than 10:1 kill ratio because he's sat at the other end of the map with a static MG shooting anything that moves, even the snipers supposed to counter him. I usually snipe, and I will die several times before I eventually find him, then I'll die again because I showed my head, and only then can I try to outsmart and take him out, while he's still racking up the kills, and even then, he's back in position in 30 seconds. My observer trying to find him? Dead too. The NCO trying to find him so he can mortar the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of that MG ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥? Dead.
-Sorry, I'm going on a bit. What I'm trying to say is, this game can be incredibly frustrating against an experienced enemy, and you will be against an experienced enemy. The playerbase is limited, a full game is rare and there is no MMR-based matchmaking. A noob like me doesn't stand a chance half the time, and that's not a fun experience.
-You need friends to overcome this. To get the most out of this game you need a squad of friends and voice comms, because if you don't, the other team will.
In brief, this is a fantastic effort, and a truly unique experience, but if you're useless at FPS like me, your milage may vary.

(This game was gifted to me fyi)
*THIS REVIEW HAS BEEN EDITED TO REFLECT THE GAME AS IT IS RIGHT NOW, AS SOME DETAILS ARE OUTDATED + I GOT GUD*
I can see the passion for this game and why it has a dedicated community. Realistic first person shooters are hard to come by, especially now. It has a steep learning curve (getting over the fact that you die in one shot from most guns is essential). Reading the game's manual is important to understanding the functions of each squad. K/D ratio does not apply to skillful play in Verdun (the officers always have more kills from mortar strikes anyway). What matters is how good you are with working with your squad and helping the team win over the trenches.
Frontlines mode is the definitive way to play this game. It's as essential to serving the game mechanics as the casual/competitive modes of CS:GO, the co-op mode of Doom, and the deathmatch mode of Quake. To understand what makes Verdun's quirks so good, Frontlines is what you play. Basically, one team defends a trench and the other attempts to take it over. If the attacking team fails, the defensive team gets to take the opposing team's trench, switching the roles up. This repeats until the match time runs out and either one team has taken more trenches or there's a draw. There's nothing more frightening than when you're on the offense and your attack fails, forcing you to run back to your trench to defend it. There's no other game mode like it, and it shows that a game based off of WWI combat can indeed be made.
The matchmaking has mostly been fixed by now, although now the opposite happens and once every fortnight, I can't join a squad a friend created.
Optimization could be a lot better. I know there’s a guide from the devs to help out people experiencing poor frame rate, but they could still do a better job with post-processing effects. Depth of field, for some reason, killed my framerate even though I'm using an Intel i5 processor and a 2GB video card while playing at 720p. Verdun's a powerhog, although that fault is more on Unity's end anyway (EDIT: Lowering shadows also helps a lot, now I can play at 1080p/60 FPS most of the time). Some maps can also drop the frame rate down to 35 or lower, which is always jarring.
Some of the mechanics are half-baked and should have been cleaned up a long time ago. Animations aren’t polished,
I'm dead wrong. You can cancel reloads, and knowing where to take cover is something that you learn eventually. Still, there are moments where my sights are on an enemy at close range and yet I somehow didn't hit him at all, Pulp Fiction style. I don't know why that happens, but it sours the experience for me.
And now my most nitpicky complaint: The community is hit or miss. Me and my friends have met some positive and friendly people who play the game strategically and are willing to help the team out with callouts. And of course, there's a lot of stubborn Call of Duty/Battlefield kiddies who don't play strategically and instead just run out into the open, get shot, and complain in the chat about it. There will always be toxic people playing online games, but Verdun has a small community that takes no♥♥♥♥♥♥ This game doesn't rock 600,000 players every day like CS:GO does. If you're not willing to learn and get better, stick to rifle deathmatch and get better at aiming or go back to COD (EDIT: This is still relevant. Also, I've seen people complain about the lack of tutorials. It's an understandable complaint, but this game already has a lot of guides available for you to read. This is really a game that you have to experience to get the hang with).
Even with all of its issues, I can't help but recommend Verdun. It's a unique FPS that needs a lot more love from players. If you stick with it like I did and go with the punches from the learning curve, you'll have an amazing time on par with Red Orchestra/Rising Storm. Hopefully Tannenburg improves the formula and brings its promised fixes over to this one.

Here's my review for Burnstar!
Release Date: 03/18/2015
Developer: Nerve Software Available on Steam for PC for a limited time for 10% off! Sale price of 8.99 (9.99 regularly) (And worth every cent!)
Purchase link :
Author's statement:
Don't worry it won't be super long, but it will be detailed enough to give whomever decides to read this to the fullest a basic to good grasp of the game in general. (Otherwise feel free to get popcorn and a drink this review isn't going anywhere for some time. It'll be here when you come back, I promise, unless you close it or something happens to cause this close.)
Prologue:
The game is fantastically fun, addictive and challenging (sometimes even outright merciless), but in such a way you don't want to throw your controller or keyboard (the controller is recommended by the fine developers at Nerve Software) through the window or monitor, but instead take a breather and go "I know I can figure this out, it's got to have some sort of pattern to it. I'm just over thinking it."
Some (myself included) just thought of this as a Bomberman clone, but after playing it. I will gladly take that back and say if it is a clone it is a definite thinking man's Bomberman. But really it's so much more than a clone, it has it's own flavor of a puzzle-action game that just so happens to have 4 way explosion bombs in it. Because once you get past that, the similarities stop to a degree.
Because the premise of the game is blow all the stuff up, burn all the things, and collect all the shinies!
The storyline:
An evil corporation (literally named Evil. Inc) has came to Burnstar's home, Fairway Island, and has laid waste to it with goo and boxes of goo everywhere! (Cue dramatic music here.) Enter Burnstar (and company) to save their island!
The Characters:
Burnstar: The main protagonist and namesake of the game who can run short bursts at an accelerated rate.
Ember:  His adoptive sister who has a shield that both blocks her from damage and drags stars toward her in a short radius, however leaves her stationary.
Coldsnap: A scientist who worked for Evil. Inc trying to develop a way to freeze the goo away and somehow stabbed herself with the syringe thus giving her Ice Man abilities! Okay that is a bit of a stretch, but does give her the ability to throw Sub-Zero freeze balls at obstacles and freeze them and as long as you're in a safe area (because you'll be stationary) control them! So take THAT Sub-Zero! (Please don't kill me, I'm only a writer.)
And
Toxo: A clone of someone who wants to kill Burnstar (that's gotta be a bit of an awkward situation). Who has the ability to reproduce more clones, albeit a clone of a clone is bound to have some issues somewhere down the line so you get a purple blob clone who can attract baddies and be a very temporary shield or a button pusher for you on top of being an instant teleport back across a large map, but is stuck swaying back and forth in a single spot waiting for something to happen.
Each have their advantages and disadvantages in each map, but the maps are designed in such a fashion that sure it may be easier for let's say, Coldsnap, to do a map. Burnstar would be able to do the same map as well with really not much more effort. And it gives the game an extra little boost so you're not just stuck with one option through out the game. To me, it makes the game a bit more replayable as well, because the way you solve the map for each character can change slightly or down right all together.
Gameplay:
As I stated before the premise of the game is to; blow all the stuff up (make sure none of the boxes are left standing because they contain the goo and the goo is bad, mmm'kay?), burn all the things (burn all the boxes of goo and the goo on the ground because, remember the goo is bad, mmm'kay?), and collect all the shinies (as you blow up all the stuff, and burn all the things, stars will appear and you're to collect all the stars). As you start out it is like you are learning to ride the bike and Nerve is holding the bike steady for you as you learn how to play (ride). But by level 4 they've now put training wheels on your Burnstar bike, they're just standing by watching you and all is right in the world of Burnstar, as you gleefully pedal faster and faster. By the time the midway point of the first tier, Nerve has slipped away while you ride your cute little tasseled Burnstar bike with the training wheels off, but they've never stop watching you. Because as they introduce new mechanics into the game you truly feel as if they're trying to help you understand it better and get used to it first before really pushing you to hard.
(Now this analogy flies out the window if you can find the hidden levels. Because, the hidden levels they've not only ripped your training wheels off they've now put you in a skate park and told you to master riding your Burnstar bike, oh and just for giggles in the hidden level skate park they've thrown lava in random areas, spikes, you know the "fun" stuff for them to laugh manically about, while you try and maintain your balance.)
As I briefly touched on, Blow up all the stuff means blow up all the boxes. Boxes range in color from Yellow (they catch fire but do not explode), Orange (they catch fire and after a short duration explode in a four way explosion much like your bombs), and Red (they act just like the orange boxes but instead of exploding in a small 4 way explosion, they explode in a large 4 way explosion.) I won't tell you all the details of how to make stuff explode, as it is better to play around and figure the puzzles out for yourself. I will say this however, you only get a certain amount of bombs per level and there are more than one way to catch things on fire and blow stuff up. Next would be burn all the things, the goo and boxes. Goo is scattered throughout the levels and catches fire  by being touched be something on fire or explosions, and (hint) causes chain-reactions sometimes. And finally, collect all the shinies, collect all the stars that appear after stuff burns and explodes. And that's pretty much it.
Overall:
I highly recommend this game and it is a definitely worth the 10 dollar price tag.
Have fun feeding your pyromaniac dreams everyone!

The game provides plenty of possibilities for the player to choose their own challenge. Five races, eight classes and 16 skills are paired with the need to form a specialized party of up to four characters. Three different difficulty settings govern the speed and thrill of the very dynamic combat system. As an Old-School RPG veteran I chose to play at the highest difficulty and preferred to draw my own maps instead of enabling the game's automap feature. Additional options exist to raise the challenge even higher. I was very happy to experience a higher difficulty setting not only in terms of more incoming damage and less output, but rather mainly in an increase of the combat's pace. I also didn't get stuck in an unfair combat situation, although different situations did often require to adapt one's strategy, which I highly appreciate in a game.
Some puzzles were really challenging, having me ask my partner and roommates for advice and inspiration. I'm proud that I never used help from a guide or an internet discussion; with a reasonable amount of creativity it is possible to solve all of the riddles. Hardly any of the harder puzzles is story-relevant, so there's also the option of moving on and returning later to loot that particular room of booty.
I mainly played in a candlelit room on a wall flat screen wearing headphones. I was often able to locate secret passages by the sounds of monsters behind walls. I could always tell from the direction of the sound in which corridor that blasted zombie was currently looking for me. On more than one occasion I heard myself scream in surprise or even fear when suddenly I realized some monster sneaked up on me! I highly recommend playing this game with an adept surround sound system!
If you love hack'n'slay games, online raiding parties, bragging about your new epic item in front of your friends and skipping story and text in favor of action, this game is NOT for you!
If you are an arachnophobiac, musophobiac, herpetophobiac, necrophobiac, nyctophobiac, hylophobiac, eremophobiac, ophidiophobiac or potamophobiac, this game is DEFINITELY not for you!
If you like games emphasizing social interaction, telling a detailed, pre-cut and pre-chewed story or featuring a lot of spoken dialogue, you might consider asking yourself if you can do without any of this. If not, don't play it, you'll just be disappointed.
To anybody else: By all means, give it a try! Chances are even if-unlike me-you don't find your next favourite video game, you will be having a great time on the beautiful Isle of Nex!

I normally don't like puzzle games, but I sat down with Burnstar and really got into it.
It does have a slight Bomber man thing going, but aside from placing bombs and being more or less gridlike it's very different than the classic game.
Your goal is to spread fire throughout a level as thoroughly as possible while using the least amount of the explosives that each level gives for your disposal. But fire spreads in a very distinct way. Big objects spread fire further and light smaller objects on fire. Smaller boxes have a harder time lighting bigger boxes but there are exceptions that you have to learn and be aware of. This isn't the exact best explanation but that's part of the "puzzle" so I'll let you figure the rest out.
But while you walk around the level you're trying to assess the best way to spread fires throughout because the number of tools you have to start fires are limited. As you get further into the game you're going to have to do the above without dying from various level hazards, and that's when I really think it pulled me in. Light all this stuff on fire in the most controllled and fast way possible, but also don't die. (There's a really quick level restart button so failure feels like failure, but you're back in it before you've really gotten down on yourself.)
Other stuff....There are four characters to choose from and each one has a unique ability, but honestly I just end up playing Burnstar because well...he's really fast and I like to go fast even if it means I die a lot.
Oh, there's actually a surprising amount of content here. The whole game has the like...I just bought an old N64 game feel where there's actually a ton of content shipped with the game..I guess what I'm trying to say is it feels complete. I've put quite a few hours in and I haven't even beat it yet. You have to work your way through all these worlds Mario style and I can't really remember how many more I have to go.

Fantastic Card Game. Can't miss it if you are card games fan!
Unique combat system: (same names but very different from Hearthstone)
- Relic weapons for your hero. This kind of weapons give your hero a certain amount of armor. If armor is depleted, the weapon is then broken. Otherwise, you can use your weapon for infinite times. If you are beginner and don't want to invest, play with AI first. Playing with AI (which is called Gauntlet mode in game) is free now, and gives you lots of awards.

Actually every pack costs 1000g and contains 12 cards. Despite the 48 cards you should get whatsoever, you earn more card packs if you win more in Draft. If you have a really good understanding of this game, you will earn a lot with some efforts.
So you don't really have to invest in this game, just earn cards when enjoying combats with many interesting decks.

WARNING - This review might be a little biased, this was my first and favourite Final Fantasy game(s)!
I was on the fence over this one for quite a while, but I decided to pick it up the other day. My concern was videos I watched made some characters look rather awful compared to in the PS2 (for example the intro, look at the faces) and I didn't find this different when I ran the game - however pretty much after that has been surpassing my expectations. The higher resolution and spruced up textures are more noticeable than you realise, some things stand out more (in a good way) than you may recall on the PS2. For example I thought the Mi'hen High Road had an awesome backdrop which I don't recall being so nice to look at on the original.
If you want the original soundtrack (in FFX) you can choose and switch between that and the remastered one, which is good since I prefer the original personally. Additionally both games are the international versions, which include extra content (FFX-2 never had this outside of Japan originally, fun fact!) so you really won't be lacking in things to do - the worry might be more the hours it will eat up.
As of the time of writing this review had absolutely no problem running the game on max settings on my medium end PC. I have had a few stutters where framerate may of dropped for a split second but this is a minor issue that has rarely happened, and I am still playing around with things to resolve this - it should be noted a mod is available that claims to be able to help with things such as this too, as well as adding other additional features. The game only runs at 30fps, and it's unlikely this will ever change due to it being an old console game originally but it works fine with the turn based gameplay.
I could keep going on but it would only become an even more unreadable mountain of text. The verdict from me is simple - if like me you are a FFX/FFX-2 fan this is a very nice buy, and worth the time if you want to play through again. If you haven't played them before FFX, though a little dated noticeably, has a fantastic story and is well worth the playthrough. FFX-2 wasn't very popular but is in its own right also a good game worth playing without doubt, just very different to what you may of played before. You'll see what I mean if you pick this up.
Ultimately if you enjoy a good rpg (or two?!) you get great value for money on this.
