Since Max Verstappen is keeping the Dutch pride high in the Formula 1, I started watching and following it. Yeah, I knew people like Schumacher, Raikonnen and Alonso because my dad watched it since he was young, but since Verstappen, the F1 took my interest as well. And after a few races on my television screen I wanted to find the possibility to get in a car myself. And now with the Summer Sale, I picked up this game for 15 bucks, since I didn't want to blow the full prize with F1 2017 so close around the corner. Here's my actual review about the game ;)
Compared to what I've seen from older F1 games on YouTube, I really think the game has the best gameplay on almost every front. It's solid, great and there's not really much to say about it!
The graphics of this game are absolutely beautiful. You will need some kind of good PC to run it on the highest settings, but even on lowest (yes, I tried and highered up until the point that my fps got too low), it still looks good. I've not seen texture glithces or whatsoever, so the graphics are awesome!
Yeah, the AI of this game. Maybe the best out there. But also maybe the most aggressive? When I get hit in the rear, sometimes it's my own stupid fault, but I see a lot of times where I have the right space and do the right thing in the moment and some AI car still brakes too late and just knocks me out of the race. This doesn't happen mid race or at the end that much, but it's almost every first corner after the start. But hey, maybe I'm complaining about it too much. The AI is besides that a great feature of this game.
Career mode is probably the most interesting thing this game has to offer. Creating your driver, choosing the team you want to drive for, you call the shots and it's awesome. The rivalries add something fun to it aswell. Only thing is the upgrades you do. I'm currently doing a career with Sauber, but I noticed that once you upgrade a lot, your car just becomes a new Mercedes or something. On one side that's nice, because it puts the competition up, on the other side it's not that realistic. But that could just be me aswell.
Overall this game is awesome and if you like Formula 1 or racing (games) at all, you could pick up this game on a sale. If it's not on sale, I think it's best to wait a little longer before F1 2017 comes out, although I can't guarantee that that game will be as good as this one, of course.

I like games which tell stories. Recently I have been enjoying a computer game genre sometimes described as "walking simulators" - games which aren't based on fast action, shooting, jumping and so on, but are instead more introspective affairs utilising exploration and story as their main elements, occasionally with a few puzzles. Last night I played Gone Home and recommend it if you're interested in this genre.
The setting:
June 7, 1995. 1:15 AM.
You arrive home after a year abroad. You expect your family to greet you, but the house is empty. Something's not right. Where is everyone? And what's happened here?
Gone home is an interactive exploration simulator. Interrogate every detail of a seemingly normal house to discover the story of the people who live there. Open any drawer and door. Pick up objects and examine them to discover clues. Uncover the events of one family's lives by investigating what they've left behind.
I have to be careful what I say since I don't want to give anything away. It hit the perfect sweet spot for me. It's not too long (you can complete it in an evening; quicker if you don't explore every nook and cranny); it inspired different emotions at different times, rather than being one-note; it has believability; it offers an interesting premise and a compelling story revealed gradually. I think most people, gamers or not, could get something from this game if you approach it in a relaxed way, a bit like curling up with a good book. I'm glad games like this exist.
[Note: despite the possibly ominous setting it is not a horror/jumpscare/Hollywood thriller type of story, so if you avoid those types of games, don't avoid Gone Home! It’s heart is about families/people.]

I thought this would be another Far Cry clone or a buggy mess.
It turns out I was wrong.
Imagine my surprise as I picked this title up and got engaged into the story about a minute in. It reminds me of the PS2 era's 'Freedom Fighters' where America is invaded by a foreign force. I realize my tastes rival the average gamer's. I found many mechanics to be intuitive and innovative. For example, instead of customizing your weapon at a work bench like most games, you can modify your weapon out in the battlefield. By pressing 'x', you can change your barrels, foregrips, sights, etc. and your character responds by holding the weapon in its newly modified state. Putting on a foregrip makes him hold it differently than before. Not many would find this amazing but I appreciate the little details like that.
Another little detail I enjoyed was looking down at my feet and seeing that my legs actually reacted with the environment. Standing in an uneven surface makes you stand in a different stance.
The environments are much more detailed than I assumed they would be. There are a lot of open buildings you can walk in and the place just tells a story. I also found that the cities/maps themselves felt alive. The game is open world and the territory you capture has your allies camped out. However, the North Koreans can always come back and take over what they believe to be rightfully theirs.
There are plenty of things to do (see FarCry 4) where you're helping the local population. I'm not one to do side quests and I usually tackle the main mission first on the easiest difficulty. It makes it much more enjoyable. I tend to come back a second time and play the side missions on the hardest setting to really give that immersive feeling.
All-in-all, I give this game a 8/10. It's a hidden gem. You can feel the effort and quality the developers put into the game. I was planning to return this before my 2 hour limit but honestly, after playing this game, I want to keep it. I want to see what happens in the end.

This has to be the most Audacious Example of Bait and Switch I have seen in years, and that includes No Man's Sky!!  I am only giving this the thumbs up because I bought it in a sale for Five Bucks and I genuinely enjoyed the story, if I had full price then I would be very angy indeed.
Firstly this is a VERY short game, I clocked it in just over Two Hours and then went back through to see if I missed anything because it was so short.  Nope, I covered the whole thing and missed out nothing, so yes, it's an incredibally short game.

Homefront: The Revolution is one of those games from the year of 2016, which was a glorious year for the First Person Shooter market, that was released months after the releases of the likes of DOOM 2016 and Overwatch, and this was one of those games that were panned by many critics and other gamers alike for some really notable flaws such as bugs, cringey characters, and the typical "Not elevating the FPS genre" excuse BS.
Now after spending quite a couple of hours with the game, let me tell you ladies and dudes out there why I'm actually recommending this title despite its flaws.
First of all, the overall theme of the game has a lot of potential since the original Homefront. North Korea taking over the USA and playing as a Freedom Fighter in Ethan Brady to fight the Red Army while climbing the ranks of a resistance group? I think that's actually something a lot of people would like to play, especially for those who wished that there are more games that would explore the idea of fighting a fictional representation of a real world threat to democracy, liberty, freedom, and the red white and blue.
Second, the Philadelphia setting is actually quite something here in Homefront: The Revolution. The City of Philly despite being taken over by those damn Norks looks really good with the ever beautiful CryEngine, and overall the graphics of the game when set in High/Ultra are very spot on, with the CryEngine showcasing its really beautiful visuals and effects.
The game also has some pretty spot on sound design for the most part. The weapons in the game actually sound powerful and effective, from the lowly pistol to the actually entertaining Freedom Launcher. The weapons actually have a good PUNCHY sound to them which honestly is a rarity among more of these military themed video games. They actually feel good to use, and I highly recommend EVERYONE to use the Battle Rifle (one of the best weapons in the game from my personal experience) to know what I mean when it comes to some really PUNCHY gun sounds.
As for the game itself, I liked the Weapon modification system here, which was borrowed and tweaked slightly from the likes of Crysis, which is of no surprise considering the game engine used. Watching a Pistol become either a Submachine Gun or even that really interesting Pneumatic pistol, or the Battle Rifle become either the Freedom Launcher or a Sniper Rifle on the fly felt really good.
As far as the general gameplay goes, its fairly above average in most aspects. Like I mentioned previously, the guns sound and feel very effective for the most part, and the game's level design caters well to how the action and the general gameplay flow together.
As for the flaws, it has to be mentioned here. The Bugs and Exploits are all over the place. There is some clipping issues between AI characters and terrain, some sounds play at awkward times. As for Exploits, its highly possible to break the immersive intentions of the game when you can easily abuse the AI in the Yellow Zone sections. Its somewhat entertaining to spend an entire half hour piling up bodies of KPA forces by simply camping in one spot. and with how the game handles its ammo generation system for your weapons, you can easily spend that entire half hour killing as many KPAs as you can in that one camping spot while easily refilling most of your currently equipped weapons.
As for the game's story, this is something that I have a mixed opinion about. I LOVE the idea, but the execution seems to be all over the place. The game wants you to feel sympathy to the city of Philly but most of the characters are hardly appealing save for the AI Resistance fighters you can recruit to fight alongside you. Most of the main resistance characters are hardly likeable yet you will remember them for how much of a bunch of clowns many of them are.
Yet for some reason, why am I recommending this game? Pretty simple. Wolfenstein 2: The New Colossus is coming a few weeks from now, and for some reason, Homefront: The Revolution was that kind of game that has a similar (but of course still very different) setting. America being conquered by a Foreign power. If you want to play a game to unleash your inner MURICA **** YEAH! in you, Homefront: The Revolution is that kind of game you may want to play, especially with the sale the game currently has. Its a flawed game, but its FAR FROM TERRIBLE as what those game reviewers and journalists claim to be. When Homefront: The Revolution works, it frickin works. The game manages to be really fun in many places even with flaws in many places. The important thing here is that the game is still fun, and FUN for me is still of significant importance than just being a technical masterpiece.

The first Homefront was a complete garbage Battlefield Wannabe. This game apparently got the message that people did not want BF lite, and instead turned this game into Far Cry: Red Dawn Lite Edition. It's a huge improvement, and while not one of the all time greats, is at least fun and worth getting on sale.
Obviously it's not as good as an actual Far Cry - more limited weapon selection, smaller maps, less upgrades overall, just to give examples. That said, there's way more to do than the first Homefront, less embarassingly awkward "Press F to hide in corpses in front of the Walmart" moments, and generally doesn't waste your time - no time to think how stupid this whole story is, you've got to get on your motorbike and blow something up!
It's a fun but forgettable open-world FPS. You get the guns to do the missions to get the upgrade points to get more of the guns to do more daring missions. Your weapons are rather anemic to begin with but can be upgraded with KPA points, or modified in the field to have 3 variants each. As in, you take your pistol, remove the receiver and put on a silenced pnemuatic receiver instead. You have a variety of IEDs (referred to as the Guerilla Tool Kit) that start at boring ol' molotovs to RC cars with an emp grenade that can convert drones to your side.
No open-world co-op, but it does feature Far Cry 3-esque missions set on the single player maps with up to 4 players. You create a character who then does missions and gets xp/money, replacing the single player tech point upgrade system. Also you can choose a character class with a starting bonus, including Timesplitter (STOP TAUNTING ME, DEEP SILVER!) and Game Developer. Not many people play, but fun with friends and features pretty much all the features of the single-player game. Not sure why open-world Co-op was not an option, but it makes a good Payday 2 Lite.
In short, pretty much the definition of a fun but forgettable 7/10 game. Get on sale - not a 30 dollar game by any stretch of the imagination, but genuinely fun if you get it 10 USD or under.

This game is amazing, I'm gonna do a quick pros/cons review:
Pro:
-Car handling is good, not enough to be called a simulator per se, but its no arcade/nfs game either.
-The atmosphere and the setting is stunning, they really captured the feeling of driving through the desert, the snow, or the green fields in central USA, the cities are also amazing and expansive.
-Very open ended, you can go to wherever you can see, no exceptions, almost no invisible walls, its awesome.
-Traffic AI is not perfect, but the sheer amount of cars on some sections make it worth it.
-Entretaining multiplayer challenges
-amazing graphics
-Lots of cars, very customizable
-Handling reacts to the terrain
cons:
-Bad soundtrack, very little variety. I found myself either listening to the classical music station, or simply playing some music on the background. This game urgently needs some kind of adaptive radio station to blend in with the atmosphere of each area. Driving through the appalachians? Why not some bluegrass? Driving through arizona/nevada/texas? Some country music would fit in perfectly, driving through the snow? Something more epic would probably be a nice addition. In the end, the soundtrack, which is mostly electronic music only serves if you are in a city, at night. For a game that depends so much on its atmosphere, that's a very significant negative
-The story is better than TDU2, but its still lacking substance.
-It gets a little repetitive, but never really "Grindy", for me at least.
To sum it all up, it manages to capture an atmosphere similar to that of Euro Truck Simulator 2, the best moments in this game weren't spent doing some obnoxious slalom challenges in detroit, but driving calmly down the road to florida. It also feels a lot like Test drive unlimited 2, but this time there is more variety and less bugs. If you like test drive, you are surely gonna want to buy this game.
Ultimately, is it worth buying?
If you care about atmosphere, driving, eventually speeding and sandbox racing, YES, totally, but if you are looking for just another Y0LOSW4G 420 ULTRA FAST CAR R4C1NGE DANK SLALOM 0V3RT4KE 666, then you better stick with games that focus more on that. THIS IS AN OPEN WORLD DRIVING GAME, NOT PURE CIRCUIT RACING GAME!

Well, From Software, you really screwed this up, didn't you.
Before you read this, you gotta know that I started with DSI, then DS3 (which I played before the 2 because it was one of the rare occasion where I could have a more expensive game). I loved them both, and DS1 made the Dark Souls series immediatly one of my favorites. However, I've heard a lot of people bashing DS2. I thought: "Why? Seems quite like the others. I gotta play it too."
And, my bad. I realized why people didn't like the poor Dark Souls 2.
I'll start with the pros, first.
Graphically, the game is pretty good. Its optimization, however, is absolutely amazing. I can run the thing in maximum settings on an Nvidia GT740 (this GPU is quite a pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥. So, the graphic argument is 20/20. Too bad they didn't keep that kind of godlike optimization on DS3, however.
The emerald herald. It's the firekeeper lady in Majula. Yeah, you can guess that I was desperate to find another good point to the game. Well, let's go with the ugly then...
And let's start by the essence of frustration itself: the gameplay. It looks like DS1, in theory, except that everything is slower. Rolling takes at least three times the stamina it used to (stamina which regenerates as slow as a snail under the grip of acid), and it's been nerfed (you gotta increase your AGL stat to gain some few frames of invulnerability while rolling, but that doesn't change that much imo). The character takes literaly hours to get his estus flask, and the regeneration it provides goes very slowly (unlike the other episodes where it just instantly filled the health bar). That, my friend, will cost you many, many deaths. Pretty much everything in the damn game became slower and incredibly frustrating. And there's also the soul memory, aka a perfectly useless system which only purpose is to prevent you from playing in coop with your friends. I mean honestly, this system has no need to exist.
But what about the bosses then? Easy. They just die so quick that you can't even focus on their theme (which are pretty meh anyway). But then, why is the game frustrating then?
Mobs. It's not that the mobs are particularly hard to beat. They're all pretty simple, to be honest. Either ranged or melee. But the thing is that the difficulty was made by number. Have fun trying to slay three knights in front of you while being assaulted by four different archers in four different, remote locations. Instead of "Scholar of the first sin", the edition could have been called "Prepare to throw your controller at the screen" or something. The game is just that frustrating: Horde of ennemies who continually staggers you, giving you no time to drink estus, and when you beat them or run past them, all you encounter is a lame boss with meh lore and a meh theme.
It's honestly a shame, since the lore over Vendrick was interesting. The passage with the memories was possibly one of my favorite concept from the game. But sadly, the rest of the game is just average/bad. Where DS1 and 3 made practically all of their bosses epic, those in DS2 are just merely a soul farming tool.
Well, back to an important point of the DS series: The music. Well, the few I've heard of the boss themes was rather dull. The only tracks I do remember in this game are Majula (the game lobby, equivalent to the other game's Firelink Shrine) and the credit song, which was in my opinion far too pretty for the dissapointment this game was.
Now I've just finished the main story, going through as much side stories as I could. I've heard that "The DLCs of DSII were actually better than the game itself" so I gave a quick try to Crown of the Iron King. What did I meet? Tons of ennemies without much characteristics, only their strenght was their number, and that is honestly a poor move to add difficulty. So after all the♥♥♥♥♥♥I went through in this game, I thought it was time to stop it; I choose not to give the DLCs a try. Maybe later on, if I'm really bored; but for now, I just don't feel like doing this. The game is too much of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to play. Perhaps if the combat wasn't so lame and clunky, the spam of ennemies wouldn't have been a problem. Perhaps...
Seeing Dark Souls 2, I feel glad that From Software went back in the right direction with Bloodborne and Dark Souls 3. I've finished Dark souls 1 with all achievements, and I'm currently trying to 100% Dark Souls 3 as well, while waiting for the next DLC to come out.

An amazing tile based dungeon crawler which, unlike the first game, has expansive outdoor sections. The visuals and art direction of this game mold an extremely impressive aesthetic appeal, taking advantage of current generation technology and bringing new life into the classic tile based RPG genre.
The difficulty Legend of Grimrock presents is just right, not consisting of too much gauntlet difficulty while not being too easy. Legend of Grimrock 2 also features and impressive soundtrack and the audio is of high quality. The level design is non-linear and effective, making a fascinating world of many paths to explore.
As a massive fan of games like Stonekeep and Wizardry, this game delivers an enjoyable experience for hardcore tile based-RPG players while being accessible to new players of the genre at the same time. Being a game of such nature it requires an in-depth party creation, stats, items, spells and good level design to keep interesting, of which Grimrock 2 delivers superbly.
This is a gift to players who are nostalgic of the 90's era RPGs who want something of the same except current, and to new players who are willing to invest some time into a different kind of RPG experience.
Legend of Grimrock 2 is a revival done right and gives me hope of the future of indie games, this is trully an extremely high quality product with a lot of love and care put into making it. Verdun is a refreshing departure from the mainstream shooters we have been seeing as of late.
It takes the best of both worlds finding a medium between games like CoD and AA or ArmA where team play is heavily promoted but at the same time a few players doing their own thing won't screw the team.
The core game-mode "front-lines" gives an actual fun representation of WW1 trench combat with a cycle between various phases of attacking and defending as you play what is effectively a tug-of-war while you move between the various trench-lines.
The game also takes an interesting approach to their class system, the players are divided into squads with each squad having up to 5 people and a specific squad "type" the squad types are unique to each faction and each come with 5 player classes/roles that the squad members can fill. To be clear if your squad has a sniper role only 1 member of that squad can be a sniper. This system creates a diversity within each team and also prevents issues liek what we sometimes see in say BF1 where half your team is hiding out sniping or mortaring, it actually forces a role balance within the team.
Finally the leveling system, this is another place where Verdun really breaks the mold. Yes you have your personal leveling through which you earn points you can spend to unlock the 2 extra variations of every role for each squad type. However you also have squad level. Squad level is determined by who is in that squad but it actively tracks how you level with another person.
For example if I play with my friends lets call them Pat, John, Bob, and Ryan a lot then we will see our squad level rise as we play together, we will earn a series of passive perks like better support calls (artillery, spotting planes, gas etc) for the squad leader, or maybe our machine gunner will be able to sprint while outside the squad leaders command radius (a whole variety of perks for each of the roles within each squad), as well as better aesthetics for your uniforms.
However if then we all split up and play with people we have never played with before we are back to 0. This system really encourages you (a) not to jump squads during a match (b) not to jump servers between matches and (c) to regularly play with some friends (real or randoms of the internet).
I could go on and I should mention the game isn't perfect, sometimes you will find yourself stuck in odd places or in a squad where the leader never gives orders/uses their abilities but all in all a phenomenal game that is realistic enough to be interesting but but simple enough to be fun and accessible to all that is worth a play for any fans of the genre.

Legend of Grimrock 2 is a proper sequel that improves on the formula and concept of the original and expands on it while still retaining the feel and gameplay of the predecessor.
The most significant change is to the world. While Grimrock 1 provided you with a dungeon crawler in the truest meaning of the phrase i.e. you were in a dungeon, just a dungeon, from start to finish in a somewhat linear journey through, but that's not true for Grimrock 2.
The world of Grimrock 2 is open to be explored and your adventure within it will be much more non-linear. In this world you will walk much more in open air but don't worry there's enough dungeons to be crawled. The game will not tell you where to go now and instead you are free to explore on your own, provided you are able to defeat the enemies and solve the puzzles that stand in your way.
The puzzles in Grimrock 2 are very well made and range from a simple push the button that clicks, to much more elaborate ones, that could take clues from every corner of the world to solve. Either way the puzzles make sense and are rewarding when solved. Their difficulty isn't too high that it should impede the progress of your adventure but there are also plethora of more advanced puzzles and sneaky secrets to be found and solved if you desire the greatest rewards.
Combat has also changed in comparison to the predecessor. The enemies move faster and react quicker and are in general more varied. There are more weapons (completely new firearms class) and armors to be found. The skill system has also been improved and allows for much more versatility.
Legend of Grimrock 2 just has much more content than the predecessor in almost all areas while it still provides the same experience and more, including some subtle humor.
In conclusion answer these questions:
Are you interested in some old school first person dungeon crawling?
Do you like a world where the lore of it is not handed to you on a silver platter but you are free to find out about it through exploration?
Do you like solving puzzles and finding secrets?
If yes, then I can wholeheartedly recommend Legend of Grimrock 2 to you.

Reverse Crawl is a bit difficult to explain. You choose a level that will reward you with something like more abilities or different troops. You then fight several battles attempting to reach your goal (such as defeat the Spider Queen). You'll be given a selection of troops (randomly chosen, but you can reroll several times for better options). So in a battle, the enemy might start off with 3 troops that have heavy armor. So you'll want to choose some troops that stack up well against those, perhaps that do magic damage. If your troops wins against those 3 enemies, another batch of enemies appear. You'll try and defeat as many of these (your troops are still weary and worn down from the first fight), before dying. If your troops are defeated, you can bring in a set of fresh troops that you'll want to counter these new enemies. So it's small strategy battles.  You get exp after each battle to level up your skills, so you can choose to make your melee stronger, or range stronger, etc. It's a fun little game that is a few hours long, but it does have replay value, because you can choose to select different spells, troops and level ups the next time you play. It's a good game to pop into, play 1-2 battles for 10-15 minutes then come back later to play again. The graphics are simple but adequate. The music and sound effects are good (wish there was a volume control though, as they seem very loud).  All-in-all, a pretty good simple but fun and addictive strategy game.

Banished is a good game. It's an addictive game. It isn't a indepth game like Skyrim or Sim City. You don't unlock buildings or complete missions. You simply try to survive. Survival is hard, and you'll likely spend most of your time trying to balance (on a very tiny needle) the fine line between flourishing town and frozen waste.
The graphics are nice, very detailed, and work well for the gameplay. The gameplay is solid, very easy to understand, and easy to get into. It does have a bit of a learning curve, and figuring out each button takes a lot of time. While the game does have some bugs, remember that this game was made by one guy. And it's probably more than most of us out there could do.
Overall I give it a 4.75/5. If it wasn't for the few bugs, then it'd be a 5/5. And remember, this game isn't meant for everyone. If you don't like it, then don't rage at the creator to add things that would make the game "better". It's his work, not yours.

I understand why people would be disappointed in this game. There's not an immense amount of interaction, and even with the limited set of actions that the game allows, there isn't a massive amount of content to interact with. If your primary determination of value from a game comes from the amount of time it takes to beat it, this will not seem like a very good value.
However, I enjoyed it immensely. As "walking simulators" go, I thought the setting was wonderful, and the story that was told in the game was perfectly constructed for the way it was gradually revealed as different pieces were uncovered. And it was the story that was the most compelling part of the game.
I think that video games are still figuring out the best ways to tell stories, and I think that Gone Home was an excellent example of how a story can be told. For me, it was well worth the price, but I am probably more interested in artsy games, casual games, and narrative-driven games. If those sorts of things appeal to you, this is a highlight of those genres.

Why don't I recommend it?
DS2 original is completely dead because of this strategic release. I beat the hell out of DS2 original. Bought all 3 DLCs as they came out. Paid over $120 for the whole thing.
I bought DS2 when it first came out.
First, it's mechanics are the chunkiest and slowest in the series.
The Estus drinking is the slowest,
The jumping is the shortest,
The stam bar drains the fastest.
The swinging of your weapon, your rolling, your attack / knockdown recovery, it all has arbitrary delays that were not present in DS1, or DS3.
The NPCs are the stupident, literally running into environmental deaths during battle.
The story sucks, too, all but departing from the original storyline of DS1, and only leaving in trace elements of story and lore, bringing in unwanted and uncharasmatic NPCs in town nobody cares about. Limited storylines with NPCs, too. Nothing as deep as DS1 or DS3.
SUDDENLY, SOTFS comes out. It's 95% the same game as DS2. All the improvements were concentrated on this new "Version" of the game, requiring $39.99 from anyone who wants to participate in the game improvements. The PvP migrated DS2 was left in the dust, and now there's literally no reason to buy or own DS2 original or the DLCs for it. I don't even want that in my library, because I might accidentally download it instead of this game.
Anyone who bought the original version and put in time and effort should be enraged FROM software pulled the rug out from under the feet of DS2 just to re-release it and re-charge people for 95% the same game. It should have been an update.

As a DS veteran, I can comfortably say this is worth paying at least 30$ for. The story is somewhat lacking, and the PvE feels static, but enjoyable. The PvP is by far capable of redeeming the whole game, and does so excellently. Every hit feels clean, and you can actually punish roll-spammers even if there is lag. Hitboxes are fair, and there is a reasonable counter to everything. Phantoms cannot heal if they are invaded, and can only use spells to heal (including the invader). Before I begin, I would like to join the chorus: COULD THE ESTUS DRINKING TIME BE ANY SLOWER? Seriously...
I should preface by saying that I have played and beaten the original Dark Souls and its DLC. I thoroughly enjoyed that title but this go around felt very different. The hours spent on the two weren't terribly different, but this game felt twice as long and half as enjoyable. Don't get me wrong. I wouldn't say that Dark Souls 2 is a BAD game, it just doesn't live up to the glory of the original and suffers from some poor design choices that really make parts of the game a chore. I think those who played the original will still get something out of the sequel, but those first entering the Dark Souls universe would be better served starting at the beginning of the series. Fighting mechanics have been improved (spare the awful hit-boxes) but new players won't be missing out on anything by passing on this one. Dark Souls 2 suffers a variety of flaws that alone would be tolerable but put together make the game fairly boring and sometimes downright miserable.
My biggest technical problem was the extraordinary lack of human effigies in the game. I never understood the purpose of humanity in the original title and so never used effigies. After learning that one could summon assistance with bosses by using them I was pleasantly surprised by how much more fun the game could be with a little help. Being hollowed-out also came with a health penalty that could be really detrimental at times. So with my new-found knowledge of effigies I began to use them often only finding out later how rare they were. The rarity of effigy drops didn't bother me at first because I figured vendors would surely sell them along the way. Problem was: vendors only sell so many before they are sold out for good. Just farm them from enemies that drop them in the field, right? That would work, except that after killing a particular enemy a certain number of times the game stops spawning it forever. You can work around this with bonfire ascetics but the increased difficulty of the area is a cost that far outweighs the benefits. The fact of the matter is that the health penalty of being hollow is far too great in this game and only serves to frustrate the player. The game is already hard enough. The developers should have made buying effigies a persistent option and just made them really expensive.
The lack of interesting environments and atmosphere was also a perpetual drag on the game. The original Dark Souls had a number of places that were really beautiful and awe-inspiring and the areas had a nice sense of scope, size, and cohesion that made sense. Dark Souls 2 is a patchwork of locations that are mostly uninteresting and offer little to no reason for return. There are no vendors, side-quests, or NPCs that make returning beneficial, so most are drive-through areas that clearly did not receive any thoughtful consideration from the devs. Some area transitions, like the one from the final elevator of Earthen Peak to the entrance of the Iron Keep, were just plain bizarre. Exploration of the world and the slaying of optional bosses doesn't yield much reward to the player either which is particularly disappointing after being brutalized by an area like the Frigid Outskirts. Touching on this point, the lack of NPCs in this game made it feel all the more hollow. Part of the charm of Dark Souls was its characters like Sir Onion and Trusty Patches who really rounded-out the game and gave it that dash of humor that was sometimes desperately needed. Their voice-acting and scripts were really fun and memorable. Dark Souls 2 is completely devoid of any interesting NPCs, save the Emerald Herald, who the protagonist rarely has any meaningful interactions with. My one hope in the game was to at least see some grand development of the Emerald Herald's story, some big animated ending that included some resolution for her. But "Alas, nothing happened": we have about 3 short dialogs with her through the course of the game with no mention of her in the end. Epic. Disappointment.
With no unique plot developments or interesting NPCs the game comes off as just a poor carbon-copy of the original game and this doesn't just apply to the story. While some of the bosses you fight along your journey are fresh many are just cut-and-paste from the original Dark Souls. The Belfry Luna gargoyles are literally bosses right out of the original game. And although both are optional the game includes two nearly-identical fights with the Smelter Demon boss. The bosses of the Iron King and the Ivory King DLCs are true to the original vision but the base game bosses are weak and unmemorable for the most part. The battle with the Ivory King, which involves the ability to hire four knights and summon two spirits to assist in a group battle with the boss, was truly epic in contrast. I really wish we were given more refreshing battles like that. More group-oriented activities would have been much-appreciated and offered the players something truly different. On the boss side of things, I will give the devs some credit: The battle with the Fume Knight was exceptionally hard and the duel with Sir Alonne nearly made my chest explode. Good work.
But what was most damning for me was the general lack of direction in the game. This was tolerable in the original Dark Souls because it was a much smaller and cohesive world; if you poked around enough you would find where you were supposed to go. The world of Dark Souls 2 is much larger in scope by comparison and the DLC worlds make it even broader. I myself spent several hours in the Brume Tower after finishing off the Fume Knight having NO idea where to go to next. I couldn't find the last smelter wedge to kill the last Ashen Idol and knew it had to be somewhere in the Brume Tower. Turns out: I was wrong. After a few hours of wandering I finally resorted to consulting the internet for direction. If a seasoned video game player is doing this in your game you know you've failed royally. There is no indication that there is nothing to do in the DLC areas when you finish off their bosses and the fact that finishing them does not affect the story or gameplay is quite a disappointment.
On top of all of this the DLC areas are locked behind doors strewn about the world. Yes, they are locked. Where are the keys, you ask? They are hidden in random places in the world as well. The dragon talon required to open the Crown of the Sunken King is hidden behind a door that itself is locked by yet ANOTHER key hidden in ANOTHER hidden area. What the ♥♥♥♥ is that about? Why on Earth would you hide access to these areas and offer no leads to finding their keys?
I would love to go on about the empty story that I just stopped trying to understand about half-way through the game, but the small amounts of muddled history and plot leave hardly anything to comment upon. The "story" is a tedious, poorly-developed afterthought. Enough said.
When I first finished this game a few days ago I didn't realize how much I didn't like it, but after writing this review I came to realize how many key areas this game fell short on. The empty ending cinematic felt like a real slap in the face after having sunk so many hellish hours into this game. I feel like I've put more effort into this game than the developers did. I can't recommend this game to new players of the series. Stick to playing the original for now. I haven't played Dark Souls 3 yet, and I've heard it's better, but this game has left me wary of trying it.
Oh, and whoever designed the Frigid Outskirts: I hope you get hit by a bus...

I have played the game for about 6 hours and I am not convinced that it is as good as many people claim it is.
I find the control scheme very annoying (needing SIX keys to walk around, and needing to right-click on weapons to use them, let alone using magic which requires numerous clicks -- and all of that in real-time). The enemies are kind-of underwhelming, just standing in front of you and hitting you -- unless you ran into enemies that are far too high-level for you, which can easily happen. There are some pretty annoying puzzles (invisible switches, items that are hidden without the game giving any indication of where you have to look, be-fast-and-move-to-the-correct-spot-or-you-die challenges, and puzzles whjch basically require you to die multiple times before you can actually get a glimpse of what you need to do to solve them). The character upgrades are too rare, and it is too easy to make a mistake in constructing your characters (I made an alchemist who uses firearms, but now I find that firearms and ammo for them are very hard to come by, while I have found fantastic bows with reusable arrows that I cannot use). Fortunately, enemies that are defeated do not return, so that's a plus. But overall, I find the fun factor not so high that I am keen to continue.
What REALLY hurts the game is the complete lack of any story. Why are you doing the things that you do? Why do you walk around here? Why not just stay on the beach, build a big fire, and kill turtles for dinner until you are rescued? I don't feel that "exploring for the sake of exploring" is very rewarding. Ultimately, the whole story seems to come down to something like: walk around until you have collected 20 power gems, and then you can unlock the final door. Hooray!
I played the first Grimrock for a while, and that game feels much better. There is an actual incentive for you to delve into the dungeon, and the atmosphere is suffocatingly claustrophobic. While in Grimrock II you are just walking through woods without rhyme or reason. The atmosphere of this game is just off.
All in all, I am on the fence as far as Grimrock II is concerned. It is not that it is a bad game, it is just not as good as the first one, and I rather play something else than more Grimrock II. So I have to rate it down, partly in compensation for all the up-ratings.

At first glance, Verde Station might seem like what some people call a "walking simulator", but it isn't. It's an adventure game. I would call it a cousin to the walking simulators... you're exploring an environment devoid of other people using a first-person perspective. But there are definite puzzles to solve and a definite ending to achieve.
More than that, I don't really want to say. It's not a long game, and as the developer warns, you can only experience it the first time once. It's definitely meant to be experienced. If you're interested in a sci-fi adventure game, grab this one.
Be aware that it's a bit buggy; if you don't hear footsteps when you walk, you should restart the game.

I played F1 2010, '11, '12, and '13 back in the day and haven't played an F1 game since. I happened upon some gameplay footage of F1 2016 and was blown away by the AI's racecraft. You can't just bully them out of your way anymore. They'll hang tight side by side for several corners if they have to. Now owning the game, the AI is everything I'd hoped for. They're aggressive and daring, which means you have to stay aware of them. If you slam the door shut on them when they're half a car length along side, it's your own fault for causing a collision. It is absolutely delightful when you nail a corner exit that enables you to try a pass on someone.
Beware, it took me about 6 hours to get back into the swing of things. It's probably best to get a feel for the game in Time Trials before moving onto Quick Races. There you can figure out what difficulty you need before moving into career mode. I went straight for career mode where you can only change difficulty in between race weekends. I also swallowed my pride and put traction control on medium so that I could get up to speed enjoying myself faster. The physics are good, but a bit numb compared to more hardcore simulators.
The game is much more complete than ever before. Each race weekend begins and ends with commentary summarizing events, as if you were watching on TV. Practice sessions now have tasks for you to perform which give you points to unlock vehicle upgrades. The safety car seems more fully integrated. Tires no longer seem to go "off a cliff." The graphics are next level. It's all well polished.
Buy this game if you want to get racey, but make sure to ease yourself in.

Great game. It's a side-scrolling platformer with an interesting mechanic: you can reverse gravity, so you choose whether you fall up or down, but only if you're already standing on something solid. You can't jump or climb, so this leads to all sorts of interesting puzzles (for example, one item you need is on the other side of a tiny block, but you have to fall "up" through a gauntlet of spikes until you can flip over and fall back down on the other side).
The object of the game is to find your five crew members, who are each stranded somewhere in the mysterious VVVVVV dimension. Each crew member is usually at the end of a series of rooms full of jumping puzzles and each series usually has its own trick that complicates things (such as lines that force you to instantly flip over or a constantly moving wall of spikes chasing you). A secondary goal is to find the 20 "trinkets" scattered around the dimension. Some are easy to get, but a couple are brutally hard to snag (two of which probably took me 100 deaths each).
The game is quite short. I think I beat it in about four hours of play time (all crew and trinkets found), but there are many player-made levels and challenges to try (such as playing the whole game upside-down or trying to avoid dying).  There are generally checkpoints everywhere and there's no penalty for dying (you immediately reappear at the last checkpoint), so you can die over and over.  I don't play many platformers, but I didn't find most of it too difficult, skill-wise. Many of the rooms require to think about how your character can maneuver to avoid spikes and moving obstacles. I found many of the puzzles really satisfying to figure out and there are great moments when you manage to traverse a room perfectly after dying a dozen times. The controls can be a finicky sometimes: there's a slight delay between hitting a button and your character responding.
The retro art style is simple, effective, and charming. I enjoyed the music a lot too. The simple dialogue and expressions of the crew are quite funny at times too. I really enjoyed just exploring the dimension and stumbling onto new areas.
Overall, I highly recommend this game. It's challenging, quick, and fun.

Built to recall days gone by, one can only feel nostalgic when playing this game. Visuals are simplistic yet effective, making good use of the color palette. Reminiscent of the Atari console era. The audio also is set in a chiptune manner that we all were so familiar with not so long ago. And yet, still, all these are brought together to the modern era, clearly, with more instruments being played at once, and with how much is happening on screen. It's what one would think a classic game to be if developed with what we're given today.
This game will test your patience. Yes. This game is the VERY DEFINITION of "Trial and error" where you'll try time and time again to overcome obstacles. Fortunately, this game is most forgiving and doesn't make use of a life system and instead gives you save points of which are within reach of the obstacle you must overcome. But, that is the meat of the game; Overcoming obstacles. You'll find very quickly that this game is short. Very short. Nothing is terribly hard to get through, though, where the trinkets scattered throughout the map will test your mettle most. But these things are not required, so you do not have to sweat about acquiring them.
Because this title is so short, I can recommend it. And at the price it is, it's hard not to be okay with it. Glorious chiptune, simple visuals, and gameplay that will measure your character, this is an indie game worth your time.

good n realistic World War 1 game.  every other FPS game i've played has been everyone running around one-man-army machine guns and hyper power sniper rifles and grenade of grenade: grenade grenade.
This game manages to avoid that using a rather simple system of zoning.
The main game mode (trenches) involves two sides on a long, narrow map, with lots of trenches and barbed wire in the way.   One side starts defending their trench while the other has to go to it and sit on it until the timer runs so it can be captured.  Enemy units that sit in the trench block the other side from capturing.  Once a trench is captured, more of the map opens up for that team to advance and fight for the next trench.  If they fail to take that trench, that section of the map is closed off to them and they're restricted to the first trench where they started out.
Ingeniously to prevent random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s wandering around one-man-armying, sneaky wannabe sneaking behind enemy lines, the portions of the map the enemy occupy are off limits as described above.  You can move onto them without issue, but a timer warns you to return to your lines within 8 (or more) seconds or you'll be shot as a traitor/deserter.
This simple design works great to replicate trench warfare and get a proper scope of just how mind-numbingly unprepared the world powers were for modern war in 1914, as you can easily spend an entire 30 minute match fighting over the same strip of map short enough to sprint across with almost enough stamina left over to sprint back.  Alternately, a match can be done in less than 8 minutes if one team is woefully inexperienced and gets steamrolled by the other.
weapons are what you expect, with the vast majority being bolt action rifles and pistols.  Machine guns are a rarity, and all but two cannot be fired until deployed, during which time you're likely to end up sniped or flank attacked by a trench invasion.
a minor nuisance is the lack of variety in terms of the Central powers, in that you only get to play as Germany, while the Entente powers let you play as France, Belgium, Canada, England, or the US, with the myriad different weapon types associated.  The German weaponry is solid enough to stand up to and even overpower all of theirs, but the lack of variety can make them get boring quickly.
cormbat is squad-based, as people in a squad have different roles with different weapon types, but it doesn't encompass the entirety of gameplay; you can work successfully as a team while being the only member of your squad, or never communicating or coordinating with your squad.  Every squad has an NCO with the ability to call in auxilary support, mostly in the form of mortar and artillery strikes, and poison gas bombs.  The dud NCOs get only recon planes and smokescreens.  Having an experienced NCO who knows how and when to deploy artillery strikes can easily shatter enemy defenses or completely disrupt attacks.  Respawns come in waves between 20-30 seconds each, so wiping out a huge portion of the enemy's soldiers gives pivotal advantages to a side to be able to capture trenches and fortify.
Due in part to the nature of the gameplay and the weapons, the game is not too hard the way Red Orchestra 2 would be, although a newbie can still be easily overwhelmed as they get constantly sniped while standing in their trench, or respawn just to be instantly hit by an enemy mortar, or more likely end up caught in barbed wire and struggle too much, like a chinese finger trap, and end up dead.
while by its name it's focused entirely on the Western Front, i would love to see this game expand and potentially include Austria-Hungary, Serbia, Russia, Greece, Bulgaria, perhaps even the Ottoman Empire

If you've never played a game similar to this in the past, you're going to feel a bit confused, and perhaps turned off at first.  Although the game is concidered first-person, think of it like this - you are a floating camera, right in front of four party members.  That's right, you control all four.  Even more jarring for many will be the grid-based movement and combat.  The levels certainly don't appear much like grids, mut you move from grid-space to grid-space without any leeway.  No diagonal moves - only forward, back, and 90-degree turns.  This is one of my only complaints - it's restricive,  seemingly an un-neccisary "old school" feature, and sometimes makes me a little dizzy if I start making too many turns.  Controls are mostly menu based, requiring you to click on the weapon of a party member to attack and actually have non-weapon items (like alchemy equipment or warhorns) if you want to use them.  The games has a very nice map system which creates a classic grid-paper like map (nothing is labled for you, if you want to make note of something the game gives you the tools to do so)
You would expect, concidering the grid system, that combat would be turn based.  Nope.  You'd better get used to the system quickly, because strafing and dodging opponent attacks are often vital tactics for survival.  This game is quite challenging at times, and I often find that I feel under-leveled for the area I'm in, even when I'm actually not.
Character progression is handeled quite well - you never feel completely satisfied with your characters, which is how it should be.  Skills only have 5 levels, but you only get one point per level, and there is something like 20 skills.  Character classes actually feel different from one another and many have very unique benefits / systems.  Alchemists actually grow more herbs once they're in their inventory.  Magic users are treated to a magic system that involves combining different elemental runes to create spells.
The environments are absolutely beautiful - this is possibly the nicest looking game I own, in my opinion.  But I'm a sucker for AA, so opinions may vary.  Everything is essentially open world.  The best comparison would probably be metroid, if only because most areas are blocked off by locked doors, the keys to which can only be found elsewhere.  That elsewhere is probably blocked off by some puzzles.  The puzzles are a nice level of difficulty, vague enough to leave you scratching your head, untill you figure them out, at which point you facepalm.
And did I mention - you can make and download custom dungeons, some of which are campaign lenth?  It's a wonderful feature that adds huge amounts of value if you want to keep playing after you've finished the original campaign.
In the Windows version, custom dungeons are held in
.  Dungeons downloaded from the Steam Workshop are immediately brought there, but there are others on the Nexus which are too large to be allowed on the Workshop.  Place those dungeons in the aforementioned file as well.  Took me forever to figure that out.

The game is quite fun, and I have spent many hours in it, and will probably spend more too. However... there are some pretty big caveats to this. The price for one; I have the Australia tax, and the base game costs $75USD, not including the exchange rate and everything. Then there is the DLC - each one is a pack of 4 extra cars, hardly worth the price considering they don't really offer too much more. And then there are the Mi-crew-transactions. Seriously? Extra in-game micro transactions on an already pretty pricey Triple A release? There are two different forms of currency in-game, one which is solely earnt through missions, skills, and stunts. And then there are CREW CREDITS. You are given 100,000 reasonably early on in the game, but that's not enough for anything good. And so... you are invited to use real life money to purchase these in order to quickly obtain cars or specs that you would otherwise spend countless hours grinding for. The grind for this game is pretty ridiculous - not only do you have to grind for in-game cash (unless you pay real money) for the cars, but then, upgrade those cars, you must complete skill challenges to acquire parts to improve your car... for each individual car. The best parts are also RNG based, so you could easily spend hours farming the same challenge to try and get that specific part you wanted.
In contrast to some others, I've had no issues with Uplay, but this could just mean I'm one of the lucky ones. Unlike some of the Trailers, the world isn't as filled - this is both a good and bad thing. If you like PVP, well, you'll be in for a long wait. But otherwise, the comparative lack of players is actually a bit of a blessing in disguise. Particularly if you are farming money or parts, the smaller population sizes actually makes it much easier to do what you want without getting in each other's way, which is extremely inconvenient and can be extremely aggravating. One of the biggest draws, the co-op, doesn't really seem to work completely as well, sometimes crews doing a mission won't finish properly. That said, it is still incredibly awesome to drive around America with a group of friends, or accept a random online invite if you prefer that instead. There can, however, still be connection issues even within a crew, so that is something to keep in mind if you plan on primarily playing the game in multiplayer. You'll also want to do this with a friend, playing with strangers online can be dicey and very hit and miss.
The campaign is pretty standard and boring despite how short it is - done and dusted in about 7 or 8 hours. The campaign really offers nothing new, interesting, or relevant. It's very cliche with some pretty glaring plot holes. I enjoyed cruising around the map in free roam doing whatever I wanted more than completing the campaign.
This brings me to by far, the best part of the game - the world map. The Drive is the best open world driving experience I've had by far, with you literally able to drive from Canada to Mexico and coast to coast with an incredibly diverse environment to explore, with vast tracks of open road and off road land to discover. Many cities are either scaled down or removed completely, understandable but potentially annoying to some - I never had an issue with it, it would not make sense to make everything completely to scale. The exploration of the map is great, although sometimes the game feels more like a tourist guide... noting landmarks like the Grand Canyon and Hoover Dam. Regardless, the environments are fantastic, from the dense urban cities of Los Angeles and New York, to snowy mountains, deserts, and swamps. The time and environmental system in The Crew is also well worth talking about. From snow, rain, cloud, and sun, the weather is quite well, although rain does not affect driving as much as it should. The day/night system is a highlight, although sometimes streetlamps and headlights turn on and off at weird times... The poor standard of NPC traffic is a let-down. Not only in terms of how they look, but also in terms of how they spawn and despawn. I understand that this is to reduce the stress of the game, but it still looks odd to see other vehicles randomly appearing or vanishing, especially at night time, where headlights are the only thing which shows other road users.
Now to the gameplay. The driving and racing offers nothing spectacular, although the game's physics and hit boxes are inconsistent. On one hand, it's pretty good to see a driving game where your car accumulates visible damage. However, repair prices are exorbitant, and the damage does not seem to effect the car's performance. Then there are odd times where you hit another car or object... sometimes you get the "crash cam", sometimes you spin to the side, sometimes you flip, sometimes you are bumped backwards or sideways... but there doesn't seem to be much  consistency. And sometimes you'll be sent flying over rocks or curbs through invisible walls. It can be entertaining to see your million-dollar car flip and tumble... but also frustrating and physically wrong. I feel the handling is quite poor in the game, with strangely large turning circles, the surprisingly high propensity to skid (not drift), something exacerbated off-road. Landing after jumps is also poorly handled, and you always land nose first, generally but not always, causing you flip and crash.
There isn't too much racing in this game, with a variety of other missions such as "disable" or "deliver", but the game's AI is very frustrating and completely unrealistic. Regardless of how your car is upgraded, the AI will always be right on your tail. Collisions will ALWAYS affect you more negatively than the other car hit, regardless of whether it's a race or police pursuit, and who intitiated the contact. And the police pursuits are not fun either. Pursuits only start if you hit a street lamp, but you will be ignored if you speed through a red light at four times the speed limit past a police car? And then, when the pursuit starts, it's actually quite impractical to see the police cars catch up to you... it just doesn't make sense that a random squad car could catch up to a supercar and then insta-stop and bust you. The speed with which you get caught, and subsequently the amount you get fined, make police pursuits far more trouble than fun. The traffic can also behave oddly, especially at lights and when merging.
And then, finally, the cars themselves. I really love the fact that most of the cars are licensed, and have official paints, rims, etc. There are exceptions though, such as the two RUF cars. The stature of the cars is further refined by the 5 different classes, or specs - Street, Dirt, Performance, Race, Circuit - which are all noticeably different to each other, in both looks and performance. This is in contrast to some other games, where differences such as Rally or Muscle cars actually really don't offer much difference in terms of gameplay. In The Crew, the different classes all have their own strengths and weaknesses, and perform differently. Even with the classes, however, the selection of cars is really quite limited, especially if you do not purchase the DLC. While there is a reasonably large range of physical modifications available (bumpers, hoods, spoilers, etc.), these customisation options lack depth and are limited. And some, like the license plates, are barely noticeable. That said, you are able to do some incredibly fun and potentially silly things. Like drive a Mini Cooper down a ski ramp like THE STIG, or hit 300km/h in a Fiat or Dodge SRT.
It's months post release, but there are still bugs  - getting stuck or going through environmental hazards, , and graphical glitches where roads vanish or turn strange colours... Don't get me wrong, I enjoy The Crew, and it isn't bad, per se, but it's hard to justify the price, especially with microtransactions thrown in.

A bitter sweet swan song from Two Tribes (Toki Tori). You can tell this is a labor of love cramming in decades of industry wisdom and every last pop culture reference on their bucket list. They’ve really gone above every expectation of themselves and the shooter genre itself.
Most of the game is progressing from arena to arena, and each arena presents special patterns and environment hazards to work around. The best sections involve gravity bubbles or popping above and below the surface of water, all while dodging spinning laser beams. Other times you’re on a speeding train, conveyer belt, or being chased by rising lava. Waves of enemies are after you the whole time and it’s all about aiming while threading the needle through them. Each enemy type has a unique attack pattern that presents interesting combinations with other enemies.
Hacking is a very small part of the game, but it allows you to turn an enemy into an ally. Usually this is for healing or a little extra fire power. Enemies drop scrap which can be used to purchase upgrades. It’s a fairly long shooter, several hours. It’s got incredible boss fights, set pieces, and a beautiful rendering style. Fast fun explosions everywhere all the time. I’d put it on the very difficult side, but except for a few of the timed chases it’s very fair about keeping you in control. There’s also several extra modes if you’re looking for additional challenge.
Probably the best shooter of the year and easily in my end of year top 25 list. If you love run and gun shooters you’ll love this.

In 1983, a team of deeply pious scientists conducted a radical experiment in an undisclosed facility. The scientists had theorized that a human without access to any senses or ways to perceive stimuli would be able to perceive the presence of God. They believed that the five senses clouded our awareness of eternity, and without them, a human could actually establish contact with God by thought. An elderly man who claimed to have “nothing left to live for” was the only test subject to volunteer. To purge him of all his senses, the scientists performed a complex operation in which every sensory nerve connection to the brain was surgically severed. Although the test subject retained full muscular function, he could not see, hear, taste, smell, or feel. With no possible way to communicate with or even sense the outside world, he was alone with his thoughts. Scientists monitored him as he spoke aloud about his state of mind in jumbled, slurred sentences that he couldn’t even hear. After four days, the man claimed to be hearing hushed, unintelligible voices in his head. Assuming it was an onset of psychosis, the scientists paid little attention to the man’s concerns. Two days later, the man cried that he could hear his dead wife speaking with him, and even more, he could communicate back. The scientists were intrigued, but were not convinced until the subject started naming dead relatives of the scientists. He repeated personal information to the scientists that only their dead spouses and parents would have known. At this point, a sizable portion of scientists left the study.
After a week of conversing with the deceased through his thoughts, the subject became distressed, saying the voices were overwhelming. In every waking moment, his consciousness was bombarded by hundreds of voices that refused to leave him alone. He frequently threw himself against the wall, trying to elicit a pain response. He begged the scientists for sedatives, so he could escape the voices by sleeping. This tactic worked for three days, until he started having severe night terrors. The subject repeatedly said that he could see and hear the deceased in his dreams.
Only a day later, the subject began to scream and claw at his non-functional eyes, hoping to sense something in the physical world. The hysterical subject now said the voices of the dead were deafening and hostile, speaking of hell and the end of the world. At one point, he yelled “No heaven, no forgiveness” for five hours straight. He continually begged to be killed, but the scientists were convinced that he was close to establishing contact with God.
After another day, the subject could no longer form coherent sentences. Seemingly mad, he started to bite off chunks of flesh from his arm. The scientists rushed into the test chamber and restrained him to a table so he could not kill himself. After a few hours of being tied down, the subject halted his struggling and screaming. He stared blankly at the ceiling as teardrops silently streaked across his face. For two weeks, the subject had to be manually rehydrated due to the constant crying. Eventually, he turned his head and, despite his blindness, made focused eye contact with a scientist for the first time in the study. He whispered “I have spoken with God, and he has abandoned us” and his vital signs stopped. There was no apparent cause of death.

This is the best Magic: The Gathering (M:TG) clone that I've seen.
Pros:
- Free to Play
- The game features nuances, such as the ability to permanently modify cards. Cards retain their modified states, regardless of where they are. As an example, if I cast +1/+1 flying on a creature, it directly adds text to the card. If the creature is killed, it still has the modifications on it. The spell, "Silence" permanently wipes out the text on the card.
One of the strangest game mechanics is called, "War Cry", where an attacking creature will blow into a horn, which gives the creature or weapon, closest to the top of the library +1/+1. So you can give random bonuses to things that you have not even seen yet, which is a weird concept for a strategy game.
- I loved playing "Forge" mode, where you draft pick 25 random cards and fight against the AI for prizes:
- The game was very generous and you can get every card in the game, just by grinding, crafting and learning to play well.
- A lot of the artwork was very beautiful. Each card has a static and animated version ( the animated version being rarer ). The animations are more subtle than the cards in "Infinity Wars" but still very cool.
- The AI difficulty scales as you level up ( their decks have better cards ).
Cons:
- As someone who played Magic: The Gathering in sealed deck tournaments, I found the tutorial / campaign a chore to wade through ( 17 wins, 3 losses ). I had seen most of the mechanics in M:TG 16 years prior.
- If you want to play draft games then you have to grind gold by playing constructed games against the AI or people. The alternative is to pay cash ( $5 per draft game ). You get to keep the cards that you draft though.
- If you have a fast effect ( spell ) in your hand, the game auto pauses. The game telegraphs your hand to your opponent, which is idiotic.
- The biggest problem is that where other modern games ( "Spectromancer"; "Infinity Wars"; "Spellweaver"; "System Crash" ) tried to fix the inherant mana problems with M:TG ( mana flood / mana drought ) "Eternal Card" still has M:TG's broken mana system. At least some of Spellweaver's elaborate mana mechanics could be copied... actually on second thought, it would be difficult to change the way mana works because white faction has Empowerment cards ( they receive boosts when you play mana ).
- Balance problems. A couple of cards are overpowered.
Tips for noobs:
You can customize your power (mana) in "Gameplay" options.
You can stack relics on top of one another.
Tips for advanced players:

How to play this game:
Imagine there are 3 clocks. One is laid down, where 12 is facing in front of you. The second is held up, with 12 aiming above you. The third is like the second, but turned 90 degrees, with the 3 and 9 meeting the 3 and 9 of the first clock, and the 3 and 9 of the second clock meeting the 12 and 6 of the first.
First, press "?" and find the controls. Load the ammo,♥♥♥♥♥♥the gun, turn off the safety/auto-fire, and get ready to aim. When ever you enter a room, check the corners. 9 by 3 by 4, 4 by 6 by 8, 8 by 10 by 2, 2 by 4 by 7. WHOOPS! You forgot 6 by 5 by 3, and there was a turret. You're dead. Restart.
Keep going until you find a tape. You listen to it. Once done, you need to find another 10. After finding 1 more, you die, and lose all progress. 24 hours into the game, you have only found 4 in a life. You give up.
The next day, you come back.
Repeat until you die.
As a proof of concept, this game is well worth the $5. Make a larger game with the same mechanics and a better and larger story, and I will play $10-20 for it.

***I've not yet finished the game, just writing some early impressions***
I think I can see what The Final Station is trying to do. Mysterious events, a plot inferred by suggestion and overheard conversation, brutal combat and resource management. It just seems like so far none of it is very well balanced.
The English translation is done poorly, leading to a loss of understanding in some phrases and others that make no sense at all. I can mostly understand what they were going for and simply asking for fan help in making sure the English is solid would do the job but for some reason it's been overlooked. I'm happy to look through the script and make recommendations if the developers want me to, no charge.
Resources are scarce, which is fine, but almost immediately you end up with too many people on your train. They starve very quickly, sometimes draining their entire food bar between 2 stations. Food is scarce and cannot be crafted like medkits and ammo, which makes sense. You're clearly not supposed to get everyone to their destinations alive.
These destinations are obfuscated though, so you can't make executive decisions about who to save and who to let perish. You get rewards for safely delivering survivours but have no idea when they'll get off the train. Sometimes the dialogue will infer destinations but the map only shows you what the next one is, so you can't work out whether it's actually worth giving John the last meal, because it's 3 stops before he gets off, or if it's worth giving it to Suzie because although she's off in 2 stops she gives you $250 and 12 bullets and you want her alive.
Exploring environments is tense and challenging, as it should be. Ammo management can be an issue though. Good resource management is built around choices but the game too often forces you into combat against multiple foes in confined spaces. Sometimes these are optional and if you're short on ammo you can just run away but too often the pack of zombies are blocking the way forward. This forces you to expend ammo and if you're short, you're pretty much screwed.
Overall I'm enjoying it so far and am looking forward to the DLC but there's definately some rebalancing to be done to take The Final Station into excellence. Also, that bad translation needs sorting. It makes a game that looks beautiful feel cheap.

Intelligent, thought-provoking, and more than a little unnerving. Verde Station follows in the footsteps of Gone Home and The Stanley Parable; it's a game about exploring an environment, and in so doing, coming to understand that environment. Or, to try anyway.
Like Gone Home or The Stanley Parable, it's easy to "win" Verde Station. You can go from the opening to the ending in half an hour if you put your mind to it. But that's not the point; don't do that. Take your time and, more to the point, think about what's going on. Expect to be confused. Expect to be misled. Expect to be surprised.
If you say the phrase "walking simulator" with contempt, you probably won't enjoy Verde Station. That's fine. But if you're willing to leap into the unknown (and Verde Station is one of the very few pieces of media that actually is improved by approaching it without knowing what's going to happen), I cannot recommend this game more highly.

Gone Home is something I decided to purchase recently on Steam as it had very positive reviews and a few reviewers I like said it was worth checking out.
I'm not unfamiliar with the concept of a "walking" simulator, in which the player is only allowed the sole mechanic of interacting with objects in game while a story plays out or is narrated or revealed. In other words, coventional gaming mechanics many associate with the idea of gaming, such as jumping alongside any form of combat mixed with very complex puzzle solving, is ignored. The Stanley Parable, with the aid of the dulcet tones of Kevan Brighting, is also such a game.
The difference between the two is substance.
The Stanley Parable is a very meta game that deliberately relies on tropes to then dismantle them in front of the players' eyes; it brings into question the players' interpretation of a game based or normative factors prevalent in other triple A titles, often referencing such games. The player finds themselves in an empty office at the beginning, dystopian vibes interwoven in the surrounding textures, as a narrator tries to give said player a "ride" through the "amusement" tracks of the gameplay itself in all its beautiful linearity. In gaming, this is basically the idea of getting from point A to point B often through arbitrary means. It's incredibly well done, in part thanks to the hilarious narration of Kevan Brighting.
However, the same can't be said for Gone Home. Gone Home is in short an interactive story lacking any substance. There are no alternatives to the path, there are no different angles in which to tackle the path and it isn't metaludological, nor is it a metanarrative. I really wanted to like it, but sadly the narrative of "this stuff really matters" teen-angst narrative is the biggest pile of trope laden crap I've experienced.
There is a reason why game mechanic "memes" that frequent some of the biggest franchises of all time, such as Mario, Zelda, WoW, Halo, Fallout, etc., are recursive, and why there exists a stark trench between story telling in novel execution and game execution for a reason. This isn't to say that story telling can't be great in games; I found myself falling for the lore of The Elder Scroll, Witcher and Deus Ex universes for the complexity of their cinematic narratives.
Yet I would have not bothered with any of them if they were solely cinematic. If something is solely cinematic with the illusion of "gameplay" through QTEs or "click X" to get a little more dialogue, then perhaps it should be a TV or animated series or a movie, or perhaps a light/visual novel or in fact novel. I don't find triple A games, or many of the indie games I tend to play, tackling small segmentary slice of life narratives for good reason; they're trite, very boring to go through and highly unplayable in terms of replay value.

Having played the Airport Tycoon series, I was thrilled to see a new title that promised just as much fun but with updated graphics. After purchasing Airport Simulator 2014 and sinking about 23 hours in it, I felt highly disappointed for the following reasons:
- There is only ONE airport that you can play with, it has 8 gates and when those are filled there's a nice queue of 5 aircraft so you'll never run out. They never start moaning about the waiting times either, keep that in mind for the next point.
- You can drive 12 vehicles around the apron. You only get one of each and many aircraft need the same vehicles at a time. This could get a bit hectic, if it wasn't for the patience of the waiting pilots. Just drive your vehicle from gate 1 to gate 2, and maybe to 3 and 4 as well, just to make your time deadlines, then get back over at gate 1 and do the actual work etc.
- This all gains you small bits of "money", and a good sum when a processed aircraft takes off, which you can then use to hire drivers for 11 of the vehicles, for each gate specific. Funny, as these drivers come with their own vehicles, so gates don't have to share a single vehicle anymore. Drivers come in three skill levels, you start with the slow ones and go up to the faster ones. (Yet the vehicles still drive at the same pace!) The 12th vehicle is a cargo container loading platform, there is no driver available for that so you have to keep doing this until the end of times.
- After earning enough "money" to upgrade all your drivers, you get a "Well done!" message, saying that your drivers are now fully automated and you can either return to the main menu or keep playing to load/unload cargo planes.
- There is no way of expanding your terminals (you only have one, and it disappears after a while!) or extending your runways. It is however advertized as such in the game description in the Steam store. False advertizing!
Conclusion: think I am going to make a couple of screenshots and then use the false advertising as reason to ask for a refund. I strongly suggest you do not buy this game.
