One of my good friends introduced me to this "game", I wish I never got it though. I have 3 main reasons why I strongly dislike this "game", each of them making more of an impact on me than the last. These are my personal opinions. I have been part of the fanbase at one point, then I saw from the view of the anti-fanbase section. I chose to stick with the anti-fanbase, because I had more evidence to back-up my opinion.
All I have to say is, look at both sides of this community, then choose. You can say whatever you want to me, but good luck changing my opinion on this subject.

3: Gameplay mechanics. When it comes to games, I don't think that graphics matter, but that is not the problem with this "game":. Give what I am about to say a little thought before you start hating on me. It is a point and click game where you have to follow a pattern in order to pass a certian night. That's it. Once you know the pattern the game isn't even fun to play. It's like trying to memorize a combination on a keypad, or the combination on a padlock. Takes you about 60 seconds, then it becomes boring doing it over and over and over again. All you do is sit in a backroom and keep repeating the same process for about 6 minutes. If you somehow don't make it because you mess up on the pattern, the "jumpscares" are nothing more than an animation to show that you died. They're not even scary the first time you see them. Just another way of saying "Game Over". This game could have been on the Nintendo Entertainment System ( An 8-bit gaming console from 1985) and still have worked the same. Not saying that console was bad, but I expect more from todays developers. I would think that kids this generation would be into some newer games, but that apperantly isn't the case. Bloody Disgusting, this game didn't deserve your Game of the Year awards because the awards where for characteristics that the game doesn't even have. The game is not even close to being scary. I expect more from you guys over there at Bloddy Disgusting. I thought you knew what you were doing, but that just simply is not the case.

A majority of the content is not even gameplay. It's a bunch of Source Film Maker content and some "animation". Once peope get involved and you do not think about the negative side of the fanbase, there is no way you're coming back out. You're stuck in a world of mediocre gameplay and animation. If you want to see some of this games content (Why would you?) find some actual gameplay. Or better, play the real game. Or even better yet, ignore this whole series. It's a simple strategy game where you, as the king of your kingdom, have lots of different squad types you can call upon in battle like archers, mages, warriors etc. You pick a squad based on what can best combat your enemy, and try to get through as many waves as you can. When that squad dies, you can pick another, and try to beat all the waves of the encounter before you use up 3 squads.
The reason it works so well is because there's a lot of choices you get to make. There's a crap load of squad types and you can choose from a selection of them with randomised traits in each scenario. You also get to choose which missions you go on, whether you want to earn new squads, abilities, upgrades etc. And even when finishing a scenario you can pick between 3 types of your chosen reward. I don't believe it affects the story a whole lot, but you also get to choose pathways at major story points.
The main gameplay is a fairly simplistic hex-based strategy but has an interesting magic system where killing enemies or changing squads gives you 'threat' to spend on spells. It's a bit boring at first but after you get some new spells and develop a few strategies you like it's more interesting. Combined with the fact that you get literally a tonne of squad types by the end, it's better than average.

This is the best Magic: The Gathering (M:TG) clone that I've seen.
Pros:
- Free to Play
- The game features nuances, such as the ability to permanently modify cards. Cards retain their modified states, regardless of where they are. As an example, if I cast +1/+1 flying on a creature, it directly adds text to the card. If the creature is killed, it still has the modifications on it. The spell, "Silence" permanently wipes out the text on the card.
One of the strangest game mechanics is called, "War Cry", where an attacking creature will blow into a horn, which gives the creature or weapon, closest to the top of the library +1/+1. So you can give random bonuses to things that you have not even seen yet, which is a weird concept for a strategy game.
- I loved playing "Forge" mode, where you draft pick 25 random cards and fight against the AI for prizes:
- The game was very generous and you can get every card in the game, just by grinding, crafting and learning to play well.
- A lot of the artwork was very beautiful. Each card has a static and animated version ( the animated version being rarer ). The animations are more subtle than the cards in "Infinity Wars" but still very cool.
- The AI difficulty scales as you level up ( their decks have better cards ).
Cons:
- As someone who played Magic: The Gathering in sealed deck tournaments, I found the tutorial / campaign a chore to wade through ( 17 wins, 3 losses ). I had seen most of the mechanics in M:TG 16 years prior.
- If you want to play draft games then you have to grind gold by playing constructed games against the AI or people. The alternative is to pay cash ( $5 per draft game ). You get to keep the cards that you draft though.
- If you have a fast effect ( spell ) in your hand, the game auto pauses. The game telegraphs your hand to your opponent, which is idiotic.
- The biggest problem is that where other modern games ( "Spectromancer"; "Infinity Wars"; "Spellweaver"; "System Crash" ) tried to fix the inherant mana problems with M:TG ( mana flood / mana drought ) "Eternal Card" still has M:TG's broken mana system. At least some of Spellweaver's elaborate mana mechanics could be copied... actually on second thought, it would be difficult to change the way mana works because white faction has Empowerment cards ( they receive boosts when you play mana ).
- Balance problems. A couple of cards are overpowered.
Tips for noobs:
You can customize your power (mana) in "Gameplay" options.
You can stack relics on top of one another.
Tips for advanced players:

I bought FFX back on PS2, then PSVita, and now Steam. Clearly this is a must have for any Final Fantasy fans if people are willing to buy it 3 times over.
Pros:
- HD graphics look crisp on PC with a few adjustable graphic options.
- In game "boosters" AKA cheats are awesome for those that have already completed the game (many times in my case).
- Turbo mode to speed things up x2 or x4 comes in handy.
- Achievements
- Autosave
- Good controller support with all the vibrating bells and whistles.
Cons:
- Game freezes up for a few seconds quite often where it looks like its crashed but if you wait a few seconds it keeps going, it isn't game breaking as you can continue playing as normal, but it does get very annoying as it happens often.
- Capped at 30fps
All in all its a decent port, I've just completed FFX without any crashes to desktop, just a few freezes that last a few seconds at a time but the game keeps going. I don't plan on playing FFX-2 again so I can't say how it plays but I'm assuming the performance would be identical.
If you're a fan of the series I would say it's definitely safe to pick this up. It was fun playing through the story again with steam achievements as well as the built in "boosters". Thumbs up from me.

Based on that lineage, I thought I was going in with pretty clear notions of what to expect, one of them being the paradoxical expectation of the unexpected. In spite of that, I was genuinely surprised by twists and turns in the narrative within 15 minutes.
I was not expecting to see an ending in under two hours. Those seeking a game to play moreso than a space to explore or a narrative to unravel will probably get there sooner, and probably be disappointed-  there are other Steam reviews that claim to have finished in 20 minutes. But Verde Station seems clearly designed for multiple playthroughs. Exposition via recursion. Nothing here is as it seems, including the fade to black. The narrative IS the game.
At this juncture, all I can definitively say is those two hours have left me itching to go back, and as a fan of these experiential setting-sims, that's worth my recommendation.

Well I have a mixed feelings about this game. I was about to recommend this game, but I was waiting for something more to be in a game before I do this. Well, it didn't work out.
First, it's very impressive to see such game to be developed by one man. I had a lot of fun providing feedback and bug reports on the forum while the game was in Early Access.
Second, the idea of the game is good. Attempt to present it looks a bit dramatic. There are some good moments in the game which can create an illusion of something interesting happening.
The idea of the game is undeveloped and presented very shallow. It looks like a very short and linear story told us via game. If you compare a game devlopment to a movie development this game reminds me of a short clips directors make to present their vision to producers before they are hired to film a full movie.
There is absolutely no challenge in this game. You just move further because you have nothing else to do.
The game interactions that affect your story progression boil out to just  moving around and using terminals. All other interactive objects are secondary and give very little benefit.
The overall design of the game is very unobvious. The game lacks explanations and player assistance. You can discover some pieces of information scattered around only if you'll be ignoring story progression and specifically looking for them. These pieces of information are very disconnected from each other and won't give you a full picture or even a hint about it. Maybe if you collect them all you'll be able to see something. It seems I haven't found them all.
The game still contains bugs.
I was expecting this game to be in development for at least a year more. I was excited about what this game could be.
I never expected it to end like this.
I can only recommed it only if you're interested in studying game design. There are very good examples of bad design decisions, and a few good ideas. I would like to read post-mortem for this game.

I think everyone who's seriously into video games as a hobby became so after they played... "THAT Game." It was a game that immediately filled him or her with the hazy and incoherent sense of wonder and excitement after playing something that wasn't just a video game, but an experience like no other.
For me personally, that was when I walked into Hasting's and bought a used copy of Fallout 3 for the Xbox 360.
Back then, my mom had gotten me an xbox 360 for my 13th birthday, and I got Halo 3: ODST and GTA 4 with it. I still mostly played TF2 and Half-Life on my crappy laptop, but I remember one day seeing a specific game's boxart. The boxart depicted a washed-out, green hued picture of a suit of armor simutaneously reminiscent of a Knight's armor, and a hazard suit at once. I knew right then and there that this "Fallout 3" was a game I had to have. I begged my mom for it and upon sitting down to play it, I had played it well into dawn by the time I gave it a rest. From the moment that I witnessed my own character's birth, even the little brat that I was knew I was in for a treat. My character went through the stages of living out his own childhood within the vault, even down to dealing with a bunch of wanna-be gangsters harassing a girl he may or may not have liked. That is, until, Dear old Dad left the vault, causing the power hungry overseer to murder one of your childhood friends, Jonas, in cold blood. When I inevitably talked him into giving me the keys to leave the vault and layed my eyes upon the Capital Wasteland for the first time... I knew this game was something special, and to this day it and the fallout series as a whole have had a huge impact on my life.
But enough about me, I feel like a game as legendary as Fallout 3 deserves a proper review.
Fallout 3 is centered around the journey of a character officially only known as "The Lone Wanderer." The Lone Wanderer's father leaves the security of Vault 101 for mysterious reasons, he or she set outs on their epic quest through the graveyard of American society in order to find him. Similar to most other open world RPG's, you will come across the occasional village or city complete with it's own set of eccentric characters, however, these locales are often cobbled together from heaps of junk or within well-fortified pre-war areas which remained relatively intact. There is certainly much to see within the ruins of DC, including but not limited to a certain dorky redhead who dreams of publishing her own little self-help book, a hammy and charismatic radio jockey who dreams of calling the wasteland at large to fight the good fight, a rather well-preserved luxury tower filled with some rather snooty and xenophobic eggheads, a woman who's entire set of life goals are based around aquiring a Soda that turns your urine a glowing mess, a literal oasis of trees and fresh water who's residents have taken to worshipping a certain long-time series staple, and  a dark and dingy city populated entirely by "Ghouls", a 'race' of people who have been violently disfigured from the copious ammounts of radiation that now exists on a global scale. Regardless of who you talk to or where you go, you still must always remember that your prime objective is to try to determine dear old Dad's whereabouts so you can ask him why the Hell he'd leave safety in Vault 101 to plunge himself back into a bleak world that would eat him up in a heartbeat.
Fallout 3 does an excellent job of filling you with an inescapable sense of wonder, and the game world is so huge and deep that 10 years since I first played this game, I'm still discovering areas i've somehow skimmed over. This vastness is aided by Fallout 3's ability to immerse the player in one of the most unique atmospheres in perhaps all of gaming. The capital wasteland is as exciting to explore as it is haunting. There's alot of pre-war houses and buildings that you'll go through scavenging for any and all loot that you can find... but every single area you visit are the remnants of a society long dead. It's really quite horrific to find a house that you think will be a prime candidate for looting, only to find the remains of children upon a bed. There's also no shortage of carnage hungry raiders, slavers, mercenaries, super mutants and deathclaws that prowl the wastelands, ready to bring yet another poor soul to their untimely end. And for as depressing as the world of Fallout 3 often is, it's not not entirely nihilistic. Despite everything that has happened to this burned world, life continues. People have formed rudimentary civilizations, down to the point of establishing the Bottle Caps of Nuka-Cola as a makeshift currency. Hope, and the human spirit as a whole, still most definately exists.
You, the player, get to decide whether you want to embrace the Carnal nature of a world without laws and watch the world burn, or if you want to stick to what's right and become the last, best hope for humanity. In addition, you get to choose how you'd like to do either of these things. Fallout 3 is as much of an RPG game as it is an exploration game. At the very start of the game, you are given access to a panel where you can determine your character's SPECIAL stats: That's Strength, Perception, Endurance, Charisma, Intelligence, Agility, and Luck. These traits will effect the skills you are able to pick. A character with high Strengh and Endurance is better suited towards Melee weapons, for example. A Character with high Agility gains bonuses to Guns and Sneak, allowing them to end fights from a distance before they even start. A Character with high Intelligence and Charisma can exploit non-combat skills such as Speech and Barter to have a better chance to sweet talk NPC's into gaining access to restricted dialogue options. Your SPECIAL, however, does not tie your character into any particular pigeon hole. If you want to have an Intelligence of 1 and be a Science and Medicine expert, then go ahead. Even further, every level up also gives you access to perks, passive skills that further specialize your build. A perk may increase the ammount of damage resistance you gain, or improve your critical chance. Some perks allow you to gib your enemies hilariously merely by shooting them with a BB Gun! The possibilities for any given character are endless, and you can roleplay to your heart's content.
As great as this game is, it's not without it's faults, unforunately. Fallout 3 is decidedly an RPG and not a very good game in terms of combat, You have no true iron sights, the guns are basically unresponsive, and feel universally weightless. Forunately, a system called V.A.T.S. makes a return, allowing you to freeze time and manually select parts of a given enemy that you'd like to specifically target. Unless you're using a machine gun or a sniper rifle, you're most likely going to use this for most combat. In addition, Fallout 3's voice acting was recorded using Bethesda's janitorial team. Seriously, that old man voice you heard in Megaton from Nathan? You're going to hear that exact same old guy for every other old guy in the game. When the voice acting is good, it's spot on, especially since Liam Neeson is your dad, but when it's not, it's laughable. Lastly, the entire metro area of Fallout 3 sucks, and you have to go through it in order to progress the story-line. It's very, very confusing and to this day it's my least favorite part of this game.
Even then, Fallout 3 was more than a good game to me. It was an experience that I'll remember until I die. I spent thousands of hours playing this game on my 360 and the PC version is just leagues better. Fallout 3 opened the door to what I would consider my second favorite gaming franchise of all time. Every single Fallout game has been an incredible experience for me, especially Fallout 3's sister game New Vegas. Still, Fallout 3 will remain my favorite. It was my first taste of how amazing games could be.

As a national guardmen and personal weapon enthusiast, I can say without a doubt that this is the most mechanically accurate handgun simulator i've ever seen. I love having the ability to operate all of the feature present on an actual handgun, and operating them together for a seamless tactical combat experience.
A few things i would like to see, and they're pretty minor: a character model, the floating gun and equipment is somewhat disoriented without context. Even two arms and hands to operate the firearm would be very welcome. Also verying wall and floor textures, just to add a bit of life to the world. The optimization is good for the most part, though i did find some minor stuttering and slowdowns here and there when loading a new cell. otherwise fantastic job to the devs this is outstanding and i hope to see more content in the future.

Fallout 3 is a sandbox-style shooter RPG. It was one of the best games of its time, and it remains one of the best games around. It's definitely more of an RPG than a shooter; you can even pause time and let the computer do the aiming. The world to explore is huge, and you can find whole adventures by just checking out that building on the horizon. The 40's-future aesthetic of everything is really neat. There are many ways to build your character and many different interesting choices you can make during the game. It's not hard to sink a lot of time into this game.
The cons: it can be a little buggy, and the moral choice system is nothing new. Also, there's no reason to play with small guns/melee.
It's worth it at its current price of $20 or $30. Definitely buy the Broken Steel DLC because it raises the level cap. Anchorage and Pitt are decent.

Sometimes some multiplayer TFC servers had a "/stuck" command that would jostle you out of the way when you managed to get yourself stuck in a corner somewhere, so I tried that in Old Vegas and nothing happend. Anyway, in this game (while you're not stuck, anyway) you play Liam Neeson's child who misses its father and has to blow up all of Vegas to get him back. I've never reviewed a game before, but here goes nothing.
I heard about this game a few months before release, when I was reading about bugs in the new SimCity.  I read a developer blog about pathing in Banished, and it intrigued me.  When I discovered it was made by one guy though, I sorta passed on it, so I stopped following it.  It wasn't until about a week before release when I started watching a few videos about it, because my SimNation™ Guild recommended it.  That's when I started to get really excited about it.  Unfortunately though, I didn't get my hopes up too high because at the time I couldn't afford to purchase it myself.  That changed when one of my fellow SimNation™ guild members purchased it as a gift for me.  I cannot thank this person enough for allowing me to play such an awesome game.
The first night I played it, I did the tutorial, as most people probably would, and then started on my first town.  Needless to say it kicked my♥♥♥♥♥ which frustrated the hell out of me.  I didn't know what I was doing wrong.  My town starved to death because I tried growing too fast.  I took a few days off from playing it, but started watching a couple videos, and started learning more about the mechanics.  I ventured back in, and still my town more or less failed.  I was starting to learn though.  And it made me want to come back for more.
I continued watching more videos and reading guides, and learned a lot more about the game.  I finally figured it out and have been playing semi-successfully for about 6 weeks.  The gameplay is fairly straightforward and simple.  Build a town for your Banished, and hope it thrives.  The execution though is far more difficult.  There are so many things to learn about buidling a successful town.  You need to manage your food, which is the number one thing, and make sure you don't grow too fast.  If you start building too many houses, your population will just continue to grow and people will reproduce, putting a huge strain on your food production.
The graphics in this game are great, even though I'm playing on a non-gaming laptop, it runs pretty smoothly.  At least until you get to a high population, and then the framerate drops a bit.  Not to an unplayable level, but definitely noticeable.  The best thing to do if you're playing on a low-end machine is to not play at 10x speed if you plan on moving around the map at all.
Lost my train of thought, so I'm going to end this review with this.  The fact that ONE GUY made this game is absolutely mindblowing.  This one man did a phenomenal job creating a town building game that is far far better than SimCity, and far less buggy.  Sure, there are a few bugs here and there, but nowhere near the amount that SimCity has had since launch.  And considering it's only $19.99, you cannot go wrong buying this game.  I cannot recommend this game enough to anyone who wants a city building or planning game.  There are definitely things that could be improved, but I have confidence that the developer will actually listen to his fans and will implement changes when he is able to.
Bottom line, this is a MUST BUY if you're into this style of game.  Hell, even if you're not, it's a great game to get you going with this genre.  I can't give it a 10/10, but that's only due to a few small issues and the fact that I don't think any game is a perfect 10.  And really, what the hell does an arbitrary number really matter anyway?
Oh, one last thing, the game uses a random map generator, using a number system, a 9 DIGIT NUMBER SYSTEM, so you do the math and figure out how many different maps there are in this game.  Sure, it can be hard to find a map that you really like and enjoy playing on, but the fact that there are so many possibilities means that there will be a map seed for everyone.
Sorry for the long rambling review, which probably is fairly pointless anyway.  But, if anybody actually reads this, and hasn't purchased the game yet, what are you waiting for?!?  BUY IT!!!

Ah VVVVVV.  What can be said about this indie hit that hasn’t already been said?  Well, I could say its a hamster served with gravy, a side of steak fries, and an ice cold cola.  Of course that would be a lie, but it probably hasn’t been said before.
This game is centered around one simple concept: You can't jump.  Instead you reverse gravity to get from point A to point B.  The goal is to find your five crew members and get them all, along with yourself, back to the ship.  While it lets you tackle some of the puzzles in the order you want, in-between it throws required puzzles at you.  And let me tell you, those puzzles are hard.  And by those puzzles I mean all of them.
The game has pretty tight controls, a good thing because many of the games puzzles rely on pulling off tight maneuvers mid-air and landing on relatively small platforms.  That being said, sometimes I did find myself slipping off of various platforms or that I continue moving when I wanted to stop.  This may have been my accidental holding of the button, or may have been momentum actually being slightly carried, I’m not sure.
The music is good, and defiantly fits into the game.  Though it is weird how sometimes it fades out, as if to start the loop again, then picks right back up and keeps going.
This is also a relatively short game and it's minimalistic on the graphics.  This brings me to my biggest complaint about the game: It felt like a Flash game.  In a world with free games available on sites such as Kongregate and Armor Games, it's hard to make an argument for buying a game when it looks like it could be played in a web browser.   Of course, the line between Flash, Mobile, and low end PC games is beginning to blur.
However, this game is defiantly worth the money.  At around $5 the game delivers, and despite feeling minimalist and Flash game-y, doesn’t make you feel like you got ripped off.
Overall, I give it a 9/10.  I have to dock a point for the loss of my sanity somewhere in the dimensions of the game.  Really, this game will steal your sanity.  I mean, I opened this review talking about serving hamster.  Regardless, this game is worth playing.
Oh yea, and it's especially definitely worth it when you can get it for less than $0.50 and the money all came from selling trading cards on the Steam marketplace.  Don't you LOVE Steam sales, I know I do!

Banished is one of those indie games that revives one of the old genres that has been abandoned by the mainstream: city building. You start as a group of exiles banished from their homeland and sent to live in the untamed new world. You build houses, set aside land for farming, chop down trees...do what you'd think you'd do to survive. One of the quirks of the game is that you have no direct control over what your citizens do. Instead, you just assign a number to a job, and free hands fill it. Honestly, while this idea mostly plays well, it can be very aggravating. Sometimes, you want your miner to live right by the mine, but he instead lives on the other side of town. Nothing you can do there. Also aggravating is citizens starving despite having stockpiled food.
The game is very unforgiving and your first town will fail quickly. Yet it's a very fun time waster, and can be relaxing. When people aren't dying, that is. It's like Dwarf Fortress, except not as complex or insane.

Notice: Before you read this, note that this is just my opinion, and you can make your own. I won't affect it.       Shoot the dang enemies.... Hook onto Kane's heli... Run like hell.... GO GO GO! Oh, hello there. I'm going to start with the basics. For anyone who loves GTA, but doesn't play it often, or it broke, or whatever, Just Cause 2 is there. At it's price, you can't beat a realistic game like this. Sorry, GTA, but JC2 is better in my opinion. In this game you play as a character named Rico, who has many missions to do with various clients. It's not the same and the same every freaking round and mission. Each mission has its own meaning, solution, cause, ect. I played the demo multiple times and waited months to finally get enough money to pay for this. This game is something else. Each structure blows up its own way. Also, pull enemies off of feet with grapple hook, 5000 out of 1000
Anyway, this game is unique for its grappling hook system. You can tether things together, pull things toward you, slap people with it, hook onto cars, drag bodies, tie two bodies together to make them slam in midair. This game is different for the colorful, but dark environment of the destructive missions, a few with multiple ways of solving them. There are amazing missions, but it still has its share of amazing free roam action. If you get into the right place, you can mess around with the environment. There is a variety of different weapons and vehicles, ranging from jeeps or pistols, to helicopters and explosives. There are quite a fair bit of special things to destroy that are found randomly around the map, many achievements, and other things to make this game quite an amazing one. If I could rate on a scale of 1-10 of everything, here's my list:
Gameplay: 8.5 - It's good but can get fairly confusing
Graphics: 9.0 - They are amazing and colorful, but if you have an old computer, you will lag quite a bit.
Destruction System: 9.5 - It is amazing. I am a rather large fan of destruction myself. I find as many games with realistic damage systems as I can. There are few. Ones like this, Battlefield, and all those others fulfill that want.
Vehicles: 8.0 - There are many to choose from, and you can hijack them, shoot the people out, blow the vehicle straight out of the road, and more. It has a realistic driving system as well.
Weapons: 9.5 - Now here's the good stuff. There is a crapton of weapons to choose from, whether it be modded or put in the game on the start. There are SMGs, MGs, LMGs, Rockets, Pistols, and other things too.
The way it is unique is the grappling hook. You don't see many games with those, do you? I give the grappling hook a 9.5 out of 10. Why not a full 10? It can be tricky to use sometimes, with a partially screwed up range. I feel it is a bit too short of a range. It is fun to use however, as it has multiple funny uses. For example, pulling people off of their feet and them saying "HELP! HE CAUGHT ME WITH HIS WIRE THINGY!" and them trying to untie it, but utterly failing, and launching into the air where you can shoot them. Another is tying them to a civillian car, and the civillian in the car having not the slightest idea there is a person they are dragging around, and killing the hitchhiker slowly.
AI: 6.5 - Why? The AI has a ridiculous amount of health, but nothing like the super aim sniper noob AI in Sniper Elite V2. This AI is smart, can detect at a reasonable skill level, and other things, but it feels a bit overpowered with its health.
Mods: (Unrated currently) - I haven't really modded it yet, only really the multiplayer mod, but I can easily imagine I'd love the mods.
Multiplayer: (Unrated Currently) - I have only one friend to play with on it, and I haven't done it yet. I can imagine there'd be a few unimaginably good players out there, but a few not so good average players out there. Others are in between. Don't get me wrong, I can imagine I'd enjoy multiplayer apart from the fact I SUCK AT FPS AND TPS!
FINALLY, THE MOMENT YOU'VE (maybe) BEEN WAITING FOR,
My overall game rating and whether or not I recommend it, 9.5 out of 10 scorpions. Yes, I know. I had so many positive things to say about it, but like any other game, it has its negative parts, and I will list those after this rating. This game is a unique third person shooter, but its AI isn't that good. I mean come on, they are social butterflies who scream a lot and are way too, um, They have way too much health. Let's just say that. I can land 3 headshots and they simply wont die. I can shoot them in the chest, or any other vitals multiple times, and they're all like "NOP EIM FYN HEEHEETEE"(Translate from Panauan) (Nope, I'm fine TeeHeeHee)
THE NEGATIVE SIDE:
Like I mentioned multiple times, it is a very laggy game for those older and weaker CPUs, and it takes up a lot of space. It works, but imagine... It could be a crapton better on old computers, but NOOOOO
And I mentioned this single thing twice: The AI is buggy.
Where to start with it. It IS a fairly good AI, but the health and voices are annoying to me. I feel like I can't even play a game without hearing that voice, and I got this game the same day I wrote this review (6/5/14) I mean, come on.
The last two things about the negatives. Price, and Graphics.
This game is worth paying, but I feel it costs a little too much for weaker computers. It's like adding a high price and slow speed for bad graphics cards (Wait, isn't that exactly what it is?) Anyway, maybe if they brought the price down to 10 dollars, then it would be more fair. I just don't find this price amazingly fair.
FINALLY, Graphics: The graphics are good, don't get me wrong, but they just BARELY work on slow graphics cards. I have a slow card, and 75 percent of my deaths in the game are from lag spikes. Maybe make the graphics less "WHOA, THIS LAGS MY SLOW GRAPHICS CARD" and there would be even MORE buys.
Overall, YES, I recommend this. It is awesome with all of the good things, but the graphics and price could be more fair for us steam (and Square Enix game) players. If you love a simple destruction sandbox with missions and a twist, look into this game and maybe even buy it. You won't regret it. Now, what are you doing reading this? GO BUY IT NOW!

As always loyal fans, my 100 hours of gameplay obligatory review... The good, the bad, and the warning.
This brave marriage of both race/roam concepts into a single game is not flawless, but is still a huge step up from the early pioneers of this genre such as Midnight Club. This game stands out in the race/roam genre due to Ivory Tower's groundbreaking philosophy of making the race essential to the roam, and vice versa, rather than just trying to use the free-roam as a bonus feature like in a Need for Speed game.
The Good: The map is incredible, and the USA begs to be explored (just don't use anything you have learned on your geography test as the locations of points of interest and the borders of the map are not very accurate). I love this game for its call to curiosity, and the open world concept is what this game is centered around. Honestly though, if you are just looking for a good racing sim rather than a free roam based game go with Assetto Corsa instead. The customization is also good and the diversity of cars is alright. The game does make up for its smaller than average car list by making each car very unique by giving it different "specs", which I love. The specs of the H1 Hummer may be just modifications to the same base vehicle, but each is so unique in appearance and handles so differently that you are taming an entirely new beast when you switch from the dirt spec to performance. This holds true for most cars, and that is a huge plus on my list. I won't ignore the story either, and it gets my two thumbs up. Though not very rich or immersive, the story in this game is meant to introduce the player into the primary features of the game, and it does this while still having a decent plot which takes the player to all corners of the map. The good part about staging the story this way is that you don't feel like the game is over when the story is, and in fact you are only more hooked on the game than when it started.
The Bad: I'll be frank, everyone, and not just audiophiles, complains about engine sounds in this game and for good reasons. Off the top of my head I really can't think of more than seven or eight unique engine sounds for the thirty or so cars in the game. You can tell when you are driving the Lamborghini, the Hummer, RUF, and a few other iconic cars, but other than those exceptions all of the audio on the cars sound very similar. At least they are divided up into engine noise classes; for example, all of small cars like the Abarth and the Mini sound the same, and so do most low-slung exotics like the Ford GT and the ZR1. The other major bummer in this game is that multiplayer lobbies are abandoned in areas and some game modes like faction vs. faction are rarely even played. This is a shame for a newly released game, and frustrating waiting ten minutes to find a match. Lastly, the soundtrack is also rather limited and you will find yourself hearing the same songs over again if you play more than an hour at a time.
The Warning: When it says "high end PC required" it isn't kidding. Thinking mine could handle it I bought the game but it lagged bigtime on even low settings. My PC can run Skyrim on high without a hiccup, but this game pushes its limits. I am running an NVIDIA GeForce 8800 GT. However, with some modding to the launch files and reducing the graphics settings manually I was able to get the game to run at a tolerable 30 fps most of the time.
Overall I would recommend this game if you like the fast paced and intense racing action of Grand Tourismo, but also enjoy the serenity and curiosity of a game like Euro Truck Sim and are willing to accept the MMO trend for new games.

I'll start this review with saying, that I loved the first LOG and once I completed it, I went straight to google and queried "games like LOG" and "LOG 2 release date", knowing full well, there wasn’t a chance it was being developed yet,  but just hoping it was, as the experience was fantastic.  Well I got my wish!  At current I have around 14hrs into the 2nd installment and have not been disappointed.
If you are reading these reviews to get an idea of gameplay, I can say the grid based movement system can be odd or awkward at first, if you have never experienced it but you really feel like you’re playing an old school dungeon crawler or a tile based board game and sink right into it after a handful of minutes.  Don’t get this confused with turn based or real time pause type games like wasteland 2 or dragon age.  This is real time with you being limited in movement to linear paths only. You move as you would with any other game using w a s and d in a linear fashion on an invisible grid.  You can rotate within a grid square using q and r or rotate by dragging and pulling your mouse.  You are also able to look around with the mouse within your FOV up, down and side to side.  You are probably wondering why even utilize this and not just use free roam?  The grid based system has a direct influence on combat, as you can only engage an enemy that is in a tile(s) directly in front of you - ranged weapon, firearms or magic can be cast/fired beyond 1 square. You cannot move diagonally.  This makes combat difficult and tricky when multiple enemies are engaged with you.  Back yourself into a corner and hope you have enough health potions to duke it out before your entire party gets wiped out.
This is a good spot to describe the party system.  It’s a four party group stacked 2 x 2.  The front two, typically are your tanks, damage dealer type heroes with the back being your spell casters and ranged weapon guys.  This is pretty standard but important to understand how that works within the grid system.  When facing directly in front of an enemy, the front two take the brunt of the damage while allowing your back row to cast and fire.  Let an enemy flank your party and the back row now becomes the focus of the full force of an attack.  This can be very troublesome as they typically don’t have the protection or armor the front row has.
Attacking can be confusing for a new player as you don’t actually click on the enemy to attack, like you would in a standard first person hacker.  As long as the party is facing the block with an enemy in it, you simply click the item/weapon in your hand to perform the attack (in party box lower right hand corner).  To cast a spell you first need to find the scroll, have the required skills/traits to cast it and finally to use, right click the hand and select the correct glyphs to perform the spell.  You have to memorize these and perform them every time you cast a spell.  There is no hot key for spells.  Spells with multiple glyphs need to be drawn, by holding and dragging the mouse across the designated glyphs.  This stumped me for a while as I was simply clicking them which are fine for single glyph spells but useless for more complex spells.
The world is full of secret chests and loot so keep an eye out for button like stones on walls.  In fact whenever I go through a new area I always look left and right at every wall surface to find hidden wall buttons.  Get used to doing this. Getting through the game will be considerably harder if you are not finding the secret items.  All secret chests need lock picks to open!  You find these in the world so search every last block.  This is not like path of exile or another action RPG where they dump items on you.  These lock picks are few and far between, in some cases you will have to make a decision which chest you want to open.  In these circumstances I simply save it and test each one out for its contents (CONTENTS ARE NOT RANDOM) when you decide which chest has the most useful loot go to it, loot it and save it.  Another great aspect of the secret chests is that some are buried around the world, so you may be given a treasure map and tasked with digging up areas looking for it.
So now to my favorite part of this game - the puzzles!  This game has the best combination of RPG elements and adventure game puzzles.  If you like complicated puzzles that you would often find in classic point and click adventure games, you will love these.  They really make you stop and think, all while testing your sanity.  They can be downright frustrating for some and near impossible for others, who don’t have the constitution or mental makeup for them.  All, however, are very logical when the solution presents itself, from either trial and error, or simply when you fold and look it up online.  Solving some of these will make you feel like a genius! And your efforts will be rewarded with a shimmering melody and a rare item or clue.
Without giving away any spoilers I would like to touch on the story and level layouts.  Each unique area you access consist of outdoor open environments, coupled with a labyrinth of dungeons beneath.  This differs significantly from the original where you were confined to the claustrophobic dark of the tunnels.  This offers a nice respite from the stress of dungeon crawling IMHO.  Its always a breath of fresh air, literally, when you make it out to the bright summer sun after spending hours, laboring in the rat infested deep.  You are able to back track to previous levels in case you want to open a locked chest or forgot to do something important.  I cant speak for the entire game, but at least to where i am, 14hrs in, i was able to go as far back to the opening beach. There is a running theme through the levels/areas, in regards to story quest items.  You are not simply leveling and grinding for the sake of leveling.  You collect story unique items which will most likely be used in some synergistic fashion at the climactic ending.  I am no where near this but seeing how the levels have progressed thus far, it would be a logical deduction.
There are many game options at the start of a new game all of which allow you to scale the difficulty.  Easy Normal and hard are the difficulty levels.  In my opinion Normal can be difficult for new players or if your party is not balanced correctly so choose wisely.  You also have the option of disabling the map function which forces you to draw your own maps on grid paper which is lots of fun tbh.  It forces you to slow down and take note of things around you, as opposed to running through the dungeon in which case you can become quickly disoriented and lost.  You will never really become lost but they are useful when running from an enemy(s) so you can keep your orientation so not to back yourself into a corner which as explained earlier can be game ending.  Another option is to allow quick save anywhere in the game (f5).  This in my opinion is too easy to spam so I choose the option to save at save crystals which are sparingly spread across the levels.  One final option is to only be allowed 1 save per crystal.  This is extreme and to be used with caution.  You can do a lot before you come across another save crystal so dying before you reach it can be disastrous and for some a game ender all together.
I can't recommend this game any higher.  Pick it up and you will have hours upon hours of fun.  I am sitting at work writing this review because I can’t wait to get home to play it!

Reverse Crawl is quick, fun, fairly simple turn Based Strategy game.
The story is your daughter, a necromancer, raises you from the dead after your castle was invaded by The Red Queen. You now must use various undead and other minions/monsters in battle to get new powers, new allioes, andgain stength to defeat her and reclaim your kingdom. The story does nothing that will really surprise you, but I liked it. It got me from point A to B and gave motivation to what I was doing.
Battle is performed in waves, both of your enemies and allies. They have X number of waves, usually around 3 (but it goes 1-5) and you have a few waves yourself. Your team will consist of premade groups of certain monsters that have their own strengths and weaknesses. Each type of unit has their own set of powers, but you also have a bar of spells that may be used on any units turn in addition to their normal actions. These can be direct damage, summons, heals, stunning, and so on. So while I say the battles are "simple" there is a good range of various actions you can take every time given the resources. The battles are pretty well balanced, though I hate the Alchemists.
I beat the main campaign in 4 hours, which to me is fine for the asking price.
There's an Endless Wave mode, and a New Game+ mode I can choose now. When going through the campaign you pick from 3 different power-ups to gain new ally groups, buff existing groups, or gain new powers, and there's an upgrade screen as well for various buffs to your team, so I imagine going through the campaign again will allow me to focus on different areas, and use other groups I didn't use much in my first play through.

If you want a way to beat the game on hard with out too much stress. It seems that they built the farmer into the game for this purpose because there is so much synergy to this strategy. I went with a Lizard Knight, Lizard Rogue, Lizard Alchemist. Human Farmer with skilled tech and fast learner. I put the 1 point into alchemy on the farmer (yes not the alchemist, the farmer). The rogue/alchemist took light weapons/accuracy and put their first point into Accuracy 2 for reach. Then straight light weapons until max, then crit until max. The alchemist is really just a rogue who sacrifices his rogue abilities for the herb spawning tech. All 3 lizards take poison immunity, the knight takes fast metabolism, and the others take endure the elements. This means the only damage that can hit the rogue/elem (usually magic [always?] through the front row has to deal with 50+ resist all, and straight immune to poison). Now that all that's out of the way, I let the farmer contribute in the early game with the sling and rocks but by the time I got the first boss I just keep him dead. The farmer is dead 99.99% of the time. This lets me stack all my best armour on the knight, convert all the herbs to health pots (at crystals when I res the farmer he makes pots and gets to partake in 1 sometimes 2 fights until he's dead again). The knight takes armor/athletics and lastly dodge techs. Since only the knight tanks when slots are broken you don't have to worry about multiple characters having slots broken, so it's less use of potions. Also with fast metabolism pots are 2x effective. (Also 3 living party members consume less food, not that it's going to matter.) Now for the poison immunity, when you get to the herder poison mushroom spawner fight, you will be around level 5-6, don't kill all the spawners, I left one alive (the back one where the orb is) and I backed my party on the tile where the bag is picked up. 3 poison immune lizards are 100% immune to the little sapling type mob, and the mushroom head guys that spam poison, those mobs cannot do a single point of dmg ever, except the 3rd mob is a mushroom type melee mob. Luckily for you, you've been paying attention and have a beefed up knight with all your best armour pieces so far. With some finesse and running around you can kill this room indefinitely, as you get higher level you will be able to hold that one tile (where the bag is) without ever moving. These mushrooms drop food (not 100%, but regularly). You will amasse this beautiful stack of mushrooms on the tile right in front of you. When you are convinced you're high enough level. Finish the encounter and go outside to the crystal (not too far) and res your farmer, take him back and have him eat all the food (don't try to carry the food, let it sit on the ground).
With a human farmer and fast learner tech, I was able to get him to level 17 when the rest of the party just got 11. Thats with leaving plenty of food for everyone to spare.
An alternative to this strategy, would be to make the farmer a lizard as well with poison immunity. There is a healing crystal that acts like a real crystal (1-time-use) that drops right in that room. You can wait until you have enough food on the ground and the place under well enough control to res the farmer, eat all the food, level him, and put him in the front line. If you don't have poison immunity and res the human he'll die immediately. If he's in front he'll be subject to the melee dmg in there too, if you intend to keep him alive the rest of the way, he'll need to be up front and tanking. For this reason you should consider giving the farmer things like Athletics/Armor/Conc[3](shielding)/Alchemy etc. I wouldn't worry about the farmer as a damage dealer, it won't be worth the extra mouse effort to click his weapon when you're dealing with the 4 rogue attacks which do more than enough dmg.
Also if you don't want to spend that much time there leveling, just get the farmer to 5 for max alchemy at this stage, and leave him dead through the whole game, doing pots at crystals.
If you want to use a non poison strategy. I recommend a knight/battlemage/rogue/alchemist I would probably make the alchemist a human with 'skilled' tech for lightweapons/accuracy/alchemy so I don't have to sacrifice points in dmg early. Obviously rogue/alch get accuracy 2 first then no more accuracy ever, you know the drill. Once light weapons is maxed you could put the alchemists points in alchemy instead of crit. I recommend rushing Con 3 for shielding on your page. The 25 Prot on the buff will be an absolute must keep active ability.
Good luck.

This is a vast improvement over previous entries in the series. They've done a great job of gamifying the race weekend in a meaningful way that was absent before. You have tasks to complete and they aren't onerous to do with a reasonable setup.
The AI can be a little dumb sometimes, like I got rammed off the track twice but simply having flashbacks enabled is a great way around this. Thats really my only criticism.
I like that you can simply select your team in career, I didn't like having to work up from the bottom in previous games in the series, it just wasn't fun to shoot for 17th place every race.
The AI is a lot better in terms of performance, if on a lower difficulty they would simply take corners unreasonably slow before, but now its more like their overall pace is lowered evenly, which makes for a more compelling race at lower difficulties.
The car handling is more predictable with correct settings. One criticism I have is that I think their default differential choice is a little strange for some setups. For instance with full downforce, the default diff setting is 90%, which is very locky and make the car be sortof all over the place coming out of some turns. Once you turn this down, its like night and day basically.
The game plays really well even on a 2 year old mid range gaming pc right out of the box. I had two framerate hickups in the race but that might have been cause I was downloading something at the same time.
I would say if you haven't bought it yet but are thinking about it cause of the sale, I'd go for it. I was on the fence about waiting till F1 2017, but my wheel stopped working with F12013 which I also own, so I figured its worth it now since its also on sale.

Reverse Crawl is an extremely additive game. I can't stop playing it. I'm always so excited to start playing it and have to pry myself away each time in order to stop playing it. It's so much fun. I really didn't think I'd like it near as much as I actually do. I'm so glad I bought it now. It's so worth the money. They make the game simple to understand and pick up, challenging enough to make you keep coming back, and engaging enough to encourage you to to keep playing and trying if you don't win a certain quest the first time around. It's everything I typically want within a turn based strategy and I have a good grasp on what I want since I grew up playing these kind of games. The only two minor critiques I can give on this game is that on the "Endless" option it gives at the end, I wish it allowed you to send out one of each group you've picked up along the way to make it even more endless versus the 3 or 4 waves (can't remember which one it is right now) they give you. The other critique is I wish that they allowed more power options after each quest. That would be especially helpful when going for a certain theme as I'm currently trying to go with a Necromancy theme as much as possible on my current run through of the game. I feel like they should allow one option for each catagory of powers (Necromancy, Saboteur, etc.) each time. Other than that, it's a fantastic game. Finally came F1 2016 and after hearing about the new features for it especially the Manual Starts where you hold down the A button on the Controller (This is different if you use a wheel) until the lights go out. While I understand to be classed as Illegal overtake is either you overtake over the white lines or under a yellow flag, But whats not classed as illegal is where a car spins or crashes out and causes a pile up with 3 or 4 cars is not an Illegal overtake, its trying to avoid the collision. This does ruin the racing for me a bit because when I get hit for Illegal overtake for passing a car thats facing the wrong way after a spin with 3 other cars piled up behind it. its classed as an Illegal overtake but Im miles ahead of them so I have to slow right down for them only then do I get hit with a penalty for not letting them through even though it was there own fault for not making the mistake in the first place!

If you are not a fan of unexplained endings and piecing the story together with your own imagination, then I would highly advise you to not buy this game!
For the record: this game is pretty linear, having those nice and simple 'manage your resources right, dont waste your ammo etc.' game mechanics placed in a charming post-apocalyptic scenery which you travel by train, driving from one station, accepting a simple task (i.e. bring this to that), to another station, ending previous task and getting a new one, all while you learn more and more that a great threat, which already accured over a 100 years ago and almost destroyed all of humankind, is on its rise again. This game feeds you up with so much main- and background-story appetizers that you'll a 100% keep on playing 'till the end because you can't wait anymore to unravel all its' secrets... well that is in fact, untill you reach the end for real.
Im trying to make an example: imagine watching your all time favorite franchise Star Wars: Episode V and right after the scene where Luke accused Vader that he killed his father, and just as Vader answered 'NO!'  the movie would cut off into commercials. But not the commercials you get from time to time while the movie is running. I mean the commercials you'd see at the end of your free-TV movie. You would never get to know that Lukes' hand gets replaced or even more important, that Lord Vader is his father.
This is The Final Station summed up in an example. All the joy and fun you had while playing this game means nothing when reaching the end of it, which comes as abrupt as your climax after getting your long time crush into having sex with you (don't lie to yourselves, you all had this).
The ending leaves you with so much open questions, which will only be answered if using your own imagination is good enough for you.
And then you remember this game has a DLC, which is basically Star Wars: Episode I - III in my stated example, ending the third episode right after Obi dropped the sh*t out of Anakin and left him on the edge of a lava-stream, cutting out the part where he got picked up by Palpatine and being made into Darth Vader. Long story short: the DLC leaves you with even more questions!
The Final Station really had some potential and it feels like the autors came up with a good story but where to lazy/busy to end it well and while still regretting buying that game, in a somewhat way I hope they make a sequel (mby even prequel?), where all the stuff gets explained since my thirst for knowledge is still not satisfied. But until then:
DON'T BUY IF YOU HATE SUCH CLIFFHANGERY ENDINGS

Rive is an action platformer heavily leaning towards shoot’em’up, or run’n’gun. And I was surprised by how good it is.
The gameplay is very smooth and fluid, with fast movements and the ability to double jump. Additionally, you can control where you shoot with the mouse, which means 360° of freedom. Add to this infinite ammo, and then picture yourself all guns blazing with very aerial movements despite being in a tank looking like those from Metal Slug. Oh, and the screen shakes when you shoot. Simply exhilarating. Just perfect.
I could criticise a bit the secondary weapons system, since you can only have one ammo at the time for different attacks (like homing missiles or EMP). I understand that it would be overpowered to access those too often, but the game is generous with ammo anyway… It just makes it less reliable than it should. Otherwise each attack has its advantage or disadvantage under specific circumstances, all good. I just also regret that the mouse wheel cannot switch between them. But it’s ok, all the keyboard buttons are rebindable at least.
The graphics are really sharp and remind me of the beautiful Rayman, even though the design itself is not as impressive. It still all works well together, but it would not be the highlight of the game for me.
The highlight of the game is the level design. So much variety. So many situations. Tons of references to other games that are even translated in how it plays. Moments in zero-g between classical platforming. Traps made of crushers, lasers and so on. Rising lava. Monsters infighting thanks to the hack system (some specific enemies can temporarily become your pet/familiar). Corridors with point blank dangerous gunfights. Arenas that move. Boss fights with interesting patterns and phases. It’s all there. It’s brilliant. The difficulty curve is great too, from easy to harder and harder. Although there is sometimes a bit too much reliance on suicide bots.
Rive is a celebration of the run’n’gun formula. A perfect blend of shooting and platforming, an excellent gameplay and a sublime level design. This game came out of nowhere, and it is exactly what I was looking for. Heartfelt recommendation.

So I told myself I'd just continue on and hope to be enlightend, and thankfully I was. The story seems to be presented to you by way of eavesdropping. You overhear bits of conversation in town, either indrectly or when you "speak" directly to someone, even though your own lines are not shown; NPCs simply respond to you in a  way that usually conveys what your character had said, such as "A phone? Sure there's one just down the road." Curiously, an exception to this occurs when you are on your train and conversing with someone via network connection, whereupon you occasionally have one or two choices of what you will say to the person on the other end. Admirably, the story presented to me kept me hooked in spite of
.
Along the way, several surreal things happen to make you wonder if something truly alien is happening and/or if your character actually has a full grip on reality. Some occurances were disturbing, some sinister, and one at the end that gave bittersweet closure to the whole thing.
All in all, I'm glad I gave this game my time. It keeps you largely in the dark at first, but gives you plenty of little revelations along the way.

What can I say. I haven't even touched the surface of this collection, however I have completed FFX.
FFX is a wonderful game. The remaster is tastefully done and many areas of the game have been visually enhanced. Still, some facial animations and character models look outdated because they were not enhanced. This does, however, not take away from the overall experience of the game.
The story is epic. You follow the journy of Tidus, who crossed into a world where he doesn't belong. He wants to find a way back to his home, but it's hard. Along his journey he meets a wonderful cast of characters, who inspire him and show him that his fate is in his own hands and that true love is something we should strive for even in times when all hope seems lost. The chemistry between the characters is great and they all play off each other and form a team, which can eliminate even death itself. Spira is not yet lost, so it is upon you and your friends to break it out of the vengeful cycle or spiral of death.
The port is good. The game's performance is locked to 30fps (at least I think, I haven't checked but it seems so), however, the lock does not worsen your enjoyment, because you just don't care. My game has never crashed and all went well. The game is long (at least 40 hours If you like to play slow, but you can easily play it for more than 100 hours with all the sidequests and dungeons + bosses). I haven't done any of the sidequests except the chocobo race, and blitzball may not be for everyone. The bosses can be tough sometimes (looking at you Seymour + the final bosses). Also, screw the insta death spell. The sphere grid is kind of confusing with its complicated upgrade paths, but you can learn it in time.
To sum it up, FFX is a really wonderful game. It's long and its story stood the test of time. You might also cry at the end, because the game is very emotional. The graphics are nice for it being a HD Remaster. Furthermore, the game offers a variety of side content, which is nice. This games is the one JRPG that I wholeheartedly recommend to anyone who is interested in playing this genre or people, who just want to play a good RPG. This is turn based combat at its best.

Great mechanics. The game throws you into a survival situation with a gun of random type in an unknown state and asks you to deal with it using detailed gun operation mechanics. It's difficult to remember all the buttons, as there is one for releasing the magazine, one for loading, one for cocking the hammer, one for toggling the safety, one for inserting magazine, one button for each storage space in the inventory, and one button which consistently drops the magazine you just released to the ground, forcing you to pick it up again using a different button(and with a released magazine the layout changes). Combining these into fluid gun operation is hard, and that's the point. This is not a point-and-click fps like call of duty which supplies you with a handy "make gun ready for firing"-button and a big nice crosshair floating in the middle of the screen. Everything you do is exactly as it would be in real life using a real handgun. You even need to put your gun away when you load rounds into a magazine.
I do have some problems with the game though. First, it's a bit repetitive and bland. You face two different enemies through the game, and both are instant death unless you're lucky. It's realistic and makes for a good demonstration of the mechanics(and the message behind it), but it doesn't work very well as a game. Secondly, the main objective of the game, which is finding 11 cassette tapes providing you with the backstory for the setting, is impossible. Most of my attempts I die after having found exactly 0 tapes. You can search through miles of this building and never find a tape. The most I've found was 3 I think. It's not worth the attempt to go for all 11, so with the main objective being moot, the mechanics is all there really is to the game.
Thirdly, the end goal of any game should simply not be to reveal the exposition. According to what you learn underway, you are a survivor of some extradimensional genocide of the human race, conditioned to fight back against them. However, as far as I can tell(as I haven't found all the tapes before), you fighting back doesn't really have much of a purpose. You don't save the human race, as they are all gone, you don't deliver a blow to them that serves as phyrric victory, you don't even get to kill a single one of them. You are just a special agent trained to survive the initial massacre so you could starve to death a bit later. So the storytelling doesn't work very well and mostly serves to confuse.
Now, I do realize that my criticism is a bit irrelevant considering the purpose and format of the game(and the fair price). The reason for my criticism is simply because I really, REALLY want to see this concept developed further.
If this game was a filled-in roguelike akin to the binding of isaac, with permanent and temporary upgrades, special items, more enemies, more varied areas and with a more direct purpose, this could be an amazing game. I believe this would be entirely possible without breaking with the principles behind the game. For example, you start with the 1911 and some bullets, then while you learn the game mechanics you earn a temporary upgrade, let's say a fluorescent front sight or a magazine of hollow point bullets(giving a high chance of disabling an enemy without a critical hit maybe?). Then you find a tape and unlock a permanent upgrade, the ability to sense whether an enemy is within a certain distance(that's sort of the stuff I would imagine considering the whole "mentally conditioned to deal with the invaders from another dimension" thing. It could be as simple as unlocking the ability to hear them better, which is one of the things that bothered me. *silence* BEEP BANG *death*). Next run you use your new ability to gain 10 enemy kills without dying and it rewards you with a new gun which you can start with or find during a run. Then maybe as you gain achievements or find things, you unlock new items you can find(and therefore the chances of finding anything), or maybe the chances of starting a run with rarer items, or unlocking a bulletproof vest which has a 80% chance of absorbing a hit and a 40% chance of being broken each time it does. It should lead somewhere and feel like you are improving and progressing.
There are a lot of things you can do with this concept, and the rogue-like format is what it's already going for, so that's just an example. I want it to have value as a game, because as a simple gun simulator the whole procedurally generated stuff and backstory is pretty wasted on it. Another potential use for the mechanics is as a proper gun-range simulator, which could be a great way to learn about gun operation and safety(I imagine with instructors who throw you out if you don't use proper safety precautions). In that case there would have to be a lot of different weapons and more realistic aiming(with the steadying and holding your breath and that whole thing).
Tl;dr: The mechanics are excellent, but the game they are used for isn't. I want to see a good game using the same amazing mechanics, and so do you.
Oh, and let me hold shift to run.

I don't know if you've heard from like, all the marketing but this is Two Tribes' last game. All I can say after playing RIVE is that's a damn shame.
RIVE is a twin stick shooter/platformer that starts off pretty easy and seems like it will be throughout because of its generous checkpoints but quickly gets super challenging and will take way longer to finish than you might think. You're a space scrappin' trucker type who ends up coming across a huge derelict but ends up trapped inside by a cute and funny but oddly sinister AI who wants you to test you against its creations.
The writing is very punny and relies a bit too much on references and memes for my taste but it does the job well enough. Your character talks frequently and I find his voice acting somewhat flat and uninteresting but again, it's serviceable.
The game play is what you should come to RIVE for and on this, it delivers. The control layout is unique, especially on a game pad but it's also intuitive and you get used to it quickly. You move with the left stick or the keyboard and fire with the right stick or the mouse. You can also hack certain electrical boxes to progress and also different kits of robots to aid you, either defensively or offensively. Enemies drop scrap which you can collect and use to purchase upgrade and special weapons. You can only hold one special weapon shot at a time but they drop frequently and one shot can be used with any special weapons you have purchased.
Much of RIVE's combat takes place in cordoned off areas of the levels that are like small combat puzzle arenas. Some just require you to fend off a massive horde of enemies, others have environmental hazards that require reflexes and timing. There are boss fights as well that will put all your skills to the test simultaneously. The checkpoints are very generous and there's no lives system or penalty for dying but don't let that fool you into thinking this game's easy. Some of these encounters will take MANY attempts to get through and require learning through iteration and persistence. Beyond the game's general challenge, there is also a combo based scoring system with online leaderboards to encourage additional playthroughs and getting better at each encounter. You don't have to care about score if you don't want to but it's nice to have and it's implemented well.
RIVE is gorgeous and sounds fantastic. Two Tribes has some phenomenal artists and they pull out all the stops for this game. They make great use of screen shake and zooms to give make combat feel hectic and satisfying. The weapons also have great punch to their sounds and everything feels high energy. Whether things are calm or hectic, RIVE is a visual and auditory feast.
I love games like this and RIVE is a top shelf entry in the genre. Again, while I respect Two Tribes' decision to leave the industry and the fact that they didn't spare a bit of effort on this, despite it being their last game, it is their last game and it's sad for that reason. This is an incredibly talented team and with so much low effort garbage being cranked out on Steam and so many pretentious art "games" being given all the attention by the press, it's frustrating to see developers like this giving up on it because they don't feel there's a place for them. This is the kind of stuff we need more of. I hope their last game does well for them.

is a gloomy zombie apocalypse/alien invasion survival tycoon game with beautiful music, decent level design, good pacing, and a setting that seems heavily inspired by
. You play as a train driver amidst a collapsing society, running errands for the higher ups while trying to save as many people as you can. Your train is the last glimmer of hope in a world overrun by weird dark creatures.
The best thing about
is its haunting and forlorn mood. While the pixel graphics are modest, the visuals are varied enough, and different locations do feel different. I also very much enjoyed the dishevelled yet semi-futuristic pseudo-Soviet architecture.
The core loop of the game is simple, but feels good.
is broken into two sections: there is the real-time train-riding that's simple, but feels stressful, and there is the exploration, that gives you room to strategize and throws you into different tactical situations. You have to manage various resources in the process.
The game's systems definitely could have used more thought. For example, first aid kits are the only items shared between the two game modes (you can either heal yourself while exploring or heal survivors on the train), which is a shame. It's also often unclear which items you can use to attack with and which you can't during exploration.
The final overly dramatic arc felt forced and unnecessary to me, but the story was unintrusive enough to not be a bother.
All in all, these gripes are minor.

I just finished my last playthrough a couple of hours ago and it left me with a mixed set of feelings.
At first, when I started the game, I thought like: "Okay, cool, I'm about to manage and explore a huge space station."
But, as things turned out, it went completely different. That's, just to say, not a bad thing, because it provided a nice surprise regarding the experience and it felt kind of nice.
On the other hand, the experience itself was not so terrific in the end. That's probably because you know exactly what's
going on when you take a close look at your surroundings. (I'm not going to mention any details.)
Take a second/minute to take in the details and you might be able to figure out what's going on yourself.
Another thing I didn't really like, but that's probably because it's still in development, is the short gameplay of each playthrough. Depending on your play speed it can be done in less than, let's say, 40 minutes.
What's good? Fear, by answering a set of questions you're supposed, or you believe, you get a custom tailored portion
of fear presented to you. If that's completely correct, I don't know, because I don't know how the game has been designed. But, it's done in a good way and makes you act careful for as long as it lasts.
I recomend the game as far as it concerns the concept, but I don't recommend it based on actual content. It's too little at this moment. The experience doesn't last long enough at this time to be regarded as a full gaming experience. It feels more like a test setup for psychologic gameplay elemenst to see what works and what doesn't. (Depending on your goal as a developer)
Conclusion:
Verde Station has potential, but needs more work. It needs longer playthrough time. At the time of writing the presented content is not enough to keep you satisfied for long. For the current price you expect more material, story and interaction with your surroundings.
But, I do recommend Verde Station, because at its core it's a great concept that does work in a fast way. And if the developers do something with the feeback, they'll be able to create an awesome game in the end.

Essentially, Banished is a very simplistic version of SimCity, placed in a time period where your biggest concerns were the ones directly related to survival. There's no technology or development tree or anything, allowing the player to freely choose in what ways to progress in his or her town. The citizens have vague needs, so you can choose how to satisfy them. A town can be based on any and all production facilities, and so long as you have some form of surplus, you can trade to acquire things that you yourself are not producing. Unlike Far Cry, there is no way to reset the Red Zones (enemy controlled areas) once you finish the game, so in terms of replayablility whilst keeping your upgrades, there isn't. Some of these upgrades are fun, but some of them you get while near the end of the game - leaving you wanting more time to play around with them but guess what? the game's over and you can't.
Enemies can pop in behind you, sometimes even in front - just so that they're far enough. That's one of the problems, enemies can respawn just from a few meteres away - making sniping kind of pointless. You can snipe enemies, but as soon as you get close, they will have already respawned.
This sucks when you love long range, but it also affects players who like to play like assassin's/ninjas. You can sneak in a stronghold and knife everyone to your liking, but some times enemies will respawn literally seconds after you turn away and they'll sound the alarm.
Eventually, you'll get used to this and develop your own sense of where and when to be most cautious - so that you won't alert the whole block, it just sucks that you even have to worry about that in the first place.
Don't get me wrong, the gameplay was OK, it's just not great. Small things like this detracts from the experience. I enjoyed it, but it just could have been more.
