Rive is a pretty looking mix of shmup and action platformer with a solid gameplay loop but a very sub par replay value.
full review:
Text:
Rive looks pretty and controls quite well, but a massive lack of weapons, upgrades or pickups make the various gameplay elements quite bland only a few hours in.
This balance choice in terms of weapon damage, special power ammo limitations and hazards, while enjoyable for the pacing, does get boring.
The game also tries to be both a speed-running title, and a shmup and misses the focus for either. A nice speedy run will be rudely interrupted by a stationary sequence to kill mobs in a single room before being able to continue.. And while the game gives you the chance to try various levels time and again and improve your score and rating, it doesn't provide any information on how to see if you are doing better or not.
The gameplay isn't bad, and nothing feels "bad" but it's all been done before and done better. an overall average experience. the upgrade system is linear and simplistic, the weapons types are limited and same old same old (shotgun, stungun, etc..)
the cool gimmick is "hacking" various NPC robots to provide a boost such as healing or extra DPS, and those are pretty cool.
For all it's flaws though, there is ltitle i can take away from the title but cool art pretty decent sound and voice assets that will provide an enjoyable Saturday for anyone that likes action platformers. Not a game-changer - but not bad either.

I really wish there was a Neutral or Mixed option for whether or not to recommend a game here on Steam so while I might have "not recommended it" my stance on it is actually mixed.
You can read the good stuff about LoG2 from other reviewers, I just want to vent what I personally disliked about the game.
Open world
The atmosphere of loneliness, isolation and claustrophobia from the first game is pretty much gone. The feeling of you being in an alienating machine which lives all around you, trying to kill you is gone. There is just something terrifying about the prospect of running out of food deep underground in a dungeon you can't get out of. About having to continuously push forward deeper down into a world unknown to you in the vague prospect of being allowed out. Because of the open world and outside environment the atmosphere is completely lost.
It doesn't help that the world feels like a themepark either or that the square design looks awful when it comes to how trees, plants rocks and especially water is designed to act as barriers. The locations like graveyard, crystal caves and the swamp don't feel natural at all. Out of nowhere you leave the regular forest area and BOOM! Now you're in a swamp and the area looks completely different. It comes across as cartoonish. There is no feeling of loneliness because there's stuff all around you. There is no feeling of isolation or claustrophobia because you can at any point just leave a dungeon. (except for a few select instances when you have to battla a boss or solve a puzzle)
Finally, the idea of allowing players to choose where to go might sound good on paper but in practice it makes the game overwhelming at times (in a bad way). You might get something that is crucial to use later on at a puzzle to get to a power gem which is vital to completing the game but because the game doesn't tell you that you might deem it irrelavent because you've combed the area you found it in and you decided you want to have more space in your inventory for stuff that is actually useful. So you throw it out and then later on you come across that puzzle and would you look at that? You can't solve it. Because the piece that would have helped made sense of this puzzle is somewhere in a dungeon but you can't remember where.
Don't get me wrong. This^ doesn't happen all the time, there is only a select few moments where things like this can happen, but it made me very uncomfortable to go 'anywhere' because I was afraid I wouldn't be doing the puzzles and♥♥♥♥♥♥in the right order.
Puzzle Design
So the puzzles... In the first game, a puzzle was pretty straightforward when it was presented to you. You're in a small'ish room where all you need to solve the puzzle are at for the most part. In the sequel, the puzzles are a mess. Sometimes you can't solve a puzzle you stumble onto until way later when you've solved other puzzles. Or you might come across a puzzle where you have to have X to finish it, a crucial plot-important puzzle that is. So what if you don't have X? What if you didn't pick it up? What if you've used all of X up? Then there are puzzles where you need to comb the entire ♥♥♥♥ing area for a button or something that is connected to it but because the game gives you no hints you tediously check every damn wall for that damn button.
See that's the thing. In the first game, secret buttons for the most part where for bonus-rooms of loot. In the second game there are times where they are crucial to your advancement in the plot and you end up feeling obligated to check every damn wall you can in order to find a button and that tediousness adds up after a while until I reached the point where every time I entered a dungeon where I had to comb walls my enjoyment dropped.
Broken Feet
So, we can break limbs in this one. For the most part it is a nice addition to the game, except the feet. See, if you break your feet (which you will do a lot because of having to go down fall doors and pits) your characters max weight drops until you heal the character with a potion. So what do you think will happen when you accidentally (or have to jump down because that is the way to advance the game) go down a hole and end up having to face enemies? That's right, you're stuck because on of your characters broke their feet and they are now overencumbered and you ran out of potions for the character because of all the other times you had to heal his/her ♥♥♥♥ing feet because of those ♥♥♥♥ing trapdoors. Best craft yet another potion to heal their feet!
Crate/Sack Screen
All right, so remember how in the first game when you open a sack or crate then it opens to the side of your inventory screen so that you can have a full view of what you're carrying, what you got equipped and what is in the additional space of the crate/sack? Remember that neat little design that allowed you full view of all of your character? Yeah. The crate/sack screen now opens 'over' you equipment screen.
Puzzle Difficulty
The game becomes too damn nonsensical at a certain point. It is not that the difficulty of the puzzles increase, it is that you don't get any hint as to what you are supposed to do a lot of the time when it comes to puzzles and without a stepping stone you're pretty much forced to look up a tip or how to do the entire puzzle because it just doesn't make any damn sense to you. You will come across puzzles that, unless you are the developers, you won't have any idea how to do them. It's like a friend of yours telling you an inside joke the two of you never had and then she laughs, sees you aren't laughing and then remembers that it was an inside joke she had with another friend. Now if you were to think, and I mean 'really' think about what she said and think about what her friends are and what they were doing and think back on stories they've told then maybe you'd eventually piece together what the inside joke was about.
Question is, is the joke still funny? It isn't for me. I sat at one of those tedious♥♥♥♥♥puzzles, refusing to look it up and was damn determined to figure it out myself and when I finally did it wasn't an "Aha!" moment, it was "...So that is how it works huh? Fun... I can finally ♥♥♥♥ing move on..." Had I been given a teensy little tip at each of those convoluted puzzles then maybe it would have been more fun because you'd at least have a freaking stepping stone, but without them you'll resort to looking it up online. There was only 2 times I had this problem in the first game, but in this one you'll start getting them more and more frequently once you reach the later stages of the game.
Now, with those things said, the world is still fun. The combat (while clumsy) is still fun. Most of the puzzles are fun. There is more variety in locations (even if they come across as cartoonishly designed sometimes). There are more ways to build characters.  And in general it's just fun up until a certain point in the game. So, I do recommend the game, I just want you to know some of the issues I encountered in the game and prepare yourself in case you encounter them as well.

In general I wouldn't consider myself to be a huge fan of the shoot 'em up. Despite that fact I really enjoyed Rive.
Rive is unique in that it is a combination of a platformer and a shoot 'em up. While the game is more shoot 'em up than platformer, both elements come into play in the game. What I liked most about the game is that it does a good job combining the two different genres. Two genres I didn't think would work well together actually make for a pretty fun game. While the game doesn't do anything highly original with either genre the game does a good job utilizing the game's mechanics to create some fun and interesting levels.
Overall the controls work really well. I would say the game is moderately difficult. It provides a challenge but it didn't feel as difficult as most shoot 'em ups. The story is pretty average but has some funny moments.
I would say the game is around six to seven hours long. After beating the game the only replay value comes from replaying the levels in either the time trial mode or the single life mode. If you like a challenge you will probably enjoy these modes.
Coming from a person that generally doesn't love shoot 'em ups, I had a lot more fun with the game than I was expecting. If you hate shoot 'em ups or don't like the combination of a shoot 'em up and a platformer, the game may not be for you. Otherwise I would recommend picking up Rive.

Going to sound like a broken record and don't often post game reviews, but I feel this one is very deserving of another positive overview.
With a UI feel familiar to Hearthstone but the majority of mechanics more similar to Magic: The Gathering, Dire Wolf hit one out of the ballpark with this one - of course assuming set development continues on a regular basis and maintains to balance/fun.
Card mechanics feel mainly inspired by both M:TG and Hearthstone, with a few more unique ones so far. Weapons exist to attach to creatures, but behave more similarly to Enchantments. Relic Weapons are similar to weapons in Hearthstone, allowing your character to attack, but have a better (IMO) feel to them as you must be wise how you attack with them and defend yourself. Relics, much like normal artifacts, exist to aid in your gameplan should you choose. And most importantly, the game differs from Hearthstone the most in 2 ways - attack/block phases much like M:TG and instant speed spells! Even better, instant speed is more user friendly than M:TG since you can only respond in a couple phases of the game, although these phases are the most commonly responded-to anyways.
There are several fun game modes already right off the bat. You can play against AI, which is great for simple, quick fun and testing. The AI modes contain a play-til-you-lose mode (Gauntlet, always free) with a final boss and another mode similar to Hearthstone's arena (Forge, free at first and then a small fee of coin or gem). Against players, you can play in a familar ranked system or draft. Oh, did I mention you keep all the cards you open for these modes, including against the AI in Forge? To top it off, you can get sweet rewards (on top of the daily quests!).
With all of that being said, the game has been very fun and one of the most consumer-friendly CCGs I've played so far. If you're at least remotely interested, I highly recommend you give it a shot.

I first played this game in 2002 when I was 12 years old and fell in love with it. Since that time, I've played through the PlayStation 2 version five or six times. For many who came into the series earlier, this game represents the point where Final Fantasy began to decline in quality and I don't fully disagree. IX is typically cited as the last good FF, but X takes that title for me (I haven't played XV yet and, though I consider XII a good game, it was a FF only in name). This is likely due somewhat to nostalgia, but I think there is a lot here for newcomers to enjoy. FFX has aged fairly well and this HD Remaster is everything I could have asked for; it makes the game easier on the eyes and ears while upholding the integrity of the original release and, in the case of the soundtrack, giving the player the choice of two arrangements. Those who played the original will not be disappointed. For newcomers, FFX is not a bad place to start. It was released recently enough to fulfill some modern expectations and it's old enough to retain some of the charm of the beloved classics on the SNES and PSone (Nobuo Uematsu's involvement doesn't hurt it either). I have thoroughly enjoyed this version of Final Fantasy X and I hope you do as well.
Note: I never played X-2 and have yet to play it here, so I cannot speak on its quality. If I decide to play through it, I may update this review.

TL;DR This is a great game for people with a basic understanding of card games, and a great game for players new to the genre provided that they put in some effort outside of the game itself (forums, articles, etc.).
Eternal is the best digital card game I have played hands down.
I enjoy TCGs and CCGs as a genre. This paragraph is mostly developing ethos, move on to the next section for the review.I currently own a Magic: the Gathering Modern deck (Lantern), many Commander decks in paper, and play pauper (UW Acid) on MTGO. My Hearthstone collection is large, with my favorite decks to play being aggro mage, Secret Pally, and Oil Rouge (RIP). I played scrolls a little. So I've been around the block when it comes to card games. I like to be competitive, but I will try to keep my review as a reference for a broader player base of the spectrum of competition. My opinion will be biased as someone who came into this game experienced and already liking the genre.
If Hearthstone was designed to appeal to the casual player, Eternal was designed to reach the dedicated (not necessarily competitive) player. If Magic is *the* paper card game, I think eternal has potential to become *the* digital card game. By investing time to play the game, you will grow a collection and create a deck you enjoy over the course of a few weeks of 1-2 hours of playtime each night. Obviously, this isn't required to have an enjoyable experience, but the fact remains that Dire Wolf Digital has done everything in their power to make this game an excellent time for players of any budget.
I decided to go Free 2 Play for my first few weeks to see how the experience was. I cannot stop giving praise to DWD for designing such a tight game. Within completing the "tutorial," I had enough cards to put together my first deck. I could tell this was supposed to be the "beginners deck" not because they forced it onto me, but because I had the cards in my collection to create it from the start. It was a great foray into deck building format and introducing me to the ladder. I am an experienced player, so I have no way to know if newer players could do that for themselves. However, a quick google search for "Budget Eternal Decks" brings up a slew of reputable choices, so while new players may need to seek outside help initially, the parts are all in your grasp for a good deck.
The combat system, mulligan system, spell system, and deck building system fall into a weird middle ground for me. It feels easy on the surface, but some restrictions and interactions can be confusing the first few times you encounter them. After these shaky footholds are developed, the only thing that will limit your skill is the time you put in. As with all strategy PvP games, the ranking system favor those who gain an understanding of the game. That being said, there is no shame in playing your own fun decks where the ladder places you. The lack of a casual mode makes it difficult to switch between gimmick decks and ranking decks, but the player base is too small to be fractured in such a way.
The Drafting system in Eternal is the absolute best drafting format I have seen in any game. It is the most fun way to play a card game that I have ever had. No, I am not being hyperbolic. I truly think this is the best draft system of any DCG, and even many paper card games. If you are a new player, no matter how bad you are at the game, I can only recommend you spend your coins on drafting. If you don't know what drafting is, look it up before you try it and learn the basics. (Math time!) A draft costs 5000 gold. A single pack costs 1000 gold. In the draft, you get to open 4 packs of cards, and get, at minimum, ~500 gold for playing. Your first win adds ~250 gold to that pile, and another win bumps that return value to ~1000 gold *and* another pack. With three chances to lose, you have good odds of making it to breaking even. And that's just the first two wins. More wins gets more prizes. I will draft in Magic: the Gathering occasionally. I will almost never draft in hearthstone. I play constructed in eternal for the 5000 gold it takes to draft (and because the constructed meta is super healthy and fun to play)
I don't play games for the lore. If you do, you may find Eternal to be lacking in that regard. For anyone who cares, this game is closer to Magic than it is to Hearthstone.
So, what have we learned?
Cons:
Lore is lacking
Skill floor is a bit higher than may initially be comfortable.
Small(ish) community, so memes are hard to come by.
Pros:
Draft may be the best in any game I ever played
Constructed is fun and has a healthy meta
The game is generous with its rewards, which means that it is easy to build a collection and work toward your first "real" deck.
Small(ish) community, so you get to know those you're playing with.
Final words: Please play this game if you have a passing interest and a few hours to spare. It is fun for both new players and seasoned card game veterans. The game is free to play, so there really is no reason not to give it a try.

This is the first time I've ever played a visual novel game before. For my first time, I became very invested into the characters. Unlike some other visual novel games I've seen, the characters in this one not only vary personality wise, but are also very different because of their physical appearance. As opposed to some other visual novels, where all the characters are average people, you have a huge variety characters that you'll meet whom are all charming in their own way. You'll need to complete at least three playthroughs in order to meet all of the characters in the game, and each one will take roughly two hours.
The idea of the game is pretty simple. Take a friend to prom, and succeed at school. You'll be spending your year becoming friends with the people who you meet in your clubs, and you'll have to become best friends with one of them. The person who you click with the most will be based on the decisions you make as you play through the game. By spending time with a person frequently, and adding to your niceness, coolness, or toughness, the person who you befriend will be different. Succeeding in school is also important, so pay close attention to details as you play the game. You'll be given four tests through the year, with four questions each. You'll have a final grade at the end of the game.
The characters are all charming and interesting in their own ways, and that's where a lot of the heart is in this game. I'll be honest, picking your best friend can be kind of difficult, mostly because many of the main characters are very likeable (I went with Cupcake from Music Club on my first playthrough). The game has some replay value to it as well. As I said, you wont get a chance to meet every character in the game on your first try. However, there are multiple endings you can get in the game if you keep playing once you complete it. Finishing the game also adds character pictures to your yearbook, and grants you points to unlock gallery images of characters and backgrounds.
I do have two complaints, however. They both have to do with my best friend in the game. I noticed first that as you progress through the game, the interactions you have with your friend at certain points are repeated. I admit that it was a little disappointing. Like I said, I became very invested in my character that I met, and wanted to see more from them. Which leads to my second complaint, which is that the game is a little too short. Perhaps I became too attached to the odd charm of my friend character, and kind of wished there was more.
Overall, I do recommend this game. Unlike other visual novels, this one had charm to it as opposed to some awkward adult theme. It feels like something Nintendo would put out. And while I wished that the game was longer, it gives a very feel-good vibe that makes you smile and chuckle all the way from start to finish.

I picked this game up quite a while ago but just got around to playing it. Overall, I am very very impressed with the game. The mechanics are novel and satisfying, the atmosphere is sufficiently creepy, and the enemies are a very enjoyable fight, and I find myself at the edge of my seat throughout every run. I eagerly recommend the game to anyone seeking an addictive challenge with near infinite replayability.
The game starts, thrusting you right in to the thick of things, with nothing but a gun and sometimes a maglite. No tutorial, no nothing. Your goal is to find and listen to 11 cassette tapes without getting shot or tased by the hovering drones or sweeping turrets. Oh, did I mention you die in one shot? Yeah, that brings a whole other level of tension and urgency to every fight. There is no HUD, so you have to either count your shots or check your magazine constantly. Running out of ammo in the middle of trying to shoot down a drone that is divebombing you, tazer buzzing, will certainly spell your doom.
I really like this game. The tapes fittingly play in any order and the guns are very satisfying. In my 4 hours of play, I have not yet beaten the game, and that speaks volumes to the challenge this game holds. The turrets are spooky and can startle you if you aren't ready for them, but easy to take out. The drones are probably the hardest enemy in the game. Very frequently, you'll hear one, step through the doorway and shoot it down, only to have another one that you didn't know about zap you from behind without warning. Luckily they aren't seen terribly often without large spaces to deal with them. The game feels very mazelike, lending to the general sense of unease and being lost and alone. For 7 days of work to create the base game, it is amazing. I only leave it wishing that you could actually
with regularity, as many rooms are so dark that even the flashlight does nothing to help you. Even if this game never sees another major update, I am quite happy to play it as it is now.

This game has a great premise and its presented very nicely, well maybe except the music. I love electronic music but there's a droning track early in the game that gets really old fast, the music gets a little better later in the game. The graphics are top notch and the atmosphere is there (especially the Lombard zone) but the core gameplay loop gets repetitive really fast, you just take over locations, turn on radios, do flashpoints and that's about it. The job board missions are very mundane tasks like taking pictures of things or kill some soldiers with a specific weapon. I enjoyed the DLC missions the most but they are VERY short. The attention to detail as you take over a zone was good. Seeing the citizens rise up and starting fires in the streets and attacking soldiers was neat as well as all the KPA propaganda being replaced with resistance stuff.
The weapon attachment system is pretty cool if you liked it in Crysis and being able to turn weapons into something else was enjoyable especially since you can do it on the fly and not have to run back to an NPC. The flamethrower was particularly enjoyable to use. You can do the same with the explosives and gadgets, improving an explosive into a controllable RC car was pretty fun. Overall it's a decent game but it does have flaws chief among them being the repetitive open world formula. There's also some really wacky spawning issues with soldiers seemingly appearing out of nowhere sometimes. I would recommend this game if you really enjoy the Far Cry formula, but grab it on sale regardless.

Legend of Grimrock 2 is a true sequal. I thought the first game was great but had many problems that left the game needing more. The main thing I love is how open the world is and how you can play the game in essentially whatever order you want, unlike the first game which was far more linear. The goal overall is to gain access to the final area, but in what order of areas to go to before that is pretty much up to you. This allowed me to work on another section or puzzle when I get stuck rather than just quitting or caving in to internet help. Speaking of internet help, you may need it. The game is very challenging and if you don't save often, you may find yourself raging...a lot. No deathes feel too cheap as eventually you'll learn to recognize everything as a potential trap, but be warned that it can be unforgiving at times. If you enjoyed the first game, then you'll enjoy it's sequal. If you didn't like the first game, this entry may have fixed what you disliked, but likely didn't. And if you haven't played the first game, I would recommend playing the sequal first and going back to the first game later on, if at all. It's a fantastic game, but it's certainly not for everyone.

This is absolutely one of the better AAA TCG games out there. Wel start with that. Using stratagy and rules of most games of this genre, ETERNAL brings it, well done and with a good artistic style that everyone will browse the cards to look at. Take steampunk apocalyptic and magic and sorcerory together/merged and vs each other with other mythological beings. It's pleasing to see something new and diffrent amongst all the card games. There is alot of simularities though, but its polished. WIth 5 types of color/powers with respective leaders, make a deck combining or soloing one color/power. Time is tan with healing and is lead by Talir( kinda of a arabian, egyption feel), Shadow is purple and led by Vara and is lifestealing and killing cards ( think rogues and assasins), Justice is green with soldiers and armor/weapons and is led by Rolant, Primal is blue and is led by Eliyn and beasties and ice magic. Rage/fire red is led by Kaleb with charging creatures and hard hitting fire magic. There is plenty of combinations of colors to go with and the themes, stratagy play styles change from power to power. Campign mode is a unlock and learn each of the powers and their scion leaders. End game boss for the campign  is a deck of all the colors called Strangers. Think ''slivers'' from Magic the Gathering, but just weird humanoid well, strangers. Beat this and off you go to Guantlet ( a beat random AI players for loot according to how well you do) Forge ( make a deck out of cards, witch you keep and face the AI for loot according to how well you do. Ranked ( playing against other people and gaining loot according to how well you do ) and Draft ( making a deck out of cards , witch you keep and playing against other people and gaining loot according to how well you do) LOOT?! is cards or booster packs or gold and gems or shards-to craft cards. Gold and gems is used to get more boosters. It's all about getting more cards. Making your own deck is very custimizable in this game, you can change deck or profile pictures and names too,  when you want. Crafting is just having enough shards to make what cards you want or destorying cards you have multiple of and need the shards to make thus cards you want... Quests of dailies and such do pop up to help nab more gold to .. get more cards. The graphics are just right up there, with neat relic banners of your choosing to the side of the board and the animation and sound effects is pretty satisfying and is definantly done right.  There are card ablility names that are simular to other games, but go by diffrent names like, endurance is like vigalance or taunt. BUT there are new abilities that I like like infiltrate, war cry and quickdraw. Enjoy a good card game and enjoy making a unique deck of a articstic theme and style that deserves a good ''nod''...

I really liked this game. I liked the story so much. It only gave you infromation piece by piece, until you could finish putting together the whole story about Sam and Lonnie. It's a love novel actually, 2 lesbian teenagers, but the story and the voice acting is just so good.
PRO:
+ very good voice acting
+ thrilling story
+ great atmosphere (storm, flashing lights, empty house)
+ pretty good graphics
+ lots of papers/diaries/pictures/books to explore in order to assemble the story
+ some easy puzzles
CON:
- no achievements
- no autosaves for diary entries you find (my PC crashed after I played like 2 hours, and my progress was gone, had to start the game again from the very beginning! )
- pretty short
- no collectibles ( it was nice if you could collect all the postcards, casettes into your inventory and have them in one place)
- no replay value
Overall it's a pretty interesting walking simulator bringing you back to the Nintendo games era (mid-90's). Definitely not for everyone. I dare to say I liked this game a lot more than I did 'Dear Esther'.
The overall playtime would be somewhere between 2-3 hours for the first playthrough, really my only point in replaying it was that my PC carshed mid-game after I opened the kitchen area, so basically had to quickly replay about 75% of the game.
Would I buy it? Definitely if it was on sale. I bought it in a bundle so really no regrets. I can recommend this game mostly beacuse of the story and the easy puzzles which really make it relaxing.

I've always been a fan of Nerdook and his games, so consider me a little bias. Reverse Crawl isn't exactly what it looks like on the surface; The game is more about controlling a group of "Evil" minions that grow in strength through your decisions during multiple turn-based battles. After every battle, you get a choice to upgrade a specific area of your strengths; This could be making your Skeleton Minions deal more damage, or one of your more powerful creatures to gain a new ability. The Campaign is about three solid hours, give or take, and there are no real penalties for losing a "Mission". Every step gives you a choice of up to 3 different pathways, save for explicit encounters, and you can grow in strength depending on what you choose.
Missions vary from taking down a Hero to gain more XP, to ambushing Merchants for loot and special upgrades, or enslaving/saving evil guys from the good guys. There's a LOT of variety and strategy, with every upgrade providing a unique and interesting ability that you can play around with. The difficulty is so-so; I didn't have any real troubles during the campaign, but I'm used to Nerdook's style of gameplay. After beating the campaign, you unlock New Game+ mode as well as Endless Mode, which becomes more or less a dungeon crawl.
If you enjoy turn-based RPGs that let you continuously grow more powerful, as well as enjoying cute (if amateur) art, then you can't go wrong with Reverse Crawl. I suggest that you go to a flash site (e.g Kongregate) to play some of his older games, like Dungeons of Kong, Cat God vs Sun King, Deadly Neighbours and more. They're all free and can give you a good example of his abilities. Still, for $5 Reverse Crawl is a steal. I can see myself playing over and over again in the future, and making new, fun decisions.
I don't review often, but this game was a day-one buy for me, so I give it my all-star 10/10 rating. I hope that you enjoy the game, Nerdook is a great guy.

Final Station isn't what it bills itself to be. I picked it up expecting a train-based scavenging roguelike, and that's what it is for a little while, but only as a disguise. What it is is a heavily narrative game hiding inside the shell of a narrative-lite experience. There's a lot of visual storytelling going on here--which is good, because the translation still feels a bit shaky in places.
Core gameplay works like this: you get on a train, play a distracting minigame to keep diesel fumes from flooding the passenger car while you eavesdrop on the conversations of your passengers, and occasionally bring them a snack or a medkit to keep them from dying. Every so often, you stop and scavenge a station for food, medkits, and crafting scraps. Zombies attack you when you do, and you spend a lot of time walking slowly backwards punching them in the belly.
If you can get your passengers to a safe station further down the line, they give you money, gear, and crafting scraps. Then you pick up more and the cycle begins again...at least for a little while.
The story of the game is told in the background, and it's a surprisingly haunting one. It's also, by design, unfinished. The plotlines don't resolve. You get left with some suspicions, and you can follow some trails of lore pretty far through the game, but ultimately it terminates in a Sopranos ending that doesn't clear up any part of what you've just played through.
This is frustrating to someone who likes there to be a meaning in things, but the game ends the way life does, messy and unfinished, and I think that's probably the point. Ultimately, you won't regret getting to dip into the gameworld, and the train gameplay elements are fun, even if they ultimately get dropped. There's some absolutely wonderful level design, despite being perfectly linear, and the soundtrack knows how to move deftly between mellow and tense as the mood changes.
This is well worth its price, and a steal on sale.

Firefights are about getting a better position and viewpoint than your enemy. But movement is so limited by "desertion" that you can't even try to outsmart you opponents by placing yourself well. Instead you have to rush back into the map in a couple of seconds just to be seen and shot. Of course the map has to have limits but enforcement of the limits could be done much better. For example by having strong robotic positions behind open ground that would be map limits. Trying to cross would have you killed.
Then there are the "experienced" opponents who can kill you behind good cover at 50 meters with a pistol when you with less experiance points have put several rifle bullets right through his fully exposed body, but you miss. Or it could be that he just has a very fast connection, regardless shooting feels way off. Pistols are way to effective at long range while machine guns are too cumbersome to use effectivly. It is also way to easy to avoid being hit by jumping around like a monkey. I have counless times been killed by players who jumps left and right through the trench at 15 meters range and all my bullets miss. Maybe I am just a lousy shot. But it seems to me that now the game is dominated by guys running around with a pistol on their own killing everyone. Somebody said this game is becoming more of a arcade game and less of a simulation. Unfourtunately I think he was right. Which I think is a great pitty. Oh, Homefront! It was not well loved on release but I really, really, really enjoyed my time in occupied Philadelphia. There's nothing quite like the feeling of planting a remote detonated explosive, waiting for a patrol to pass and then watching things go boom from (relative) safety. And then you realise you weren't quite as safe as you thought and suddenly Norks are appearing from everywhere and I;m blindly running into alleyways trying to find a bin to hide in.
You walk in a small circle and enemies have just popped in out of nowehere (in one case, threatening a civilian whilst standing on top of the corpse of the previous soldier who'd been stabbed in the neck for doing the same, and not apparently being bothered by it...) I blew people up with RC cars, turned an assault rifle into a sticky grenade launcher and turned the enemies guns against themselves.

A final send off for Homefront: the Revolution.
I finally beat the game after 27.3 hours and would've probably been able to beet it just under 18 hours if I hadn't gone ahead and tried to capture all strike points. Unfortunately, a bug causing Lombard Red Zone's Recon Post to be uncapturable prevented me from doing this and thus prevented me from getting the achievement of capturing all 65 strike points. If you are an achievement hunter you will be disappointed.
So the game ends with a very cinematic ending but unfortunately does not let you continue off in "free roam" after that. You can load up an old save BEFORE you choose to accept the last mission in order to continue free roaming. One thing that disappointed me was a ziplinning mechanic that you can only perform once in the end credits. I was hoping it would've been a bigger part of the game. There aren't that many levels of verticality either even though there are tons of abandoned skyscrapers, I was also hoping to explore.
Okay briefly on the gameplay: its just your average run of the mill FPS really with upgrades you can purchase. About 75% of the time you will be solving basic puzzles in order to capture strike points. The gunplay feels okay but you will need to burst on most your full auto guns or at least aim because recoil does have an effect on where your bullets land. Several guns like the crossbow and shotgun feel useless since you have access to the Battle Rifle (M14) or LMG (some weird belt felt upper that attaches to an M4 lower) which are extreme high powered. The enemies are also pretty weak and are only powerful when they swarm. Enemies have a detection range and time it takes for them to attack you if you expose yourself too long so you can stealth more scenarios by knifing them or using a silenced weapon.
Graphics are excellent, probably some of the best I've seen in a first person shooter and why I decided to play the game til the end. I ran this at 50-60fps depending on the zone. Day night cycle and weather cycle too. Gorgeous apocalyptic night scenary. Smoke looks like smoke and shadows and lighting were really well done. They didn't overdo the overexposed spectacular/shininess you get in most games that try to make their graphics pretty. Color palette is pretty consistent and gloomy too which is 100x better than the eyesore of a game you got with the original Homefront. This game really makes me wish Deep Silver could acquire a license to make a Terminator game and commission it to Dambuster because the environmental artists behind Revolution are on top of it!
Some gripes I had with the game besides the strike point bug: Stale story, boring characters, with a main cast spanning only about 7-8 named characters that die. They spent 4 years in development but couldn't crank out a good story that connects players emotionally to the characters? Missions. There are usually really well done cut scenes between each major mission and the motion captured animations are really good too. But the the missions usually consist of killing X, Y, Z, reaching location X, Y, Z and then always, spend 3-4 hours wreaking havoc in the city or capturing strike points or saving civilians or switching on radios to raise the "Hearts and Minds" level of an area in order to organize an uprising against the North Koreans. This gets very old very fast and if it weren't for the pleasing visuals, I would've shut it off a long time ago. Bugs: sometimes Norks will swarm you infinitely no matter how many times you kill them. You can't hide and you can't transport to another zone so the only way to get out of it is to get yourself killed. One last gripe: script isn't proofread well and they spell many words in the English manner. They got the Americans to do the voicing and even made the environment look American (New England) which is impressive seeing how different London and Philedelphia look, so why couldn't they hire one (American) dude to proofread everything?
Co-op: a very short grind. A few missions to spam a couple of times on hard in order to reach levelcap. The only reason why you'd want to keep playing is to unlock every cosmetic/item or you have friends.
Overall, a very bittersweet reboot to the Homefront series. I don't think I'd every recommend buying this game at full price. I got this in the Deep Silver  humble bundle. For what its worth, its a good time killer, really pleasing to the eye but definitely not one of the most memorable experiences you'll have with a lack of PvP multiplayer and repititive gameplay. But I would recommend anyone with an eye for art and wanting to try an FPS like no other on the market try it. I will be uninstalling the game after writing this review as I have nothing to get out of this game anymore.

Pros:
Cons:
Overall, I found this game phenomenal. It steadily increases the challenge both through new variety in monsters and puzzles throughout a lengthy game in a natural way. The music is astounding and boss fights are intense. There are very few cheap traps and most puzzles can be solved quickly if you find and comprehend the hints provided. Secret doors are usually (almost always) audible from the location of the object that opens them so if you pay attention you can find them. If you get stuck, you can go to a different area for most of the game and come back later thanks to the free roam design. Enemies respawn (and get more difficult as your level increases) but it takes a considerable amount of time to the point where I've never seen them respawn in the current dungeon (note that I rarely slept throughout the game though). Progression is consistent and if you get stumped, walkthroughs will make you facepalm because the solution is usually right in front of your face. If you are looking for a challenging, enjoyable, long (compared to modern games), cheap (again compared to modern games), and gratifying game, Legend of Grimrock 2 could be the game for you.

I've been playing card games for nearly 20 years. I started with Decipher's Star Wars TCG and graduated to Magic when Mirage came out in 96'. I've been hooked on them ever since.
We live in interesting times for card game players. There's now a plethora of digital CCG's out there — perhaps so many that it's difficult to find the one that's right for you. I'm not going to tell you Eternal is better than X — that it's a Hearthstone killer or anything like that. What I'm going to tell you is it's a marvelous game and it is more than worth your time.
In the last two years alone I've played Might & Magic: Duels of Champions (now dead), Solforge, HEX, Shadowverse, Hearthstone, Star Crusade, Infinity Wars (I kickstarted this one, regrettably), Spellweaver, most recently Elder Scrolls Legends, and now Eternal. I have spent money in practically all of these. After playing them all, I can say that Eternal is by far my favorite. Here are some reasons why:
1. The combat is more based on M:TG than Hearthstone. That is to say, you attack with your creatures and the opponent deals with how blocks are handled. You cannot directly attack another creature (without the creature ability Killer, anyway).
2. Instant spells exist, and as such, so does priority and the stack.
3. Eternal uses a mana system. You have to play your sources of power; they are not given to you freely like in Hearthstone. As such, mana screw / flood is a possibility. There is a mulligan mechanic that (I believe) guarantees at least two sources of mana if you redraw without dropping you a card.
5. Chests. You earn chests from completing quests and participating in the game modes. Each one has a 10% chance to "upgrade" to a higher chest level when you open one. Bronze give a common card and ~50 gold. Silver give an uncommon and ~250 gold. Gold give a pack of cards and ~500 gold. Diamond give a pack of cards, a random premium card, and ~2000 gold.
4. Free to play is incredibly possible. The game features several modes of play:
Ranked Constructed: Use your constructed deck on the ladder. 3 wins will get you 2 bronze chests and a silver chest before resetting.
Gauntlet (Free): Test your deck against a string of 7 AI opponents in a single-elimination gauntlet. Rewards increase as you defeat more enemies.
Draft (5000 gold): Asymmetrical draft. You get four packs and keep the cards you draft. Pick a card from a pack and it gets passed off to some other random person. Win 7 or lose 3. You only need to win 2 games to break even. Incredibly easy to build a collection if you're decent at drafting, or even "go infinite" if you're really skilled.
Forge (2500): Draft a deck and play against AI opponents. Keep the cards you pick. Cheaper than Draft, and a good inaugaral game mode to familiarize yourself with drafting and the card pool.
5. Shards and wedges. If you were a fan of the guilds in Ravnica, or the Alara wedges, this game is for you. Mix your factions without having to worry about buying expensive resource cards.
6. Lots of mechanics and unique decks. There are token decks, control decks, reanimator decks, burn decks, aggressive voltron type decks, decks where you win by beating your opponent with equipped weapons.
7. The game is designed by magic pros like Luis Scott Vargas, who ruthlessly brutalized me in a draft match.
In just a short time I've been able to build decent decks, and I've been having a blast drafting. If you liked Magic the Gathering and want something deeper than Hearthstone, then Eternal is your best bet. It has the fast paced gameplay of Hearthstone with some of the complexity of Magic. If you don't care for Magics mechanics, then you may want to stay clear — but I urge you to reconsider.
Direwolf Digital has done a great job of balancing Elder Scrolls Legends (except for sort of absolutely dismantling Control Mage, but oh well) so far, and has been proactive about addressing imbalances in Eternal thusfar. Please, please, please give this game a chance. You can easily start building a collection.
And if you find you like the game, kick it some money. A small investment of $35 can easily set you up to crush gauntlet and start drafting regularly.

Cook, Serve, Delicious is a restaurant "super mini game" where you manage a menu (selecting your dishes and their options), unlock new meals to make, and participate in a few sundry mini games.
The meat of the game is in the daily cooking, which progresses through a morning, noon, afternoon, and evening - each punctuated by rush hours, inspections, chores, and picky persnicky customers that demand you make their food JUST SO. Like some other typing game, you make your food by assembling it with hotkeys on the keyboard (or you can use the mouse if you're not feeling awesome that day) and the faster you type the quicker you cook. Rush hours can get pretty intense, especially if you have complex food items with many options like hamburgers or pizza, where you also have to manage the oven and deliver the hot food to the customer while in the middle of prepping the next one!
Additionally, with the cooking arena, daily challenges, a rather nice "combo" system to force you to keep the menu fresh and a few side quests (like dating or gambling), CSD keeps an enjoyable experience reasonably well seasoned and fresh in small portions. Wholeheartedly worth the money, and a big tip to boot!

The gameplay combines the depth of MTG with the fluency of Hearthstone. This means deep strategy and fast turns. While playing alone all the time (1v1) might get a little lonely and repetitive after a while, I am still hoping the devs consider implementing 2v2 or other team-based modes in the future. Even MTG would not have been such a hit if it weren't for the multiplayer modes featuring more than two players on the same battlefield.
Before getting into the nitpicking, I would like to state that Eternal's model for acquiring cards is leaps and bounds ahead of Hearthstone and completely crushes Magic the Gathering: Online in comparison. It is therefore a huge leap for collectible card games.
As for the fairness of collecting cards; legendaries can be acquired in decent numbers when drafting, even against the AI. At first this seems like a fair deal but when crunching the numbers needed for a full set the task seems undoable by F2P means.
Lets do some math:
55 different kinds of legendaries -> 660 total legendaries to be acquired.
After first 15 hours of gameplay I've managed to gather 13 legendaries (including the starters so the number is extra forgiving in favor of the game). This amounts to 2% of all total legendaries.
As an extra note, most of this acquisition was done by playing Forge (draft vs. AI), which seems to be the recommended mode for new players (as suggested in Reddit).
While it seems kind of silly to complain about this sort of grind in a F2P game we also have to consider them adding more sets which might set the bar a little too high for new players to even consider the game.
Maybe the developers will take this into account in the future and alter the propability distributions when appropriate.
However, I cannot yet recommend this game to other players.
This is due to the tendency of collectible card games trying to make you pay large amounts of money just to level the playing field or even build a single super optimized deck (which you may only want to play for so long before getting bored of it).
Crafting is an option for the common cards, but crafting a single legendary takes 3200 common cards in exchange. Now combine that number with the fact that you may actually need 4 of the same legendary card in your deck that means you need to destroy 12800 common cards in the process. It is also good to remember new card sets in the future will also feature more legendaries. If said legendaries are more powerful in regards to the new meta when comparing to the old cards...well, you get the point.
I'm also concerned the developers, old card sharks as they are, will go the MTG route and introduce some rare and seriously overpowered cards each new set. This means you either pay or start losing tons to other people who payed.
Just because MTG tries to grab your whole wallet doesn't mean every other card game should try to behave in the same economical way.
This is put into an especially strong contrast when comparing to other F2P games which don't place major gameplay elements behind paywalls or a multiple year long grind.
tl;dr; Go google Karmic Guardian and Sandstorm Titan. Compare them side by side to know what you are going to get into.

Gone Home is a pretentious, boring walking simulator that received glowing reviews for its "groundbreaking and progressive" story from biased journalists (some of whom were friends with the creators) who somehow didn't realize how boring and predictable this game's cookie-cutter coming-of-age plot is because they haven't read a book since high school. I really wanted to like Gone Home because of its atmosphere and premise alone- girl comes home from abroad to find her house abandoned- but the plot- the one thing that this non-game has to fall back on- quickly became predictable and unfulfilling. It never really goes anywhere, and you can already tell how it's going to play out just from the first couple audio journals. There actually are some interesting subplots involving the protagonist's parents and uncle, and I felt that they could have lent a little more depth to the story, but ultimately, they both take a backseat to the main story of the game, which sucked.
This "game" did not surprise me in any way, and the fact that gamers are putting it on a pedestal makes me question those people. Super fun restaurant-themed game! I wouldn't call it a sim because you don't have a huge amount of control over the restaurant. It's more of a fast-paced strategy game that requires good memory and quick reflexes.
You are basically a one-person restaurant. You have to set a menu each day, and you don't want to keep the same food on for too long because you'll recieve a penalty (keeps you from just breezing through the game after getting good with a few foods). This becomes deceptively complicated as you go. Too many unhealthy foods and people will find your restaurant less appealing (resulting in less customers), but people tend to like comfort foods when it's raining. More complex recipes generally make you more money, but so does getting an unbroken streak of perfect orders, which complicated dishes make it harder to do. And then what do you do when you get one of the special challenges that offers a huge cash bonus if you use certain recipes and get a long streak with them, but they're ones you're not very good at?
The recipes themselves amount to QTEs, effectively. Each key (or button, if using a controller) corresponds to an ingredient or action. I haven't played with a controller, but the keybindings for each recipe are fully customizable so you can go with makes the most sense to you. And you'll need to do that, because you can't be as fast as the game requires without memorizing some combos. It's very challenging and nerve-wracking at first, but it feels really satisfying when you get to the point where your fingers just fly over the keys so fast, the ingredient screen barely showed up.
There's also a significant time management factor when you're serving customers. You might want to start steaks and potatoes before fast things like ice cream and drinks because you know the former will have a cooking time after you get the ingredients together... But maybe it's rush hour and you're trying to shove as many people out the door as possible, so you take all the fast orders as they come and only get the slow ones when the customer is about to ditch.
Profits are the main way you progress through the game. You'll advance in restaurant stars as you go, unlocking more and more twists and challenges, such as dealing with health inspectors or getting robbed. The money you earn can buy upgrades for your restaurant, new recipes, or upgrades for existing recipes (which raise the price of the dish but also add complexity).
The game can get reptitive because it ramps up slowly, but I think that's also a plus. This means more levels, so the fun lasts longer. This isn't the sort of game you marathon anyway, but one you pick up and play a few levels whenever you've got the time.
The game is definitely worth its full price, so if you see it on sale, jump on it.

Final Fantasy X might be my favorite in the series. It's got a unique setting, a great turn-based combat system that demands strategy, and a heartfelt story that once again shows you don't necessarily need happily ever after to have a satisfying conclusion. The graphics hold up well and look great in HD. The music is wonderful and you can choose between the remastered soundtrack or the original version - something the PS3 and Vita releases didn't offer. It's on the linear side though, which I know bothers some folks, and the lack of skippable cutscenes hurts replay value somewhat. I love the story and characters, but it'd be nice to skip over the more uneventful scenes after a few times through.
Final Fantasy X-2 is a whole different beast. While it has the same setting and some returning characters, it takes place a few years after the original and has a much more light-hearted tone - although there's a story worthy of Final Fantasy underneath its bubbly exterior. It's also got a great take on the series trademark job system and boasts the best version of the classic ATB combat system to date. Notably, the game abandons its prequel's linearity in favor of a very open-ended structure that lets you tackle things in whatever order you want. This one's hit or miss among fans, but I personally like it.
As far as ports go, it's one of Square's better PC offerings. It runs at a steady framerate - although it's worth mentioning it's locked at 30 FPS - and looks really nice. I never experienced any bugs or crashes, and overall was impressed by the polish of it all after the disappointing FFXIII ports. Plus you're getting two great full-length RPGs for the price of one, which is tough to beat. This release also has the typical "cheats" that come with Square HD releases - you can max out your money, levels, items, etc; alter encounter rates, super power your characters, and more. In my opinion they kinda of undermine the point of playing the game, but they're there for folks who like to use those things.
I recommend this to anyone looking to revisit these classics and / or wanting more quality JRPGs on their PC.

Playing this game is probably one of the best decisions I have ever made in my life.
To the simple man, this game may seem a simple button masher, but look beneath its simple exterior, and a whole world of truths unfolds. We see the story of a few simple people coming to a simple resteraunt, but as the resteraunt grows, so do the bonds between them.
We see Leo, a major playah, and his never ending battles with the cruel, relentless Dennis.
We see Darren, as he trys to win the heart of the ever kind, ever drinking Phil. Alas, Darren has never been able to muster up the courage to win the heart of Phil, so he decides to drown his sorrows in fish and grape sodas.
I eagerly look forward to the turning of the next page of this gripping, tear-jerking story.
There may be no story set out for you by the game itself, but isn't the point of life to experience it to the fullest? You must create your own path, your own story, and as Phil has said:
"The people who you love must care for who you are, not what you are."
So are you willing to dive into the deep lore, the rich passion, that this game has to offer? Do you have what it takes?
Don't be a Darren, be strong in yourself, BELIEVE in yourself. Don't look back. Don't let the regrets of yesterday inflict apon the hopes of today, or the promise of of the future. Take the plunge into the greatest experince of your life.

The level of skill required to master the game is in most aspects to a higher difficulty than that of other FPS games. Accompanying the base game, community made modifications including maps, skins or game modes can be found in the server browser. Unlike other common games however, Counter-Strike does not award players constantly with rewards or achievements nor does it have a leveling system. For a game made 10 years ago, the quality in development and execution is tremendous. These characteristics are reverberated throughout each of the Counter-Strike games and thus makes it one of my most favourite series of all.

Here's the biggest disappointment: The very important subtleties are missing:
If you play Dirt 2, and you drive over a dirt bump, you'll see it, hear it, and feel it in the controller.
If you play The Crew, and you drive through a corn field at 90 mph, the car looks like it's driving on flattened asphalt.

This game is a game that I have been waiting on for years. I have always wanted to play a WW1 game that focused on trench warfare and the western front. The level of detail that is put into these maps are above and beyond what other mainstream developers go to. The trenches are THE most realistic trenches I have seen in any game with the small details like covered up dead bodies laying on the ground and tiny little dug-outs for infantry to sleep. Even in the crater-filled No Man's Land I was taking cover from an enemy MG and just saw a pocket watch laying next to me. Just seeing this, I knew that the devs are really trying to get this as accurate as they can. Things likl pocket watches, spades, helmets and boots are scattered everywhere because they would be the sort of thing that would be dug up today.
At times it can be confusing with all of these different soldiers most commonly on the allied side, where some soldiers are French, British or American all in one trench. Because in a game like this, you wopuld be looking out for different uniforms. So there have been a few times when I have been in an enemy trench and have turned a corner and accidently fired at a French soldier becuase their uniform almost looks like the German uniform.
I absolutley love this game, if you buy this game (which you should be doing right now), definately plat the tench warfare game-mode (forgot what its called, you'll know it when you see it). I've clocked almost 50 hours in The Crew - an obvious recommendation. I am currently level 27 and still exploring the first of 5 regions (more about that later). Why is it fun?
The Crew has a huge map, a huge number of difficult races and skill challenges, reasonable AI, the longest races I have ever seen in a computer game, a varied selection of cars right from the start, and a good system for levelling up cars, doing PvP, and doing co-op PvE with or without friends. It is a bit of a cross between FUEL (its game world is bigger, but emptier) and NFS:World (which has a more crowded MMO-feeling, but is pay2win and not as social). It has Burnout Paradise's ability to initiate challenges right in the game world without going to an instance, so you may be driving along and see a car flying through the air because you're passing a jump challenge and someone's doing it; or see everyone else's police pursuits (join in if you like).
The level cap is at 50, there are 5 regions, you can go anywhere at any time, but the events and cars of a new region unlock every 10 levels. So in theory, since my main focus is still the first region (Mid-West - of course you start in Detroit), I shouldn't be over level 10, upgrading my car with level 1-10 parts won from skill challenges available in that region, and generally having a good time; and I should be able to level out of that region by following the storyline missions, if I like, which I probably am. But the game also provides other ways to level up: you can grind story missions (even accidentally, if you want to improve your score from bronze to gold; and the game also makes you, because other player will invite you on coop runs - of course you can decline), you can do faction missions once you are level 10 (out of curiosity), or you can do PvP (a dozen races was enough to get me from level 21 to 27). This will unlock other car types (good) and the parts sets that come with the level (bad, because I now could just buy me all level 20 parts for my car and skip the East Coast region altogether, and with a bit more PvP, skip the South, too). Maybe The Crew should have taken a slice from GuildWars, where you're a) PvP-ready from the beginning with competitive gear (but you can use your own high-end PvE gear as well), and b) levels and player capabilities are adjusted on the fly depending on the level of the region you're in so that co-op works well.
Right now, I exercise some restraint and explore and do the skill challenges and the exploration anyway, and the nice thing about The Crew is that even though my cars are somewhat overpowered for the zone (what with the stat boost levelling up gives them -- why, exactly?), the challenges are still tough to get golden. At the rate I'm going, there'll be many more hours of fun in this game.
If I could do it over, I would play each story mission only once and stay away from anything social (PvP, Factions, co-op) until level 40 at least. Recommended.

Playing this game is probably one of the best decisions I have ever made in my life.
To the simple man, this game may seem a simple button masher, but look beneath its simple exterior, and a whole world of truths unfolds. We see the story of a few simple people coming to a simple resteraunt, but as the resteraunt grows, so do the bonds between them.
We see Leo, a major playah, and his never ending battles with the cruel, relentless Dennis.
We see Darren, as he trys to win the heart of the ever kind, ever drinking Phil. Alas, Darren has never been able to muster up the courage to win the heart of Phil, so he decides to drown his sorrows in fish and grape sodas.
I eagerly look forward to the turning of the next page of this gripping, tear-jerking story.
There may be no story set out for you by the game itself, but isn't the point of life to experience it to the fullest? You must create your own path, your own story, and as Phil has said:
"The people who you love must care for who you are, not what you are."
So are you willing to dive into the deep lore, the rich passion, that this game has to offer? Do you have what it takes?
Don't be a Darren, be strong in yourself, BELIEVE in yourself. Don't look back. Don't let the regrets of yesterday inflict apon the hopes of today, or the promise of of the future. Take the plunge into the greatest experince of your life.

Good tile based combat game for a cheap price!
The storyline is light and cheesy with an unconventional storyline. Via its manga style dialogues, you play a king resurrected by his necromancer daughter, trying to get his kingdom back from the Red Queen. Along the way you will battle heroes and monsters, as well as gain allies that will join your cause.
All this is done through the core gameplay of tile based tactical combat, and, like the story, the combat is light but surprisingly with a level of depth. You command limited groups of summoned minions (which includes the revenant king and his necromancer daughter), and duke it out with similiarly limited groups of enemy monsters. There are some tactical varieties such as the ability to flank as well as melee engagement rules. Also, you will gain threat during combat which is essentially mana for you to cast spells. There are a variety of enemies, as well as "hero" enemies who will appear again and again throughout the game, getting stronger as you progress.
As you win each battle, you will be given a choice of rewards (new spells, new allies, upgrades), as well as a choice of which storyline path to tackle next. These are randomly picked, thus ensuring a level of replayability to the game. The same is true when you lose battles, as the game does not end but instead you will take a pick of which negative choices to pick.
Overall the game is fun and engaging, and never does it take itself too seriously with its silly anime humour. For the price, it is definitely recommended for those wishing for something a casual tactical tile based combat game with a solid story.

Reverse Crawl is a lighthearted turn-based combat game sporting a charming art style, funny story and a good amount of quests/ units to choose from.
-the cartoonish art style is well done
-good amount of different unit models
-the story doesn't take itself too seriously and, while simple, does elicit quite a few chuckles due to the funny dialogue
-there's a good number of units to unlock through quest and then use in combat
-several passive skills to choose from after each completed quest lets you upgrade the units/ spells you like most
-the actual combat features quite a few strategic elements such as flanking, an attack with a chance to miss but a guaranteed critical, units with bonus damage towards certain unit classes, powers you can use to heal/ damage/ summon units etc...
-decent replay value due to the amount of offered quests and units to unlock paired with the fact you can only complete and gather some of them in each playthrough: there's also a few decisions that'll provide different bonuses to certain heroes and two different endings. An endless mode is included once you beat the game for those interested in high scores and you can also select the new game+ option to start over while keeping 5 upgrades from the previous game
-the battle area is a bit small and might get cluttered during fights involving several units
-no way to know turn order for heroes/ units
-a few units/ upgrades feel weaker than others or just too situational to be useful
-basic options menu
-pretty easy overall
-despite the replay value each playthrough is somewhat short, at around 3 hours
I had a very good time with Reverse Crawl, despite its simple premise and looks there's a decent layer of complexity to the actual combat and, even though the fights are somewhat easy, you'll still have to choose the right units for the job and use some strategy to be victorious. You'll be able to choose between three different quests each time you're back to the world map and they all have different rewards such as unlocking units, heroes or spells: as said you won't be able to tackle them all so you'll have to pick the ones that give you unlocks better suited to your playstyle.
There were a few times when units clustered together made distinguishing who's who and/ or movement somewhat difficult but that's just a minor annoyance and the result of the small-ish combat area: the short campaign also make this a bite-sized experience that can be done in an afternoon but one you could be playing through at least twice if you're interested in seeing what happens with the other dialogue choices and what the other ending entails.
I can see Reverse Crawl being a worthy purchase for veterans looking for a diversion from more complex games or newcomers looking to either jump into the genre or try their skills with an easy game that still requires strategy to beat: it's a good game and, for what it offers and its length, priced fairly even when not on sale.

Reverse Crawl is a wave fighter game. Enemies, oh i'm sorry, "good guys" come in waves and we as the "badguys" must deploy our waves to kill them.
Unfortunately It gets really repetitive really fast and I know why.
The game uses a hex grid system like Heroes of Might & Magic games so while fights should be tactical and played smartly, the AI doesn't offer a great challenge so often you are just clickling through waves.
Its a shame really as its a nice twist on the usual wave fighter game since you must pick a unit type, such as archers and fend of various waves until you win or that group dies and then you select your next unit type. I feel the system would be very good in a PvP game but I don't know if there would be enough public interest to warrant a PvP mode/standalone game which is a bit of a shame.
I also feel the game wouldn't be so bad if the game as a whole didn't feel so uninspired, it isn't bad but it feels bland and devoid of charm. It doesn't offend you but doesn't entice you either.
The concept itself is original in that when your party/squad/wave gets wiped out, you have reserves. Thats the only original idea though, everything else is a forgettable reprint RPG Grindfest.
I liked Vertical Drop Heroes (By the same developer) but that also suffered from a lack of life and charm too although the co-op was fun so I find myself going back to play it every now and again.
I'm not sure what could save this game really, but I know this game will divide opinions.
If you've never played any of the Heroes of Might & Magic games then I imagine you will really enjoy this game, or Braveland.

Also on the plus side its not another "free to play" game, so there is that.

I have played three versions of this game but instead of repeating what other's have written about the features that make this game better than the other versions many of us have access to and to choose from, I'll give you advice from a seasoned FFX player (I haven't played X-2 so I can't help with that)....
* Before you start playing, look up the list of Al Bhed Primers and get them as you progress throguh the game instead of having to find them all later.
* Check out the web for info on the Celestial Weapons, you'll need at least one of them to speed through the final part of the story (damage dealt is capped without these weapons).
* There is no such thing as "too much sphere level grinding" essentially, a well rounded party will progress through the game easily and you'll have fun doing it, once you get to the last third of the story, a party that hasn't gotten many sphere levels will be dead before you know what's hit you. So don't skip levelling.
* Like most Final Fantasy titles, the main story is about 10  - 20 hours long. But the rest of the game will keep you occupied for more than 100 hours, maybe triple that, so accept now that this game will own you for a good couple of months.
* But MOST IMPORTANT!!! Choose the EXPERT GRID even if you are new to the game, partly because it's far more open and is going to allow you to basically handpick your party in terms of their abilities from the very get-go and partly beccause the STANDARD GRID BLOWS CHUNKS!!!
There is no such thing as too much research, too much time, or too much patience with this game. Unlike a lot of games that promise you this and fail, this succeeds, you'll get out of this game what you put in to it. Nothing more, nothing less. This is a game that was remastered, not changed in any way (as far as I can tell) and is still everything it was in the beginning. Years of gaming with other developer's products, playing different genres, even other Final Fantasy titles, and this game is sheer excellence and will always remain so.

First, I should disclose that the copy I played was a free copy provided for a review.
Reverse Crawl is a turn-based strategy RPG in which you gather minions and upgrades in order to take back your kingdom from the Red Queen. The twist here is that you play as the traditional enemies, with your main units being the Necromancer Princess and her newly-risen Revenant King father. Together with an army of skeletons, zombies, and wraiths, you must gather some unlikely allies such as wolves, goblins, and a wizard with a particularly soft and luxurious beard, alongside many more.
The art style is charming, the music is lovely, and the story, though simple, plucks at the heart strings of anyone with sympathy for our favorite rotting villains, the undead. Though the combat is easy to learn, the game still provides a challenge, as simply trying to rush down your opponents may easily result in a loss. Your units may also be summoned with randomized traits, which can result in them being weaker or stronger at times, preventing you from building up a singular group of badasses to steamroll every encounter. The game also provides branching paths, allowing you to decide what allies or abilities you would like to gain next. Overall, this game provides tremendous value for its low price.
