This game, VVVVVV, it calls itself. A mess of letters that blend together into a mess of jagged lines, as if to trace one's path through life in a retrospective essay of Adobe Flash and Steam winter sales. It infuriates me. But not for the reasons one might expect, no, not the usual cries of difficulty and despair.
I double-click the name in my Steam library and prepare for the worst. Forty nine cents, I say. This game cost me less than a round of slightly clogged arteries from the local fast food joint and was paid for entirely by selling virtual headwear and trading cards to those less fortunate than myself. Surely I will be able to find some modicum of enjoyment of this mess of Flash. Flash? Perhaps not! The forums of the Internet tell me that at one point it was remade in a proper programming language. As such, the game can suffer random slowdowns in fullscreen and neither the Steam overlay nor capture software such as Fraps will recognize the game. I found myself unable to take and upload screenshots of my trials in this pixelated, single-colored world, for all to see but none to comment on. A Google search leads to a Steam forum post regarding then-'soon' updates for overlays, achievements and the Cloud. The famous Cloud. At the original time of writing, this post dated from over two years ago. The Cloud has since been implemented to questionable effect, but now there are a host of colorful trinket achievements to chase. Did you already play the game to completion before their appearance? You're out of luck, friend, do it again, they say. Alt-tabbing the game will lock your cursor in the corner of your screen and sometimes just crash to desktop. This game was not built on Source, they tell me. They're lying to me.
The game itself controls acceptably. Sometimes I find myself sliding off platforms and into hazards and sometimes getting stuck inside either. Platformers should not have slippery controls like this, but the air control is precise and exact. Why is there such a difference? Is there an underlying message to be found here, perhaps describing the trials of Man trapped in his earthly plane? I would hope not, as this game predates the trend of waves upon waves of lazy, 'deep' indie
by several years. To the untrained eye it appears to fit quite well, though, with the simplistic graphics and chiptune soundtrack.
This. This is where this executable of poor optimization and developer laziness gets to me. The game's art style is obviously meant to harken back to an era of dial-up and diskettes, in truth even earlier than both. Simple graphics and single color palettes attempt to imitate the limitations of old, yet miss the mark entirely. The developers want you to think you're playing a Commodore 64 game, down to including an imitation tape deck load screen upon startup, and yet they so clearly miss the appeal of the C64. Why go for plain, blocky graphics when it was capable of so much more? Why use a soundtrack consisting entirely of generic chiptunes churned out in Fruityloops in an afternoon when the Commodore was famous for its SID chip, used even today for its unique sound and characteristics? This was perhaps the biggest indicator of Vee Six's origins.
Vee Six? Yes, that will do. I feel it fits this game nicely. You wanted the big American V8 with more displacement than the total Coke bottles in a shopping cart at Wal-Mart, but instead went for the more frugal six-cylinder for better gas mileage. Perhaps it shows up under a different name, like Grand Sport or Touring, but the illusion disappears as soon as the hood is opened and the guts of the machine become visible. Likewise, you wanted a game that harkens back to the days of incredible difficulty, but without actually playing a game from that era, so you bought Vee Six.
It was quite ahead of its time, really, this poor little game. Perhaps it actually started the trend of retro-throwback games that only appear as such to the untrained, Mountain Dew chugging eye, taking a small break from his endless stacks of semi-futuristic first person shooters starring Sgt. Master Sgt. Technician of Operations Captain Slabmeat and his sidekicks, Alpha Team Bravo Charlie Omega. I have doubts about his ability to find such a game, though. This seems like one meant for that other audience, the one that cuddles into their woolen hat at the corner coffee house while typing on their ridiculously overpriced, shining white laptop and adjusting their lensless, thick-framed glasses. A game for those who want to go back... but not really, because they never experienced what they would be going back to in the first place. An imitation that falls apart like that disgusting hipster's Volkswagen as it gets driven around a small upstate city in New York looking for guys in skinny jeans and no shoes while struggling from no oil changes to no oil changes.
So. An interesting word, 'so.' Both a statement and a question. So what? So this is a review, after all. Reviews have to have one final word, else the whole page might as well be used as a paper airplane to send your thoughts and dreams. In these modern times of instant messaging and ironic tendencies, no one has time to read more than exactly one hundred forty-four characters without requesting a short-form so their attention deficit disorder-afflicted minds can process that one tidbit of information before riding the rollercoaster of latest trends down the next incline while that child in the back row vomits all over himself and the poor sod sitting beside. Do I recommend this game? The question weighed heavily on my mind for days on end, pervading every waking moment with its incessant inquisition.
Yes. I suppose I can recommend this game, if you enjoy throwing money at walls to throw a small, single-color, virtual person at a wall over and over. I move my mouse and hesitantly click the checkmark instead of the thumbs-down icon. Nobody reads negative reviews, after all, and unfortunately there is no option for 'indifference' or perhaps 'Yes, but only if on sale first.' I paid forty nine American pennies for a sadomasochism simulator in the guise of a 'retro' platformer game.
I should have found two more quarters in my couch and bought a burger.

Before i start this review i would like to point out that i’ve personally only played around 15-20 hours of this game. The rest of the hours were played by my father who seems to keep coming back to this when he wants to play for an hour or two. And seeing the amount of hours we have played he must enjoy it. But this review will be from my own opinion.
I guess I need to start by saying that I know very little when it comes to the sport of F1. I know most of the drivers names and I have a basic knowledge of the rules; as in I know that there are cars and they race around a track for a large number of laps. So given my knowledge of the sport and the fact that I don’t really play racing sims, I wasn’t sure how I would get on with the game.
Thankfully, F1 2016 welcomes drivers of all levels. If simulations are your thing, players can switch all of the assists off and experience the game at its most challenging. The management of the car can be completely left to the game, or the player can intervene and set the car up as they so choose. This means that all of the technical stuff that the game simulates and that fans will love, can easily be sidestepped by those not in the know; something that I really appreciated.
And when you do finally get behind the wheel and put your foot down, well that's when F1 2016 really comes into its own. The first time i took part in a race with the assists off and the laps turned up to full takes the kind of discipline and mental focus you would usually associate with a hour-long boss battle. Races are mentally demanding and physically draining, but they're also incredibly satisfying, especially if you manage to come out with a place on the podium.
Codemasters caps it off with some of the most impressive visuals we've seen from an F1 game to date, especially when the heavens open and it starts to rain. If only they would've put the same effort into the character models and crowds, but hey you can’t win them all right?
F1 2016 isn't just the best game in the Formula One series, it's also one of the finest racing sims available right now. It's a tough game with a steep learning curve and lots to get your head around, but it's also genuinely rewarding. Although it  won’t be for everyone, it is a testament to Codemasters’ appreciation to the genre and their commitment to their fans. Taking lessons learned from previous games and applying their expertise, Codemasters has developed an almost perfect simulation of the greatest racing competition on earth.
This is an F1 game for F1 fans, but exciting enough to pull in those who'd never normally sit through qualifying. You can't really ask for more than that.

I have to say that this game was a lot of fun and the puzzles are really really challenging, some were even too absurd to be figured out without the understanding of hints or things you even may have forgotten over time in the game.
Youtube was especially "RPGDivision" was a great help here. He helped me many times when I already gave up solving the puzzle my own. Given I spent nearly 70 hours on normal difficulty you can imagine what kind of a work it was, to solve them.

-> the music is much better as in the first part, and often I even had goosebumps and felt fear. But even though every level has an own "soundtrack" it becomes repetitive. It would be a great addition if the music would be tense or dynamic regarding the situation.
-> The final fight against the Island master is horrific. I've slain the dragon quite easy but then all the new diversity brought into the game how you can skill characters is rendered useless if you want to defeat the Island Master. It is all about HP, DMG and best elemental resistance at the end. It is a must to have strong built party, with certain equipment and spells etc to stand this last fight.
It find it very very sad that this final boss is actually so hard to be defeated, if you have not chosen an "ideal" party. During the game you can compensate any lacks but speed or exploiting monsters, but this boss will tear you apart if you are not properly equipped and skilled, so the diversity is simply not useful at the end.
-> All Ingridients, except blooddrop cap (healing) and crystal flower (skillpoints) are very plenty so on normal difficulty I was too savy using them.
-> a great well thought story
-> very very challenging puzzles
-> very good diversity in graphics, character building (with limitations) and monsters
-> much better music
-> great levels and landscape and lovely details
-> an intro and end scenes makes more rich, what you missed in Grimrock 1.
-> it is good that there are enough keys to unlock quite all gold caches and chests, but you need to be careful to find them all
-> because of the higher environmental and graphical diversity "secrets" are much more hard to find as in Grimrock 1
-> Workshop (Modding) support

A sequel that seems to improve from the original in every way.
Pros:
- Fantastic level design. Features an outside world that can lead to dungeons, and then dungeons that can connect to other dungeons. It makes the world feel interconnected and organic.
- Clever puzzles. The majority of the puzzles in the game are very mind-bending while also being reasonable enough to solve on your own.
- Improved Combat. The enemy AI isn't perfect, but it's pretty damn good. Enemys will often move try to pin you down, dodge, and even flee. Also, if you're a wizard-lover like me, you'll greatly appreciate the improvements to the spell system, and the skill tree system as a whole.
- VARIETY. This game does a fantastic job of making the world varied enough to keep it fresh while also making it consistant enough to make the world feel connected. Just when you start getting sick of an enemy type or a weapon that you have. the game will throw in something new. Even the puzzles have a decent amount of variety to them with some being reflex-based, being observent of your surroundings, thinking outside the box, and even cracking codes!
Cons (I'm gonna be honest, these are pretty nitpicky):
- While the inclusion of guns is nice, I feel as though they were a bit of a missed opportunity. I came across maybe a total of 3 or 4 firearms on my 1st playthrough, and for the often pitiful damage they do they aren't worth it for the amount of times they seem to malfunction and backfire. There is a firearm that's good, but you'll hardly use it out of fear of wasting the very small amount of ammo it has. Hopefully, they'll be buffed for Grimrock 3. *crossing every finger I got*
- 2 or 3 puzzles in the game felt a bit lazy or too ambiguous, but they're greatly overshadowed by the amount of good puzzles in the game.
- Legend of Grimrock 3 hasn't been made yet.

i grew up on wwf wrestlemania 2000, and to a lesser degree wwf no mercy 64.  then i discovered the joy of the Gamecube WWE games where collision detection was added and a giant swing in a 4+ man match meant everyone got their asses knocked over.
then i did smackdown vs raw 2008, 2009, 2010, and they were terrible.  wwe 13 was the last good game i did.
WWE 2k16 is basically that, but with more stuff, and that's pretty good.
it's got probably the most diverse roster of any game i ever played.  i told a friend about it who is not a current wrestling fan, and they basically asked me "is insert-obscure-80s/90s-wrestler-name in it?" expecting me to say no, and I ended up saying Yes to every single one (names like iron sheik, though as colonel mustafa, dude love, randy savage, x-pac)
they even have a large number of NXT roster in it so even almost a year after the game is out, it's current with stupidstars like enzo and cass, the vaudevillains, binn falor, samoan yusuf, KENTAAAAAAA, baron von chickenpants, killsteenkill, and so on.  this is the first double-e game where i've actually wanted to play as almost everyone in it.
the new campaign mode is also something remarkable despite being a rehash of the exact same thing almost every we game has had fantasizing over the attitude era and bone cold beave austin.  this time you play as him throughout several matches in his career, following objectives to advance the matches as they historically unfolded,  with exact in-game recreations of events, movement, and motion from the matches, as well as clips of the original audio and audience noise.  even lets you play as STUNNING STEVE AUSTIN where you can marvel that wcw also had jerry lawler and jr on commentary wow
the steam-included DLC contains individual missionmatches in teh same vein for the wwe 2015 hall of famers, allowing you to unlock a bunch of excessive skins, variations of wrestlers, etc, from The Rock, to The Rock 97, to The Rock 00, even to The Rock 03.
the in-game handling of grapples and strikes feels much smoother than before, though there's basically no information on the controls for certain grapples, leaving you to figure it out yourself or look it up online.
to counter boring counter-fests, counters are now limited and have to recharge over time, so if a cheating computer is countering everything you do, they can only do it up to 5 times in a short period of time before they can't counter anymore, although even then sometimes the cheating computer will cheat and be able to counter despite having no counter.
the MyCareer mode has some fun and innovative bits like starting out in NXt, choosing which titles to pursue and earning your way to title shots, having story interactions where you can make bad decisions and give horribly generic interviews which can turn you face or heel.  the problem with MyCareer is that this is pretty much all it has for all the championships and it costs stat points and VIRTUAL CURRENCY to upgrade your stats, and you gain very little of those at first, and even when you start earning more after each match, everything starts costing more, so you end up going year after year in MyCareer mode grinding for points unless you cheat using CheatEngine and give yourself more.
MyUNIVERSE mode is basically the same but you don't play as one custom superstar.  you don't even have to play as a superstar, but just arrange shows, set up rivalries, and see greater in-world interaction with stuff like injuries and women wrestlers.  little icons appear after each match showing some trait loss or gain, but there's no explanation anywhere as to what these icons even represent so i have no idea what any of them even mean, one of them is literally like a pyramid or something.
there's also great deal of customization of arenas, i made one that looks like paint and puke, and is atrocious and has a Turkish flag on the side of the ring beneath an LED board for no reason at all.
the wrestler customizations are limited, as it seems every year they completely pick at random what things to include or disclude from the games in terms of features and customization options.
the new facial morphing system allows for greater freedom of movement, but at the cost of being excessively difficult to manipulate, and having some seemingly arbitrary limits which leave you with such oddities as being able to smooth down the right jaw, but not the left jaw ever.  it's all very dependent on the new photo-face capture feature, where you have to take a very precise photograph of someone's face, then messily staple it onto the CAW's face.  some of these looks surprisingly good, but none of it even matters because the CAW facial animations end up making every face-morphed CAW look the same.
some other things i really like are the little details in the game.  por ejemplo, iffin when you play as Bray Wyatt and you do a taunt, youll hear his voice shouting "follow the buzzards!" or "i'm the eater of worlds!" like real.  Paige also shouts and says "this is my house" and cass loudly spells out "S" "A" "W" "F" "T" with his siganature or finisher thing.

This game is getting a lot of hate nowadays. Like other reviewers said, its not for everyone, but it was for me. Playing this game is like solving a mystery that at first is very external, and then becomes more of an internal journey of coming of age. Sweet, touching, beautiful in its details, and even dark in several ways that are easily skipped over. Its really nice to play a game that wasn't pandering soley to the demographic of straight male. For someone not in that category it was relatable, affirming, and a breath of fresh air.
It's short (def get it on sale <$10), and "not perfect" in the sense that it isnt a "game" in that it doesnt have gameplay. But it is truly an innovative storytelling mechanic, seeing the human story through objects left behind. Its like 90's archaeology. Walking through my house after I finished it felt like I was seeing everything with new eyes.
If you like puzzles or explosions or chase scenes in your games then this isnt for you so there is no point to buy it and then whine about how bad it is just because it doesnt resound with you.

If you're a fan of guns or want to learn how a gun works, how to eject a bullet out of a pistol, How the ballistic's of a pistol bullet works, and so fourth, you may like this game.
Story: Well, when I started out on this game, I had no idea what I was doing, but there are cassets that you can find that will give you the backstory, I found two. So far it has too do with some kind of.. war that will happen.
Gameplay: Simple and bare with mechanics hardly found anywhere else.
You start in a abandoned building with a pistols which ranges from a Colt 1911 pistol, S&W Model 10 "Victory" revolver, and a Glock 10 with full auto mod. Everything is random, your ammo count, placement of ammo, and enemies.
I should mention that ALL enemies make a sound and lights when they spot you. These are only two enemies in the game that I have seen.
Enemy types:
Sentries: are stationary, but once they spot you, they fire at you as you would expect.
Drones: These little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s chase after you once they spot you, choosing to close in at close range to taser you, I have yet to see with with a gun mounted on it.. or destory one.
Challange: Think Dark Souls, but First Person Shooter with mechanics that fit more in a military sim. (Roughly)
Replay ability: This one is a hard one for me, but it does get a bit tedious after a few tries. So it's doesn't have much replay value.
Verdict: 8/10 With deep mechanics with the weapon types and detail of how it works. The Enemy types is dissapointing and the variety of weapons is quite lacking. The reply value is a bit hard for me to say due to the fact you spawn with different weapons at the start of every game and the enemy placement appears to change.

A really cool technical game. Basically it breaks down all the physical actions required to operate a gun, then binds (nearly) every individual action to a key, then puts it on top of a standard FPS control setup.
So it's fun to manage bullets, but it's more difficult than it really should be due to luck. Which leads me to my only real gripe with the game.
Every time you start a new game the world is randomly generated from a set of premade areas that connect in a linear fashion. Since item placement, starting equipment, and enemy placement is randomized as well, you can end up with a bad start and find no ammo but run into tons of enemies.
Lastly, when moving from one prefab-area to another, the game seems to hitch for a second while it loads stuff, this has killed me so many times I think it's probably the biggest flaw. Not being able to react to a flying killbot coming at you for even half a second can easily be the difference between life and death.

Given the fact I'm switching from positive to negative review and back and back and back I'm just gonna stick with my original review, because even if this game dies for lack of interest of other players it was still a good ride.
It's hard to review and recommend card games as with the wiiiide selection we have today it is all about the personal taste (and not gonna lie - about what your friends play).
Eternal started as MtG/HS rip-off that is evolving into its own style. If you like MtG for its complexity or HS for its quicker style you definitely should give Eternal a try. Don't be scared by one of the worst campaigns in game history (not kidding there, if you have any TCG experience it's gonna get boring a lot and challenging for wrong reasons - some of the opps play deck that's few ranks above yours and you don't have any answers to beat them in a fair game) and delve into PvP experience as that is the thing we're all looking for, right?
As for person experience: I played a lot during closed beta, stopped and came back once they put it here on Steam. Some cards got nerfed, some got stronger. Some disappeared completely and some new showed up. Can't say I loved all the changes, but they sure turned out good. Even with the very limiting card pool at the moment (Feb 2017) the meta is still healthy and didn't produce one or two decks to beat it all and that's a really good sign that someone (looking at you devs) know at least a little what they are doing.
Overall I'm not afraid to recommend this and even if I stop playing to go back to only true game of them all (paper MtG) I will for sure drop by every now and then to check on the new cards and to play a game or two.

I bought this game in the sale on a bit of a whim, but even though it was less than £6.00, i'm starting to regret my decision.
As the many other reviews will tell you, this game is not exactly cutting edge in terms of graphics or gameplay, but what did you expect for this much!?!
Initially I was disappointed with the limited gameplay "move truck A, to this place, in this time", "move truck B, to this place, in this time" etc, but I stuck with it in the hope it got better as the number of planes you handle ramps up. Again, I was wrong. As you go on, the only way to get by is to automate the airport functions by hiring helpers. At first, they are desperately slow (you have to pay more to make them go faster) which frustrates you into upgrading everything as fast as possible. The problem is, you are effectively upgrading yourself out of the gameplay! There are perhaps 2 functions left that you have to do manually, and that's allocate a gate, and load/unload cargo. The latter is probably one of the more redeeming features of this game, in that the cargo lifter requires a little bit of effort as you have to line it up fairly precisely, and that it has some legitimate animation! If they had extended these features to more of the equipment, so you actually connected and sealed the stairs and the skybridges etc, I might have been inclined to stick around a bit longer.
In summary, a bit tedious and a bit limited. Save your money...
For the sake of constructive feedback to any of the development team who might see this (unlikely I know):
- they get close to their goal on some tasks and then just abandon it altogether
- In case of the above, I had no way to step in!
- Connecting the walkways, and seeing people in the buses can't be that hard to do if you can do containers in and out of a cargo hold!
- Maybe designing and building a new terminal? Extending the current one? Upgrading equipment? Replacing old equipment with newer kit?!?
There was a fair bit of potential for this game but it just fell short of my expectations, even for this price. Deep down inside I hoped it was going to be like 'Air Mogul' with the customisation of the buildings as well as the operation of the equipment, and i'd definitely come back to it if these things were patched in at some point, but for now, I bid you adieu, Airport Simulator 2014...

It's a cheap game that's worth a look if you've ever wanted to try a hex based tactics game, but were never willing to spend a big amount of money on the idea. It's basic strategy elements have been done before, but the replayability does get boosted with the ability to grab skills based on the missions you take on. There's an element of strategy that's present here in the way that you grab minions and their specific strategies and weaknesses they have against each other. It's not going to stick around long, while there is some replayability, it's too simple at the surface, and the game isn't too complicated in the end. But it's solid for a cheap price, and has a couple of cheesy moments to help make the game a little bit more out there in the end. There will be a bug here and there, and it's not the most visually appealing game out there, but it does the job where it needs to in its gameplay.

Reverse Crawl is a simplistic looking game that hides a challenging and entertaining title that offers a decent amount of replay value.
The game's story might not appear to be much more than a spin on the stable RPG genre of playing a hero and defeating villains and their minions; instead in Reverse Crawl you play a king who was revived via necromancy who wishes to reclaim the land that was stolen by the Red Queen and the heroes she recruited. The game's story also features a branching storyline with each task you choose (each chapter allows you to pick 1 of 3 tasks) potentially altering the game.
The combat provides a decent challenge for new players, but over time the challenge is easily overcome when you recruit overpowered minions such as a golem or a swarm of rats.
In terms of replay value, the campaign is only about four hours long, but upon completing the game you have the option of doing an endless dungeon, taking on the Red Queen or entering New Game+.
The game's major negative comes from its options menu, which is nearly nonexistent; the menu only contains three options: sound, music and full screen, all three of which can only be turned on or off.
Hard but really fun, especially with friends.

This game had huge potential and was fun at first when you dive into the aspects of just driving around a huge country and exploring. It's pretty satisfying when a good song comes on the radio and you just blast away full speed through a curvy mountain/forest road or something...
But it ENDS THERE. It quickly gets boring, landscapes just don't feel open (there's always very little open scenery visible no matter where you are, and the wonky camera controls and insanely low field of view makes it even worse).
Performance is awful, barely jsut BARELY getting 60 FPS with two GTX 980's in SLI, and visuals are decent at best. Not to mention the FPS caps at 60, which is a huge turn-off if you have a 120/144hz monitor. SLI scaling IS good, but with only decent looking visuals that somehow are very demanding, it doesn't matter. There's also issues with stuttering, every 10-30 seconds or so the entire image "shakes" for about 5 seconds or so. I've confirmed this is NOT an SLI issue as it happens with SLI disabled aswell (and then it's just not playable either). Not only the graphical aspects are wonky, but the controls are so clumsy and lack freedom. You can never properly stop and look around without the automatic camera rotation jerking the immersion right out of the game, and cockpit view is like using a pair of binoculars to look through a keyhole.
The story is boring, the missions are extremely repetitive and have no meaning. Online interaction is a joke, as I've yet to be able to see one of my friends ingame. My router NAT is ♥♥♥♥ING OPEN, yet I can never join/invite a friend or see them in freeroam. As for other players I DO see, trying any coop is almost impossible.
And don't get me started on Uplay. It's just an abomination that shouldn't exist, and needs to go. Surprisingly this is one of Ubisoft's less bug and problem ridden games, but it's far away from being a proper finished and polished game, like the trend has been in the past years.
It had it's fun moments, but ultimately it's a waste of money buying. If you get to opportunity to try the game from someone who already has it, it's worth playing for a bit, but paying the full price for something like this is just stupid.
Ubisoft needs to seriously start improving on their quality, and people.. STOP PRE-ORDERING GAMES.

I enjoyed the concept of the first Homeworld, so I was looking forward to this entry. However, there was news on the development of this game that I missed. Apparently, the developer went under and they were picked up by someone else, and then had to work with a really small team. This all gets discussed in a message after beating the main story. Thus, I will forgive the number of bugs in the game and a lack of polish. However, I want to note that NO BUG or lack of polish is game killing. Everything is stuff you'll think to yourself "Oh, they clearly had an issue there", but you can continue playing without issue.
That all being said, I enjoyed the hell out of this game.
I like FPSs and I like modern weaponry. Combine that with a timeline where the U.S. is the occupied country, and you have a great atmosphere. The story here is excellent despite moments where you know they were rushed due to the stuff mentioned earlier.
You're Ethan Brady and you're a new recruit in the Resistance. You're based in Philly and the leader of the Resistance, Walker, is on his way. Things go south and now you're fighting to keep the Resistance going against the KPA, who are essentially North Korea, but if I remember from the first game, they're all of Korea? They're also very technologically advanced.
More on the story in a bit because this game does something I've never seen before.
The game play feels good. It didn't initially. I was actually thrown WAY off by the aiming and even dropped mouse sensitivity to its lowest level. I was pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥thinking I would be shelving this game as unplayable. I even stopped playing it for two nights. Then I returned and gave it an hour. I am very glad I did. Maybe it had been a while since I had played any FPS other than Rust, but I was not prepared for the inaccuracy they give you as a rookie recruit. Once I realized that recoil and your shakiness improves as you purchase new equipment, all my fears disappeared. By the end, I was a killing machine, yet still able to be dropped quite easily. I guess it does get easier after that first one...
Anyway, I played on "normal" difficulty, which isn't called that, but you'll figure it out. Very nice challenge. At times I felt like I was the ultimate killing machine that couldn't be stopped, but I could still be stopped quite easily. It's not a one shot=you die game, but you also can't tank your way through enemies.
Enemies are almost all human and come in different favors: Normal, Slightly Tougher Captains, Chemsuit wearing dudes, Fireproof guys, female Snipers, and heavily armored guys with miniguns. The non-human enemies are: Seekers (Drones that spot you and call baddies to you), Jeeps with an AI(?) minigun on top, a Wolverine that is an AI laster turret on treads, and the Goliath which is a rocket shooting tank. You also need to avoid enemy cameras.
Levels range from pretty big to tiny. Objectives vary throughout the story, and with the optional side missions given out as jobs at a job board. These jobs are a great example of where you can see issues in development. If you're a completionist, you'll want to knock these out before advancing the story at all. Some jobs become impossible yet still available if you drive the story forward too far. For example, one job has you photographing collaborators, but if you've inspired the people in their district to fight back, there are no more clabs to photo. Some of the jobs might require a quick Google search to see what the hell you're looking for too.
Ammo and health can be found around the city in stashes the Stronghold have hidden. Look for blue paint. There are also dirt bikes around the city that can be ridden. Another example of ideas they had that they had to abandon. Riding them is slightly wonky, but manageable. Only twice in the story do you have to ride one, and it's almost on rails, so no concerns there.
Back to the story, once I finished it I realized there were three other stories aside from the main one. Each is a good 30 minutes, give or take, in length. The first is a prequel to the main story, and it wouldn't hurt anything if you played it prior to the main story. In fact, you might get a kick out of it. The other two take place after the events of the story and reflect what's been happening. "Aftermath" was decent and ties up a dangling plot thread. The ending of the third one "Beyond the Walls" is pretty kick♥♥♥♥♥ I honestly wonder if those little bits were the original game or something added on later? Very different feel. Don't forget to quickly convert your weapons when you start each one or your aim will be wonky again.
I definitely got my money's worth here and I hope they are able to give us a sequel. I'd recommend this game to anyone that enjoys FPSs, particularly ones set in a more realistic, modern setting and not in Hell or on an alien planet.
Ignore the bugs, there's a really good game and story here that's all the more impressive considering the obstacles the developers faced.

2K16 is a pretty solid game that is a good gateway to understanding the appeal of professional wrestling. Not only does it cover the highlights of the poster child of WWE's Attitude Era "Stone Cold" Steve Austin, but high points of the newest Hall of Famers like Alundra Blayze, Rikishi, and "Macho Man" Randy Savage. Needless to say, experiencing Career Mode is a good place to start for anyone that wants to know why people tune in to buff guys pretending to hate each other (sometimes) and not-so-pretending to beat the Hell out of each other.
For those who want just a match, the roster is enormous and the modes are varied.
Wrestling is an inherently creative endeavor, and with 2K16's tools, creativity is encouraged. Build custom wrestlers with their entrances, arenas, shows, tag teams, championship belts.
Universe Mode is like being in charge of your WWE programming lineup, which means you can make something better than current programming easily.
While no means an absoultely complete and flawless experience, it's pretty close.

Now I beat this one on my Xbox One. The PC port is great too. A Great Souls Game, though I feel that It lost some of what the first one (Dark Souls not Demon souls) did right. I have some issues with the combat speed of the game. It feels slowed down compared to the first and 3rd installment of the series. For Example when swinging light attacks with a melee weapon like a longsword or a katana. There is a pause between attacks where you cannot roll or attack after doing such untill the whole animation is over. On the First and Third game you can immediately roll after an attack which i believe is a strength of the two games and is one of the things that drew me away from the 2nd one and stopped me from doing a second playthrough of the game.
What I will say I am pleased about is I think it was in the right place with the stamina usage, where rolling and attacking would use much more stamina than the third game. Alot of the game seem's very polished and you have to be certain about the moves you make when engaging in a pvp battle with another player. Also this game has a much more cinematic experience than the Third and First installment. And it is a beautiful and dark game as it should be. Another thing is the Bosses. There is so many bosses and each are challenging. You will also be pitted against the pursuer in the worst situations, a difficult foe that either never seems to die or there is many of. A Great Installment of the series.
Also I did love the Character Creation in this game compared to the other 2. Sure It was a little more anime looking than the others but it was kind of refreshing. It wasn't as hard to make a good looking character on this as it was in Dark Souls 3. And the Female Models Look somewhat Feminine in this game when in armor, compared to 3.
An Important thing to mention is that this version of the game is an improvement of the normal game with the DLC packaged in. This version improved many things the Vanilla Dark Souls 2 had wrong such as placements of items, and enemies as well as a graphical overhaul. Well Done Fromsoft. Let us praise the sun and hope that in Dark Souls 3's End state, it will be as polished as this.
Pros: -Long and Challenging Experience
-More Cinimatic than the others of the series
-Fully Patched and Polished game state
-Great Character Movement and Animation as Well as Accurate Stamina costs
-Character Design and Creation is Great
-Scholar Cut version of the game fixed alot of what was wrong with the game originally.
Cons: -Slower Combat than the First and Third.
-Combat also feels a tad clunky with the stagger rate of the enemies as well as yourself.
-Some of the I-Frames Feel improperly placed.
-I just can't get over how slow the combat felt in the game.Hard to Roll after attacks to escape death dealing blows                   -Lore feels a tad seperate from the first and 3rd. Hard to place where this game takes place in the convoluted                                                        timeline of the series.
Overall this game is considered a great sequel by many Souls fan's and Gamers alike. I myself did not have a good time with the combat but you may. I did still enjoy the story and the lore the game had and the overall experience of beating it was a joy in itself. Really I think my Dark Souls 3 Review applies to my feelings of the Dark Souls series in general. But Good luck, happy slaying my sunbros and sunsisters.

The story itself is generic and predictable. The game has you go from point A to B, interact with objects to take strongholds, and occasionally go to the location of a random event to save allies from the KPA for a reward.
There are much better games out there for a much better value. I wouldn't pay more than 10 or 20 bucks for this. I only have it because it came in the Humble Bundle.
TL;DR: If you're bored and want something to keep you mildly entertained, go for it. Pick it up on a sale if you want a generic FPS game.

Main Game
- Whilst running the train you can miss out on exposition as well as keeping your passangers living.
- Depending on who you decide to save/find you'll see different conversations play out.
- Depending on who is with you at the next safe populated station changes rewards as well as what exposition you hear.

DLC

- The more sociable the character the better the discussions.

This game compares favourably to Hyper Light Drifter in storytelling, gameplay mechanics and overall artistic integration -- everything fits together excellently. I found my train troublesome to maintain, but the quick little "minigames" associated with it were enough fun to keep me fond of the thing. On the other hand, I found myself getting genuinely angry at certain passengers for: (a) acting like spoiled children; (b) bleeding too much; (c) requiring food. I like to think this is how the character himself felt. Combat is fun, and most of the stations have unique characters to them -- you feel like you're exploring real places, each with its own purpose, rather than just a series of levels. Resource management can be challenging, but if you ration your bullets well in the easy confrontations, you'll typically have enough to handle the next horde. Somehow I was constantly on the edge of running out of food, but never faced starvation. Medpacks were also scarce in early game, but by late game I had a bunch of em, thanks to the crafting system.
Despite a dubious translation, the writing is excellent. One thing that impressed me was that in a game where you're already piecing together the story from little fragments, the main character was the most mysterious of all, up until the end. He speaks to other characters, but you don't get to see what he says*, and so everything about him has to be inferred.
Other than genre, The Last Station differs from HLD in being pretty short and linear, which I think worked well. It's also not as polished, and there were a couple of control issues that I found annoying. Still, it's high on my list of great games.
* With the exception of in-game text messages you send and receive on your train.

Terrible game. Basically, all you get to do is drive around various airport vehicles (stairs, buses, luggage carts...) and assign planes to gates. However, it doesn't really matter which gate you assign a plane to, and there's not much you can do wrong with driving the vehicles around. The "management" part of the game has you paying money for upgrades of the various vehicles, where the first upgrade automates a vehicle (you no longer need to drive it yourself, but you also can't take control if you want to), and subsequent upgrades speed up those vehicles.
Automated vehicles are slower than manually driven vehicles (which are also pretty slow), so you might think you'd cleverly automate only some vehicles or some gates or what have you and do the rest by hand. However, as soon as you're using more than one gate, you run into a problem with manually driving the vehicles: you only get one of each type. So if you need, say, a passenger bus on gate two while it's already loading or unloading passengers on gate one, you're out of luck. But as you have a time limit for getting any vehicle in place, you'll probably end up driving the bus from plane one to plane two, then back so that unloading can continue - once an activity is started, there is no deadline, but they only continue if the vehicle is present. Except stairs. You can remove stairs and the passengers will continue loading from the bus into the plane.
The strangest part about this "game" is that the aim of it is to make yourself mostly useless, as you're supposed to get all gates fully automated at upgrade level three. Obviously, just watching the game take care of the planes for ten to fifteen minutes at a time before you get to assign a plane to a gate (one click), then watch again, isn't really that much fun. Apparently even the developers realised this, so they gave us cargo planes. Unloading and loading cargo planes is the one thing you can't automate, so you have to drive the cargo lift yourself. It's a shame though that the game is only capable of keeping track of the loading state of one cargo plane at a time - if you have more than one cargo plane at a gate, the second (and third etc.) planes will have to wait until the first one leaves.
The only thing you can do "wrong" in the game is be too slow getting a vehicle in place, which will result in money being subtracted from your account - one Euro per second until you get it done. Actually managing to be that slow is almost impossible though. One might think that as the frequency of landing planes increases, a penalty for not getting rid of planes fast enough will occur - not so. They will simply queue up on the taxiway until it is full if you don't assign them to a gate, and once it is full planes will stop landing.
All in all, the only thing this "Simulator" simulates is a horrible attempt at making a game, but it simulates that very well.

Just finished the single-player campaign, or whatever you wanna call the story missions, cause you can do them in co-op as well. Anyway, the game is not finished, yet enjoyable for a very specific crowd. Let me explain. At a very technical level, the game is not where it should be. Laggy and stuttery even on an FX-9590 and 290x, tendency to cook a water cooled processor that doesn't go past 58 in Prime95, and almost unplayable on a mobile platform with an A10-5750M and M290x. If you can muster better specs and get it to be playable and responsive, you'll run into their side of the hardware issues, meaning the server. It might not pe hardware though, but still technical. On some networks it works, on others it doesn't, and it will disconnect every now and then in the middle of one of those hour long races, and you'll have to do it all over again. So, if these are things that you think you can look past just to get a glimpse of the sunset from the Grand Canyon behind the wheel of a LaFerrari, this is the game for you. It looks amazing, the cars sound fantastic, and on hardcore driving mode the driving model is brilliantly tuned for a very good mix of arcade and sort of simulator. Not a simulator in the actual sense, just that it follows a few rules that arcade racers usually don't. Say you're in a controlled power slide, or a drift, and one of your back wheels hits the dirt on the outside of the bend, or the snow, or even a wet patch, you will lose control of the car, because the back end loses grip completely. That is a very nice touch. So, driving model not bad at all, but not a full on simulator by any means. The story itself is a cliche, obviously, you've heard it a million times if you're into this culture, or have ever played a NFS game or seen an FnF movie. Bad guy kills/betrays your brother/mother/sister/any other signifcant family members and then you seek to get revenge by driving fast and breaking the law almost all the way. Nevertheless, this story is told well, with good quality cut-scenes and voice acting. Also, the missions themselves are quite fun, at least at first, because later on the same challanges are presented for the lack of more then 3 or 4 modes. You get the normal checkpoint race, checkpoint time trial, a sort of destruction derby against the clock, where you need to catch and bash into the opponent several times until a health bar hovering over his/her car is depleted. This one is quite interesting and fun, until they pit you against a prison bus that can keep up with a modified Mustang that can do 300 KM/h. Funny, but frustrating after the fifth try. Also has the health or relisience of a prison bus. There's another mode which I shall call "touch the package" because it can be interpreted in several ways, and I love a good internal debate. Anyway, this one puts you on a course, against the time, in which there are 100 packages on the ground, the story will explain why they are there, don't worry, not as stupid as it sounds. You have to, within that time limit, hit 80 of those boxes. Sounds easy? Pah. Difficult, but fun.
As a whole experience, because there is much more to talk about, and I can't be bothered because it's my night off, and I just wanted to share my general opinion about The Crew, the game is enjoyable if you like cars and the whole customization, FnF and NFSU heritage stuff. For the car enthusiast, the flaws are not there to disturb, we keep hoping that eventually they will be patched, because they are obvious, yet we look beyond them and enjoy good looking and sounding cars, that drive in an impressively fun and engaging manner, amongst scenery that you will probably only get to see in game. By the way, the map is a smaller version of the United States, with little versions of New York, Detroit, Las Vegas, Los Angeles and many other major US cities. Basically, you get to drive across America. And, also important, in my opinion, you can modify your cars in pretty fine detail, and the body parts available are very good looking, and have that racy feel, not the silly Underground toy looking things. You can put together a very good looking off-road version of a 2011 Mustang with 800 horses under the hood. Pretty cool. Thumbs up, but please work on those performance issues at least. Thank you.

This is what every digital MTG game should have been and very well could be the best digital CCG on the market.
It plays very similar to Magic however with some of the more complex elements stripped down, some alterations that are only possible with a digital game, and and some attempts to fix common issues like mana screw while retaining a complex mana system.
In terms of simplification, the biggest one is likely the priority system. Unlike Hearthstone it posseses instant speed spells ("fast spells" in this game) which makes each players turn far more engaging. This is, however, simplified from Magic by only giving players priority at certain moments (when a spell is cast, when attackers are declared, at end of turn, etc) and removing the ability to play a spell, retain priority before it resolves, and then play another spell. Instead once a fast spell is played in response priority passes, this goes back and forth until neither player make another play, It allows for the counterspell and buff wars everyone loves but prevents things like pitching your entire hand to Phantasmagorian's ability turn 1.
The mana system is simplified in that there is now "Power" and "Sigils" inplace of lands. When a power card is played it increases your power by 1, this is your mana used to cast spells and is colorless. Most power cards also grant you a specific color sigil (sometimes multiple). This is essentially permanent colored mana. Even if you only have 1 sigil of a color you can cast as many cards of that color as you have the power for (although some cards require you have multiple sigils). This makes it far easier to diversify your mana pool and helps to alleviate the terrible feeling of having an all blue hand and only drawing mountains.
The mulligan system is designed to alleviate mana issues as well, as it guarantees you draw at least 2 power cards. The downside is this does nothing to prevent mana flood. It's also incredibly beneficial for lean aggro decks that run mostly low-cost spells. To avoid people creating decks with only one or two power cards and all 1-2 mana cards, it is mandatory that a deck contain 1/3rd power cards. At first I reeled against this restriction but 1/3rd is still less than the 20+lands in an average 60card Magic deck so it has less of an impact than it seeems.
I do currently have a minor qualm with deck construction, which is the minimum of 75 cards. Deck size being this large means you will have games where you just don't hit a key card for the situation. It can be remedied to an extent with draw cards and tutors however the game could stand to have more of those. That being said there are some combos that allow you to draw through plenty of your deck. I do feel like the deck size (and card pool) do hinder combo based decks though.
At the moment it seems like straight aggro and midrange are two of the more dominant strategies, which is disappointing, however I've been playing control with good success and hear there are tier 1/2 control decks so aside from combo being weak and a large chunk of play being creature based the metagame seems healthy. I've yet to encounter anything too cancerous.
At this point I'm rambling so I'll cut it short and list bullet points:
-More polished than other digital MTG games
-More complex than Hearthstone with more rooms for outplay and less RNG
-Simpler than MTG
-Long standing issues like mana screw have been lessened however can still occur on occasion
-Combo seems weak in the current cardset
-Additional polish, cards, balance tweaks are bound to happen
-It's FREE just download it

This game combines an action packed open world game, with plenty of wacky physics to abuse. It's a game that's certainly a bit dated by today's standards, but it's still a lot of fun. But what makes this game really special is the mod called Just Cause 2 Multiplayer, which adds a multiplayer component to the single player game.
You still get to free roam in the world, jumping in every vehicle you see together with dozens or even hundreds of players. It's frantic, it's fun and a bit laggy at times when too many players are residing in the same general area. Which seems to be the airport mostly. There's other minigames that you can play such as racing and destruction derby or hunting down a player with a bounty. These will award you with ingame currency which can be used to buy items in game. Most items are free to spawn at any time you want, but the more powerful weapons or vehicles may cost money.
Servers do enforce a donor system similar to Garry's mod. Where some items are restricted to people who have donated to keep the server up.

Cons: Lacks mission variety. Outside of missions and races, all you can do is blow stuff up, and that does get old. No real consequences, dying(outside of a mission) doesn't "cost" anything, you don't even lose progress.
I recommend this to any fan of GTA and/or open-world games in general.

Gone Home is a fairly straightforward exploration game.  You're basically on a scavanger hunt in an old mansion to find clues why the family home is deserted after returning from a trip overseas.  The game requires a keen eye and meticulous searching to find each clue to find the doohickey that will unlock the cabinet so you can find the combination to the safe to find the key to open the door, and so on and so on.
In the end, the story is somewhat sad, two lovers separated by closed-minded parents (the lovers are ♥♥♥), one of which has left home to find the other, while the parents just happen to be away from home at the time on some mundane errand.  No ghosts, no monsters, no grizzly murders.  I found the story to be sad, yet all very mundane and the kind of hardship and injustice that many people from all walks of life--men and women, ♥♥♥ and straight, white and black--face every day.
The game deserves more recognition that it's getting.  Unortunately, the publisher, Fullbright, pulled the game from PAX (a trade show or Indie game developers) because they didn't agree with the PAX organizers' political views--the PAX people don't cowtow to political correctness or feminist dogma, which I applaud them for.  So I think that's a stupid reason for pulling a game--at the very least, Fullbright should recognize the importance of freedom of speech.
But as for the game, I recommend it.  As long as the ♥♥♥ theme doesn't upset you, the game is basically a benign puzzle game with a sad ending.

This is essentially Legend of Grimrock, but more. There's a greater variety of enemies, the skill point system is tighter, there are different environments to traverse instead of an eternity of brick-and-moss walls to bump listlessly into, the fan community is generally helpful, and the game *can* be beaten by a casual dungeon-crawler without the need to refer to a walkthrough every five steps. That said, there are several major optional dungeons, old areas repopulate with new encounters after milestones in the plot, puzzle hints are scattered between zones to make back-tracks more productive, and classes have been added to the game, supplementing the new races with a broader range of build options at the game's start.
Grim II is substantially more intuitive, with the worst puzzles being largely optional and timing-gimmick traps an occasional thing, rather than a whenever-the-developers-got-bored kind of affair. Pixel-hunt walls are also less in evidence (although the workshop community is working dilligently to fix that,) and fish restock themselves in ponds and rivers to cut down on starvation-induced unwinnable game-states.
It is still possible to get locked into an unrecoverable state (invincible golems start appearing midway through the plot, and they can wall-abuse you into a corner if you're unlucky,) but rotating your saves will prevent this handidly.
Basically: if you even sort of liked the original game, you're going to have a good time.
If you didn't much care for Grim 1's formula, but you liked Eye of the Beholder or Ultima Underworld or similar titles, this is still worth a try.
The only people I'd suggest give this a miss are people who want a smooth, continuous flow of play ala Halo, CoD, Skyrim, etc. Grimrock is largely about stopping and thinking about how you're going to proceed, and folks who have a strong negative reaction to things like substitution ciphers would do well to stay clear.

TL;DR - You know how sometimes garbage can still be fun? Well this game is absolute garbage that can still be fun. Why are you even bothering with reviews? You have no other choice, either buy this piece of crap or give up wrestling gaming. 2K have us by the balls and they know it, exploit it and love it.
Okay, first of all, let's be fair here. Recommendations are absolutely useless when it comes to the only game brand offering a solution (or at least a sad excuse for one) to us wrestling fans in the past two years. So of course I would say you should wait for the lowest price possible and get it. However, under absolutely no circumstances am I able to in good conscience mark this as “recommended”.
True, it is awesome to finally be able to play wrestling on PC after having to make do with the holy work of Rawmodders and their constant releases of mods for the 1995 RAW game. Nice of you to remember PC exists after 20 years, 2K! The graphics are spectacular, the audio quality as well. You are able to recreate your favorite WWE moments, or create your own new ones as you choose. Very nice.
Besides that? It is obvious that everything besides graphics has been given the absolute minimal possible attention, without any QA or beta testing (even though I’m sure thousands of you, just like me, would have happily done it for free). The controllers are the most atrocious I have EVER experienced in my life as a 31 year old gamer. Don’t believe me? Try playing a Triple Threat or Fatal 4-Way, I dare you. An opponent could be outside the ring 70 ft. away from you, and still when you try to break the pin count the game will for some reason think you wish to kick the air in hopes of hitting said opponent (what, you aren't a Jedi?). Nothing is more fun then having one of your oponents pinning another one right under your nose while you desperately pray that hitting the required button will actually have the meant effect. "Smack your TV", huh? More like smack your keyboard. The referee also works in a 1.5-2 seconds delay regardless to your specs, meaning you only have to the count of 8-9 to get back in the ring, causing a lot of frustration and turning skills like “relentless force” (extra damage outside of the ring) and the best OMG moments (like smashing you opponent through the table) irrelevant, as they WILL cause you to get counted out. In summary, you will do everything right and the less than amateur controllers will still make sure you lose. Yeah, I know, it could have been easily fixed, but why should they when so many of us will still buy the game having no alternatives? I know what you might think, I'm probably just not that good. Fair enough. As I've said, try it. Apology accepted.
Now let’s talk about My Career. Hooray, I get to create my own superstar with his own appearance, move set, entrance and what not! Great, right? Wrong. Why can’t we use custom music or titantron movies? Because it would have taken some work. Why will 95% of your matches be regular mundane 1 on 1 regardless to occurrences? Because anything else would have actually taken some programing effort. Why will the game decide that you are a Heel after about 20 hours of game time in complete contrary to your actions thus far, and won’t let you change it even though the crowd loves you and you are a Face in all ways possible? Because taking care of bugs and actually offering customer service is beneath 2k. Try it, write to them about that bug (or any bug). I wouldn't hold my breath though.
Let us continue. Oh, I see these two superstars are scheduled to be in a 1 on 1 title match on this weekend’s pay per view. What would be the most realistic and logical thing to do? Wait! I got it! Let’s put them in a 1 on 1 match in both programs this week, nothing draws the crowd more than watching the same goddamn match three times in a row! (said no GM ever). Seriously, what dim witted never-watched-an-episode-in-my-life degenerate now lives with the shame of being responsible for this?! And another thing. Is this a game, or a cellular app pay2win? Because the SP awarded for 5 star matches make you wonder where you buy more in order to actually upgrade your superstar before WWE 2K35 is released. The amounts of useless redundant boring grinding is embarrassing, maxing-out your created superstar should be challenging, not invoke suicidal thoughts.
Many say this year’s My Career is a lot better than last year’s, to which I say hogwash. Last year was terrible for its reasons, and this year’s terrible for it’s reasons. Narrators no longer use the name you chose, the entire match is the same dialogue about your opponent (they know our move set, can’t they say anything about that? What, Cole, King and JBL were too busy to record?). The highlights are complete garbage, showing every reversal done by your opponent but hardly ever your OMG moments or hard grapples. Also, remember how last year we got extra SP for being in the pay per view? Well now your superstar is in every single pay per view without getting squat. Keep grinding, don’t worry about getting bored, the extra sophisticated game engine will make sure to give you the same match over and over and over (and over) again. How exciting!
And of course, the reversal engine! Nothing could have been more terrible, I have no idea what bunch of 5 year olds decided on that system. I get it, they had to do something, but this? Disgusting. Last year you simply had to hit F at the exact micro-second, as your opponent dominates you while you attempt to figure out how. Now superstars have a limited number of reversals (which get replenished according to your Reversal stat, just as long as your opponent's get replenished faster). Not to mention the system is buggy as hell, and your opponent WILL use magically conjured reversals without them being removed from his current reversal counter. Why? Because f*** you, that’s why. In addition, you can create a superheavyweight and he will still be tossed around and dropped by the tiniest of wrestlers. Makes perfect sense, right? Just like the fact that every time you are down on the floor outside the ring ANY AND ALL opponents will run to the ring and wait for you to be counted out (as you helplessly push the button to enter the ring, which only works on occasion). Just the way John Cena and The Undertaker like to win matches, right? Let the other guy get counted out! Superstars don’t drag the opponent back to the ring on RAW and Smackdown in order to beat them honorably, right? Right.

F1 2012: I literally played it for 2 hours to find out it was the opposite of F1 2011, it would understeer LITERALLY everywhere, handling felt terrible.

Objective view: It is a loyal remaster of a well respected game, if you enjoyed the game before, the game has not changed beyond visual updates and quality of life addition such as the OPTIONS of auto combat, faster movement, and some optional cheats the devs put in themselves, like max gil, 99 of every item(not key items), and all skills unlocked. These are optional, they will not make your gameplay easier if you ignore them. Other additions include the option to hide hud, reduce or remove random encounters at will (toggle like auto combat), and a 'supercharge' feature which I have not tried yet. All in all, an honored game got memorialized on steam with a good polish.
Subjective view: I loved the game before, the auto combat feature is nice for small conflict, and will be nice for when I'm grinding levels. I'm personally not going to use the cheats since that defeats why I enjoy the game, but it's awesome the devs thought "Why NOT put these in? More options never hurts." And who knows, I may want to do a crazy playthrough next!
Summed up: love the game before, you will love the game now. If you didn't like the grind, there are options to make it easier or remove parts of it entirely. And for your money? 2 huge games and bonus content for the christmas price of 18 bucks? (30 bucks doesn't hurt for two solid games either) I don't know about the rest of you, but I've paid 20 bucks for a meal before.

Just Cause 2 may not be my favorite out of the games that reside in my library, that title is reserved for The Binding of Isaac. However, I can say with 100% confidence that it is the most fun open-world game I have ever played in my entire life. Just Cause 2 holds this high honor on my personal favorites list for a number of reasons:
1. Just Cause 2's world is breathtakingly beautiful. In my opinion, this makes it superior to any of the Grand Theft Auto game worlds, as they are gritty and urban, while the fictional Asian island of Panau is filled with lush tropical landscapes, barren deserts, and even snow-covered mountains.
2. Just Cause 2's selection of vehicles is extremely eclectic, and all of the cars, boats, planes, motorcycles and helicopters are insanely fun to use. My personal favorite is the DLC addon "Tuk-Tuk Boom-Boom."
3. Just Cause 2's selection of weapons is also extremely eclectic and each weapon is fun to use. Tearing apart the Panauan military (and helpless civilians) is ceaselessly satisfying and feels like playing a zany action movie akin to Machete or even Tropic Thunder.
4. Just Cause 2's missions are reliably fun. Some of them may be somewhat generic, but each one is worth playing in its own right. On top of the main story missions, there are three criminal factions to do dirty work for in the form of "Faction Missions."
5. Just Cause 2 has extreme replayability, as it's fun to hop into just to cause destruction and have fun, with the varying map locations to tear apart (over 300 scattered across the massive map).
6. Just Cause 2's modding community is absolutely amazing, offering new character skins, extra weapons and vehicles, and fun cheats. My personal favorite mods are the Extreme Heat mod, which makes the military much more formidible and erratic, and the Insane Civilian Mod, which causes the civillian NPCs to mimic the actions of the military, creating widespread chaos.
My personal score for Just Cause 2 is 9.75/10. It's a fantastic gaming experience for even more reasons than I've listed, and I strongly encourage everyone with access to M-rated games to play it.

This game has a lot of potential, but it hamstrings itself with a series of deck-building rules that I struggle to see as anything other than a cash-grab.
I'll lay it out short and sweet: You get cards by playing the two Draft modes, either against AI for 2500 gold or against players for 5000 gold.  In order to get gold to play draft modes, you either play ranked matches (slow) or play against AI (fast if you win reliably).  The AI only pays off if you can reliably win 7 games.
Now here's the problem: your deck is unplayable unless it consists of 33% mana and a minimum of 75 cards, or 50 cards and 25 mana.  That's a large enough percentage that you /will/ run in to situations where you get mana starved or mana flooded - either you have a hand with 3 mana and all your cards cost 4+ to cast or you have a fistful of mana and nothing else.
Now, will this happen every game?  Of course not!  A well-balanced deck with a good mix of cards will only be left helpless at the mercy of RNG occasionally.  However, anecdotally, it feels like it happens at least once every 7 games, and there's no option to design your deck in such a way that you can eliminate this problem and get more reliable results.
Sometimes you just draw 6 mana sources from turns 15 through 21 and watch yourself lose the game despite playing to the best of your ability, and the frustration when that happens on game 7 of a Gauntlet run spoils the rest of the gameplay.  This enforced lack of reliability in a mode that dangles rewards over your head for winning consistently is a bad gameplay experience.  It feels designed to tease people with the possibility of getting better cards without actually offering a realistic chance of doing so.
This is the hook in Eternal's "free to play" model - sure, you can play the game for free, if you're the sort of fortunate soul who can make a profit by buying boxes of magic cards and selling the foils for more than the cost of the box.

Right off the bat, it's more tech demo than game - everything about Receiver is incredibly barebones in every aspect.
There are three different weapons you start with, randomly decided on startup. There are two enemy types and only one is a real threat. Aside from collecting 11 short tapes that detail the world, over and over again, your only real pickups are bullets for your one gun with the occasional moderately useless flashlight.
But despite its barebones nature, Receiver is an incredibly fun tech demo.
You control each and every minute aspect of the weapon. From manually ejecting the magazine and inserting each bullet, to inspecting the chamber and messing with the slide lock, your firearm is a precise instrument of beauty when being handled. This has the side of effect of slowing the gameplay down to a crawl, which when provided with the mostly stationary enemies and emphasis on not being seen, and especially that each enemy has five or six weak points that mandate precise aiming, Receiver is the essence of a survival game. Perhaps even survival horror, given the stress.
It's not difficult to explain why Receiver has captured the interest of so many. It is an incredibly engrossing game. It's far from a perfect or even polished game, however.
All of the art in the game is incredibly simple - apart from the looming cityscape, it's all very simple geometric shapes with no textures and no complexity. It is, therefore, such a surprise that the game runs so badly. Even running at the lowest resolution with the fastest graphics option enabled and no other programs or windows up, I was still experiencing slowdown. Whether or not this is a side effect of developing for Unity is for someone else to decide.
As mentioned before, the procedural generation is incredibly vapid. There's also only about two dozen room types, and whether or not you succeed at the game very quickly becomes a question of if you can avoid an encounter of a room packed with flying killdrones long enough to gather all the tapes to hear the story and end the game, which just ends the process. There's not even a save function.
For the story itself - there's a sense of enlightenment that you can experience regularly on the internet. It's when you're viewing a perfectly normal image, and then it dawns on you that you're actually flicking through pornography. This is like that, except with somebody's paranoid fantasy. The "Mindkill" and the media being instruments of mass destruction is a hilariously tinfoil to say the least.
However, with all this in mind and that the biggest disappointment is the lack of content, the gameplay itself is ultimately fun enough to override all concerns. It's fun enough that despite being one of the most shallow "rogue-lites" yet, it's also one of the best.
If you're in the market for a "one of a kind" survival game set in a Cyberpunk Dreamscape, then I couldn't recommend Receiver more. Just don't expect an overwhelming amount of actual stuff in it.

Legend of Grimrock 2 (here on referred to as LoG 2) is everything you could want for a sequel and more. I look forward to what the future holds with user generated content.
The Legend of Grimrock series are a set of real time, grid based, dungeon crawlers with pleasing graphics and a good aesthetic.
Movement is based on grid and you can turn left and right also move left, right, forward and backwards.  You attack by clicking the weapon of choice from the character portraits. While this is not for everyone, it's stays true to it's roots and will please many after they have adapted.
While the story is a little weak, you will find yourself enjoying the neatly packaged puzzles that are littered throughout the world. I had a problem with the first game where you had to search each wall for secret buttons or risk missing one. LoG 2 improves on this by giving some subtle and some not so subtle hints that the player is missing something and should look deeper, resulting in a less difficult search.
Another area that LoG 2 improves upon is allowing the user access to outside areas, giving more varied feel to the game. There are now many more types of enemies and many of which have varied A.I.
The soundtrack has seen improvements since the first game and has a lovely score of atmospheric ambient noise and battle music for boss fights. The theme tune is catchy but I still see myself returning to the theme song of the first game.
In conclusion my experience with Legend of Grimrock 2 was amazing and to top off it all, there is extensive support of modifications, I look forward to seeing what people create.

Seeing that this title is on sale for the start of the 2017 season, I feel obligated to post a review to interested F1 fans who are yet to pull the trigger.
This game is very nearly a masterpiece for an F1 fanatic. It's well optimized, it controls well, and you can customize the game settings and assists on your vehicle to make the game as hard or as easy as you'd like.
This is the first F1 game for me. I've been playing using all three practice sessions and qualifying before taking on the full length race. I have to say that it is an incredible experience to progress through each step leading up to lights out.  The progression of learning the track, advancing your skills, and testing different tire, car setup, and fuel strategies pays off on race day.
The tracks look gorgeous, and they are very true to their real life counterparts including the brand new Baku Circuit.  Weather affects your control heavily, and you can absolutely feel the difference in your vehicle's grip from the start of P1 to the end of Quali as more rubber is put down on the track.
The AI is challanging in my opinion. They are agressive and they don't all mirror each other's strategies. You'll see a variety of tire compounds starting on race day and different pit strategies. Every once in a while you'll have an opponent spin you out from behind, but hey, that's what flashbacks are for!
Last item of the positives: Voice commands for pit crew / race updates! So awesome!
The only negatives I've found:
Tire strategies during weather events are difficult because the AI has an advantage of knowing the better time to switch between slicks and intermediates/wets.
Multiplayer doesn't have the same "feel" as single player.
Sometimes AI will pull clearly illegal moves, but hey, can't be perfect all the time.
In conclusion, It really feels like you are competing at the F1 level until you have to pause mid race to use the restroom.
9.5/10

Flying is possibly the best thing in the game, and it feels amazing, as the game allows you to fly to ludicrous heights, taking whole minutes of freefall to hit the ground. There is always a sense of freedom in the open world, where you can just jump in and blow up a plane or two. The guns feel very powerful, and some of the dlc has some interesting weapons available. And then theres the grappling hook, which allows you to latch onto anything in the world and pull off some impressive stunts that make you feel like a baddass afterwards. So yes, I highly recomend this game just cuz.

Firstly, I'd like to say how glad I am that I took a chance on this game during a sale. After all the negativity, which may have been warranted at launch, I was super hesitant to pull the trigger on this one. But wow, this game is legitimately fun. Like really, really fun. Not only is it fun, but it's actually quite superb in many areas that I judge a FPS. Number one, the shooting over course. The guns and the way they control FEEL GOOD. The Battle Rifle in particular, feels remarkable. Now not only that, the way the game allows you to modify the weapons in the field and on the go at any time is the best thing I've seen and should easily be in every FPS moving forward.
Now it's not just the shooting, the game has a stealth mechanic and it works supremely well. Basically, this game is Far-Cry. The stealth takedowns are addictive and amazing. They're simply brutal and fun to pull off on unaware enemies. The detection works and I enjoy playing with a crossbow, silent pistol and picking off enemies one by one.
Add to all this, the completely open world, that really does feel like a warzone, in the red zones. It almost feels like Judgement Day from terminator happened, especially at night. And the music/atmosphere is chill inducing.
All I can say is, whatever issues this game had, they've been fixed. If you like Far Cry 3 & 4. You will simply love this game. Buy it now or wait for a sale. It's great and I'm enjoying my time with it.
