James: "What's that Walter? We've declared war? Well I'll be! I bet the country'll need some soldiers, eh?"
Walter; "Sure will. I'm going to hand in my attestation papers in today. To hell with the Jerries!"
James: "I think I shall sign up along with you. Perhaps we'll go off to war together, eh?"
Walter: "Sounds like a plan to me James. Brothers in arms, we'll be. Heroes we'll be!"
James: "My, that sounds like a dream to me. I will go fill out these forms now! I'll be seing ye around Walter."
Walter and James, two nineteen year old young men, inspired by the propaganda. Wanting to prove themselves to their community, wanting to be heroes, sign up for The Great War, as they feel excited by war, and feel a need to fight for their country. Together these men go through training camp at the famous Canadian Valcartier training camp. After that, it's off to war.
So off to Ypres the men were sent, in the same division, same platoon, same squadron, even.
They were sent to the front lines of the dirty and cold trenches. The two men realized what a horror this war was. This was no dream, this was indeed a nightmare.  But this didn't get their hopes down.
-Sounds of artillery and explosions are ongoing outside well Walter and James sit in their dugout-
Once the artillery fire stops, the men are pointed out to defend the trench.
James: "Walter, here come the jerries, get ready, and make sure you have your mask with you!"
The axis forces make a good effort, but the allied forces hold of on the defence.
Officer: "OVER THE TOP!"
Walter: "Here we go James! Onwards!"
As they try and make their way across the rough landscape, James spots a German soldier. He puts his iron sight up to his face, takes aim, and puts his hand on the trigger. He hesistates for a moment, thinking about this man's life before the war, but stops these thoughts. The trigger pulls and the man in the distance go down. Onward the men rush, not stopping for a moment. James and Walter eventually make it to the enemy trench.
All of a sudden, Walter gets shot in the stomach as they are turning a corner. He cries out in pain as he bleeds out in front of James. James takes him into cover, and looks at him, holding him in his arms. Walter  slowly goes lifeless and becomes nothing but a body. No life is left in him. James kisses his good friend on the forehead, and goes back out to the war. He and his allies push up, and force the Germans out of the trench, pushing them back.
Although the allies may have won a good days battle, James feels otherwise. The coldness of the trenches, the stench, men dieing of trench foot, shortages of food... James is left to go through this without his best friend. He can only imagine the look on Walter's parents faces when reading that letter. 2 months later, James is sent home. Although his family sees him as a hero, James is never the same.
War isn't pretty, and this game shows it. Every man you kill is a man with a family. He has a life, but your goal is to kill the enemy, and you must do what it takes to win the war. This game shows the true horror of world war 1. The trenches are so detailed, the poison gas and gore is horrific... If you like world war 1 or realistic shooters, this game is a must.

Just wow. It is not very often that a sequel to a game that I thought was "meh" comes around blows me way the ♥♥♥♥ away. This is one of them. I have been having an absolute blast playing this game, closet comparison I think I can make for Grimrock is Wizardry (mainly 8.)  One of the things that I really liked about the first Grimrock game was the replay value and Level Editor that was added, and my god did Grimrock 2 deliver in those areas too! The level editor is fleshed out in a pretty serious manner, mods have already been developed for the game. The way the story is told, outside of the opening cutscene is pretty much through things you discover for yourself, letters in the world, things you see, the closest comparison I can make is to Dark Souls where the lore is indirectly fed to you, I like the setup, and it adds to the mystery of the Island. One of the new things they added was outside areas, which was one of the best editions this game could have made, for one, it allows for some serious modding potential, (Eye of the Beholder anyone?), the other thing is it just expands more on the world itself allowing you to be a bit more immersed. Another thing that was added was a Day and Night Cycle, it is also very well done and definetly adds to the atmosphere in a few areas (The Cemetery.) Next, I would like to give a big shout out to the guns. There are guns in this game! They added Guns! I really shouldn't have to go on any farther on that subject, although mechanically speaking they can be weak, they jam, and bullets are hard to come by. VVVVVV is an incredible game and one of the best puzzle games ever.
It starts by showing that all your crew has vanished and it's your job to find them, by exploring the rooms of your ship. The story isn't the selling point of the game, but it complements the game really well. It's probably the only way to give the game some logic. The twist here is that you have the power to change gravity, just by the push of a button. You can only change gravity when your in the ground/ceiling/surface or when you touch a "gravity beam". This power gives a lot of room for good game design and VVVVVV delivers it. It makes great use of this power and makes you think in ways you would never think before.
But with this also comes a lot of frustration. Thankfully, VVVVVV shows that frustration may not lead to a rage quit. It's the type of frustration you get but you want to keep playing the game.
Another very good thing VVVVVV delivers is it's music. The music is incredible and really brings nostalgic feelings of the 8bit era. Some of my favourite musics of this era are now from this game, which is odd, knowing this game was published in 2010.
VVVVVV is a game that I highly recomend to a lot of people. Just don't expect the story to be the next final fantasy...

I've put nearly 42 hours into this game over the course of under a week. Grimrock 1 was a really good modernization of the dungeon crawler that I didn't realize I had been missing. Grimrock 2 is possibly the best game I've played this year, which is drawing to a close at the time of writing.
The game is gorgeous. A lot of fans of the first were put off by the game being even partly outdoors, but there are a lot of touches that disguise the grid-based nature of the game, like uneven sands and the like. I never looked at the game and thought 'Now this here doesn't look good.'
Gameplay is much improved from the first. Gone are the days of circle-strafing around every enemy and cheesing the game. Most enemies function in unique ways and require different tactics to approach... I mean, some of them can be circle-strafed, but it's not a reliable tactic for all of them this time, which I appreciate. But I digress, the biggest improvement comes from game feel in a lot of regards. A major boon that you didn't even know you wanted is that each party member has dual weapon slots ala Diablo 2, so you can switch between gear on the fly without having to pull up a menu every time.
Additionally, character selection has variety now. Gone are the 3 classes to go with your 4 party members, as there are a whopping 8 classes to choose from, ranging from nearly essential to wonderfully bizarre. Variety is the spice of life and, honestly, Grimrock 1 was sorely lacking in this regard.
tl;dr Grimrock 1 was good, Grimrock 2 is one of the better games I've ever played. Now if you'll excuse me I have a second campaign to start.

So, I've clocked in FORTY* hours in The Crew, and I figure I'll give my review in the wake of everyone else's. I'm a fan of racing games; From Daytona USA to Nascar (bleh) to Blur to Forza, so I generally know what to expect from racing games.
I got exactly what I expected from The Crew. It's a open-world semi-arcade (Simcade is the term, right?) racer with a story and a buttload of missions and challenges to take on. And you know what? It's fun. I enjoyed my first couple of hours. Despite what people say... I never encountered any noticeable bugs, and what the game offers is *perfectly fine.*
-----------------------------------
"Sub par car selection." "There's nothing iconic in this!" "Not even fifty cars?! Lame!"
If you're looking for a game that has hundreds of iconic cars, go play Forza or Gran Turismo. The Crew was meant to be a game that you could pick up and play without having to think too much about a vast array of choices. That's fine. If I wanted car porn, I'll boot up Forza Motorsports 4 and play around in the Autovista feature.
-----------------------------------
"The customization sucks!"
Again; Go play Forza Motorsports or Gran Turismo.
-----------------------------------
"The handling is terrible!" "I can never keep my car straight!" "I slide all the time!"
I'm not going to weigh in my opinion on this, because I'm currently playing The Crew with a keyboard. It's generally known that keyboards are poorly suited for driving games, and for good reason. A keyboard doesn't allow you to "ease" into your turns, brakes, and throttles. It's 0% or 100%, never in between. So yes, at higher speeds, I would expect a slippy sensation when I do more than tap the keys.
Despite this, I'm completely satisfied with how they did the physics, and it reminds me of the GRID series. You can't round corners at 80, 90, 100 miles per hour. You're going to crush into the wall, but I can also feel a great sense of power in the steering (Again, probably due to the keyboard). Just like circuit racing: Bad entrances and extreme speeds will send you careening off the track and simply ruin your day. So I advise two things for those complaining about the handling.
A) Grab a controller. It's... $20 for a simple one, and if it has sensitivity flaws, you can adjust the dead zones for the sticks in the game settings. You'll have a significant level of control that the keyboard can't give you.
B) For God's sakes, learn your apexes and limits. A car can only do so much before it gives, even if it's made to drift. If you can't stay within the limits of your car, then you'll fail. This is no excuse to blame the handling and physics. They're fine.
-----------------------------------
"Bad navigation" "Nav sucks."
Maybe it's because I got the game after the initial tweaks, but I don't know what you're talking about. The nav system acts very much like the nav system in my car and phone. It doesn't send me in circles, and while there's a bit of a delay, it's unnoticeable if you also use the mini-map and common sense.
-----------------------------------
"AI is cheap!" "AI cheats!" "AI is unfair!"
If you talk about the 5-0, then definitely. I'm not a fan of how they're able to clip and phase through traffic, and I realy don't like how they can send you from 150mph to 0 in under a second. But most of all... They're always on your heels. I have watched them go from 600 yards behind me at my speed up to my bumper in a couple seconds, even though there's no logical way for them to do so.
If you're talking about the missions... Nope. Again, I don't know what you're talking about. There's no "slingshot AI," if the AI gets the gain on you, it's because you took a turn in a horrible fashion or they made use of nitro (Which is something you too can use.) The only issue I see is that you can never knock the AI out of commission. I've rammed many into walls and threw out their back end, but they somehow stick with the pack.
Car level... I'm running around in missions with a L. 165+ Camaro against AI with car levels of 70-80. It was *heavily* implied that car levels do upgrade a car's performance, and despite having a level twice my AI opponents (And even 100+ levels than some newbies), I can't leave them in the dust. Maybe it's so everyone is on an "even" playing field, so that you can't grind challenges before the story and so you can't troll new players, but I don't feel the sense of progression or power. And that sucks.
-----------------------------------
"Pay 2 win!"
...What kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥are you smoking here? If you're saying that you can buy a couple of cars with Crew Credits, then maybe... Until you realize that the only way to progress and develop new kits is to actually play. The only way to get tuning parts to improve your ride is to actually play. The only way to increase your car level and it's general power is to actually play. I don't like microtransactions as much as the next guy, but microtransactions don't equal "PAY TO WIN" unless they give a significant advantage. I got a McLaren MP4-12C, but until I get 30 more levels, I can't play with it or get anything out of it beyond showing it off in free roam. I still have to work and play to be able to tune it and use it in missions.
There's no pay to win. Knock if off with this slander.
-----------------------------------
"MMO was just a marketing term to get more sales."
I agree 150%. With the size of the map, and with the attitude and concept the advertisements touted around... I expected at least 64 drivers on the whole map. I say "at least" because it's totally possible to have 64 drivers in an instance radius that follows you while having a map filled with 200-300 players. instead, I get to drive around with seven others. In total. That was... Disappointing, to say the least. I was told that I could race in quick co-ops, develop a crew that I could ease into, then break it off when necessary and find another crew to hop into with absolute ease. Essentially: A highly social experience that changes with the people I drive the nation with. What I got was Criterion's "Most Wanted" with a metric ♥♥♥♥ton of map to drive. Not impressed.
-----------------------------------
Is the game good? Yes, without a doubt. I had a decent time playing The Crew so far, and I plan on continuing later down the road, when I have some time to kill. Would I recommend it? No. The game plays a lot like GRID, and from what some say, TDU. Which is fine. I have no problem with these games, and I find the former enjoyable on its own. But Ubisoft's main selling point that supposedly made The Crew different was the "MMO-like gameplay." Ubisoft did not deliver this. 7 players around me does not constitude as "MMO-like gameplay." You have better interaction and a denser playercount in Euro Truck Simulator. I am *not* joking here.
The Crew just feels... Empty, and if my opinion means anything, I would recommend getting GRID (For PC), Forza (For Xbox), or Gran Turismo (For Playstation) in place of this game. You'll save a bit more money, and you'll have everything The Crew offers and a ♥♥♥♥ ton more.

Warframe has a lot of pedigree behind it, being made by the same people who made Crysis and the original Far Cry, and perhaps in another world it would have been something truly special. Sadly, that's not how Crytek made this game and it shows every single trapping of those "Free" to Play multiplayer military shooters; the over reliance on microtransactions, a good deal of hackers, optimization problems to the point my gaming setup couldn't run at a decent framerate on anything but the lowest settings (which makes the game look awful, by the way), a general feel of Pay2Win (though nowhere near as bad as other examples), the community being a bit annoying, the insultingly poorly designed maps, the endless and rampart spawn killing, the list just goes on and on.
Oh, and playing the Medic class as an actual medic is pointless. Trust me, no-one lives long enough to make use of that equipment and trying to revive someone mid-game is both pointless and suicidal.
Pretty much the only reason I'm saying you should try it? Well, to be fair, it's perhaps the best example of its class. The gameplay is solid, the financial side is nowhere near as bad as others make it out to be (though it IS still a problem), it has a few more gamemodes and co-op missions going for it and - provided you have the right sort of setup - it looks dang good. It's not levels of Pre-Gun Mettle Team Fortress 2, nor can it really hold a candle to what any paid shooter, even a certain fish-acronym shooter of scorn, can provide. But it's free, and it works, and it's better than its brethren. Not that that's really saying anything.

As a long time fan of the series, FFX was one of whcih that I had to get as soon as it recieved its HD treament and was availble on PC. At the time of its initial release, the quality of graphics and gameplay was at the top of all others, possibly the best on the PS2. After all those years, this game still holds up in terms of gameplay. The game features a turn based system, that incorporates more strategic actions requiring the player to understand that each character is built around the idea that they are a specific counter to certain enemies. Taking that into consideration the system creates a situation in which every battle will require a different party composition per enemy groups encountered.
In terms of story, we begin with our protagonist thrown into a group that is just about to embark on a journey to save the world from a seemingly natural calamity. (possible spoilers ahead) Originating from a very modern world, the player is able to empathize with the protagonist as he inquires about this new world with antiquated technologies and traditions. However, as he learns more about the world, he finds that this world seems to hold things that belonged to the world he came from. A city known as Zanakand is also in this world, the Blitzball victory pose has turn into a prayer pose for the dominant religion, and most notably a man named Jecht, the father of the protagonist who turned missing for a decade, is now a well known hero whom perished in battle, also a decade prior.

DISCLAIMER: Don't pay full price.
Story? Terrible.
Graphics? Pretty nice!
Sound? Decent, voice acting is bad or cheesy (which is funny sometimes, but gets annoying).
Gameplay? Pretty fun, but it wears off.
I think I paid 3 bucks for this game on sale and I don't feel bad about that at all. If I had paid a bunch more, I would've been upset. The game is pretty fun to play, but to me, I couldn't keep playing it forever.
I love games like Grand Theft Auto, or I guess a more fitting comparison, Saints Row, simply because Saints Row has gone for the more ridiculous (e.g., super powers). Your character in Just Cause is a cheesy action hero who can repeatedly use his grappling hook and infinite parachutes to do crazy maneuvers and fly through the air.
The game is pretty fun when you first start out, but I got decently bored with it after a while, which has never happened with me in GTA or Saints Row (except for searching for the 1000s of collectibles in SR4). I had lots of fun being crazy and blasting people away, but the game really doesn't have much life to it. It's a sort of playground, but it's not a very inventive playground.
It looks nice and the map is big, but it's lifeless. There's people around and some funny characters, but it's all carbon-copied, essentially. Even the cutscenes are carbon-copied where the developers couldn't take the time to "film" some of them and instead avoid showing characters' faces and just provide voice-overs so they don't have to lip-sync.
There's not that many main missions, and once you get through them, everything else is identical. There are much more side missions and they're all generally the same--go kill this specific guy 1km away from here, or drive this car 7km away while not losing its cargo, etc. Sure, there's repetitive behavior in GTA or SR or many other action-type games, but I guess the characters and the environments keep me more interested than the islands in Just Cause.
I will still put recommend if you want to take the time to just jump in the middle of something without feeling obligated to play it continuously. But if you want a serious (or even just interesting) storyline, or interesting characters or world, then look elsewhere.

How does one describe Receiver? Tis a weird little game with a bunch of cool features. Aight, we're gonna hafta split this up into pieces.
STORY: The story of Receiver is similar to the first Hotline Miami in that the exposition is delivered in cutscenes in the form of various cassette tapes you find and have to play to finish the game. The story is that you are a Receiver, a survivor of the Mindkill event, an event that wipes the life off of the world you're on. Done by machines who had begun controlling the world, you are tasked to find all 11 cassette tapes and ascent to The World Not Filled With Turrets and Flying Tasers all the while dealing with the fact said machines are dropping in sentry guns and taser drones that can both drop your♥♥♥♥♥in 1 hit.

GAMEPLAY: Gameplay in Receiver is the most interesting. It is similar to realistic shooters such as say Red Orchestra 2, Project Reality and so on. You get one of three guns, a Colt M1911A1, A S&W Model 10 "Victory" revolver and a modified Glock 17 each with their own specialties, the Glock can fire in full auto, the Model 10 can be fired in single and double action and so on and so forth. Also different in Receiver is that you have to do many things via key presses, ranging from loading individual rounds into gun magazines, releasing slides, using the ejector rod in the Model 10 and so on. It seems complex at the beginning but become almost instictive after an hour or two.
ENEMIES: As I said earlier, the enemies in the game are very basic, one is a sentry turret, the other a drone with a taser, or the ATF Special. Both of these are different as if you shoot specific parts of them, they do more damage. You can disable sentries by either shooting the CPU off to break it, disable it's battery or break the camera. As for the tazer bots, shoot it repeatedly, cause they're more annoying than the tazers in PAYDAY 2.
IS IT WORTH IT?: The gameplay is rather solid and the gunplay is fun as well as realistic, and it sits at a nice $5 dollars. If you feel like spending $5 dollars on a small FPS then go ahead, if not, wait for a sale and nab it for cheaper.
